StellarHub is a space station building and management game from indie developers, Casualogic.
In StellarHub, your role is to manage the construction and maintenance of a space station. Starting with a single hub module and a group of eager people, your job is to develop and grow the station, attracting trade and tourists, and defending against pirates and wandering asteroids.
StellarHub's graphics are really rather good.
Each level displays your station, made up of different 'plus-shaped' modules joined together in a grid layout. There are two modes of display for your station: interior and exterior mode. Interior mode is where you'll play most of the game. This shows each of your station inhabitants wandering around performing their daily tasks, and allows you to interact with them. Exterior mode is used for monitoring approaching trade or pirate ships, as well as asteroids that impinge upon station space.
Characters are small, but have a number of animations. Each profession wears a different colour jumpsuit, providing reuse of graphics resources while allowing for relatively quick differentiation between characters. Most of the modules look fairly bland in internal mode. External mode looks a little better, with good attention to detail in each component, but the grid layout of the station does look a bit weird and somewhat unnatural.
The whole lot is rendered in front of a number of lovely animated backgrounds, each showing the planet about which your station presumably orbits as well as the star system's primary star. These look very nice, indeed, with one of them being used in the beautiful title screen.
The interface is very clean and easy to use, with tooltips for almost everything, making the components that lack them stand out. There are no graphics options beyond full screen/windowed selection and resolution. I haven't experienced any slowdowns.
StellarHub's soundtrack is lovely. There are only a few different trucks, in a nice ambient electronic style with haunting light melodies and slow beats. It's like a good chill-out album.
Sound effects are mostly good, too. Interface sounds are responsive and well synchronised, with electronic bleeps and bloops appropriate to the setting. The "pewpewpew" lasers are good, and the explosions and warning klaxons are suitably loud and sudden enough to jolt you out of the casual, meditative state that the rest of the game can invoke.
There are no voices, but there are occasional groaning sounds.
At its heart, StellarHub is a relatively simple city builder in space station format. Your station is made up of modules connected in a grid layout. Each module requires a certain amount of metal and plastic to construct and consumes a certain amount of power on an ongoing basis. You can only place modules if they are connected to the existing structure, maintaining the X/Y grid.
When you begin a level you have access to the basic module types, which is more than enough to keep you busy for a while. One of these modules is a research module, which unlocks the use of the scientist profession. Assign someone to the research module and you can select items from the technology tree to research, further unlocking new module types and upgrades for your existing modules, as well as further items to research in each branch. Initially the research available seems quite varied, but your researchers are fairly efficient, so you'll find yourself progressing quickly through what's available.
Resources include first-level basic resources such as oxygen, food, power, or ore, and second-level processed items, such as metal, plastic, meals, or ammunition. You produce first-level resources through the construction of certain modules and assignment of appropriate people to professions, while second-level resources must then be processed in a manufacturing plant. It's a simple model, but it works well enough. Given that some of the first-level resources come from special zones in the local area, it's possible to run out of something, effectively stalling your station growth or worse. If you've built a supply or trade ship landing pad, then all is not lost even then, as ships may pass by and offer you what you need -- for a price.
Your station inhabitants have a large range of skills and professions available, and you can swap profession almost whenever you feel like it. They also have a range of personality traits and attributes, adding variability and interest to the game. You don't normally control them directly, instead assigning them a profession and leaving them to it, but you can order them to perform certain tasks, such as going to work or visiting the medbay. This can decrease their mood. They'll occasionally make their thoughts known through little text bubbles over their heads; these are amusing, but could do with a bit of editing.
The game features asteroids and pirates that will damage your station, and defensive modules that you can place to destroy them before they destroy you. There's no real combat, as such, though. The standard pause, play, and accelerated time controls are available, and I'm thankful the developers decided to allow control of most of the game's features while paused; things can get a bit hectic on occasion.
The game comprises two tutorials set in the Sol system, six missions of varying difficulty and size in other star systems, and a random system mode. The tutorials do a reasonable job of introducing the basics, though some of the grammar is terrible, and it's not yet clear to me whether there's a set goal in each of the system missions or whether they're just more structured sandbox modes. If there is a win condition then it's not explained and I haven't managed to reach it yet. The random mode doesn't allow any configuration or selection of parameters, which is a shame; being able to tailor the level to your liking would be a big benefit to replayability.
The game does have a few gameplay issues. The AI of the station inhabitants seems a bit off, for example. People often seem to wander about aimlessly; you might find your technician hanging about in a spaceport that hasn't even started construction yet while another module leaks precious oxygen into space. Sick people won't go for treatment on their own either, even if they happen to be walking past a medbay, and they often wait to eat, sleep, or 'get fun' until their needs are making them downright miserable. My stations always seem to eventually devolve into two groups: the stupidly happy who have asked for pay rises and seem to think I can't do anything wrong, and the eternally miserable who complain until they have no 'moral' (sic) and then refuse to do anything except sit in the lounge.
It's a little buggy, too. So far I've had two CTDs -- both when starting a level, so at least I didn't lose progress -- and I've noticed that some of the module information screens don't work, either at all or they show the wrong screen.

To be clear, this is not a bad game. It has many novel and interesting systems well covered elsewhere, most of which work quite well. However it has one gaping flaw:
The hex based tactical engine simply doesn't work with the other systems.
You control three units. Maps are relatively open. Many attacks are ranged and characters of any side don't block line of sight. It is therefor impossible to reliably protect someone from getting hit. You lose the game by losing all your resolve points, and you lose one resolve every time someone is incapacitated in the tactical map. Thus bringing anyone who can't survive reasonably on the tactical map is a recipe for failure.
Apart from the occasional area that heals anyone on it at the start of their turn, terrain is either passable, impassable and blocks LOS, or impassable and doesn't.
All of this combined means that save the rare AOE ability, positioning barely matters. So why have it?
Scrap the hexes and simply have lines of units on each side of the screen like the old Final Fantasy games. You can still play with AOE effects, all the other systems remain in place, the only thing you lose is range. and tedium.
I have some other minor quibbles but they're all picking nits. It's a charming presentation, the exploration is good, the between expedition stuff is okay but nothing special. I really want to like this game. But the tactical side is tedius, about 40 percent of the gameplay time, and where you always lose. I hold out no hope it will be changed, and unless it is I can't recommend this game.

So, Besiege. This is a really unique game, and I'd really recommend it to a lot of people. If you're deciding whether or not to buy this game, just spend 5 minutes on reading this review.
Below is a more detailed breakdown.
Gameplay is the main point of Besiege. Just to list a few things off, this game provides you with a nice campaign (even though there are not so many levels yet, but every level has a ton of replayability potential). There are also a couple of sandbox maps. The player is equipped with infinite amounts of different varieties of building blocks and elements. There is literally everything, starting with a simple cube and going right to holders, pistons, different versions of cannons, bombs, wings and a lot of other stuff. The best thing is that anything you will build will work and people have already came up with some really crazy ideas. Ever wanted to create a huge flying carrier? Or a machine that swings a giant hammer around itself, smashing everything to pieces? You can basically do that. Also, slow-motion is epic.
I like the graphics. There is not much to say, but the visual style is pretty unique and is just enjoyable. Fire, water, explosions, the machines themselves look great and organic.
There is some nice ambient music that I really enjoy listening to. The sounds produced by machines and structures are simply great.
This is not some kind of an official criteria, but I just wanted to mention how flexible Besiege really is. First off, in any level (including the campaign ones), you are able to disable the small building box that limits you and build anything. The sky is the limit (and your computers hardware, of course). There are quite a few cheats on the options panel, that can give you something like zero gravity or infinite ammo (most of the weapons fire only once or just can be held on for around 10 seconds). There are 3 large sandbox levels. And, as I've already mentioned, a level editor and a full multiplayer system are coming in 2017 (well, hopefully in 2017. The devs promised at least.)
As for a sandbox fan, it's pretty much a 10/10. I would rate is as the best "wait, did this just
work?" simulator.

First of all, this game is brilliant.  I was totally drawn in by the story and how well it unfolded considering that it depends on the player. Considering all the rave reviews, I guess most people agree.  But there is one MAJOR flaw that doesn't seem to get mentioned in these reviews - The Ending.  SPOILER ALERT?: there isn't one.  There is a chat that comes up once enough of the clips are viewed that basically asks you if you want to stop and credits roll, but it's not exactly satisfactory. That's actually a strength though. The story sticks with you and is ambiguous enough for different interpretations. But how do you know you're done?  For a game to get you so invested in a story just to say, "ok stop whenever you heard enough" feels incomplete.  There could have been a way to give the player closure while still leaving some questions un answered.
Still I have to recommend the game for the singular experience.  But what could have been 5 stars is more like 3

The computer version of CoH is a faithful representation of classic tactical level wargaming.  Units are individual vehicles/ordnance and squads.  Hexes are probably on the order of 30-50 yards, and maps represent the fields, forests, and villages of WW II.  The action point system makes the game feel like a mix of real time and turn based, as players take turns back and forth many times moving units and playing actions within larger game turns (as opposed to one side moving/action while the other takes the occasional reaction fire shot, then repeat.  Some scenarios can be played as quickly as 30 minutes, while others are quite intensive and could take several hours.  The game supports computer opponent, online opponents, and PBEM...which seems like it would take an eternity to finish some games.
If you're a fan of tactical WWII board gaming, you should love CoH.

F.E.A.R. 2: Project Origin quite simply isn't a F.E.A.R. game. It's Call of Duty with its only tie to the first game being the little telepathic supernatural undead psycho chick Alma.
All the highpoints of the first game, the atmosphere, the alternation between fast unforgiving gunplay and atmospheric level progression are not present in this sequel. The first game's expansion packs of Extraction Point and Perseus Mandate were weaker than the original game but far stronger in design + story than this. The Mech suits are interesting but the rest of the game is unoriginal as dirt.
Furthermore, F.E.A.R. core gameplay involves the Replica soldiers, supernatural monsters, and the U.S. Army unit of First Encounter Assault Recon. This game starts you out with a lengthy section of fighting Armachan soldiers murdering Armachan employees. You're not fighting as the F.E.A.R. Point Man or operative (as in Perseus Mandate) but a Delta force squad practically taken from COD: Modern Warfare.
In conclusion, I would only recommend this game if you're a COD addict and need another cheap fix. The original F.E.A.R. with its expansion packs and F.3.A.R. are better than this. At least in F.3.A.R. you get some interesting gameplay  as Paxton Fettel, the undead brother from hell.

This game has overtaken FTL as the best roguelike in my library. That should be the only recommendation you need before buying the game, really.
The combat mechanics are surprisingly deep, the 'choose-your-own-adventure-storybook' vibe is a welcome breath of fresh air and the overworld phase adds a juicy layer of long term strategy. While the amount of maps and encounters is somewhat limited, I thoroughly admire how different the encounters play out based on your party composition and prior choices. Plus, there's oodles of unique 'epic' enounters which lure you into trying them when they show up, even though you might not be fully ready for them yet. You get a *real* sense of story here, you get to know your party members in such a way that you don't skip over the text of every encounter, like you would in FTL after a couple of playthoughs.
Don't get me wrong, while the story element is great this is still an unforgiving roguelike if you play it on that difficulty setting. Your first few games should probably not be played on that difficulty setting. But after two games, when you have a feel for the combat, dive into the richest, most colorful and most tactical roguelike of recent years.
The only criticisms I could make against this game are a slightly clunky overworld map and a poor optimization of the graphic engine (a 2D game should be 100% smooth and polished, not 98%). But those  are such minor complaints that I feel petty for mentioning them. This is an expertly crafted game worth every penny of its low cost.

Final Fantasy 5 is often considered one of the "Forgotten" Final Fantasies. It wasn't properly released stateside for many years and as a result very few played it compared to the vastly more popular 6 and 7.
5 was a very natural progression of mechanics from 3 and 4. It took the job system from previous games and gave it a new spin. Now in 5 you could switch out your class at will. And you would gain XP in a particular class which would level it up and gain it abilities. Which you could swap in and out with other classes. It's a very modular game that lets you play it in whatever way you could concievably want. Like you can play the game with 4 warriors while still having 4 white mage skills attatched to them. You unlock jobs gradually throughout the game and there are even hidden ones.
The story to 5 feels like a spiritual predecessor to 6. It features things like multiple overworlds and a floating island at one point. But it's in general a more simple and straight forward story. It's a better paced and shorter game overall, and one that can appeal to newcomers of the franchise a lot more than some of the more intimidating later entries. The characters in 5 are all likeable and memorable enough. The only real thing I'd say that holds 5 back is the game feels a little samey overtime and I feel like if it lacked it's job system it would've really gotten dull. If you're exclusively playing FF5 for it's story it won't hold your attention as well as 6 and 7 do.
The port for FF5 on PC is based on the iOS remake that released some time ago. The sprites were completely redrawn alongside the user interface and character portraits. It also includes the additional content that came with the GBA port of FF5. I'd recommend finding a mod that disables the character portraits since they don't match the sprites and were based on the concept art for the game, so they look very out of place compared to the more modern sprites the game has. It also doesn't feature mouse control so if that's a turn off for you I'd suggest not purchasing this port.
It's a fine JRPG and if you can find it for a good price I recommend it a great deal.

Many, many people told me, that FFV is not a great, amazing piece. It has great gameplay, but the story is bland. I could not disagree more.
If FFIV is a classic grand epic, a great tale of huge proportions, with heavy emphasis on characters, FFV is grand adventure. It is not as much about the characters, or the plot itself, or the setting, but about the overall feel of it. I really have enjoyed all the interactions, all the small comedic moments in this game far more, than in any other FF. And it actually has one of best "just evil" villains of all time, and one of best side characters of all time. It also doesn't really have any plot-holes, or inconsistencies. It really is well written, and presented, making me actually shed tear more than once.
It's themes may not be the best, and are indeed fairly in the background for the most part, but the setting has so much life to it. Whereas FFIV had some setting, but it was basicly still fairly undefined, FFV has just as definite lore, as future installments of the series. You don't need a lot to fully understand the differences between this peacfull land, and future settings. And granted, I actually hold FFV's setting high on my list, actually being far better than both FFIV's and FFVI's respective worlds.
The music and gameplay shine. Gameplay is singular THE BEST job system I have seen in Final Fantasies. It has just as much of customization as FFVII, or FFVI, but just like in Dark Souls, you can always add a little variance, you can always modify your strategy, but not to a point of complete change. And characters are leveling, not your items like in FFVII. And what's even better, is that the game truly is challenging. In both FFVI and FFVII although the main antagonists were epic as hell, I actually blazed through final bosses. It could still get challenging, but it was nothing realy hard. Final boss of FFV actually had me retrying modifying strategies for four hours, before I was able to truly beat him. I could count on my fingers amount of times, were final boss was a true challenge, both difficult and enjoyable - and FFV would be high on this list.
If you love good gameplay, you should get into this game immidiately. If you enjoy adventure-like feel, this one is definiately for ya. It may feel off compared to other FF's, but trust me, it's a welcome change of pace, feeling and themes, being both singulary the funniest, and most fun to play FF in the entire series. Add to that really well-written characters - there aren't many of them, but when they receive focus, they are not worse in any way than other main parties - excellent villain and you get one of the best jrpg's ever made. BUY IT NOW! :D

So, I'm giving this game a very mixed yes review. Should you buy it full price? I wouldn't. I bought it in a bundle, though, and I've been really happy with it. How's the multiplayer? I have no idea--maybe I'll get to that someday (if anyone is still playing it when I decide to give it a try...which is distinctly unlikely).
I really like the story mode. It could stand to have more levels, but the wide variety of characters and the frantic pace of the combat make it a great option if you just want to tap into the old Halo-like joy of blowing up hundreds of cartoonish enemies for 30 minutes or so. It's like Borderlands 2 but smoother in a lot of ways--there aren't 50000 guns, but you also don't have to stop every 2 minutes to cycle through inventory. The characters feel more varied because their skills and main weapons are all they have (if you go with a melee champ, you have no option but melee--which can suck but also makes you adapt). The voice acting is fun and has enough variety that you can play through the same levels a few times without getting annoyed at it.
The game has problems. A lot of them, as other posters have pointed out. But if you can pick it up cheap in a sale and you're looking for Halo meets Saturday morning cartoons, I'd give it a look.

Penumbra: Overture is arguably a prime example to the tired idea of "It's not how much time, but it's what you do with it." Throughout the 4 or so hours I took on this first playthrough, I experienced genuine fear as I crawled through the dusty abandoned mine that would set the stage for most of Philip's first chapter. It's not a stretch to call Penumbra: Overture a terrifying game. More terrifying than Amnesia: The Dark Descent and more on the level of Alien: Isolation, Penumbra: Overture makes you dread turning every corner for fear of a flesh-eating dog or deadly spider. The atmosphere is amplified by the well-told story and excellent sound design (especially the soundtrack). The gameplay is also done really well, aside from the half-baked combat system and few difficult moments (like the first spider cave). I will be coming back to Penmubra: Overture for years, but the atmosphere, story, and sound truly sell the game. It may be 5-6 hours long (maybe more depending on how you play), but it's a well spent time.

Penumbra Overture is a strange one. It is classed survival/horror, but I felt neither of those. It felt more like a trial-by-death rage game. Try to do anything, you die, until you die enough times to feel out what specific actions you need to take to not die so quickly. Granted, I played on the hardest difficulty so it probably would have been quite a bit more manageable on lower difficulties, but the lack of direction killed it for me. Not on a macro story level, but on a micro encounter level.
For example, hopefully without spoilers, one level immediately drops you into an encounter where the character states, in subtitles, that they need to seal "that door" whilst looking at a door that obviously can't be the target of the statement. You are then in a large room with somewhat of a gauntlet arrayed before you, and if you take more than half a second to look around, even to get your bearings for the first time, you are dead. It took me at least a couple dozen attempts to coincidentally use that half second in the right spot facing the right direction to realize there was a button. Then I died again. And that was just the first leg of the gauntlet. There were at least two of these situations, together probably representing half of the time I put into this short game. Half the time the game decides to ignore its own mechanics, such as an enemy completely ignoring a distraction that should have worked, and had worked on previous occassions, for no discernable reason. There were also several cases where I would be hiding behind cover, such as a box or around a corner, waiting for the chance to sneak by, and the dog I was hiding from would suddenly start growling and teleport right next to me to rip my throat out. This game made me feel as though there were some hidden timer, and I weren't allowed to go more than a half-minute without dying, usually for no fault of my own.
The controls aren't very intuitive when it comes to the use of tools. I often found myself swinging short or my goal, or in a different manner than I wanted, which in itself got me killed quite often. There wasn't much story, nor was I particularly captivated, but this is only the first chapter in a trilogy. I did like the character Red very much however, in both his voice acting and portrayal. I will also admit that even with all these things, once the credits rolled I was surprised to find how small the crew was, and for the team size I think the game was pretty good.
Context aside though, as the game itself stands I don't find myself compelled to recommend it.

First off, I do recommend the next episode, and if you are buying that, this episode will likely come in a bundle with that. But regardless I found this episode to be kind of lackluster.
The game controls like a typical first person game, except the bulk of the gameplay is puzzle solving similar to that found in classic point and click adventure games. These puzzles are nothing special but managed not to bore me too much. There is however a fair amount of finding a locked door then finding a key, literal or figurative, in some random place. Fortunately the areas are small enough that they are not usually hard to find.
Where the episode fell flat for me was the supposed horror elements. In between the rooms with all the puzzles in them there are some kind of mutant dogs or wolves roaming the hallways. These to me were not scary and were just kind of annoying. The strategy for getting past them is generally just walking slowly and hiding slightly out of sight when one is in the way until it moves away. There are some other creatures you come across which you have to run away from and these sections are very trial and error. At least one of the creatures would be scary but when you've played the same part repeatedly because of the trial and error nature of the gameplay, it loses any scariness it once had.
There isn't a whole lot to the story. You're trying to enter an underground facility to find out what happened to your father who mysteriously dissappeared. There are various obstacles in your way and some crazy guy talks to you over a radio to guide you along. If you were to start with the second episode, you'd find yourself in the middle of the facility without knowing how you got there but there isn't really that much necessary background information needed to enjoy the second episode.

I want to put a break in the train of hatred this game seems to be getting. First off, yes. I have not played Coaster Planet. Does Coaster Planet look nice? Yes. So does this, however. Are there things that I'd like to see improve? Well sure. That can be said about many games and this, fortunately, is still being worked on. For what I've got, I'm more than happy. Now that my little rant is over, allow me to explaid why I recomment this game:
Gameplay: Overall, the game plays more or less exactly like RollerCoaster Tycoon 3. The game does try to move away from the grid system, however there is an optional grid you can enable to make your work more precise. While the grid feature does require some touching up to allow for things to be more exact, it still works and helps. The Coaster Builder is also updated to bring a, in my opinion, more indepth and detailed construction process. You no longer are restricted to certain angles allowing you to have a lot more freedom in your design. It will also display data on how your speed is distributed on the track, how fast you are going at a given place, etc. I had a good amount of fun playing with it. Going back to paths, you can also make curved paths this time removing your restriction to blocky pathways. Overall the game plays the same, just with some slight tweeks and updates.
Graphics: This seems to be another contested area. The game definitely went away from the cartoonish theme of old in favor of realism. This doesn't bother me too much (Yes, I've played every RCT game. Yes, I understand the style was cartoony in all of them. Sure, go ahead and call me a casual, not a fan, etcc.) The overall user interface looks clean, perhaps not "super uber professional" with its art direction like some may desire. However, it works, it looks good, and I like it. A lot of what you would expect out of a RCT interface is there.
Overall: There really isn't a whole lot for me to pick on with this game. It is exactly what I'd expect from a RollerCoaster Tycoon game, there are definitely some improvements over RCT3, but there are defintely areas to improve on. I will still continue to play it and enjoy it and definitely looks forward to what will come in the game's future. If you are on the fence of buying this game, do understand this is a work in progress, and understand that it really is not half as bad as people seem to think it is. You will enjoy it nonetheless if you enjoyed past RCT games.

Renowned Explorers: International Society is one of those rogue-lite games that have come into vogue recently, but this game stands out among them due to it's unique design, concepts, and combat mechanics.
The art design and premise of the story is akin to a choose your own adventure book--and that means if you dislike reading or are prone to skipping dialogue, this game may not be for you. That being said, I was super into these books in my childhood, so as I played through the game it often time made me feel as if each choice mattered dearly making the game that much more immersive to me.
So, if you dislike the theme of the game is there any other reason to buy it? Yes, the combat system of the game is not just shooting and killing your opponents. This game has a mood system, both for the characters and for the entire battle. The three moods, aggressive, devious, and friendly are absolutely vital to your success on any particular adventure. That being said, on the higher difficulties event the most mundane encounters can threaten your entire expedition, so learning to master moods and the various ways to influence it is vital to winning the game.
An average playthrough takes around 2-4 hours on classic difficulty, but this doesn't mean that the game lacks replayability, in fact there are well over 16 explorers to chose from all with unique abilities and traits. There are also 6-7 expeditions in the game, and as others have pointed out, the lack of variety in that sense can make the game rather dull to run through after you've sunk in around 10 hours.
Despite all of this, as the game currently stands I absolutely recommend buying the game at full price or otherwise!

Okay let's start off with the basics, shall we?
Pros:
- The soundtrack is incredible, as one would expect from a FF game
- It's on PC and Steam, which opens it up for modding. You can replace the ugly portraits, too. So that's a plus.
- It stays faithful to the original. The job system, etc. is still there and it works as well as it did when it came out. It's still pretty fun to play around with.
- The way they redid the graphics is somewhat appealing.
Cons:
- The battle menu is obviously designed for touchscreens, which I feel alienates a large majority of the people playing the game/buying it. Should have just stuck with original battle menu. Much easier to navigate/use.
- I don't expect much in the graphics department, with this game first having came out in 1992 and all and having a lot of adaptions without too many improvements graphically. However, this particular version was released in 2015. Where there are probably programs specifically designed to help remedy this.
- The tiles and backgrounds are awful. As well as the sprites. It's like someone just remade the whole game with RPGMaker.
All in all, I'd reccomend it if you're looking to legally own the game and you want to scratch an itch for FFV. And don't get me wrong-- this isn't a bad port. Just a lackluster one.  But yeah.
tl;dr:
Good for scratching an itch, but a lackluster port of an otherwise excellent game.

There's a lot of arguing going on right now, but the fact that almost every negative review has the words "Planet Coaster" in them is worrying. I'm going to try my absolute hardest to give a review on the game without resorting to comparisons. Any point of interest I place an asterisk (*) at the end of is possibly subject to change, and reflects the March 30th launch only.
The good:
Coaster builder - Very useful and well-made. The color safety guide is also very helpful for setting up your coaster in advance as well, so that you can know what does, and does not work.
Area themes - Adds an interesting way for scenery variation to effect certain areas. Also contains variations of each building as well.
Steamworks support - Modding adds unlimited potential in every game.
Terrain editing - Excellent terrain manipulation tool. Not really much else to say without adding pointless padding.
The okay:
Paths - We finally have curved paths, along with several variations. Only problem is that it can occasionally get wonky with terrain collision, or pathing intersection. No curved queue lines, sadly.*
Scenery selection - Decent amount of stock scenery with the base game, however certain themes such as Sci-Fi are lacking in options. Modding could fix.*
Difficulty - This is bad for me, but some people prefer it easy. I'm a veteran of RCT and RCT2, so I prefer biting my nails when it comes to funding, however just building a small portion of the park, and working on a coaster can set you for a good while in terms of funds.
The bad:
Fences - Fences are badly implemented. Can only place them one at a time, and at angled intervals. Hopeful they will add line tools, or at least an option to place along paths.*
Staff - Staff control is basically minimal at this point. Place the building down, select how many you want hired, and hope they do their job, let alone efficiently.*
Performance - There are certain options to minimize graphical load in exchange for increased performance, however certain tools, will bring your frame rate to a crawl under certain circumstances. (EX: Path tool works fine unless it's clipped to an existing path, in which case my frame rate drops by at least half.)*
Graphics - Not great, to say the least, but they could be much worse. I don't really come in to Unity games with high expectations, though.
Overall, it's not as amazing as RCT1 and RCT2 obviously, but I do like it more than RCT3, which I never really transitioned into. On launch, it's a 6/10 for me. I'm curious to see where the future updates will bring this though, as I really do see potential.

As a huge RCT fan, this is a tough one. On one hand this game is (head scratchingly) in early access. On the other hand, they've had multiple games in the series to pull from in terms of content and roadmapping as well as several delays before the official release date. As an early access game, it's not bad. It's completely playable with the money and simulation basics in there to actually run a park.
However, as an RCT game it is a major letdown. We were promised an evolution in the series and what's here is simply the framework for the next step. Is that a bad thing? Not exactly, if something isn't broke then don't fix it. But it's nowhere near what Planet Coaster is doing. Right now you have 3 themes and over half of the scenery/props are locked. I'm not sure if they are locked behind some sort of in-game system or locked out because they aren't finished yet... the game doesn't say. My park ran smoothly enough for me but after I had built 3 coasters and 8 flat rides, I had 1,300 peeps in my park. At one point my menu disappeared so I had to exit out and reload from the main menu. After it sluggishly reloaded, the framerate was in the single digits. Making it unplayable in my eyes.
As for the coaster builder, I didn't care for it much at first. I made a clunky and ugly first coaster. The second was a bit better and the third was almost exactly what I wanted. It's not a bad system and I actually think it works great once you learn how to use it. You can attach set pieces, just like in the older RCT games, or you can go off the grid and make whatever you want! You just have to play with it. So, the coaster builder is on the short list of positives for this game.
The biggest problems I see right now is the amount of content, lack of in depth management tools (staff management, etc.), ugly peeps, and poor optimization. Luckily these are things that can be addressed and fixed. The menus aren't particularly eye pleasing but that's not a big deal.
Also, the mission objectives that are given to you in game are so HUGE they sometimes occupy 75% of the screen so you can't look at the tasks while playing with your park. You have to look at them, close it out, try to finish the task, then open it back up to see the next one. It's mind bogglingly annoying!
The truth is that there is a lot of potential here but right now it's not worth the asking price. Wait for a sale or the full version to see if they can polish this up a bit.

By removing the Shooter element from the FPS, 'Penumbra' created an eerie FIRST PERSON SURVIVAL PUZZLE genre that surprisingly features some unexpected, nicely paced, action sequences without any direct combat from time to time. You can actually melee some foes or trap them but you'll most likely just sneak past them in the dark (unless you're being swarmed by spiders). The interface is mostly a point and click plus, where not only you get to combine elements to make your way through doors and passageways in endless halls and corridors, you also get to interact with the environment in 3D (with the occasional frustration of not turning a wheel quite right to open a hatch or not thrusting a rock hard enough to break something). It's indie games like this that paved the way for something like 'Alien Isolation' and it's still today one of the coolest games out there with a great storyline and level design. In some ways I prefer this to 'Amnesia', specially because here the dark is your friend and doesn't drive you mad like in the later game (A mechanic that was introduced in order to force you to use lights as if it was food, to recharge your sanity).

I've played and beat this game many of times, and I always come back to it. If you didn't know by now. The people who made the Penumbra series, Frictional Games, also made Amnesia and the upcoming SOMA. If you like puzzles and horror games. This is for you.

Renowned Explorers is a game about the golden days of scientific research and exploration in the late 19th century, when all you needed to get funded was a willingness to travel to the Scottish Highlands and hurl insults at sheep until their will was broken.
Renowned Explorers: International Society is difficult to pin down into a single genre, though in very broad strokes it's half resource management, half turn based strategy.  The premise of the game is that you belong to a group of scientists and explorers, and each game sees you setting out with a group of three explorers of your choice to travel the globe, visiting exotic locales and collecting treasures.  You've been sleighted by another member of the society, and over the course of 5 expeditions you have to collect more Renown than him in order to win.  During expeditions, you manage your resources as you travel from node to node, dealing with events and occasionally finding yourself battling strange locals and/or wildlife.
Each game begins with you assembling your party, selecting 3 explorers from 20 available and electing one to be your Captain (Which provides a unique perk for the game).  Characters are broken up into 4 classes, and each character come with a unique mix of actions, skills, and upgrades.  The crew select screen is where the feel of each run will be decided, and there's a wide variety of party types available.  You want to befriend enemies to death while accumulating prodigious amounts of reasearch?  There's a crew for that.  Do you desire to do nothing more than smack your enemies until gold pops out?  There's a crew for that, too.
From there, you're taken to the expedition.  On the expedition map, you travel from node to node to collect as many resources as possible, keeping an eye out for potential treasure.  The majority of nodes with resources available usually feature a challenge that you can choose to have an explorer attempt.  Challenges have percent chance to succeed/fail, often modified by the traits and class of the explorer chosen.  As you would expect, challenges offer greater rewards if successful, though often carry some sort of penalty if you fail (Anything from a minor stat loss for the rest of the expedition to losing resource tokens). You obviously want to maximize your resources gained by hitting many nodes, but your ability to do so is limited by supplies, so it's important to exercise judgment and figure out the optimal way to travel through an expedition (if you do run out, you being to incur rather large stat penalties).  Not all nodes have challenges, however. Some are empty, and some feature encounters.
Encounters are where the meat of the game lies, and probably the most time consuming part of any run.  The overlying battle system is turn based, with each encounter utilizing a procedurally generated hex-based map.  You move your three units, and then the enemy moves theirs, etc. etc.   You obviously want to be as efficient as possible when dispatching the opponents (Who often outnumber you), and the best way to do this is through EMOTIONS!
This is the hook: the mood system.  You and your opponent each have a certain attitude in an encounter, which generates a mood that can be advantageous (or not) for you.  The three attitudes are Aggressive, Friendly, and Devious, and they exist in a rock-paper-scissors relationship.  For example, Aggressive beats Friendly but is weak to Devious.  So, if you are against a Friendly opponent, it is in your best to interest to generate and maintain an Aggressive attitude since it provides bonus Speech Defense.  However, if you generate a Devious attitude in contrast to their Friendly one, you'll take a Speech Defense penalty (which is bad).  You can generate a better attitude by utilizing attacks of that attitude, contributing points until it rolls over.  So in the case of a Friendly enemy, you want to use Friendly or Aggressive attacks until you switch to that attitude, generating a less disadvantageous attitude.
Friendly/Devious attacks also have an emotion component to them, which can provide buffs or debuffs to a target enemy depending on their "state of mind", which is essentially a meter that goes up with Friendly attacks and down with Devious attacks.  There's a lot to manage and it's a ton of fun, and there's a surprising depth that doesn't come through in screenshots.
I'm skipping over a lot in the interest of brevity, though I hope I've communicated the core mechanics.  I haven't even touched on the preparation stage, or how resources work, or skills.  This is very board game-like in the sense that the rules and mechanics are simple, but the way everything interacts creates a good amount of depth that never feels clunky or counter-intuitive.  While the game rewards good decision making and tactical acumen, the most important thing is developing mastery over the game.  You never fail because the game was unfair to you, or because you got unlucky.  Every failure will be your fault, even if you don't know it at that time, and the best way to improve is to learn something from your failures and carry it with you into the future.
While the core mechanics are sound and fun, the package it comes in is incredibly charming.  The art is great and fits the overall feel of the game, the writing is funny through and through, and the music is enjoyable.  It look like a fun, light-hearted game about being an explorer in the late 19th century, and it certainly feels like it.
I love this game, and for me it scratches an itch that only FTL has ever been able to.  Each run takes about 2-3 hours from start to finish, and it's incredibly easy to drop in, form a crew, and set out if you have a bit of time to kill.  I'd also like to give props to the dev team, who are active on the forum and communicate with the fans.  They're constantly tweaking and balancing stuff even now, which is massively appreciated.  The game is better than it was when I first bought it because of their efforts, and it was incredibly enjoyable even then.
I suspect that people who enjoy board game sensibilities or solid turn based strategy will get the most out of this title, though I suspect anyone who just enjoys resource management games would find it enjoyable.

A lot of people have had some pretty negative things to say about this port. It isn't that bad. Yes there are some occasional graphical glitches, and it may not be as clean as the GBA version, but it's still a very solid port of an AMAZING game. It's certainly better than the US PSX version that came with Anthology back in the day.
Anyway, if you've never played this game, and you're a fan of the Final Fantasy series as a whole, you owe it to yourself to check this title out. The story is pretty simple and uninspired, but it's more than made up for in the gameplay. The job system introduced in FF3 is expanded and reworked to become something truly impressive in this game. The soundtrack is, as always, impressive as hell. The combat is interesting, and the bosses are challenging. My only real wish is for a bit more balance between some of the job classes, but for a game that's 20+ years old, they did a pretty damn fine job.
This may not be the perfect port, but it's a very solid one, and the game itself is just incredible. Definitely one to add to your collection.

To me, V is one of the gold standards of the Final Fantasy franchise. Now before I go any further, I should establish that I have enjoyed almost every main-line FF game. The sole exceptions are II, XI, and XIV, and that's mainly because I don't play MMOs. FFV is something special because everything clicks. This is one of those rare games where every aspect is perfect. "Every aspect is perfect". Wait... what? Why not just say "FFV is a perfect game"? Uhhh...huh. To this I say that if FFV is a perfect game, then what would be the point of playing other games unless they too were perfect? Would I be able to devote an equal amount of time to all these perfect games? Would one game be more perfect than the other? Besides, today's perfection is tomorrow's mediocrity. We should all strive to-ENOUGH!
How about we focus on actually discussing FFV? God frikkin' dammit!
This entry in the series is notable for its Job system. Early on, the four warriors of light are introduced to the crystal shards. These allow the heroes to change their job(class) at any moment outside of combat. While FFIII did it first, FFV expands upon the system, by allowing players to mix and match abilities. So your White Mage, who usually twiddles their thumbs during a random encounter, can use their bare hands almost as well as any Monk. The trade-off is that White Mages don't get the Monk's large HP pool. In any case, this system allows players innumerable options for dealing with monsters. Grinding, as always, is a last resort. If your party is failing to beat a boss, maybe their jobs need to be changed, or their abilities aren't adaptable.
While I applaud Square-Enix for adding additional content to FFV: Advance (which this port is loosely based-on), I'm not too fond of the end/post-game. As any FFV fan will tell you, a party of Freelancers with every job mastered is absurdly over-powered. The original version of FFV takes note of this, hence the super-bosses Omega Weapon and Shinryu. FFV:A goes a few steps further with an additional dungeon, enhanced versions of those bosses, and a Super de-duper ultimate final boss to boot. Oh and everything loves to counter your !rapidfire attacks. After a certain point, it all becomes just a little absurd.
So let's take a step back and look at the main game, the "story mode" if you will. The real brilliance of the job system is not in combining all of the abilities to make super-boss smashing Gods, but in making for hundreds of ways to play through the game. The challenge-run is a long-standing Final Fantasy tradition. Ever played a party of all White Mages in FFI? A no-esper run in FFVI? FFV is hardly any different. This is an RPG that can be beaten with literally any combination of jobs. Yes, even a single berserker can defeat the final boss. They have to be level 99, have specialized equipment, and it's still a 1 in 249484140 chance, but it can be done. The point is, there is no wrong way to play through FFV. Your heroes can be whatever you want, and by using all of the tools available to you, you can see the game to the end.
FFV also wisely chooses to avoid large cinematic set-pieces or overly-extensive conversations. This is a game made up almost entirely of overworld and dungeons. Later FF games have a lot of memorable sequences, but for me they don't hold up when being replayed. Take FFVI for example. I'm one of those rare players that prefers the second half of the game. I like the freedom that comes with exploring a world, choosing party-members, and building their abilities. The focus of FFV is exactly just that. Also, like with the other early FFs, this game is appropriately-paced. You can see and do everything in a reasonable amount of time. This, in my opinion, makes FF5 the kind of game that you could afford to devote one play-through a year to.
As for this port of the game...well...eh...I don't like it. At first I was stunned to silence by the awful interlacing, the frame-rate*, and the fact that mashing the fight command can sometimes lead to characters choosing to defend, switch rows, or ???? As I recall, the last time something like that happened was in FFIV: Advance, and I was not happy with that port either. After enough time, I got past these issues and beat this edition of the game, but it's still disappointing.
I'm of mixed opinions on the sprites. As always, the enemies look great, but the characters look weird. Aside from the jarring inconsistencies (Why did they use Amano's artwork for the portraits?), the actual character sprites are just strange at times. To give an example: Bartz always has this "RAWR!" face whenever he raises his hands in the air. This happens at several points in the story, like when he's breaking free from something, celebrating, or is getting pumped up. This is getting really nitpicky, but it showcases what I prefer about FFV's original sprites. The characters in FFV are expected to show a wide range of emotions, but they're tiny sprites with a dozen animation frames between them. However, this simplicity works to the story's advantage, because you can always tell the current mood of the situation. With this version all I can think about is "Why does Bartz get angry so often?" as he gesticulates wildly like Stan S. Stanman.
Overall, this port of FFV is serviceable, but it deserves better. This is a fantastic JRPG, one of the best of its kind, but it's the victim of yet another lazy port. Maybe one day Square-enix will get the bright idea to hire M2 or a similar team to do their previous games justice. Still, it could be worse...it could always be worse.
*Yep. I will complain about the frame-rate in an RPG, especially if it's worse than the previous edition's.

FEAR 2 is the sequel to FEAR (obviously). You play as a Delta Force soldier named Michael Beckett who is sent to capture Armacham (the bad guys from 1) president.
There are some dramatic gameplay changes from the 1st game, and they are all absolutely terrible. No more awesome gunfights with smart AI. Now you just fight waves of dumb enemies. AI is really inconsistent. They go from not even noticing you after you've shot two of their team mates in the same room and circling around a grenade you've just thrown to having the reactions of someone who just snorted crack and with aimbotting accuracy. I will also note they have serious trouble throwing grenades.
Another change was the removal of peak buttons. This wouldn't♥♥♥♥♥♥me off so much if this game actually gave you a reasonable amount of health but instead you are forced to hide by corners and pick enemies off. No more running into rooms with slow-motion on. Try that and you better hope you kill all enemies before slow mo runs out. If I really need to manipulate cover, I need more than a press E to flip over a ♥♥♥♥ing table here.
To begin with the guns all feel incredibly useless. The SMG sounds okay at best, and the pistol sounds like it's less useful than harsh language. The combat shotgun's sound is laughable and pathetic. Even some of the better weapons like the assault rifle, (semi) automatic shotgun and sniper rifle don't feel extremely powerful. There aren't many new weapons. Most of them are re-skins. Only new are the automatic shotgun, sniper rifle and laser gun which are somewhat welcome additions.
The one thing I thought could save the game was the sections where you get to pilot a mech, but some idiot decided that there should be some grainly filter over the screen that gets even worse as you take damage. It absolutely looked horrible and I found it incredible distracting.
About the only thing improved from the original game is the fact that there are more varied environments for levels, but that's nothing if I'm not enjoying the time spent in said environments.
All in all the gameplay felt like a cookie cutter shooter which needed to give the player one or two more health packs and armour pickups (at least on hard).
Story wise this game is kinda like the first. It gets very predictable, especially if you've played the first game. The scares are the same, although I did feel this game was a little more scary than the first, it still failed to terrify me. Most of the jumpscares were fairly predictable, and there was only so many times that seeing Alma and bloody rooms could be even somewhat unsettling.
All in all, I'd advise you play the first FEAR game. It runs rings around this game. If you need something else to hit that slow-motion Hollywood badass fix go check out the Max Payne series. The only reason I could possibly recommend this game is if you've played the first FEAR and wish to see how the story plays out.

Rating: 7.5/10
Overview: FPS with the ability to go into slow-mo
The Good:
+Game looks good both artisically and technically. Game also makes good use of lighting
+ Game has a variety of weapons and grenades. Certain weapons are very creative while others are what you would expect in a FPS
+ The game has really solid level design. In addition, the game takes place over a series of different environments and locations. One of my biggest complaints in the first FEAR was that the environments were too similar and felt repetitive so it's nice to see this was fixed in the sequel.
+The shooting mechanics feel good, going into slow-mo and shooting enemies is always fun.  The game also introduces sections where you ride a mech to change up the gameplay.
The Average:
The AI feels average compared to the first FEAR. The first game was renowned for its amazing AI and to this day I still think it sets the standard for AI in a FPS game. This game though doesn't seem to have that.  The AI is not bad by any means, however compared to the first game it doesn't feel close.
The horror elements are not as a good as the first game. Between finding a balance between action and horror the developers chose action.  There are certainly plenty of times the game tries to invoke scares but sometimes it just comes across as flat.
One of the most satisfying weapons in any FPS game was the shotgun from the first game. In this game, the shotgun doesn't even feel close to satisfying.
I found the game to be very easy even on the normal setting, play on hard if you want a challenge.
The Bad:
- The dialogue in this game is terrible. It makes the story feel like a straight to home video release. It becomes difficult to take the story seriously or be afraid of what's around the corner when the characters are saying things that just make you shake your head.
-The game has a certain flow to it but the entire ending gameplay segment feels frustrating and out of place.
-Multiplayer is dead
Conclusion
On the one hand this game does things a lot better than the first, on the other hand it also doesn't seem to improve any of the flaws and in some cases makes it worse. What could have been a really great horror FPS game turns into you standard run of the mill FPS game.  For a FPS game it is very solid and should provide you with a 5-6 hours of fun.

Despite having loved the first FEAR, its sequel is a seriously mixed bag.  The weapons are fairly satisfying, although the energy weapon and laser are stupidly awkward.  Gunplay in general still feels right, but the AI lacks the level of skill and more believable squad tactics that made the gunfights in original so dynamic and enjoyable.  Things feel much more scripted now, which while not necessarily bad, certainly makes for less engaging fights overall.
This almost goes without saying, but the game looks far better than the original. but it generally lacks the same unnerving tension that FEAR managed to create so regularly.  It definitely has its moments, to be sure, but it's far more sporadic.  Put differently, a lot of the scares (jump or otherwise) felt extremely formulaic at this point, with even sightings of Alma being generally unremarkable.
There were definitely some good (albeit disturbing) revelations--like the purpose of the school, or the extent of the experiments on Alma, the prototypes, and all the would-be candidates for the Program--but a lot of it still felt a bit perfunctory to me.  Maybe it's because a lot of the mystery was gone by that point.
I don't want to give it away, but I found the ending totally unexpected, disturbing, but also appropriate to the kind of dark, adult story being told--particularly considering its many troublesome implications.  However, my "liking" of the ending and FEAR2 overall was also predicated on FEAR3 finally connecting all the dots in a satisfying and sufficiently harrowing way, which it most definitely did not do.
I'm seriously torn here, but I'm going to have to down-vote this one: I don't regret playing it per say, but I also can't recommend it with a straight face.  Come for the tight gunplay and lukewarm scares if you like, but if that doesn't do much for you then just play the original again and pretend that its progressively less satisfying sequels never hit store shelves.

Wow. Awesome experience. I call it an experience because it's not really a game. There is interaction, definitely. You are tasked with parsing through old police tapes (7 of them, I think), but they're all chopped up in pieces but you have to search for the pieces you want to view. How? Well, you do a keyword search, but you don't know what's important until you watch some videos, get some more keywords to search for, then find a few more, etc. The challenge comes from the fact that you only get to watch the first 5 results that come up from any search, so you have to be clever with your search terms. The game is well designed because there are a lot of recurring themes and words that come up a lot, like repeating numbers even for different situations, so searching for a number in a given situation can give you the same number but in a way you didn't expect. The order in which you unlock the information is all up to you. I actually stumbled upon a very crucial reveal early on but didn't realize its implication until way later.
Pros:
+ Story. This game is 90% story, and it's a good one.
+ Interaction. The way you are uncovering the clues means you always feel like a genius when you discover something new, or when going out on a limb gives you new results. The game never railroads you into a certain order; it's up to you to bring order to the chaos.
+ The look. The film snippets take place in '94, and the computer you're working on has an old Windows 95-esque computer feel to it, down to the icons, low res and screen glare that makes it clear it's an old CRT monitor.
+ Sound design. Very minimal, not very much music, but police sirens now and then make you think you're actually sitting at a desk in a police station. The monitor even makes a static sort of hum like an old CRT screen, and dims occasionally (I noticed a correlation that it dimmed whenever I stumbled upon a truly crucial snippet)
+ Acting. It was just awesome. Especially since the medium you're really working with is film, this could have gone so much differently without good acting.
Neutral:
~ Length. I'm putting this as a neutral because I actually felt like it was the perfect length, but others may feel it too short. According to a YouTube video with all the clips stitched together in order that I watched after I was finished to see what I missed, there's only about 1 hour 45 minutes of footage. My gameplay took about two hours, including occasional rewatching of clips, taking notes, and typing.
Cons:
- Uh... maybe people won't like the fact that it's more of a visual novel (albeit one out of order) than a "game". If you think of it more like a puzzle or an interactive experience, you won't be disappointed. Personally, I loved it. It was one of the most inventive games I've ever played. Just be aware of what you're buying. But honestly, this is the only con I can think of, and it's a stretch.
10/10

This game is a full motion video (FMV) game. Using point and click mechanics you watch a series of pre-recorded videos acted by real people. Each video lasts seconds, and tells a small snippet of a story. Each video has two things in common: they always feature the protagonist and they are always set in what appears to be some sort of interview room.
As you watch the videos, you can use keywords to search the police database afterwards to find related snippets in an attempt to piece the story together.
I have never played a game like this and I appreciated its approach to storytelling. The detective-like puzzle of using keywords you identify during the videos to figure out the story was compelling, challenging and enjoyable. The videos themselves were well-acted and written. For the price, I highly recommend this game.

Her Story is a short interactive movie with one good idea. The gameplay, if it can be called that, consists of typing random keywords into a search bar and watching video clips of a narrative play out in nonlinear fashion. Depending on how clever/lucky you are in selecting keywords, you'll piece together the story in about 45 minutes to an hour, and the game will end shortly after that.
There is a kernel of a good game here, and the keyword search mechanic is diverting for the first 30 minutes or so. Unfortunately, the story is more contrived than clever, and in a game that relies almost entirely upon plot, this is a fatal flaw. Additionally, the whole endeavour feels more than a little creepy and voyeuristic as you pry into "her" sex life and other intimate details. Actress Viva Seifert is totally game though, and her performance softens what could otherwise be an uncomfortable experience.
I'd like to see this game mechanic in a more substantial title (perhaps as a new investigation mechanic in Capcom's Ace Attorney series), but as a standalone game, Her Story disappoints.

Rated “F” for ♥♥♥♥balls, The Angry Video Game Nerd Adventures lives up to its rating. Developed by FreakZone Games and published by Screw Attack Entertainment this game has been a long time coming and many have looked forward to its release for some time. AVGNA is actually really hard, and almost makes me wonder what the Angry Video Game Nerd himself would say. The game fits into the online series perfectly and any Angry Video Game Nerd fan will love everything that they have incorporated into it.
Covered in nostalgia this game stays true to the 16 bit era, and doesn’t stray from the path at all. I could think of a 100 things that would make this game better, but by adding them in it would drastically change how the game is perceived. When I first started, it almost felt like 1991, coming home from the video store after renting a new Nintendo game. The AVGNA logo sits on a black background with 3 choices, Start, Options and Quit, and reminded me a lot of the old 8 bit style games like Dig Dug or Excite Bike. The language in this game reminds me of Farrah Abraham’s porno, a bunch of awkwardly placed swears revolving around the words♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and♥♥♥♥♥♥ whereas in this case its actually funny on purpose. Adding to the awesomeness of the game, not only is your main weapon an old school Nintendo Zapper, but you have enemies like Rob E. Robot and a defecating Rudolph the reindeer.
The story starts off with the Nerd and his friends playing a “♥♥♥♥♥♥” game together, when suddenly his friends are zapped into the TV. The Nerd escapes into the basement but an arm comes out of the TV and grabs him but the balls and pulls him inside. The game begins in Gameland, 3AM. From there the game brings you into a small training level to learn the controls and dynamics. After the tutorial, you are brought to a map screen where you have the choice of 8 worlds. Each are individually themed and named accordingly. To name a few, “♥♥♥♥♥♥♥vania” is reminicient of Castlevania and holds many obstacles similar to the ones you would have encountered playing it, “Beat It & Eat It” has elements of the adult themed Atari game Beat Em & Eat Em. Your ultimate goal throughout the game is to beat the boss at the end of each level and try to get yourself out of GameLand.
At times during gameplay I found myself almost trying to like this game, because upon initial gameplay I was almost taken back by the tremendous difficulty, I feel like this is one of those games where its simplicity makes it almost impossible. Your health is comprised of beer bottles, depending on the difficulty setting you choose you will start with either 3 or 5 beers. Like most platformers the bottles are scattered throughout each level and usually appear after a seemly impossible section to help replenish your life before its so callously taken away. Your main weapon is a Nintendo Zapper and if you can find the upgrade you also have the SNES Super Scope which fires faster and more effectively. Each world has hidden secrets and you can even discover new playable characters with different weapons and abilities. 1UPs are scattered throughout the levels to help replenish the lives lost along the way, as well as a few one time use abilities that have a variety of effects.
I think what it all comes down to with this game is price and how its not reflected in gameplay. I respect the old school retro effect and any of my readers will agree with that, but this game would be amazing and I would love it 10 times more for 4.99. Due to the marketing of the game and the already house hold name of AVGN amongst gamers this game would be understandable at 9.99, but the 14.99 price mark is almost a dig at the fans. What it all boils down to is the game at its base and if its good or not. The graphics are a little more pixelated than I would have expected, and the ratio is a little larger than your normal platformer. The controls are on point and flow well with the game. Overall The Angry Video Game Nerd Adventures is certainly worth checking out, and will leave you just as angry as the Nerd himself.

Full of pop culture references, nods to old school gaming, and a great sensor of humour, Guacamelee combines the exploration of the metroid games, and later castlevania games, precision platforming, and beat em up mechanics, similar to final fight and streets of rage.
Guacamelee does not have any game overs, or give you any lives, rather, checkpoints are plentiful, but while they are plentiful, they are also well placed.  Later stages in the game demand absolute precision, concentration, and perfection platforming, yet the sense of relief when you pull these parts of with a reward of a checkpoint is fantastic.  While the demands of the platforming parts are in place, you will not ever feel frustrated, as the game encourages you to try to tackle a piece of platforming, and your worse case scenario is your back at the start of the room, and if you run out of health, you return back to the last checkpoint.
Combat is plentiful.  Combat is simple, but there is plenty of depth.  Along the course of the game, as you unlock more moves and abilities, you can combine these moves into one gigantic combo.  There are various enemy types, and of course, like any good platformer, some of the enemy placements are quite strategically placed.  When your precision platforming and a flying dragon is trying to knock you off, you instantly remember the older days of platforming on the NES.  Combo attacking, and juggling mid air is encouraged, and the game encourages you to rack up a high combo, rewarding you with extra money.  The potential and depth of the combat system is up to you to discover, but the game does a very good job teaching you the overall basics (One of the side quests involves you linking up different abilities to pull of a combo)
The overall pacing of the game is also quite good.  The game never makes you feel like it is a drag.  Just when you feel comfortable, or you come across an area where you need an ability, you usually come across a chozo statue (Yes, right out of metroid) that grants a new ability, which then encourages you to go and further explore.
That all said, the game does not take a very long time to complete, and even 100% the story will take just over 10 hours.  Fortunately, there is a hard mode, and there is challenge rooms to keep you interested, while multiple costumes give you specific extra and negative abilities (For example, one suit grants infinity stamina, but you are also unable to regain health) so for people who do like to set their own challenges, there are options here.
Overall, if you like humour, metroid style games, or platformers, this is a must buy.

Often called as best Hitman game and for a good reason.

Even though I fully recommend it the game has few issues. In some way it still feels more like a puzzle game than a stealth game. While the brilliant level design allows for many ways of finishing each mission, the game always playes the same way. The "accident" deaths (the best kind of kills score wise) are quite scripted and the game seems to really push you toward using these limited ways of finishing the levels. The guard patrols always follow the same patterns and they are not very reactive. They either discover you and try to kill you (in which case you can restart the mission or shot your way through the level which isn't very fun,) or they ignore you. There is no middle ground, which would complicate things for you but not make it impossible to progress stealthily. Because of that the game almost feels like it has an instant failure state whenever you get discovered. Because of that you will constantly restart missions figuring out the best route for you. Once you figure it out the same route will work just fine every time to play. The missions difficuly falls drastically down as soon as you get a good disguise. While in Hitman 2 a disguise would delay the guard recognizing you, in Blood Money a good disguise will allow you to walk freely throughout the whole mission. Beating a level often comes down to figuring out what is the strongest disguise in the game and getting it as quickly as possible.
Writing is dodgy at best. I think the devs were trying to make you now feel bad by killing your targets but jokes and chatter are quite crude. Game would benefit greatly from a better script.
Still messing around with levels and trying different approaches and strategies is always fun.

This game is a full motion video (FMV) game. Using point and click mechanics you watch a series of pre-recorded videos acted by real people. Each video lasts seconds, and tells a small snippet of a story. Each video has two things in common: they always feature the protagonist and they are always set in what appears to be some sort of interview room.
As you watch the videos, you can use keywords to search the police database afterwards to find related snippets in an attempt to piece the story together.
I have never played a game like this and I appreciated its approach to storytelling. The detective-like puzzle of using keywords you identify during the videos to figure out the story was compelling, challenging and enjoyable. The videos themselves were well-acted and written. For the price, I highly recommend this game.

Her Story is a short interactive movie with one good idea. The gameplay, if it can be called that, consists of typing random keywords into a search bar and watching video clips of a narrative play out in nonlinear fashion. Depending on how clever/lucky you are in selecting keywords, you'll piece together the story in about 45 minutes to an hour, and the game will end shortly after that.
There is a kernel of a good game here, and the keyword search mechanic is diverting for the first 30 minutes or so. Unfortunately, the story is more contrived than clever, and in a game that relies almost entirely upon plot, this is a fatal flaw. Additionally, the whole endeavour feels more than a little creepy and voyeuristic as you pry into "her" sex life and other intimate details. Actress Viva Seifert is totally game though, and her performance softens what could otherwise be an uncomfortable experience.
I'd like to see this game mechanic in a more substantial title (perhaps as a new investigation mechanic in Capcom's Ace Attorney series), but as a standalone game, Her Story disappoints.

You find your own clues, you go with your own hunches, and there's no glowing icon or [Blue Tinted Keyword] to click on. When you finish this game, it's because you actually figured it out, not because you kept pushing "A" until the developers ran out of content.
The only complaint I have is that getting 100% completion is a little tedious because so many of the videos are extremely short and difficult to find with searches, but that's a very minor nitpick and is even alleviated with some in-game cheats unlocked after finishing the story.
Playing Her Story made me feel like I solved a mystery in an organic, real way that I've never seen done in any other form of media before. Its nonlinear nature is uniquely suited to being a video game. Unlike so many Games As Art™ things I've played, this advances the medium and could never work as anything else.

Battleborn is an exciting, original game with an impressive amount of content that will keep me busy for a good long while. It has some serious problems, but these are sufficiently outweighed by the game's quality to offer a lot of fun. I've more than got my money's worth already and there's much more to do. Pick it up on sale (it's very cheap on Amazon right now) and have a go.
Pros:
- Superb writing and narrative concept. It has all the quirky humour of Borderlands 2, with even richer characterisation and better dialogue. There's also a lot of writing in each story episode: every playthrough can have a different script.
- Soon to be 30 playable characters, each with their own abilities and skills. Huge potential for individual playstyle, and lots of replyability.
- Extended support is in place, with more content coming out. Gearbox are actively working on improving and balancing the game.
- A pretty good community once you get in-game.
- Challenges, skins, taunts, and lore to unlock for the completionist in you.
- Three different PvP modes and a number of story missions which let you practice and get gear.
Cons:
- Really low player base. The game was marketed abysmally and has suffered from it... But it's quite fun seeing familiar faces in versus.
- Poor matchmaking. There's often a big skill gap in games. Gearbox are working on it but until numbers pick up it's a challenge.
- It's irritating constantly hearing assertions that the game is dead or seeing inappropraite comparisons to Overwatch. Battleborn is a unique game and I'm still having great fun with it.

If you loved the Borderlands series, you'll more than likely really like Battleborn, too. Before the game was out, I watched some closed beta PvP gameplay, and I wasn't too interested. But before I wrote the game off, I figured I'd give it a try during the open beta. I'm glad I did! The story missions were so Borderlands like in the gameplay, that I was immediately hooked. My girlfriend and I played through the three available missions, and we pre-ordered immediately after.  Over 200 hours in, and no regrets!
The replayability of the eight story missions is pretty incredible.  The first run through on normal difficulty, took the two of us about an hour each mission, not including failed attempts. Add in all the different characters and their unique playstyles, and running through the missions stays fun and feeling fresh with each new Battleborn you try out.  There is so much diversity in playstyle between characters and even within the same character when you delve more into the helix and gear loadout possibilities.  The game has depth and incredible humor!
After fully mastering my first Battleborn, I tried out PvP finally.  I've never really done PvP outside of MMOs, so it has taken me a while to feel like I can actually be a vital part of a team.  When you get to that point, though, PvPing is soooo much fun!  If you're looking for a game where you can just button mash and quick kill everyone around without working with your teammates, you're going to have a bad game experience, as will your teammates.  Successful PvP in this game requires teamwork and communication.  If you don't have friends playing the game, it's easy to make new ones in the game.  I've befriended some amazingly fun players, and that makes all the difference.  Have someone playing and communicating well in a match? Send them a friend request in game, and don’t be surprised when that friend request is sent to you after a good match, too!
The player base is low, but contrary to the doomsayers, this game is far from dead.  Maximum wait time for a match has been about five minutes.  Gearbox continues to do weekly updates with a lot more big updates coming down the line: DLCs, new maps and play modes, and new characters.  If you're waiting for Borderlands 3 to come out, Battelborn should do well in tiding you over until we return to Pandora!  If the price is an issue, keep an eye out for a sale.
