While it certainly is good for AVGN fans and it certainly is difficult, it is by no means fair. Rather than building the game around a particular structure and then making that difficult, the game is built around the difficulty itself. This means that almost every part of the game is designed to kill you, particularly in certain areas. Fantastic music and stylized graphics are overshadowed by areas that get so difficult, they no longer feel like levels but like a path of obstacles created in a predesigned level builder. Many of the faults that the AVGN has pointed out in numerous bad games have been built into this one, and by doing so it's less of a parody and more of a bad game itself. All in all, AVGN fans will be pleased by the pretty colors and references, but anyone else will find this a very frustrating experience.

Final Thoughts:
Preferably, it's best to get a copy of the GBA, SNES, or PS version. Or you know, emulate them. The game feels better with the older sprites because they feel like they actually belong in the game. The battle menu makes you look in the correct spots and the music fits the game. This is a problematic port, there is no question about that, but I would have to say that, despite its issues, the game is still a lot of fun.  Final Fantasy V has always been a great SNES-era RPG, and that has not changed, even with the problems present in the Steam port.
I think my biggest problem with the port, which is mentioned in most of the other reviews here, is the tile seams are very obviously visible.  This, more than anything else, bothered me, as it just makes certain areas and objects in the game look terrible to the point of distraction.  This also has the result of making certain areas of the game look really bad while your character are in motion.
The character sprites are another issue that a lot of people have with this version.  While I will say they look a lot less distracting in-game than in screen shots, they still take a lot of getting used to.  And even then, something about them just makes them look odd and out of place compared to the look of the rest of the game.  On the flip side, though, the redone enemy sprites look pretty fantastic.
On a positive note, this version of the game contains all of the additional content that was originally added to the Gameboy Advance version, which includes a handful of new jobs, new bosses, and a new post game dungeon.  So, if you've never had access to the GBA version and don't want to play on a mobile device, this a way to be able to experience these additions.
Overall, the game seems to run fine on my PC.  In my 30-plus hours of playtime, I have personally not run into any noticeable bugs or crashes, and load times are non-existent.
I debated on whether to give the game a thumbs or down at the end, since while I enjoy the game, the bad porting is an issue which I don't really think should be condoned.  But, when it really gets down to it, what I want to see answered in reviews is essentially "is the game fun", and in the end, I have to answer "yes".

An example is in the void, there is an enemy that when physically attacked, it vasts protect. This by itself is not bad, but it casts it EVERY time. There is no check to see if it already has this status. If you have dual-wield and hit it with both weapons it casts this twice in succession, dragging out the battle unneccesarily. It is this kind of reliance on enemy counter attacks to drag out battles and increase the difficulty that I find unpalatable. Compounding this is this is many ememies counter even if you miss.
I feel obligated to pointout that you will miss a lot. What is the point of dual wielding weapons if the second hit misses >50% of the time? Enemy attcks seem to miss me so infrequently unless I'm a samurai or using the zephyr cape which doesn't help if you don't have enough to go around...
I like a challenge, but when critical attacks by the enemy are unleashed at any time bacuse instead of using RNG, they were added into the monsters move sets which canbe seen when you manipulate them.
This is overall very disappointing, and I'm sad to say it is just a port of the old game with none of the flaws fixed, with some fancy visual fluff. Unlike with FF IV where they added in augments, or FF VI where there was a good an solid game to start with, this is a poor offering. You can't polish a turd as the expression goes.
Save your money and buy the FF IV or FF VI remakes instead.

: Square-Enix
: Square-Enix
==========
Final Fantasy V is the fifth and in my opinion a very underrated entry in the esteemed Final Fantasy franchise. It took the Job System introduced in Final Fantasy III and refined it, delivering a highly customizable and adaptive experience for the player. It also features a small handful of memorable characters, and doesn't fall prey to "the REAL villian comes out of nowhere at the end" trope that a handful of RPGs typically use.
The Steam version is based on the iOS port, and as such comes with the bugs, flaws, and complaints that version had. The most notable of which are the character portraits and character sprites. Put those minor complaints aside, and you have yourself a great RPG. Please do not let the graphics put you off of this grand adventure!
==========
As said above, Final Fantasy V takes the Job System of Final Fantasy III and improved it. Instead of the formulaic, behind-the-scenes way FF3 handled how Jobs leveled up, FFV favors a simpler approach. After every battle you earn Experience Points, Gil, and Job Points. Every Job levels up a few times, and each level requires more and more Job Points. The first level can be anywhere between 10 and 30 Job Points, depending on the Job, and as they level higher, you may see numbers like 150, 200, or even 999 for a select few Jobs! As you gain levels in each Job, you learn an ability from that Job that you can then assign to your characters
This opens up a plethora of customization opportunites and different playstyles.
As for the game itself, the game utilizes the tried and true turn-based ATB system. When the ATB gauge fills up you are able to give commands to your party, then wait for the gauge to fill up again to take another action. Basic stuff, but it works very well. There are a lot of abilities and spells to learn, including White Magic, Black Magic, Blue Magic, Songs, Summons, and Time Magic. All of these can be mixed and matched in the Job System to create some truly flexible battle setups. While the game doesn't really present any truly challenging battles (apart from the super bosses), much of the game can be completed with a simple setup like 2 Knights, a White Mage, and a Black Mage.
==========
This version comes with updated sprites and character portraits. This is a point of contention with some of the playerbase, as many do not like the "new look". For those where this is a major concern, a mod was created that you can find online that replaced the character portraits with art that matches the sprites. Barring that complaint, the rest of the game looks okay. In some areas you can clearly see the borders of each tile, and in some places it sticks out like a sore thumb. This was another complaint. While not major, it's VERY noticeable, and depending on how you are or how you like your games to look, this may or may not be a problem. Check out the game's screenshots before making a buying decision.
==========
Another game soundtrack composed by the legendary Nobuo Uematsu! Final Fantasy V has some iconic themes of it's own, such as Battle on the Big Bridge. Each track contributes to the situation at hand and enhances the player's attachment to the characters and story. This is music done right. Here's Battle on the Big Bridge:
Sound effects are pretty basic, but do their job. Nothing really groundbreaking, but the soundtrack more than makes up for the shortcomings in the sound effects department.
==========
PC specs are on my profile. The game ran very well, no major problems occured. It's an older RPG, so FPS isn't really a concern in this case. I used a Logitech F310 controller for the entirety of my playthough, and it worked just fine by default. Didn't have to change anything for it to work properly.
==========
If you never got the chance to play Final Fantasy V back in the day, this would be a great opportunity to do so. Great characters, great story, and a superb character customization system makes Final Fantasy V a fantastic entry in the series...although it is frequently overlooked. Don't make that mistake, give it a shot!

I've owned and played all of the Hitman franchise, both on consoles and on the PC (non-steam), and I've thoroughly enjoyed each one. I think my favorite games in the franchise are Silent Assassin and Contracts, however, each game is a wonderful experience and should be given at least one playthrough if you have the chance.
If you like stealth-oriented (or guns-blazing) gameplay, being a dangerous assassin, and open-ended, challenging missions, then you will really, really enjoy this game. The Hitman franchise has consistently been able to provide the experience of being a world-renown and package it into a fun, fresh, and user-friendly game for all types of gamers to enjoy.
The aesthetics are fantastic - the detail in the environments and character models are very well-done. The music and sounds in the franchise have always been solid, and the score used in Blood Money adds a sense of grandiosity and elegance to the gameplay. The story has always been interesting, and this installation chronicles the FBI's hunt for Agent 47. The "ending" is quite satisfying, and offers a great segue into the next game.
The controls are not too difficult to familiarize yourself with, and the tutorial mission is both fun and very helpful - it feels less like a hold-your-hand mission compared to other games that may restrict your actions initially. The learning curve is minimal to moderate, further influenced by the difficulty you select (no notoriety on Rookie) and playstyle you use (stealth vs. bloodshed).
Before you begin your missions, you will be able to select which weapons to take with you, as well as upgrade each primary weapon you own - more options are unlocked as you progress. The money you accumulate is based on your rating upon completing your missions (generally, more stealtheir approaches lead to higher rewards).
Your performance rating is provided in the form of a newspaper article, with the headline "Silent Assassin" if you achieve a perfect playthrough. I really liked this feature, as it will comment on your most used weapon, firearm accuracy (ex: the 4 headshots and unwasted bullets suggest a deadly professional), number of witnesses and casualties, and how the targets were killed. Each mission has a mechanic available to make each target die in what appears to be an accident (ex: a pallet of crates falling on top of someone), allowing you to achieve full stealth.
Notoriety is affected by your performance, and the more attention you draw to yourself, the higher your notoriety gain. As it climbs, NPCs will react faster to your presence and may even call for help from guards. You can pay a fee to reduce your notoriety, and obtaining the CCTV tapes (if you are spotted on camera) will eliminate that hit to your notoriety.
My favorite mission involved
You can challenge yourself in many ways - try doing a mission without switching into a disguise, being seen (causing an alert), killing, using weapons, etc. I beat Blood Money on the hardest difficulty on my 3rd playthrough (full stealth), and I encourage everyone to NOT try the game on Rookie (the notoriety feature adds a lot of intensity and fun). For my first playthrough, I did full stealth and normal. For my second, I tried a Rambo-style method - both provided me with a satisfying, badass assassin feel. Watching NPCs running away in fear while helpless guards fall to your expertly-placed shots can be just as fulfilling as entering a restricted area without anyone knowing.
Overall, the game is very enjoyable if you are the least bit interested in assassinations (stealth or non-stealth), and everyone should definitely give this game a try.
Highly recommend!
Cheers,

There is a fun game concept here, but the implementation is lacking. A combination of frustrating design decisions and occasional severe bugs makes this into an unpleasant experience, and if one continues playing until one has beaten the game, it's more likely due to stubbornness than enjoyment.
In the beginning of the game, combat is tedious, a boring cycle of killing weak enemies that take too long to dispatch while waiting to find a weapon upgrade which may or may not ever materialize. Later in the game, most actual threats feel as though their danger comes from clumsy game mechanics rather than appropriate challenge. Various aspects of the game feel unpolished; a shop appears at the beginning of the game when the player cannot possibly have anything to sell or any money to spend, the visual indication of the boundary of the level is much too subtle, etc.
Finally, frustrating bugs often take what enjoyment there is out of the experience. Sometimes, after finishing a level, all real progress will be lost; score is reset and items and upgrades are gone (seems to happen most frequently when alt-tabbing during level end). Some enemies can be rendered impossible to kill (an abyss enemy in the -goblin family has an invulnerable portion and a vulnerable portion; usually these can be killed by depleting their vulnerable portions' health and then harpooning them off, but a Berserk elite has enough bonus health to actually survive this process, leaving only the invulnerable portion to swim around and attack indefinitely). Finally, the game actually crashed after finishing the final level, so I have no idea whether there is supposed to be an end-game sequence, and I've no patience left to find out.

Her Story is an inventive adventure game with an interface and means of storytelling that I haven't experienced in a game before. The basic gist is that you're someone using an old computer terminal to pull up interview clips from a woman about a crime. You're not given the question she was asked, just the answer and from that answer you have to listen for key words for phrases. You then search for these words or phrases and bring up more relevant video clips. It's up to you to determine when you've learned enough about the events that transpired as you piece together clues.
This game is highly recommended for anyone a fan of adventure games, the crime genre, or just wants to experience something unique. Also big props to the actress for delivering a great performance!

3 - Building base - in SC1 we need to overlap shields (paying attention to energy consumption) and hope they would hold long enought while your defense structures and units take care of the enemey. In SC2, just one shield will do for everything.

Anyway, the devs maybe were drunk, in a bad mood or just left their kids in charge, i don't know. But they just took everything that make SC1 an remarkable game and throw them in the trash. And painted everything with neon paint....too childish.

One of the most frustrating, yet fun to play platformers I've ever had the pleasure of playing. A game based on the hit, internet sensation the Angry Video Game Nerd, a character portrayed by James Rolfe whom reviews older games ranging from the Atari, to the SEGA Genesis to the NES and a bunch more.
Off the bat, the game starts out by introducing the Angry Video Game Nerd (or AVGN for short) before he is sucked into the TV (by the balls no less!) and is forced to play through what he calls hell. The stages, quotes, etc are references to older video games and episodes he has done in the past. The game itself conveys a traditional 8-Bit art style for the majority of assets used in the game aswell as play the expected 8-bit style music to go along with them.
Now, personally, I love this game and actively recommend it to everyone that loves/loved watching AVGN and likes tough platformers in general. The game plays out very similarly to classic MegaMan games and Mario Bros, since the Nerd has his standard jump, shoot and crouch, as well as a few nifty temporary power-ups you can pick up across the stages - these range from the Glitch Gremlin (a green creature that glitches the game and often helps with progression as it halts both stage hazards and enemies), the Super Mega Death Christ (Yes lol, a power up that destroys every enemy present on the screen at the time.), an upgraded gun for the Nerd (Has a much bigger hitbox than his standard light gun) and rocks (Yes rocks, like those found on one of his older episodes that he says is useless because of the low travel distance and low damage).
The game has a 3 damage health system and lives (unless you pick a higher or lower difficulty setting in which the game alters these). 3 beer bottles pretty much signal how many more hits you can take before dying, and the lives, like in older Megaman games, means how many times you can retry before being kicked out from the stages. There are also toasters (checkpoints) scattered across the stage to mark your progress on any given stage, but they are optional to activate as there are also beer bottles scattered across to help restore health to you - and there's also secret characters you can unlock all based on his show.
Stage Progression~ Generally, excluding the tutorial stage - you pick a stage in a similar fashion to MegaMan games, there are 8 in total. Each stage has their own deathtraps, some will take a point of damage, and some, like the golden skull blocks found across every stage, will kill you in one hit. Some zones are based around very careful and timing based jumps, movement, etc - like some zones will have an enemy type that is there to hinder you while you do a section, it's all very much reminiscent of the old formula of games back in the day - and like those games, this game isn't very forgiving.
In general, if you're a fan of the AVGN no doubt you'll already have this, but if you're a fan of tough NES-like platformers, get this game. From the obscenely ridiculous references to the appealing art style, this game screams AVGN charm.

Overall F.E.A.R 2 is a solid, fun shooter with a horror undertone; nice to look at, but perhaps doesn't quite have the same magic as the original F.E.A.R.
It has a relatively quick but enjoyable campaign, containing lots of intense fire fights, vehicle and turret sections without holding your hand too much or dragging you through too many cut scenes.
I gave this a quick run through on 'Normal' and found it mostly quite easy due to the frequent placement of armour and medkits. However the enemy AI provide a decent challenge regardless as you can never stay in one place for too long before you are flanked, outnumbered or grenaded.
As far as the horror aspect goes, it doesn't build tension as well its predecessor, which undermines the "jump scares" somewhat, but F.E.A.R 2 is a little less predictable in this respect and does provide a lot of disturbing moments none the less.
I'd also recommend playing the first F.E.A.R and its DLC if you want to follow the plotline as having some context makes it a little better I think.

Well, it's FFV. If you liked old school Final Fantasy games, you will probably like this. It's polished, decently well translated, and moderately difficult, just like the original.
Looks like it has a bit of extra content, though I haven't played far enough to get to it in this version. Not convinced that it adds much to the experience, but Steam cards and achievements are nice if you're into that (I am). There are a few annoying glitches with the ATB menu, but it's not a deal-breaker.
The downsides include the fact that they used a rather half-baked graphics filter to smooth out the pixels, and in fullscreen mode, there is a horrid amount of what looks like screen tearing that could be fixed by using v-sync, which is not an option in the graphics menu.
I didn't like this translation as much as the RPGe one from the late 90s, but it's far, far better than the one from the PSX release of this game. I didn't play the GBA version, so I can't comment on that.
The addition of the Amano concept art to the dialog boxes was a nice touch, even though they look NOTHING at all like the character sprites.
My other complaints with the game were mostly centred around the fact that I forgot how awfully GRINDY this game is (as were most RPGs at the time). Can't really hold that against it though, since it's not a remake, just a rerelease.
Final verdict, if you've already played this on other platforms, you can safely skip it, unless you want to push your nostalgia buttons, otherwise, it does a much better job of that than the butchery that was the FFIV DS port, so recommended. I'd still have preferred a direct port of the original though.

This is one of the worst versions of FFV available.
That said, I will explain exactly why.
I have played through Final Fantasy V twice.  Once on the ps1, once on the GBA.  This Steam port is a port of a port.  The GBA version was the original (not counting the SNES/PS1 versions) and its contents were ported to IOS devices with major graphical changes.  I would call them enhancements, but I find the quality of the enhancements a little subjective.  I personally like them, but not everybody really does.
From the IOS devices, this port sprang up.  And I must say... you're better off just playing this on an iPhone.
For starters, the graphics are significantly worse on PC.  The PC version does use IOS assets, but the tiles are so clearly visible on the overworld that it just breaks any sort of emersion.  I can see where they weren't able to properly adjust the display output of the IOS, therefore you can see each and every single tile on the screen.
Every problem that people would have with this game would probably apply to the IOS version, too.  The character models on the overworld and battle are pretty terrible looking compared to, say, the character models in the psp games (final fantasy I, II, and IV for psp) and they suffer from extreme stiffness for the kind of animation they were trying to achieve.  However, you can control the steam edition with an Xbox controller or a keyboard (HOWEVER, holding the accept button does not auto-select a command).
This isn't a bad game, it's just a bad port.  The gameplay isn't completely butchered.  It's essentially chocked full of the same content you could get in the GBA version, and the GBA version is probably my personal favorite version of the versions I've played thus far.
If you want to play this version, you're not worse off with the IOS version.  And I'm fairly certain the GBA version isn't that hard to find (I'm saying this because I got my GBA copy for $20 at Half-Priced books).  I would only purchase this version of FFV if you have absolutely no other options.

This is my second attempt to write a review for this game, since the first one ended up being fifteen pages long.  Battleborn is... complicated.  It's a game that tries to do a lot but never quite nails anything perfectly, and trying to explain why requires pages and pages of explanation about interactions between gameplay mechanics.  So, in an attempt to keep it short:
The game gets compared a lot to Overwatch and Dota.  Like Overwatch, the game is a first person shooter, where you play as a quirky, colorful character with unique abilities.  Like Dota, the game has RPG elements, with you starting every map at level 1 and having to level up and buy equipment and stuff until the end of the game, when everything resets.
There's a lot of pushback for comparing this game to Overwatch, because Overwatch is laser focused on it's payload and control point maps, polishing that type of gameplay to a mirror shine, while Battleborn is... not that.  A lot of reviews say that the game is basically FPS Dota, with lanes and minions and towers and so on, but that describes just one mode out of three PvP modes (the other two being a control point mode and an "escort the minions" mode like Arena in Smite) and also ignores the PvE Story mode.  Which is why I think it makes sense to compare the game to Overwatch: the main difference, to me, is that Overwatch is super focused on it's one, very specific gametype and Battleborn is extremely unfocused.  If you pick up Overwatch and said "man, I wish I could just play through a single player campaign as one of these characters" or something then Overwatch will not give you that, while Battleborn will... but the tradeoff is that everything in Battleborn is way less polished and ends up kind of a mess.
This is where my last review ended up dragging on for page after page because Battleborn does a lot of stuff and almost none of it is really executed smoothly.  The movement mechanics are awkward and clunky, hit detection is inconsistent, body blocking is a constant nuisance.  The item system is a convoluted mess, the UI is kludgy and tedious to navigate and was obviously designed with consoles in mind, graphical optimization is terrible for certain setups and produces single digit framerates even on systems that can run more impressive games with no problems.  Map design is a cluttered mess, littered with ankle-high platforms that you need to jump over or chest high obstacles where you're not sure if you can jump over it or juuuuust barely not.  You can play the game single player, but you still need a constant internet connection or you get instantly kicked out of the game, and the bots tend to glitch out and spend the entire map with their face mashed against a wall or wandering pointlessly around an empty area near the base. There's not a single element of the game that you can point to and say "this ruins EVERYTHING" but at the same time, everything is just a little poorly put together, feels a little unpolished, doesn't work quite the way it should...
It's hard to give this one a thumbs up or thumbs down.  If you want a solid FPS, Overwatch has much smoother gameplay and a more lively community and is cheaper.  If you want a really competitive MOBA, then Dota or League of Legends are probably going to give you a more satisfying experience than this game, and are also cheaper.  But there's a lot this game does that Dota doesn't, that Overwatch doesn't, and if you're in the mood for the weird cocktail that Battleborn serves, then it's the only game in town.  If you're not sure, it's price tag is a bit high at full price, but if it gets discounted (and looking at the player count, I suspect it will fairly often) then you might want to take a chance and check it out.

Tiny Brains is a cooperative puzzle game with a kid friendly aesthetic.
You control and swap between 4 different mice with different powers: 1) sucks up inaniminate objects, 2) blow inaniminate objects, 3) swabs inaniminate objects, and 4) creates ice blocks that help you reach up vertically through levels. You'll enter different puzzle rooms which are all variations of hit this button, or put this box on this switch etc. 2 other level variations involve pushing and pulling a ball with your powers through a Marble Madness like arena, and the last is a Horde Mode mini-game where you defend an objective against... umm.... chickens. Of these the puzzles are the most satisfying, with the other 2 being boring to frustrated. "Dying" in levels is very lightly penalized with a 5 second respawn. Dying actually becomes a strategy for completing some levels even, not a mechanic I particularly find satisfying.
Tiny Brains biggest issue is it simply runs out of ideas. You'll solve puzzles that are just minor variations of each other. Maneuvering the big sphere quickly becomes a chore as does the Defense missions.
Graphically the game looks good enough. Polygon counts are low but the bright colors and well lit environments are nice to wander around. Its reasonably well voice acted but it tries way too hard to be funny.
The puzzles make this game too hard for kids, and everything else is too similar for adults.

I've owned and played all of the Hitman franchise, both on consoles and on the PC (non-steam), and I've thoroughly enjoyed each one. I think my favorite games in the franchise are Silent Assassin and Contracts, however, each game is a wonderful experience and should be given at least one playthrough if you have the chance.
If you like stealth-oriented (or guns-blazing) gameplay, being a dangerous assassin, and open-ended, challenging missions, then you will really, really enjoy this game. The Hitman franchise has consistently been able to provide the experience of being a world-renown and package it into a fun, fresh, and user-friendly game for all types of gamers to enjoy.
The aesthetics are fantastic - the detail in the environments and character models are very well-done. The music and sounds in the franchise have always been solid, and the score used in Blood Money adds a sense of grandiosity and elegance to the gameplay. The story has always been interesting, and this installation chronicles the FBI's hunt for Agent 47. The "ending" is quite satisfying, and offers a great segue into the next game.
The controls are not too difficult to familiarize yourself with, and the tutorial mission is both fun and very helpful - it feels less like a hold-your-hand mission compared to other games that may restrict your actions initially. The learning curve is minimal to moderate, further influenced by the difficulty you select (no notoriety on Rookie) and playstyle you use (stealth vs. bloodshed).
Before you begin your missions, you will be able to select which weapons to take with you, as well as upgrade each primary weapon you own - more options are unlocked as you progress. The money you accumulate is based on your rating upon completing your missions (generally, more stealtheir approaches lead to higher rewards).
Your performance rating is provided in the form of a newspaper article, with the headline "Silent Assassin" if you achieve a perfect playthrough. I really liked this feature, as it will comment on your most used weapon, firearm accuracy (ex: the 4 headshots and unwasted bullets suggest a deadly professional), number of witnesses and casualties, and how the targets were killed. Each mission has a mechanic available to make each target die in what appears to be an accident (ex: a pallet of crates falling on top of someone), allowing you to achieve full stealth.
Notoriety is affected by your performance, and the more attention you draw to yourself, the higher your notoriety gain. As it climbs, NPCs will react faster to your presence and may even call for help from guards. You can pay a fee to reduce your notoriety, and obtaining the CCTV tapes (if you are spotted on camera) will eliminate that hit to your notoriety.
My favorite mission involved
You can challenge yourself in many ways - try doing a mission without switching into a disguise, being seen (causing an alert), killing, using weapons, etc. I beat Blood Money on the hardest difficulty on my 3rd playthrough (full stealth), and I encourage everyone to NOT try the game on Rookie (the notoriety feature adds a lot of intensity and fun). For my first playthrough, I did full stealth and normal. For my second, I tried a Rambo-style method - both provided me with a satisfying, badass assassin feel. Watching NPCs running away in fear while helpless guards fall to your expertly-placed shots can be just as fulfilling as entering a restricted area without anyone knowing.
Overall, the game is very enjoyable if you are the least bit interested in assassinations (stealth or non-stealth), and everyone should definitely give this game a try.
Highly recommend!
Cheers,
DJSF

I really wanted to like this game...
Roguelight? Check
Nice visual style? Check
Interesting theme? Check
Sounds promising right? Unfortunately I feel like Renowned Explorers is a case of almost but not quite, all of the elements of a great roguelike are here but it falls short in a number of different areas that ultimately resulted in the game leaving a sour taste in my mouth.
I think my biggest issue with the game is the severe lack of content available to play with at the moment, in one playthrough you can visit the vast majority of explorable areas in one playthrough. The areas themselves are basically the same each playthrough except for a few minor RNG differnces. Seeing as one playthrough lasts for at most just under three hours there really isn't a lot to keep you coming back for more.
If the game was in early access or in open beta this might be excusable but with only one new piece of DLC available since it's "full release" I could never reccomened this game at full price and would do so cautiously when it is on sale.
My second issue with the game is that I feel it's a little to RNG heavy. I like a little randomness in my games as the next person but this game turns it up to eleven... the vast majority of your overworld interactions are going to be decided on the roll of a dice, and even the combat has fixed %chance to hit for some abilities. It's incredibly frustating to be completing the final expedition only for a 5% dice role to take away two resolve (basically life in this game) and end your playthrough.
Renowned explorers does have a few interesting and well executed ideas though, for one thing whenever you click on a decision on the map with a percentage chance instead of just resolving, it brings up a spinner wheel. The simple addition of this spinner wheel adds a lot of tension into what is usually quite a mundane part of rougelikes. Another thing I thought was relatively well executed was the emotion combat system, which basically gave stat buffs or debuffs depending on how you chose to handle the encounter wether it be peacefully, deviously or agressively. This had it's own problems however, as to min-max in this game you basically have to optimise your encounters to one particular mood to get consistent benefits.
I enjoyed my first couple of playthroughs of this game, but after I started to understand the game more and progress I became increasingly frustrated with the amount of luck compared to skill especially for someone not amasingly skilled at roguelikes. Overall I guess that's my overall opinion of this game, if you like the theme of this game and are really good at roguelikes and don't mind heavy RNG elements, great. For everyone else, go back to FTL or Dungeons of Dreadmore.

A fun rogue-like in which you create a party composition of characters to find ancient treasures. I particularly enjoyed this game because you could choose to seek out skill based events instead of just pure combat, with success percentages changing depending on your party's explorers were skilled in.
Game play takes place on a board where you can move to different nodes that have possible events listed on them. You can choose nodes with skill based story events or go for combat nodes, which revolves around a novel rock-paper-scissors type of attacking.
While the combat was interesting, I found clearing the events to be much more fun, as the well-written events all calculated your success by formulating the characters physical stats as well as their skills, such as diplomacy, engineering, archaelogy, etc. The game then animates a spinner that makes you hold your breath as it makes that one last tick between success or failure.
The setting is incredibly novel and charming as you explore the world as a turn of the century exploring league searching unkown and wild lands for rare artifacts.
The replayability is very high; each playthrough doesn't take that much time, and the urge to replay again with a better more effecient setup or completely different exploring party is very strong.
Still learning the mechanics but I am already enjoying it.

Not a proper review, but I just had a few thoughts.
MGS V is a colossal letdown, but I will likely finish it because I want to experience the story beats for myself.  I'm only doing this because I loved MGS 1-3 growing up.  Here are some things I really dislike about the game.
• The open world is very bland and uninteresting, has next to no features besides the enemy emplacements - and the only thing you have to do besides the missions is hunt and capture animals or pick flowers.  The Witcher 3 (which has major problems for sure) pulled off general exploration much better, and the progression felt good because once you captured something it stayed captured and you felt like you were making meaningful progress.  This game just feels like Far Cry 2 because everything always respawns.  It makes the exploration feel gamey and takes the satisfaction out of taking over something since it will just have enemies the next time you come back.
• The helicopter travel time around the Mother Base is unnecessarily slow, going from strut to strut takes like 30-40 seconds not including the pickup and landing, and driving between strut takes about as long (it's really far).  The box transfer system is faster but wasn't made clear at the outset.  It seems odd to place a convenient time saver behind a semi-obscure easter egg mechanic, especially if you consider some people might be coming to your game for the first time due to it being the first game that's had a wider release.
• The building and managing of Mother Base is a neat idea in concept, another persistence mechanic in a single player can always be fun and interesting if there's a reason to do it and it's rewarding.  It's just a shame that it never feels like it matters that much.  Selecting the option to auto sort is usually good enough unless you stocked up a bunch of guys with bad ratings early on, and what you do in the base really doesn't effect how the missions play whatsoever.
• If you're not extremely meticulous and don't want to spend several hours sussing out each mission's objectives, you will miss a lot of side objectives that have rewards that are tied in to each mission.  This makes you have to go back to SAME areas and take out the guards again and explore an area that's still unchanged, just to finish an objective or find a blueprint - most of which are not important at all or don't change how the game is played.  It seems like there are too many options when any of said options will do the job you want them to just fine.
• The PC controls have some issues.  Navigating the menus is done by pressing 1 and 3 for left and right, and W and S for up and down.  You can also use the arrow keys.  There is also a delay on inputs in some contexts, where it takes a second for the game to register your menu input (this includes skipping a cutscene you might have seen before).  To interrogate someone or use the radial menu while subduing a guy you have to hold Q and press 3 and 4, or 4 and 5 as options open up later in the game.  Holding a guy while shooting someone else requires you to hold mouse 1, but clicking mouse 1 to shoot someone while holding another guy makes you release the button and let go of the guy you're holding, which leads to a lot of situations of just having to re-subdue the guy you lost control of.  In some situations this has led to my reflex action triggering and this of course subtracts points from the mission score.  It's worth nothing that you can turn the reflex mode off if you want to.
•  The game also has long loads (sometimes 2 to 3 seconds) in between menu selection screens on the iDroid.  Even on an SSD this gets old fast, and it makes me want to not use the menu if I can help it.  The loads are even longer if you have any problems staying connected or connecting to their servers for the online functionality.  Several times I have timed out while trying to upgrade a base feature or weapon.  The loading symbol will just spin for 10-15 seconds then you will get an error message.
• Suppresors have a limited use, allowing only a select number of bullets fired from them before they are rendered obsolete.  You can get an upgrade later which makes a supressor for a given gun be unlimited use, but it takes a while.  Like 10 shots at ranks 2 and 3 and your supressor's toast.  This game takes place in 1984.  Not every gun is a freaking Welrod, Kojima!  I realize supressors ("silencers") don't make guns silent and in fact most guns are still incredibly loud even with supressors, but this is a METAL GEAR SOLID game, and as long as you DO have a supressor the guards don't have a clue.  You will often shoot way too many bullets trying to perform a headshot, which makes your supressor degrade faster than it would if you were just shooting a single bullet. The fact that there isn't an option to change fire modes is insane.
• D-Horse often gets stuck on tiny objects and loses all momentum - this frequently happens around enemy compounds causing you to lose all speed and become an easy target for getting knocked off the horse.
• The camera changes when you get on the horse a lot and this makes the first couple seconds of controlling it impossible because even if you try to turn the horse based on where you think you are the cinematic camera just prevents you from doing it consistently.  This is super annoying.
• Most of the time I'm playing this game I just keep thinking that none of the small things matter at all.  Nothing feels meaningful.  It all feels shallow, as if they couldn't think of anything interesting to do with the environments so they just added some stuff on top of just doing the missions, extra objectives and things/people to capture.  It feels very lazy.
• Helicopter travel time at the beginning and at the end of missions is also lengthy.  I really don't need a 30 second cutscene before each mission (including dropping in to freely roam around for a side operation or something) showing Snake's face and then a pan into his point of view, then him opening the helicopter door and waiting to land.  IT'S COOL THE FIRST FEW TIMES BUT TAKES TOO LONG AND GETS OLD FAST - JUST FADE TO BLACK, LOAD, AND FADE FROM BLACK AND LET ME PLAY THE GAME.
• Snake is a mute.  He barely says a word.  Idk how the development process went, but you hire Keifer for your character, and he barely even speaks, even in the cutscenes?  He speaks more in the tape recordings than in the cutscenes or when interacting with people in the world.  Also, for someone who's the boss and progenitor of building the Mother Base back up, Snake really hasn't done any work fresh out of the hospital, and he barely even comments on anything.
In short, none of the extra stuff matters or feels satisfying to spend time with.  If you care about the Metal Gear series, just play the story missions as fast as possible - that's what I decided to do.

If you haven’t played Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes then do that first before starting Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain. If you have then strap yourself in for a fun, roller-coaster ride of betrayal, intrigue and murder as you slither and sneak your way across Afghanistan, Africa and your Diamond dogs base in order to enact revenge on those who destroyed your MSF base and killed all who were stationed on it.
This game is a masterpiece- the story twists and turns at every angle, and there are so many references to the Phantom Pain suffered by all major characters (not just the loss of your arm before being fitted with a replacement). Those who are new to the series might be confused as to who everyone is and about some of the previous events as they are mentioned regularly, but there is enough information provided (either through direct cut scenes or collectables) that by the middle to end of the game you can figure out majority of what is happening, only for the rug to be pulled out from underneath your feet right at the end.
The game is controlled as a open world 3rd person shooter, but vastly rewards players for not killing (killing will lower your overall mission rank). The 3rd person viewpoint is critical as it allows you to see a wider range, so you can spot anything that might detect you and give you away. It’s mostly open world, with missions limiting you to parts of the overall map, but giving you the freedom to tackle the mission how you want. I thought this was a great setup, and when the mission is done you can usually continue on your way with the open world exploration- there is lots to see, do and collect. You can use support characters that you gain throughout the game to support you in each mission, from Quiet, the mute female sniper to D.D. an orphaned wolf puppy that you find and raise. Each comes with their own equipment and abilities, and their usefulness will vary depending on mission. If you don’t look after them in mission then you have to wait for them to heal, so you can’t just send them in and expect them to do all the work. If you feel like a challenge you can do missions as someone other than Snake, each character has a full bio of abilities and stats. You can request supply drops and extra equipment as needed though it will cost you either money, materials or vehicles. The missions themselves are great, and many aren’t unlocked until others are complete, some just seeming to be there as filler, but others advancing side stories in conjunction of the main story as all the plot pieces slowly fall into place.
The graphics and attention to detail are amazing, you can see the rain roll down Snakes armor, when you do kill an enemy if you pick them up (to hide the body) Snake gets covered in blood. If you don’t shower when returning to base the soldiers stationed there will comment on your appearance and stench. Your actions in game also influence your appearance- if you continuously murder enemies or commit immoral actions (building a nuke) then you will gain a darker appearance, blood will always be on your armor and the shrapnel in your head will look like a large horn. If you perform good actions, such as rescuing hostages, stunning enemies (or destroying nukes) then this effect is reversed.
The music soundtrack is amazing as well, you pick up cassettes throughout the game and play them in your Walkman. You will likely need to stop listening to it quite regularly as you need to listen to mission briefs and updates that happen throughout the game, but that’s not an issue, and the voice work for all the characters is amazing.
The characterization and growth of characters displayed is amazing, from watching Snake try and fumble his way out of the hospital in the first mission, to replaying it at the end but with all the knowledge you have learned and seeing all the details that were initially missed is an eye opener. Watching Snake cope with the signs of PSTD when discovering mementoes of Paz, and dealing with Huey to finding out Quiets history all add character development and keeps on reinforcing the idea of Phantom Pain. The base building concept is great, making you want to go out of your way to collect base materials and collect soldiers with good stats. There is a point in the middle of the game where this concept is turned on its head (I thought it was an evil trick and I didn’t see it coming but well played) that again really drives home the concept of Phantom Pain.
The multiplayer component comes in the form of raiding other players bases for resources, staff and nukes. This adds an interesting dimension to the game, as you need all of the above items (except nukes) to upgrade your base and equipment, but if you stockpile it too long others can take it. If you don’t have the hero status, you can’t assault a base that has a nuke, but having a nuke makes you a very large target (and ruins your appearance).
If you are aiming for 100% achievements then it’s possible, but you will have to sink a lot of hours into the game, as there are a lot of side missions and collectables. I would recommend doing it, or at least finishing all the side missions as a fair chuck of the games plot isn’t explained until you do (Quiets disappearance)
There is a lot of DLC, but none of it is needed unless you like extra costumes for your characters to dress in, many which are references to previous games.

F.E.A.R. 2 improves on many things that were bothersome in the first game, but also changed things that didn't necessarily need to be changed from the first game. The combat is vastly improved and more fun than ever, but the horror element are not as effective as it was originally. The graphics have been buffed up significantly since the series debut, with better lighting effects, a deeper color palette, and some cool ghostly visual effects. However, the new engine the game uses seems to strongly favor a console design which is apparant through the enlarged UI, unnecessary quick-time events, and other additions to the gameplay design.
So let's get right into it, what makes FEAR 2's gameplay so different? For one, level design has been changed dramatically. In the original FEAR, levels were sporadic hallways that twisted around in an endless maze of confusing warehouse and office building design. Thankfully, FEAR 2 has more believable environments with larger outdoor areas that feature plenty of cover to play with the weapons you want. The game allows you to carry an additional weapon, now maxing out at 4 but reduces the amount of healthkits you are allowed to carry from 10 down to a measly 3. This never really bothered me though, I played straight through the game and probably died only once on the normal difficulty setting. Enemies are very easy to overcome thanks to the ability to slow down time whenever the situation gets out of hand. Unlike the original, enemies take a lot less damage to kill and all of the weapons feel effective including the SMG. The melee in this game is still terrible. I used it in a few situations, but never did it down an enemy in one hit, so I felt as though i had wasted time meleeing when I could have just been reloading one of my guns. The game offers quite a few large weapons like a rocket launcher, sniper rifle, laser gun, and even some experimental blue shock gun. But I never felt as though any of them were really necessary. The game offers these huge weapons but never really presents an enemy that they felt effective against other than the one or two big mechs you have to take down. There's also a few levels that give you access to your very own mech which is fun to use. You can mow down countless enemies with powerful miniguns and launch a load of rockets at heavily armered mechs whilst using a cool thermal vision. The horror element that the game's title would imply just doesn't seem to be there anymore. ALMA no longer appears as a little girl in creepy places, and instead the big jump scares in the game are just the teenage naked ALMA running at you and forcing you into another repetitive quicktime event. I kept waiting for a big scare but it just never happened.
The story picks up close to the end of the first game, right when the nuke goes off. You take the roll of a new silent protagonist who also happens to have the ability to slow down time and shoot people, which makes absolutely no sense because now you're not even remotely related to ALMA in any way. The game has some more interesting characters than the first game, but not interesting enough for me to even remember their names. They feel more like disposable puppets used to shock you whenever ALMA shows up and decides to kill them, and never did I feel emotional towards any of their inevitable deaths, despite the music and other character reactions implying that I should. Unfortunetly, FEAR 2 removes the cool answering machine background storylines that helped give more life to the world and instead replaces them with boring PDA text files that you are told to find in every level. I liked the answering machines more because they didn't interupt the gameplay itself and allowed me to listen while I was looking for the next exit. So overall the story, just like the game itself, does some things better but then does some things worse.
The graphics have taken an inevitable leap forward, with an engine that really gives me that "Unreal 3" vibe. Especially when you shoot enemies and they turn into ridiculous bloody red mists and yell out similarly to the "Boomers" in the "Gears of War" franchise. While the game as a whole has more interesting colors, especially in the Elementary School level, the game as a whole felt like a blur of red, gray, and a slightly darker gray. The UI is enlarged to rediculous proportions (most likely to make it more readable for console users) and large prompts appear on screen whenever you approach an object to interact with like a door. Everything about the game itself implied that it was a console port, but thankfully the game has aged well and performance is without any faults throughout the entire game.
So to summarize, the gameplay is more action oriented and more fun than ever, but the horror element behind the game suffers deeply because of this. The storyline is pretty uneventful, save for the ending that cliffhangs into the sequel, but it's easier to follow and more interesting than it was in the first game. The graphics are better, but there are many indications that this game is simply a console port and considering it came out in 2009, it could have looked a lot better had it not been held back. Definitely recommend giving the game a try as it was a fun simple shooter, but it certainly isn't the masterpiece that I've been told it is.

To start: I used to add a longer header describing my reviewing ethos, but it made some reviews too long to submit, so I've left it on my Backloggery page.
Gameplay: Odds are that if you're looking at this game, you've played the Amnesia games. They're pretty much one and the same, these series. In fact, there's such a high probability that you've played Amesia or at least seen Amnesia that I'm not going to bother going into too much depth as far as the gameplay goes. Instead, I'll just keep things shorter and compare and contrast the two. For starters, both games have an emphasis on hiding from enemies, since combat is kinda spotty at best. However, that's by design, so there's not much point whinging about that. Unlike Amnesia, you don't have to worry about sanity. The screen just goes all wibbly whenever you look at the enemy. All in all, there's three things you've gotta worry about: puppies, carnivorous spiders, and the worm. The puppies will patrol the area, but you can distract them with bits of beef jerky... sometimes. It doesn't work all the time, though; even if you've got a whole pile of jerky in front of the dog. The other two you just run away from.
Puzzles are, again, very akin to Amnesia. There were a few puzzles that were kinda annoying or suffered from 90's Adventure Syndrome, but they're generally pretty alright. You can brute force a few puzzles; a favorite solution to one where you have to knock down a ladder is to build a tower of barrels. Yes, that works. I'm still surprised that it works. There wasn't really anything that blew me away as far as clever puzzle design, though. It's just pretty run of the mill puzzle design.
As far as the atmosphere goes, Amesia wins by a LONG shot. There really weren't any gripping moments for me in this game. It's not bad, and to someone who's more susceptible to horror than I am, it might be quite a thrill. However, the game didn't grab me in the same way that Amnesia did. Then again, this is the first episode of the Penumbra series; maybe Black Plague can step it up a few notches. 6/10.
Story: It's a pretty typical supernatural-based story. I can tell a lot of the questions the game brought up (that I didn't find myself asking, actually; the game kinda shoved the questions down my throat) are gonna be answered in later installments, but for just the first game, I didn't find myself really caring all that much. Red should have been a lot creepier of a character, but he was more of an annoyance than anything else. At the end, I didn't feel pity; I just felt relief that I wouldn't have to hear his stereotypical rambling. Also, just because your game is episodic, that doesn't mean that you've gotta have a cliffhanger. It only works if you're really invested in the series. Otherwise, it just seems silly. Oh well; at least they got better at writing by Amnesia. 5/10.
Graphics: I'm quite impressed that they were able to do this much in only a ~300MB download. All of the textures look pretty good, the worlds are pretty well made, and everything just looks pretty good. Too bad that the mine environment didn't allow for much on the art style front. Enemies aren't really too interesting art design-wise, either. Certainly nothing as discomforting as Mr. No-Jaw-McGee. It does get kinda boring looking at mine section after mine section after mine section, but I guess that couldn't be helped. The game will run at 1080p easily, and I'd imagine that if you have any graphics card whatsoever, you should be able to run this game without any problems. For a fair bit of technical finesse from an indie team with an unfortunately lacking art direction, I'll give it a 3/5.
Sound: Frictional has always been pretty good at sound design. While this isn't their best example of sound design capabilities, it is still a good show. It does get a bit silly and overdone at times, but for the most part, it does a pretty good job at setting the atmosphere. As far as the voice actor (singular; Red is pretty much the only one), it wasn't bad. It's only bad  that his dialogue made me get rather tired of him fast. As far as the music, there really isn't much. It does set the mood, though, so I guess there's that. 4/5.
Overall scores are: 6/5/3/4; cumulative score of 5.7/10. Overall a pretty middling surivival horror game. Hopefully Black Plague picks up the pace.

Story
Reading like a cross between Moby♥♥♥♥♥♥by Herman Melville and The Island of Dr Moreau by H.G. Wells, you are one of the best hunters in the galaxy and in competition against others, you must find and hunt down the elusive White Whale or die trying.
Gameplay
I recommend to hit the tutorial first as this will guide you through your movement, fire and other quest keys. Also to get you use to the slightly weird use of WASD. Weird only because I am not use to it, but over time you can master it. W is to go up, S is to go down, A is to go left and D is to go right. Those using a control pad will be use to this. LMB is throw spear, RMB is power up throw (very handy) a second click of RMB will rip limbs off if powered throw is a success. Shift is power boost to your ship, if you need to do a quick get away or to ram some terrain out of your way.
You start of with the Old Man, who looks more like Neptune from The Little Mermaid, only more bad♥♥♥♥♥space marine style and a crude spear (you get to unlock three more Hunters and a boatload of WTF spears later).
You meet at the main Saloon and listen (read) to some banter from your competitors, some of it can scroll through a bit too fast, so brush up on your speed reading. Then you from a space map you pick which Monster bounty you wish to go hunt for. These will have a lvl of difficulty and bounty listed with them but don’t be fooled, even lvl 1 monsters will kick your butt, hard! Select then hit the road..um space.
You fly around the area, keeping a close eye on your radar in the bottom left corner, if a red ping shows then you have a monster near by.  The map is filled with space flora (shrooms) that can cause psychedelic hallucinations, so avoid at all costs. Also minor monsters that can pack a punch or swarm you to death.
All kills will earn you money and points so hunt away, but you need pick you opportunity as most monsters have some form of hardshell armour and your spears will just bounce off, aim for the soft fleshy parts. You can power up the throw by holding the RMB, let loose and land a hit, RMB click again and you can start to dismember your prey, piece by piece (Calamari anyone!).
Some of your prey will drop coins and even keys if your lucky. Take a key and scan for a hidden chest, to claim loot. Most loot is power-ups for your spear or ship or both. Above all do not die as this is a permadeath game and there is no health boosts or aids unless in a chest. Once you have killed you bounty you return to the Saloon and rinse and repeat.
Everything else
Main menu and options are well thrashed out giving you options on graphics and sound as well as key binding and feedback vibration (for those who play with their controller between legs, you sickos!)
Graphics are cartoonish Southpark style, are crisp and clean and work very well here. Back ground music is subtle and upbeat and is not annoying so leave it on. Movement is crisp and very responsive, sometimes a little too responsive but at the same time it will save your butt a tonne load.
My only small grips with this game is that a) monsters can hide behind the space debris from you as you need to either blow it out of the way or go around, but you can hide behind it because monsters just glide through it as if it’s not there.
b) It has a very steep (not steep, it’s a bloody sheer cliff) learning curve that even low level monsters eat you up for breakfast, lunch and tea!
c) Story is bare exists but maybe a bit more tweaking it could beef up the game a bit more.
Outside of these, Blacksea Odyssey by Blacksea Odyssey (still no resemblance) is a fun action shooter/Harpooner that needs to be in your library.

ROGUE-LIKE!! If any of you read my Eldritch review, you must already know I have a soft spot in my cold, dark heart for rogue-likes. It all started with the original Binding of Isaac, there Is something about the randomness of the items and your progression that appeals to me, and this game does that rather well, there is room for improvement, but at it's current state, it's really fun.
Many years in the future, The Galaxy holds a sacred tournament that happens once a decade, The Blacksea odyssey, in which every hunter must prove their worth by hunting down and killing the most ferocious creatures that exist in the known universe, in which the winner, aside from insurmountable riches, gets a chance to battle the legendary Titan of the Stars.
Well, the story is a bit lackluster, but it does add something to one of the characters, in which there are 4, all really well designed and colourful, and the one you start with is The Old Man, who is one of the oldest humans to still roam the galaxy, and he is in search of revenge from the Titan, who took his arm in his youth, and he is poised to do whatever is necessary to defeat the blasted space whale.
Does it sound familiar? It's because it is, The Old Man is basically Captain Ahab, from Moby Dyck, and the Titan is the whale himself.
The game is a top-down rogue-like, with Nuclear Throne like controls, in this game you've got two active item slots, a boost system, and spear and a harpoon, and an amazing combat mechanic, you can weaken the monster's limbs, and after they've been weakened enough, you can harpoon them and rip them off, which limits the monster's attacks and mobility, that is such a cool mechanic, and it works so well, it is amazing to rip off the bosses's arms and spiked tails, sooo satisfying. You can also improve your spears and your ship with runes, changing your playstyle a bit, and at the start of each game you can also pick one of the 4 characters and one spear, each of them with their own playstyle as well.
Also, every part of the map's terrain is breakable, you can use your active bomb items to blow them up, or just boost trough them, this prevents the enemies to pin you at walls and just murder you, which still happens at times.
There is one peeve I had with this game, some things clearly need rebalancing, your boost clearly needs to last longer, it's barely a boost as it is right now, you've got to use it to dodge the boss's attacks, but then it enters an ungodly cooldown. Also Megalodon is just absurd, it turns way too fast, Jackdaw needs to have a weak spot in his mouth, not just block everything. And the frogs at the early levels are really annoying when you still have no runes to boost damage.
The graphics are OK, there is a bit of room for improvement, but I like the game's style, the designs being what I love the most, every enemy has a really cool design which complements their fighting style. Some of the bosses are MASSIVE, like REALLY HUGE, they easily dwarf your view range, and I like that Shadow of The Colossus type of huge bosses.
The music is also kind of catchy, but I am one to prefer podcasts and other types of music while playing video games.
Overall, this game has the potential to be great, and as is, it's really fun, and the developers literally updated the game on the 18th, so it still has their support. I recommend it, you're sure to have several hours of fun with this.
Just remember to disable the screen shaking under the options, it's really headache inducing.

This dull exercise in frustration is arguably the last "classic" Final Fantasy.   Seemingly, however, Squaresoft did us a favor by not localizing this game when it originally released on the SNES.   Frequently tedious random encounters sap your desire to explore and boss difficulty curves that ramp up excessively force you to reload and double back in order to grind on the same monsters you already didn't want to deal with for 40-60 minute intervals in order to progress.   The game's claim to fame is a more robust class system than it's predecessor, Final Fantasy III, and while the mechanics of this system are certainly enjoyable to play around with, it also forces you to track yet another thing you need to spend a great deal of time grinding on.   What really irritates me about Final Fantasy V is not that it is difficult.   Like a typical 90s jRPG, there is nothing in FFV that cannot be handled with copious amounts of leveling.  The real frustration comes in the fact that you can't simply sit back and enjoy the story.   As worlds go, FFV's is pretty interesting with a multi-world mechanic and a pretty memorable core cast of characters.   This update's inclusion of original Amano artwork as character portraits only makes the story more enjoyable to experience.   Unfortunately those few minutes of story are punctuated by frustrating gameplay that seems to have attracted little interest in balancing from the original dev team.   Serious Final Fantasy fans will want to play this game but for the casual fan there are far better entries in this venerable series to sink your teeth into.

Strictly from a gameplay perspective, Final Fantasy V is easily my favorite in the series. With a job system that is more in-depth than any other game in the series, this game offers more in the way of customizability than any Final Fantasy title to date. The music, as with any Final Fantasy title, is just plain awesome, with the recurring motif "Battle on the Big Bridge" making its debut here alongside series fan-favorite character Gilgamesh.
The downside to all of this is that the PC version of the game is little more than a port of the mobile version of FFV. While this by no means makes it a bad game, the graphics and player UI suffer a bit as a result. If you're a fan of hardcore RPGs, however, this game will still offer you a challenging and engaging experience.

I actually really enjoyed the personality of this game. The colors, the art, the music, the characters, it all comes together really well. The game is well made and I enjoyed just about every moment I had with it.
The pacing to how the mechanics are tolled out is polished, but I do have to say that I wish they allowed things to simmer more. Every time I got comfortable with a new mechanic they were introducing another one with its own little challenge room. I would have appreciated a bit more time with each. The game is challenging at times, and gives some room for exploration. The level design is focused and cohesive, while still allowing for a good amount of exploration. The movement and the combat is one and the same and it leads to skills developed platforming translating right into the combat in a satisfying way.
The story told is a fun twist on a simple story. The world is detailed enough to give context and motivation.
All in all I finished the story in 4 hours and don’t really feel any motivation to go back and find hidden items. I might spend some time in secondary combat stuff later, but if your looking for a really polished experience that won’t overstay it’s welcome I’d happily recommend Guacamelee.

The best Hitman game. Ever. While it did change some gameplay aspects from the earlier games and doesn't look amazing like the latest, it's still the greatest. Why? I'll tell you why.
-It's got a pretty good story, for starters. I mean, it's not as deep as the story in let's say Hitman: Contracts, but it really does  make the player ask questions for most of the game. "Who is this ex-CIA guy in the wheelchair?" and  "Why is he so interested in 47?", and so then the story adds up to that near the end.
-The gameplay is possibly the greatest designed out of all the Hitman games. Definitely takes a hold of the open world and each character plays a moving part in a large level. As the assassin, you have to learn and observe every of these moving parts before you can make your own move and make sure you don't screw everything up. You always have to come prepared for the next mission, and it always feels so much more rewarding when you accomplish Silent Assassin rating on a level (and then shows a newspaper headline starring the mysterious person known as you!).
-I can't say much for the visuals (the game is several years old, so I'm not complaining) but they don't really matter in a game as amazing as this.
-The musical score has to be the most amazing thing to ever exist. I mean, seriously, Jesper Kyd is one of the video game music gods among Kelly Bailey and Michael McCann. He knows how to capture each moment in the game with a perfect musical tone settling it. My favorite track from the game has to be Apocalypse
after you eliminate a target perfectly and that evil grin appears on your face.
Overall, I could say it's a 9.5/10 (I wish it was longer though, at least another mission or two!)

I just want to preface my review with the fact that I genuinely love this game. This game is not the most complex, but its fun. This game takes a genre I love (pulp adventure and exploration, like the RPG's Spirit of the Century and Hollow Earth Expedition) and turns it into a short and heavily replayable strategy game for the ages.
Pros: The characters: While this game may not have a Bioware dialogue tree, this game still gives each of the possible party members a unique personality. The moves, the skills, the speech bubbles all give each character a different feel and a different strategy going in.
The comedy: Your rivals are as over the top as Gaston. Your characters get into rediculous situations where you have to going into a conflict because the locals are too friendly, or where you accidentally drop a safe from a treehouse. Even the expressions can be funny.
The Replayablity: Why not try a different location? A different party? A different strategy? Get different treasures this time? There are a lot fo reasons to replay the game.
Cons: Minor gameplay issues: Sometimes movement grids don't show up until you start and cancel an attack. Sometimes targeting can be misjudged by a few pixels (an issue even Shadowrun has). Its unfortunate, but doesn't always ruin the gameplay.
Achievement Hunters: As much as I love the stories that can be told with this game, one of the major calls of this game is the achievements. Complete the game with a certain personality, complete the game with every character as a leader, get a bunch of treasures, do it all on iron man mode. If that's not your thing, you might not get as much enjoyment from this game.

There's no question whether MGS5 is worth MSRP or not, but the faults this game has are critical and frustrating. First the good: the gun play and stealth are incredible and unique. Anyone can play the game for a few hours and feel like they're actually Big Boss himself. This is largely due to the controls- it's like they had a team of mathematicians and physicists making sure every single thing Snake did was immaculate. Speaking of breathtaking: the Fox Engine amazes me every single time I boot the game up. It's gorgeous, it's versatile, and it's incredibly stable. The team that made it needs a medal.
What of the problems? The story is the main offender. Kojima has always been scatterbrained and unrefined (but that hasn't stopped his rabid fans from trying to rationalize the most asinine of mistakes) but this is just unfinished. You play chapter 1 and you think "How could they mess it up from here?" Then you play chapter 2 and you can almost pinpoint the second when Konami pulled the plug on the funding. In retrospect, even the second environment seems smaller and underdeveloped compared to the first.
Next, although the action elements of the gameplay are perfect, the base building sections feel soulless. Mother Base was clearly intended to be less of a plot device and series of menus than it turned out to be. Even the UI feels primitive. Development project trees are somehow confusing in their simplicity. Soldiers are pretty much a spreadsheet management minigame, and the game does expect you to care about them both narratively and mechanically. However, even with these faults, MGS5 isn't a game to skip. You can wait for a sale if you want, but the game is worth it.

In game Cops pretty much arrive in waves the millisecond you start to look at someone the wrong way. Just like Payday 2 there are special enemies in the way of Tasers, cloakers, shields, bulldozers and snipers that spawn in frequently to stop you from getting your pay dirt. However unlike payday 2 the special enemies often act quite differently. For instance Bull dozers move much more faster than they do in payday 2, though they don't have as much health, still if you get shot twice from them it’s more often than not 'man down'. Tasers will often come in pairs and strike instantly. Cloakers have no warning sound that they are close by and most of the time will pounce on you when you’re trying to interact with something or someone. Shields other than the Gl40, there is no other gun which can penetrate their shield. Forget you’re Gl40 and the only answer left is to quickly try and flank them. Snipers in the droves are undoubtedly the worst. Every time I try the level undercover on 145+ I openly weep when I'm informed I have to go to the roof.
The second biggest difference between this and Payday 2 is that ALL the maps are LOUD. None of them are 'True' stealth. Granted 'Diamond Heist' can be done stealthily on the easier levels, but try it on 145+ and it’s all guns blazing again. Sadly the stealth side of things was never properly instituted in this version of payday and so playing as a pacifist would never be a real option most of the time. There are only 9 maps in total with four different difficulty settings with 145+ being the hardest. (This is not including the fact that someone has created a mod which creates a 193+ level for those that love to experience sheer pain).
The developers Overkill have finished with the game and have moved all their focus on Payday 2 even recreating the same levels from this one to there. So most people ask the obvious question, 'Why bother to play PAYDAY the Heist?'
1) For the experience. Since both the skill tree and the special enemies react differently there is a much more rewarding experience in the level of difficulty fighting in comradery with three other team mates against the relentless sheer hell of countless waves in this one than you might experience in Payday 2. Since all capped 193 players have the same instruments at each other’s disposal it’s all about game play and team work. Have one person acting alone and it’s probably game over for the whole team. This game is so much harder, that I’ve actually seen people who have spent 5,000 hrs plus be taken out within seconds by a cloaker or a taser. Having said that the game also offers fewer enemies for those that try each map solo without bots. This has given rise to the gauntlet of challenges from die-hard fans in the fool hardy attempt of showing off their skills as they venture alone. Here is an example of two professionals who have raised to that challenge...
2) The history of the Original secret vault and what gamers had to do to get there is also a rich part of gaming history and to attempt it yourself is a 'must do' for any serious gamer out there . Here is a video explaining it all in detail...
So, basically first you need to do all the heists on 145+ to get the golden mask. Then play the first world bank with three other people each wearing a golden mask standing in your respective positions, next you will have a 2hr constant onslaught of the hardest enemies  while you wait for the drill to get through. Only to be confronted by another room which requires a correct code to be entered into the floor tiles to avoid being gassed to death. Then you will get rewarded with one of the most beautiful vaults you will ever see. Some even claim that sending the video of the above adventure to Overkill will result with you getting a special secret mask.
3) Another challenge I would recommend is doing the last level 'No Mercy' Loud all the way on 145+, without the bag glitch, there are no achievements for this challenge, the reward is simply knowing the fact that you have done the hardest level, on the hardest difficulty, the hardest way.
The Payday Story stops abruptly and hints towards left for dead more than it does Payday 2. It honestly feels that something is missing like a payday 1.5 maybe?
True there are plenty of Trolls, Hackers and Noobs in this game just like there is in Payday 2. True there are only 9 levels to grind away at while trying to reach that coveted 193 level, but it’s the level of difficulty and the constant dedication of the professional players who remain behind throwing out challenges and helping new ones that can make this game a really rewarding experience and a thumbs up.
In final it is a great game to vent off some steam if you ever get a speeding fine, Thanks Overkill. Wish you were still here...
