Decided to come back to this from Payday 2, and this game does not ♥♥♥♥ing dissapoint.  Whereas Payday 2 has more options and an RPG style progression, Payday: The Heist is much more linear in how the game unfolds.  You can unlock all of the skills in the game, there are a small selection of weapons, and at most the "skills" are designed to work around a party of 4.
What this game lacks in choice, it makes up for one of the best heist/action movie simulators you're going to play in a long damn time.  Straight up recreations of scenes from movies, or entire movies themselves.  Rather than throw 20+ different options to complete at a heist at you, you often have one objective to complete at a time, often with dozens of cops throwing themselves at you.
Holed up on a rooftop with SWAT climbing up the sides and jumping from adjacent buildings at you? Check.  Fighting your way down a crowd downtown street, chasing a traitor who stole your cash ala HEAT? Check.  Sneaking into a highrise building to steal a buttload of diamonds while holding various corporate members hostage for negotiation?  Check and check.
The graphics have aged a bit, being a 5 year old game, but they get the job done and it's well optimized.  The music is absolutely amazing, and in many aspects I would count it as better than Payday 2's soundtrack.  Rather than dubstep/DnB tracks, P:TH opts for breakbeat loops with emphasis on bass, giving it a lower key but higher overall intensity feeling to the shootouts.  Rather than spending the entire match in a constant shootout with cops regardless if there's an assault in progress or not, the game gives you downtime inbetween assaults, letting the tension build before dropping you into a balls out assault wave from every direction.  It gets you in the mood and honestly keeps me coming back to the game again and again.  I particularly enjoy the Panic Room Theme, which slowly builds up as you fight your way up the derelict apartment building to the saferoom filled with cash.
At $15 this game is a steal, the WolfPack DLC is unnecessary but does come with some nice skills and weapons, it's your call though since it's 66% the price of the actual vanilla game.

I find it'll be easier and less messy if I just put this as a Pro's and Con's list rather than an essay type review. At least for the most part.
The Pro's:
-The graphics are quite good (player models, environments, etc), even by today's standards.
-Similarly, lighting and shadows are similarly fantastic.
-The voice acting is quite good as well. Notable actors such as Jen Taylor (Halo Series), Phil LaMarr (Halo, Metal Gear Solid Series) and John Patrick Lowrie (Half Life 2, Team Fortress 2) make an appearance in this game.
-While I see that some disagree, I quite liked the story, and thought it elaborated more on Alma and the Armacham Corporation's backstories and helped make me more sympathetic towards Alma.
-I also thought the environments were a bit more varied than the first, although there are still a couple cut and paste corridors now and then.
-The physics and game engine are quite good, and you don't need top of the line specs to run a good looking game like this.

-Several improvements were added (IMO) such as ADS, Sprinting, moveable cover, destructable environments (kind of), and more.
-Sound effects (except for a couple weapons) and overall audio are top notch, easily some of the best I've heard in a game.
-The sense of tension from the first game is still there, albeit toned down a little bit.
-The Elementary School level 'nuff said.
-Also unlike some, I enjoyed the ending, even if it was a bit WTF? at first.
-There's also an awesome
, even if it is a little out of place in a "Horror" game.
-There's a lot more, but those are the major things.
The Con's:
-The game isn't as scary as the first, while I wouldn't call any of the F.E.A.R.'s genuinely horrifying (I'm pretty hard to scare however, not true for some people) the game often made noises, or flickered my HUD and either did nothing with it, or focused the scare somewhere where the player's attention wasn't designed to be focused.
-Some of the gun's lacked the "Oomph" they had in the first game, particulary the Shotgun and the Sniper Rifle (The latter wasn't in the first game). I quite enjoyed the feel of the shotgun in the first F.E.A.R, the one in F.E.A.R. 2 though feels and sounds particularly lackluster. Grenades also lack that "Bam, Pow!" sound when they explode, even if the explosion looks cool.
-The game is easier than the first one, which is caused by several things. On Moderate difficulty (a.k.a Normal) I often found myself just walking out and shooting enemies using Slow-Mo without even touching any sort of cover, something that you couldn't get away with nearly as much in the first game. Slow-Mo also lasts longer than the first game, at some points later in the game (after collecting reflex boosters) I could finish entire firefights in one use of Slow-Mo. I also didn't die very much, something I can't say from the last game either. Also, enemies aren't quite the bullet sponges they were in the first game (not a bad thing IMO), but this makes for firefights being a LOT easier, even with lots of enemies.
-The game is also shorter than the last one, the last one took me around 8-9 hours to beat, this one only about 7.
-The Enemy A.I. has definitely been tuned down from the first game, it's not awful, but many enemies will run out of cover, or rush you for no reason, which is a big change from how they acted in the first game. I've also watched A.I. blow themselves up with grenades and just not run away from them in general (Although this was rare.)
Personal Cons (less important stuff and silly nitpicking, but maybe these things bug you as well):
-
isn't in the MAIN game aside from being mentioned in documents. (I know he is in the DLC. But I liked him quite a bit in F.E.A.R  1)
-They took out the option to lean in and out of cover.
-The game has a more CoD/ modern shooter feel, rather than it's more unique first game feel.
-Speaking of which, this game added QTE's, there's not a crazy amount and their done with a decent amount of taste, but I still think they were unnecessary.
-The default controls are really odd, Shift to aim, right mouse to melee, V for thermal vision (which you use only once or twice in the whole game AND it's not necessary) the first game had similarly wonky controls, but it's still an odd thing to not change with a sequel. However, the controls are easily rebindable.
-The film grain visual option is on by default, it adds a nice atmosphere to the look of the game, but after a while began to give me a headache when combined with the motion blur, so I turned the film grain off.
-There's a turret section, two of them to be exact.
-All
look pretty much the same, aside from the visual differences based on the "type" of enemy. They also don't sound as badass as they did in the first game. Hearing a Replica soldier yell "Flashlight!" in a gruff voice was kinda awesome.
-The game also uses the horror game trope of somehow magically seperating you from your squadmates, and the FPS trope of having the environment become destroyed to become a perfect pathway to get somewhere.

-For such a good looking game, most of the skyboxes in this game look pretty bad and you can even see that the skyboxes go under the level in some places.
-You are also a stereotypical mute protagonist, which makes for a couple of odd "conversations" with your squadmates.
Now, I don't usually give a number score with my reviews, (be it Steam or elsewhere), but I feel it's necessary with this one. Why? Because despite me having seemingly more gripes than likes about this game, I don't want you to feel that impression.
I like this game quite a bit, almost as much as the first game, and would highly recommend you buy it. $14.99 is pretty good price to pay, or about 9.18 Quid/British Pounds. It's a good shooter overall, and a pretty decent horror game besides that, which makes for an pretty good game all around.
Finally, for the magic number, I'd give it an 8.5/10.

This game is enthralling.
Now, it might not be for everyone, but that's a mechanics thing. I also highly recommend going into this game as blind as possible. As such, I won't be reviewing the story, but I love it and recommend the story to everyone.
What I will be reviewing are the mechanics. This game puts you, as the player, in control of an old-school computer interface. You are logged into a L.O.G.I.C system which you can control. When you first log in, there are 5 videos, each with a yellow eye icon on them. As you watch the videos, this icon disappears. This is how the story is presented, through videos of a length of anywhere from 2 seconds to a minute and a half. You get new videos by searching for different key words.
Does this sound borning to you? Would these mechanics bore you no matter the story? Well, then I don't know if I'd recommend the game to you. There are YouTube playthroughs of the chronological story or there's an easy way to watch the videos in chronological order, although if you want to experience the story, don't do this first. You can simply search the keyword "blank" and remove it from each video after watching. Again, I DO NOT RECOMMEND YOU DO THIS ON THE FIRST PLAYTRHOUGH. The magic of the mystery (and the ending) are spoiled by systematically scrolling through the videos like this.
Anyway, the narritive is great and the game is little more than an interactive novel for less than a movie ticket. The game, if played, will give you somewhere between 2-4 hours, and if watched about an hour and a half. Still a great bang for your buck, and it has a better narrative than many movies.
Still not sure what really happened, but that doesn't stop this game from being an awesome puzzle for the amateur sleuth.

If instead of just "yes" or "no", I could select "recommended for some", I would, because I know this product has generally good ratings and understand that different tastes exist. In this case, I wouldn't say the product is horrible, it mostly all just comes down to if you like specifically what it's doing or not.
So this negative rating is true for me, without saying that the product is inherently bad or good, just giving you my honest opinion, which is the best one can try to do in a review, I think. If what I don't like seems good for you, this product will more than likely be something you'd want to try.
It's similar in principle to some other products that came out in the last few years, mostly from independent developers it seems, trying something totally experimental. I have to say, and this will give you a clue as to who I am and why I didn't like Her Story all that much, but I find that those experiments cut most or all but one gameplay element in a way that I don't fully get. I just want to know why would you do that in something that is sold as a game where you could have some gameplay while introducing experimental ideas? But while I will always feel right in at least asking this question (which could be responded with some valid answers, I'm sure), you can forgive the lack of gameplay to some extent if the experiment is good enough for you by itself. This is where it all comes down to personal tastes, I didn't get much out of Her Story.
But here is my description of the game, I'll say it can be an intriguing video experience at times. You enter search terms in a computer interface and if those terms are said in a police interview video contained in the computer, you get results. The thing is all about not knowing specifically what you're searching for, but listening closely enough to get a sense of what's going on and finally having a better guess at what search terms could help you understand what the whole interview was about.
In my personal experience, I didn't find it very different from watching a movie, I would even say potentially not as good for me since I didn't find something good out of the interactive system as it was and it was mostly effective at standing in the way of getting access to more story immediately. But you might very well be different and you could consider this basic gameplay element to be the puzzle in itself. There's no wrong or right about this, it's all a matter of whether you like it or not.
This didn't want to be what I'm going to describe to fix it, it was just trying something else that wasn't and probably will never be for me, but I'll say what could have worked for me anyway. Perhaps something more along the lines of a real adventure game, even a basic one, but it could keep the same foundation as Her Story. Let's say you'd have those interviews which would give you clues and you'd have to use them to understand how to complete some objectives or to conduct a game investigation that would really have an in-game goal of figuring out what is true, what is a lie. Perhaps even only having to answer questions after seeing the whole thing would start looking more like something I personally am looking for.
I played it all the way through, I enjoyed trying it even though I didn't end up liking the interactive video experience that was this product. It's not horrible and once again, buy it if you think my description of it was interesting. It's not too costly and I find it good at doing something that is just not what I personally want or like.

this game's concept is absolutely amazing.  it's never felt better to rip apart a massive boss with the most satisfying noise ever when you tear off a hulking monster's arm, or to absolutely destroy entire ecosystems.
however, this game is so unpolished and unfinished with so many bugs that I just can't recommend it to anyone.  If the developer irons out all these bugs and uses spellcheck, then I will change this review, but for now we have an absolute gem covered with grim.
EDIT: as of 01/18/17, the developer is updating the game with bug fixes.  I haven't had time to experience these fixes myself, although I have noticed the update bringing new bugs with it like the taco bomb not working.

On a serious note: it's, as you saw from videos and screenshots, game with shump elements (it's closer to western type of shmups, than to a super-mega-ultra-hardcore Japanese shmup) and rogue-like elements (random encounters and loot). So how does it work in practise? Gameplay cycle is as follows:
* kill trash monsters in their camps;
* slay relatively big boss monster;
* buy/sell loot;
* repeat this until the last battle against ... little bunny with a carrot-sword (not really).
Followed by item-stacking (or creation of build), heavy use of the surroundings, analysis of enemy behaviour patterns and other nuances that has to be learnt.
Man, I like the game a lot, but sometimes it can be kind of a "celestial dumpsterfire".
Pros:
* different space beasts with different behaviour patterns. One of the most impressive aspects was their ability to defend themselves in different ways even when approached from back.
* upgrades that require time to learn (like Pimpernel in Borderlands 2). Of course, there are your standard movement speed, attack speed, damage boosts, but that's just how it is.
* art style is great. It succeeds to deliver an atmosphere of harsh, cold and unforgiving space filled with creatures who don't give a damn about humans (it's a little bit influenced by Lovecraft's work (I know man didn't write about space hunter, but the feel is on some level similar)).
* most of the boss fights are really entertaining (at some level, at least, haha).
* environments are destructible and may be harmful, I really liked seeing debris drifting, awesome attention to detail.
* music is ok.
Cons:
* overlapping, disappearing and distorted audio (sometimes);
* bullet-spongy enemies; they can really be irritating, sure, if one has enough damage runes, the job can be done pretty quickly, otherwise drops are in the hands of RNGesus. So, I guess, it depends on one's preferences.
* some AI is really stubborn, especially that
. Man, it is annoying, because that a-hole keeps on turning (very) fast when I tried to flank him. It seems that the boss does not have any turning limit like other bosses. Another example
- this majestic creature just flies around and do not attack me. I, like some kind of idiot, have to play catch with it. Not cool, dude, not cool. Also, some trash mobs (in void biome) are really fast - faster than my spear, especially when combined with speed modification. Jesus flippin Christ.
* this is where attrition comes in. There were some fights where I just gave up because battle became solid stalemate.
Oh, and I forgot,
and
, go to Hell, not to mention the last d-bag.
Verdict: game's between average and solid, in my opinion. If you are still curious or long boss battles are your thing, then sure, try it out. Otherwise - purchase if you have some "creds to burn". For me it lacks flexibility in dififculty, but I understand and respect design decisions.

Blacksea Odyssey is a highly enjoyable game.
If you need further encouragement: Blacksea Odyssey feels like
meets
.  It's a top-down Roguelike-like, with many unique weapon mods and destructible terrain.  The emphasis of the game is on boss battles: the end of each of the rounds is a boss that you select at the Bounty Select screen, so you know what to expect.  The stages between bosses are incredibly fluid, relying completely on your focus to advance and defeat the boss.  But even more than that, each mob fight feels like a mini-boss fight.  To defeat enemies, you have to focus their weak spots, then rip them off with a secondary-fire (a harpoon shot).
To me, this feels like what many Roguelikes (or Roquelites, or Roquelite-likes, you know what I mean) have been missing over the years.  I don't want to just beat♥♥♥♥♥♥up,
I want to feel like a Master, more than just a Badass.  And Blacksea Odyssey does that for me.
In all fairness, I did encounter a bug that resulted in me dying.  But was that enough to make me want to stop playing?
(The Krakhammer boss became invulnerable, getting stuck at 100% health, more than halfway through the battle.  But I'm almost positive that the bug was a result of me pausing the game during combat, which was due to me jotting down a note of how awesome that boss battle was.)  It is likely that you will encounter bugs, but very few (if any) of these will be game-affecting.  Most are graphical or text bugs (I unlocked 135,000 chests!?), and the ones that do affect the game are forgivable.
And on to the polish.  The polish on this game is fantastic.  It's more than I've come to expect in most indie studios.  It's more than I've come to expect in games beyond indie studios.  You can feel the love the developers put into this game.  Background layers in stages, boss reveals, music tracks, character animations, destructible terrain, lighting effects on walls, character sheets, stage types, itemization, their spin on character creation, harpoon ripping physics... I could have a list a hundred items long, and still miss things that I appreciate.
Blacksea Odyssey is a great game.  I enjoyed it more than Everspace, and that's saying a lot.  You should buy it.

If you're looking for a very basic demonstration of Metroidvania power-ups and ideas, this is it. It's like a game design prototype that Robert Alvarez just decided to release on Steam.
And I think it's great.
There isn't a map, nor is there a ton of power-ups to find. As far as I know there's only one "gun" upgrade, so it's all just jump and shoot (and a tiny bit more with upgrades.) But, as basic as it is, it does capture the essence of what makes a good action game - except for one thing.
The difficulty curve is something like if you were riding on a bicycle with training wheels, then suddenly someone runs over and shoots the training wheels off with a shotgun and pushes you down a hill. That might be a little hyperbolic, but I think that for less experienced gamers this game is going to be an exercise in frustration, since there's little in the way of intuitive tutorialization. But if you like a challenge and don't mind dying over and over until you get it right, I definitely recommend this one.

‘Hitman: Blood Money’ is the fourth entry in the iconic Stealth / Strategy RPG Hitman series, and is simply put, the best game of the franchise. Gorgeous visuals, well designed levels, intuitive gameplay and a compelling storyline make this title Agent 47’s defining moment.

Released by Eidos / IO Interactive in 2007, ‘Blood Money’ puts gamers back in the familiar shoes of Agent 47 – a professional assassin who is both ruthlessly efficient and disarmingly charming at the same time. The campaign details 47’s first foray across the Atlantic, and its 13 missions take you around the world to varying locales and vastly differing settings - from mountain retreats in the Rockies to Opera Houses in Paris, from Casino’s in Las Vegas to Jungle Hideaway’s in Chile. The missions are seamlessly woven into a broader narrative of the FBI’s efforts to connect the dots in a series of high profile assassinations and the surprising twist ending ensures your attention is kept throughout.
Graphically, the game is beautiful, with detailed, lush environments, atmospheric sound and some of the best level design seen in modern gaming. Each mission has several objectives that need to be completed – but be aware – there is no handholding here. True to its ‘Hitman’ roots, ‘Blood Money’ drops you into a large open world level with the freedom to accomplish your objectives in any order you see fit, and you are largely left to figure out the best way to get at your targets and escape unnoticed. Every mission, even every target, can be approached in multiple ways limited seemingly only by your imagination – Sniper kills from afar, close up strangulation with Piano Wire, a poisoned beverage to a distracted gory death are but some of the options at your disposal.  Tight and intuitive K&M controls, a broad selection of weapons, tools and distraction items, and upgradable items available for purchase in-between missions round out your toolkit.
The game also addresses many of the core gameplay issues and complaints of previous installments while at the same time moving the series forward – the inclusion of plentiful in-game save options, much improved AI, ability to play in both 3rd person and first-person views and high replayability make finding fault difficult. If pressed, a few gripes would be some clunky character animations and a close adherence to the Hitman formula making things seem quite familiar to veterans of the series.

Overall, ‘Hitman: Blood Money’ is 47’s finest hour – a visually stunning, atmospheric, Stealth / Strategy RPG that puts you in the shoes of the iconic assassin and where you are ultimately limited only by your imagination in finding new ways to eliminate your target. Highly Recommended – Rated (9/10)

This game is not a copy/paste of SupCom FA, and though I originally liked FA more, after awhile I found that SupCom2 just fit my playstyle better.
I enjoy the research tree and find that a centralized research window such as this is easy to navigate and plan with and is quite informative about what each upgrade does..
The story was kind of meh, but it was enough that I played through it and did not regret it, but have no desire to play through it again. The skirmishes are great though and very satisfying.
AI originally was horrible, but now a hard AI can be a real pain (mainly due to the increases resource and production handicap they get) but you can design a "Custom" difficulty setting right in the game setup when you are adding AI players, so you can really set the AI to however you want.
The actual play ability of AI...well it seems to have been improved since the start, but it's still pretty easy to get an idea of what they are going to do after you play 5-10 skirmish matches, but again, you can change some of this in custom AI settings.
Overall, especially being on sale, I would definitely say pick this game up AND THE DLC. The original price for the game and DLC (adds a bunch of stuff, worth the original DLC price of $5) would come to about $18. Would I pay that price for this game? Depends on my financial situation, but it's still under 20$ and I have spent more for less.
Graphics 8/10. You won't be zooming in super close very often, but when you do, they look nice. The terrain looks nice though and you see that a whole lot more.
Story 5/10. At least they had one, and it was worth playing it once. I would suggest they keep their marketing to saying about that much and not more in regards to their story in this game.
Gameplay 8/10. Can't complain too much here, it keeps me coming back to play more. Wouldn't mind more AI customization, or at least make them much more dynamic and able to adapt. When they see me building 5 artillery cannons and raining hell upon them, they should probably try to take out those cannons, you know what I mean?
Voice acting 6/10. It's there, it gets the job done, but when you have someone just read a paragraph here and there it really comes through like someone is reading a book and trying to give it a character personality. Could use more dialogue in the game, and that would also make it seem much more personable.
Sounds 8/10. They are nice, high quality, and get the job done.
Complaints:
Take away the damn unit cap or at least let us customize it to what we want. My computer can easily handle 3x as many units as what we cap out at and the maps are HUGE. Let me use more of it!

I'm a PvP Player and i have some issues with some design choices here.
The game runs not good (smooth) at all, which is really bad for a PvP Game. FPS should come before everything else.
The screen gets cluttered easily with special effects which can get really chaotic, especially when you play a melee character. Reduce the effects and the game might even run smoother and gets less chaotic.
First Person vs. Third Person: Do it like Savage. First Person with ranged weapons, third person with melee. Also since every character has a melee attack, make the weapons switchable so every character can use their melee weapon to get into third person mode to have a better overview of the situation when needed.
Now to two things that are abysmal for a PvP Game:
The Helix third tree: make it available for everyone at level one in PvP. Its okay to have to unlock it for the coop missions, but for PvP that's a no go! It should be about skill, not about who just played the most.
Same thing goes for the item sets. It's a nice idea for coop missions, but it's bad for PvP. You chose an item set with shield penetration and you play against a team with barely any shields: you're screwed because you wasted slots. F.E.A.R. 2: Project Origin takes the great gameplay from F.E.A.R 1 and improves on it. There are more guns to use, more grenades to throw, you can now flip objects to make cover, and they fixed the melee system so you can't speedrun by kicking everyone in the knee. My biggest complaint is that the Intel you collect is no longer in audio form, but written out. It's not really a big deal but I don't want to have to stop the game and read what is going on.
F.E.A.R. 2: Project Origin is only as scary as you make it, literally. The game relies a lot on events that are triggered by the player rather than being scripted. While this sounds great in theory, you can miss a whole bunch of stuff if you don't take the time to explore. The biggest fault with the horror is that sometimes Alma jumps out at you and you fight her off... with a quicktime event. The game itself runs some tropes with a hospital and a subway setting, but surprisingly avoids the little ghost girl trope by making Alma older.
It's not quite as good as F.E.A.R 1, but F.E.A.R. 2: Project Origin is definitely worth playing and is worthy to be called a sequel to F.E.A.R

This is a seriously well done roguelike with pulp fiction elements and one amazing cast of characters.
Pros:
- Characters, there's plenty of diverse explorers, each neatly designed
from the Luchadora to the Russian 'bear' to street orphans, all the cliches of a good adventure are here

No doubt, get it.

If you're looking at this game, it's most likely because you've heard of or played the famous Amnesia: The Dark Descent made by the same developers.  Penumbra: Overture is Frictional Game's first game and it definitely shares characteristics with Amnesia.
The mood and style of the game is similar to Amnesia.  The lighting and eeriness of the locations set the tone of places you'd rather not be at.  Notes are scattered throughout the game, providing background history of the places you travel through.  The game is also physics based, but unlike Amnesia, you are allowed to have weapons, which does suggest that there is some form of defense.  However, the physics nature of the game requires the player to manually swing melee weapons by moving your mouse back and forth.  Nothing quite as fun as swinging in panic!  In addition to these, there are quite a bit more puzzles to solve, but nothing that is frustrating and some have satisfying complexity.
If you're buying this game thinking you'll get the same experience as you did when playing Amnesia: The Dark Descent then you will be off the mark.  While it does share Amnesia's atmosphere of horror, its level of execution isn't the same.  A play through the game shows that a lot of thought went into finding ways to instill fear into the player, but it's unable to maintain the same pressure throughout the game.  If you want to get the same scares as one would get playing Amnesia, then you'll be disappointed.  But if you're interested in playing a horror game or seeing Frictional Game's earlier works, then it's worth picking up this title.

Before anything, this game is only for diehard fans of JRPG style games. Not being elitist, this game can be incredibly boring, even for a fan of the series. If you don't want to do a lot of grinding, you probably won't like this game.
So for the rest of you still here:
Pros
-Soundtrack is one of the best in the Final Fantasy series, and improved graphics from the original game.
-Job System for an insane degree of party customizations
-One of the more difficult Final Fantasy games. Hard fights, difficult classes like the Chemist and Cannoneer, this game won't be a cakewalk. And that's before we get to the superbosses! With bosses like Omega, Shinryu, ExDeath, Enuo, Gilgamesh, and many more, this has some of the toughest bosses in the series.
-Game is a bit more streamlined. Resting at an inn is much faster, you can end a battle with usually a single button press, and the game doesn't auto-optimise your equipment every time you change your Job Skills
-The legendary "Rapid Fire" and "Dual Wield" combo. Definitely worth grinding for.
Cons:
-Easily one of the most grind-heavy game in the Final Fantasy series. You have to level characters and their jobs seperately, and ABP is incredibly tedious to farm.
-On top of grinding, the best skills and gear aren't available until nearly the end of the game. By then, your character can be truly overpowered, but it can be a turnoff to people without the free time to get there.
-Weak story compared to the rest of the Final Fantasy series. Story is fairly generic with few twists, and is fairly predictable stuff. Also some cringe-inducing attempts at humor, such as refrences to the Simpsons, lame puns, a main character being a crossdressing woman for no real reason, and naming the player character's sick mother "Stella" just for a one-off, immersion breaking reference to A Streetcar named Desire.
-Yet again from Square-Enix, obviously a mobile port. While the ingame UI and battle interface isn't so bad, there's still vestiges of it (IE, "Tap the sprint button", with a giant button in the bottom right corner that doesn't do anything). In all fairness, WAY better than Square's other mobile ports on Steam, but it's a mobile game all the same, and I know that's a turn-off for some Steam users.
Basically, if you've already played and loved Final Fantasy V, you've probably already bought this. But for newcomers to Final Fantasy? It's a hard call to make. Personally I love this game, despite it's many flaws. In terms of story, it might disappoint compared to Final Fantasy IV and VI. This game's real selling point is the Job System, and even from that point-of-view Bravely Default on the 3DS improves on this mechanic a lot.
The story isn't as good as Final Fantasy IV or VI. It lacks the presentation of Final Fantasy VII-onwards. But in terms of gameplay, I personally think Final Fantasy V is the strongest. For people who really enjoy micro-management and really getting into the nitty-gritty of party building and synergizing certain skills, this is the Final Fantasy for them.

This is a pretty good game content-wise. The textures obvioulsy are NOT stitched very well, and the sprites compared to the full body pic are WAY off, but the overall gameplay is fine. Please fix some of these issues Square Enix!

After having read a substantial amount of reviews criticizing glitches and performance issues within this game, I was somewhat trepidatious about purchasing it when it was first released. Nevertheless, being an ardent Final Fantasy fan since I was a kid when the Final Fantasy 1 debuted on the NES in the U.S. (definitely showing my age here) I had to buy it. I must say after 15 hours of play, I haven't found anything that has diminished the gameplay and no glaring graphical errors.
My first experience with this title was when it was reissued for the first time as a compilation package with Final Fantasy VI for the PlayStation One system. I find this one a serious improvement over that version with a much improved (albeit still inconsistent) English translation, better looking (in my opinion) character sprites, extra dungeons/sidequests/jobs and steam achievements...which are the proverbial "icing on the cake." Going back through a classic game such as this and collecting all the achievements for things you accomplished years back is strangely satisfying.
Like countless others have mentioned in other reviews, the Job system is this game's greatest strength whilst the story is passable...bordering on formulaic/mediocre. In my opinion, the job system in Final Fantasy V is the deepest out of the entire series. With all that being said, I would strongly recommend this to anyone who is interested in classic JRPG's as this one is definitely a "standard" of the genre.

A great match with having a lot to do is being able to make the party how you want it with its job system. Want lotsa melee? Want indirect attacks or magic oriented. Or a well thought out strategy of your own. Why not try it all?
These two together give this game a ridiculously high replay value.
Gameplay aside, the music is alright. (I prefer the GBA version probably due to nostalgia, but I feel like this soundtrack doesn't really want to be here. It's the SNES soundtrack for whoever didn't know.)  Still, some songs are still just lovely.
Looks: ... well... In this version of the game it definately takes some getting used to. Textures are a bit weird, (Though I didn't notice until like 15 hours in.)   But the character sprites look really nice.  The portraits are the most shocking at the start probably. They don't fit at all with the rest. I got used to them after like 3 hours though. In fact, this classic Final Fantasy portrait box art artist guy is REALLY good at some portraits. Galuf and Dorgann look incredibly handsome, while Krile and Faris are still my cuties.  I think the shock was extra hard on people because the main character looks so awful. Even at the end of the game I couldn't understand how he could look like that. It just looks so wrong.  The other ones that make you go Uechh are Cid & Mid.

Simple metroidvania with ugly graphics and a difficulty which will lead you to rage.
Main character (box?) is not only simple, but expressionless. It's number of animations is very low.
You get hearts for increasing your health, but then most of the common enemies hurt you for two hearts. This nullifies the sense of doubling your health.
One of the bosses pattern consists on increasing its speed as its life goes down. The problem is that it also jumps when it is near you. Combine this two things and you will have to position yourself in order to provoke the boss jump in places where it can be dodged. The game tricks you into believing that the corners are this place, but this place is relative to you. This pattern is very counterintuitive.
Other bosses have extreme difficulty, such as the wall of eyes. Funnily enough, Zolthan is the easiest of them all.
Given the very specific movements the game expects from you, save points should actually not exist, respawning the player at the entrance of each screen.
Music becomes repetitive as it is only a single melody.
Overall, it's a short game whose problem is an excess of difficulty. Probably not worth your time if you have some others games from the same genre.

To start: I used to add a header to these reviews, but since it often made the review too long to submit, I've decided to just leave it on my Backloggery page.
Gameplay: As with every other stealth game I do these reviews on, I feel the need to point out that I'm not good at stealth. At all. Fortunately, Hitman: Blood Money takes stealth in a bit different of a direction. While you can always spend your days creeping around corners and walking very close to armed thugs but not too close otherwise they'll notice you, you also have the option to disguise yourself. I tended to go for the latter more than the former, since as mentioned earlier, I'm not good at all at stealth. Of course, there are consequences to both sides. From these two initial decision factors a lot of the missions become surprisingly non-linear, allowing for a multitude of ways to hit your man.
Most of the levels in the game are very good about allowing for a multitude of ways to take down your target, although a couple toward the end become very linear and not that interesting in terms of strategy. As for the AI, they're pretty dang smart, I must say. They'll notice blood pools and trails and will investigate accordingly. The AI did sometimes see through my disguise even though I had done nothing wrong to blow my cover, which can be very annoying, but if you've saved fairly recently, it's not too big of a deal. Regarding saving, you can save anytime in the level (except for the highest difficulty), but the amount of times you can save per level changes with difficulty. On easy you can save as much as you want, on normal the count is 7, and on hard it's 3. This system is much better than checkpoints in my eyes given the non-linear nature of the game, but it still can be very frustrating to lose a good bit of progress just because you didn't save frequently enough. There was only one level that I found myself brushing the 7 save cap (obviously I played on Normal), but that's because there were so much man hitting to do.
Apart from that, there really isn't much  else to go on about. The level design for the most part allows for many, many ways of approaching the challenge; there's plenty of tools to allow you to adapt to the scenario; the AI is for the most part very good, even on normal, and it's just a great deal of fun. 9/10.
Story: A surprisingly good aspect of the game. There isn't much in the way of character development, but there's a lot of intrigue; that's for sure. Since this is my first Hitman game, I can't attest for how well it fits into the series' story arc, but it seems like a good place to wrap up the franchise, given what all happens. Without spoiling too much, I'll just say that the storyline becomes more and more tense until the final mission where things actually get pretty dang cool. If you like the Bond movies, odds are that you'll like this quite a bit as well. They definitely have a very similar feel to them. 8/10.
Graphics: Oh cool, a game from 2006 that didn't abuse the hell out of bloom. Since this game goes for more of a realistic feel for the visual presentation, there isn't much sense going on about art style and all that. Rather, I'll talk about how this game would stack up against games from 2006. If you haven't guessed already, this game does a lot better than its 2006 bloom-theren. It's of course silly to ask how it holds up today; Quake 2 held up for a while until 2001 or so. For 2006, though, this game looks pretty great. As for the technical aspects of the game, I (as I just assume I'll have to do for most games) had to go into the options menu to change to a more not-terrible resolution, but it worked just fine. When you launch the game, it gives you the option to bring up a configuration menu, but I didn't find too much use for it. Beyond that, the game ran without a hitch at 1080p max settings on my GTX 760. Average temperature from a few trials was about 48degC, so it's not gonna push your hardware too hard. Overall, the graphics side of things is very good and it works great to this day. There is an issue of the realistic style dating itself, but for now at least it's still pretty nice looking. 5/5.
Sound: As one would expect from such a game like this, the voice acting isn't exactly dramatic. In fact, whenever things do get hairy, Agent 47's voice acting does sound a little silly. Apart from that, the voice acting is just kinda alright, but it doesn't need to be too terribly bombastic anyways. As for the soundtrack, there's a lot of electronic music as well as orchestral music. Apparently it's a sort of blending of the prior game's soundtrack styles. Again, I can't attest for the quality of those soundtracks, but for what's presented here it's once again not bad. Not anything I'd want to go out and get the OST for, but I can at least appreciate the somewhat wide scale of the OST. Overall, on the audio front, it's not bad. Nothing too memorable, but it serves its function. 3/5.
Overall scores are: 9/8/5/3; 8.3/10. I was quite pleased with this game, but I do recognise that when I eventually go back and play the prior games, they're probably not gonna be as good based solely on the fact that I played this first. Oh well; at the very least I had a good time with this one.

I’ve heard some people say FEAR 2 is inferior to the original game, but I actually prefer it over FEAR 1. Most notably, the graphics of FEAR 2 are greatly improved, now comparable to other Xbox 360 games/ports. There’s still an issue with default key bindings being weird compared to other modern FPS games, but you can change those easily.
FEAR 2 picks up a little before the end of FEAR 1, ignoring the FEAR 1 expansion DLCs. This time your character has a name and you actually feel like part of a team, instead of just having a lot of people talk to you on the radio. However, similar to the first game you’re on your own most of the time when the bullets start flying. Your team is tasked with rescuing the CEO of Armacham Corporation, the private military contractor with more firepower than most first world nations. The Armacham leadership is trying to cover its♥♥♥♥♥by blaming the disaster from FEAR 1 on the CEO and sending in black ops teams to wipe out everyone and everything that could tie them to illegal activities. Not to mention *SPOILER* at the end of Fear 1, Alma was released, so she seems to have awakened all the replica forces around the city. You have a lot of visions of her wandering the halls and tearing people apart like Phoenix in the worst Xmen movie (you know which one).
Like its predecessor, FEAR 2 is a first person shooter with a time slowing power that you can use to achieve tactical supremacy. The game seems a lot easier than FEAR 1 for some reason, possibly because the enemies don’t seem to have perfect aim anymore. There’re at least half a dozen new weapons, some of which are pretty cool (Lasers and electro grenades) and a pretty badass mechanized power armor that you can use to lay down the pain. Of course there are a lot of new enemies as well to soak up your bullets. This time around there are non-human enemies that have either been created by Armacham or were summoned by Alma’s psychic presence. You also need to fight some enemies with their own power armor (at least you have a missile launcher). A minor gripe of mine is that not all the weapons seem to have designated “roles.” For example the assault rifle and the submachine gun are basically the same thing. One is weaker but fires faster, that’s about the only difference. There’s also an energy weapon that is basically the same thing as the missile launcher. I won’t complain too much about it though since more variety is nice in a game with modern graphics. I wish there was better documentation of how enemy armor works. Most of the enemies seem to be wearing heavy armor. Does it randomly deflect bullets like in Rage, or just lower the received damage like in the Fallout games? The Hammerhead rifle is supposed to be great against armored enemies, but in a fast paced game like this, it’s really hard to see the difference. This is really kind of nitpicky though and it’s just something that stuck out in my mind, not a real problem.
EDIT: I was wrong about the energy weapon being the same as the missile launcher. It seems to be more like a BFG 10k (from Doom) with lightning bolts shooting out of the main blast to fry people around it.
Pros:
+Great visuals and some unique looking monsters. The ghost summoner is pretty cool
+A lot of “intel” items can be found in the game, which give you a flavor for the game world. It’s disgusting the kind of things that Armacham has been up to.
+Slow-mo + sniper rifle = fun
+Good story and a lot of replay potential
Cons:
-There’s this weird issue where each time a level loads, it seems to pause around 50% and not move until I alt+tab out of the game and go back in. I don’t know if this is specific to my computer but it also happened with my old non-steam version a few years ago.
-The game has no Steam achievements despite having game achievements built right in (like 10 headshots or 10 melee kills).
-FEAR 2 is kind of short. I went through it in about 6 hours on normal mode. It may take longer for someone who hasn’t played it before.
Overall if you liked FEAR 1 you should like FEAR 2. I find it superior in pretty much every way. As much as I liked the first FEAR, I doubt I’ll replay it again because the outdated graphics really take away from the experience. With FEAR 2 I’ll keep it around to replay in a few months (smaller download size too). If you have this game in your inventory from the Humble Bundle, give it a try.

I find that nearly all horror games have jump-scares, so I went in head first into this game thinking that probably most horror elements would be presented in this way. I had a lot of fun playing Fear 2, it took me 7 hours to beat but it felt longer for some reason. The atmosphere is great, much more environment changes than Fear 1. Great lighting effects, but the textures are ugly. The first thing that came to mind when I played Fear 2 is how similar it is to Doom 3 - the Intels (PDA in Doom 3) laying on the floor, the jump scares, style of the corridors, those moments when a person is being swallowed by Almas darkness or whatever one may call it, and the guns even felt Doom 3-ish to me. Fear 2 also nails the difficulty curve quite well IMO, if you put it on hard its challenging but not frustrating. I think this is a topic often forgotten in many modern games, usually there's too many annoying difficulty spikes or the descriptions at the start about each difficulty are inaccurate. The ending is one sure to be remembered, it's unique.

What a really unique game. It was about time that I got around to looking at this game as it has been on my list of games to play for a while now. Anyway, this game has an impeccable execution that really makes it shine. Everything from the story to the presentation is fantastic. For those who don't know (maybe there's some people out there) your essentially sitting in front of an old 90's computer going through a database of small clips from seven different interviews of a woman who is being accused for murder. There's a search bar on the top that allows you to sift through these clips based on keywords. Want to find all the clips where she says "murder," just search "murder" and the list will be brought up for you...although you can only look at the top 5 (if there are 61 clips, for example). This requires you to narrow down your search terms, getting more specific as you slowly start to learn the story behind this woman and the murder she is being accused for.
The woman (who's name I can't remember off the top of my head) gives a fantastic performance. She really sells the part and brings you into the story. It's a fascinating story...one full of weird twists and darker secrets. By nature of the game's search mechanic, you aren't going to experience the story chronologically, but instead in bits and pieces that you have to puzzle together. The game doesn't hold your hand and leaves you to interpret the woman's story and it's meaning. There's no "objective" to the game. If you feel like you've seen enough or think you know what's going on, you can simply leave and that's that. That's the beauty of this game. Some might find it frustrating, but I found it very powerful. You're truly on your own on this one. You draw the conclusions.
I don't want to say much else in fear of spoiling things, so I'll just say this. This is definitely a game worth a try if you haven't gotten around to playing it yet. Really great on all fronts.

Got this in the humble bundle for £15 and have thoroughly enjoyed my time so far.
Co-op and story was a blast, but very short. While I've almost done all the levels with gold ranking on each difficulty level, it feels a little copy-paste and lacking compared to the previous series developed by Gearbox. The humor is there and there are some very memorable lines, however, overall I feel like I wanted more to the story. Not much is explained in terms of why the main bad guys are doing what they do, and the best way to find out is character lore (which requires certain challenges and play time). Each level follows a very specific layout (minion fight-mini boss-minion fight/escort-main boss) and can get boring if you don't get lost in doing lore/fighting/trying to pull off cool skill combos. The key factor is to set yourself in-game challenges and work towards those, being either character lore or score-based medals.
Multiplayer was hard at first with the pretty unbalanced matchmaking due to the low player base, but good games and bad games come along. I play with two other level 80+ players and we can still get rolled through games if we have low level players. We do try our best to encourage and teach mechanics (as long as they actually want to learn!) so to best try and keep players in the community. While there is three different multiplayer game modes, I feel only Incursion is the game mode where players will thrive in a tactical-MOBA-esque mode. Games can be frustrating if you don't have people willing to fill character gaps (healer/tank/melee damage) and these will quickly ruin your experience. It is best when a player embraces their role and tries their best to help the team, which is difficult with most players as the past years of games have promoted self-play, instead of team-play. Choosing when, and if, to initiate and sacrifice your kda for a team fight is a skill upon itself.
The character cast itself is diverse and quirky, with each characters personality popping out of the screen. Some good voice acting mixed with strange character traits provides the player with loveable rogues they get attached to. The art style is very typical Gearbox, and I personally enjoy this. It may feel a bit gimmicky with the casts over-the-top personalities, and can be tiresome to hear the same cheesy voice lines from characters you personally dislike.
Overall, a very enjoyable game with friends, sometimes frustrating multiplayer, but shines through in its moments of glory when all the same pieces come together.

Guacamelee is a game that mixes a lot of game mechanics at once. It has platforming, exploration, combat, dimension-swapping and more.
The game does a great job of introducing new abilities and mechanics to you as you progress, so the game never gets repetitive.
The combat feels fresh and unique because of the ability to perform your own combos and the ability to grab your opponents and throw them in any direction.
The dimension-swapping mechanic adds some neat puzzles to the game, but it also adds the ability to see 2 different dimensions of the same universe (the "dead" dimension and the "real" one) at any time, which is really cool.
One thing I didn't like about this game is that all these mechanics don't always blend in so well during combat. This is more complicated, but I'll explain.
As you unlock new abilities, the combat gradually becomes more interesting, but it also ends up being more tedious. Near the end, it almost becomes an annoyance. They give you more moves, which are very fun to use for platforming and puzzle-solving, but since they constantly add more depth to the combat, they end up just throwing tons of enemies at you at once. But it doesn't stop there. They make it so that you can only hit enemies if you break their shields, which will only break if you do certain moves, and these moves cost stamina, which takes time to regenerate. Also, all enemies can damage you in both dimensions, but you can only hit them in their dimension, etc. It gets overwhelming.
Some enemies even throw objects at you, but even after unlocking new attacks, you can't even break them. Like, you can't punch or kick a flying bone to break it. It just hits you anyway. Ranged attacks are literally indestructible, so you HAVE to dodge them. But the thing is, this isn't a shoot'em up: you can't attack and dodge at the same time. So you'll inevitably end up getting hit. The thing is, I shouldn't feel weaker as I progress through the game. I should feel stronger.
The game is pretty forgiving, so you won't necessarily die too often, and even if you do, you'll respawn just before the fight. But getting completely stopped because of a random little flying bone or an enemy from the other dimension? That completely breaks the flow of the game.
Also, when you use a controller, the button to dodge is R2 and you can't rebind it. This might seem like a minor complaint, but when you make a game about accurately dodging things, you don't put the dodge button on an analog trigger...
Anyway, I'm being overly critical here. I actually enjoyed the game a lot, it's just that combat gets pretty tedious and less fun near the end. The visuals and the characters are always charming, the humor in the dialogue and presentation is genuinely funny (except when it resorts to memes, but that rarely happens), and the music is fitting and pretty catchy!
I'd give this game an 8 out of 10.

Guacamelee is a joy to play platforming beat'em up done in a Metroidvania style with a lot of flair and fresh ideas for an old genre. The combat is excellent. Easy to play, tough to master. Attack button, special attack, roll trigger and jump are the basics you need to know. You can uppercut enemies into the air, jump and punch them, roll through enemy attacks and hazards, grapple enemies to throw them in any direction you want. There is good stuff here. Then as the game progresses, you unlock special moves, like jumping uppercuts, wall jumps, double jumps, headbutts, frog stomps, wall climbs where you shoot yourself straight until something stops you. All of this is considered combat, but in Guacamelee it is also a means of traversing. Jump uppercut will let you break red walls or its used as an extra boost while in mid air. Now just that, but the game's enemies will eventually have shields that can only be broken by special attacks. The shields are all color coated, such as jumping uppercuts break red walls and red shields. Yellow shields and walls are broken by headbutts and so on. Then on top of that there's an extra layer of day and night worlds or living and dead worlds. You flip through them to traverse or take out enemies that can only take damage in the living or day. They still hit you if you're not in their world, but you just can't hit them.
Each world full of bright, vibrant and beautiful colors. The game is a joy to look at as well as play. Great simple story, the president's daughter has been kidnapped and you are killed, but resurrected by a luchadore mask. Everything has a lucha Mexican vibe to it and that makes the game feel so fresh and different instead of space worlds or never ending castles. The world isn't that big and really it feels like there are a few specific combat areas tied together by a major town. There's no real chance to get lost, since you have a map and the map will always point you to your objective, without revealing rooms that you've been in.
While the combat is easy and joyful enough, the game really starts getting tricky with your powers. Such as having to wall jump back and forth all while switching between the living and dead worlds. Timing plays a big part in the later areas. There are plenty of side rooms with parts of heart and stamina containers that will really test your skills and timing, but since there are frequent easy challenges, it makes the big challenges seem less daunting and have a 'one more try' mentality.
I have completed the game on PSN and it seems like the Gold Edition on Steam is just easier when it comes to bosses. The bosses are simpler and I can't say that's a bad thing. Maybe its because there is no difficulty setting for the Gold Edition. Steam also offers character skins in the Steam Workshop, which is always nice.
On PSN I completed the game in 4 or so hours and that's when it was more difficult. That might not be enough play time in some people's opinion, but it was an absolute joy to play and well worth the time and money. I'd much rather have a game be short and sweet than long and boring.

Penumbra: Overture is a first-person game about Phillip (the player) who ventures into an abandoned mine in search of his father. The game takes a dark turn when Phillip is trapped and forced to survive the horror of the mines while looking for clues.
Overture is only slightly scary in my opinion, but that's just fine. It's more about survival, and is incredibly realistic. What it lacks in scariness, it makes up for in realism.
For example, the main enemy is packs of demonic dogs that stalk the player. You can fight them, but it's hard. You aren't a superhero, and you can't just click to swing your instrument of destruction over and over. You have to time attacks carefully, and swish the mouse in the direction you want your weapon to swing.
Another example is the physics engine. Like Amnesia, you can pick up/throw/push almost anything by cicking on it and dragging the mouse in the corresponding directon. You feel like you're really there, like your character has wieght and realness. This makes the game totally immersive, and really heightens the "survival" aspect.
You'll have to solve puzzles and escape monsters all the way through while feeling helpless and alone--so it perfectly captures what the survival horror genre is about.
The mad rantings of your only friend, Red, wrap it all up. Red is wonderfully voice acted and his insanity is creepy, eerily setting the mood.
If you want a dark, macabre, realistic, true survival horror game that doesn't pull punches or hold your hand, Penumbra: Overture is it. 10/10.

Dungeon of Zolthan has its own simplicity and uniqueness to it. The goal and controls of the game are pretty basic, where your goal is to defeat 3 bosses via shooting and using certain tricks and strategies. I was able to complete the game within ½ an hour or so, and much quickly when aiming for the 20 minute achievement. Thankfully the game had check points, and after each boss battle you can find/unlock a new ability for your character. It has a good progress-reward system, with the latter as well as the achievements.
The metroidvania genre is what really gives it some flair in the design. Some reviews have remarks of how low-quality and shabby the graphics are, but to me they were decent. The bright, neon coloured outlines over a black BG is quite relaxing for the eye, and helped me better my focus throughout the time. There isn’t much effects or animations though; killing an enemy results in them shrinking and disappearing. This also goes to being hit or dying as a result, where nothing too flashy happens.
The audio included noises that trigger when you jump, shoot and hit and destroy an enemy. There was also background music. It swaps between casual (where you are roaming in the dungeon) and boss music, when facing a boss. I find it suiting to the theme of the game.
Overall, Dungeon of Zolthan plays out very well as a basic platformer, but nothing more. No bugs, glitches or any other difficulties were encountered during my entire game play, much to my satisfaction. Kudos to the developers for polishing the game well.  At the price it’s currently at, I’d say it’s worth giving the game a try.

Hitman: Blood Money is my favorite game in the Hitman Series. There is a story to it but you play the missions how you want to play them. Each mission has a target, or more, to kill and some have additional objectives. You must complete these objectives to beat the level but you may go about it however you wish. You can be sneaky and use disguises to get close to and fiberwire choke them, then disappear; you can load up your M4 assault rifle with a 100 round drum and take out everything between you and your target [my personal favorite method ;)] ; you can find a vantage point with your modified W2000 sniper rifle and pick off your targets and then disappear; you can beef up your silverballer pistol with armor piercing rounds and a suppressor to walk through the level picking off guards/threats in silence, leaving a wake of bodies to be found long after you've left the area.
As you can tell, I've played this game in many different ways. Much of it just screwing around.
For each level you complete, you are rated on your violence and noise. You can be a Ghost leaving a dead target with no trace of foul play or be a mass murderer with bullet holes, empty mags, blood, and bodies everywhere. The more silent and less violent you are, the more money you will earn to upgrade your equipment. Did I mention you can upgrade your equipment?
You can upgrade your core weapons: pistol, shotgun, SMG, M4, and W2000 Sniper with suppressors, ammo types, and other modifications to make your killing more efficient. You can also upgrade your Hitman with better lockpicks, better armor, more equipment, and more.
After completing the game, you can go back through the levels with your upgraded assassin and glide through them like butter.
If you haven't played this game, PLAY IT! It is an impressive game for being 8 years old (2006). I remember playing this game on my playstation 2 when it came out, good times... and it also explain my murderous tendencies... and I wasted all that money on therapy...

The game Blacksea Odyssey follows the paths of four interstellar bounty hunters who "fish" in deep sea for giant monsters. Honestly, the story may as well not be there, as it's only told during cartrige-era text boxes, but for the amusing conversations that take place between the four hunters between missions, which if you take the time to read are actually quite amusing.
As far as gameplay goes, you control your spaceship with WASD and fire with the mouse. There is gamepad support but I would recommend not using it. I've tried both, and even after taking a half hour getting used to it with the gamepad it still wasn't worth it. The controls simply don't work.
Your only customization going into the game is which of the characters you play as and what "spear" you use. Each one has different effects, pros, and cons. None of the bounty hunters are genericly better than the others. The standard indie random loot and infinite replayability rears its head here, with ship and spear upgrades being "runes" which are acquired by opening chests and defeating enemies. It's all comprehensive enough, although I've found the runes to be very unbalanced within teirs, and some runes are almost useless.
Controling the ship is a little clunky, as it controls more like a boat than a space ship. However, once you've adjusted for the controls and stop running into the projectile you were trying to dodge, the game flows very nicely and intuitively.
Map design is a little boring, with four teirs of space and each one only having recoloured rocks. Enemy design is a little more inspired, though it doesn't take a genius to realize that there are about five categories of enemies and you just need to slot them in for each layer you travel to.
Now I will talk about the two biggest selling points of the game, which are the reasons the game is teeth-gnashingly difficult and extremely fun.
First is the enemy AI. Whoever did the programming for the puffer fish AI on the second level, hats off to you, I can never hit those guys from long range. Most enemies in the game have unique AI that determines their attack patterns, and it's enough that even after slaying a few hundred of the same enemy you can still be blindsided by their routine.
The second big selling point is the boss fights. There are seven levels to the game, and each one you get to choose which of a handful of bosses you'll be going after. Bosses range from insultingly easy (looking at you Puff Daddy) to basicly impossible without a perfect build (Charybdis). Almost every boss has some unique gimmick, and the level major bosses are as rewarding to fight as the challenge implies.
I have a few minor problems, like the rune issue above and the fact that you can never just strafe to dodge those stunrocks from the level three bosses, but in the end the game is very solid. Not something to be played all day and beat, but a fun thing to do with a few hours to kill.
Oh, and on the subject of spears, I've been using the spear you get for completing the in-game beastiary, but I'm only done with 60% of it, so I have no idea how I unlocked it.

I can sincerly recommend this game to video game players or rpg fans in general. It has an effective combat system with the class system being my personal favorite in the Final Fantasy series. Want to combine Monk with Summoner? The customizability is nearly limitless. The story elements are very excellent and the humor elements work to help the audience to cope with the horrificically dark story. Some may object to the over-the-top behavior of Exdeath. I personally disagree with this analysis. In fact he is my second Final Fantasy villain (just behind Golbez). His maniacal behavior highlights the threat that Exdeath poses to everyone and everything. He is also an effective strategist who uses the heroes and others to achieve his goals on mutiple occasions. Furthermore his minions were able to stay loyal to him over several decades. The scene with Galuf at the midpoint of the game was my personal favorite of the entire Final Fantasy series.
Even though I have played little time for the Steam version I have played the game elsewhere. I beat the game on the playstation 1 port and I just beat the Android port earlier this year. The main criticism of the game has some validity. The character sprites do look terrible but I can forgive that. This format is one of the first occasions where gamers could easily access this game. There had been three official ports: The Playstation 1 Port (which can be purchaseon PS3) THE gba Port and the ios port.There were few ways that non-Japanese gamers could legitimately play FFV. Now to conclude my long-winded thoughts I recommend this game thoroughly.
Final Score: 9.5/10

I have played all main Final Fantasy games and for some reason Final Fantasy V is my favourite. Before playing steam version, I have played the game on psone.
The story is very simple. First you need to save four crystals. After that you need to save the world by stopping main antagonist, who is simply just evil. Story is sometimes very serious, but it has a lot of funny moments so it's never too serious.
Job system is awesome. You can choose one job class at a time for each of the four characters. Then you can train the job until you get skill that you like or until you master the job. I only wish that you could choose more skills on default class. You can choose two skills on default class or thee on one other class. Still mastering different jobs do pay off by giving better stats. It's just fun to master many different classes.
I've noticed that some people have complained that game doesn't run smoothly. For me the counter said 60 fps all the time and I didn't notice any problems. Some people have complained that music is just the original music. I didn't mind that since I loved the music and it didn't need any fixing in my opinion. New sprites do look nice. I'm just happy that they didn't change animation much, since I loved the old animations. Only real issue for me in this game was when someone talked, there was a portray of the person talking. Most of these portrays didn't look anything like the character in the game.
This game had new classes and new dungeon compared to the psone version. New classes were nice and the dungeon seems cool. Unfortunately I haven't gone far in the dungeon yet, since you can enter there only after finishing the game.
Still if you own any other version of the game and you are not hardcore fan of Final Fantasy V, I'm not sure if you should buy this version unless it's on sale. Steam version has only few new things added compared to psone version and I believe that compared to GBA or iOS version, this has even less new features.

In a quantum leap of effort over F.E.A.R., the producers of F.E.A.R. 2 have decided to eschew the generic character naming convention of the first game, and give the protagonist of F.E.A.R. 2 a proper name. In the first game, the lead character was imaginatively named Point Man after Gun Man was rejected as being too specific since he can do Matrix style slow-mo kung-fu and kill without guns. Violent Guy was also considered but rejected as being too generic. Neo was already taken. This time you play a special-ops soldier named Michael Becket.
Continuing the story from the first game, the incredibly powerful ghost Alma has just been released from containment. Alma had previous been locked up in a science lab for over 20 years. Naturally being surrounded by nerdy science types for over 20 years and having to endure their annoying and incessant chatter on Hadron-colliders, Star Trek and whether Anakin really had a father or not, has driven Alma completely insane. Her top priorities are understandably to kill everyone (especially nerds) and getting a (non-nerd) boyfriend. Being a violent and vengeful ghost she sees a kindred spirit in trained-killer Becket and falls madly in love with him. Not only is Becket a hunky special-ops type that's good with guns, he's also handy about the house and not a bad cook. Unfortunately Alma being out of the dating scene for over 20 years does not know that the rules of dating have changed significantly since her time. Instead of the more sensible dinner and movie, Alma proceeds to woo Michael by killing all his friends and scaring the bejesus out of him. Tragically this doesn't work out too well.
For those familiar with the first game, the narrative style is identical and predictable, vacillating between fast-paced action set pieces and slow-burn psychological horror. Slow-mo is back but Mechs are a new addition. F.E.A.R. 2 is a worthy addition to the franchise and fans of the first game will probably enjoy this one. Best played at night and in the dark - just watch out for the Puppetmaster.

What a really unique game. It was about time that I got around to looking at this game as it has been on my list of games to play for a while now. Anyway, this game has an impeccable execution that really makes it shine. Everything from the story to the presentation is fantastic. For those who don't know (maybe there's some people out there) your essentially sitting in front of an old 90's computer going through a database of small clips from seven different interviews of a woman who is being accused for murder. There's a search bar on the top that allows you to sift through these clips based on keywords. Want to find all the clips where she says "murder," just search "murder" and the list will be brought up for you...although you can only look at the top 5 (if there are 61 clips, for example). This requires you to narrow down your search terms, getting more specific as you slowly start to learn the story behind this woman and the murder she is being accused for.
The woman (who's name I can't remember off the top of my head) gives a fantastic performance. She really sells the part and brings you into the story. It's a fascinating story...one full of weird twists and darker secrets. By nature of the game's search mechanic, you aren't going to experience the story chronologically, but instead in bits and pieces that you have to puzzle together. The game doesn't hold your hand and leaves you to interpret the woman's story and it's meaning. There's no "objective" to the game. If you feel like you've seen enough or think you know what's going on, you can simply leave and that's that. That's the beauty of this game. Some might find it frustrating, but I found it very powerful. You're truly on your own on this one. You draw the conclusions.
I don't want to say much else in fear of spoiling things, so I'll just say this. This is definitely a game worth a try if you haven't gotten around to playing it yet. Really great on all fronts.
Solid Gold

Captivating story told through a surprisingly simple mechanic. One can compare it to “Stanley Parable” as both games use unpretentious yet unique mechanic to deliver complex narrative, and as both games carefully balance player's freedom and story consistency.

A brilliant game -- one that uses the interactivity of gaming to present a story in a way that could not have been accomplished if you were merely watching the videos straight through.  To know too much ahead of time is to invite spoilers, but I'd highly recommend this game to anyone interested in why we create and tell -- and listen -- to stories.
Some reviewers have suggested the game lacks an ending.  But to the contrary, there is indeed an ending, one I find very emotionally satisfying and which successfully changes a player's perspective on the game.  (You will know it when you find it.)  Another common criticism is that the game lacks basic gameplay elements, and that the "play" aspect merely consists of keyword searches.  That is a valid criticism, up to a point; after all, the game isn't Overwatch, nor does it try to be.  But if your appreciation of gaming also includes those games that exist primarily to tell stories and to develop characters with whom you can empathize -- in short, if you enjoyed, e.g., To The Moon -- I think there's a strong likelihood you'll also enjoy Her Story.

A new way of telling stories. Brilliant!

Go play it!

This title was definitely an experience worth having. The fascinating way of traversing information to discover the entirety of the story was certainly a clever idea and while it wouldn't yield additional playthroughs, it was an interesting take on both, telling a story AND letting the player discover it at their own pace, having them feel like they've put in the work into the discovery of the story.
Presuming that you don't mind giving unusual games a bit of a bash, I'd recomment trying this one out just to see what in all it has in store. The story is interesting enough, but what it really nails is the setting and how it genuinely feels like you're in the place of the protagonist, genuinely doing research on the situation.
Now, that being said, I will say that discovering 100% of the information is not, strictly speaking, necessary. Depending on how clveer you are, you should be able to get the full story after finding about half the clips (more or less). However, once you're done with playing through the game, I'd recommend going into the game files. The reason why is that the individual videos are stored there, unencrypted and labeled in the exact chronological order that they should be to view all the interviews front to back. Queue all of those up in your favorite video player and enjoy, this way you can get the fully complete story without having to figure out what the last two or three bloody words are.

You play as Philip, a 30 year old physics teacher. After his mother's funeral, he receives a letter from his father, who has been presumed dead ever since Philip's birth. In his letter, he asks Philip to destroy certain cryptic documents, but out of curiosity, Philip decides to do some research and finds out the location of a mine in Greenland. He then goes on to investigate the mine on his own, which is where the game begins.
Penumbra Overture is a blend of survival horror, psychological horror, and adventure game. You will solve puzzles to progress further, while avoiding and outsmarting enemies. While there is a combat system, the game encourages you to be stealthy and cautions. Combat is pretty clunky and ineffective, mainly because Philip is just a regular guy, not an action hero. Puzzles are interesting and done well, but I did get stuck once or twice (however, I was never good at puzzle games anyway).
What makes this game shine is its atmosphere, sense of tension, immersion and isolation. Mysterious story only enhances that, but since this is the first episode in the series, not much is explained. Most of the information comes from notes lying around the place, and you better read them if you want to get the full back-story of the area.
In the terms of technical features, the graphics and sounds are solid and do the job, and the physics engine works well. Level design is decent, but since you are in a mine expect to see a lot of similar areas. Voice acting is not the best, but it's not cringe worthy either. Music is pretty good, it really keeps the tension going on and improves the overall atmosphere.
Because of the nature of the game the AI is not that complex and that's perfectly fine - enemies patrol the area and if they spot you, they'll chase you.
My complaints would be that after some time, enemies started to annoy me and get in my way. Probably because the enemy variety is pretty weak - there are only three different types of them and two of them are encountered only once or twice. Also, I didn't find this game really scary, especially in comparison to some of the later games from Frictional.
Overall it's a solid game, worth your time if you're a fan of adventure games with horror elements. It does a good job of setting up the basis for the series.
