I started this series with Supreme Commander and then moved on to Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance. I've played thousands of fun and amazing hours of the first two games and it only took me a few hours to find the horrible flaws in this one.
This game is nothing like either of the first two games in function or in spirit . It is an all around disappointment, with so many things changed for the worse. For example, build queues beyond your current resources (the ability to plan ahead) are gone. Units have been simplified and unit numbers reduced. The overall game has taken on the per-game-leveling mechanics as those seen in the Battle for Middle-earth II and Command and Conquer: Generals RTS games. Map sizes have been greatly reduced and the graphics are terrible: the units look like fisher price toys.
Basically, if you've never played the series, this game will be overly difficult to learn for what you get back from it and if you're a huge fan, like me, you'll absolutely hate the changes they've made.
One reviewer said something like "Chris Taylor has created a game that is, simultaneously, too simple for experienced players and too complicated for new ones". That about sums it up. This one should be nominated for "The Worst Sequel Ever" award.

As a stand alone strategy game it isn't bad. It's not great, and it's kind of bland, and the story is extremely lackluster, but it isn't awful. That said in comparison to the game it's supposed to be a sequel to (Supreme Commander Forged Alliance) it's absolute garbage. My recommendation is that if you want a GOOD strategy game then don't spend your money on this. Buy Supreme Commander Forged Alliance, bask in how it is a superior game in basically all ways, and deny that SupCom2 was ever made.
TLDR- Not a bad game as a stand alone, absolutely terrible game when put up in comparison to the game it's supposed to be the sequel to.

Ok I will start off this game by saying personally, while I do enjoy this game, I do not think that it is worth the $60 price tag that it is listed as here on steam.
Pros:
-Competitive multiplayer game modes are incredibly fun to play. It is not a literal FPS MOBA as some people say it is, but there are elements similar to a MOBA, such as minions, and sieging your enemies base or territory.
-Very broad lineup of unique characters. 25 were released with the game, and 5 more are to be added as DLC. Currently at the time of this review there are 27 characters.
-Has RPG elements that makes the game very addictive to completionists (like me.)
-Weekly updates and balance changes from the developers to make sure everything is in order.
-While its strongest aspect is the competitive modes, this game does have a story mode. Although, I would not consider it a full story mode. If you play through the whole thing at once you could probably knock it out in less than 5 hours.  Although, bosses in story can drop loot that you can put in loadouts to be used for your characters in all modes, so if you like the thrill of farming for loot and getting legendary drops, it stays quite interesting.
Cons
-Player base is low, so queue times for multiplayer matches are decently longer than what you are used to in other games. Also because of this it is common for low level new players to be put against high level veterans, which isnt fun for anyone.
-Story mode in my opinion is only good for farming challenges or for good gear drops.  If you are thinking of getting this game because you were a fan of the Borderlands series and you are expecting something like it, you will end up VERY disappointed. The story to me is very boring and repetitive, although the character lore is interesting.
-This game is overpriced, do not pay $60 for this. You can get this game on on other sites for less than $10. Honestly this game should have been released without the story mode as a free to play game, the model of this game already would work so well as a free to play game.
So personally, I think this game is fun, I will be playing it until it dies. The biggest enemy that this game has I feel is the fact that it is a $60 game. I along with many other people am hoping this game goes free to play because its the games only hope, I wouldn't even care if it was like Evolve and I lost all of my progress. This game is awesome and needs more people playing it.

This is a very surprising and surprisingly impressive game. It seems like such a simple premise but here's what makes it work:
- Over 200 video clips to go through and scrutinise
- An exceptional performance by the actress playing the suspect
- You only hear her side of the conversations so you figure out what questions are asked from her responses, facial expressions and body language.
- You view the videos out of order depending on your search terms so uncover the story in bits and pieces, and then must make sense of it.
- Completely believable writing, this comes across like a real crime. A very strong example of the 'unreliable narrator' - how much can you believe of what you're being told? You are basing your conclusions on only testimony, with almost no other evidence being presented.
- Once finished with the footage, you get a message from the detective, explaining a crucial bit of information you were without.
This doesn't feel like a game, it feels like a documentary showing 1990's grainy video footage of interviews with a suspect. It feels real and you get engrossed in uncovering the entire story, using more and more random keywords to find more footage... and you do. By the time you finally run out of footage to watch, you have a solid and quite tragic overview of the case.
This game requires patience but is well worth the effort. It is not that long but you feel satisfied when you're done, like you definitely got your money's worth.

This game is getting such bad reviews lately but I am here to recommend. The game does have a few small issues as far as the artwork goes, but the character portraits that appear during conversations give us the level of detail that the simple sprites cannot. The music is everything we know and love, so thats another plus. Here is my review on how I see things.
THE GOOD: Its freaking FFV! The job system allows for customization options that hardly any game truly allows. (want to be a monk with white or black magic? We got you covered. Each job that is mastered adds the base stats of said job to the freelancer class which is the default class you start out as. This gives incentive to master as many of the jobs as possible to maximize your stat potential. For instance, you mastered the thief, warrior, black mage, red mage, and white mage. This allows for you to doublecast black or white magic from mastering the mage class, while hitting like a truck because of the warrior stat in strength, high magic stats from the white and black mages, while wielding whatever weapon you want and filling the ATB gauge very fast, with the option of hitting for double the power using focus from the monk class! Be what you want to be.
THE BAD: Nothing is really changed from the mobile port besides the new boss they added and the portraits.
THE UGLY: Taking my nostalgia goggles off for a moment, the art direction is a bit odd, some grammar issues still exist, and of course there is no new real content. The new jobs at the end of the game from the GBA remake are virtually useless, but provide something new if you really wish to use them. The monster art looks better than the sprites themselves!
FINAL THOUGHTS: This game gets about an 8.5/10 from me. With enough support from the fans, we can get the game "fixed" to other fans expectations. The game is still the great FFV we all know and love, just with a wierd art direction this time around. If the art is nonappealing to you then wait about a month or two for the steam sale and see if its on there, either way I recommend this game for all who love final fantasy in hopes that this game sells well enough for a port of FFIX! I think most bases are covered in a lot of the other negative reviews with more views but I will say this, as a long time fan of this franchise Final Fantasy V and VI get no love... and here's just another chalk mark on the black board.
This remake was designed as a quick cash grab for mobile users, it was never Square's intention to port it to consoles / steam and it shows... If the screenshots weren't indication enough, it just looks incredibly shoddy.
I'm among the minority when I say I actually like the character portraits in the dialog boxes because that is the original art design for the game. It was hard to convey that level of detail in pixel form which explains why all the characters have wonky, vibrant colors on their clothing and outrageous hair colors. For example, Terra's hair in Final Fantasy VI isn't even green, it's blonde like Celes' but they had to give the character some kind of uniqueness other than the clothes they wear. Faris should technically look more like Edgar from FFVI as well but then people would get confused.
Until a true 3D remake is realized, this is as good as it's going to get. I can understand where Square was going with this, they wanted to keep the nostalgia alive and honestly, they did a good job on that front. The game literally plays identical to it's Famicom counterpart, the way the characters move, the way the cutscenes play out and of course, the untainted original soundtrack (which I'm actually thankful for because that Walse theme is tight)
Enemy sprites are just insanely well done, the character sprites however are lackluster and that's really a shame considering how much exposure they get so quickly. You literally aquire all 4 party members within a half an hour of gameplay and aquire your first 6 jobs in about an hour. I always remembered switching jobs and looking different was a fun process but considering how tacky the models look in this game, some of the uglier job costumes look even uglier.
If you have an itch to re-play Final Fantasy V, then I would look for a discount, I got mine from GMG. You could also just grab an emulated version because the new jobs (from the GBA version) are garbage and you aquire them way too late in to the game for them to have any kind of relevant impact on your success. I never did like the tacked on crap that artificially extended the games beyond the final dungeons... that stuff is meant for newer age games, not retro stuff, it just doesn't fit and seems really corny. I was never a fan of artifically extending the life of video games any way... like collectables and junk... waste of time.
If you've never played Final Fantasy V in your life, I'd suggest getting it if you REALLY want the experience... however, I would recommened both parties not buy it at full price and try not to support this level of incompetence. We'll never get proper remakes of these games (FFV and VI) if people keep supporting garbage that's just barely passable.

Guacamelee! is a well-designed game where the backtracking isn't frustrating and you're fed new powers at a good (albeit predictable) pace.
Some parts are really hard (there are several "Chac Mool" arenas that test your various skills and a general challenge arena) but optional. I'm not great at the game, and I've made it to the final boss, so it's not impossible (although I don't know if I'll beat the boss).
I've definitely had some euphoric moments when I finally got good enough to progress past a challenge -- and I kept at it because it felt like I was making progress. I often give up on notoriously hard games because I feel like I hit a wall. That's not a big problem in Guacamelee!. I gave up on some of the "Chac Mool" arenas that test your various skills and some rooms in the challenge arena, but they're optional. Yesterday, I hit a wall at the final boss (but I might come back to fight another day).
The humour is good, but the fourth-wall breaking varies from hilarious to grating (eventually I grew tired of the homages to other games). The atmosphere is great (I love Mexican themes) and the music is pretty good.
Overall, I think Guacamelee! is a lot of fun and the drop in coop is great.

Part strategy, part adventure, part hex grid turn-based combat Renowned Explorers gives you control of three adventures of your choosing as you tackle expeditions around the world trying to be recognized as the best explorer in the International Society.
The aforementioned mix of genres works quite well and makes Renowned Explorers a good game with lots to offer despite its lacking tutorial and somewhat repetitive nature.
-nice comic book graphics
-it's a pretty lighthearted game with funny encounters and dialogues
-a good selection of different explorers with specializations and skills
-light RPG elements (level up bonuses, equipment slots) help you develop your group as you see fit
-procedurally generated levels help replay value
-simple to learn but hard to master gameplay mechanics
-several difficulty levels to choose from can give you a more relaxed or truly roguelike experience
-if you like the genre and trying new adventuring groups you'll find a good amount of replay value
-the tutorial is ok when explaining the basic mechanics but fails to explain others properly leaving you trying to learn how some things work by trial and error
-while they are procedurally generated there isn't a huge amount of different expeditions to choose from, so it can feel repetitive after a while
-some difficulty spikes, especially around bosses
Renowned Explorers was a bit hard for me at the beginning, the tutorial leaves you a bit stranded and it took a bit to properly understand how the various moods/ actions worked during combat, its rock paper scissors take on strategic fights can feel overwhelming at first and you'll either need to try (and fail) a few times or read some guides before you're comfortable with it: the same goes for its somewhat intricate token system that represents the resources gathered from each expedition and how it interacts with your entourage choices.
Once you're comfortable with it the game is truly fun and provides a good challenge, the fact you can choose a balanced team or one leaning more towards a certain interaction style ( aggressive, devious or friendly) will let you try different explorers to see how they do when faced with certain challenges and bosses: all things considered Renowned Explorers feels like a solo boardgame with somewhat complex but well oiled mechanics, one that rewards a deep knowledge of its design while giving you a good amount of freedom in how you decide to face its challenges.
You can expect a few difficult encounters though, some bosses can especially be a bit aggravating due to their abilities or a constant stream of reinforcements, and if your team is weak against a certain opponent's attacks you'll have an even worse chance of winning: the other problem I see in the game is that the number of expeditions is somewhat limited, while the levels are randomly generated the enemies within and final bosses will largely stay the same so things can feel a bit too same-ish after a few playthroughs. I'd also point out that there's no persistent bonuses or character growth so each playthrough starts as a clean slate, this will be ok for some but others will be disappointed you have nothing to show or gain from your past adventures.
All things considered Renowned Explorers is a very good game and an easy recommendation for lovers of the genre that don't mind taking the time to learn its mechanics and its reliance on repeated playthroughs.

It allows the franchise to evolve with players pulling and dragging the tracks making it more flexible. The second game in the series basically had lots of customisation and built on the first title however the newest game lacks themes and other objects but with more from the developers it soon might improve, the game also has user generated support so lots might be provided from the community of tycoon fans. The third game in the series bacially went 3d and wanted to expand everywhere which in my opinion didnt work and pushed many gamers back to the 2 originals, the UI and campaign were so bad I continued playing RCT2 as it seems the developers went crazy with zoos and water parks however with the newest game going back to its roots and starting again its seems the franchise can get back to its best! Many of the newest games features are very promising and deserve some time to be made perfect, Im willing to wait and share my experience with the developers to make the game decent and a standard which the originals set!

Ok I will start off this game by saying personally, while I do enjoy this game, I do not think that it is worth the $60 price tag that it is listed as here on steam.
Pros:
-Competitive multiplayer game modes are incredibly fun to play. It is not a literal FPS MOBA as some people say it is, but there are elements similar to a MOBA, such as minions, and sieging your enemies base or territory.
-Very broad lineup of unique characters. 25 were released with the game, and 5 more are to be added as DLC. Currently at the time of this review there are 27 characters.
-Has RPG elements that makes the game very addictive to completionists (like me.)
-Weekly updates and balance changes from the developers to make sure everything is in order.
-While its strongest aspect is the competitive modes, this game does have a story mode. Although, I would not consider it a full story mode. If you play through the whole thing at once you could probably knock it out in less than 5 hours.  Although, bosses in story can drop loot that you can put in loadouts to be used for your characters in all modes, so if you like the thrill of farming for loot and getting legendary drops, it stays quite interesting.
Cons
-Player base is low, so queue times for multiplayer matches are decently longer than what you are used to in other games. Also because of this it is common for low level new players to be put against high level veterans, which isnt fun for anyone.
-Story mode in my opinion is only good for farming challenges or for good gear drops.  If you are thinking of getting this game because you were a fan of the Borderlands series and you are expecting something like it, you will end up VERY disappointed. The story to me is very boring and repetitive, although the character lore is interesting.
-This game is overpriced, do not pay $60 for this. You can get this game on on other sites for less than $10. Honestly this game should have been released without the story mode as a free to play game, the model of this game already would work so well as a free to play game.
So personally, I think this game is fun, I will be playing it until it dies. The biggest enemy that this game has I feel is the fact that it is a $60 game. I along with many other people am hoping this game goes free to play because its the games only hope, I wouldn't even care if it was like Evolve and I lost all of my progress. This game is awesome and needs more people playing it.

Short version: play this game. It's good, klunky at times, but good. Also, DISCLAIMER: I'm an active community member and an amateur caster for the game. I'm neck deep in this. Just saying.
Long version: Battleborn has a certain charm and charisma to it that is indicative of the developers past achievements (these are the folks that created Borderlands) and that is by far the strongest point of it. The writing, characters, world it's all oozing with the same style of humor. In one mission you have to escort a walking sentry called Wolf that has had his survival inhibitors removed so he has no idea that death is fatal and permanent, all so he can do a suicide attack easier. Throughout the mission, he keeps blissfully talking about returning home and asking what the characters are doing after the "suicide mission that he totally will make out of". A bit cheesy, but the voice acting delivery of every character is fantastic.
Battleborn is a huge package of a game. Like, EXTREMELY HUGE. While the story PvP uses the same assets as the story mode (and vice-versa) no level is repeated and everything is always brand-new, which means that the devs have created 14 huge levels, all unique in their own way, filled with randomized locations for the 5-item chests (best chests in the Story mode).
Every character has at least 20-30 minutes of dialogue each, with more lines coming in every time we have an update (keep in mind we have 27 characters at the moment, do the math).
You can level up individual characters and your own level to unlock more powerful skills and special skins and unique gear for that character.
Characters are unlocked through hard work, not bought (with the excepetion of the DLC characters that can be bought with in-game currency)
Every characters is good, every character is fun, every characters is funny. So it begs the question: why isn't this game more popular?
Because people don't understand it and quite honestly, I don't blame them.
You have shooting, but it's not a traditional FPS. You have grinding, but it's not a RPG. You have unique characters with active and passives skills and an ultimate, but it's not a MOBA. Battleborn is a mixed bag of mechanics borrowed from those genres to create its own thing and it's very confusing. Heck, I go into it thinking I'd only play the Story mode and now I'm going into PVP all the time. That's how weird this game is: it made a non-competitive player become competitive.
However, it's because of this weirdness that people are put off by it. They compare it to other games and then people get in and feel lost when in reality, Battleborn works because of that crazy combo. Sadly, it is still an online multiplayer game and without people to play, it loses the appeal (not to mention lack of world servers is really bad, I had to change my Steam download servers to US - New York region just so I could get some matches going)
But perhaps you're not convinced that this game deserves your attention (and more importantly, money). Perfectly understandable. But if you want a game that can pull some laughs out of you even in the middle of a crazy heated battle, Battleborn is that game. If you want a game full of achievements and grinding (Near 100 hours and only 80-something% on the Story achievements) Battleborn is that game. And most importantly: if you want to have fun with a nice community that is actively trying to make the game more fun and better, Battleborn is that game.
I should know, that's one of the main reasons I'm still writing. They welcomed me as a caster and I have been having a blast playing and narrating the matches ever since.

Pretty much none.  Most of, if not all the missions you play in this game are extremely isolated and I like that, very much.  The base story is that you, and three of your friends are proffesional bank robbers taking on the biggest and most elaborate hits.  Ranging some simple bank heists, to raiding a panic room for cash, to even stealing blood from a patient in a hospital.  While the mission total is short, (With the games expansion pack only offering an additonal two) there can only be around 9 heists.  But the RNG makes for great staying power.
PAYDAY: The Heist is  of the two, one of the more grounded games.  It knows its engines limitations, and is sparing with the spectacles.  PAYDAY 2 on the other hand, is a much more... Outstanding game.  With PAYDAY: The Heist, you are only able to go loud for a majority of the missions, or heists.  Only one two can be stealthed, by not fully.  Working in horde based siege modes, there are four phases to a mission:
You and the crew are just casing the joint.  Taking in security previsions, placements and looking for objectives
The heist has just gone loud.  The police have just showed up, and it's about to go down.
The police will, in favor of tacticallly approching your arrest, will instead besiege the area with armed forces.  Overwhelimg your defensives, on the higher difficulty.  They have a tendancy to really throw down the gauntlet.

This is the phase where the police pull a tactical withdrawl.  Though only briefly.  You use this time, to med-up and restock.  In certain cases, trade allies from custody.
This is, where the PAYDAY series has always managed to impress.  The Soundtrack, compased by Simon Viklund, then Overkill's inhouse music producer and dialogue director, impresses as always with a booming soundtrack.  While the songs can not be interchanged, like in PD2, they are much more tied into the heist you're playing.

This game has one of the best random terrain generations I've ever seen. Combined with decent FPS experience and good fighting vs mining ratio, I am happy to recommend it, despite not having a lot of content at this moment.
In Rogue Islands you take control of a dwarf on a journey to save his tribe. It’s an FPS-meets-minecraft kind of game, with voxel graphics and heavy use of roguelite principles. You travel from island to island on your boat and complete simple missions: simply gathering enough fuel to move forward, visiting the “spirit tree” to meditate on top of it or fighting the boss. The gameplay on every island can be split into three parts: exploration, resource gathering, fighting. As for the gathering part: at the very least, you need to gather enough fuel to move to the next island, but there’s much more resources (food / magic gems) at each location. The monster hunting part is pretty straight forward: use your spells to kill monsters, they drop “souls” that can be used for upgrades later on.
-	The islands are huge. The random terrain generation is also very well done, generating caves / mountains / ponds and placing random resources. I don’t know how they did it, but most of the time you get the feeling that no way the current map you’re playing on could have been randomly generated. I’m very impressed.
-	The graphics are well done: very colorful, lots of effects and due to the right sound choice you get the feeling like you are in 8-bit world. The monster death effects deserve extra mention: killing stuff is just cool.
-	The FPS mechanics are alright. It’s not impossible to dodge the enemy projectiles, but you need to make an effort to do this. The projectile impacts are well done, but the weapon shooting does not always feel powerful. Don’t get me wrong, the weapons are in fact quite powerful, it’s just your first weapon, wand, which you are going to use most of the time, does not give impression of power. Projectiles just sort of fly away from it. It’s just an aesthetic feeling: impacts done right, shots – not so much.
-	The difficulty seems just right. If you make mistakes: you die and reset, if you play / dodge correctly – you progress further. There’s not much random involved in the combat itself, which makes it deterministic and not luck-based.
-	As of now, not big enough variety of monsters: first two boss models are the same. At the first ¾ islands, you are going to encounter 3-4 types of enemies at most. Again, this is OK for the early access title, but I think it’s fair that I warn you.
-	If you are playing with keyboard/mouse, but have controller connected, it’s still going to vibrate (which essentially means that you’ll have to disconnect it from your pc when playing).
-	No hotkeys to switch between weapons (spells). You have to press right mouse key, then the circular menu opens and you need to navigate to the one you need.
-	As of the current moment, the game crashed `4 times upon my death within ~6h of playing. Not a huge deal (since you died anyway), but still gets on your nerves occasionally. After patch today I played for ~3 hours and did not encounter any crashes.
-	After alt-tabbing, the mouse pointer is not captured inside the game window (meaning it can go over the game window bounds if you have 2 monitors like I do – meaning you’ll probably die since the game is not pausing on alt-tab).
I don’t think it’s bad trait, but I have to warn you that it’s a roguelite after all, so all who like hoard resources are going to be disappointed as there’s really no easy mode :) Despite the lack of content in Early Access version on launch and some inconveniences, the main gameplay loop is really well-done and I had fun playing for about ~9 hours at the current point. The terrain generation is really original and all the randomly generated landscapes/islands never felt repetitive, as I was eager to explore them and find the resources every single time. The game is really fun even at this point and I can confidently recommend it: there’s not much content yet, but the developers mentioned that it’s going to cost $9.99 during early access. For this price - it’s a steal and if you like the idea of it – there’s no reason not to buy it.

Gone is the intrigue. Gone is the intelligent gunfights. Gone is the sense of 'FEAR'.
FEAR 2 is unfortunately a game that virtually feels lost during its development. Monolith is the studio who made the popular Shogan game previous to FEAR, and FEAR 2 is some kind of bizarre cross-over. The franchise at this point has become lost in translation. It no longer has the slow pace, building tension, between amazing gunfights. The whole game has become a B-movie sci-fi chiller. Enemies now consist of dumb sparsely populated goons in crappy generic-looking masks.
But as initially fun as it may seem to jump into a mechanical military exo-suit, and start blowing everything up - you soon realise Monolith have succumbed to the Call Of Duty cliché. The fun wears off very quick and you remember you wanted to play FEAR, not Mechwarrior.
It's a damn shame. FEAR with its smart enemies should have been the template for future FPS games but instead we're stuck with dumb AI and scripted events thanks to the obsession of console-oriented games (COD).
I can only reommend this on the strength of a half decent FPS, it nearly has nothing in common with the first game. Big disappointment.

I'm not going to compare this version with the others. I'll just say what this game is for people who never played it.
This game is pretty awesome! The story is a bit cheesy but entertaining, but the gameplay is really the star of the game. You can pick the character's jobs and combine them with abilities you learned with them to improve what your characters can do in the game. For example, if you play enough as a Black Mage, you can add the option to cast black magic on your Knight. If you learned Knight's "Guard", you can put it on a Monk, which can naturally use "Counter" and it will counter-attack any attack while not getting hit at all.
The game is huge, has lots of enemies to fight, with lots of different tactics to fight them. Add the customization of the jobs and abilities, and you have a lot to play with.
The game uses sprites, as it's just a remaster of the old SNES/GBA version of the game. It's not high-tech or anything, but it preserves all the gameplay elements of when it was released. It was a very good game back then and it continues a very good game now.
Have you wondered why people like Final Fantasy so much? This is not a Final-Fantasy-like game, this is the real deal. Buy it.

A truly fantastic platformer/fighting game. Combat system is a bit slow at first, but after a while getting used to it, feels incredibly smooth. Sountrack is nothing short of amazing, graphics are colourful and lively and humour... depends on your tastes I guess. I found it charming with amount of references this game manages to make, although at least half of those are internet memes.
One of most amazing features is that platforming puzzles, excluding two or three, can not kill you. Failing a jump, game teleports you back and you can repeat jumps until you perfect it. And speaking about platforming, while beating game normally won't have any extremely hard challenges, there are few very tough ones if you want to see alternate ending.
The only downside for me is that base game difficulty is very low. Until very last showdown, it was tough to actually die to combat even after making ton of mistakes. That includes killing bosses you never saw patterns before. Thanksfully beating game, or putting code in, unlocks hard mode, requiring more skillfull combat, and bosses change their behaviour and attacks making them real threat.

This was my 2nd favourite of all the FF games, only behind Tactics. I feel it's worth the buy, a great nostalgia trip and a few new job classes added to the game.
I only have a couple gripes about the game, the first being the character portraits. They look great, but if you have any issues with consistency, it will bug the hell out of you that Lenna and Faris' portraits have them with whiteand blonde hair, when their in-game sprites have pink and purple. A simple to fix oversight, but it doesn't take anything away from the game itself.
The bigger issue I have is that the cursor will occasionally move to random selections on its own. It's quite frustrating when you're in a simple battle that only requires some mashing of the A button to win, and instead of attacking (the top selection of your actions) you randomly waste an elixir on a character with full health because the cursor moved to items for no reason whatsoever. This issue is more relevant to gameplay, but nothing worth saying you shouldn't buy the game.
Overall, the game is fun just as it was when it originally released, just make sure you pay attention to what your cursor is doing so you don't waste powerful items. And if you have OCD, just try not to pay attention to the portraits when Lenna and Faris talk.
Happy adventuring!

As of this current review 15 hours put in.
Why am I recommending this? Because, despite the obvious lackluster character sprites and other random graphical issues that have come up. I have willingly put 15 hours of my life into playing this game that so many seem to call "garbage" because of some of the most asinine reasons.
Do I think this could have been a better game if some actual attention was put into some aspects? Of course, but that could be said for a large number of games that have been released recently, and even more in the past.
Did I get a huge hit of nostalgia causing me to think, 'Here I go again...' when the overworld music started or a particular scene occurred? Absolutely, and that's what makes this game a recommended choice for me.
Not because it looks good but because the story in this game resonated enough with me to actually put forth the effort to play it once again on a different platform, willing to enjoy it and actually work the grind of leveling jobs.
Shoot this down as a "fanboy" approach if you want, but Final Fantasy V is one of the games back before we got writing such as FFX, and to an extent FFXIII.

So far, I am about at the water crystal, so not very far into the game. (I have completed other versions of the game.)
I am enjoying this version of Final Fantasy V. While not a remaster, the sound quality is improved over the original version, and the enemy sprites look quite good. I am not a big fan of the character sprites, but they don't look "bad". Just a little too basic for my personal taste. The job system is just as addictive as ever, and will provide hours of enjoyment.
I have heard there are some technical issues with stuttering and framerate, but I have not personally experienced any of these issues (using an i5 and GTX 970). Some of the minor graphical issues with the tiles are slightly annoying, but don't detract from the overall experience.
This won't go down as the greatest port of a game of all time (I would have been overjoyed to see character sprites like the FF IV PSP remake), but it's definitely worth checking out if you are a fan of the series.

Simply can't recommend this for Supreme Commander, Forged Alliance, and Total Annihilation fans.
Gas powered drop everything that made Supreme Commander and Forged Alliance (and Total Annihilation for that matter since SupCom 1 is a spiritual successor) great and unique. They instead end up making a C&C/StarCraft clone with supreme commander skin slap on it to feed to the masses.
Unit selection is super small, using a upgrade system pretty much like C&C/StarCraft use, experimental unit go from Massive Godzilla like monsters that cost a fortune as they were in SupCom 1 to little more then High end units that are a dime a dozen, and they also dropped the whole tiered unit/Structure system (tier 1 units building tier 2 etc).  Maps are super tiny, and the streaming build system of supreme commander/FA (and TA) is drop in favor of the same system that C&C/StarCraft and nearly every other RTS uses.
For those not experience with this, Supcom 1 and TA had systems where you could start building unit/Structures and their construction would slow down or stall if you ran out of resources. But you could build high end unit and Structures even if you lack the upfront resources, with it just taking a while to do so, slowly add to them as you get the resources.
This build system on top of large maps (to very large maps) and a broad choose of units, is what made SupCom 1 and TA so different then nearly every RTS and allowed for a large variety of play styles and strategies. In SupCom 2 they chose to instead dropped all this, with the game using the same style of systems that nearly every RTS uses.
So if you prefer Starcraft 1&2 and C&C over SupCom 1 you might like the game, but if your a Total Annihilation and supreme commander player and prefer their play style you most likely will not care for this game.
I force myself to play though the campaign, and a few skirmishes before uninstall the game. Personally I could possible deal with the unit style changes but the tiny maps and the build system changes just turned it into a another clone of many other games.
Doesn't have the epic scope of the first game or Forged Alliance, but it's still pretty fun.

In all honestly, For those who have never played supcom 1 or forged alliance (nor own them),  I would not see you a fool to get this game, it does have some things going for it, like smoother graphics, faster pace (very good for multiplayer games), and they
add a little more flavor to commanders in places where it was non-existent.
But what tears me straight toward saying "No, I would not recommend this game." is that it is a HORRID sequel compared to the two stars behind it. First we were graced with Supreme commander, which practically gave birth to the level of RTS we see so much of now (or surpassed in scale as Sins of a Solar Empire did). Forged alliance enhanced the graphics of supcom 1 and added a whole new faction that was mentioned several times in supcom 1, the seraphim, and a multitude of new units. Sins of a Solar Empire Rebellion and Supreme Commander: Forged alliance are literally the only two RTS games I play anymore, I am such a huge fan of them.
I like many other fans of the series got this game expecting the same magic, but when I realized Square Enix was involved in this project and not THQ (A company who I later learned had essentially fallen apart on hard times). My heart sank slightly, as I knew because of that, there were going to be some serious shifts in gameplay mechanics. It really hit rock bottom as I jumped in and started playing...
I immediately walked into the campaign, and after seeing the sheer madness of the Forged alliance campaign.... I beat the Supreme commander 2 campaign in just a day or two...
a good start. The whole story lacked much of the attention grabbing that could be found in Supcom 1 and Supcom Fa, it seemed to just guide my hand the entire way like I was a child that didnt know what to do, RTS games shouldnt do that... EVER (Aside from a newbie campaigh which I have no objection over). I will give credit in that the story of supcom 2 did have a rich background like that in supcom 1 and supcom FA... but it seemed like I was playing in a game set in an alternate dimension rather than a game set not very long after the end of the seraphim threat... the only character from supcom 1 and FA that carried over at all, was Gustaf Brackman... a shame... especially since the end credits of FA showed QAI rebooting... so that bonus bit no longer fits in, further supporting my say that this game hardly lines up with being set after forged alliance. The story that takes place
supreme commander 2 was like a crap sequel to not one but two emmy nominated blockbusters (Supreme commander 1 and FA)
Back to the gameplay for a moment. I do want to give the devs of this, and chris taylor, credit for keeping some little flair from the original two games, like the cybrans having ships that can walk on land, etc. But I dont know what was going on, either Chris Taylor had far less say in how this game was developed or he was on some sort of drug when he was working on it. There is extremely little reason to
use naval units as there is such a lack of variety of them from what I recall. Naval units weren't the only thing lacking, as there was a sense of emptiness in the manner of units, so all I ever ended up doing was nuking AI or spamming so many of a single unit that it didn't matter
what the AI did, they would get annihilated, even with the considerably smaller max amount of units compared to the first two games. The experimentals don't even look like they would hold up against their prequel counterparts, the Megalith II looks like a baby scorpion compared to the Megalith I, which outsized the monkeylord (which I
crack a smile that they put into this game as DLC.). When using them in supcom 2, they feel ludicrously more fragile than their supcom 1 counterparts, which i don't see the reason for really considering that in supcom 1 and FA you could easily take them out by just spamming what they are weakest against... (for galactic colossi, GUNSHIPS... LOTS OF GUNSHIPS).
What hit the final nail of the coffin for me was research..... just....
? What is the point if i don't get to use everything in the research tree? WHY DID YOU NOT KEEP THE UPGRADE SYSTEM THAT WORKED SO PERFECTLY!?
Knowing Square Enix's background, i know that they likely did as much as they could to keep the ship afloat, but man, Chris Taylor made a doozie, though a good one if he meant to kill the series here.
If you want a great RTS for multiplayer though, I WOULD recommend this SOLELY for multiplayer... otherwise...
.

+ AI reacts to gameplay styles, encouraging various playstyles to develop

+ Characters have interesting dialogue, and the cutscenes aren't boring/awful.
+ Research/development gameplay is intuitive. I spent a lot of time kidnapping Russians to make new guns.

+ Movement is fluid, never clunky.
+ Each mission encourages multiple approaches and replayability, especially when trying to get a high mission score.
+ The funny aspects are consistent, completing the whole off-the-wall vibe the game gives off.
- DLC list is a little long, but it is only filled with cosmetic stuff.
- Research/development sometimes has really long arbitrary wait times.
- The few side quests that repeat can be repetitive. (negigible)

This game is by far the best Hitman in the series, even till this day. The playability, even on this platform, is exceptional. No lagging, rendering and most of all no crashing (windows 8). Despite having a lot of options and weapons and ways to use them etc... everything is easy to use after the tutorial mission, nothing too complex. The graphics are awesome, especially taking into account that this game was released over 8 years ago!
Hours of fun is to be had with this game, it's entertaining to go and play the game back to do things a little different and see which route to take is the most rewarding one. The introduction of new systems in the series such as a cash system, notoriety system and conventionally a rating system. Each one tying everything in the game together, demontrating why your approach has earned you your reputation/money whether good or bad. Axiomatically the stealth route is the most fruitful, but to blast your way through the game and become notorious can be extremely fun too.
There are 13 immersive and addicting levels in the game, each taking around 30-60 minutes to complete, so you will certainly have hours of fun. Each level is beautifully designed and shrewdly thought out, making Agent 47's world one which you will want to go back to again and again. Despite the linear narrative in the game and the ineviable ending, how you get there is what makes this game unique. You notice new things as you go back and play again, noticing different geographical approaches or the fact you completely missed a secure room which takes you on a different route to achieve your assassination(s).
The AI need a mention in my review for the vast improvement the developers have made, contrasting previous titles. They are much more intelligent in every sense you can think of when approaching a conventional stealth assassin game. They no longer blow your brains out for wanting to go through a door that is restricted, they just become aware and suspicious of you for wanting to do so. They will ask you to leave, if you do not comply, that's when they logically gun you down. Also, you can no longer hide in the most ridiculous place as the AI will look if they're suspicious of you being in there... for instance, if you shoot from a building and your notoriety shoots up, if you're in a building with a closet and you get in, they will get you out of there... the game prepares you to be more of a stealth killer, or just more prepared for the mini army about to come and get you.  A final mention on the AI is the fact they can see right through your disguise if you do not use them wisely. If you put on a disguise, but have irregular patterns or do suspicious things, their awareness will raise and they'll eventually warn all other staff and before you know it everybody is coming after you. This again engages you to be much more shrewd about your assassination if you take the stealth approach to the game.
All in all a beautiful looking and atmospheric game which captivates throughout. The rebuild of the engine has made for great animation with amazing lighting effects and shadows and immaculate detail for a 2006 title. The only negative I can possibly fathom is that the camera can sometimes be a little awkward in tight spaces, such as an elevator, however this takes nothing from the overall playability of the game. It's definitely worth picking up at normal price, but at it's current discounted rate it would be crazy not to!
Pros:
- Enthralling and story-line that gives many hours to feast upon.
- Beautiful scenery in each level and a great atmosphere.
- Extremely easy to pick up and play due to it's incredible playability.
Cons:
- Camera can be awkward at times.
Rating: A stolid 9.8 out of 10.

I think at this point most people who know anything about the series have heard that Blood Money is the best. It is. The levels are surprisingly big, for a start. Well, they're not huge compared to say, any shooter, but they're packed full of stuff. Even on my fourth playthrough I still found new things. New ways to kill people, new ways to hide their bodies, etc.
It's also very open ended. There's refreshingly little guidance. No annoying helper character telling you which way to go, no big floating arrows, it just puts you in an area with instructions to ruin some poor sod's day and off you go. Yeah there are some optional hints to buy but besides that you're pretty much left to work it out for yourself.
This approach does cause some problems, sadly. It means that save scumming is heavily encouraged, as there's a lot you can only work out through experimentation. Often it's not entirely clear which disguises will allow you in which area, but thankfully you're usually allowed to leave the area and find another way in rather than being shot on sight, so that's handy, but it's less forgiving with the actual kills. The NPCs are very unpredictable. It's quite likely that another character will walk in while you're busy killing someone, and there's no way to see it coming or prevent them from spotting you once you've started. Once you have been spotted it's usually easiest to just reload a save. You can try to shoot your way out, but while you can finish the level this way it won't be nearly as satisfying. You can also leg it and put on a different disguise, but a couple of times the guards would shoot me on sight even after doing this. Why? I don't know.
This sort of thing can get very frustrating at times, but thankfully the positives of the game outweigh this. Walking into a building, killing your target with little extra damage and walking out again unnoticed is a great feeling. The newspapers at the end of every level add to the sense of acheivement, sure, but they are pretty limited. There's only a couple of things they can say. It'll say what weapon you used, whether you killed anyone besides the target and if there were any witnesses. It'll also criticise your aiming skills every damn time because the guns are just shockingly inaccurate. Even when I was sure I hit every shot it'll still tell me that I missed like 50 of them. I felt insulted.
One final note: the notoriety system. The basic idea that you get ranked based on how well you performed the kill and how many witnesses you left is good, but in practice it basically changes nothing. You can just pay to have it reduced, and I could easily afford it every time. It supposedly means that NPCs will be more suspicious of you but as I never actually had any notoriety I don't know how true this is.
Despite these issues the game is still great. There are few games that do anything similar. Even the older Hitman games kind of feel more like spy games than assassin games. You'd generally deal with the military rather than being in any public areas, whereas Blood Money offers a wide range of levels in which to be a total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. There's just nothing else like it and it's a whole lot of fun.

While on the load screen for the encounter the game crashed at 5%. I thought maybe it was a one-time thing, after all the first time launching games isn't always perfect, so I tried again. I went through the intro and related process again only to have the game crash once more upon entering the loading screen for an encounter at 5%. I did this a few more times with similar results. Encounter loading screen crashes at 5%. Every. Time. At this point I'm convinced it just won't work on my PC and I can't for the life of me figure out why. It looks like a really fun game so it's a real shame I can't play it. I've seen on the support forums other people having the exact same "5% Crash" issue and the only response from the developer that I've seen was a sincere apology but no real solution. Don't spend money on this unless you're willing to gamble that it just won't work for your PC.

If you're looking for a game to capture the magic of Ernest Hemingway's The Old Man and the Sea, this is probably the closest you'll get.  It's a rogue-lite top-down shoot-em-up set in space and you're on a rocket powered surfboard as you fly through the black sea (re: space) throwing spears at space-fish and using your harpoon to violently rip body parts off of these space-fish.
It sounds like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t but nothing I said is false or exaggerated.  It's all genuine gameplay and it feels awesome.  It feels great to rip the leg off of a giant space-frog and then finish perforating it with your infinite supply of javelins.  The items all add significant choice of how you alter your gameplay, and the consumables are all fairly interesting.  It's a fun roguelite with a creative setting and a unique aesthetic.
The description claims RPG, but I wish it were removed because the only remotely RPG-like feature is the inventory.
A few complaints:
- the terrain kinda sucks and is frustrating to move around and is pretty dull in general
- it's annoying/tedious to find things in the world because the sonar (radar) is small and local and doesn't show chests
- some elements of the UI don't quite match aesthetically, so there's a weird disconnect (minor complaint at best)
- the screenshots on this Steam page shows a lot of items but items seem much more rare than the screenshots suggest, leaving you starving for something to equip half the time
- chests are very underwhelming for how tedious/annoying they are to hunt down
These complaints are all acceptable to me considering how fun the game already is and the fact that this game is in early access makes me hopeful that the devs will address these complaints over time.  And they've promised updates EVERY 7 DAYS.  That's awesome!

My overall experience before writing this review (2 hours) has been great. I don't normally prefer the top down look, but the artwork fits the camera angle well. Gameplay is smooth and you feel in total control of all your actions. Finding new runes to upgrade your weapon and ship is always a blast! My most favorite aspect about this game at this very moment has to be the epic boss battles! I won't spoil much about them, but they are most definitely a challenge that feels amazing to overcome. Each run, (so far) if you expect to go all five rounds, should take about 30-50 minutes. This time for a game session is actually pretty perfect for a quick game every now and then.
TL:DR, if you're at all a fan of rogue-likes then give this game a shot. The devs are extremely passionate about this title so you'll have no worries of lack of feedback and content as this game progresses. Looking forward to checking out more new characters and bosses soon!

The bosses were incredible and interesting. Puff Daddy was far too difficult at first, but after I got used to him, it became a lot easier. I mean, the whirpool mouth insta-kill, the crazy under the screen tentacles, the vast number of little sucker-like poison shooters... I mean, I can't find anything to dislike. Here are my only problems. 1. Wyv the Elder has such a fast breath recharge that it's nearly impossible to rip out his tails. Also, his attack range is a bit too wide. 2. Belch Brothers are waaaaaaaaay to easy. 3. Can you even rip off ANYTHING from Puff Daddy? Enemies are all great, except for one stupid little bugger that makes my blood boil... THE SKITTISH LEAP-FROG. The idiotic little monstrosity looks great on the outside, but of the inside he's a green little ball of PURE EVIL. Overall, this game has been an amazing experience and I am proud to have just unlocked Gungnir ;). 4.5 out of 5 stars.

F.E.A.R. was an incredible game with an AI the likes of which had never been seen. It had a decent enough of a storyline that acted as a great vehicle for getting to explore a very Akira-esque underground facility. It's still visually stunning to this day (I played it a few months back).
All of those traits are dumped for F.E.A.R. 2. An alarming percentage of the enemies will stand off in the distance as you shoot them repeatedly in the head. If they aren't standing perfectly still, they will abandon cover and run straight at you. The storyline  is much more limited than the first. While I think the J-horror jump scares of the original were pretty dumb, the story was at least compelling enough to create a real sympathy for Alma. Alma plays a minor role at most in Project Origin, with the devs perferring you to have a strong bond with your mindless, soulless teammates while giving you no reason to feel connected to them except by telling you how close you all are. All of the imagination that went into the original facility is gone here. The sense of scale has been scaled down, if you will, to a couple of small buildings and an itty bitty underground lab.
Everything about it feels more like an ambitious yet terrible expansion pack than a real sequel. If you adore the original as much as I do, I would definitely suggest you just appreciate it and it's second expansion pack, Perseus Mandate, and leave F.E.A.R. 2 alone as to not spoil your fondness for the original.

So, I got a few bundles of
games that were mostly garbage to be tossed in the trash.  After digging through some bad titles, my eyes were set on
.  Immediately, I get a nostalgic Atari-age feel from the title, the graphics, and the gameplay.  So, when I booted it up, I had to know if the retro urge would be satisfied.  I was pleasantly impressed by the end result.
is a short Metroidvania that includes 4 bosses and can be speedrun in about 20 minutes (my best time is about 16 minutes).  You don't get a story.  You don't get a tutorial.  Instead, you get a simple plug-and-play game that essentially teaches you through an "Instinctive" tutorial you get from games like
or
had (if you've seen Egoraptor's
, then we're basically on the same page).  You run, you jump, you shoot, you dash.
I LOVE the neon look the developer was going for and I LOVE how true it stays to the retro conventions.  It really reminds me of Atari-age and NES-age games.  Back when games ranged from reasonably hard to Konami hard.  Though this game did have some rage-moments (mostly speedruns, few deaths, and perfect boss runs), but after a while, it's all manageable.
I also love the retro music, especially for the final boss himself.  In the end, I had a great experience from this title.  Is it worth the price?   Possibly so, but you still can't beat finding a good discount.  Suggested price range between 50-75 cents.

What is Dungeon of Zolthan?
Dungeon of Zolthan is a small Metroidvania game.
Gameplay
The game is controlled exclusively with the keyboard, there is no controller support. You use the WASD keys to walk around, Shift to dash and Space to shoot. You start off with just a basic weapon and jump, but can gain a higher jump, double jump, dash, rapid fire and eventually invinicibility while dashing. You have three hearts, and while basic enemies and traps take away one heart, mines and advanced enemies take away two hearts. Spike blocks instakill you, regardless of your hearts.
You can find up to four additional hearts, when finding one your life is fully restored. Most upgrades are gotten after boss fights, the hearts are completely optional after rooms with minor challenges.
The game is difficult at first but once you figured out how to correctly do even the more difficult passages, you can do that every time, kind of like in Super Meat Boy.
The few bosses are also niciely designed, and while they might not be completely original, at least each boss is unique and needs a different strategy to beat, without ever becoming overly difficult. In fact, experienced players will find the whole game and especially the bosses too easy.
The play time is short. I needed under 40 minutes on my first playthrough, but I skipped all optional upgrades by accident or rather luck.
Graphics
The graphics are very basic, the game looks like an 80s game, but plays fluid most of the time. The screenshots on the store page show how the game really looks like.
Sound
The sound is basic, although every action has a sound, but the background music is nicely done. Overall I can't complain as it fits with the chiptune character the overall style of the game.
As I said, the game is short, and in fact there is even an achievement for beating it in under 20 minutes. Getting all achievements took me around two to two and a half hours, but can probably be done faster by better players.
Recommended: If you know what you get, yes!

I've been a fan of Final Fantasy ever since I can remember. I remember playing on the SNES as a kid, enjoying the wonderful setting, story, and gameplay. This Final Fantasy V PC port doesn't lose that magic. I have thoroughly enjoyed this port so far, and I've played the original FFV game all the way through at least 3 times, so I feel I have a good base to compare with. I think Square Enix did a good job with this port, and at least a couple of "problems" other reviewers have with this game are simply config options that can be turned off in game. That being said, there are a couple of issues, and I'll list out the pros and cons.
Pros:
It still feels like the original game, just more polished
New animations are great
New art is pretty
Job system is addicting surprisingly in depth
The story is quite good
Optional autobattle - very nice for grinding
Cons:
Occasional glitches with the battle selection menu causes me switch rows or defend when I meant to attack
The texture tiling still has the same issue as the original, in that it's slightly off and you can sometimes see the lines between texture squares.
Portraits sometimes don't match character sprites (Faris portrait has blond hair, sprite has purple hair. Wut.)
If you like Final Fantasy, just get the dang game. It's great, just be prepared for plenty of grinding to get those job levels. If you've played the original FFV and liked it, get this game. It really twangs on the nostalgia chords and it's so much more fluid and pretty.

Where to start.
I love this game thorugh and through. It has grace and style i have not seen before. Right down to the angles of the polygons themselves, there is artistic quality. This is not to mention the extensive roster of heroes to enjoy. Yes, enjoy. As it is now there are 10 levels you gain as you move through each instance. Each level up you get to choose 1 of 2 different skills from the Helix. If you have that character maxed in rank (r15) you will have all of their 'mutations' unlocked which give 5 of those Helix levels a 3rd choice. This is good and you can level up to fit the situtaion at hand.
Now! The main 'action currency' is shards. You gain them around levels to upgrade your gear that you have put into a predetermined loadout. As is gearbox style they range from common (white) all the way to legendary (yellow-gold), with greens, purps and blues ofc. These may be activated using shards. There is gear to gain shards per second and is usually good to pop first when doing PvP. Shards can also be used to build things around the levels like traps, turrets and drone bots.
Are you a solo gamer? No probs. I played this game until command rank 40 (max100) without even touching the PvP mode. You like action and gankage to the max? PvP mode is more than a fun experience.
Story mode is comprised of 4 different modes. Normal (obv), Advanced, and both of those modes have hardcore mode which means if you die, you die. There is much challenge to be found in all of the above modes. You need help with heliophage on advanced? You can queue with a party. You can leave your lobby open to the public or just friends or no one!

Let's be honest this game isn't for everybody but there's a lot of heart and soul in Battleborn if you truly give it a try it doesn't disappoint. Behind the cartoon graphics (very much like Borderlands) and overwhelming amount of partical effects on your screen is a truly in-depth next gen game. The amount of titles, achievements, character levelling and in game customisation via the item and helix system makes for truly customisable gameplay and strategy. The game does have issues, the graphics aren't up-to-scratch (this is done on purpose tho) and the gameplay isn't for everybody as for a FPS there's rather large learning curve.
Yet this game truly has so much to offer and if you give yourself the chance to learn the helix system, learn the characters and enjoy the fresh and vibrant world either with your friends or against the world this game has a lot to offer. This game is for people who like games who take a chance on a concept and run with it, it's explosive and volatile but the payoff is a game I will be playing for years to come.

My frustration with, and the subsequent hazing by the Steam Community over, FTL has been well documented.  The game was solid, but far too random, frustrating, and unrewarding an experience for me to recommend.
Renowned Explorers is, in my opinion, FTL done right.  Instead of space, you are in the age of exploration with a crew of allies looking for treasure all around the world, so if that setting doesn't do it for you, I don't blame you for giving the game a pass, but everything else is great.  It's a turn based tactical combat game focusing on using both strength and speech to win the day, with the option to hit, insult, or chat with enemies to win them over to your side, each with benefits and drawbacks.  Say, you meet a nasty pirate captain.  Maybe, after you talk nice to him and win him over, he decides to go with you as a lobbyist, to bolster your rep...or maybe you pound him into the dirt and turn him in for an extra bounty...different solutions lead to different outcomes here.
Alongside the interesting combat mechanics, the game uses a spinner to determine success in many randomly generated actions, such as studying plants, climbing perilous cliffs, searching for treasure, dashing out of a collapsing tomb, etc. and this spinner uses your inherent % for success to give you a visual representation for these challenges, which is much more satisfying than a basic pass/fail.
You begin the game choosing a team of 3 explorers out of a total of 20, with one captain and two subordinates.  The captain perks and the synergy with certain people allow for some really interesting ways to play and combinations and this is aided further by a robust upgrade system which gives bonuses for research, which can affect all or some of your crew.
Overall, what I love most about this game though is how approachable it is.  FTL has a cripplingly high difficulty at times, making it easy for anyone to give up on it in frustration.  Explorers though, has multiple difficulty settings, each scaling well and allowing you to cater your experience, along with two modes, one which lets you retry encounters you fail and another which ends your game, allowing for another layer of challenge.  I feel in control when I play.  And while I haven't been Classic difficulty, which is on par with FTL, normal has been very good to me.  This is a game which, when jacked up in challenge, will make hardcore min maxers cry, but when played on easy or normal is easily approachable by kids or families.  It's a game which I think suits all ages, especially with the charming art style.
Explorers is, in my opinion, a great game.  It's fun and approachable, has a lot of variety, and there's many teams to try out and treasures to collect, with the devs adding new, free expeditions to go through all the time.  This game rocks.  Give it a look.

BSO actually almost reminds me of a top-down Shadow of the Collosus. The majority of the game-play revolves around hunting down and killing giant bounties, with each bounty requiring a unique approach. Each enemy in the game, even the small trash mobs that you will have to fight through to get to the big bosses, have components that you can destroy that will weaken their overall fighting capabilities. For example, if fighting a boss that shoots lasers out of it's eye, you can actually focus fire the eye and eventually removing the boss's ability to shoot lasers out of that eye.
BSO also features a Diablo-esque drop system, where the each enemy killed can drop items, including executables that have cool on-cast effects and equipables that give passive boosts. This drop system was actually one of the highlights of the game for me. Once the player accumulates a selection of equipable runes, the game-play starts to become very fun. You go from slowly chipping away at an enemy's defences to destroying entire sections of bosses in only a couple attacks.
My biggest complaint about the game in it's current state is that the early game can be rather off-putting. You kill slow and move slow until you find some rune drops. However, once you find a couple runes, thats when the real game starts. You kill trash mobs super quick, and actually start to feel like the legendary space hunter that you supposedly are.
In review...
Overall, it is difficult to write a proper review for the game, as it is currently missing many components that the developers plan on adding, ranging from entire play modes, to additional playable characters and levels. In it's current iteration, however, BSO is a game that should be watched, as it definitely has great potential.

is somewhat hard to describe in common terms. The best way to describe it would be as a twin stick shooter at its core, with permadeath, loot and epic boss fights. Levels are procedurally generated,fully destructible and come with dozens of different creatures to fight against. The tutorial also explains the controls both for keyboard and mouse and controller at the same time so you can choose whichever you prefer.
The main premisse of the game is pretty simple. Once in every decade, four contestants compete in a hunting tournament to find out who is the greatest hunstman and you play as one of these contestants. This tournament is divided in 5 rounds. Between rounds you’ll be placed on the Blacksea map, here there is some text dialogue between the contestants, they brag about previous deeds and mock each other. It is on the Blacksea map that you can visit the shop to sell your unwanted items or buy new ones and it is also here that you can choose different bounties to take.
Each bounty has its own description, such as difficulty level and stats such as “-% enemy damage” or “-% credits dropped”, aswell as the amount of credits you’ll earn upon completion. They are also divided into different biomes such as Tropical (green) and Crystal (blue). Each biome will reflect the enemies you’ll encounter once you’re there.
The boss and overall creature design is pretty damn good. The game does a really good job in showing you which body parts are weak spots and what kind of attacks that enemy has. Not only that, but no two creatures look the same.
During bounties you can choose either to farm credits by killing lesser creatures or you can go right away for the boss. After killing the boss you’ll complete the bounty and then you’ll be awarded score points based on your performance. It is these points that will rank you in comparison with the other contestants.
While playing you’ll also find chests that contain loot and that can be opened with keys, keys which you’ll find by killing enemies. In Blacksea Odyssey, loot is presented in the form of runes and potions that improve both your ship and your weapon. That said, this is where progression comes into place. Right now there is only one playable character, The Old Man, but more are on the way and I assume that each will fit a specific playstyle and each  will have its ups and downs. You’ll also be able to choose one of various spears to choose from. each with its own passive bonus and specific stats.
This is main part of the game so let me do my best to explain how it works. Besides attacking with your spear, you can also throw your harpoon into the creatures and use it to rip body parts off or to slow down said creature. However you can’t just spam both your spear and harpoon because some enemies have armoured body parts. This forces you to keep moving and flanking your enemies so you can deliver a fatal blow to their weak spots.
It is also worth mentioning that your ship has a booster built into it. This booster is divided into three different types, short boost, medium boost or long boost. Using the short one will use up one boost bar, the medium will use two bars and the long one will use three bars. This is very helpfull to escape from tight situations and to open passage on terrain, thus proving to be a life saver at times.
So, if you haven’t guessed already, the combat is very fast paced and you’ll find yourself using your boost to dodge and using your harpoon  at the right moment to slow down your foes and deal tons of damage.
One thing that bothered me at first was the fact that the camera is very close to your ship, but you also have a sonar to guide you, which will show you where creatures are on your minimap, as well as rock formations.
Blacksea Odyssey is as solid as a rock can be. It has tons of potential and I trust the developers to improve the game, since they update every 7 days if I’m not mistaken. The only thing that it needs right now is more unlockable characters and weapons (perhaps ships as well?). The combat is refined and extremely enjoyable and everytime you defeat a boss you feel like you’ve accomplished something great.
I highly recommend Blacksea Odyssey to people who enjoy hectic and fast paced fights with enough enemy variety to force you to adapt to new situations.

I just completed this game and would like to address a couple things that I read in the negative reviews.
A lot of the negative reviews mentioned that the game did not have controller support and they felt the controls were bad because you could not disable the double click to dash and they would often inadvertently activate it killing themselves. Both of these issues have been fixed. There is now controller support and you can bind the dash to a separate key with the option of turning double click to dash on or off. Other than that, I played with the keyboard and felt that the controls were very responsive and I had no problems.
I'm not sure why people are saying this is a very difficult rage game. I did not find it that difficult at all and completed it without many deaths. There is no permanent death and the game gives you very frequent checkpoints which you instantly respawn at when you die. Most of the reviewers saying that this game was difficult have probably never played an NES game or have forgotten what they were like. Everything in this game is designed very simple and follows a pattern. If you take a few seconds to understand how a mechanic works instead of just trying to run through the game blindly respawning every 5 seconds when you die, it will become quite easy.
The only negative thing I have to say about this game is that it is short. I took my time exploring everything I could and even backtracked through most of the game to make sure I didn't miss anything after getting an upgrade that would allow me to reach new areas and it still only took me 64 minutes to complete the entire game.
I feel that the current price of 99 cents is exactly where this game should be priced, it's like spending a few quarters on an arcade machine. I would recommend it to anyone that thinks they would be interested in this type of game knowing that it is very basic and is only an hour long.

I'll be upfront - I generally hate platformers. So while this game is a platformer, I'm not marking it down because it's a platformer. Let me at least address the one thing it does right - aesthetic design. With the exception of the final boss, the entire game seems consistent in design. Sorta feels like an anti-virus adventure to delete all of the viruses. Not bad. Now let's move onto the bad things.
One sound track. That's all there is. Okay, you'll hear 3 distinct-ish soundtracks in the game, but it's the same one soundtrack with either increased tempo or increased tempo and instrument changes? Octave changes? It's really annoying after the first 5 minutes. Boss fights seem unfair. In games like Castlevania: Symphony of the Night or Dark Souls, the bosses have tells. Each boss fight becomes reading your opponent and reacting to their moves. In this game? There's no such thing. You can't "get better" at the game, you can only jump and hope you don't hit the boss as they move. It's really terrible boss design. Your health is designed in such a way that you get two shot very frequently. This isn't necessarily bad, but it can be annoying when it comes time to fight bosses. My biggest gripe with this game is the sheer amount of instakill spikes. They're EVERYWHERE. The game becomes less about platforming and timing jumps than it is about making sure you jump in exactly the right way so as to not hit the instakill spikes. Which - spoiler alert - get used to them. The entire platforming seems to have been balanced around them. It's annoying.
Definitely pass. A $1 game I'd say,

Guacamelee feels like a mix-tape of "best-of" 2d side scrollers. It's one part hardcore platformer, one part open metroidvania, and one part action game. The parts make greater whole, which a fantastic game. Levels are interesting. The jumps are great. And the combat is emmaculate and meaty. One of the best combat engine to be found in a 2d game.
The music and visuals are most definatley a highlight. While most video-games go for a try-hard "epic" score or bad butt rock, Guacamelee draws on a unique source of inspiration (traditonal Mexican music) and fuses it with a very classic video game sound for a soundtrack unlike anything else. The Mexican inspiration  also carries over the visuals. The results is very aesthetically excellecent complient to the some great mechanics.
The humor and reference are hit-or-miss. The video games tend to be charming as hell, while the meme ones are cringe-worth, in my opinion.
With that said, Guacamelee is excellent game in nearly all regards. It the type of game that's not afraid to have some fun. If you like 2-d action games at all, buy it. You won't regret it.
