To sum it up, its a generic FPS thats based off the original but in no way recreates it or really continues the lineage of FEAR but rather takes inspiration from that game in the form of bullets on a powerpoint. Its not bad, I have played far worse but its definetly not good either.
It felt like they looked at F.E.A.R. and just made a casualised/consolised version of the game instead of taking the first game and building onto that.
Unfortunately it dousn't take anything that was good from the first game and build onto that and feels more like a generic FPS of these days rather than anything like the, now classic, original. The great AI is gone and feels much more basic now while they still attempt to recreate the original they feel much more stupid. The maps have alot more detail but sit at either at being simplistic places to run through or overly complicated areas where you get turned around and confused where to go. The areas though do look nice and the graphics in general are a huge jump forward in fidelity but something is lost in the transfer. The 1st game had a very flat and empty graphical design (either due to intended design or hardware limits of the time) that added towards the atmosphere which is lost with 2.
There is also alot more involvement with NPCs but unfortunately the story isn't exactly the easiest to understand or make sense at all. Honestly with this type of story there isn't much sense to be made and its more of a thriller than a story book.
The scaryness isn't really there aside from a handfull of jump and other scares but its not a scary game anymore than the first and probably less so. Its mainly a shooter like the original game, but you end up fighting the same enemies over and over and scenarios reminiscent of the original game. Unfortunately the AI of the old game and feeling of a dynamic shootout escapes this one as the experience feels more canned than homemade.
I would only recommend playing this if you just played FEAR and want more of that type of game or if you just want to play a generic style FPS and know what your getting into.
The cinematics and writing is pretty good, but if you wanting something super serious all the way through than the writing will fail you from the very start of the game. But it tries to be serious at certain points but its hard to care about the characters in a game where the gameplay feels generic and bland.
Its also very easy, for the most part you can either just blaze through areas or take advantage of faults in the AI to get past enemies more easily.

Tiny Brains wants to treat you like its minuscule rodent protagonists.
A coop focused puzzle game, you play as one of four furballs who through some bizarre experiment have been given superpowers and are now naturally stuck running through tests to deduce just how intelligent they've become. Where Spearhead takes this so far however is in seemingly forgetting to design its puzzles as anything requiring involved thought or clever utilization of its awkwardly implemented mechanics.
There's this feeling throughout playing Tiny Brains like you're running on a treadmill through the tutorial for all of its four very brief levels. It reuses the same puzzle types, repeats similar level designs, and never gets around to taking the training wheels off. You're a rat in a maze doing the same things again and again. And that's really boring.
More frustrating still is how poorly it makes use of its coop component. It's very clearly the way Tiny Brains was designed to play, but puzzles rarely requires the use of more than one or two different powers, essentially meaning if you're playing a full game of four you'll be trading off who gets to actually do anything instead of using your combined efforts to progress. It's at this point that you're probably asking why you wouldn't simply play solo, and the answer to that lies in the aggravating handful of levels that make playing solo immensely difficult or downright impossible. I'm fairly certain I cheated through several of the last levels as there didn't seem any way to possibly get through them without the help of more players, and at one point was attempting to use two controllers simultaneously to get past what was still a very rudimentary puzzle.
And then there are all the portions which don't center around puzzle solving at all, but instead rolling a giant ball through an obstacle course or protecting a little pink chick from a horde of rampaging chickens. These are without question the worst parts of an already miserable game, and besides being terribly boring are often obnoxiously difficult because of the poor controls and annoying cooldown timer. These portions probably take up about a third of the game, which is only an hour or two long to begin with. I'd take a moment here to write a bit more about how the before mention pink chick, ostensibly the sole female character in the game, is used solely as a victim and a villain and feels just a little sinister and problematic, but the dialogue is so cringe inducing and the narrative flimsy that there's hardly any point.
Everything just comes together like a giant mess of bad design, not helped by the abundant technical issues (as of this writing online coop is all but entirely broken, and even playing solo I experienced crashes after every chapter). I love what Tiny Brains was going for with a coop puzzle game with some unusual means with which to solve them, but it fumbles the whole way and never does anything with its concepts that it just wants to keep introducing over and over. Getting through Tiny Brains would have been a chore even had it worked as intended, but the sort of disrepair its in just makes it sad and embarrassing, and I feel a little bad for having made others play it with it.

Her Story is an excellent example of video game/interactive narrative done well. Not the first of its kind but definitely an amazing perspective of the medium. That's not even the best part, it goes beyond being a unique experience with impressive narrative and a memorable conclusion, all in resonance with its gameplay elements.
To give a gist of what I adore about this game, let me talk about video game narratives for a bit. Games are a medium, much like film and animation but what sets it apart is the idea of interaction while telling a story/providing an experience. Most games boil down interaction to decision making and branching stories which is fine in itself but the options are ultimately static and very  limited at any point. Other games eschew any sort of interactive story telling and restrict it to a challenge, games as a medium for story telling is still at its infancy in contrast to film, animation or books despite years of diversification and expansion as an industry. Very few dare to take a risk from the convention at this point but there have been efforts into pushing the medium further in the Indie scene: Dear Esther, Gone Home etc. unfortunately these games are far too familiar to most of us after numerous first person titles but that doesn't mean they are poor attempts at all, just that they are quite overwhelming in this impatient world that isn't fully acquainted with the idea of environmental story telling. What sets apart Her Story from these is its fresh take on interaction/gameplay - the entire game follows a Windows 95 style UI and a gameplay element we are familiar with not thanks to other games but something we do everyday: searching key words from a data base.
A simple gameplay element and probably not even impressive on its own but in relevance to the story, its effect is pronounced. With no tutorial or guide at the beginning, game relays its story through interaction, I opened the readme file before I did anything which gave a gist of our task without detracting from the theme/story quickly adding to the immersion but I won't be surprised if people started getting into the meat of it right away (as did my dad).
We get to watch a number of FMV on the interrogation of a woman in bits and pieces. The player is tasked, rather suggested/implied to piece together these bits and pieces they hear from the videos. You don't understand why but you are nonetheless pushed to solve this mystery in hopes that you will. What's incredible at this point is that there's next to nothing that detracts you from believing that everything on your screen is short of reality, the suspension of disbelief slides in with little to no effort thanks to the UI, the interactive tools (keyboard and mouse) and the utter lack of videogame-centric hints or information. Every bit of it is in sync with its story. There were a few moments that the game does detract but that was only because it deliberately wants to but not that there was a short coming of it, I wasn't aware why as I played but I later came across Sam Barlow's GDC presentation on the game and he mentioned that it gives us a moment reflect the events of the game in our own life.

[MINOR SPOILER TERRITORY, READ AT YOUR OWN RISK]
This was important with respect to how it concluded, it asks for a simple answer, yet one of the more difficult choices I had to make in a video game which felt a lot more intimate than anything I've ever played. I played quite a few games that left me in a bind when it came to decision making but none felt as intimate and personal as this. It didn't matter what sort of outcome the game would have as result of it but the answer it expected would only affect us, as players than the game itself.
Forget the characters of the game, would you be okay with it? Whatever your answer may be, it's alright, perhaps it's what makes you you.

Anyway, if you have any interest at all in police investigation and crime mysteries, GET THIS GAME! It is just so very weel made, the developer really put his soul in it. There's lots and lots of details, and many, many ways to get to the truth.
The gameplay is simple, and some people may find it strange at first: You're basically in control of a person that has access to a police computer, searching for videos of the interrogations of a certain suspect of a cold case. You can type stuff in a search bar, and view the videos. That's basically it. You can also see what videos you already found. You have to pay attention to what the suspect says in the videos, and try to identify keywords for your next search. There's nothing indicated, you just search for the words you found interesting. Little by little, you begin to understand the story, what happened on that case, what was the suspect's role in it. After "unlocking" enough key videos, there is an option to leave. That's when the game decides you probably already know what happened. But you can still continue, trying to find all the videos to complete everything. After you leave, there is an additional bit of the story that gets revealed.
Anyway, it's awesome. One of those games that you will never forget.

Blacksea Odyssey is a twin-stick shooter about space whaling.
You are one of the badass looking whalers, who entered the competition to beat everyone else (and not die in the process).
Generally, the game's more or less your typical rogue-lite twin-stick shooter.
You get to fly around, shoot spears at space fish (I guess that's fish?), buy upgrades and consumables, upgrade your spear and your ship (which looks more like a hoverboard).
Additionally, you can unlock more characters with different stats and perks and arm them with variety of spears that also have different stats.
That'd be pretty average if this game didn't have two things that distinguish it from the rest.
First thing is absolutely crazy art style and monsters design. I can imagine some people might not like it, but I personally loving it - it fits the game very well.
The second, more important, thing is "rip off" mechanic.
The idea is that all monsters you hunt have vulnerable parts. And if you want to defeat them quicker - you can weaken those parts and then use your harpoon to rip them off dealing massive damage.
It's not easy to pull this off, especially on more protected monsters, but it feels pretty awesome being able to pull this move off :D
You can of course just keep shooting and kill monsters the traditional way, although it takes quite some time this way.
There are couple of issues and minor annoyances in the game at the moment.
Chests are not shown on the minimap so it's a bit tricky and somewhat annoying to search for them.
Minor UI glitches, spears missing targets (my guess is hitboxes need tweaking) and other small things.
Nothing game breaking was noticed. And devs are promising updates every 7 days.
So, if you like rogue-lite twin-stick shooters and theme with new mechanic does sounds good - go for it.
The game's pretty cheap and very enjoyable for what it is.

Blacksea Odyssey is slick, highly replayable and has some of the best bosses ever seen in a 2D game.
Your character fights with a spear (basically an infinite ammo pistol), and a harpoon that needs to be charged up to use, but does more damage and can tear off weakened pieces of enemies to inflict major damage and reduce their functionality.
This harpoon adds depth to all encounters. Instead of indiscriminate firing, you can repeatedly spear a particular body part (such as an eye that shoots poison darts) and eventually harpoon it and rip it out. As a result, no more poison darts while you finish it off.
Gameplay video, including four bosses:
Each round of the game (out of 5), you choose a bounty to go after. You'll always have a choice of 2-4 randomly chosen bosses, each offering different difficulty and potential rewards.
Then you launch into space. You start by exploring, looking for regions where you can encounter groups of smaller enemies, which will earn you small bounty, and if you're lucky, power-ups. If you're very lucky, a dead fish will drop a key that opens a chest that may contain runes - more on that later. And if you kill all enemies in a region, that results in bonus bounty at the level's end (as does speedrunning the level).
Once you've done everything you want to, you can go and find the boss, which will be lurking under the surface (of, er, space). Fight the boss, earn a huge bounty explosion, and move onto the next round.
But man, the bosses! They're brilliantly designed with a great art style and each demanding different fight strategies. Some are more traditional bullet-sponges, others level-swallowing mouths with vast tentacles. Others are armoured pyramids with a death-star exhaust port to fire into. And the biggest boss, the leviathan, can fill half the level and has teeth for DAYS.
Each boss (like all enemies, in fact) is designed to scale to different sizes. At "elite" scale, the leviathan's mouth ALONE is several screens long. These encounters can be genuinely breathtaking.
It helps that your old man controls so well, once you get used to the "surf-like" turning. Once you master it, it allows you to dodge all manner of bullet hells. A controller is ideal for this movement, but I ended up on keys and mouse because I found aiming easier (and the game struggled to interpret some of the gamepad buttons reliably for me).
Roguelike elements mean each level is created afresh, although none of the layouts are particularly memorable, they're just arenas for the fighting and make you have to explore a bit.
What is more memorable is the rune system - this is a great game for people who love to repeatedly play to hope to come across the rarest runes. They power up your ship and spear, but come in different rarities - some of the most powerful rare ones are nuts, but you'll hardly ever get to use them. You can also fiddle with the rune loadout to pick the ones that suit your play style. Shame nothing carries over from game to game (at time of writing, at least).
Only real niggles - the spear collision on some of the smaller enemies can be a bit off. You can use either mouse & keyboard or controller, but each have their weakness. Some of the easier bosses can be a chore once you've fought them a lot. You can have bad runs where you simply never find any power-ups.
In summary, I love this. There's still loads of new content to come over early access, but it's great already. Highly recommended.

Let's get serious here. I'm putting on my serious face for this review, as FEAR is my second favorite FPS of all time right behind Fallout 3. FEAR 2, I should start out by saying, is not a bad game. It's decent compared to any other FPS you play these days, but what ends up making it a pile of waste to be trudged through is when you compare it to the original FEAR. For instance, a common theme in FEAR 1 is that when you kill a enemy in slow-motion, they often die still fireing the gun, allowing you to be clipped if you're not careful enough. In FEAR 2, I only saw that happen exactly 5 times. All the guns in FEAR 2 sound like BB guns, and aren't satisfying to use, whilst in FEAR 1 you actually fired bullets instead of what sounds like nerf darts. Also the shotgun got downgraded, and that is just a crime. The only part that I thought FEAR 2 did get right was the setting, but that was only for the School portion of the game. All in all, FEAR 2 is a okay game, but does not live up to the expectations of the FEAR franchise. 5/10.

Don't even worry about the overly complex and melodramatic story. The game is too fun to get caught up in the details. You play as cyborg Sam Fisher, with a team-building and customization mechanic that is somewhere between a JRPG and a Mechwarrior/Dawn of War game, with a classic RTS approach to research and development of your tech and capabilities, all set on a Battlefield 2 map with all the hilarious, game-breaking physics exploits that entails. Having trouble engaging a sniper? Call in a support drop to land right on his head. Need to abduct several enemy soldiers? Knock them unconscious, put them all in a car, and attach the car to a C-130 with a Fulton device. Trouble with armored units? Trick them into chasing you right off a cliff. Intense stealth action meets wacky exploding fun, when suddenly you're being attacked by a giant flaming monster right out of Final Fantasy.
Don't think too hard about it. Just pop your inflatable decoy, ready your C4 under your cardboard box, and enjoy your adjutant Miller's ridiculous commentary as you strafe dance around while jamming 80's hits on your Walkman. Imagine if The Boss from Saint's Row was the protagonist of HITMAN with some Resident Evil thrown in and you have just one small part of this massive game, tightly balanced and never repetitive.
It's a game and an experience that is only as serious as you take it, never impeding the sheer fun and challenge. Your vendetta against Skull Face is intense and engaging, in spite of the laborious Melville references, lengthy cutscenes, and Professor Kazuhira Miller's comically overserious ruminations. Yes Miller, things that are made of fire will tend to avoid water, and yes, you should have known the guys with lame disguises and evil mustaches were enemy infiltrators. The mid-game plot twist still reaches out of the screen and slaps you for not seeing it coming. Not to spoil it, but it makes you feel as stupid as Miller sounds, which is impressive. The plot is overwrought, sure, but it still adds a special dimension to the game.
You will not be disappointed.

Original review:
Compared to its closest FPS rivals the controls are a bit janky and the overall game design is a little quirky, but what it lacks in polish it makes up for in strategic depth and complexity. The MOBA elements truly make Battleborn unique and more engaging over the long term than a simple point capture team FPS. The unpretentious Borderlands style humor and wacky character designs are also really fun.
The main downsides are the grinding required to unlock characters, abilities, and gear, and the small PC community making it hard to find games during non-peak hours. WRT unlocks it's actually surprisingly easy to unlock characters, I'd unlocked all but two by the time I finished the story missions and unlocked the other two shortly thereafter. Still, it's annoying that you can't just play whoever you want from the get go.
Also, even the single player maps are hosted on their servers. Consider this game a rental, especially until the community gets larger. However as previously stated, the game is very fun and unique. For these reasons I would recommend purchasing it, but wait for a deep discount. I got it for $15 in a Humble Bundle and do feel that I've gotten my money's worth, probably twice that.
Played a round or two. Seems fun. I'll play a few more to be sure.

Sure, the community is tiny. I don't think the game was marketed well in light of Overwatch's success, but it's not fair to compare Battleborn to Blizzard's game. The two are entirely different games.
Gameplay feels like Borderlands. This is good.
Humor feels like it, too. Also good.
PvP feels unbalanced for many (as of just a couple months after release) because the player base is so small. High skill players are regularly put into matches with newbies fresh out of tutorial. This can't really be fixed without more players, unfortunately. I will say, though, that as someone with quote a bit of experience with MOBAs and FPSs alike, I feel like I play nearly as well as max level players. The only thing holding me back is a shallow understanding of most characters and map dynamics.
If this goes free-to-play or even sub-$30, it's well worth it. Harsh critics may think it doesn't hold up to expectations, but the game is fun. Plain and simple. I'll be playing this for a while (currently have 30 hours or so), and I'll update if my opinions change.

This is a good game, i had a ton of fun with it.
First Let's go over the positives:
1. The Loot, I LOVE LOOT, to the point i started collecting legendaries and got to a total of 33 unique legendaries, each legendary feels really unique and feels as if they have a meaningful impact on the game, the moment you recieve the legendary you've been looking for is amazing. and finding cool combos for PVP is fun and interesting
2. Art Style. ever since i played TF2 or Borderlands i love this cel-shaded style of art, i feel it's a strong style that can hold up to the test of time. the simple colors allows immediate info of the surrounding battlefield
3. Boss Battles. Most boss battles feel epic, like you are actually doing something different in each one. each one has different goals and sorta like mini-games to make the boss vulnerable, coupled with the intro cutscene to most bosses this is one of my favorite reasons to play the game.
4. PVP. when you get a game that feels fair, it's an amazing display of skill on both sides, it feels like your individual actions actually effect the game, regardless of who you play. i've seen some op strats come and go but usually a well coordinated team can beat these strats.
5. THE WRITING - i almost forgot, the writing in this game is perfect, each character has depth and feels unique to one another. each character has their nuances and they all have jokes and taunts that perfectly fit them
But, there are a ton of problems with it, these may be long, but i try to provide proof for every point on why i think this way:
1. The community on steam is NONEXISTENT, 533 people playing as im writing this (obviously i understand the conundrum behind not recommending a game because of a small community as no new players will increase the size of the community if they don't get the game) The community has always been small, even since release, at release it had somewhere around 12k people at one time - Dead By Daylight has 16k people right now. Battleborn's release hype barely compares to that. The community itself is also toxic, they were advocating writing good reviews to increase the games overall rating when it was starting to die.
2. Reused resources everywhere... there's an enemy called the sheppard in PVP, this is also an enemy in the mission "The Algorithm" and it is also an allied ship (several times larger) in "The Renegade". The enemy ship, i believe it's called a Viper, is used for a single enemy in "The Saboteur", literally one enemy, remove the enemy and it's a unique resource, the game would be better. i can not count how many times i saw the same dragon bones on different maps, also no matter which planet you go to for a story mission they are the same exact enemies, some enemies don't even make sense - like the robot minions in "The Experiment", you ally ISIC, controller of these minions, in the previous mission - Also, the minions are made on "Bliss" and "The Experiment" is based on "Ekkunar". It would have been SOOO cool to fight the Bliss bugs that plague bliss, or fight the monstrous enemies leaving these bones behind, or fight hostile creatures on "Ekkunar" that weren't just a variation of the swarmers or sentinels you already saw on a DIFFERENT PLANET in the previous mission. All but a few bosses are just larger versions of other enemies, ISIC and Rendain are the only unique enemy bosses. I feel, with less repeating content this game would be better. even if it meant making the content overall less.
3. The game is sloppy.... you can see out of bounds in an overwhelming amount of spots. It's hard to believe the same amount of effort was put into this game as say Borderlands. The PVP looks good, but reused resources exist, the balance is not the greatest, and there's no one to play with so every match is unbalanced. And the PVE side of things suffers from sloppily created maps and enemies. It's almost as if the devs spread their efforts to thin trying to create a game that satisfies both PVP and PVE players. Beyond this, during helix selection some choices are just 100% inferior to the other, it's not a real choice but feels more like a QTE that if you fail you just become weaker for the rest of the game.
4. Lack of info. Everything, and i mean EVERYTHING has very poor descriptions on what they do for you, no cooldowns on skills are given in the character pages, no distance of projectile skills, or area of effect size. there is no info on if it is skill or attack damage (which may seem simple but there are skills that deal attack damage). Next: Items, all the descriptions are vague and i have found hidden stats on several items, like the Symbiotic Gauntlet. it's nigh impossible to plan anything efficently in this game.
5. Unbalanced PVP. item combos can be broken, and some strats are absolutely ridiculous (like multi heal teams, or my personal favorite, infini-stun) some characters are just completely unviable because they dont offer anything to a broken combo, Montana, benedict, phoebe are all great characters but doesn't offer anything to a broken combo so he is left in the dust, this is the same story for a lot of people. Also, the Balance for all versions of the game (console and PC) are the same, so a sniper on console is weaker than a sniper on pc, and most of the time a PC sniper is better than console, so one of these will be balanced and the other will be weak or overpowered. I believe the game is being balanced for console.
I got this game during release, and i had fun, a lot of fun. speed-running the story missions was great, and dominating an enemy team with galilea and kelvin was amazing. But in it's current state, as of mid august 2016, I do not recommend this game, it feels incomplete (as a lot of games do nowadays). If you can look past the problems i have mentioned here, get the game, you will prolly get your money's worth of fun out of it. But in all honesty the game is better on console.

Every once in a while, a game comes along that really thrills me in every way, I like to play vg, from every genre and dev, I consider myself someone that can usually spot duds from the get go, so in that sense, I’m super stoked to say that Battleborn is one of the best MP gaming experiences currently on the market.
Everything, from its design to its frenetic gameplay is spot on, in this genre of hero shooters this one is the most complex and mature of the ones currently on the market, I own Overwatch, but it lacks content and depth, Battleborn has.
The story missions are challenging and fun, some levels are amazingly well designed, and with its huge roster of heroes’ u can be sure that it won’t get boring fast, on to its competitive modes, a capture the point ordeal not unlike the one UT had in the old days, a MOBA like creep grind affair that is very fun and finally a kill the opponent super robot at the end of the map, which for me at least, showcases this games most intricate aspects of party composition and mad dashes for glory!
Alas, Overwatch game modes feel just the same over and over again, in shallow matches that last aa little over 10 mins, while in Battleborn, if the teams are balanced, sometimes the match is decided at the last possible second of a very frantic and intense tug of war, and herein lies its shortcomings, matchmaking is kind of iffy at times, making teams of high level pros against teams of low level newbies that will get roflstomped, as this fames needs a deep understanding of its underlying complex mechanics, personally I’d rather play something complex and deep over something shallow like Overwatch, now don’t get me wrong, OW is fun, but for me it’s not in the same category as BB.
Graphics and sound are top notch, the hero design and quirks blow Overwatch ultra clean design away, in Battleborn some characters do really feel as if they really do come from different planets, love the funny banter and the sheer madness and carnage that gets  going, sadly, very few companies an compete against Blizzard, and some technical issues, of which I haven’t found any yet, have thinned this games player base, but I’m certain that once the Overwatch tedium sets in, Battleborn will find a resurgence, Gearbox still has plenty of DLCs  to come so the best is yet to come!
So if you are looking for a complex and fast paced shooter, give Battleborn a try, it’s amazing once its gears get set in motion, gather some friends and give it a go, you won’t be disappointed, this is really an overlooked game, beyond anything on the market right now!
On a side note, high level players on the matchmaking aren’t all pros, as the level jut unlocks some cosmetics, sure they might have played a lot, and might know the maps and characters more, but believe me when I say that if u play smart and don’t Rambo away into oblivion, they can be taken and beaten, I’ve won games while being in low level teams, and lost some with higher level ones, so don’t fret, learning the game is super fun.
So overall this is a must play if you like shooters, MOBAS and overall having fun, if you are expecting a shallow super accessible game though, then yeah, it might take a while for you to enjoy it, if u are ready for the challenge, then see you on the field of battle, glorious death awaits!

Whether you are just starting the PAYDAY series with this, or you are coming back here after playing Payday 2, this is a phoenominal game. Also, I ask that you read the whole guide. I may have some of my information wrong as I have not played in a while.
HEISTS
The game itself has 7 heists, with 2 from the DLC, each completely different.
First World Bank is kind of obvious, you rob a bank.
Heat Street is surely something else, as you rush your way down a street to intercept a fellow heister who has betrayed you, but it doesn't go so well for him.
The Diamond Heist sends you into a high security building with diamonds, rubies, and other jewels, which are your main objective.
In Green Bridge, you obliterate a bridge in order to rob a prison convoy of one of its prisoners.
In the Panic Room heist, you raid a drug dealer's den to grab his panic room containing loads of money, however, it is not as easy as it sounds.
The Slaughterhouse heist sends you to intercept a Murkywater convoy, but, again, it's not as easy as it may sound.
*DLC* Undercover is all about intercepting "The Taxman" and stealing the server he's carrying that is the key to $25 million.
*DLC* My personal favorite heist in both Payday 2 and Payday the Heist, Counterfeit throws you all the way down to Florida to grab the printing plates of money launderer, Mitchell.
The final heist included in the PC version is No Mercy, which is the uncanon start to Left 4 Dead (at least I think it's L4D).
WEAPONS
There's only around 10 weapons in the base game, and 3 more with the DLC, but they're all great in what they're meant to do.
-First off, the primaries.
AMCAR Assault Rifle: The basic primary gun, it is an assault rifle which is good all around, and can be upgraded through all skill trees. Medium capacity, low damage, medium firerate, and long range.
Brenner LMG: Part of the Assault tree, it's a great primary at short-mid range. High capacity, medium damage, low-medium firerate, medium range.
Reinfield Shotgun: Part of the Medic tree, awesome at short range, but can't really do anything at long range (it's a shotgun). Low capacity, very high damage, very low firerate, low range, CAN HIT MULTIPLE TARGETS.
M308 Marksman Rifle: Part of the Sharpshooter tree, this is my personal favorite, it's a marksman rifle. Low capacity, firerate depends on how fast you can click, high damage, very long range.
*DLC* AK Assault Rifle: Part of the Technician tree, the AK is like the AMCAR, but different. Medium capacity, medium damage, high firerate, and medium range.
-Pistols
B9 Silenced Pistol: The default pistol and can be upgraded through the Sharpshooter tree. Medium capacity, low damage, medium firerate, medium range, SILENCED.
Bronco Revolver: A great weapon from the Medic tree, and although not my personal favorite, it is claimed through the community the best pistol. Very low capacity, very high damage, very low firerate, and very long range.
Crosskill Pistol: My personal favorite base game pistol, it comes from the Assault tree. Low capacity, high damage, low firerate, and long range.
*DLC* STRYK Automatic Pistol: My favorite pistol in the hole game comes from the Technician tree, and is great for rushing into different rooms. Very high capacity, very low damage, ludicrous firerate, and short range.

Payday: The Heist by Overkill Software is an amazing game and the best out of the 2 Payday games.
PayDay 1 puts you in a crime group tha goes around and pulls off heists while trying not to get killed/arrested by the police.
You can play as either Chains, Hoxton, Wolf or Dallas. Each Character has a unique personality to them so they dont get boring after playing for a while.
The Game offers 6 different heists in the base game while the DLC adds another 2-3 heists. You can rob a bank, pull off a diamond heist, etc.
Reputation levels is the XP system in the game, you gain Reputation by completing objectives during heists, picking up small money bundles in the heists, completing challenges and finishing heists. Each time you level your Rep you gain upgrades to weapons, upgrades to your characters health, and a variety of other rewards that can be used to benefit you in the heist.
The guns are very well balanced and different from each other so no weapon is better than the other. however the number of guns in the game are a tad low its not something that bothers me because each weapon is good at something. So I played the game over the weekend pretty much none stop and I can say I was super excited about this game. The graphics are pretty awesome.
I like some of the news things they have put into this game but it still is nothing like the original. Which to me this is a good and bad thing. It is great that we have so much more customization to this game. Circle paths, large, small, medium paths, lights, trash cans, benches, etc.
I enjoy the fact that you can make a roller coaster now almost as you wish and it is not constrained as it was in the old Roller Coaster Tycoon. But with that being said, the magic of the old games is not completely present here.
I want to build a roller-caster, test, add my scenery, my queue and be off. I don't want to spend almost 2 hours on building a coaster and than not be able to finish it because my train car is always hitting a bar that was placed in the wrong area by the game. I don't want to spend close to an hour and a half just to complete laying out my track. I want to put able to select the section of the track and place it how I like. There are alot of advantages to this new UI and I do recognize them but I am not a roller coaster designer. I am a average player that wants to build a roller coaster in the game as quickly and have it enjoyable. At the point, it is not that enjoyable to build a roller coaster because it is super frustrating.
Here is an example on why it is so frustrating, If I am building my roller coaster and I am zoomed out to see what it looks like. If I click on a portion of the map where i would like for my track to be laid, that game from now where lays a very large piece of track randomly that the end of the new piece of track is laid down all the way to the edge of the park. WHAT?!!!!! That is not what I wanted. Now I have to zoom back in to make the track smaller, than angle the camera just right, and than either shift and any of the 4 number to adjust the track as I want. That is just ridiculous.
If you are going to show a grid, as I like building on a grid, don't give me just a small piece of grid. Just display it on the whole map.
For sure there is a learning curve for this game. But so far my initial review of this game is not all the stellar when building coaster. This is something that is NOT going to change for this is pretty much the hole core of the game.
I am still at a maybe..... I wouldn't recommend this game but at the same time if you are a die hard fan as I am, I wouldn't turn you away either.

Game is all good but there are a few issues that should be sorted by the time it is fully complete don't be fooled by the crazy amount of negative feedback its getting, some are genuine and some are abit longed out getting an unfinished product after waiting so long but a huge amount is just people comparing and bashing it because of PC.
Pros -
-Coaster builder is really cool and much more stable compared to the beta. It does take some getting used to but once you've mastered 1-4 the creations you come out with look epic.
-Tycoon elements are kind of there setting the price for rides and entry is key to staying on top and not going into debt.
-Map looks great and they are really fun to build on. The devs have already said a flat map mode will be added but I'm pretty happy with the 3 already here.
-Decor also really cool will be good once there is alot more but whats here looks sweet and it can really make your park look cool.
-Other rides the time and attention put in is noticable they look really good especially compared to RCT3.
-UI, I get loads of people don't like it but I've not had any issues other than one thing but I'll put it in the cons it was by no means a deal breaker though.
-Build a massive coaster and pay after is a really good move can really help push time along just building some beast and not having to pay for the completed ride until you wish to open it. Was always long running out of money back in RCT2,3.
Cons-
-Alot is missing, some might feel ripped off paying so much for what you get and how unstable it can be at times.
-Glitchy I've had peeps all spawn by the entrance after loading. I've had my money drop at 10,000 a second after the heat tab bugged out, not sure if this is a bug but cant seem to build anything beyond zero depth if I put a coaster drop at -1 depth it will always crash.
-Unstable only at times I would build a few coasters and Ill start to get major slow down it goes back to normal speed after a while but it does remind you your playing a early access game.
-Some plants vanish from view if you go more than 1 foot away from them it might sound silly to some but after spending a few hours making some sick flower display it can really grind your gears that its all invisible when zoomed the slightest bit out!
-UI only issues I have is with the heat panel it makes me go minus in money other than this one thing its all good.
-Peeps getting bored of rides it sounds like a really good idea to put this in but it just ends up making sure you will always fail. After 9 years in game time no one other than the odd one or two peeps would ride anything in the first 3 zones of my map they desperately need to add a scenario maker and add the option to restrict what % peeps will get bored at so they never fully find any ride boring.
-Lack of management for any in park services. This is something they said they will be working on but it is something that needs to be sorted asap not one of my 100+ mechanics would fix the circus and there is no way to find them or set them to do a task or even give them a radius in which to patrol. I'm not feeling just put down a building and hope they are working, it does not work.
-No colour change tab for any of the pre build family, junior and thrill rides they look good but dont see why this isnt just a normal feature.
-Long load times its not a deal breaker for me but in this day and age any long loading screen is a con.
Things that need to be added please -
-Smaller rollercoaster entrances.
-More decor, rides and shops.
-Being able to build rides through mountains and at minus depth and maybe tunnels in water?
-Camera to take peeps pictures on rides was surprised this wasn't in the build panel.

-Staff tab and general commands just like the previous game would work fine.
-Balloons that float off and the ability to pop the kids ones to ruin there day.
-Water rides, gokart rides, zoo stuff and water world stuff im sure it'll all come but want to be able to build an epic gokart track again soon.
-More music and themes.
-Option added to sandbox mode to set starting money if the scenario maker takes too long to come.
- Map grid mode improvements. Just put the grid over the whole map and let it change size as it does now just over the whole map. Its not bad how it is but it can be off putting at times all moving about.
Overall
It's a really fun game as is but I will look forward to all the updates, it might have awful reviews but dont be put off by them. It will freeze on occasion and it is a little glitchy but so are loads of EA games. People need to be more patient and stop bashing it and filling the forums up with comparison discussions. This is the best Metroidvania I've played in a long time. There are parts that mirror the GBA Metroids really well: Flying across multiple screens for secrets, and hidden 'morph ball' tunnels, to name a few. The nostalgia is incredible, but it is very much its own game.
The combat system feels pretty decent: It's not anything groundbreaking, but it never gets in the way, and killing crap always feels nice. Throwing enemies was a neat (And fitting) addition, though. With enough enemies on the screen, you can just keep throwing them around, racking up massive combos and killing them without getting touched.
The secrets scattered throughout the game (As any Metroidvania should have) are satisfying to find and oh so numerous. What I really enjoyed, though, was rather than having 'energy tanks' that instantly increase your health cap, you have 'heart pieces,' which are instantly reminscent of Zelda. Some areas for secret items get notoriously difficult, and the platforming skills it asks for have been compared to Super Meat Boy (Which, personally, I love a good difficult platformer). The main game, though, is a nice difficulty to get through: It isn't a stroll through the park, but it's not too tricky. And it's still rewarding to finish.
The game is also absolutely filled with very-unsubtle references to... Everything. Classic games, internet icons, memes, you name it. The lack of subtlety makes it pretty hilarious. And lastly- This is a game I will never get tired of looking at. It's so gorgeous.
Buy this game. Buy it now.

There are three levels of strategy to this game -
World - deciding what to invest your resources into improving
Expedition - choosing which encounters / events to activate, and which route to take before running out of supplies
Encounter - ordering your three explorers around to defeat enemies.
The encounter turn based strategy game is the weakest part, and unfortunately is also the largest part of the game. Encounters are either trivially easy or punishingly hard. The best "strategy" i've found is trapping enemies with no ranged attack behind a "chokepoint" that they could walk around in 2 turns if the AI wasn't so bad. Otherwise the strategy is to burn down the boss before the minions can kill you too many times.
Overall this game is pretty good and well polished, especially considering the price point. I just wish they would balance the encounters so they're not so hit or miss.

You lead a team of 3 explorers (picked from 20 different characters in 4 main classes) on 5 explorations around the world (2 new targets of increasing difficulty after each successful exploration). Your goal: gain enough Renown on those 5 adventures to beat your main Rival in the society of explorers.
Lots of exploration (both in the game and in my review) which basically has you make a choice of route across a partially randomized map with partially randomized encounters towards the boss (including traps, choices) which will always be the same. The loot is chosen from among a pool per encounter increasing your Renown, as do some ressources you gather along the route you chose.
Some fighting tests your skill in positioning and in using the right mix of attacks against specific enemy setups. If you don't pay attention you won't beat the game on the adventure mode, which is the regular mode granting access to all achievements. Your group setup can make certain encounters easy, others rather difficult. You'll learn over time what works and which destinations suit some setups better.
This time learning and the resulting success, combined with needing to have every character succeed as a leader to achieve the list of achievements is the mid to long-term appeal of the game. It is fun, worth the money definitely and turns into casual gaming after you have seen every destination repeatedly. That repetition might give you a feeling of "again?" and is the only downside I can list (while I leave out lots of positive things in the small deatils), but my playtime can tell you, it didn't bother me much.
A huge bonus is the support. Listening to customers, asking for input, feedback, shelling out a free DLC and Halloween event just like that. Best-in-class.

MGSV: TPP would make a great stealth game but there is one HUGE problem with it. Score system encourages players to finish missions as fast as possible. In reality that means it doesn't really matter how well you execute the missions as long as you speedrun them. The score wouldn't bother me but game actually gives you rewards for getting S rank in missions so they aren't just meaningless numbers.
I'll give an example.
In one of the missions your objective is to eliminate 2 tanks and colonel. You can get bonus points for capturing him alive ofc. It took me about 3 hours of retries to execute the mission in the most perfect stealth way possible. Meaning I didn't kill anyone, didn't trigger reflex mode or any alerts whatsoever. I extracted the colonel alive, destroyed tanks with c4 instead of RPG so they never saw it coming. My final try took me around 30 minutes. Not bad huh? Well guess what.
After all this work the game rewarded me with A. If you want to get the highest possible rank (S) all u need to do is come to the convoy and slaughter everyone with RPG Saint's Row style in 5 minutes. As an extra time bonus you will get around 150 000 points.
On the other side, capturing colonel alive is not a simple task at all since he is located in the middle of valley surrounded by guards. The game gives you 5000 points for it. 5000 points!!!
That means I could probably commit a genocide if it happens within short time and still be rewarded with highest rank, it's just ridiculous.
Punishing methodical stealth approach while rewarding dumb reckless tactics seems really unfair and kills most of the fun for me. It's a shame because gameplay is pretty smooth and addictive.

In short, one of the best JRPGs I've ever had the pleasure of playing. A port is a port, and I'm sad that there's no mouse support still, but on the other hand, mechanically this is probably the best Final Fantasy in the main series. Some of the models look awkward, but if you're like me and gameplay is better than graphics, then pick this game up and treat yourself to a really fun, flexible, and intuitive job system that lets you mix and match different abilities to your heart's content. As someone who played through the game multiple times earlier in life, I can guarantee that someone looking for a JRPG experience will not be disappointed.
However, one bug I will mention that is somewhat irritating is that sometimes the game doesn't correctly remember what your last action was. For example, one round you might attack, and the next the default action will inexplicably be to guard or use an item. It's minor in the grand scheme of things since it doesn't happen consistently, but nonetheless it is an issue. I haven't run into the screen tearing and other issues that others apparently are running into, either.
I am also not the biggest fan of the music "remaster," but the in-battle models have been reworked and are exceptional- each character has unique animations for each action for each different job. One character casting a spell as a mystic knight will look different casting that spell as a ranger, for example. It feels like a loving recreation of an underrated game.

I've played every version of FFV from translated SNES ROMs to the PSX port to the GBA version. The first 45 minutes alone were enough to put a bad enough taste in my mouth to request a refund.
Pros:
It's FFV
Updated Textures
Worked well with controller
Cons:
Tile lines very noticeable with updated textures
Font choice looks terrible against all the updated textures and menus.
Frame rate. I don't know what it's locked to, but it was a stuttering jerky mess.
Amano character portraits. I get using the original character artwork for the portraits, but there's a reason it tends not to make it into the actual games.

Was pretty obvious what the game would look like by just checking the preview images. Yet, people still bought it and complains far and wide. Though most of the complaints come from people who -didn't- buy it. Whatever.
Yes, the tiles look wonky, as does the text fonts and the character portraits doesn't match with the overworld sprites, but... I honestly don't give a ****.
I wasn't duped into buying it nor did I buy it to then act appalled and surprised at what I had purchased. I made the choice to buy it, with or without flaws, myself.
My nostalgia goggles are hard-bolted into my skull. This game is great and I'm having a blast re-playing it for the first time again after 15+ years. And that's why I'd recommend it, and I have, to my friends who also grew up playing these early entries of Final Fantasy.

It really bugs me that so many of the reviews that tell you to not play this game have placed less than an hour into it. I was a big critic of the art style when I saw FFV hit the Steam Store, but since it's my second favorite in the series I wanted a go at it again. I've played the GBA version and an emulated version. Now for some points.
I can say with certainty if you liked FFV, you'll enjoy this adaptation. The artwork is not so bad after all. I have quite enjoyed the animations used. Watching Faris as a Monk using a spell. it just works. It does not feel odd or out of place. It does not feel rushed. Story animations are as funny or sorrowful as they were in the SNES version. The music is not remastered, but that does not take away any points. It's exactly the soundtrack you fell in love with before. And if you're new to FFV, you wont be dissapointed. People in the reviews encourage you to go emulate the game because it's better. At this point, it does not matter what version of the game you play, it's still FFV at it's core.
If you never played FFV, let me just say the job system will sell you on this game. It's fun, addicting and it will push you to mix things up. You unlock a lot of jobs really fast, so you're not stuck being just a simple mage, or just a fighter. Most fights can't just be spammed auto attacks and win, you have to go into them with some thought.
By the end of the day, if you like RPGs, depths, or Final Fantasy games. Get it. Enjoy it, and don't worry about the sub 1 hour reviews throwing a hissy fit.

Okay then. I have a small disclaimer: I bought this on PS4 initially so 99% of my hours are from playing there, I have put quite a bit of time in it there. I recently got PC via humble bundle as well to play with other friends not on PS4. My laptop barely runs it without lag after some modification. Completely playable still like this and still as good of an experience as I've had on PS4.
This game is absolutely fantastic.
Remember that this is a MOBA in every way that just is using FPS as a way to play it.  There are three multiplayer modes: Incursion (more traditional and the best imo), Meltdown (pushing minions to a checkpoint rather than a tower), and Capture Points (your basic Nodes or Conquest mode, closest thing to a deathmatch you can get)
The visuals are great, while somewhat chaotic, it isn't hard to get used to it. Melee characters are harder to get used to it though, but still very doable. (I main a melee character, a few games in and I was set)
I have heard complaints that you hear the same stuff over and over from each character, but this is in all multiplayer games with voices. In this game they are spaced out far from each other as well so you don't hear someone say the same thing more than *maybe* 3 time max in a game and even that is rare. I can't tell you how many of the same phrase I have heard while playing Battlefield 3 in a single match, yet that isn't a complaint you really hear from people. These kind of quips are especially common throughout MOBA styled games.
The voice acting is actually very well done in the game. Each character unique and you can immediately tell what kind of personality they have.
Some people complain about a difficulty curve.  There is a bit of a difficulty curve, yes, but seriously what MOBA (or shooter or fighter or puzzle, etc) doesn't have that? This is simpler than most MOBAs anyway because you generally are just pushing minions and having team fights, you don't have to worry about lane towers and you especially don't have to worry about Jungle. Jungle in this game is minimal, there are just NPC units you can kill and get out into lane as one of your own.  These units attack the sentries in the mode Incursion with a *ton* of damage so they are vital to get on your team.
Shards are the other Jungle type element.  All powerups, or gear as it is called, in this game are bought with shards on a kit that you get to customize for your character. This is similar to creating a loadout in CoD or Battlefield. You could also compare them to perks you get in Cod, though not with a killstreak, it is with the aformentioned shards you collect.  These become a very important element in your playstyle and team play. I have one for example, while expensive on shards, grants my entire team 20% shared shards. After that point, the team almost never has to worry about shards again, one person going to get a shard collection benefits the team greatly. Shards are also used to build turrets and health stations on the battlefield, which are also needed in strategic play.
Characters are diverse and cater to many many playstyles. Each one will take time to learn, but again, it's a MOBA, ALL characters take time to learn in these types of games no matter what you do. I personally main Boldur, a melee character. I got used to the "screen chaos" fairly quickly and it poses no issues. I've heard complaints that when someone played a melee character you just had to run in and hope your attacks something because of the visuals. This is completely not true. You have a reticle for a reason. If you just learn to use it, you can hit anything you want, especially because it TURNS RED when you are in range to hit something. Use what tools they give to you and it isn't hard.
Story Mode is great, however there isn't a whole lot to it. It is fun to replay the missions, there are little incentives to replay them. For example if you go through an area it will have the characters you are playing as give input to the mission, usually it picks one at random. But they all say different things which is entertaining to hear them all. In one of them a Sentry you are escorting doesn't know he is about to die and asks to hang out after the mission. Boldur will talk to himself over the intercom saying "does Boldur tell him? No, no, awkward situation avoided!" where Benedict will quip "man this guy doesn't have a CLUE, haha!".  I do believe they are going to come out with some more story missions in the future, however. Each one will last you roughly 20-40 mins, depending on the mission, difficulty (may make it longer), and team coordination.
Now the game isn't without flaws. Matchmaking options could be better, though I personally haven't had much issue with it, I usually find a match within a minute or two, a pretty standard waiting time. What should be fixed is allowing everyone to vote on all story missions during a public session and give people the ability to rematch a team or story.  They also need to add some sort of punishing system for afk players. Right now it kicks them out fairly quickly, but that's it. So currently, people who can't deal with finishing a game or actually *trying* to win even when you are currently losing will call for a surrender and sit at their TV/PC giving slight inputs so they aren't kicked. They will refuse to help in any way because they didn't get their way for chickening out in a surrender. This does need fixed because it drags everyone else down and the person can 100% get away with it without any reports.
This issue I have only encountered a couple of times, but still it needs fixed.
This game has a ton of replayability, even with the story missions. As I said before, playing through them with multiple characters gives a different experience both in game play and in dialogue. Speaking of dialogue, the humor in the game is in the vein of Borderlands. If you don't like Borderlands humor, you won't like it here. If you did like it, you'll love it just the same in Battleborn. Personally, the humor for me is spot on, everything is great about it.
Overall, if you enjoy MOBAs, you'll definitely enjoy this game for it's gameplay. It is for sure better to play with a team, but not impossible without one. I make many comparisons to this game to SMITE as a MOBA and  Battlefield as an FPS, especially with the pacing of the a match. Everything flows extremely well in a game.  I find that this is easily a game to keep returning to for it's charm and especially it's gameplay. Absolutely a blast!
Quite honestly, the only reason it is doing poorly is because it released in the same month as Overwatch and so they get compared. This is unfortunate because Overwatch playes absolutely nothing like Battleborn does and after the FPS and Hero selections, there are no comparisons between them whatsoever. Battleborn gives much more content with a different playstyle. If it had released a few months later, the game would be full of players. People look at it and say it looks fun but there aren't players to play with. Well the only way to change that is to get in on it yourself.  The more people that pick it up depsite the players, the more will be playing and the sooner than you realize the game booming. Just like with any trend, it has to start somewhere regardless of what people think.
I look forward to seeing new players in the game and to the extra content that is still planned for release!

Oozing with style, Battleborn mixes several well established genres into a moshpit of humor, gunplay, and first-person melee. And, it gets most of it right.
Battleborn is trying to be so many things, it's a wonder that it succeeds at enough to make it hold together. Witty, funny dialogue for a cast of zany and unique characters helps polish the whole deal, but the gameplay is what shines through.
Slicing, dicing, and punching feels as satisfying as the gunplay (something the makers of Borderlands know a bit about), and somehow works in the pvp multiplay, and not just in the co-op campaign.
Colorful, cartoon styled graphics steal the show with bright and vivid scenes that leap out of the screen.
Every fight is littered with witty one-liners and quips from loveable characters.
Now, for all this, the game does suffer from a touch of an identity crisis as it tries to fulfill your every desire.
You get a bit of a story-driven campaign that will leave you wanting more.
You get a few moba-style incursion maps.
You get a touch of capture-the-point
You get some tug-of-war robot battles.
All of these are playable solo (with bots in most cases), or online (though you will need to have an internet connection to run the game).
There is another issue: the online community can be difficult to get involved with in the most popular (I believe) game mode, Incursion. It's easy to get trolled, or get owned.
Finally, Battleborn can be a bit of a performance hog at times.
I fully recommend the purchase with the above in mind. This is a game that happened to be in the wrong place at the wrong time. It is worthy of adoring fans and worth being laughed at, immersed in, and enjoyed.
While not palatable at 60$ (I took advantage of the humble bundle), it is a good game.

F.E.A.R. 2 has to be my favourite of the series, the fluidity, the graphics, the scares make this game a great one.

F,E,A,R, 2 is a two steps forward, two steps back kind of sequel. On one hand we have better looking levels, (Fear 1 was just grey office buildings) more variety (more weapons, more varried levels) and better graphical quality. But on the other hand, we have AI that are not as good, this is probably because people got sick of getting lost in Fear 1 because of all the different doorways to an area (which allowed the AI to be more tactical and flank). The gunplay is also lacking, weapons are more varried, yes, but they have much less recoil. However, they still have good impact, bullets ripping through enemies looks arguably better and because they reduced recoil you spend less time in bullet-time mode because you needed to do that A LOT in F.E.A.R. 1.
As for the scare factor, it can sometimes be scary but don't let that discourage you if you are interested in this game. The scares serve more as an adrenaline booster than to leave you with absolute horror.
This game is one of my favorite FPS of all time mainly because of how varried it is, It has a lot better pacing then the previous games and more variety then I see in most big budget titles. I give it a full reccomendation if you like FPS.

I spent a little time with this game, and I can't say that it was terrible, but it's not a game that I would recommend, unless you literally only have a dollar to spend on a game, or if you've exhasted every other Metroidvania there is out there.  It's a serviceable Metroidvania with a jump-and-shoot mechanic that is reminscent of Mega Man in that you can only have 3 shots on screen at a time.  There are several design decisions I'm not a fan of.  The enemies feel like bullet sponges.  The music restarts everytime you die, and you can die a lot.  Jump is initially mapped to the up arrow (which thankfully can be changed) but prompts still exist in the game that ask you to press up that no longer work, despite being specifically prompted (though the new jump button works).  When you unlock the power dash, you're told to double tap left or right, which doesn't work anywhere near as reliably as I'd like.  If you decided to check the control screen, you'll find this is also mapped to the shift key.  Why the game didn't direct you to this much easier alternative, I have no clue.  The one boss I fought did not feel terribly inspired, it just moved in a giant circle around the room, shooting discs at you.
All that said, I wouldn't call it a terrible game, it's just that there are many other titles out there that should be able to scratch this itch, if you're so inclined.

A good analogy to describe Renowned Explorers is that of an Iceberg. Looking at screenshots or even just one playthrough, you can be guiled into thinking you've seen all the game can offer. The game offers a high level of replayability as there are many possible combinations of explorers and exploration scenarios.
It's hard to describe RE because it doesnt quite fit into a conventional genre such as FPS, RTS, etc. You pick 3 explorers - these explorers are typified into classes (speaker, scientist, scout, fighter) that have their own strengths and weaknesses -and lead them across an exploration scenario collecting tokens. Through combat, diplomacy, or cunning, you resolve challenges across the exploration scenario - the makeup and stats of your explorers will determine your overall success.
Tokens earned can be spent on upgrading a research tech tree, attracting more followers, or purchasing loot.
Combat in RE is especially well done. During combat, 'moods' can offer a significant bonus/penalty. Manipulating the mood of the combat situation is key to winning battles in harder difficulties. You can resolve a battle by being friendly, aggressive, or devious.
Overall, RE is easy and fun to play but will take some learning and effort to master. The game offers alot of depth and replayability.

While a little dated now, and certainly guilty of some pretty horrendous character stereotyping, Hitman: Blood Money remains a powerful game and my favourite of the series. It isn't as linear as the previous offerings, and the ability to interact with characters and objects in new ways, and approach the same mission from numerous different angles, means you can play each mission a dozen times and still not experience everything the game has to offer.
(From my old Amazon review:)
I would primarily recommend this game to people looking for something more intelligent and stealthy than your typical action game. While 47 can certainly go in guns blazing, the game is clearly designed for more than that. If you run into a gun fight you'll find he has an annoying tendency to reload his guns while taking fire - when the character in a standard FPS would opt for the more sensible approach of ducking for cover and grabbing a different gun. If you want a lot of 'constant guns blazing' action this trait will no doubt annoy you. But if, instead of thinking "there are only 20 guys - I can take them" you think more like "I wonder whether shooting a single bullet into that glass roof will cause the shards to fall and impale the guards, giving me enough time to make my sneaky getaway" then this game is for you.

Overkill's Payday The Heist (PDTH) is the first game of the 2 Payday games, and unlike Payday 2, features only 2 DLC's, from which only one affects gameplay in one way or another. Pro:
- Cheap DLC.
- Kind playerbase.
- Easy to pickup.
- Nice looking and cool masks for all four characters.
- Voice actors are top-notch.
- Fun with friends.
- Many cop types.
- Nice and challenging achievements.
- High level cap.
Con:
- Cops sometimes bug out and don't move.
- Very few weapons and maps.
- Some masks are done poorly.
- Bugs.
- Gets boring after awhile.
- Glitches with Steam Matchmaking which makes hard to find a match.
- Some kick you just before you're ending a match so you don't get any money.
Summary:
Buy the game if you don't want to spend a ton of money on some game and DLC's, play it till it becomes boring, wait a month or two, play again till it gets boring, repeat. Very nice also for casual gaming.

- FFV (enough said)
- GBA features with SNES music + 8 way movement
- AMAZING redrawn enemy sprites.
- I personally like the new character sprites too but opinions.
The Cons
- Tileset has some issues. I've ran it at 720p with good-ish results and 800x600 res seems to help as well.
- Framerate seems locked at 30 FPS despite running the game at full speed I think? Not really a big issue. Could just be my rig.
Are the technical issues enough for me to not recommend the game? Likely not. The new interface can be a bit weird and intrusive at times, but overall the port is workable enough to play if that makes any sense. Granted if you're concerned with the negatives greatly, a patch will likely be released for this game I imagine. The issues are fairly minor compared to the robust, amazing game it delivers. Additionally, the new menu controls are AMAZING! Being able to instantly exit menus on the fly is an awesome feature, alongside being able to pause the game at ANY instance even during an active battle (in case you have to attend to other business or use the washroom.)
Overall if you're concerned with some of the minor graphical issues and the framerate potentially, I'd say wait for a patch. If you love this game as much as I do however, these issues are fairly minor and do not get in the way of the core game experience, which is delightful. Otherwise I'd recommend playing the GBA port with the enhanced music patch (google it!)
I recommend this game if you don't mind the minor nuanced issues. Lots of people are complaining (and rightfully so if they're that upset) but I can't say the product is unplayably bad because I'd be lying. Overall, it's FF5 with nice new redrawn stuff and some minor graphical issues. Take it or leave it, but I overall recommend it personally.

This is a review of the first beta.
This game looks very promising to me. I think the coasters and scenery look fantastic so far, and the coaster editor looks like it will provide a lot more opportunities than in previous RCT versions. The editor could benefit from some modifications, but I think with some modifications and/or a tutorial in the final game, users should be able to get over its learning curve (which is a little steep right now).
Pros:
- Excellent scenery. I want to commend the developers on how nice the roller coasters, stations, trees, statues, park entrance, etc. look.  It's amazing!
- Excellent degree of control of scenery orientation (much higher than in previous RCTs).
- High degree of customizability with roller coaster design. Right now it takes a few hours to get a handle on a lot of the main elements (in particular, the three degrees of rotation at every node), but I think the end product is very rewarding.
- Path customizability. I have not fiddled around with this nearly as much as the coaster editor at this point, so I'm sure I don't have all of the details sorted out...but it looks very good!
- General commands (outside of the coaster editor) are pretty intuitive, especially if you are familiar with previous versions of RCT.
Cons:
- Strange train crashes. I found my trains often had a hard time going over the lift hill, and either some or all of the cars would fall off the track. I'm guessing this arises from track curves being too steep, or is some kind of bug I don't understand. (I lean to the first explanation only because I ran into this issue far less frequently after my first few coasters.)
- Unclear coaster ratings system. In the previous RCTs, I thought the Excitement/Intensity/Nausea system was pretty straightforward. Here, I was surprised at some of the values and unclear whether the new 4th metric ("Safety") should be high or low. I kept getting very low values for all the parameters other than safety, even for large coasters (with the highest excitement reaching ~3 only after adding lots of trees). Were they unsafe coasters (lowering the other values), or were they just tame? It's probably too early to nitpick this, but in the final version it would be great to have some more clarity.
- Inherent linking of rotations *combined* with needing to move your mouse to click certain buttons. (For instance, when you are about to place a new node, but then you want to bank the curve a little, you have to reach over to the bottom right of the screen, which might introduce some new curve into your track section that you then need to take out. Rotate your view, and something similar can happen. This could take a couple of iterations for a user to fix, and even when you understand it, you will have to spend some time correcting for it.)
My primary suggestion for the developers (as others have said) would be to have an "Expert Mode" and a "Basic Mode" for the coaster editor, where the "Expert Mode" is much like the current setup, and the "Basic Mode" removes some complexities (e.g. uses some elements of the previous RCTs or, for instance, turns off rotations along the track axis) to make coaster design more straightforward. I know people who didn't get too heavy into coaster design in the previous games (e.g. they never banked their coasters' turns), but they still loved the RCT series, so I'd expect the same to hold here in light of all the other improvements over previous iterations.
In summary, I think this game has a lot of potential and the final product will be worth buying, though I would only recommend pre-ordering if you are very experienced with coaster design and the previous RCT games. I think the new coaster editor looks outstanding so far, though it has a steep learning curve. I look forward to seeing the next beta and the final game release!

This is the perfect description for the game (Description on steam): "Black Hole Hazard is an action puzzle spacewalking game with unique control and a fascinating sci-fi story."
It is a game about a senior researcher at International Nuclear Research Center(INRC). He was participating in an experiment to create an artificial black hole. During the experiment, an unexpected explosion occurred and he was knocked unconscious. He woke up to find himself floating in a mysterious cosmic space.
My review:
I loved this game, you move by firing a gas-firing jet gun with the left click of the mouse and it pushes him exactly in the opposite direction. To shoot you use the right click of the mouse. The objective of the game is to reach a portal to continue to the next level, each level gets harder and harder by adding new enemies, new blocks and new traps. Each stage of the game has 8 levels, after you pass the 8 levels you have a boss fight. The game has amazing physics and a very good story. The game is simple but is of high quality.
The only problem I found was that after you pass a checkpoint and die, all the enemies that you killed before passing the checkpoint comes back too, instead of only coming back the ones you killed after the checkpoint.

To begin my review I have to say that I didn't play with other titles in the franchise (except with Ground Zeroes) so I might be a little biased.
The intro sequence is a bit weird if this is your first MGS title but after it does a great job explaining the Big Boss mythology and the events of Ground Zeroes.  That brings me to one of the most critised part of the game, the storytelling. Unfortunately Kojima thought it would a good idea to switch to casette tapes when it comes to storytelling devices. That doesn't mean there aren't any cutscenes but they are far and few between. I believe the story suffers from this kind of storytelling because you feel so disconnected from the happenings during the game.
The gameplay is loads of fun because it feels like a real sandbox. You have a lot of opportunity to carry out your missions with variety of gadgets and devices that game provides (of course they are only available if you have good enough R&D department on your base). There are side ops which can be bit boring if you are doing the 20th mine clearing mission in a row. The basebuilding is fun early game but weeding out your troublesome soldiers will be a tedious task once you reach mid or late game. The only annoying thing is that most interfaces were designed with consoles in mind so they are a bit hard to navigate with a mouse and keyboard.
The soundtrack is mostly made up of licensed hit songs from '80s, they can be listened on your "iDroid" during missions, or you can set them to your helicopter's landing music. Of course you have get them from Soviet and milita camps.
The engine is a technial marvel. The optimisation is great, the game looks good even on older hardware. The controls are tight but unfortunately the game assumes you are using a controller so there are a few things that you have to find out yourself.
To conclude it, I must say that this is brilliant title with a few shortcomings. I recommend this title to everyone who loves stealth games and/or games that gives you a lot of freedom.
