Renowned Explorers: International Society (RE:IS) is a nice mix of FTL-style exploration and classic hex-field turn-based strategy (such as Heroes of Might and Magic). The game really shines as a complex system of resources and synergies; it's a lot of fun to try out different ways of generating the ultimate ressource in the game - renown. Another element standing out is the combat mood system. Based on your actions and your opponents' actions, the encounters have a different mood, which gives your units certain buffs and debuffs. This really encourages you to use all abilities of your explorers, rather than just using the 'strongest' or 'juicest' (which you can also do and is a challenge of its own). I think in this sense, RE:IS is a great developmental step from REUS, the studio's previous game. REUS had bautiful synergistic mechanics, but the game played more like a simulation. In RE:IS, the devs managed to forge the synergies into a great interdependent game system that is very enjoyable and rewarding - especially if you're into building systems/resource engines.
In general, I think that the game is also a bit too short (many others have mentioned that as well). You're done after a handful of explorations; to compare it with a card game: it feels a bit like playing Race for the Galaxy -- you're taking some turns building a great resource engine, but there's not much time to actually see it run. This being said: The replay value is great, but I think some additional campaigns, or some sort of ongoing exploration with limited lives ("resolve") could be a great addition. (The good news is that the devs are still working on some additional content and modes.)
As much as I do like the mechanics and the complex resource system, I do think that the representations of different cultures and individuals are reinforcing problematic stereotypes. I do believe that 'exploration' type games do have a tendency to reinforce hegemonic world-views; in the case of RE:IS, I believe that the  "explorer" setting is indeed strongly reinforcing a eurocentric idea of exploration, and in fact, of cultural exploitation (and more than that: it refers to a style of colonialist exploration that actually did happen, and it romanticizes it).
Many encounters involve helpless or fumbling natives that need the help of the explorers. In my opinion this does have an undertone of cultural inequality, and contains an imlicit message that suggests a cultural inferiority in the cultures we explore in the game. It is also important to note that  all of the places we explore are depicted as technologically, and culturally less advanced.
On one side, the game gives me the choice to resolve encounters agressively or via persuasion. But even if I use persuasion, or 'friendly' tactics, I am still taking something away from the culture (e.g. artifacts). In fact, there is no way to progress in the game without taking artifacts away from their originating culture.  For example, I talk myself into a monastery and convince the nuns to give me one of their relics. Cultural exchange is great - but in RE:IS, a classic colonialist (one-sided, and hegemonic) way of exploration is a constitutional part of the game setting, and game play.
In conclusion: The irony in RE:IS is that the game mechanics are so bautifully synergistic - but the setting is colonialist. Overall I think that this is a game worth playing, set in a game setting worth problematizing and talking about.

This review is probably old at this point but here goes -
The next evolution of the F.E.A.R series: A challenging, deep and scary game. F.E.A.R 2, while probably not as interesting as its predecessor, is an excellent continuation of the series. Its a first person shooter with horror eliments, nuff said. Many improvements have been made; combat system is deffinetely more fluid, weapons feel weak though. Overall interesting story, deffinetely a lot of freaky and dissarming moments that really scare the sh@t out of you. Alma is in your face from start to finish....

The F.E.A.R franchise has always been & always will be a game about "The Paranormal" expect a lot of Ghosts in each of the games more so in F.E.A.R 1 & 2. That generally has a solid story line and to be expected in a game about the paranormal plenty of gore & jump scares. THESE ARE NOT BAD THINGS!
F.E.A.R had you playing in the shoes of an unknown solider for the "First Encounter Assault Recon Team" or F.E.A.R for short, you went in and you were tasked to capture a test subject who was designed to control these "Super Soldiers" for a war. The project was a success except things went wrong & the leader went nutso & so you're here to clean up the mess.
F.E.A.R 2 has you playing the role of a new solider named "Micheal Becket for the "First Encounter Assault Recon" who is in another squad & is deployed just before
released Alma in the first game, you were tasked to find & capture a doctor who was working on the test subject & then you are to eliminate the test subject & attempt to shut down project Origin by eliminate the main "Ghost" who was causing all the mayhem around the city, unfortunatly things don't pan out so well & then ♥♥♥♥ hits the fan & of course once more you're trying to battle your way out of the storm.
F.E.A.R 2 starts off right before you're deployed into the field, the first conversation from your squad fills you in on the parts you may have missed or if you didn't play the first installment fills you in on what has been happening for the first team. From here you're given a good understanding of your team & then you're plopped into the game and off to start your adventure.
F.E.A.R 2 focuses on it's story more than F.E.A.R 1 did & it adds even more into it's "creepy atmosphere" by giving you a lot more of the Ghosts you knew and loved in the first game, it also adds more fluent combat in the game by making combat seem more stable and flow well, unlike in F.E.A.R 1 where combat felt kind of chunky.
F.E.A.R 2 also saw a huge improvement in the Graphics department with a better engine, more impressive textures & even better shadows than F.E.A.R 1. (That game had some very impressive Textures & Shadows & even games today (2014) have trouble matching.)
The Gameplay in F.E.A.R 2: Project Origin is based more on exploring & reading the many stewn about conversations & lab notes dotted throughout each map filling you in on the story & what has been happening with the Origin Project with a hint of action and a lot of Ghosts to spice things up from time to time. Expect nothing much different here as there was in F.E.A.R 1 where you were fighting Mercinaries, Super Soldiers & the occasional Mech, except this time you won't always be fighting on your own 2 feet, sometimes you get some help from your own Mechs.
While F.E.A.R 2 is very impressive & most certainly improves on every aspect of the first F.E.A.R it's not what i could call better if anything F.E.A.R 1 & F.E.A.R 2 are very much at the exact same level as each other and it's hard to recommend either of them over the other, you really need to get both of them.
F.E.A.R 2 brings you better graphics, more fluent combat & more creepy ghostly moments than F.E.A.R 1 but it doesn't beat the initial feeling that F.E.A.R 1 brought to the gaming world, where it added the ability to carry a gun during moments of intense action & still managed to make you be♥♥♥♥♥♥scared of an unknown presence waiting to tear your face off.
F.E.A.R 2 also brought you an expanded version of the first F.E.A.R's story & made it's self well preserved in the sequal.
My final rating for F.E.A.R 2: Project Origin is a 7/10
F.E.A.R 2: Project Origin brings you everything i said above, improved graphics, more scares & better gun play but it also feels somewhat lacking of what F.E.A.R 1 brought us. It could just be me feeling nastalgic about F.E.A.R because it was nothing short of another DOOM 3 experience when i was younger.
And now i ask myself the question.
My recommendation is most certainly a YES, this game deserves a playthrough at least once just because it's a good game & it expands on F.E.A.R 1's design flawlessly.
Buy this & F.E.A.R 1 if you're able to and you'll most certainly have an enjoyable experience.

The review that points out that this game is for you if you like the theme of the game and can deal with a bit of jankiness was spot on for me. I like the theme of this game and I hadn't played any of the other games included in the bundle, so I have been having fun.
However, there is definitely jankiness in these games. There is little in the way of polish, the animations can be quite slow (which would be okay, except that you can't always que up the next action until they reach a certain point of the animation e.g. changing to the hydraulic cutters for your firemen and then ordering them to cut open a wrecked car, you must wait until they begin to grab the cutter until you can issue the order), the micromanagement is pretty hellish without a lot of tools to help mitigate.
Having said all that, though, I like the game because it is unique and because it does create a good amount of tension. If they smoothed out some of the nonsense (e.g. in Emergency 20, where you play the remastered missions, there is no tactical pause, while in Emergency 17, there is.) it would be a really great game. As it is, if you like the idea of a game that has you managing emergencies, and you haven't played/bought any of these titles before, and you're prepared to deal with some warts, you can have fun with this game.

This is one of these rare cases of Early Acces Done Right! Hats off to the developers so far!
As I'm writing this version 0.45 has just been released and the most important new features are the Level Editor and the Multiplayer Mode. I haven't even tried these yet but already this game delivers so much more content than many fully released and fully priced AAA-games. On top of that it looks amazing and the controls are smooth and easy to handle.
If you're someone who likes messing around with a box of Lego blocks to see what you can come up with, this game is Virtual Heaven.
If you love Kerbal SP but would like a change of pace and perspective, say with some Low Tech, slightly more Ground Based with a tad more focus on Purposeful Destruction, this is a fantastic addition to your virtual toybox.
If you like a Campaign that, altough still small in size, demands some serious creative thinking with perhaps lots of trial and error and lots of replay value, this game is so much fun.
If you like building siege engines, supercars, fighter jets, battleships, transformers and whatnot from wooden blocks and iron fittings, with physics that actually feel realistic, buy this game and embark on a rampage of creativity.
If you like to challenge your friends into a match of medieval Robot Wars in your DIY-arena then do yourself a great favour and try this one out.
If the (ridiculously) Low Price of the game makes you suspicious of the (lack of) depth of this game just browse the Workshop or the many YouTube video's and feel your lower jaw drop to the floor.
If even the (ridiculously) Low Price is too much for your budget wait for the next time it goes on sale (I think I picked it up for around three bucks!).
Do not buy this game if you don't like creative building, if you're put off by a slight learning curve or if you don't have any patience to wait for the rare kind of devs who somehow seem to be able to take the time they need to make something good!
So yeah, consider this a strong recommendation.

It's really simple. If you've played/own SC1 and/or FA, this game will probably disappoint you. In general, lots of options have been taken out which were present in the predecessors, including diversity and lots of tactical features, especially the latter being very important aspect of RTS genre.
However, this has been happening with most of (RTS, but also others as well) games recently. This game fits into this new category of "next-gen" games. The UI and Graphics have been updated (although in SC2 it isn't as fake flashy as in other new games), so it appeals to new and probably young players (who otherwise lose their attention if they aren't surprised in the first few seconds of seeing a new game, and the very first thing you see in a game is how it looks like). Also, it has been simplified a lot (or, I think it was both partly, it wasn't really finished yet), but that again can have its positive effects, like new players get into it faster and you can convince friends to play it easier.
So for situations where you've got some time for a long battle, together with other RTS-dedicated friends, SC1 and FA fits better.
However, especially if you haven't (yet) played the previous ones in the series, this game can really be awesome and fun to play. The largest maps in the game, while far from the size of SC1's and FA's 81x81km games where you really wish you had some Homeworld hyperspace modules, they still give some lengthy plays and tactical options. The smaller maps are good for quick plays, when you don't have that much time.
You've still got control of exlusions of what can't be built in Skirmish/MP and the game can be modded quite easily (although not many mods are made),  so for some casual battles you can change things slightly (like I find it relaxing to sometimes play without nukes and/or air units). Also, some mods are actually quite good, and some bring back some SC1/FA features.
So to conclude, if you want lots of tactics, slow(er) gameplay, grand scale and planning, you'll probably like SC1 and FA better. However, if you want some quick matches, easier play/calmer learning curve, or want some friends to join you quickly who might not be into RTS games that much, SC2 is a quite nice game to play.
I'd certainly recommend buying it in a sale, it really is worth the price when it's reduced like that.
Oh, and don't forget to buy the Infinite War DLC, it is a must for the game!

Tiny Brains is a decent enough puzzle-platformer for two or more players. I can not imagine playing it alone, so make sure you have someone with you, as the game is not just for two players, it is pretty much only enjoyable this way.
Anyway, you control four mice that have unique powers(Push, Suck, Switch-positions, and Freezing) and all their powers combine to help you get through the increasingly harder levels. The game has a cute look and the puzzles are usually quite satisfying to solve.
However, the game does lean towards being very rage-inducing. Some of the puzzles involve keeping a little critter alive while it is being attacked by waves on enemies. It's not fun and can drive just about anyone made. Other puzzles involve pushing a ball through a complicated hole-filled maze. They are not fun, either.
The majority of the puzzles, though, are wonderful little rooms(think of Portal) that require solving something in order to open the exit. These are all great and a lot of fun to solve with a friend. If they make a sequel, they should focus on these kind of puzzles exclusively.
Room puzzles - 8/10
Non-room puzzles - 4/10
Overall, this game is worth 6/10 to me.

As this stands, I cannot recommend it.  This is yet another instance of a game being released while it's still horribly unoptimized.  30 fps, laggy and jankity screen moment even on a good PC.. that's unforgiveable as far as a remake goes.  It just looks like trash.  I got it to stream it and play through it with some friends, but it's just not worth it, people will get seizures from watching it.
The sprites are hit and miss... Bartz/Butz/Dude's sprite looks like he's puffing out his chest beyond what humans are capable of, but ones like Lenna's look alright.  The character portraits are Amano, but as per usual they don't look like the characters at all.. so that's up to you whether it's cool or not.
Tileset is a friggin' mess.  Considering there are games out there made in RPG maker that have a smoother set than this says leagues.  The majority of tiles don't blend together, and look like they are all mashed together.
My major battle complaint is that you can't just hold down the attack key.. you have to push it every time.  Not a big deal, but why would they take this function out in a remake?  Did they not play the old one?  When older RPGs get re-released, they typically have things to speed up the game, not slow them down.  It's really just nitpicking, but it slows down things considerably.
I wish I could say I recommend this, but I can't.  Not unless they patch it.  Pass unless you read about a lot of patch notes!  I'm tired of getting burned for pre-ordering PC games.

I really like the Final Fantasy series and loved playing it on ps1 as a teenager.
When I saw those games were available on steam I got a bit excited and just to get it.
However, after playing this game for 40 minutes I'm kinda done.
- Screen Tearing / Flickering
You can't play this game in fullscreen... or well, I can't. It seriously hurts my eyes as through all the cut scenes, there is major 'flickering' going on. After 10minutes of playing I choose a smaller resolution and unchecked fullscreen.
- Graphic
I did not expect anything good and overall the Graphics of the game are 'OK'...
That being said.. you will always see the 'grid' / the 'tiles' of the game, others mentioned it before and I thought at first I'd be OK with it.. but after playing 40minutes it already takes it toll on me.
Others also mentioned the characters look nothing like their potrait.
- Audio
This to me is actually the tipping point. 8bit melody / sound effects none stop. I actually shrug up the first time I entered a fight because the audio/ soundeffect hurt my ears a little bit.
If I were to continue playing this game I would actually mute the sound and play some music with it, that's how much I dislike it at this point.
- Conclusion
It honestly seems like Square Enix just ported this game with little care or work being done to it. It will appeal to the hardcore FinalFantasy fans that absolutly want this game on pc - for me, it feels like I payed ~14€ for a game from the 90's.
Honestly just put a little work in it and you got a great game, work on the audio and visuals and make it a bit more appealing Square Enix..
.. don't get me wrong FF V is a great game.. but this is just a port.. you can play this on a GameBoy Advanced and will not be worse of than the pc version - this is to me what makes it so 'dissapointing' they seem to have put in little effort to make this an enjoyable experience.

I have somewhat of a soft spot for old school turn-based JRPGS, and this is one of my favorites. FFV tragically gets overlooked quite a bit because it didn't have an official U.S. release/translation until 1999, seven years after it came out. This is really a shame because I think FFV outshines the other SNES era Final Fantasy games in a lot of ways. I'm sure this is a controversial opinion as debating which games in the Final Fantasy series always tends to get heated, but if you don't believe me and you haven't played this game, you really should.
FFV's story is kind of... ehhh. It's pretty standard template "heroes save the world" writing. Story is not where this game shines, but pretty early in the game, you’ll unlock FFV’s job system. FFV's job system is what sets this game apart from other Final Fantasy titles, for better or for worse. The various jobs are slowly unlocked at key story points as you progress through the game. You initially unlock knight, monk, thief, white mage, black mage and blue mage but will eventually unlock all 21 jobs (25 in the enhanced remake). You can assign any of your 4 party members any job and can reassign them at any time. Changing jobs will affect your character’s stats and what items they're able to equip as well as grant them different abilities to use in battle. Once you master a job’s ability you can carry it over to use with other jobs. This, to me, is where FFV is at its best. Trying to figure out which combinations of jobs and abilities were powerful and which were useless was really fun and rewarding. For instance, combining the Ninja job's "dual wield" ability with the knight class' high innate defense and ability to equip high damage longswords was pretty good if my memory serves. FFV is paced pretty well such that you'll unlock more jobs just as you were mastering previous ones so you always have new combinations and tricks to try out and experiment with. The ending of the game comes right about the time you've mastered enough jobs to be dangerous. Unleashing all of your ridiculous tricks and crazy combinations on the final boss feels like an adequate final exam of your mastery of the job system.
I think FFV is one of Nobuo Uematsu’s first really excellent soundtracks . Not that any that came before were inferior, but FFV really showcases Uematsu's musical range and his ability to create timeless and catchy tunes one right after the other, over and over again. “To the North Mountain”, “Home, Sweet Home" and "Clash on the Big Bridge" are some of my favorite tracks.
Summary:
If you enjoy old school RPGs or are a FF fan who missed out on this game the first time around, you should check this game out. If you don't mind the slower pacing of the turn-based combat, I've found experimenting with FFV's job system while listening to the genius of Uematsu to be a really enjoyable experience

It's freaking Final Fantasy V. If you've played the other versions you'll like this one.
-It has a sort of autosave-function I'm not willing to trust entirely yet, but then again it seems to be very good. Seems to save after entering new area and after winning a battle.
-New sprites look weird at first compared to the classic sprites, but you get used to them pretty quick. Besides, they emote very much in the same way as the classics. (Weird to see King Tycoon's head!)
-Documentation is very extensive if you come in as a new player.
-I've seen complaints about running in 30fps instead of 60fps and honestly I have no idea what the problem is. I get it in a modern action game, but this is a SNES era JRPG. You want your party to chop at air smoothly? Anyhow, I'm sure some wizard will unlock it.
-Some people are having graphical issues like tearing, but I haven't seen any, so YMMV.
-Music is the classic old stuff, no weird new remixes.
Overall I can recommend this especially to fans of the old games and other versions of FFV (you have the handheld goodies in this one). I can also recommend this to people who enjoy classic JRPGs. You can read more extensively about the actual game online, but basically it's a very "standard" FInal Fantasy: Group of heroes destined to save the world with the help of the Crystals. Considerably more lighthearted and humoristic than FFIV or FFVI. The Job system is awesome.
PS. If you're new to the game don't check the achievements, since they spoil several plot points straight out!
Nice to own Final Fantasy V again. Despite the negative reviews I've found my time so far in FFV to be enjoyable.

A bit of a preface. The Final Fantasy series was what got me into rpg's some 20 odd years ago. I own multiple copies of the games spread across multiple consoles and I have beaten all of them. While I am not a diehard player I can certainly say that I really love this series. Which is why it pains me to say this but I cannot recommend the Final Fantasy V port.
The positives about the game are that I really like the re-done sprites for the monsters and some of the background sprites for objects and buildings do look nice. You have free movement instead of tile movement and you can quickly quit out of the menus by hitting the menu button. Unfortunately though, those is the only positives.
The first thing bad about this port is what everybody already knows, the character sprites. While I personally don't mind the new sprites, the problem is that they just dont fit in graphically with how the world looks. They look like they were going for a psudo 3D look to them which makes them stick out like a sore thumb against the backgrounds.  Plus their color pallets are exceptionally bright making them stick out even more. It is more or less distracting and constanly pulls me from the experience.
The second bad thing is the profile pics when they talk. While I am all for seeing the original artwork and I actually like how the characters are designed in it, they just dont fit into how the game looks. This is of course is also distracting seeing the clear difference between the simple sprites in the game, and the highly detailed character portraits.
The the third bad thing are the tiling textures, which actually don't tile at all. Around all of the tiles there is an extremely visible seam along all four sides which is, you guessed it, distracting. While moving around you don't really notice it but definately during cutscenes you will. I did read that if you put the game into 720p windowed mode it isnt as bad, but the problem is that it is still there and I want to play my game in fullscreen 1080p.
The fourth and final bad thing is the UI. Being an iOS/Android port the interface was changed to accomondate that. The problem is that SE did nothing to try and get it back to how it was, or done something to remotely change it. Not to mention there is a bug where if you mash the attack button in battle the cursor moves to the row button, wasting a characters turn and weakening them by moving them to the back row. You can move them back to the front but by then you have wasted two turns.
So in the end all we have is a game with a bunch of graphical elements that distract the player from enjoying the game and an uninspired mobile UI. While the game itself is great and it is Final Fantasy V, the lack of art direction really pulls me from the game. I probably won't refund the game as I do wish to own this on PC, but going forth I will definately wait to buy any other games in the series at a steep discount. My only worry is that when FInal Fantasy VI will eventually come to PC, that it will be in the same sad, disappointing shape this game was put in.

I got this game during the winter steam sale and found it to be very good. You play as Catherine Stockholmes, an amnesiac girl that woke up in a prison chamber. You soon find out that the place you are in is your father's factory and must retrieve 5 different type of keys in order to escape the factory. There are a few different criterias that make this game stand out to me:
Characters:
- First off, this game has beautiful character designs. As for the characters themselves, Catherine isn't that great of a protagonist. But the two characters that I really like are the the doll and the boy. Both are characters have very intriguing personality that kept me wanting to know more.
Story:
- The story starts off strong, with many possibilities but drops off a bit later on. The twist at the end caught me by surprise and while it is not the best of ending, it is definitely a great ending.
Puzzles:
- The puzzle designs are very good, they feel very rewarding when you solve them. All of the puzzles are different from each other so they never feel repetitive.
Graphic:
- The artwork is very well done. I really like the special effect that some of the artworks have, it is unique compared to other games. Only downside is that a few of the arts are inconsistent.
Sound:
- I like the bit of voice acting in the game, it brings the character to live for me. Also, the music is good as well and does not feel out of place at any time.
For its value this is a great game that the developers put a lot of effort in. Hoping for a sequel soon :)

I may not be the biggest fan of horror games, however this one hits a lot of the right notes and excels in a lot of places many others don't.   I dislike how in a lot of top-down horror games the point A to point B segments sometimes come off as complete random.  Stitched however does a good job at railroading the player so they never get lost, while at the same time not ever coming off as handholdy.
The story is a little cliche for this type of game, however it is very well written to the point of which you don't notice that often.  The characters are all likable, and have interesting mysteries surrounding them.  There are also these detailed and sometimes gory digitally painted visuals that very much add to the experience.
Great horror game and a pretty great RPGMaker game as well.

Bottom line at the top for the short version of my review: Game is enjoyable despite some obvious flaws and I'll be on the lookout for any other game this Studio might release in the future.
I'm a huge fan of puzzle RPGMaker games, especially horror ones, so I nearly jumped on this game as soon as I saw it.
I can say I enjoyed it and the pill system made it more challenging than your basic puzzle game, which I appreciated.
The artstyle is overall pretty, though uneven. The music is simple but works perfectly.
Chasing scenes are usually my bane and can quickly frustrate me but the rest was fun enough for me to easily overlook this. I will have to say that if you hate those kind of things, some of them might make you bang your head on your desk and ask yourself what o what did you ever do to the developpers to deserve this.
Lastly, while the story starts strong with some very interesting possibilites, the ending(s) feel a bit flat and abrupt. The only explanation I can think of is a buildup for a sequel.

I thought I knew this game was going to just another one of the many titles in the Steam Store, but it's completely not just another game. Stitched is a Top-Down game such as The Witch's House and such so, has a scary atmosphere with blood and gore. It contains spooks and jumpscares that comes along with unique art. You get the bare essentials of the plot behind the game, but still contains strange mysterys and secrets. It's fun so far and I would very much recommend you get this game. Tread carefully.

I grew up playing games in the 90s so this takes me back. The gameplay seems pretty simple: you interact with objects and find solutions to puzzles in order to progress. What makes this game interesting, however, is that it provides a feel of a real horror story with its eerie sound and ambience. The storyline also seems pretty engaging, which I feel a need to mention as many games tend to focus on animations and graphics with a lacking storyline. Stitched tells the story of a girl awaken in a doll factory with no memory of how she got there. Throughout the game, the player has to navigate obstables, solves puzzles, meets interesting characters, avoids dangerous threats, discovers secrets and find keys to escape the factory.
Pros:
- Atmosphere fits the theme of the game
- Great artstyle, great use of the color purple
- Some puzzles are well designed
- Story is engaging and interesting
- Well developed cast of characters
- Good attention to details, has small touches here and there
- Nice gallery feature
So-so:
- GUI could be improved a bit
- Backtracking is required to get more out of the story
- Some arts are inconsistent
Cons:
- Fullscreen support not available
- Mouse is not very useful
Overall, Stitched was an enjoyable experience for me and I would recommend it for those interested in horror adventure games with good storyline.

Well lets see ouch look at that current review 195 with a 41% postive...... Well this is a Beta review first off, just a little FYI.
(Beta 1 Review)
So lets get started if you ever was a fan of Rollercoaster tycoon 1,2, and maybe even 3. Then this is the game you have been waiting for, or is it. Well we currently are testing the first public beta, or atleast the people that pre-ordered the game are. It's limited to just the coaster builder system, the path builder system, and some props and the ablity to edit the terrain with out a grid system like in the old RCT games.
(The Coaster Builder System)
You have several different coaster to try out and test.
Each coast has a few options for the stations.
You can change the colors of your coaster in 3 different areas rails, core, and supports.
You can change some of your coasters trains.
The new coaster builder system is kinda like a string that you can pull and turn and twist in to a pretty crazy looking rollercoaster. It sure is not the easiest thing to use by any means, infact sometimes it down right frustrating. It really shouldnt be this hard to build a coaster. I really do like the new system tho it really allows you to make a one of a kind coaster. After messing around with the coaster builder, it did get easier to use and I kinda started to enjoy making these crazy coasters.
Tho with that being said I have seen some pretty crazy bugs with the new coaster system. The main bug I see is that the supports sometimes are missing where there is no reason for it to be missing and then sometimes the coaster supports are right in the middle of another peice of track.
Not locked to a grid or a set of peices really does add to the over all freedom of the new coaster builder.
(The Path Building System)
You get a lot of different paths to pick from you even get 3 different sizes.
You are able to do straight paths , curved paths, and que lines for your rides, tho it would seem you cant do curved que paths.
You can raise the path and make some really cool path systems, saddly tho no steps but they have said they were looking into it.
(Props)
Not much to say really you get a bunch of trees, some rocks, some statues, a few different trashcans, benchs, tables, light poles, even some halloween items.
About the only thing that seemed off to me was their double flag poles where not the same ingame as they showed in the menu...
(Peeps)
You see the peeps but they are just ghosted out they look much better then last time I saw them at PAX i think it was. They was kinda like power sliding every where.
( HOW DOES IT RUN )
Well it crashes a lot...... and i can not say this enough but i mean a ungodly amount. But remember this is a beta..... When it does start up and work it seems like the game has memory problem or something. I have 8 gb of DDR 3 and they recoment 6GB and i can watch it peg my memory out over just 3 coasters and some trees...... what about all them flat rides and peeps... i Still feel like they have alot of work to do before this is ready but then again maybe this is just a older version of the game they are leting us play on. I have faith they well make this game great so i would Recommend this game but i would atleast hold out till late nov as that is when beta 2 should be out and they will open more of the game out to the public to test out.

Presentation Review

First of all, I am getting this out of the way. RE:IS is a very compelling , Refined , Well-paced and simply epic way of telling story using every mechanic to support the idea of upbeat adventure. Which might be praised  for a hundreds of time already.
So I am going to focus on presentation this game has to offer instead. First of all, I am pretty much a sucker for anything that has a strong theme. whatever it might sound weird , serious , stupid or unrealistic it is, If the game living in it's own world and take advantage on it's own theme then it's doing presentation right (example : Darkest Dungeon , Hunnie Pop, Don't Starve , Recettear)
For limited budget game like REIS to shine out,  It has to need every aspect of the game to help represent the theme of
the game and gladly they did almost everything right. the visual is bright and colorful in pop up book style , this might just look too simple on screenshots but when you playing it yourself it feel a hundred times more impressive. This is one of the game that design everything to support the theme itself. Characters design is vivid , a little goofy but they can be mixed together not just for create an efficient party but to change the story telling itself too. Also , to support the idea of combat system that based on "Friendly" , "Devious" and "Aggressive" ways, Every character has their own traits and personality fitting what they are. A small but important details like how they gain buffs or making facial expression on dialogue encounters helping a lot!  So even not in combat this game still keep getting interesting by well made story telling (which you have part of writing it too). It's not hard to find an epic funny story along the way and still this is not the end of how smart they using this system, Because the way they keep changing how encounters and event approach you. Eventually , You will find  most of them but it will hardly goes stale because you will still get different vibe with different party anyway. Even Combat system is created to compliment the theme , battle can be resolved in ways and it's really funny that you can even bully a giant monster until he cry and run away! (and that is A F**KING Brilliant way to make this game appealing).
The weakest point of presentation might be the soundtracks of the game, However it's not actually bad but comparing with all amazing aspect of this game, music in this game got a little off feeling (feel like it should be more upbeat and epic than this), And While it has a good feedback interface that giving most information you need to know. some of them are still lacking (like no tool-tips of unlock buildings in world map and some unclear combat tiles connection). Anyway these are just very tiny dot in this masterpiece.
Bottom line. Just shove money into this game as hard as you can! this game deserve more sale and attention than it is!
(I don't know if pricing in USD maybe a bit higher but in Thailand it's about $10 which is a very good deal)
Exceptional game, if you like games like FTL or other roguelites then this one is definitely for you! Love the fantasy setting as well!

Level 1-7 in particular was designed by a sadist.

Intro 4/10
Music 8/10 (could change up sometimes)
Graphics 6/10 (Good for what the game is, but could be more varied)
Gameplay 9/10

If they add more variety and different challenges, obstacles, sprites, and music as the game goes on I think it will keep a players interest for a long time.

This game is a love song to Super Metroid played by a nerdy mariachi band.
Instead of an arm cannon, you use your fists. Instead of a morph ball, you turn into a chicken. Instead of color-coded doors to be opened with the appropriate weapon, there are colored blocks to be smashed with your varied slam attacks. You even gain your powers by destroying precious Chozo statues (more on that later.)
The best part of this game, hands down, is the combat. The multitude of useful attacks at your disposal, combined with the responsive dodging mechanic and the fun and powerful grapples means that the combo system is both useful and rewarding. Battles in this game just resonate with me as being really fun, as you can bash some skeletons around, throw them into other skeletons, and just keep it going as the numbers on your screen go up and up and you get a bigger money reward when the fight is finished. It's just really fun, and the enemies are well designed to let you take advantage of combos and such if you're good.
The level design is nice, and they manage to keep the levels fresh with mixtures of new and old elements that let you make use of your powers. Backtracking when you have new powers, a staple of any "Metroidvania" game, is present in this game, but also quite simplified. Areas that are blocked off from you are marked in bright, unmistakeable colors on your map, and correspond to certain powerups. While this is unfortunate if you enjoy more subtle or clever ways to impede progress, there are a few secret areas scattered about that have very little indication on the map, meaning you have to be perceptive to find them. The art style and design of the levels are also overall pretty good, but while the backgrounds are vibrant and creative, the walls of the levels are all dark and square, making areas seem kind of cramped, and it's just not as visually entertaining as it could be.
Unfortunately, there is a lot of untapped potential in Guacamelee. There were a few levels that were pretty barren as far as secrets and backtracking goes, which sort of made them simply linear puzzle dungeons. The last few hours of gameplay for me could have been a lot better if I had more reasons to revist older areas. Due to the linearity of how and when you get your abilities, most of the secret areas just contained health and stamina upgrades. I would have liked if there were optional powerups or attacks that I could find, or perhaps more villager sidequests that required you to visit other areas. There are only two towns in Guacamelee, and all of the "quests" are pretty much just completed inside those towns, when there's no reason not to use other areas for them.
My main gripe with this game is how shallow the world feels, and there is one big reason for this: instead of worldbuilding and lore, the game opted for silly references and jokes. I think that the developers got kind of lazy in this regard, because the world concept is a pretty cool one, and the art and character design is top notch. But even though the game was inviting me to care about the world inside through its visuals, it just completely falls flat whenever it wants to convey information about the world directly. The towns are littered with posters of famous luchadores and advertisements, and 100% of those are jokes or references to nerd stuff. They were cute and funny the first couple times I saw them, but then I realized that these areas that could have been vibrant with character were just a platform for showing me some mexican versions of memes.
I mentioned that you gain your powers by smashing Chozo statues, and I mean really. There are Chozo statues laying around in the dungeons, like, actual Chozo statues from Metroid. And you smash them, and then the goatman cometh and yells at you for smashing his rare Chozo statue, and gives you a new power. Again, this was funny the first time, like, haha, we're trying to make a Metroid game guys! Haha! But really, that's a missed opportunity for something more creative or fitting for the game's world. You could still make a lazy Metroid reference, but instead of it being a Chozo make it a Luchadore or something. I hate saying this, but the over-reliance on jokes in this game smashes ~my immersion~. I know, I would roll my eyes if someone told me that, but it's true. It just ticks me off because the lazy world-building sours what would otherwise be a fantastic game.
Despite all that, I really do love this game. It's a blast to play, and I had a good time exploring and taking on the secret challenges. The game can get pretty tough when it wants to, and those difficult areas are really satisfying to beat. The music is great, and the gameplay is superb. I would only write such a big effortpost review if I actually cared enough about the game, so at least there's that. I highly recommend you give Guacamelee! a try.

If you mixed Metroid with Super Meat Boy and sprinkled in a little bit of brawler fighting (maybe TMNT: Turtles Through Time?), wrapped it all up in a Mexican "Day of the Dead" aesthetic with beautiful artwork, and threw in a few laughs for good measure, you would get Guacamelee.
I'm not quite finished with the game as of writing this but I've had an absolute blast playing.

Metroidvaina + Castle Crashers with just a dash of Super Meat Boy! = Guacamelee!
I purchased this game as soon as I saw that Metroidvaina was the general design of the game. I intended to test it out when I installed but ended up playing for 3 straight hours.
You'll play as Juan who dons the mask of legacy and becomes the Luchador. The game is filled with Mexican culture with modern internet-isms (memes as well) masked throughout. Don't let that push you away however, seeing iconic internet..uhh things in the game actually provide a bit of subjective art as I felt more connected as if the developers are one of us who are playing.
The controls are extremely fluid, with the ability to cancel out of any action with an air or ground dodge and the combat has just as much flow. You do a regular melee attack that can combo up to 3 hits with cardinal directional moves depending on if you are in the air or ground. Add another button dedicated to Special moves also with 4 directions of variety and you got a simplistic yet intricate combat system. Oh you can also toss opponents across the arena and into other skeletal hombres.
The exploration aspect is top notch with nook and crannys begging to be searched. You'll find places you can't reach due to some obstruction and be rewarded if you remember later down the road. At one point in the game, you'll have the power to switch from the light world to the dead world with platforming and combat creatively incoporated. While some secrets are obvious, you'll need to put on your master explorer hat to find everything Gucamelee! has to offer. The difficulty is just right, with the enemies requiring more finesse and the platforming demanding 2 or 3 actions in short time. For the daring, to 100% the game, Guacamelee! demands you to channel your inner Super Meat Boy and do some sadistc platforming challenges.
The soundtrack is fantastic with each area giving you a different Mexcian vibe. I always enjoyed hearing all of the pieces each and everytime I entered an area.
You can even have local 2 player coop!
There is a ton to say about Guacamelee! but I think you should save it for yourself. I personally recommend this game to anyone who enjoys beat-em ups/platformers/and exploration adventures (Castle Crashers, Metroid, Castlevaina, Super Meat Boy)
To fully complete the game (100% completion including Steam Achievements) I clocked in at about 10 hours.

My first attempt at cooking got me the following feedback: "it's good, but I don't like it" I didn't know what to do with that statement, because I thought I had done a horrible job and my family was just nice enough not to hurt my feelings. Today I am in the controversial position of having similar thoughts about Battleborn, though I still can't fathom the paradox of the prior statement in its full glory. I have a FPS history and I loved action RPGs like Mass Effect and The Witcher from the very start. I loved borderlands too, especially in coop and was thus probably also biased into buying the season pass - at full price upon release, mind you - for Battleborn, which I've uninstalled just two weeks ago. I still cannot completely wrap my mind around why I'm not ready to go on with the game and uninstalling it felt like a failure, either by the game, or by myself.
I'm an occasional gamer, having a family, children, a demanding job and not endless time available. Gaming is my hobby, not like it used to, but still part of my everyday life. It's a vent, it's joy and mostly I understand the games. I didn't understand Battleborn though. When I keep rushing through BF4 even with a bunch of strangers, the goal is clear, people mostly know the map and if they don't, you help out. Maybe I'm old but I didn't understand battleborn and probably what really got me away from it was the lack of collaboration the game expects from it's players. 40 hours in I basically just played Miko since on multiplayer nobody else seemed to care about the necessity of having a healer around. I've missed the hero feeling and the gratefulness of my fellow mates who just dashed off to find shards, destroy sentries in an uncoordinated manner and just don't giving a sh*t about who was fighting alongside them. But I wanted to try MOBA.
"Hey did you see that?! My spore mushroom just killed Boldur, all the while healing your lazy a** trapped in the corner and I slowed down the minions so you could recover" No, you probably didn't. "Oh f*ck, how did Montana get so close to me, I'm done for... when some well mannered Orendi had the grace to save my skin" - so cool, open chat: "Hey, you're great, I thought it was my last breath when Montana came rushing. Thanks Orendi!" Too much happening to read the chat? Maybe didn't find the settings to have it displayed long enough? No problem: try voip... to no avail. Well, I can keep talking to myself...
No feeling, no connection with my fellow mates. If there was much interaction, then it was a "hi" at the character selction screen and only if I've started the conversation. Probably I am old fashioned but there never really was a "GL & HF" feeling. But maybe it's not about interaction with others in this game and I kept enjoying every round of it, no matter how frustrating it sometimes could become. I still like the game, I just don't have enough incentive to go back. BF4 is much more rewarding and less overwhelming - to me.
So, what it is with "It's good but I don't like it"? I think Battleborn is a very cool game and probably I wish I had enough friends around trying to play it. I've never come to see all the levels and I've played levels a dozen times, where there are still corners I've never come close to - since Miko isn't the tank type. I still have the feeling I just scratched the surface of something bigger, something deeper, something much more rewarding but all I'm left with is just the feeling and not the motivation to go on and dig deeper - maybe one day.
To close the story I'm a pretty decent household cook in the meanwhile, which took many failures to get me there - and passion, lots of it. I just don't feel the same for Battleborn. It's like seeing a good street musician: you wish you could play the guitar the same way, but just don't see how you could get there with a busy life. In the end, would I recommend the game, yes - definitely, with a suggestion: be part of the community, contribute, no matter how shallow the effort. And take your time, don't leave your mates in mid-game struggling like football team after a red card. Try to support beginners. I had some hilarious fun when tanks shouted at me "I'm the tank, just stay with me" in my first couple of rounds. I'm just not made for MOBA. Too frenetic, too many things to take care for (why Miko suited me well in the background) and lack of attention of most people who are playing it for the sake of gathering achievements, finding the next best lore and artifact.
In short: It's not a game for me, though I liked playing it. My player "persona" is just not cut out for it. I am not angry at having payed the full price and I still feel like I got a lot for my money. I'm left with the doubt about me being uncapable of enjoying it fully or the game not being capable of enabling me to - why it's good, but probably not made for me.

tl;dr version Far better loadtimes, fewer bugs, and a few QoL advantages over the PS1 port.  But this comes at the cost of inferior graphics on the overworld/dungeons/town sprites. Combat sprites are still okay.
LONG VERSION
This is a PC port of the cellphone version of one of my favorite FF titles.  I'm not here to discuss FF5 as a whole (love the game), but as a voice of rebuttal aganst some reviews I've seen posted for this game.
I have not personally seen the extreme screen tearing or refusal to bootup some users claim.
GAMPLAY PROs
+ 8 way diagonal movement
+ Autobattle is great for grinding or going through easy areas.  (Either all Attack or all repeat last action, based on how you set cursor memory in config)
+ Sprint on world map
+ Automatic quicksaves
GAMEPLAY CONs
- Game runs slow in areas that involve room layouts changing (I've only seen two such rooms, both lategame, as of entering the final main storyline dungeon).
- Cellphone interface means buying multiple items is half as bad/annoying as FF1 NES version.
GRAPHIC PROs
+ Combat sprites have addition animation/poses, based on which job/character it is.
GRAPHIC CONs
- Different character sprites for noncombat (map, story, etc). Initially HATED the new sprites during pre-release screenshots, but they've grown on me after seeing them in motion.
- Portaits, while from the original character designer and decent art on their own, often look almost nothing like the ingame character.
- Very noticibly poor tiling/tile seams in some areas
- Not true fullscreen/widescreen, and supposedly very noticeable on dual monitors.
- A certain portrait and sprite spoils the impact of a famous earlygame plot point.
NOTE: Users have found ways to mod the character portraits.
MISC PROs
Title Menu offers bestiary (filled as you fight) and music player (all unlocked by default).
OTHER Vs GBA
+ Not $40-$80+, and no risk of getting a bootleg or dead save battery.
+ 15 Save slots
OTHER Vs PS1
+ No save menu graphic glitch (PS2), constant freezing (PS3), or insane loadtimes (all)
+ GBA bonus content included
- Sprint feature now requires Thief. As such you can't double-up on the Sprint speed bonus.
? Different translation.  Probably better, given all the Y-Burns (Wyverns) and such in PS1.
If SE would have "fixed" the cellphone graphics and interface changes, this would be the hands-down definitive version of FF5.  But in the current state, this version makes the "best FF5" debate even more complicated.
Is it worth the full $16 Square is asking for in the current state?  Debatable, depending on how you feel about the genre, FF5 itself, and "lazy" ports of cellphone games.  But for the $8 or less that it'll probably eventually go on sale for later, I'd say it's worthwhile, even if they left it as-is.
[Note: Pricing info based on USA pricing as of launch].

An underappreciated classic, Final Fantasy V was originally released in 1992 for the Super Famicom and never saw an official US release until 1999 for the Playstation as part of Final Fantasy Anthology. In 2006, the game was re-released with bonus content for the Gameboy Advance.
What we have here is an enhanced remake of the Gameboy Advance version. The graphics and battle system have changed greatly, as has some of the translation. This can be a good thing or a bad thing. If you're a purist of the original Super Famicom version, then seeing the updates would probably make you feel uneasy and will take some getting used to. If you've never had a chance to play the see in the past, then you won't really care.
The graphics itself are really clean and crisp. They hold the 16-bit charm of yesterday while still presenting itself as something pleasing to the eyes of today. Sure, the portraits of the characters do not look like their sprites, but it's a 16-bit game, so imagination sometimes comes into play. Besides, this is traditional of any Final Fantasy remake in years past  (I'm thinking of Final Fantasy II here). The only issue I had was when the characters move their limbs or do some sort of action on screen. I'm not saying it's bad, but having played the original, seeing these events transpire with updates does cause me to chuckle.
The nostalgia factor kicks in big with the music. I literally have not heard a single change in quality from the original Super Famicom release, as if the music files were taken straight from the original source with no editing whatsoever. As a fan of the original game, this is pleasing to me, but as a fan of modern games, I will say that this is also appreciated. Even without an enhanced music track, the soundtrack is one of Nobuo Uematsu's finest and sounds great even by today's standards. It fits the style of the game itself and the story to go with it.
The story is very well done, albeit typical and to a point even cliché; evil guy threatens the world, four unsuspecting heroes set off on a quest to stop him, yada, yada, yada. There are plenty of twists and turns to keep the averge player involved, and there is also humor splashed in all over the place. There is enough mystery and suspense to make you think and wonder what is coming up next. Everything is presented well overall.
The gameplay, in my honest opinion, still holds up to this day. If you've played any Final Fantasy game, or any RPG in general, then grasping the concept of battle won't be difficult. Battle is simple, exploration is easy, dungeons are challenging, but fair. But what really sets Final Fantasy V apart from the others is the Job System. Yes, a lot of Final Fantasy games instituted a Job System of some sort (in all actuality, this type of system was taken from Final Fantasy III), but this game takes it a step further. As you battle, you gain AP to grow the job you assign your characters. When your Job levels up, you learn an ability (say Black Magic). But, perhaps later you want a character to change their job (we'll use Thief as an example). When you change your job, you can choose one ability that you have previously learned from another job to add it to your arsenal (like Black Magic). So in essence, you will then have a Thief who can cast Black Magic. It doesn't end there and the combinations are near limitless, however, getting everything requires a lot of grinding, something very common in older RPGs.
Overall, this version of the game is just as good as the original. The differences are minor except maybe to the diehard purists out there. This game looks better, but it lacks the nostalgic feel from playing the original. But, if that doesn't bother you, or if you have missed out on this gem in the past, it is worth picking it up and playing for yourself.

In my first experience with the now long-term beta of this game, I must say it's really in need of optimizations. As of right now, this game is still not ready for a full release (thank goodness they went EA if they HAD to release it now,
). So, how has the fourth installment of the Roller Coaster Tycoon franchise fared? Not as well as I'd hoped.
They're not bad, but they're not good either. Visually, they're very pleasing. However, the peeps are flat skins (clothing is not a separate layer) which is disillusioning. In addition, the feel of the ride textures leave the tiniest bit of nagging that something's missing. Overall, though, the graphics are actually very good to look at.
, good luck getting a good framerate even with a Titan. The game set my settings on high and I run a GTX 970. There is 1 setting above that which a single GTX 980 or Titan should be capable of running at 60 fps. For the graphics, to be honest, I'm surprised my computer couldn't run 60 fps.
There is a plus, though. Since the devs know framerate is bad, they went and added a tickbox that reduces the graphics demand in favor of a more playable framerate, so that you almost never dip below 20 fps. Almost. When building new things in a park that already is a bit crowded, you can dip down all the way to the 1-3 fps region.
Well, it definitely feels like a more open and controllable world than previous RCT games. Because nothing is stuck to the grid, a whole new variety of layout options become available. That said, because of the size of the park, a whole lot of creativity has been thrown out the window.
This park is only big enough to house 1 large coaster or 2 smaller ones (what the ♥♥♥♥, right?), in addition to your arsenal of small rides needed to keep the less extreme peeps happy. Speaking of those peeps, the way they scream when on a ride is all at once, so you just have an occasional scream that hurts your ears instead of constant enjoyment from your peeps.
The path and stall building tools are fairly intuitive. With the freeform option, you draw in any direction you like. With the
turned on, you can keep everything aligned to a coordinate system (perpendicular and parallel to the park entrance, mind you). With
turned on (this will turn off grid, and vice versa), you can place your paths at 90 degree angles to each other, even if they're not on the grid angle. It also allows for a few other things, like placing stalls directly onto existing paths, and more controllably placing trees and other objects adjacent to paths. All in all, having the three building modes is very useful, but I would like a localized grid aligned with a path I just drew if I had both grid and snap enabled. That would be very useful.
While this tool is great for building paths on the ground, you don't have nearly enough control with the path height. The only interval for heigh is 7 feet, which is too much, especially given the small spacing the grid has.
Well, it's just placement and angle rotation. On the other hand, unlike in previous RCT games, you can't choose the locations for the entrance and exit to the ride, which was part of how we were able to tightly pack tons of rides into a small space in the last games. And given how much smaller this game's parks are, we really need as much control of the arrangement as possible.
The roller coaster building tool really isn't bad anymore. Unlike in the beta weekend, coasters no longer crash for no reason, and the tool is relatively intuitive. That said, the station platforms are very sparse in selection and have MASSIVE footprints. There's already a significant queue and a horrendously long exit walk for every single station platform. And you can't pick where the entrance and/or exit come from, or the direction of the train. Also, track banking doesn't actually listen to what you say. For example, if I have a tight turn on an incline with steep banking, the track is actually rendered as flat and level. Decrease the banking, and the track banks outward (why?). Most of the time, using the building tools is fairly intutive. You have pre-built segments that you can adjust the scale of, or you can click on the ground away from nodes and build your own track. Working with nodes is intutive, but not getting to node mode. If you make a mistake, I have no clue how to abort the new piece without quitting the editor entirely. But on the plus side, you can create and delete nodes in the middle of the track without disconnecting it all. Overall, it still needs a bit of work, but coasters don't crash for no reason, and using it is largely intutive.
This game is labeled appropriately as something that's in Early Access. It's glitchy somewhat, and some of the controls don't feel quite finished. That said, there are other problems with this game. Flat rides don't have configurable exits, roller coaster stations are massive and just as unconfigurable (and lacking in variety), and the park size is WAY TOO ♥♥♥♥ING TINY! Will Atari and Nvizzio Creations pull it all together? Maybe. I wouldn't put any money on it happening this year. I would LOVE for them to pull it together and give us something amazing as though they've been holding out, but it really doesn't seem like RCT is on top any more. Planet Coaster, even being in alpha, is already incredibly customizable, allowing for every building to be custom made, a huge park size, and lots more detail. On top of that they're the brains behind RCT3 who did a very good job for the first 3D implementation of the series(no offense, Nvizzio). I expect a lot more from Planet Coaster in the near and far future than I do from Roller Coaster Tycoon World. For now, I'm getting my refund.

+Terrain editing and manipulation is FANTASTIC. Very easy to use and navigate, much more so than any of the previous games. Creating valleys, hills, mountains, holes, etc. is super easy and intuitive, and the water tool is much simpler than in previous games.
+Pathing is also a huge improvement in RCTW. You can change the size of paths, as well as create curved paths. Much easier and less tedious to lay down as well.
+Game itself is very pretty to look at.
+Camera works like RCT3, a positive in my eyes.
+I don't hate the coaster editor like some other reviews have stated. To be fair, I rarely messed around with it in the previous games. I'm not creative or talented enough to create anything worthy of laying down in a park, so I always relied on pre-built designs and online downloads for my coaster needs. That said, I found it simple enough to use after getting through a relatively steep learning curve. My biggest complaint with it is that the mouse sensitivity is too high, but I'm assuming (hoping) that we will have the option to tone it down upon release.
-Physics seem way, way off. Coasters seem much too slow, and coaster stats appear to be questionable at best.
-Time passes, way, way too fast. An in-game day goes by in what seems like 15 seconds, even on the slowest setting.
-Everything seems too "big". This is a difficult one to explain.
-This seems like a game that is six months to a year from release, not one a month and a half away. Menus are basic and ugly to look at, there are very, very few decoration items (assuming that there will be mcuh more at release), and descriptive text in menus is completely missing, or occupied by generic placeholder text.

I saw this game through Total Biscuit's WTF is... episode (see it here if you are interested:
and bought it instantly. I regret nothing.
It is a very entertaining rougelite experience, with tactical turn based combat. There are similar games out there, but RE:IS has some features that make it stand out from the crowd.
Firstly theme and aesthetics. Game is set in XIXth century from the pulp novels of the era. It is the world of high adventure, voodoo pirates, mummies rising from their sarcophagi, travels around the world and exploration. Characters are embodiments of the tropes associated with that genre and they are given decent personality through simple things like their visual design and animation, despite almost complete lack of dialogue.
Secondly, combat. It is relatively simple, but uses a "mood" system to create interesting variations with each encounter. Video linked above explains it in more detail, but in short - each move in battle fits one of three moods: Friendly, Devious, Aggresive. Depending in each side's mood, party is affected by buffs or debufss. Add to it the fact, that ending encounter in certain ways may give different rewards and it creates a set of decisions going far past spamming the strongest available attacks.
Thirdly, the charming narrative. It strongly connects with the first point. Each encounter (in verty FTL-esque) manner has a short description (or set of descriptions) which capture the adventureous feeling of the whole thing.
There is one problem with the game, namely number of different adventures available. Within few hours it is possible to see every one of them (but not to see everything they offer - supplies acting as a time limit make it difficult to see everything on any map within one play). This is however prone to change since devs promised to keep content patches coming through the 2015 and in 2016, provided they can afford it.
So here's the selfish part - go buy and play RE:IS. You'll have fun and I'll get chance for more content :P.

Renowned Explorers is, as it says, a tactical rogue-like where you play a team of explorers seeking to become the greatest of all time!  Set in a 19th century vaguely steampunkish setting, the world has a lot of charisma and each expedition stage has its own quirks and charms.  I especially enjoyed the wide variety of crew members and I hope one of the things the developers release is more of them, as they add a real splash of color to the proceedings, especially as you realize that each explorer has hidden traits and abilities as well.
The goal is to become the most renowned explorer in the world, racing against a rival and his own crew of explorers.  You gain renown by, well, exploring and the fun is deciding what path you will take to both explore and to deal with the variety of challenges before you.  There are both choose-your-own-adventure moments, the random outcomes decided by the Adventure Wheel and influenced by the skills and stats of your explorers (sometimes also with those hidden character influences coming up), and tactical encounters.  Though simpler than something like the X-COM games, it still has engaging strategin elements, helped along by the emotion and three-part attitude systems.
Conflicts can be resolved by Agressive (straight up combat), Devious (trickery or intimidation), or by Friendly (diplomacy and enthusiasm) means.  Resolving encounters with different attitudes leads to different rewards, told to you on the battle screen.  Also, the emotions of characters can shift through different states, both positive and negative, each with added buffs and debuffs based on the emotion.  Performing repeated actions of a particular attiude can shift the overall attitude of the battle, which ALSO has a variety of buffs and debuffs.  Even blending some of one attitude during a round can shift the attitude to a different style of the current one.  There's a lot to discover and understand here, especially early on.
While I love the encounter system, it does have its flaws.  My biggest gripe is that there is only one 'health bar', Spirit, meaning that all forms of influence take from that bar.  It's not usually a problem, but it feels just a little off that both insults and gunfire do the same harm and are healed the same way.  When it comes to the Adventure Wheel, it can be a bit rough early on, especially as you are learning the system and the kinds of challenges, and sometimes the rogue-lite elements can bite you on the♥♥♥♥♥ throwing you into hard-to-handle situations just because of the arrangement of an expedition.
Overall, though, I greatly enjoy the game and look forward to many more playthroughs.  So many more teams to try and Captains to unlock!
Pros:
+ Interesting tactical encounter system
+ Bright and colorful art style
+ Charismatic cast of playable characters and plenty of things to unlock
+ Rogue-lite elements lead to lots of variety in playthroughs
+ Variety of expeditions to undertake, multiplied by the rogue-lite elements
Cons
- One health bar for all kinds of attacks feels funny
- Rogue-lite elements sometimes bite you on the♥♥♥♥♥br>- Might be a bit overwhelming at first to completely grasp the emotion/attitude systems

After many hours in the world of metal gear solid V i can safely say that I have experienced almost everything this game has to offer. This game is by far the peak of the series when it comes to gameplay and while the story is unfinshed and falls behind the greats like MGS3 and MGS4 it does what it needs to do and the casset tapes add a lot of fun interactions between characters.  I mentioned that this is the gameplay peak of the series and i dont say that lightly, the gameplay in other metal gear games have blown me away on many occasions, but the sheer open nature of this game allows for you to take on a scenario in almost anyway imaginable, if you want to sneak in and do a no-kill and no-detection run, there are tools to do that, want to do a full on frontal assault, there are even more tools for that. a tradeoff for this open ended nature is that the game is entirely open world, which souns good on paper, but actually means that a good portion of the game is spend running around an open world with very little in it, small amount of collectables and a few gaurd posts here and there populate the mostly empty map, but you cant just run, since if an enemy sees you it slows down the game and alerts all of the surrounding bases, meaning that you ofen need to take long winding pats as to avoid the large bases.
in short despite its shortcomings, metal gear solid is a phenomenal game, and all the issues mentioned are more like small annoyences rather than glaring issues that could ruin the game. if you have tha chance, id highly recommend trying this masterpiece out, and since the series in essentially dead, now that kojima left, you may as well play his old games in anticipation for death stranding.

Black Hole Hazard takes us to a surreal journey trough space, where we will take control of Dr. Albert Armstrong who disappeared in the middle of an experiment. The International Nuclear Research Center (INRC) tried to warn him, but it was already too late, and he ended up lost in space without any idea of how to return to Earth.
In this intriguing platformer, we'll get across seven different chapters in order to unveil the truth and find a way back home. Although the story may sound a bit cliche at first, we discover shortly afterwards that there is a misterious signal that is going to play with both the character and the player's mind.
The game is set in a 2d perspective and we can control our character with just a mouse. The movement starts whenever we press the left click button to activate his gas-firing jet gun, which works like a hand jetpack. The thing is, gravity and physics will affect every moment, and that's what makes Black Hole Hazard an unique game in it's genre. Some walls will make us bounce, others will kill us in an instant with spikes, and the list goes on. We also have a fire weapon at our disposal (with limited ammo that recharges over time) that can be upgraded by finding hidden items troughout the game.
In terms of level design, Black Hole Hazard's first chapter feels like a huge tutorial. We start seeing the first enemies we'll encounter, and learning how to get around in space without dying too much. The difficulty never stops increasing, but the game feels like a relaxing challenge and the player will always fall in the trap of “just one more try before I go to bed”. It's amazing what the developers have achieved with such a simple premise.
The story has a decent length with around 150 levels to complete, they all have a Time Counter so we can compete in Leaderboards, and there are hidden logs that will help us to travel deeper into the story. We can also find a Bosses at the end of each chapter, two different endings and a Survival Mode.
- Interesting story with two different endings, cutscenes and a boss encounter at the end of each level.
- A solid gameplay that benefits from variation and great level design that keeps evolving throughout the game.
- Awesome soundtrack!
- Sound effects could use some work
Overall, Black Hole Hazard is an entertaining experience that everyone should try. I feel like the mechanics could have been used in a much larger adventure, but that's a positive thing for the development team. The gameplay is solid and addictive, and I can't wait to see what they are planning for the future.

Black Hole Hazard has been developed and published by Superthumb. Far from your regular 2D platformer, BHH is story-driven and dependent upon the many collectible log files which help unravel its storyline across a large variety of levels.
I was more than pleased by its novel use of jetpacks, gun recoil and gravity instead of the far too common platform jumping, you may be accustomed to in this game genre. Black Hole Hazard is relying on both several enemy types as well as the level environments themselves, in order to offer a fair challenge. It is exactly the right level of difficulty with the combat and obstacle avoiding sections being sprinkled with gravity based puzzles to ensure a well paced gameplay, never becoming stale and also far from causing any rage quitting. You’ll also feel compelled to seek out the aforementioned log files, each revealing a new bite-sized clue into the game’s mysterious background. And since they are well scattered across very many levels, you can add that too, on the list of features this game provides in order to stand out from the platformer crowd.
The game is certainly not lacking in the looks department, with detailed sprites, chromatic effects and well drawn cut-scenes. The sounds do feel a bit flat and repetitive but as far as I’m concerned this might be the title’s only flaw and far from an Achilles' heel. Lackluster sounds are the pitfall of many platforming games so I’m willing to cut some slack to BHH since the well detailed storyline and pleasant looking levels hold their own without having much interference from the sounds.
