is an action, indie, sci-fi, platformer, puzzle game with particle physics, gravitational pull and portal physics. In Black Hole Hazard you play as the main character, Dr. Albert Armstrong whom was in his lab testing a new discovery in his research when suddenly, something in the machinery of the space shuttle broke. You are still stuck outside on the back panel before, within seconds, you get electrically shocked. Now that the experiment of quantum mechanics is amiss, you have to go out into space and restore the gaps in the black hole. There are many dangers as you lurk through the depths chapter to chapter within these galaxies of the universe. You have spikes, pitfalls, lasers, bouncing walls and did I mention the terrible saws that you find in
,
and
.
Now, if that was not enough, you have geometric shapes similar to the ones in
that you shoot with your attached laser while trying to flip, transverse, propel and drive your character around enormous pieces of a black hole. The main purpose and goal of this game is to get through each level unharmed while avoiding death around every bend and corner. You reach the end of the level once you find a purple portal which transports you back to the main HUD.


Particle combustion is best defined as operating against the black hole environment in order to kill all the geometric shapes in sight. You have a laser and your jetpack to be able to shoot these geometric shapes. In the earlier chapters, chapters one through two, you mainly go up against rhombuses which have three different variants. One is just a basic yellow color that takes around one shot to kill it, the second type are larger red rhombuses that take slightly more and lastly, the red rhombuses with shields take around eight to nine shots to defeat.

In each level, your enemy is the gravity and obstacles that will try to deflect your steadiness to shift the direction constantly where you are moving toward. For example, there are many levels with panels and switches in them. The panels are like the hidden blocks in Mario where you have to be right under them first before they appear. This can be very frustrating in case it bounces you toward saw hazards. You can manipulate gravity based on the direction your character is facing. What I mean by this is you can perform 180 degrees and 360 degree flips to avoid gravitational pulls and an easy death.
The easiest way is controlling the jetpack in the opposite direction you are going. If you have to go up for example, make sure that the Jetpack propels you from the opposite end. Once you reach the levels in which you have to go between two pillars, sometimes pillars of saws; you have to wait until those saws and pillars transverse which is the first time they side-scroll across the area usually left to right, also, up and down. If you remain in the middle it will crush you in half, whereas if you wait, you have to be directly in the middle and you will have to carefully control your jetpack in order to prevent you from going too far to the right or left on either side.

The user interface, hud is graphically like The Undergarden, another puzzle; platformer game that have portals per chapter section. For example, in chapter one, there will be individual areas labeled off in sections such as 2-1, 2-2 located in corners around a circular area. You must enter the portal based on which level you want to play, once you do beat a level it will mark out the portal in gray instead of the original purple so you know you have played through that level at least once. There are fourteen logs separated into fourteen chapters and 150 separate levels. Likewise, of most puzzle based action, indie, platformer type games within this genre, the levels always get progressively harder as you move on taking much more patience and time. Another objective of the game,although not the main objective, is beating your friend's scores and that against others in the world based on their clear times.

•Challenging levels with a great variety of level design, enemy differentiation
•Each chapter is given a separate color landscape in the main hud which transfers over to the main color for the levels located in each chapter
•Complex quantum mechanics and physics based platforming in order to solve levels by hitting switches, avoiding potential hazards and propelling through the madness
•Unlike many big publishers, the trailers have no false promises nor advertising that would undermine the game's potential
•Simple controls

Guacamelee is a great game. It's like Metroid mixed with a beat 'em up game but done so well that I'd definitely say it was a must have game, the Steam community also enhances this experience by adding tons of customised skins like Batman, Johnny Bravo and even Samus (who I played as, of course).
The world is well designed, consisting of towns with villagers and sidequests, big open explorable locations and then temples. It plays just like Metroid but with less back tracking and is easier to navigate through the diverse areas. There are many hidden chests all over the world, I found them all without much trouble, so seasoned Metroid Veterans will likely find them easily.
The combat is also very fun, all of your attacks are general melee based attacks, as you could probably guess from the title. You will unlock special attacks and upgrades which are used for both battle and for navigation; they use up some of your stamina as you use them so you can't over use them to kill all enemies easily. The twist on the combat is that once an enemy is weakened, it can be grabbed and then thrown at other enemies or into walls using the analog for direction. A lot of challenges revolve around good use of this throwing ability and it does make the game feel different from other side scrollers.
The game has great sound design; the music is also greatly composed and enchanced the atmosphere of the areas. The sound effects fit perfectly and make the game feel cartoonish and matches the art style perfectly.
Once you're finished with the game, there is still a hard mode to play through, lots of achievements to get and an online normal and hard speed run leaderboard for both clearing the game and clearing the game with 100%. There is also an area with 17 challenges to test the limits of your skills and to attempt to best your hi-scores. Giving plenty of replay value for those who enjoy the game.
All in all, a fantastic game that I recommend very highly. Why wait for a new Metroid game when you can play this?

Full-motion video games are often the subject of ridicule, usually due to the legitimately awful gameplay and story/acting featured within these games. Despite this, FMV games, much like point-and-click adventure games, seem to have made a slight resurgence. It is because of games such as this one, Her Story, receiving high praise and attention for employing bold new strategies and gameplay styles. However, this game, unfortunately, still does not hold up to snuff.
First, I will say that indeed, the gameplay is strange but quite unique and, ultimately, designed in about the only way in which this game could've possibly worked at all. It is for this reason the game receives praise, for adding an interesting layer of discovery to this mystery within the video clips you must search for. This is a system unlike any other, and despite being entirely unrealistic, it does give the game a unique edge not found in any other game.
But that doesn't entirely matter because the actual story and even some of the acting is quite bad. There are initially moments of great intrigue peppered through these video clips, and some of the acting is actually serviceable. However, the story ultimately delves into silly ham-fisted attempts at symbolism, almost as if the symbolism was more important than the story itself. I like symbolism and searching and finding its myriad ways which can connect a story's pieces together, but this symbolism was not only forced and anvilicious, the story suffered as a result, turning into an entirely unrealistic tale where suspension of disbelief becomes increasingly difficult. This is unfortunate considering the game otherwise could have been recommendable.
I don't always not recommend games based on the story, but this is a case of what I consider "Other M Syndrome," where the story is particularly bad and the gameplay just doesn't cut the mustard in order to make the experience worth it even if that in particular isn't bad. But at least, unlike Metroid: Other M, this game is cheap enough, and I could still see someone desiring to attempt a playthrough of Her Story for that reason anyway. Just be warned, the only reason to pick this up at all is for the uniqueness of the game, which you won't find anywhere else at this time. Avoid otherwise.

Not a game in the traditional sense, but a highly entertaining narrative puzzle with an excellent hook and a simple interface. A clever and captivating use of FMV.  You'll finish in about 4 hours, which seems fair for the relatively low price of admission.

Enjoyed this game... took me only a few hours to get a reasonably good grasp of the mystery -- I was happily surprised to see that even with a little less than half of the database explored you can sort it all out, even though going into the files and watching the whole interviews in sequence was a treat in itself just to confirm or deny what of my hunches where correct, as well as there is a big differnce between THINKING you know the story and knowing the story -- which is the razors edge this game dances on. I give extra points for being simple and yet innovative -- and having such an interesting story to tell, and in an interesting way. I enjoyed this title very much. I recommend it for a puzzle-together with a loved one (swap theories and insights!) or as a solo pleasure for a long plane ride or broken over several commutes. Rewarding.

Her Story is a pleasing interactive movie-type game that kept me interested throughout.
Pros:
- I liked the fact that you had to search for the right words to reveal of the clips. You probably could have searched a bunch of common words to find most clips, but I made an effort to make a list of useful words to search for.
- Stimulating story. I've played too many games where the stories in them were way too lackluster. This one kept me wanting to find out what is going on.
- I liked the atmosphere this game made. I wouldn't necessarily say it was a scary feel, but spending the entire time in a police database felt tense.
- Great acting by the actress. The line reading wasn't cheesy and seemed believeable.
- The amount of time it took me to finish felt right. My time was about 4 hours or so. Any shorter and it would have felt rushed. Any longer and it would have dragged on.
Cons:
- Some of the words you needed to search were so obscure I wouldn't have ever thought to search them (spoiler: like "yes" with quotes).
- I appreciate an ending with a vague note up for interpretation as much as the next guy, but there are times where this isn't appropriate. This is one of these cases. I wanted to know or at least be revealed to me with more detail was going on with Hannah. It would have been that much more of a zinger.
- Was the singing necessary? I'm bias though because I dislike singing in general in things.
Overally, I was impressed with Her Story. My expectations for it weren't high or low, and I walked away feeling satisfied that I completed it. I recommend!

I'm not going to waste time trying to make this post presentable, so here's a stream of consciousness (all comparisons are held against F.E.A.R. 1):
Dirty dirty console port, cell shaded graphics do not fit the theme, aiming feels inaccurate, the AI is stupider, there are no graphics settings other than to change the resolution, spawn points are blatantly obvious and depressingly-purposefully annoying, the game speed is slow enough where you don't even need slo mo (fear1 is so fast you actually need it), overall it's too easy to really get into combat yet I get instakilled frequently by things I can't see (enemies spawn right behind you). FEAR1 had sprawling levels where squads could strategically engage you (or be engaged by you)- FEAR2 is all cheap spawn points in linear, uninspired level design. Ammo is dropped every two inches, it can't differentiate between left CTRL and right CTRL (fear1 could), it bugs out if you press too many keys at once (it often gets stuck strafing right, it often doesn't register keypresses, etc). Moreover the story is filled with cheap thrills and the plot is insanely stupid- they've never heard of "less is more". And the way alma is rendered is also less scary.
FEAR1's plot wasn't a masterpiece by any stretch; it had some really good and unique ideas in the meat of the story, but the frame-plot / getting to the meat of the story was pretty blatantly stupid. However it was at least *paced*; seems to me like they just wanted to play with some neat horror ideas and didn't really care too much about the rest of the plot- any excuse to get the player alone in some creepy environments would do. The game is about exploring ideas, and it is about exploring Alma's backstory; clearly not a lot of effort was put into leading up to that. Knowing that the plot was largely bad, they interspersed truly intriguing elements along the way and approached the more interesting ideas *slowly*.
FEAR2's approach to storytelling is to have some guy call you up and explain just about everything to you. There's no suspense or pacing. It's just... all bad.

Review:
is designed to keep you playing, and that's not always a good thing. The game is packed with so many things to do and items to research and develop (R&D), and even starts off by giving you full reign by letting you decide how to accomplish the task of re-building Mother Base. It starts humbly enough, but soon you'll discover the truth:
is little more than a gateway to spend cash on microtransactions, and it does this by prolonging gameplay.
The trifecta gameplay loop of exploration, running missions, and R&D will keep you busy for 100+ hours if you are intent on completing a good bulk of the game. This isn't necessarily bad, per se. However, the amount of time you spend playing the game is actually regulated through Gross Military Product (GMP), an in-game currency which is earned by completing missions. Not only that, every piece of equipment you use on missions costs resources in addition to GMP. The more equipment and higher the rank, the more resources and GMP you will spend per mission. (
: An average sortie might cost you 20,000 GMP plus 50 metal and 18 plants.)  Helicopter pick-ups alone can cost over 20,000 GMP and will be sure to drain your GMP if you aren't farming regularly. Luckily, you can make around 100,000 to 500,000 GMP per mission... That might sound like GMP is easy to come by, but if you think you can farm GMP by doing the same mission over and over, you're wrong. You're actually prevented gaining the same amount of GMP through a mission cooldown period where the reward is reduced to 25% or 50% of the total GMP it normally offers until you complete a few of the other missions.
's design elements act as a series of floodgates to control how much you're allowed freedom and, really, control how much fun you have. The game slowly implements gambling features, like combat dispatch missions and forward operating base (FOB) system. Taking the game's online combat dispatch into consideration, it's clear there's a gambling element here, and the main game is just addictive enough in the hopes you gamble a combat unit to get more talented staff. Starting a dispatch missions is akin to placing a bet with house odds: a max. ceiling chance of mission success at 95%, and min. floor chance to lose 3% of your combat unit. (
: You can succeed a mission and still lose staff, the way its calculated is a little under the hood).
There are two types of combat dispatch missions: online and offline deployments. In offline deployments, you send a combat unit and wait anywhere from 10 to 60 minutes for the mission to complete. But most of the offline missions have token rewards and are low-risk. The online dispatch missions are more lucrative, but missions time can take up to 3-4 days at the
rank, that way you are tempted to spend real money to get Mother Base Coins (MB Coins) to speed-up the process by completing them immediately... Enter The Microtransaction. And, in order to incentivize you to spend MB Coin, you are given a tiny amount of coins each day you log on.
But if you can get more staff simply by playing, why would you want MB Coins you ask? That involves explaining the FOB system.
The FOB system is both a persistent online experience and competitive multiplayer feature that allows you to raid and be raided, which means losing hard-earned resources and staff members in the process- of course, you can turn around and invade an enemy player. FOB is by design to be a high-risk/high-reward feature, but at least it involves some player skill unlike combat dispatch missions. The real sin by Konami, however, is that Konami keeps 90% of your total GMP to
you to stay connected online. So, if you wish to circumvent this online feature, you're reduced to playing the game with less than optimal GMP. If your base ever goes in the red, your average GMP will need to be carefully managed and you will need to recoup GMP losses through selling resources, or face a mass exodus by your staff. While you will most likely never need MB Coins, regular FOB losses might change your mind. So it's either deal with FOB tug-of-war, or play offline and have access to only 10% of your total GMP, a lame move by Konami.
So, in order to be able to regularly fund FOB invasions of your own, or simply to have insurance against them, MB Coins can help you get there. Manually getting good staff takes time, resources, and GMP. This itself is a gamble, you have to be lucky enough to spot one on the field and recover them. Hero Points allow you to passively gain A++ or S rank soldiers, but that's only after a certain amount of play time (around 100 hours). Thus, MB Coins allow you to gamble for high-ranking soldiers, but only if you have the soldiers to bet with. So, investing in MB Coins is only buying the right to gamble more often and have an edge over other players... not exactly pay-to-win, more like pay-to-not-lose-more.
Moving onto the other features of gameplay: it has an interesting Revenge System, a decent base management feature to keep you busy, and player customization to round off the experience. Through the Revenge System, soldier protocols and tactics change based upon how you run missions. Mother Base planning includes staff management, deciding on which technology to develop (which is where most of your GMP will go). Customization, while not something to write home about, is still there to allow some choice in how to
Where the game falls short, however, is the heavily rushed final chapter, and a bland
, the point of which is either to explore or sabotage a base to make a future mission much easier. Expanses between bases render much of free-roam unexciting through guardposts and patrols, but there's just not enough happening in free-roam to warrant spending more than a fraction of your time doing that. The game funnels you toward completing missions, advancing the story, and slowly adding on the FOB system which is the point of no return when the game flexes its maximum gambling design feature to make your FOB vulnerable to player attack.
While the game isn't designed to push you over the edge with its gambling design, it doesn't allow for ultimate freedom either. The game is somewhere in between a complete pleasure and a task: It's not really a dealbreaker, but it also becomes a chore at a certain point. Some players will reach that point faster than others, some may not even notice it. Luckily, the mod Infinite Heaven helps bring back some of that control to the players.
By itself, I cannot recommend
. But, with some modding, it is more than playable.

The game isn't bad per se. I've had fun with it. But there are boatloads of little problems. All in all, it's a less well done Far Cry.
The problems start with the intro. The whole hour of intro mission is neither really connected to the rest of the game, at least not as far as I came yet, and it's "Cutscene: The game". for each 5 minutes of gameplay, there are 10 minutes of cutscenes. There are nonsensical things galore, like sprinklers not starting despite the fire all around but suddenly doing so when the main char (not you, as you can't play that part) shoots them, or people, not superhuman ones, being ablaze and still pretty determined to move towards the character, again in a cutscene.
Later in the game, many problems arise because it's an awful port. For example, in the menu, switching from one category to the next has you press the 1 and 3 number keys instead of, you know, using the mouse. Switching weapons in game can also only being done the same way, using the mouse wheel is way too novel a concept. In fact, the mouse wheel has no use at all, not for zooming (with weapons), not for switching, not for scrolling in menus, only for zooming with your binoculars.
The other things are mosty small problems that amass. Enemies being able to shoot you with an AK47 at a distance where you have problems hitting them with a sniper rifle, not being able to jump without any AC-style freerunning, having to slowly walk (or horsey ride) vast distances which are often long for no reason, like in your own base, because there's no usable fast travel system (there is a way with the copter, but it requires you to first go to the 'aerial command centre' and all in all takes ages), a checkpoint system that has it's checkpoints so weirdly set that I had to repeat 3 side missions at once because saving between them never occured to the devs (why can't console ports give us free save FFS?) and so on.
One last thing that bugged me were so many cutscenes that had cool stuff to play in them that would be playable in any game but this one.
Let me give you an example: There I was trying to go to a side mission. What looked like a way to squeeze in between two mountains wasn't so I had to use a huge detour. Suddenly at one place I was stopped dead in my tracks because a sniper shot at me, which started a main mission, 11, while I was at 6 or so. This in and on itself wouldn't be that bad, I would just have liked a warning because, well, I was trying to do the side mission. Anyway, a fight later and the dilemma of letting the sniper live or kill them comes up. Ocelot and a Miller (which I don't remember, maybe he appears in a mission between 6 and 11) both take the opposite position and tell me to kill or capture them respectively. I decided.. I decided for jack sh*t because the game didn't let me decide, it was all in a cutscene. After putting them in a copter, I ride off towards the side mission I was planning to do on my trusty steed. As soon as I leave the area, a cutscene played and the horse transformed in a copter, aparently, because I was flying it with the sniper. A jet attacks. All the while I was like "grab that friggin mounted machine gun already and let me shoot it!" Quite a while later, snake doesn't seem to be too fast on the uptake, he did grab the gun. And fell over. And grabbed it again. And fell again. And the same thing yet again. As so often in the game, I was screaming at the screen 'get ON with it!". Alas, instead of a sequence where I was shooting at the jet and letting loose flares when a rocket came, which would have been sweet.. none of that happened. it was all just a cutscene.
It's like that several times through the game.
The good parts of the game are pretty much points you could make about far cry. I enjoyed far cry so that's great, but it didn't feel any different.
To wrap it up, MSG V is NOT a bad game. but it is way less than I expected from the hype.
Why do I downvote it when I didn't think it was crap, you might ask. It's because steam gives me just the absolutes of recommend or don't recommend, no neutral. I'd do neither if someone asked me. But I'd probably say something like "get far cry instead", which is pretty much equal to "not recommend"
EDIT having played some more:
The game is repetative as all hell.
You have a pool of like 5 different side objectives, basically all "kill all of them" or "rescue that guy" or "optain that ressource". Stuff like "Eliminate the heavy infantry" and "eliminate the tank command" are really the same, just one with tanks, so I don't count them as different.
You have a whopping 157 of them. And they all play in the same ~20 bases/towns, and for most of them, the bases are just restocked with the default staff and a prisoner put somewhere or a "highly skilled soldier" is among them (fun fact, nearly every time, that one was less skilled than all his buddies, aparently because it was skilled for the starting hero level you have, even if ou just unlock that side mission way further in the game. The game is riddled with such little problems, as I said).
Hell, you even have stuff like "extract a guy from OKB0" and as soon as you get back to the chopper, you get a new side mission: extract a guy from OKB0!
Ths one really got on my nerves as that base is freaking huge and as soon as you finally managed to get through it, you have to do this again.
You do the ame stuff time and time and time again, it's just artifically prolonging the game.
Also, the game punishes you for not going non-lethal. That would have been kinda OK, if all he non-lethal weapons didn't suck and people wouldn't wake up from tranquilizers way too fast. I spent much money developing a stunning assault rifle only to find out, not only is it not silenced, I can't put on any silencer from any other gun, making it pretty useless. Maybe the version of the gun at higher levels has it, but I had already go to level 5 or so just to get it non-lethal.
One time I tranqued two guys from like 15m away and before I got to them they woke up again because a tank beeped its horn for no reason (I wasn't discovered, neither were they, putting them to sleep again I could even extract them without someone noticing). There's not a single thing that will keep them knocked out. I like to clean out bases, but as soon as the base is a bit bigger, there's no chance to do that.
but if you go lethal, you get less score, less "hero points" which means worse staff and on top of it, you get a bloody skin permanently put on your char. Game, why don't you let me play the way I see fit? Why give me 90% lethal weapons and tanks and stuff if I can't even use them? Why do you make non-lethal weapons so bad?
So, after putting more time in the game, I'm a bit of a completionist or I would just not care about the side ops, I can recommend this game even less than before. play far cry, it may not have 157 side missions, but those it has are actually a bit different from each other

While this game does a lot of things right, it fails in a few key aspects. The game is supposed to be about an intrepid band of explorers venturing into the unknown and discovering lost lands, lost peoples, and lost treasures, but ultimately, it fails to deliver on that.
For example, you're supposed to be exploring the unknown, but in reality the path you're taking is fairly predictable. You know exactly how long your supplies will last, exactly what kind of challenge you'll run into, and exactly how best to deal with that challenge. There is certainy random chance involved, which is good, but it's in the wrong place. Instead of throwing you into the unknown and making you figure out how to get out of the mess you're in, you are instead encouraged to look forward, figure out what lies in store for you, and then meticulously plan out where you go and in what order to have the best chance of success. This isn't a bad mechanic per se, and in a different game it could make for some great gameplay, but for a game about exploring the unknown, it just doesn't click.
The combat is another example this. While I like the idea of using a combination of weapons, words, and trickery to defeat your enemies, the way it was done just makes everything feel gamey and contrived. Everything is boiled down to an attack on the enemy's HP, and at best you might get something that inflicts an unreliable status effect or changes the "mood" of the combat. Trying to be diplomatic or sneaky just ends up feeling the same as any other combat, rather than being it's own, interesting way to tackle challenges.

Funny how with all the complaining about the game, it's still impossible to argue that the PS1 version is better. I feel the need to state that because of how much complaining there is about TILES. "Oh noes, a graphical bug! Whatever shall I do but complain about it?"  But I digress.
This is my favorite version of FFV. It has all the added stuff from the Advance version, the music of the original, and a nice graphical update that doesn't look like Square crapped it out one night and said, "We should recycle! Let's use this for our next game!"
The job system is still just as good as in the SNES, GBA, and PS1 versions. You can equip different abilities from different jobs to other jobs after leveling them up. In my opinion, this is the best class system the series ever got, and if a modern FF game brought this back, I might actually consider buying it.

To preface this review: I would recommend Final Fantasy V as a game in its own right any day of the week. While the plot is fairly bare, the characters are cool and the storytelling full of that old-school JRPG charm from the days before everything became about anime and angst. The gameplay sets it as one of the most-solid games in the franchise, both for its dungeon design and combat/skill mechanics. The job system introduced in Final Fantasy III returns here with a flexible cross-job skill system and there's a reason this same set of mechanics would appear in later Square games such as Final Fantasy Tactics, Final Fantasy XI, and Bravely Default.
The reason this review is negative is because of this port in particular. It could not be more obvious that the graphics in this version were designed for a smaller screen--at most HD-or-higher resolutions you can clearly see many of the seams between environment tiles, even in objects such as the skull-and-crossbones banner or the meteorite that crash-lands at the start of the game. The art style used for the character sprites is also weird and jarring when set alongside the animations used in the original FF5, which are almost entirely unchanged here to suit the art change. To cap it off, the jarring dissonance between the Yoshitaka Amano stylized dialogue portraits and characters' sprite designs, which bothered me in the GameBoy Advance version, is more obvious than ever here, in spite of some of the sprite designs having been altered to closer resemble Amano's designs (Galuf's new sprite, for example, has a mustache rather than a beard, and it looks pretty good).
Adding insult to injury, Square once again couldn't be half-arsed to license a decent text font for the game, so as with previous mobile/Steam remakes and ports, the text font is jarringly stock and unstylized against the admittedly nice menu and textbox designs. Between this and the environment tile seam problem, this port of the mobile remake ends up feeling like an incredibly amateurish RPG Maker rebuild of the game.
Thankfully I haven't had any of the screen-tearing issues reported in other reviews and fullscreen mode seems to work just fine. (I am running an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 760, for the record.) I need to play further through this version of the game to be one hundred percent sure, but it at least seems to be solid on a technical level, although it's definitely not playing at 60fps--not that this bothers me in a game where most animations are three frames long at best anyway.
Still, if you're going for the all-in Final Fantasy V experience, you're better off playing the GameBoy Advance version--all of the content with almost none of the problems, and even the text font looks better. I sincerely hope Square pays attention to the negative reception this version has received and smooths out the graphics, but just in case... are any of you intrepid fan-patch-makers up for smoothing out the graphics, maybe?

In it's current form, this game is hardly playable. Technically and graphically, the game functions poorly and I would recommend investing into an older not-PC remake of the game instead of this (until it gets updated).
I've had many issues with controls: not only can I only use the menu function in one safe spot in the second dungeon, but I cannot exit that menu unless I save the game as pressing the back button only switches between the "inventory" and "save" screens". The game also has problems registering 2 different input keys at the same time (excluding directional keys); button mashing to figure out the controls will do nothing for you, give each key a second or two to fully register. You should also be aware that this game is fairly unstable: multiple crashes within the first 10 minutes of play, mostly around naming your character (caution: keyboard keys still function while typing the characters name and you may unexpectedly accept a half-finished name, like I did with the name "The" before the game crashed). Graphically, you can take a look at other reviews: the graphics are updated and improved, but there are plenty of tiling issues, the portraits (as great art pieces as they are) do not look like the game sprites and become very off-putting, and the game looks like it's 480p stretched to larger resolutions (don't hold me to that, but the main menu is very much low resolution).
The plus side is that there is controller support for the game, and it worked just as well as my keyboard (that is to say I still couldn't access the inventory/save menus); the 8-directional movement, though weird, is nice to have when traveling lengthy diagonal distances; and the gameplay is very much unchanged aside from the improvements of latter FFV iterations (that's more of a neutral point).
In summary, hold off until an update arrives or you may find out you can't save.

Note: This is a review for the single player portion of the game.
Pros:
- pretty enough, prettier than SupCom1
- decent time waster
Cons:
- horrible AI. All but the last levels on hard difficulty are won by just slapping static defenses onto the route of approach the AI uses. It will never wary what groups of units it sends, nor change their paths even by a bit, except when a new script activates at a given moment and it adds another group and path to its permament schedule. It can afford to just keep doing that (not that fighting it is difficult anyway) because it doesn't even pretend it has limited resources like you.
- bad fanfiction level of writing (can be seen as a pro sometimes, there are moments it falls down to so-bad-it's-good, like when your commander brings out his verbal trump card against an enemy bent on massacring civilians. It is literally "How would YOU feel if YOU were being attacked like this?")
- unskipable cutscenes that often take forever
- awful, awful, AWFUL pathfinding
- scripted dangers which are either a non-issue breeze or an insta-loss, with little room inbetween, depending on the size of your army by the time they get triggered. Since they're usually triggered by advancing towards objectives, they tend to fall on the "non-issue" side if you turtle up against the zombie waves and then build ludicrously overwhelming forces before destroying everything in one sweep.
The game is not bad. But then, the game could have been good, and isn't. You can feel quite a bit of lost potential. Overall, get it if it happens to be in a bundle, otherwise avoid.

Even in levels that can be completed the physics are somewhat questionable (if a ball hits a spring it should be catapulted back based on its weight and the speed with which it hit the spring...this is clearly not the case...at all, it's just random). That's why it gets an automatic "not recommended". Apart from that the game launches at least.
To give you an example of 1-7: There are 3 barrels that need to be delivered into the end zone in a particular order. However, the barrels don't move the way they should at the start (where you can't even influence them). I was able to get all barrels into the end zone, but the order is impossible to achieve, which results in mission failure. I tried it with a guide, I watched YouTube videos. The barrels just behave differently. I even tried the integrated solution system in the game, which auto solves a level. Well, that one can't even get all barrels to the end zone. They get stuck well before. So, it's clearly a PhysX issue. I refuse to go through the hassle of uninstalling PhysX and reinstalling the old version. Since it is not possible to have 2 versions installed and all other games might break if I do that and because it's generally a lot of hassle...
So, I'll just finish what's possible. At least there are cheats out there to unlock all levels.

So, I recently replayed the original F.E.A.R. and also gave it a review and ultimately determined that nearly 10 years later, F.E.A.R. is not only still a great game but a game worthy of being a bonafide classic.  But what about it's... erm, divisive sequel?  Well, to be honest when it first came out I didn't even beat it.  It was just so monumentally disappointing and ultimately boring that I didn't polish it off and it dropped the F.E.A.R. series off my radar, so no F.E.A.R. 3 for me at its release.  However, with that said - I don't feel I can properly review a game without having beaten it, and not only that - I am always willing to give a movie, game, book, or song I didn't like before another chance to see if maybe I could appreciate it for what it was and since 5 years had passed, I decided to give F.E.A.R. 2 another go with fresh eyes that weren't spoiled by the hype and excitement for a sequel to one of the best shooters of its time, and put it in the sunlight away from its predecessors shadow where I could judge it for what it was on its own.
Sadly, even then - I can't bring myself to recommend F.E.A.R. 2.  With that said, I did enjoy it more the second time around and if I were to ultimately get down to the nitty gritty, I can honestly say that F.E.A.R. 2 is by no means "awful," nor is it really THAT bad per se - but it is still bad.  It's just ultimately kind of boring.  It is competent but unmemorable.  One of the problems is that the combat just feels... off.  It is hard to articulate what I'm talking about to someone who hasn't played the first game, but it simply isn't as visceral, intense, dynamic and ultimately it isn't anywhere near as fun as it once was.  This is due to several factors, the first being the fact that the weapons themselves don't feel that great.  While F.E.A.R. 1 did have mostly familiar and kind of generic weapons based on real world guns, they at least made up for it by making each one feel different with its strengths and weaknesses made clear once the player had time to get a feel for them, and most importantly they all were fun to shoot.  From the SMG which made a great sweeper for small crowds, to the shotgun that could tear a man clean in half, to the powerful burst fire rifle that practically ignored armour - they were all great.  In F.E.A.R. 2, however, they feel wimpy and they don't feel distinct.  For example, there are two kinds of shotguns in this, and yet they are so similar that at one point I didn't even realize which one I was holding until I wondered why the hell I was walking over a shotgun but getting no ammo.  The only difference between the two is the model and the fact one shoots slightly faster and only pumps at reload.  Otherwise they sound the same, feel the same, and are easily disposable.  There are really only two weapons in the game I liked:  One was the Sniper rifle, which could cut people into some of the nastiest shreds possible, and the other was the Laser lifted wholesale from Extraction Point (I thought Monolith wanted to ignore that one?).  They were pretty fun to use.
The A.I. also doesn't seem as smart as before, which is odd because it's actually the exact same A.I. and while there are times where it can be as brilliant, it just feels as though they don't know how to use the environment as well.  Maybe its because said environments are much more cramped than before, and open combat areas are not as frequent.  Its really odd seeing an A.I. that actually feels as though its legitimately confused with its environment.  This also, once again, detracts from the combat.
Another aspect of this game that is ultimately disappointing is the story.  I actually really liked F.E.A.R. 1's story, it had flaws like the fact that at times Armacham felt maybe a little too cartoonishly evil and admittedly there were aspects of the story that made no sense.  F.E.A.R. 2's story however barely offers anything new, it picks one new story device, which can be summed up as bumbling around a seemingly normal environment (Like a penthouse, a hospital, a school, etc.) and then learning OMFG THERE'S REALLY AN EVIL UNDERGROUND LAIR HERE WHERE EXPERIMENTS WERE DONE! DUNDUNDUN!  It pulls this trick at LEAST 4 times.  It gets repetitive.  Worse still, it actually repeats the first games story.  Towards the end of the game, one of your squadmates says she has a recording that ultimately explains Alma and yet his big revelation is basically everything you learned during the course of the original F.E.A.R.
*SPOILER ALERT!!! I AM ABOUT TO REVEAL THE ENDING TO THIS GAME.  SKIP THIS PARAGRAPH IF YOU DON'T WANNA KNOW HOW IT ENDS!*
I also despised the ending.  On one hand, it has absolutely no ♥♥♥♥ing closure.  Granted I know a F.E.A.R. 3 exists at this point and had I played this game when it came out, I would have known a F.E.A.R. 3 was coming.  But it isn't even a proper cliffhanger, since it barely resolves any of the lingering plot threads that this particular game brought up, it felt more like an author had 1 more chapter in store but he decided to cut off in the middle of the 2nd to last chapter and then decided to stop and start writing the sequel and never bothered to finish off the end of the previous entry.  On the other hand - I legitimately foun it offensive.  It takes a LOT to offend me.  But there is one topic that will invariably get my nickers in a twist if it is exploited: ♥♥♥♥♥♥  There has been one and only one game in the history of existince that managed the topic without exploiting it and its victims, and that was Silent Hill 2.  But F.E.A.R. 2 has none of the brains of Silent Hill 2, and having Alma♥♥♥♥♥♥your character isn't scary or creepy - its just sick and ♥♥♥♥ed up.  I'm absolutely shocked that no one got angry, but then I got madder because I realized the reason it probably didn't stir any controversy is there are still dozens of idiots and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who think that men can't be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥by women.  And to be honest?  That actually makes me even angrier, because I'm sure there are plenty of people who didn't even think of the scene as♥♥♥♥♥♥despite the fact your protagonist actively fights back against it and it is forced upon him.  Now, I new that Alma was to be pregnant in F.E.A.R. 3, but to be honest I thought they were going to go with the idea of Alma seducing and corrupting either you or one of your teammates and then coercing them into having twisted sex, and that actually would have been a way of getting her pregnant without offending me and also coming off as genuinely ♥♥♥♥ing creepy.  She actually DOES seduce on of your teammates, and he even gets mad that she chooses you. My favourite from the FEAR franchise. Monolith kept all the core elements of the original game (slow-motion ability) and they added some extra features, as well: occasionally you can jump into a huge mech and literally destroy everything in your path. These are great scenes - they are uplifting and bring some extra action the original game lacked. I know it is a psychological horror in essence, but there's nothing wrong with upping the action if you already have the slo-mo making combat fun.
The player can now push objects, e.g. you can now turn over tables and hide behind them. I think fast reflexes serve you better so I did not really care about the cover-based approach, at all. Overall, the game looks and runs better than the original and it uses more vivid colours - the psychological aspect they could still keep without having to apply too many dark colours and shadows. There are more enemy types, more supernatural encounters and - in my opinion - a more interesting story.
Instead of Point Man you now take control over a member from a delta squad which is tasked to protect the president of Armacham. The first level takes place just before the ending of FEAR so you can see the explosion from a distance and then go through the city only to see the devastation caused by Alma. There are some interesting findings and many collectibles that further explain the background of the Origin project so I'm not spoiling anything further here.
The game wasn't exactly praised much upon its release. A lot of people from media considered it just an average shooter, a shooter that can easily be forgotten. I disagree with this - I believe FEAR 2 is a very good sequel and great care and attention was put into the making of it. I suggest you buy it and skip its awfully short DLC content.

I was pleasantly surprised by this one.  I was unsure of what exactly to expect - it seemed like a cartoony XCOM type game, but it comes across as more like FTL meets Carmen Sandiego.  That being said, I HATED what felt like the unfairness of the RNG in FTL - I would blow hours in a game and see nothing for it after one lousy encounter. OK, background first: I loved RCT2, played it tons and just wanted a newer up to date version on that.
The beta is not this!
There are 2 main issues that probably won't be resolved because I disagree fundamentally with what they have done.
1. The Artwork resembles any bland MAC application with some grey boring icons and grey paths, grey coasters, low colour vibrancy where there is colour. It's like they looked at RCT2 and thought 'No, we dont like colours. We like grey and black and white. Borders? No, we don't like borders, we like MINIMAL feel'. End result: the game has no soul, no feeling of Theme Parks, you are like an engineer or town planner, NOT MR Eccentric Tycoon with a funny moustache and wacky clothing! And the game is called TYCOON, you would think the devs would know this, but apparently smart people can be stupid!!!!!
2. The coaster building is slow and fiddly. There's a number of reasons for this, but it's never going to be fixed as there's no QUICK way to build coasters like in RCT2. You have to do tests and after waiting 3-4 mins for the carriages to get to the corner in question, only then do you find out if it works or not. Then you spend the next 5-10 mins trying to minimise the g-force (which is the usual issue), but you have no idea if you have done enough until you do a test! This feels like a 'Pro Mode', or Kerbal Space Program, with realistic physics, and no way for you to easily tell if your track is ok. And I'm no idiot, I built 3 coasters today and first one only took 15-20 mins, but it was just stupid the effort I had to put in!!
No-one should fork over money for this if they liked RCT2. I loved that game, so the choice is yours. If you want a bland simulator then buy this game, if you want a game that is, you know, FUN, then play something else.

At this time, I could not recommend this game to anyone. I'll change this review later if the game redeems itself, but for now, there's just too much to be disappointed with. This is currently not looking to be the fun the first three games were.
First off, the coaster editor.
Yes, it's a spline based system which means more flexibility in how you can design your coaster, but it also means more weirdness. I've had issues where a stright, flat, non-banked piece of track gives me the error "Curve too steep", and similar issues with a gigantic turn (probably at least 150 feet in radius) giving me the same error with little to no banking. After I figured out a few of the quirks I was finally able to build a coaster, but that took almost the full half hour I played.
Second, the actual coaster operation.
Say you manage to actually complete your coaster. Now it's time to test it. Which, by the way, you can't do while paused. Perhaps it'll crash into one of the nodes mysteriously left by the editor that didn't get removed. All right, it's a beta, weird things happen. Next run, it'll pass through it just fine, only to clip into the track and crash a bit before the station. Next run, it'll crash into the *other* node left by the editor. Finally, we get a run that succeeds.

Not every game has to break the mold. There’s a certain comfort to fighting familiar orcs and ghosts with familiar swords and scrolls. But a fundamentally simple game still has to get the fundamentals right, and Ananias does just that. It doesn’t aspire to be much more than a basic fantasy roguelike, but does so with solid mechanics and accessible gameplay. And just when you think you’ve seen what it has to offer, it might manage to surprise you with the few curveballs it does throw.
A great evil (this time a serpent) has descended on the good and decent folk and ♥♥♥♥ed everything up for them. A great hero (that’s you) has scoured the land for the Ring of Ananias, a relic of a powerful king that contains the power to save the world. The trail leads to a labyrinth of ancient secrets and vile creatures which you must conquer if the land is to know peace once more. With your trusty animal companion by your side, you’ll collect gear, battle monsters, and worship deities all in the name of reaching the magical macguffin of salvation.
Doubtless you’ve heard all this before, and I’m confident you’re already familiar with the mechanics behind it, too. Ananias is built in the image of genre classics like NetHack where every move around the gridded, randomized maps is a turn and you bump enemies to death. In a slight departure from the classics, though, each floor of the dungeon is divided into rooms that you tackle one at a time. Enemies can move to and from adjacent rooms but you can’t see what’s in the next until you move there yourself. Conveniently-placed arrows let you scoot right to the connecting hallway if you’ve finished clearing the enemies out, too.
Convenience is a major design pillar of Ananias, evidenced by how the entire interface is driven with single mouse clicks. You can leave your numpad behind on this one, because all you have to do to move, attack, or grab items is click. It’s honestly a clean and intuitive system that makes the game more inviting than ones where you need to learn a dozen different buttons or commands. This does limit the interaction potential, though, as you won’t have multiple options for using your different items or weapons. A lack of variety tends to plague the combat, even with ten different classes and different animal companions to bring along for the ride. Most of the time you’ll be doing the standard bump melee or single-target ranged attacks to whittle down foes, unless you really focus on special skills.
Active skills like shooting ice and raising skeletons are learned between dungeon levels when you’re given the opportunity to worship a deity or pick up a new skill. Deities provide permanent bonuses like combat stats or inventory slots, so while fresh spells might be appealing you won’t want to neglect your gods. You’ll also find single-use scrolls with varied effects like charming monsters and summoning pillars of flame, and ingredients for mixing potions that can heal, boost, or explode in your face. Equipment tends to be simple stat increases, perhaps because every sword and shield and glove wears out over time and needs to be replaced. It’s certainly a departure from other roguelikes but doesn’t feel like a worthwhile trade for more interesting gear.
With clean graphics and understated sound effects, Ananias looks the part of a rote, user-friendly fantasy romp. The intuitive mouse controls make it easy to get started squashing centipedes and whacking wargs, and just when you think you’re getting tired of it you’ll find a new potion concoction or an NPC with another bit of the story for you. There’s just enough variety and innovation to hold your attention, whether it be using your pet to outmaneuver a gaggle of foes or turning the tables with a well-timed scroll. I can’t say there’s much you haven’t seen before here, but I can say it’s usually not presented in such an inviting way. Ananias would make a great first roguelike or coffee-break diversion, giving it a place in any adventurer’s library.

Ananias is a throwback to classic floppy disk RPGs with new modernised elements. Explore various levels as you attempt to recover the one ring to rule them all; the one artifact that can kill the evil Serpent.
Ananias Roguelike resembles what many floppy disk games looked like, but that isn't necessarily a bad thing. While it isn't as beautiful as, say, The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, it is pretty in it's own unique way. If you are a fan of old-school pixel graphics, then this game fits your bill. One thing the developers could add relieve a bit of the burden on the eyes is to add animations which would make things that much better.
Ananias Roguelike is a turn-based roguelike dungeon-crawler that is heavily randomised. Each level is unique with different items scattered around that you can use to aid your journey through the dungeons. Quite a bit of strategy is required in order to minimise the amount of damage to you and your companion. There are several different classes in Ananias that you can use with differing abilities. My favourite class so far would have to be the Arcane Master, who is fundamentally a wizard. The replayability in Ananias is insane. Every playthrough is quite different. You can experiment with the 9 different classes, 4 different companions, and endless combinations of stats, spells, and equipment. There is a crafting system which you can exploit to craft potions with differing effects. One thing that I like to do in Ananias is entering a room full of enemies and backing out, luring them one by one to their deaths.
The only thing wrong with the gameplay and combat mechanics in Ananias is the fact that your companion is prone to dying very early in the game. If you're a ranged class, such as the Arcane Master, your companion will have a tendency of moving in front of you, preventing you from attacking your potential killer.
I quite like the soundtrack in Ananias Roguelike. It fits the dungeon-crawler theme and doesn't really distract you. There is quite a bit of ambient sounds that play throughout the dungeons, such as wind and other sounds you would expect in a dark dungeon/evil lair. There is a choir track that plays that really fits the mood quite nicely. Most of the music in Ananias Roguelike resembles what I would call evil church music. There's things like the aforementioned choirs and organs that really make you feel like a heretic fighting off a cult.
Right from the get go of the game, you are greeted with short slides that explains the story of Ananias. There was an evil serpent that rose from the Underworld (aka HELL) that somehow managed to nearly wipe humanity off of the face of the world. However, there is one thing that can save the world. The lost ring of the King Ananias. The story really is quite Lord of the Rings-ish, but Slashware Interactive did a great job of crafting a world of their own without copying too many ideas from the world of J.R.R Tolkien.
As previously mentioned, adding in animations for things such as movement and combat would greatly help the aesthetics portion of your game, however, since Slashware Interactive is clearly going for the nostalgic look and gameplay for 80s RPGs, it's unnecessary. Improving the AI for the companions would also greatly improve the game, because even though they do help you face the perils of the dungeons, they also end up being counter-productive by blocking ranged shots as well as dying quite frequently.
I enjoyed Ananias Roguelike for the time that I played it. Although the companions did annoy me quite a bit, the game itself was quite fun. If you want to reminisce about 80s floppy disk RPGs, I suggest you buy the game, as it's quite cheap. The developer selflessly put the game up FOR FREE on their own website, so if you want to try out Ananias for your self before purchasing, head to the Ananias game website. If you prefer to play games on mobile, Ananias is also availible on iOS and the Google Play Store. The developer is frequently updating Ananias (the last update as of writing this review was less than 2 weeks ago), and I see great potential in this game if the developer continues to support it.

An unusual concept turned into a really unique game. Basically, you sit in front of an old police computer and sort through a  database of short video clips from an old investigation, trying to figure out what happened. The story is well written and surprising, but I especially love the non-linearity of the whole thing. It's only up to you which video clips you'll find first, and, what's more, you may never be sure if the interviewee is lying or not. There's a certain point when you start to understand what happened and this moment, I can asure you, is one of those magic moments only games can give you.
Definitely worth a try, but probably not for everyone.

My review for PAYDAY The Heist will be about pros and cons for the game, adding a summary at the end.
Pros:
+Gameplay
+Good missions
+Fun with friends
+No micro-transactions
+Friendly staff
+Amazing weapons
+Great texture/detail
Cons:
-Not a lot of people play it anymore
-Hardly any servers
-Good weapons but not enough
-Barely any playable maps
-A lot of hackers
-Missions seem too easy
-Skill system/upgrades
Summary:
I listed 7 pros and 7 cons that I can come up with that make me recommend this game. Overall, since PAYDAY 2 came out, everyone's been buying that and ditched this game. No one ever plays it so you don't see much people host servers. The gameplay is nice, along with the textures and details, it runs smoothly. The weapons are good but there's not enough to use. Basically only 3 for each skill set. You bump into hackers every now and then which isn't fun. Instead of buying skills like you do in PAYDAY 2, you need to level up for it which might take forever depending on how well you do in games and a rarity of achieving that item. After a while when you level up, the missions get too easy, even on overkill. Playing with friends might be fun, but the maps get boring which means there isn't enough to play on. The staff are very nice and didn't add micro-transactions onto the game. I guess they went down the right road. I will recommend this game as I am a PAYDAY fan and I've had experience with this game already. It's a good game, I recommend you buy it if you're looking at an easy, fun game to play!

Go back to where it all began, with the 4 original heisters... Payday: The Heist. If you want a game that actually challenges you and focuses on team play, then grab this gem. With only 1 DLC ever made (excluding the in game soundtrack), this is a true video game, not a DLC fest, like Payday 2 has become.
This is a straightforward team based shooter with no strings attached and has some similiar game mechanics of Left 4 Dead. It is a game where you must work hard as a team or die as a team! It is an unforgiving game and the challenges become harder as you progress, until you get to the dreaded Overkill 145+ difficulty, which is much harder than the Deathwish on Payday 2.
In this game, you do not have Skills, Perk Decks, Armror or fancy weapons (RPGs) at your disposal. Because of the lack of these things, you will need to work hard and be smart with your team, to overcome the Overkill 145+ achievements.
The only negative is finding a team to play with. There is only a very small amount of people who play this (probably a maximum of 300 people online at any one time). But there is plenty Payday The Heist groups and of course the forum is still reasonably active. There will always be someone out there to help you, if you don't have friends to play with.
So what does this mean for you? Well, go Steal, Kill and make a Deal, in the best Payday game made.
Pros:
-Original concept, before it got ruined in Payday 2
-Very team focused game play
-Very challenging experience
-No DLC every month
-No micro-transactions
-No cross-overs (with game or film companies)
-No large downloads every month (2gigs or more, are standard updates in PD2)
Cons:
-Small amount of players (this can be over come by finding groups / forums to get a team)
-Game can lag a lot more than Payday 2 (especially if your team is from around the world)
-Some minor bugs in game, that will probably never be repaired
I give this game 4 out of 5 Beers.
Cheers,

Ah, Final Fantasy V.  I still remember playing this game on an SNES emulator way back before the PS1 release.  Back when the main character was given his literal translation name of Butz before being changed to Bartz in later releases.  Quite possibly my favorite game in the entire series, second only to Final Fantasy IX, and only then because I can't choose between them.  I have been looking forward to this release since it appeared in the Upcoming Releases section.  Now, has it been worth the wait?
HELL YES!
This is the same Final Fantasy V I fell in love with so long ago.  The characterization is spot on from what I expected from this release, the graphics are pretty good, sprite work isn't as great as the GBA version, but still good, and the musical score and gameplay are just as great as I remember.  Playing with the job system is just as fun as in previous releases, making your own army of customized fighters with skill sets of your own making.  Want a Knight with the healing abilities of a White Mage?  A Black Mage with the fighting power of a Monk?  A dual-wielding Berserker?  All possible.
Some of the animations and scenes look a little odd now, like when you check in on Faris in Tule.  In the original game, Faris turns her (not a big spoiler) head while sleeping, which makes her hair slip so the characters Butz and Galuf can get a good look at her face, but in this game, she turns completely over onto her front, I think, so the scene makes far less sense.  Whoever did these animations should have paid more attention to the source material, to get not only the animations right, but also the context of each scene.
All in all, a pretty good port, if you ask me.  It's still the game I love in every aspect and I cannot recommend it enough.

Sadly, as it stands now I can’t recommend getting this version of FF5. I’d like to, as I quite enjoy FF5 and I was hoping for a nice updated version, but this has too many issues to make it worth your while. It isn’t that it is a mobile port, but a bad mobile port. It just does not look or perform that well on the PC. It isn’t awful, but I just don’t feel like it really justifies purchasing the “update” in this state.
To break down specifics:
The Good:
--Nice updated sprites.
--Supports keyboard and controller and does a decent job on both, they can both be fully remapped.
--More features than the Super Famicom/PSX version.
The Mediocre:
--No music remaster. The music is just a recorded version of the SPC700 soundtrack. They didn’t redo it using modern samples or a live orchestra.
--Character portraits look almost nothing like their in game sprites.
The Bad:
--Very obvious tile seams. The tile graphics were updated along with everything else, but they do not tile smoothly. You can see really, really, obvious seams between most tiles on the map.
--Wonky fonts. The fonts are not anti-aliased for whatever reason, and they don’t line up well, so they look strange/jerky.
--Problematic fullscreen support. On the system I tested it on, which is Windows 10 with a GeForce, it won’t go fullscreen. The game’s GL plugin NeHe GL says the fullscreen mode isn’t supported, no matter what that mode is, despite fullscreen working fine in other titles. Also, this means it uses OpenGL despite listing DX10 as the requirement.
--Looks like it only runs at 30fps. I haven’t put a counter on it to confirm, but it is far too jerky when scrolling for a nice 60fps game.
It just seems really half-baked. It isn’t awful. If you want to play FF5 on your PC it’ll do the trick, but it is not a very competent port at this point. It looks like they just grabbed the mobile code and did the bare minimum to make it run on Windows. I’d give it a miss, personally.

A good middle-ground Roguelike with an excellent User Interface. While it's not incorrect to call it a simplified Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup, it also isn't simplified at the cost of fun or depth.
Ananias is extemely accessible and quick to get started with an interface that is clear, concise and doesn't leave you with a lot of questions as to how the game operates. You'll be playing in seconds.
Procedural dungeons and multiple classes should provide a decent amount of replayability. Online leaderboards let you compare your overall achievements with a community.
This is a roguelike that tried to streamline the process of playing by allowing quicker movement between rooms whenever enemies aren't present. While leveling is streamlined as well and based simply on making it to the next foor, players still have a wealth of weapons, equipment, familiars(pets), bandages mixable potions and more to give more player-choice. Leveling-up also comes with a choice of how one wishes to build their character as you delve deeper into the dungeon.
For $4.99US, I think this is a fun contribution to the roguelike genre that does a great job of being a little simpler than a "hardcore" roguelike, but not at the expense of fun - and it still has some welcome RPG-like depth

Ananias is a great Roguelike, blending classic gameplay with a modern interface. Originally conceived back in 2014 on the "7DRL Challenge", an event for developers to make a roguelike game in seven days, Ananias became so much more as the years passed by, and it certainly deserves to be in your library if you're a fan of this kind of game.
I have played Ananias for the first time on my smartphone, but it's way more comfortable (to me, at least) on the desktop. You can play the free version on your browser if you wish to know how it is on PC:
The Steam version is the best one if you want all classes unlocked and the best price, since it's localized according to your country, and not sold with a dollar tag.
The game itself is very balanced and it's a joy to play, with responsive controls, an awesome and intimist soundtrack and a lot of secrets to discover. I love how the procedural generation is handled here - it really will surprise you from time to time. Another game I like a lot on this genre is the - excellent - Dungeons of Dredmor (DoD), and despite my love for that game, DoD is more or less the same on some ways. Ananias, on the other hand, is unpredictable. It can throw some very high level monsters at you, put a dress to loot on the floor (even if you're playing with a male character), and make every run feel really unique - it's a real Pandora's Box, and it's gorgeous.
All in all, you can't beat this price for an awesome roguelike. Play the free version (on browser or on your smartphone) and if you like the game, buy it to support this awesome project. See you in the depths of the dungeons!

Welcome to my review of Her Story!
In A Nutshell:
Pros:
-Fantastic Storyline (And an intriguing, original method of uncovering it!)
-Ending Open for Interpretation (Could be a Con?)
-Retro-Licious Graphics
-Quality Acting
-Steam Trading Cards and Achievements
-Lots of Surprise Plot Twists
Cons:
-No True Ending (No real resolution, since the player draws their own conclusions.)
-Minimal Replay Value
-Dated Graphics (Even if Intentional.)
-Fairly Short (Ignore Time-on-Record, I was finished in roughly 2-3 hours!)
Full Review:
Her Story is essentially an interactive, visual novel, in which the player searches through a database of achieved videos from the ‘90s to piece together the whole puzzle of a murder. It’s incredibly immersive, and a psychological ride at times; I absolutely loved trying to figure out what had happened. Players use search terms to find videos, looking for clues within them for their next search entry; you can save videos for later review – and best of all, tag them with your own keywords! Some are a few seconds long, and others are over a minute.
The whole narrative takes place over several interviews with the suspect, a woman who initially goes by Hannah. As the story unfolds, it gets more and more convoluted; in the end, the player has to decipher what they believe happened, and the Developer no doubt intentionally left it open-ended for exactly that purpose.
As someone who loves mysteries and psychological thrillers, Her Story was a perfect mix for me. At first, it felt like a Herculean task to figure out what key words would work best. However, things snowball quickly, and before long you’re uncovering lots of backstory and nitty-gritty details. It’s touching at times, unsettling at others, and in the end I was vaguely dissatisfied with my conviction on what exactly happened. Her Story is one of the few open-ended games where I would have preferred a final conclusion, if only because of the police investigation –oriented theme. In the end, I highly recommend it, especially if you can nab this one on sale.
In Conclusion: 8/10

On it's most basic level it's not entirely unfair to compare it to FTL in some ways ie branching path progression, limited supplies for upgrades, skills that allow random interactions to have various outcomes. But ultimately it's a lot more than just an FTL like, a better description might be if FTL and a board game had a baby.
1 full play through takes 2-3 hours roughly (assuming you make it through all the adventures that make up 1 play through). Though it has a ton of replay-ability via different team configurations and strategies (gold/research/status). At it's core it's a pretty simple system of trade offs between resources and fights/encounters but it's got some hidden depth that makes it stay fresh (emotional combat states/character skill progressions/etc)
It's quite a bit of fun and frankly a pretty decent value at it's base price due to amount of content/replay that's included. Not to mention the developer seems pretty committed to continuing to release content/support the for the game and seems pretty responsive.

Honestly, I was surprised by how good it is.
The artstyle is good, character designs being one of the things that I liked the most. The gameplay is engaging, highlights being the exploration of the different areas. It can sometimes be difficult, but the more you play it, the easier it gets imo. The sound design is great, love the atmospheric sound in the stages and the goofy sounds that the characters make. Seems to have quite a lot of replayability to it with the team customization and with the unlocking of other characters as captains.
Though, I do have a slight issues with this game.
While the visuals are good, they, in combat, look a bit too blurry and have barely any detail. I also think the sprite animations need a few more frames during the attacks to make it a bit smoother, and maybe add a reaction to the characters/enemies being damaged when attacked. I also noticed that there was no sound to the mummies attack. Tiny issues, but they do make a difference.
Besides those slight problems, I ran into a few glitches. One where my character attacked the enemy, went the other way (away from the enemy, not towards it) and attacked. Then there was some random lines of codes popping up on my screen after I had made a purchase in one of the stores.

Well, the game has a good content and the developers are working to further improve the number of locations you can travel to.

I hope this review helps you in your choice.

Had BB came out a year or even 6 months ago i'm sure it wouldn't be stagnating with a player base of slightly under/over 1k players at any given time. On the surface this looks like an Overwatch clone. But that's just it... most people don't look below the surface and most people chose Overwatch.
It's really that simple. Wrong place, wrong time! So now we have a vicious snowball effect going on with the game. People come in, que takes forever, people blow through the co-op in mere days, people leave. Over and over again. There is simply not enough people to form a stable environment with a healthy matchmaking system.
Even when you do get matched up, expect to be STOMPED! Pre-made lvl 100's make up a significant portion of this games playerbase. What happens when people can't get an evenly matched opponent? They get frustrated and they LEAVE!
I bought this game on humble bundle with 10 other games for a mere $15, i more than got my monies worth. But will you? And at full price!? No... no you will not. I can not recommend this game until either
A. A miracle should befall it and people decide they are tired of Overwatch and check the game out only to find it's actually NOT an Overwatch clone and is a very deep and satisfying MOBA.
B. They go free to play so people can actually see it's NOT an Overwatch clone and is a very deep and satisfying MOBA.
The game has been misjudged and swept under the rug before it even had a chance! The humble bundle brought in a few people like myself but we mostly all left after exhausting the PvE and tiring of the PvP que times.
TL;DR: The game is dead, only grab it on a HUGE sale if you are interested and bring some friends, or you'll be one lonely, one very outmatched Battleborn.

This is a weird game.  Let's get that out of the way first.  Tiny Brains is a fun little romp, created by indie startup Spearhead Games.  These guys made, easily, one of the funniest little bits of gaming I've ever seen in recent memory.  That being said, Tiny Brains does miscalculate at points and occasionally it feels like you already went through something.  Bear with me here.
First, let's talk gameplay.
You play as one of four superpowered rodents (Technically five, although I'm not divulging due to spoilers), which all have a unique, physics-bending, power.  One can pull stuff in, another can create a block of ice which can either act as a trampoline or wall, or can be affected by the other Brains' powers, another shoves stuff away, and another swaps places with some object, BUT cannot affect the Brains themselves.  The game is, put bluntly, a puzzler.  You need to combine and conquer with powers, using two, three, sometimes all four at once just to get past a puzzle.  It's a devious piece of work - At times I was forced to take a step back, re-analyze my strategy, and then adapt to whatever I was coming up on.
That's the good news of gameplay.  The bad news?
The Brains, for starters, move a tad bit too slow.  It's not a HUGE issue, but in some cases, it does glare right through, most notably in the challenge mode.  Also, unfortunatly for the poor install base (I think it's small), this game was MEANT to be a co-op game, and playing single-player can sometimes feel less like a game and more an exercise in how to non-standardize puzzles.  It's still OK, but friends = Good.
Now, for the graphics.  They're...Weird.  This game was meant to be a PS4 release title, but it got shoved back some.  The graphics themselves are cartoony fun, mixed with horrifically dark themes.  It makes for an oddball experience, oftentimes completely clashing with it's silly premise.
The game itself takes, at best, two and a half hours to complete, more if you want to see everything ever.  This game is good fun, but I'd get it on a sale - 20$ seems a little too much an asking price for a package this tiny (Heh).
Overall, I'd buy Tiny Brains.  And so should you.

A brief but memorable experience. Tiny Brains is a commendable attempt at creating a unique co-operative multiplayer experience that can be enjoyed in a single play session. The controls and concepts are straight forward enough for less experienced players to succeed, while still presenting an entertaining challenge to gaming veterans. It's a great title to play with a few friends on Steam Big Picture for an enjoyable evening of collaborative physics-based puzzle solving.
Some areas of the game can be difficult to execute and may try your patience, but conquering these sections is bolstered by a wonderful feeling of group accomplishment.
Tiny Brains is easy to recommend to anyone looking for a fun and unique title to explore with family or a few friends. With any luck more developers will take chances on games like Tiny Brains.

Graphics: Very poor quality; you can see the outlines of the tiles and the textures don't match up with eachother. An RPG Maker game would be more consistent. Plus, the sprites seem amateurish compared to earlier remakes, especially since the chatbox heads don't fit at all with them (everybody has white hair). Overall, the GBA remake has better graphics in every point, and that was quite a while ago.
Gameplay: Controls are pretty fluid, though the eight-directional feature seems pretty weird and out of place. The combat is also a significiant notch below earlier remakes due to the fact that you have to press the button each time you want to do an action, as opposed to holding it.  You also can't run, and the texts are slow.  Again, the GBA remake is better.
UI: It may be touch-control friendly but on PC, it's just too big and invasive. GBA wins again.
Audio: Literally the only instance where it's actually better than the GBA remake; the audio in this is absolutely beautiful for most tracks. Some musics are badly mixed though, like Battle on Big Bridge where it sounds like they didn't know whether to make it mono or stereo and decided to just make it cavernous in order to hide their doubts.
Overall: Just get the GBA remake, even if you're a big-time fan. You can just listen to the OST later on Youtube.
UPDATE: Tried out different resolutions and on 720p, the environmental graphics are actually pretty good.
UPDATE #2: You can actually run, but only if you have a Thief in your party.
