Ananias is a straightforward traditional rogue-like that the developer has adapted for modern media - including both on mobile phones as well as on computer. The game features full integration of the mouse along with the keyboard, to the point that you can play through the game with just the mouse alone if you wish. At this time, the game isn't totally playable with the keyboard, but the developer has promised to enable this in the future.
As for playing the game itself, Ananias has simple but deep gameplay. You can play with reagents to concoct potions for use against your enemies or your own personal use. You can play with a companion, which you can order around. Different classes have their own gameplay quirks and bonus for different forms of play. Items have durability which degrades and reduces in effectiveness....
And that isn't saying anything about the diverse enemy set which will all have their own unique abilities and attacks for you to deal with as well.
Being newly released to Steam, there are some things that may be wanting at this time. Their are no Steam Achievements, there are no Trading Cards, and while there is a help button to get a lot of useful information - that component of the game will throw you to desktop to read a file instead of keeping you in the game.
I recommend this game primarily if you want a simple rogue-like that has decent replayability. It is likely best for those playing on mobile phones, though it can be fun to play on the computer too.
Oh, did I mention you could play the standard edition from the developers website for free? You won't get access to the Slayer, Barbarian, Sage, or Monk, but for the most part you'll get to fully experience the game and see if it matches with your tastes.

Such a great game. Not huge, but big enough to definetly be fun. It has three 'aspects': exploration, fighting, and humor.
Exploration is reminscent of metroid, except all the puzzles are jummping puzzles. They're still quite challenging, but it doesn't have the flavor of the genre namesake - no exotic architecture to figure out, no mechanisms to activate in the right order, just acrobatics. Still fun, though.
The fighting is the meat of the game, and reminds me of Viewtiful Joe somewhat, or Devil May Cry in 2d. It's all about the stylish combos, and its fun to rack them up. A lot of the enemies require specific powers to damage, so you have to set up a combo so that your upward attack can actually hit them, or so that they're off balance enough that your attack can get through their block. It's really fun.
Finally, there's the humor, which is pretty funny. It made me laugh out loud more than once. The flavor of the setting is also intruiging to me - to others it may not feel so mysterious, but I only know hints of mexican folkore, so it's exciting to experiance it. Note that if I'm totally off, I didn't mean to insult anyone who geniuinly knows about mexican folklore.
Overall, the game is great, but only that. Despite it sucking up quite a bit of my time, I felt dissatisfied afterwards, because I wanted more. Maybe I'm just greedy, but 50% - 100% more content would have been great - I feel like there was more that could have been explored in the setting.

Renowned Explorers is an innovative title from Abbey Games, an independent developer and publisher. It tells the tale of a group of ambitious explorers, out to gain fame and best their rivals by plundering treasures from across the globe.
Over the course of a game, you'll pick your crew of three explorers and send them on a series of expeditions to exotic locales such as the Egyptian desert or the forests of Transylvania. The encounters in each setting are procedurally generated, making each game a new adventure and offering great replayability. Fans of games like FTL will find much to love here.
The tactical combat system has a surprising level of depth. Each explorer in your party has his or her own set of abilities, and can be further specialised based on your skill selections and item choices. Additionally, combats feature a clever Attitude system, which grants bonuses or penalties based on how well you've optimised your use of Friendly, Devious and Aggressive abilities. In practice, you might end up charming a ghost pirate, insulting a nun, or even punching a cheeky monkey right in the mouth.
The game is remarkably well-polished, with charming graphics and a smooth user interface. It also provides an impressive level of feedback to the player at each decision point, even down to your odds of success on any given action and the factors which generated those odds.
Abbey Games continues to offer excellent support for this title, with regular patches and free content updates.

I want to like this game, I mean I do like it. But it's constantly giving me reasons not too, the multiplayer is an unbalanced mess. The majority of the time you play versus it'll be against a full team of LV 100s. While your team maybe has one person over 20! The gameplay is great in almost every way, I love the characters and dialogue. The short campaign is fun, even the multiplayer is fun. About half the time you play someone from your team will just leave out of the blue, there's no replacement coming. Not even a buff for the rest of your team when it's 4 or 3 versus 5.
PROS:
Graphics/Art Style: It's a beautiful game, gearbox really knows how to create worlds.
Dialogue/Story: It has much of the comedic timing and banter you'd expect from Borderlands
Gameplay: Tight controls, great mechanics. All feels very fluid.
Multiplayer: The maps, the character abilities, the game modes. All work great, if only there was a larger community.
Cons:
Tiny online community: Those who have had the game since around launch all have characters at least level 75. Those who just got the game off the steam sale or humble bundle (Me) are outmatched.
People dropping out of your game: When your team starts losing and sometimes badly, almost always someone will leave. This puts you at an instant disadvantage in every way. There's no matchmaking to find a replacement. I feel like a team wide buff would work well to balance out if someone leaves, i.e. more health/damage for the team with less people.
In conlusion:
I like this game, it's great. But it'd be so much better with people and at the price it's hard to justify it. It needs a price cut, to make it evenly priced with overwatch. (Which is was falsely compared too at launch and suffered)
All in all, I do recommend it since it really just needs a larger community.

Tiny Brains is an excellent co-op puzzle game that I think anyone can enjoy. It's not portal, but it's still an excellent game, what really makes this game shine is when you play it with a bunch of friends- and that's the point. If you're going to solo play this, I think your time is better spent, but as a co-op game its definitely a great experience to test friendships working out puzzles, since each person is handed a single tool in your toolkit.
My only complaint about the game is that I wish there were more puzzles, DLC is likely in the future, but even so when my friends and I did our first playthrough it only took us 90 minutes- there are some challenge modes, which are definitely great to extend it's lifetime, as let me tell you, working together with 3 other people to keep the ball on the endless rotating pillar is pretty exhillarting and full of suspense, and when you do fail you just try to do it better again.
Finally, I will say this, the game is available on the PS4, and if you have one I would reccomend you get this game for the PS4 instead. The game's strength is as a couch co-op/party game. Its easy to play, it's kid friendly (if you're wondering) and the single player mode just honestly doesn't bring the same entertainment playing it with friends is. As of this moment, I think this is the best party game to get for a PS4, definitely something to grab if you were looking for a reason to invite your buddies over to play your PS4 with you.

It isn't often a game as polished and riveting as Penumbra comes along at all, let alone from a debut effort by an independent studio. A lack of weapons makes enemies far more terrifying than most survival games, demanding some ingenuity rather than an itchy trigger finger, a feat few games succeed in pulling off so well. Along with a tense, immersive atmosphere that is equally unmatched, Penumbra:  Overture is a spectacular, uniquely engaging experience. The less that is known about it before starting it, the better the experie... I've said too much.

Penumbra: Overture is very much worth the money! This game is scary, but it doesn't rely on random scares(jumpscares) most of the time to make it scary, this game relies on it's environment and ambience to give the player that unsettling feeling so they can get the full experience out of the game! If you enjoy horror games, this will most likely feed your hunger for horror and some!

This recommendation applies to both the Overture and Black Plague episodes of Penumbra.
Both remind me a little of the survival-horror System Shock atmosphere, crossed with a classic puzzle-solving adventure game.  There are also small homages to Half-Life in the story and gameplay.
If you like spooky atmosphere mixed with a bit of action and puzzle solving, you'll really like the first two Penumbra games.
Avoid Requiem, however.  It's little more than a Portal-esque rip-off with some horror tidbits thrown in. The only possible reason to bother with the episode is to see the ending, which ties in to the first two and adds an extra layer to the story.  But it's really not worth the price of admission, unless you can pick up Requiem super-cheap.

In short - a more casual version of SupCom 1. Easier to play, but there's much less to enjoy. Good for casual occasional games with friends. Ultimately, it fails as a Supreme Commander's successor, but stands well as a standalone game.
Although Supreme Commander 1 was meant to be /the/ strategy game, with large maps and huge unit caps, where build orders gave place to thought-out tactics, it ultimately ended up being a base-building simulator, as people grew to refer to it. Supreme Commander 2 trades the large scales for a tighter gameplay, shifting focus from the base to the units.
The units are fewer in variety, each having a distinct role. There is much less fiddling with assembling a perfect mix of the hundreds of different bots, tanks, and airplanes. Choosing your tactics is now more clearly resembling rock-paper-scissors, which is both good and bad, depending on the player.
Also, there are only either big badass mother♥♥♥♥ing guns, or cannon fodder. You don't build a tactical missile launcher to fend off your enemies. It's either a small artillery installation, or a nuke. Same with units vs. experimentals.
But wait, speaking of experimental units, it's not as black and white. As before, they are pretty much useless alone when facing a critical mass of smaller units. Perhaps even more so than in SupCom 1, you will want to provide escorts to your big guys. Here, they are easier to build and to destroy, but having one early enough can still mean a victory.
There is a new resource - Research - gained through battle and boosted by research stations. Tech tiers gave way to global upgrades (purchased with research points) that are applied to all units, buildings, or else - existing and future. This serves to speed up the game, though it takes away from the complexity. Whereas in SupCom 1 destroying an upgraded outpost with tech 3 factories was a big hit, here it doesn't take much to rebuild it. Experiments units are also unlocked with research.
Instead of choosing between spending resources on improving your economy/units and building more units, you just do both simultaneously, while spending any excessive mass/energy you have on research stations.
Speaking of resources, here you don't get to build mass/energy storages - they are unlimited. Instead of draining your money during construction, the cost is deduced at the beginning of the process. Finally, there are no mass fabricators, and I have never seen someone have a problem with energy, for the reactors are very cheap and effective.
There is not much to say of the base. Just as unites, the buildings are also fewer. At the beginning of the game, you are presented with a choice of 8 "normal" structures and one "advanced" - the radar. As you research the upgrades for the structures, you unlock things like artillery, nukes, and others.
Engineers now cannot assist each other when building structures (they can, however, assist factories).
Everything is built much faster in comparison to SupCom 1 (where 30-minute build times weren't extraordinary, though improved in FA) - you won't find an experimental who takes much more than 3 minutes to build.
I haven't completed the story, but from what I played it wasn't incredibly interesting. Perhaps as a tool for honing your skills, it would do.
The visual style of the game is nice - it is also simplified, as if to underline the idea the developers had in mind. Similar to Planetary Annihilation - almost a bit cartoonish. Although now outdated and no eye candy at all, it is still pleasant to look at while playing.
I would recommend this game to people who want to play a SupCom-esque game with friends, but don't want to take the days to teach them how to play it. It's simple, bright, fun, and fast. There is not much depth to it, but the gameplay is satisfying and victories sweet.
Personally, I couldn't stand to play it for more than a few hours a month, as I kept switching to Supreme Commander 1. And if you want a fun match with friends, I would recommend Starcraft 2 over this.

Good game. I started out playing this before i played F.E.A.R. and it was then and still a really nice game. It is less scary than it is creepy in its atmosphere. The scariest thing in the entire game were the replica assassins, while everything else was either weird or creepy. But even with that the game was really nice to play because of this aesthetic. The multiplayer if not laggy can be extremely fun when played with a lot of people or with a few friends, and if you like an unsettling industrial atmosphere with fps this provides the perfect setting for that. As far as i remember though, the multiplayer was almost non-existent after a few months back of its release and after the more recent release on the humble indie bundle in nov 2013 it might gave a small kick to the revival of the multiplayer, i can't confirm that it will always be as active as it did on release. The multiplayer is really fun, but unfortunately people find other new gen alternatives and maybe even the gloomy atmosphere turns them off.
I played this game on the highest difficulty and though some parts can get very difficult, especially near the end, it was very satisfying taking on interestingly designed enemy encounters and overcoming them by being smart about using your surroundings and your weapons. The slow motion perk can be an added help if you're encountering rough situations, but i almost never used it for an added challenge, so if you want the real tactical experience i suggest not using it either even though the option is there. If you don't compare this to F.E.A.R. you will see that this game is really great. Most who played this game though, usually played F.E.A.R. and had to compare it with a bias, which had a lower scoring mostly due to its lesser scare factor. It's definitely not as scary as F.E.A.R. and since it is not developed by the same developers of F.E.A.R. the story became slightly more nonsensical in actually making sense of the whole situation and explaining it, which was left as a mini objective of picking up notes around levels to make sense as to why the projects were happening and what was involved in the project but for the most part remained as cryptic as it was nonsensical until you saw the actual cutscenes, and this heavily reflected in F.E.A.R. 3 where the nonsense literally went too far. But aside from that as a developmental story it did well in clouding the experiments in mystery and the hypothetical.
In summary, If you like a dark atmosphere and a polished fps with tactical situations, this is a game for you.

The first thing you notice about the game is that it's gorgeous.  Everything from environments to characters to animations are lovingly and wonderfully designed.
Gameplaywise, it's also engaging.  Watching the map unfold as you trot from location to location is always a treat.  There's a huge variety of events as well.  I'm still finding new events, and get excite when I find a new treasure.
If you don't normally like roguelikes, don't worry!  You can play the whole game on "Explorer" mode, and restart any expedition you fail, with no loss.  This is great for finding all of the treasures in the game, some of which are deviously hidden and going after them can completely change the way you perform your expedition.
Enconters/battles are awesome as well,  Not only do you get to admire the characters close-up, but there's a surprising amount of tactical depth, using emotions to buff, debuff, and exploit weaknesses.  in fact, how you battle a boss can affect the boss's behavior and even the outcome of the event.

Though hampered by the occasional bout of unpredictably frustrating physics, Tiny Brains is unique and creative enough that you forget to care. It's clear that the game was designed with multiplayer at the forefront, as playing solo is possible but significantly less rewarding. Multiplayer can be in the form of couch or online co-op or competitive play, and features gameplay so fun that it's difficult to get too worked up over the potential failures of your teammates.
The game never wants you to take it seriously, and that framework is part of what makes the game work so well. It's charming, packs a killer ear-wormy soundtrack, and offers brain teasing gameplay that will no doubt remind you of Portal. Though the main story campaign is pretty short, the package you get from the multiplayer is more than worth the price tag.

So, originally I had a really bad taste in my mouth after 9 hrs of gameplay and putting up with difficult coaster editor and items not locking to the grid.  This led me to give a negative review.  The thing I didnt realize was that if i looked past the bugs in the editor, like the twisting of the track, the support columns being placed in irritating places causing the coaster to run into them, or items not lining up with the grid, the editor was, in fact, the most powerful piece of software I have seen in a coaster game (RCT 1/2/3, No Limits 2, etc. etc.)  I took the time today to really attempt to figure out how the software was to work for me instead of fighting it.  After 2 hrs today, I have finally figured it out and have build a coaster that was IMO, free drawn.  After testing the coaster, you see where sh*t crashes and a few of the bugs causing this (pillars) but this is the point.   It is a process of perfecting your design.  Build, test, tweak, build, test, tweak.  The ability to allow such freehand movement has "in a way" made me feel as though i was using a design software such as AutoCAD.  Yes, this beta is bare bones and there are hardly any features unlocked, but they are breaking the game down into the bare-bones in order to ask the communitry what we like or do not like.  Imagine if they released a beta with all the bells and whistles.  You would not notice very minute problems in the 3 days they test for.  Yes, the editor takes time.  You almost have to train yourself (which in a video game, is not what I look for, for fun) but it does present a challenge, and challenges I like.  So, after refunded the game last night after being a little disappointed, I have decided to give it another go.  I'm glad I did.  These are not gamebreaking issues and I have absolute faith that these folks developing the game are striving to create one of the best.
For those people who like to place "premade" coasters (which I also love to do when I'm not in the mood to build), there will be a slew of them according to the devs along with Steam Workshop support and mods.  Besides that, I believe there will be tons of content in free DLC and updates as the devs have promised.  There will also be the "old" track editor in the game like we are all used to in the old RCTs if you want to place tracks that way.  The point is, you don't HAVE to use the coaster editor but I want them to keep it, just fix it.
Although, I judged the game on the beta, I have learned not to do this as it is not indicative of the final product.   But do not take my review as saying "buy this game" because I'm not saying that.  I am saying "WAIT" to buy this game or if you are easily frustrated, wait until the second beta.

Intel Core i7 2.5Ghz, 16 GB RAM, Nvidia Geforce 980M 4 GB VRAM, Windows 10

Coaster editor bugs:

When clicking on a node mid track, the track should not move until you apply whatever adjustments you are making (right now when clicking, the node will jump randomly of the screen and mess up what u have created"

Not bugs but add this: No "undo" button, add edge of screen scrolling or right clicking on map to drag camera
Decorations:
Items snap into areas you dont want them to go, once again, using freehand placement and grid (this is one of the issues that doesn't allow me to feel as though I have control over what I'm doing (which is premise of this whole game).  Example was, placed a path laid out according to the grid.  Attempted to place light posts, bushes, and benches.  They would line up on one side of the path, but on the other side, the bench or the posts would be off increasing my OCD.  I turned off the grid to attempt it freehand.  Same thing. So this needs fixing
The ability to "change path color" without deleting the path.  This is annoying.  It also defaults to the ugly red color even after you have been using the other paths so you place the path and realize, you have to delete and choose the right one and do it again.

TL:DR:
This is a "beta" more like an "alpha" but the game is stripped of the bells and whistles to address a select few items as to focus beta tester's attention to just those items in order to collect as much data and feedback to be able to fix the issues and give us as players what we want.

Well, it's been 5 months, and there's content. Now we get to have a massive flood of User Generated Content thrown at it via the workshop. My experience with the workshop implementation has been pleasing. I'm happy with the 'social hub' button.
Nvizzio definitely listened to the complaints from October. Every complaint of my has been eliminated.
It's very clear that the game was nowhere near ready for full release... but it's leaps and bounds more solid than the engine preview was. The coaster builder now has classic building style as well as the freeform method... and it's seamless; you can, say, build the lift chain using the classic style, and then put in the first drop using freeform, and then finish it off with classic. Fantastic work.
I was able to get my first coaster with excellent ratings knocked out in under 20min... something that took me nearly 4 hours to do during the engine preview weekend. This is a massive improvement. I do kinda miss the live intensity preview on the track building - instead, I have to guess if it's going to work, go with it, finish the track, test it, and tweak it to perfection.
The prebuild blueprints of coasters need to be looked at by the devs, as they end up testing as complete garbage on many of them - my guess is that they were designed with the older system that they had.
Achievements... *fixed. Enjoy!
Camera control is finally able to be completely bound to the mouse, which is a giant relief - that was one of my chief complaints in the preview. In minutes I was able to master the control and look at things exactly how I wanted, instead of fighting it the whole time.
Bugs happen - it's in early access. Textures go funky, AI goes stupid, and things can get weird. I've seen full released games with more issues than this, but the RCT legacy deserves nothing less than perfect; and it's up to the fans to help Nvizzio and Atari make that happen.
Play the game, and tell them when something goes wrong, or right, or weird... just don't expect them to pull up a Ouiji board to guess what is happening to everyone... because sometimes it takes the stars to align to highlight a problem - and that's where crowdsourced testing (Early Access) plays the biggest benefit. We all win when you share your grievances and pleasures.
The day 1 patch has improved upon many of the bugs. Lots of new content was added, as well. This shows much potential for the future of the game.

There was a moment, a while after starting my time within the fragmented narrative of ‘Her Story’, where a simple 10 second video clip led to a blinding degree of clarity. Suddenly, many different things clicked into place – the inconsistencies I’d spotted just previously, the cryptic meaning behind the scene I’d seen an hour before. The story I’d been piecing together finally started to take shape, but for as much as many of my questions had been answered, new ones had only sprouted in their place. So my search continued, digging deeper, looking for those last pieces of the puzzle – and that’s when it struck me how unique and brilliant this game really is.
From the beginning, it doesn’t take long to realise how oddly unsettling this experience can be. You’re faced with the view of a dim CRT computer screen, with vibrant scan lines and harsh strip lights from the room you’re in reflecting off the screen. You’re tasked with searching an archaic database of police interview clips via looking for words from their transcript – “Murder”, “Knife”, and so on. From watching and listening to these, you start to unravel the story of what has happened, slowly but surely realising how deep the rabbit hole goes. All the potential unease this gameplay style can stir within you, however, is equally matched with a compulsion to keep digging until you find answers. To step back, to let things remain unsolved, rapidly doesn’t become an option. It’s a game that sinks its teeth into you from the start, and will not let go.
The broken nature of the plot not only creates a desire to dig into the mystery of things, however, but also effectively lets you shape how the narrative pans out yourself. It’s theoretically possible to uncover massive revelations about what’s going on within your first few searches, although their meaning may not be clear at first glance. Equally, all your confidence in a theory growing vividly in your mind can be shattered within the space of a 20 second clip, forcing you to take a different approach. For all the game is called ‘Her Story’, the reality is it’s YOUR story, with the way things unfold for you perhaps being the most interesting outcome of offer here. Everyone who plays this game will have their own story to tell, their own little eureka moments and things to share around the water cooler, and that’s really a neat thing to see.
While the game has something that could be seen as an ending, the outcome to what has truly happened is left in the end to your own interpretation.  Reading online after playing through the game, I saw many others who had come to different final conclusions, with perfectly justifiable reasoning of their own. In a sense it’s slightly frustrating that there is no definitive answer to the riddles the game puts forward, but I freely admit that after saying the game is excellent at letting you carve your own path, to have one set ending would only cheapen things somewhat. If anything, it’s an excuse to dive back into the archives with a new opinion, perhaps finding more out along the way.
In short, Her Story is a title that I can’t recommend enough. It takes traditional storytelling rules, tosses them out the window, and then rewrites them into something remarkably addicting. It’s not the biggest or most epic game out there, true, but it’s certainly one you’ll remember your time with.

This game dissapoints me. It runs fun on my computer and I have no trouble getting it running on any of my laptops but as an incredible machine style game it fails on several levels.
The first is the Part variety, now there is a wide range of interesting parts and even some that use Nvidia physx, I particularly like the water physics, HOWEVER there is a distinct lack of things like walls, floors and slopes in player made puzzles. Yeah you see all those curved walls everywhere in the screenshots? To the best of my knowledge you either have to unlock those or cannot use those at all in your own puzzles. Also the only walls you can make can be broken and both the shelves and walls have very limited size.
This leaves me feeling creatively stunted as it looks like I more or less have to use everything they give me in very specific ways rather than letting me expeiriment with using things in ways other than its primary use.
The other thing that dissapoints me about this game is that they slapped a completely arbitrary limit on how many of every item you can use in free build mode, granted its 20 per item but its still dissapointing to see item limits applied to specific items rather than across the entire contraption as a whole.
I did not have trouble getting the game to run, it started up completely fine for me but I've heard that some people have issues with getting the game to run and I cannot comment on that because I don't have that issue.
Now when I saw this game back whenever I bought it several years ago I had three things on my mind that sold me on it "its the incredible machine, it has physx, and its in 3d." Having spent a LONG time as a kid throwing together rube goldberg contraptions in the incredible machine this sounded like a dream come true for me. And then the let downs started rolling in:
First: you don't have all the parts unlocked at the start, you have to go through the campaign to unlock them, this is bad because you don't have all the tools nessasary to start building puzzles on your own.
Second: the way the basic walls and floors are discourages building more interesting puzzles because you cannot effectively seperate things out to force the player to think the way you want them to
Third: the campaign puzzles seem arbitrary and lack a lot of the life puzzles in the incredible machine had, the decoration elements are very much lacking compared to what you could do in the incredible machine(meaning I hope you like the brick background because you'll be seeing it a LOT)
Fourth: Physx is cool but I get the impression that even with the fluids dlc(which came out some years after the game itself) that it isn't being used effectively, it seems to work fine for solid body physics but considering the trouble it causes for people to install the game I would have liked to have more things be destructable(like some of the floor blocks in the incredible machine)
All in all I'm dissapointed in Crazy Machines 2 as a follow up to the incredible machine because I think moving to 3d put a lot of the basic mechanics a step back even while it added more advanced mechanics. I don't feel like these new mechanics have as much potential for interesting puzzles or are as open ended or well thought out as some of the things in the original Incredible Machine game.

Crazy Machines 2 is a sequel to Crazy Machine, not counting Crazy Machines 1.5, released in 2008. It's a game of genre of Incredible Machines, where you build a machines out of many details that will accomplish the goals in one way or another. Or more exactly, you feel the needed spaces with limited amount of elements to find one of few correct solution. More of classic puzzle than anything sandboxy you see lately.
Game even supported PhysX new-by-then hardware.
And now, about how it runs nowadays on Steam.
It runs badly!
First, many people have trouble at making this game start at all. I didn't had problem with launching it. You should check demo version first somewhere to see if game will run for sure or not. If you will have trouble then try to find and (re)install OpenAL.
Then I personally had physics not work in this game. Managed to fix it by reinstalling PsyhX and then rebooting computer. Though I have feeling that rebooting was enough, after all game itself should install PsyhX drivers. Anyway. Try to reboot computer first after installing game.
Get demo off Internet and try it first!
Once you are past launch troubles (which you may not have), you still have the amazingly screwed physics in game itself, which is quite a really bad thing for physics-based puzzle.
The thing is that physics are not reliable. Tweaking some elements may change the resulting behavior of other elements that aren't connected to the one being tweaked in any way. You may be changing gears around in one part of map and it will somehow make baseball miss the bucked while rolling off slope somewhere else, for example. It's quite frustrating when you got solution right, yet it may not work until you play around with objects.
That, and the way that physics work in game seemed to slightly change from when it originally came out. What it means is that some solution don't work anymore. Now, it doesn't affect Crazy Machines 2 much, I enjoyed beating it fully. but there is a single puzzle in Bonus Labs, puzzle number 18, where official full (with bonus objectives) solution doesn't work. You can however get to see the full solution that community figured out in a list of high score records, by watching replay, once you rush through puzzle without completing bonus objectives.
DLCes seem to have more of broken puzzles, so watch out for those.
Puzzle instructions, which funny professor with overgrown moustaches narrates (instead of being annoying by popping in randomly for some always-repeated comment like in the original CM), also have small problems. The on-screen drawings that point out objectives appear much slower than voice reads the text. Even more, I noticed that some of the later puzzles have intros where voice narrations and text have little differences. And there was even a puzzle where text and voice instructions put "in what order it should be done" incorrectly, different from on-screen drawings!
As you can see, Crazy Machines 2 is full of technical flaws. Which is quite a shame, because it's superb sequel to Crazy Machines.
It has a much more "high-budget" feel to it than previous title, sporting modern-by-then shiny graphics, support of more complex physics (Like, ropes can be hanged without being connected to anything, useful for just pushing objects.), even 15 themes, with their own decoration and music. Soundtrack is a bit too much of "stereotypical local", but got nice pieces, like Caribbean theme that sounds slightly like something from Monkey Island . On bad side it's hard to understand whole puzzle system from the first look, new graphics/style are quite messy, also having useless decorations mixed in.
It also introduced new complex systems of gears and laser, making them often main focus of puzzle. There are also robots made of 3 parts and switches on which you can place switch of any given type, like button or timer clock. Instead of puzzles being one-trick physics stuff, you often will have to manipulate whole system of gears, lasers, electricity, switches. Which isn't such bad thing, especially knowing that physics are buggy here.
And every puzzle in this sequel concentrates on mostly figuring out where in the system to place each elements. There are almost no puzzles where the only thing you have to do is pixel-perfect placing of elements, unlike original Crazy Machines. I mean, not when you figure out how it should work, but when you are busy tweaking placement, being frustrated with it. I like Crazy Machines 2 approach so much more!
Not to mentioning that it saves some work when it comes to precise placement after all by having a minimal step which elements can be moved by, so to say.
Game also gives you mandatory and bonus objectives, while also providing with text clues and other hints, giving it less frustrating moments. Unlike Crazy Machines, where you either figure out solution to some-super-tricky puzzles or don't progress at all.
Overall, you will get 150 main puzzles to solve, with last 40 of which being hidden until you beat all previous ones properly. There is also 10 tutorial puzzles that you should do. 20 more Bonus puzzles. And 20 more bonus puzzles that were made exclusively for PhysX hardware. No, you can't access those. So no idea what to expect in them.
You also can design your own puzzles for your own amusement or to send it to others. Yes, you can download and upload your labs in the game to the server. And editor lets you do quite a lot of things too. Though, for some reason it has some elements locked. The requirements for those is to get some awards in main campaign, by, for example, using fireworks few times. Bad thing is that it doesn't tell you what exactly you are supposed to do to unlock them, from what I know. In all honesty, I didn't try making my own labs or try using others, so I can be wrong.
Overall, I can recommend this to only those who are ready to handle technical difficulties and those who loved Incredibly Machines games. It's good sequel and I can overlook all trouble I sometimes had for all fun I had with puzzles that didn't feel unfair.
Everybody who doesn't want to bother, well, eh, should avoid this one.

F.E.A.R. 2 is a decent shooter with a couple interesting additions to the F.E.A.R. formula. Unfortunately several things that were present in the first game and made it feel as good as it did to play are completely absent or changed for the worse in the sequel. The slide kick requires an extra buton imput to perform, making it much harder to use in the middle of combat. There are fewer weapons overall. The appearances of ghosts/Alma occur when you come near them and not when you are actually looking at them, causing you to completely miss many of the smaller scripted events. The game will semi-regularly wrest control away from the player to show them a story event or other happenings in the game world, breaking the flow of the game and making it feel a lot more like other modern shooters. One welcome addition to the game that really broke up the monotony were the sequences where you pilot one of the enemy mechs and rampage through the destroyed city for a few minutes of satisfying action. Overall F.E.A.R. 2 is a bit more bland than it's predecessor and I can not reccomend it over F.E.A.R. 1 and it's expansions. I do however highly reccomend it over F.E.A.R 3.

Utterly ridiculous, vulgar, irreverent, laughable, and shameless: Metal Gear Solid V. In it, doctors perform hypnosis and plastic surgery on a medic loyal to the PF corporation commander Venom Snake so he can create Outer Heaven, a utopia of warriors with “No greater good. No just cause.” In the words of his enemy, Skull Face:
The chain of retaliation is what will truly bind this world together as one … Sans lingua franca, the world will be torn asunder. And then, it shall be free. People will suffer, of course - a phantom pain. The world will need a new common tongue. A language of nukes. My Metal Gears shall be the thread by which all countries are bound together, in equality. No words will be needed. Every man will be forced to recognize his neighbor. People will swallow their pain. They will link lost hands. And the world will become one. This war is peace.
This game is, undoubtedly, a masterpiece. The gameplay is incomparable. Every subtle shift in the route of an enemy, the redirecting of a turret, the coming of dawn is fluid and graceful--something lacking in many other stealth games. In MGSV, time seems to condense and expand at the sight of a chopper, a trigger, or the sudden recognition of red light blinking discretely in the foliage--blink, blink; be careful. But more importantly, the game is weird. No, absurd. It has the je ne sais quoi one sometimes witnesses in a certain an image, a 10-second sound, a story--anything, but very few things. This has it. It gives the deep impression of a long past and a bad future. Something bigger always seems hidden from view, poised, but ready to crash down at any moment. It seems important, that something deeply unsettling are at the center of Snake's actions. People complain about the story. The story is not about events, but a certain feeling or fear that lingers. Moreover, this game is deeply melancholy. Motherbase is silent except for the mechanical whirr of helicopters and the bark of a soldier. It has long, dead avenues. This game regrets life, but lives it to the fullest. MGSV is, in the best sense, a somber paradox. It is adolescent and immature on the surface, but has unintended valleys and trenches. People complain about the story because it seems giddy and cheap. Life is cheap.

1) The graphics on this game are brilliant, it is clean and has a level of beauty in HD.
2) Steampowered games pu alot into the story of the games, The campain is split into three, each having their very own campain.
The first campaign (dedicated to the UEF or United Earth Federation) follows Dominic Maddox, a UEF officer who is married to an Illuminate. Maddox fights off Cybran until the UEF Commander he serves declared that all Illuminate are terrorists and orders him on a mission to "round up" the Illuminate from his home city. Maddox refuses, goes rogue, and decides to go on his own campaign to remove his old commanding officer from power. Immediately following the defeat of the UEF Commander, he discovers a portal that leads to Seraphim VII, unlocking the second campaign.
The second campaign (dedicated to the Illuminate) follows Commander Thalia Kael as she fights to restore the Illuminate to their former glory before turning against her former comrades and realizing her mistake.
The Cybran campaign follows Ivan Brackman (an experimental genetic composite clone of Dr. Brackman and Elite Commander Dostya), an old roommate of Maddox, who fights under the direction of Dr. Brackman (whom Ivan refers to as "father" while attempting to help his friends).
3) Changes from Supreme Commander
While there are many differences between Supreme Commander (together with its expansion, "Forged Alliance") and Supreme Commander 2, the two primary changes are the introduction of a new resource – research – and a complete reworking of the resource-gathering mechanism.
Research
Research is a new form of resource which is accumulated by building research labs. The rate at which research is acquired is based on the number of research labs built. Research points can be spent to acquire new technology in a hierarchical fashion at any time during the game. This produces an entirely different game from the original because it often results in a multiplayer game where one side will suddenly acquire a significant technological advantage (for example the ability to use a loyalty gun, which converts lots of enemy units to one's own side, or the ability to fire a nuclear missile). It is often this sudden, game-changing acquisition of technological advantage which leads to the end of a multiplayer or skirmish game.
Resource Gathering
The primary resources in Supreme Commander 2 are still mass and energy. However, the way these resources are accumulated and used by the player has been drastically changed from the first game in the series. The Xbox 360 version is considered "broken" by many players due to an economic glitch involving two engineers and an unfinished structure.[citation needed]
In the game's first release, the resource-system functioned as it does in most other RTS games (resources can only be spent after being acquired, and build orders cannot be placed if there are insufficient resources to complete the build - starting a build reduced a player's resources by the total cost of the build immediately). However, patch 1.23 significantly changed the economy system.[12] Resources are deducted from the total during the build. If there are insufficient resources to complete the build then engineers and factories will build as far as current resources allow and then remain in a quasi-paused state until more resources become available. With this change, the building mechanic more closely resembles that of the previous game.
Mass fabricators (which in Supreme Commander changed energy into mass at a pre-determined rate) have been replaced with mass converters, which must be manually triggered to change a fixed amount of energy into a corresponding amount of mass.

Star Wars - Knights of the Old Republic or otherwise known amongst the community as KOTOR is a classic Star Wars game.
Start during a time of war and chaos that propels you into the heart of battle as you seek to survive and topple odds that work against you. Develop skills and abilities that will help you overcome obstacles that you encounter - be it in the battlefield against Sith troopers or in the cantina speaking with an influential patron, where you choose to invest your capacities will determine different outcomes.
Just as different paths lie before you so too, can you choose your fate. Will you tread the path of the Jedi and use goodness and tranquility to show the light? Or will you aggressively stride forward in the path of the Sith and force darkness upon those you meet? Your decisions and behaviors will carry consequences that will impact all who come across you in your journey.
A predecessor and inspiration to the acclaimed Mass Effect series, Star Wars - KOTOR serves as a primary example of what RPG elements, nail-biting moments of action and a great story can do to drive a game into history to be considered one of the best games of all time. Live, breathe and fight your way in this Star Wars universe with your crew of the Ebon Hawk on an adventure like none other. Experience the moment and times of Star Wars was and is during the time of the Old Republic.
Buckle up and make ready to jump to hyperspace - you're going to be in for one helluva adventure.

This is a visual novel in which you are given a strangely limited 'search engine' for video clips from some kind of police record. A collection of videos of a series of interviews with a woman above a murder have been indexed by their script, and you can type in a search box, and any videos in which those words were spoken will appear for you to watch. You can't get away with simply typing a common word like "the," as only the first 5 relevant videos will ever display.
You discover the story by searching for keywords you think are interesting, and as you watch the videos, you'll hear her mention people, places, and things that you might want to know more about, so you search for those. As you learn more about the story, you'll start to search for more specific or complex phrases.
The game will mark videos you have yet to see with a little icon, so you don't have to rewatch videos you've already seen again and again. You can also add custom keywords to all videos you find, so you can easily search them again later. You can also add videos to your "session" which is kind of like a personal saved playlist of videos. You can't remove videos from here, however, without deleting your entire save data, it seems, which is my only complaint about the game (either that or I just don't understand how to do it).
That's about the extent of what there is to do in the game; like any visual novel, the game is purely about the story. Because of the extremely non-linear method used to discover the story, you'll constantly be curious and guessing and trying to find more videos. It makes the story very exciting to discover. The writing is pretty good, so the story is quite interesting, plus it's written in such a way that many of the video clips will mention other topics without giving away much about them to encourage you to search for more.
There were many times I thought I had figured something out or guessing what had happened or what something had meant, but then as I found more videos later, realized my assumptions were wrong, which lead to me trying to find more videos on that subject. It's really amazing how much depth there is to the storytelling from such a simple method.
There's quite a bit to the story, and you'll be surprised at the amount of content you can find, and you'll keep stumbling upon new aspects or characters or events that you didn't even realize existed when you think you've finally pieced things together. You'll learn about the woman and many other people in her life, and her life story. There's so much to discover. There are a few other little secrets in the game that are better left to finding out by playing, but pretty much it's nothing more than search terms and clicking videos and searching again.
I've only played for two sessions and seen enough of the story to at least feel like I've pieced together a basic version of it with some missing details, and I really enjoyed the story a lot. I'm going to play through again after deleting my data and take notes this time and try to discover as much as possible.
I highly recommend this game if you like unique visual novels. I also very strongly recommend trying to discover as much as you can without using guides or help. The way in which the story unfolds with the limitations and mechanics the game places is a large part of the fun and intrigue of this game. I only plan on "cheating" when I finally give up on trying to find anything new.

Her Story isn't awesome, but it is a hint of something that could be awesome. I enjoyed HS but it struck me as more of a proof of concept or pitch for a game idea than a fully realized game. All of the elements of something pretty cool are there, but they aren't developed or fleshed-out enough to really come together.
Her Story should have a compelling story; "story" is in the title after all. And using a real actor to tell a story is a great idea, but the extreme out of order nature of the story telling makes it pretty muddy. After "completing" the game, and watching almost all of the videos, I really had no idea what happened and had to look it up. Some may call that a feature rather than a bug, and I agree that an open ended experience can be cool. But this wasn't open ended, it was just really unclear. More could have been done to help the player string together the story without sacrificing the free nature of the experience. For example, if there was some way to relate videos to eachother other than via time code, or if watching videos somehow lead to other clues or videos.
The other major problem with HS is that there just isn't enough here for a game. Searching through videos, watching them, and trying to put the pieces together was cool and did feel kind of like detective work, but it just wasn't enough to really be satisfying. Examining evidence would have ben awesome.Maybe searching through case notes and pictures of the crime scene. Interviews with other people mentioned in the story would have been killer, etc.
Overall I do reccomend Her Story because it was an engaging and interesting 2 hour experience. That said I do not think the praise it was showered with is warrented. It is definitely not GoTY material;in its current state I wouldn't call it a game at all. But it does indicate that cool things can be done with FMV games and I hope it inspires people to do better and more complete versions of this concept.

Penumbra is a horror/adventure series by Frictional Games, the developers of Amnesia: The Dark Descent. While not nearly as good as that horror masterpiece, there is still a lot to enjoy in Penumbra. In fact, it's very easy to see how Amnesia eventually came to be what it is - its elements are on full display here, albeit in early forms. While the games do have some scary bits, overall the fright-factor is not quite where it could be. This is mainly due to the somewhat dated graphics and easily thwarted enemies (which, unlike in Amnesia, can usually be killed). The puzzles are generally pretty decent, with only a few solutions being particularly obtuse. So, while not perfect, the series is still worth a look for horror/adventure game fans, especially those who enjoyed Amnesia and are interested in seeing the roots of that game and supporting its developers.

I have to say, though...not quite sure why its "spiritual successor" got so much of the praise, when it's a virtual remake of this, albiet in a slightly quainter setting? To be sure, Amnesia is a tad more refined, but it wouldn't exist without this blueprint/"test run" laying the groundwork first. And any game that keeps me in constant suspense with just a handful of feral dogs, some carnivorous fist-sized spiders, and the occasional epic worm is clearly doing SOMETHING right!
In short, if you adored Amnesia you should at least get a kick out of this one, though you may well suffer a slight case of deja vu. An absolute MUST-HAVE, in any case, for anyone fascinated with just where the hell The Dark Descent came from. Underrated, to say the least!

This creative band had themselves a smashing debut with Reus, and it's always difficult to top a powerful first record. How did they do? Well, in a word, amgyes.
Upon playing this everyone will notice the cleverness, smoothness and fun-ness of it all. When the loading screen animations still crack you up after 20+ times, you know they pulled something off.
This game is all replay value, to an extent that will make some gamers feel awkward (I may be referring to the type of players who specifically enjoy cinematic RPG's with many cutscenes and after each and every corner go F5, try this, die, F9, try that, die, F9, etc). Replaying this game is integral to the whole experience, and makes you tweak your tactics bit by bit until you have a formula that works well. Because this game is so appetizing and creative, the whole tactical puzzle becomes something wonderful. Instead of "oh snap I died again, NOOOO", it makes one go "oh yeah? well how about I do it THIS way". In any case, as a gamer you're being challenged to be EXPERIMENTAL, and try numerous combinations of tactics until you're beefed up enough to gain special items and level-ups.
The most bizarre thing is that after Reus, a godgame in an arena devoid of godgames, they have pulled off their magic trick again of creating a game that is so original and flamboyant that it can only become a niche in itself.

I have been fortunate enough to be allowed to play RE:IS when it was still being developed and it is amazing to see how much it has changed in the last stages of development. I am lucky enough to know one of the designers for Abbey Games and I was eating with him a few months prior to the release and he said: "We are going to change EVERYTHING!". And I am glad they did! It has gotten so good.
RE:IS is one of those games that you can come back to time and time again and it will be different and exciting and beautifull. The lovely hand drawn animations and backgrounds are candy for the eye, the dialogs and characters full of odd references and bad jokes. Lastly, there are so many mechanics and little systems hidden beneath it surface it will take you a long time to master them all. There is a bit of a learning curve here, and sometimes it can be very overwhelming to see all the little things you can take into consideration. It can easily scare away the more casual gamers from trying to understand this game.
It has some aspects of FTL in it that work very well with the genre, I feel. The risk/reward choices you make to travel along a certain route in an expedition is the part of the game I enjoy the most. That and hugging it out with your "frienemies" instead of kicking their butt. But you can do that too if you want!
In short, love the game, love the looks, love the characters and I love the free content that keeps being added to make the game even better than it already was. Making it more playable for the casual and hardcore gamer in one simple update, and more content to come.
9/10 for my part!

Overview:  A stellar game with elements of party management, resource management and tactical combat. The game consists of short, challenging play-throughs that build familiarity with the game levels and concepts. As you improve, the game provides re-playability through selection of different combinations of party members and/or attempts to refine your strategy for high score. Not only is the game already fun, but the developers are very active in the steam community to fix bugs and implement suggestions for improvement.
Read on for a description of the game play elements.
Party Selection: The first challenge is picking a captain and two crew members from a selection of 12 characters with a variety of strengths and weaknesses. The characters are divided into 4 classes, each with 2 of 9 traits, a variety of attacks, and semi-hidden personality traits with hints in the character description. The game provides plenty of advice for selecting your team, including description of a character’s strengths and weaknesses, recommended party members, and symbols for a party’s relative strength in each of the three offensive areas – allowing you to quickly select a balanced or specialized party. There is plenty to appeal to min-maxers, challenge runs, or leisure players that just want to select a quick party and go exploring.
Expeditions: After choosing a party you are cast into your 1st of 5 expeditions, in which you explore a location for resources (gold, campaign and research) and renown (victory points). The map shows the location of the final boss and a couple of nearby locations. Each location gives a hint of the challenges and rewards you may find. Some spaces give rewards automatically, some required the roll on a an adventure wheel, where your chance of success is determined by your party’s class, traits and stats. Some challenges provide an opportunity to avoid the roll for a lesser reward, others impose penalties for failure, including a loss of resolve (game over at 0). Your goal is to choose the route that will provide the most reward on the way to the final boss. You can take as long a path as you like, but if you run out of supplies, your team starts suffering stat penalties.
Encounters: Encounters are brief tactical combats that occur during expeditions. During combat, your characters can use aggressive attacks (physical), devious speech (insults) or friendly speech (compliments) to reduce your opponents’ spirit (hit points). Speech abilities also have 4 debuffs and 2 buffs (friendly speech) that can be applied to a target. Friendly abilities can be used on your own party to heal or remove debuffs. The debuffs/buffs only apply when a character has a positive or negative state of mind, which can be manipulated through use of devious or friendly speech. Also, using aggressive, devious, or friendly abilities will affect the mood of which is how the enemy perceives your actions. The enemy also has its own mood showing their preferred method of attack. The game applies bonuses in a RPS format based on your and your opponents’ mood, where aggressive > friendly > devious > aggressive. If your mood matches your opponent, you receive a bonus to abilities in the superior mood. If your mood is superior to your opponent, you receive a defensive bonus. If your mood is inferior, you receive a defensive penalty. If your characters die in combat, you lose one resolve. Characters can also be revived in lieu of attacking your opponents.

Preparation: After each successful expedition, you are given the chance to spend your resources to improve your characters. Research can be spent to improve your ability to earn rewards, or to make combat easier. Campaign is used to upgrade your shops or hire an entourage, which can improve the value of future reward tokens or increase the number of reward tokens you receive for certain events. Gold is spent on items. Each character can hold one offensive item, one defensive item and one trinket that provides unique bonuses. Will you buy quality armor for a single character, or spread the wealth for small improvements for all of your characters? Finding treasure during expeditions also earns insight, which can be spent during preparation to earn more research, campaign, or gold tokens – you decide.
Ending the Game: You win the game if you successfully complete 5 expeditions AND finish with more renown than your arch rival. You lose if your party is wiped out during combat, loses all of its resolve during expedition or combat, or if you complete 5 expeditions but don’t earn enough renown to be the top explorer.
If you like strategy and tactics, this game is for you.

Summary
Honestly, I felt kind of dissapointed with the beta. But don't get me wrong, this game has major potential to be something big and unique but at the current stance of the beta, I'm kind of iffy on what was only given to us to provide feedback. But anyways, the beta included great elements in the coaster builder which included a lot more coaster customization when laying out the tracks. It didn't feel like it was only a set of pre-modeled tracks and looked like it gave peeps whiplash when making tilted turns (like in rct3) and allowed me to make smooth, curvy tracks. The only thing that gave me a problem in the coaster builder is that there was no way to remove added carts! This is a major key feature in the coaster builder! But if there was a way to remove carts, feel free to correct me.
The pathway design improved a lot since the previous RCT game. Now there is the ability to make curved paths which is fantastic, and also realistic! There was also a variety of pathways to choose from and also had different sizes which allowed a lot more customization to the game. Not only there was a variety of pathways, but also a variety of scenery to decorate your park. This included many lampposts, benches, trees, etc to use! And to even add onto that, the Terrain Deformation Tool allows you to customize your park with pretty, vibrant hills with also the use of the terrain sprayer. It also included a water tool to make lakes or ponds.
Now don't think the beta was all fine and dandy! There was also many things that I was dissapointed about which was the lack of a tutorial, which pretty much there to show you how to play. It was pretty much get into the game and figure out what to do. Although it did not take long, I eventually figured out some of the controls. And one thing that bugged me the most was the placement of pathways, stations, and scenery since there was no grid to make things neat. It also helps alot when creating straight pathways. Also the game pretty much crashed a lot in the loading screens, framerate was all over the place, and there was no options to customize your game. Hopefully this will get added soon for the second beta!
But yeah, to conclude this review, I do not reccomend this game yet because it can go either way. It could go terrific or can go bad. If you are really considering, I reccomend it if you are a fan of the RCT series like me, and support the developers of the game and provide tons of feedback for them to read!

(Written during Beta Weekend 1)
I can understand where people are coming from with the new coaster builder. It does take some time to adjust if you're used to the older games' way of building. From what I've experienced so far it's been great, but that's not to say there aren't any problems with it.
The biggest problem I've encountered so far are the restraints. For example, wooden coasters can barely be tilted whereas in real life there are some that do corkscrews just fine. Similar constraints apply to the paths placement as well; I couldn't make a path up to my ride because the game (as it stands during Beta Weekend 1) doesn't have stairs and as a result, you have to elevate your paths over a long distance. Even then I could only build a queue to the ride entrance and not the exit, for what reason I have no idea.
The physics seems to be a bit iffy as well. I made a drop coaster that curved upwards into a loop, but as soon as the coaster hit around 60mph it just fell off the track, regardless of how insignificant the curve was.
The decorations are good, although it would be nice to have local build limitations (such as hitboxes on other objects) displayed. I tried to wall off one of the gold statues but I had a pretty difficult time with it because of the hitbox being larger than what the model actually shows when you hold it.
The game itself was also having a few issues. When I tabbed out and back in sometimes my camera would be locked and the UI buttons wouldn't do anything forcing me to restart from my last save point. The ability to view your coasters in first person is also seemingly random; you have to test it and hope the coaster editor bar doesn't show up at the bottom so you can click the coaster again to get to the camera button.
Overall, it's a relatively enjoyable experience. If you do encounter any issues I would highly recommend providing feedback on the RollerCoaster Tycoon World forums. It's important to bear in mind that this is a limited development build and some of the issues we're having may already be addressed. Is it worth £29.99? As of beta weekend 1, no. I'd wait for release reviews if you're not interested in bugs.
Any further review past Beta Weekend 1 will be added below this. I'll keep editing the original during the weekend the more I play.

NOTICE: this review is lengthy, if tldr, check pros/cons
In short, there seems to be a lot to look forward too for RCTW, however there are many tweaks that need to be made. That said, from what I see from forums, this game will not be as popular as the original trilogy because the coaster designer is much more complex to use than in previous itterations.
There are only 7 or 8 different coaster types currently present in RCTW and many classics from the second and even first games are missing. My guess is that additional coaster types will be offered via paid DLC, the thought leaves a bad taste in my mouth, but I can't think of another reason why certain 'cornerstone' rollercoasters such as corkscrew coasters aren't available already.
The 'innovative' Spline based coaster designer is an interesting take on coaster design, it works well if you plan on building a coaster without any inversions. However, as soon as you plan on including corkscrews, loops or any other inversion. You will almost instantly get frustrated. I found it extremely difficult to create straight lines of coaster track, perhaps because the track is always attached to your cursor before you place it, and while trying to move around simultaneously, the track quickly becomes twisted and messed up. There is a premade loop that can be used, however it does not look realistic and is way too steep. The other premade track piece is a 'vertical corkscrew'. Were the developers smoking crack when they came up with that one?
One of the only things that made me actually feel like I was playing a RollerCoaster Tycoon series game was when it came to choosing the colour design of the coaster. Perhaps this is because they did little to no innovation in this area, as none was needed.
I designed a hypercoaster in RCTW that seemed fairly successful in design, but the test statistics showed that the ride was hardly 'fun' at all. I know for certain that this coaster would've had atleast 5 excitement if I had made it with any of the original games.
It was impossible for me to judge the physics engine this game has because it was impossible to have the coaster running while maintaining a decent framerate. This, despite my computer exceeding the system requirements of the game.
There is no Options menu and there is no way to change the resolution, change graphics settings or even any audio settings. I yearn for the ability to mute the annoying music that comes on if you scroll out far enough. As well, the sounds that I am assuming come from the rollercoaster stations are really obnoxious and need to be changed. However this may work itself out as more features and other sounds are added.
Controlling the game is a bit of hit and miss, You move around the map with the arrow keys or WASD, I was unable to move around by dragging my cursor to the edge of the screen, something I think is critical for this kind of game.
There are a large variety of paths in the game and the system seems to be fairly fleshed out and competent.
All in all, if the developers manage a way to include a simplified coaster designer, in the vein of the coaster designer from the original games, I feel this game will see massive success. Aesthetically pleasing and once fully optimized, I will give this game another shot.

This game has enough reviews already taken its age. So I'll just say this: it's a hell of a game! ... most of the time.
I really enjoyed the first 3/4 of it. It had a nice pacing, alternating between an hostile and creepy atmosphere and a normal fps.
That last 1/4 of it was... more of an on-rails fps, unfortunately. Very few "horror-ish" scenes, which made for a more generic experience. Also, the difficulty spiked, becoming far harder out of nowhere.
But, it was definitely worth it for the rest of the game. The designers knew how to get the player uncomfortable, in a very good way. There were memorable situations. There were a few jumpscares, but they were well placed, so that's not an issue.
It's not a very scary game, but it had its moments. Quality over quantity. I'd recommend it to anyone looking for a creepier fps. But, it falls for some of the modern shooter trappings closer to the ending, unfortunately.
Also, sound and visual design was great! This game still looks good, and sounds even better, even after 5 years.

As a fan of strategy games, I thought I would give this game a try. Not all strategy games play alike and that is not a bad thing. In fact, its a distinguishing feature of the genre. For no other purpose but to create a catchy hook to this review, I want to compare strategy games to cakes. Yes, delicious, sugary, scrumptious cakes. Cakes, just like strategy games, are made up of some core ingredients. The basic ingredients of cake are flour, eggs, and sugar.  That's all you need to make cake. Strategy games also have core ingredients such as offering the player the ability to respond and adapt to situations while balancing certain requirements. No two cakes are alike in the same way that no two strategy games are alike. The whistles and the thrills we attach to our favorite cake are different just like the components a game developer can utilize to create a good strategy game are different. All this to say, Project Tarvotan is a game that succeeds on some ingredients whereas other ingredients could have used a bit more time cooking in the oven.
For those who just want the short and sweet of it, this game exceeds at visually creating a unique image for itself. No computer is going to have a hard time visually displaying this game at its highest setting, but the visuals create a unique atmosphere that gives the game identity. I would go as far as saying that Project Tarvotan has the most beautiful game over screen I have ever seen in any video game. The gameplay music compliments the visuals and helps immerse the player into the environment of space. The User Interface is rather simple which I think is a bit of detractor. It also might take the user a bit of time to figure out what exacty is what on the screen. The developers have added the option to play the tutorial which helps a bit.
This is a turn-based strategy game through and through. I found myself having a lot of freedom to pick and choose a play-through style. I think that is one of the better things Project Tarvotan is good at. Most of the gameplay involves choosing where to navigate and what to do once you get there to best help you balance your science, fuel, materials, and such. Beyond the Milky Way, I think most of the solar systems are fictitious, but the maps are interactive. In the Milky Way, the sun expands swallowing up planets forcing you to navigate only outward. Other planets have different environmental elements that force the user to adapt their strategy to fit the solar system.  As I mentioned before, there are a few things that I think could have been given a little more polishing up. For example, we are asked if we want to accept a quest but there is really no reason why we would ever not want to accept a quest. This is especially odd since we are never told what the quest is before we are given the option to accept it. Another complaint I have is that the combat system is relatively simple and not very engaging. However it is a game that deals more in strategy than it does in action, so that is where the true fun of this game lies. The technologies you unlock are a bit lackluster in character and diversity. None the less, this game is worth a try in spite of these flaws. Its a good game to go back to because you know that no one play-through is going to be the same. To me, its not a game that I am going to spend hours and hours playing in a row, but it is one that I can see myself coming back to time and time again just to see what new challenges I will have to face and adapt to.
Buy this now.

As a big fan of the cold war era and political-related games (and on a budget), I thought I'd give this game a try. After quite a bit of gameplay, I thought I'd go ahead and give this game a review, because like many others I've seen a mix of reviews on steam and I was reconsidering buying it. So I'll give an honest review.
I empathize with many others complaining about the lack of tutorials offered for this game. There is quite a bit of a learning curve, as with any other grand strategy game. But to be fair this is an old game and Battlegoat has released a better version of supreme ruler cold war in supreme ruler ultimate. This version would be wise to get if your are on a budget, and there is info on
as well as a manual that comes with the steam version. There are also video tutorials on youtube so if you have internet access, better check those out. As long as you use your resources and practice, you'll find this game actually quite enjoyable.
The gameplay interface is similar to that of any other geopolitical strategy concept i.e superpower 2, hoi, etc. Although its not as complex as hoi, its more in-depth than superpower 2. The AI in this game isn't as impressive, but it still does the job and provides some interesting outcomes. But still i'm not as pleased with the predicbility of the AI, but keep in mind this issue is updated in supreme ruler ultimate.
In this version, I feel like alot of improvements could be made with the AI and user interface (i.e lack of military organization, cabinet confusion), and tutorials. Other than that, everything else is fine IMO i.e diplomacy, economics, research, etc. the only complaint is the lack of proper AI compared to today's games.
I recommend this game to junkies who are big fans of the cold war era or who downright enjoy geopolitcal or grand strategy games in general. If you are on a budget, buy this game. But if you can, I'd say your better off buying supreme ruler ultimate because they have a better version of the cold war era.

Talking about old, MGS series certainly is. The last major canon was literally about getting old. And it sucked! so hard.

p.p.s. I don't know why the game keeps titling 'solid' even though we all know the most interesting character in the genre is Big Boss (and maybe Ocelot too).
This review is a comparative opinion on the series, with highlight of this game.
The series spans decades and multiple shifts in style, both in gameplay and story-telling. There are ups and downs. This game, MGS5, is definitely an Up.
The Up is firstly the gameplay, this game plays like a modern action game: with enough degrees of freedom, a sense of streamlined action to consequence feedback loop and impactful tactical elements. Previously in gameplay, either it was too tactical or non-actionable.
Next Up, is story, the essence of MGS. Story is a sum of plots and character. We have plots deepening since the MGS1 but the characters start to shine when the serie take a look at Big Boss in Snake Eater. In TPP we get to witness a few fantasitic, lively characters that previous MGS games don't even have the materials for. In my opinion, the MGS series ended with Sons of Liberty in New York Manhatton. That game was more about philosophy than story, and was certainly entirely about post-modernism. The lack of character was on purpose. However Konami drags on to Guns of the patriots, so Kojima fill up all the plot holes to justify the drag. The TPP, however, has all the freedom it needs because it's not about Solid Snake the uninteresting, but the confounded yet determined 'freedom' warrior Big Boss (alert, there is a catch). So the character is a real person, flesh and blood real: we get to experience the bloody path he walks, understand his mission and give out sympathy as a human being. Drama, is an upgrade to this genre.
Finally, style. The setting sets the style. Blizzard (not the company) sets the tone for MGS1,  Ocean and sense of Isolation sets for MGS2, Jungle for 3 and Sand and Savanna for 5. There are limited factors in previous works that those settings are not well presented and resonated in the game but for TPP, with open world (somewhat) mechanism, they form a good synergy and it plays great.
At the end, MGS5 TPP is a fun game to play and thus time flies.
p.p.p.s. I need to bash MGS4 before I hit the submit button. That game tarnished the MGS legacy, although I enjoyed the clichés and the plugged plot holes... But come on, MGS2 was an art. MGS4 was a forced interpretation of the said art.
