For people looking forf Supreme Commander FA 2, you will not find it here. SC 2 Sacrifices a lot of fidelity found in the first game- normal units can no longer miss, there are no tech tiers, economy is changed into old-school standard and the selection of units is cut. But it doesn't mean Supreme Commander 2 doesn't bring anything new to the table.
The biggest one, research trees, bring the whole new level to the game, basically allowing players to specialize and chose whatever technologies they want. This allows everybody to improve their units in varriety of ways (for example, adding personal shields, range, anti air cannons or improving health of existing units). Every unit is viable in the result and will scale well into the lategame, unlike the previous game where there was no point building weaker units.
The factions also differ a lot more in the sequel. They all still have access to simmilar types of units (each faction has access to some different permutations though) but the technologies you can get for them make them differ a lot in a long run. For example, playing as cybran you start of a little weaker due to not having tanks, but you can upgrade your bots to have "mega armor" ability, making them really tough and equip them with jetpacks that allow them to fly across water and cover long distance quickly which can be used to bypass enemy defences. On the other hand, when you play Aeon, you don't have any navy, but your units are nearly all amphibian (forgot to mention, all cybran water units can walk on the land now, which is completly crazy!) and you can upgrade each of them to have a teleporter, wchih works simmilarly to jetpacks- smaller distance but instant effect. UEF is probably the most boring, solid on all fronts without any special gimmicks.
The last thing that we all love the most are experimental units. In SC 2, you can get them faster and also have more options, since every faction has about 7 of them! Also, they are all very creative and every one of them adds something new to the table. Playing UEF and want more units? Why don't you construck an Experimental Unit cannon that produces units at 10x rate and can launch them across the map? If you are playing Aeon and having difficulty with air, you can get an experimental Airt Defence unit or fortify your defences with Loyality gun, that captures enemy units at a very fast rate! Also, why don't you build a GIANT FLAME-BREATHING LIZZARD as a cybran?! With the help of research system, you can get access to lesser experimental very fast (even 15minutes in the game!) and get to the big beasts not that much slower.
All of this, makes SC 2 a very enjoyable srategy game. Just treat it as a stand-alone game, not as a sequel to one of the most advanced and difficult RTS games of all time. The campaign is really cool and enjoyable, and the skirmishes against bots are also very satisfying (you can customize every bot to change it's playstyle and give him bonuses). The only problem is the multiplayer. It works fine, but finding a ranked game after getting a few wins is next to impossible, leaving you with custom games that are occupied by veteran players. So, unless you play with a friend, forget about multiplayer.

Her story starts you off in an old looking computer with what looks like Windows 95, or perhaps a previous version. Once there you are presented with a database of footage from a 1990s, where you must piece together what happened.
Without spoiling anything, since this game is all story based, you are revisiting video clips of seven separate interviews trying to piece together what exactly happened. When you start off, you are placed in front the pc with the word “murder” already typed in. With this simple word, you are given, you must, delve deeper into the story, and form your own conclusion as to what happened, but the more you go deeper into the mystery, the more confused you may become; perhaps even discarding your previous assumption many times before coming to a conclusion that does not go against her story.
This game is not a conventional game in terms of gameplay. Instead, you are watching videos and finding potential terms that could lead you to more videos which will reveal more as to her past and what, and who was involved in this incident. Some might not like this, so if the idea of an exclusively story based game does not appeal, do not bother. It is an interesting concept, and very captivating if you play it without any distractions, perhaps more interesting if you play it with a friend and try to piece the mystery together (much like I did).

I loved this... game? I want to recommend it so much, but I worry the average gamer would be turned off by the mechanics. The object of the game is trying to uncover the story by going over a database of over 200 clips ranging anywhere from a second to a few minutes in length, taken from seven different police interrogations. Each clip is found by entering a keyword, which brings up each clip the word was used in. If you’re into story and puzzle based games, this is an original game that just might be for you.
On a different note, I would recommend creating an organization system to keep track of the clips you found if you need to go back and rewatch them in context. There is a space for each clip that allows you to add your own keywords, so what I did was type the date and time of the clip, which is shown in the right hand corner of the screen in each clip.

An average story with a unique delivery.
I'm a sucker for a "FMV" game so Her Story already had an edge with me to begin with. But I considered giving this a thumbs down as it was a bit short, the story is very quickly predictable (which shortens the experience further), and it fits a niche not the masses. Also, for me, the final player's character twist fell flat. The game's delivery of this so-so story saves it though. It isn't revolutionary or anything in my eyes. It's just simple, but done right. It works. Your character you play is interfacing with an old computer system searching through snippets of police interviews about a disappearance/murder. You type in a word, results pop up. Through theses short video snippets (4sec ~ 2mins a piece) a story is divulged and you deduce or note more words to search to yield more results until the end. Unfortunately the end is obvious for a large amount of time before you get to activate the end but its still interesting enough.
I originally played this on GOG closer to release and put in about an hour of searching words. I more or less figured I figured it out. I took a break but never returned to the game to confirm my suspicions. That first play experience I had busted out a pencil and paper and methodically listed each and every word I wanted to search next and I was very into the experience. Yet it somehow still never called back out to me. It just doesn't have that "it" factor to it. When I got it on Steam a year later and went for round 2 I took another approach. I just went off the top of my head prioritizing what I felt was thee most important term to search for next. This very much expedited the process and I was done before I knew it. And yes, the story was as I had figured a year earlier. I will applaud the game's database though, as I feel like both my experiences were unique paths to the same stuff. Then after having been done, out of curiosity, I used a guide to get every video and achievement. Not usually my style to achievement hunt or use a guide but my "FMV" weakness was the reason I played the game. And I wanted to see them all! This still hardly had me reach 3hrs of playtime.
My rambling story aside, simply put; The FMV quirk works if you like that sort of thing. That's why you would buy this game. The interface and delivery works for enjoying a tale in a new way. And despite being predictable the story is indeed actually interesting. It could've used a lot more nuance and mystery. A lot. I almost feel like you miss out on truly figuring out or discovering anything for yourself within the game universe and it all comes outside of game. There's no detective work to be applied save for two visual cues that made for satisfying search results. For the most part the story just kind of unravels itself when you search for every dumb word spoken. You're pretty much along for the ride more than getting as sense of discovery or satisfaction from detective work. An opportunity or two was definitely missed somewhere in there. And part of me thinks that the game originally had different intentions when it was conceived. That the reason there's only one sided answers in the videos is because it was originally going to be some sort of multiple choice question asking detective, interrogation type, game. Not some run down database search. But who knows...
It also most definitely came out at a time that earned it much undeserved criticism AND praise. Both paint an unrealistic picture of the product. This isn't a super innovative, artistic, something, something. And likewise it isn't some weird assault on gaming as we know it. It is most definitely NOT a top 100 game. It is most definitely NOT a bottom 100 game. Pretty much the only list it belongs on is one of FMV games and it falls somewhere in the middle on that. Its a one sitting experience that is by all means worth some loose change on sale if FMV and interactive stories is your thing. Or a thing you can enjoy as a sensible person. Otherwise, it would be common sense and wise to move along to the next thing.

Hey, hombre, you're probably looking at this game wondering if it's worth your hard-earned pesos.  Why else would you be reading a review from a perfect stranger?  'Cause if I know you, I've probably already told you to pick this game up.  And if you haven't already done so, why not, Ryan??
However, for a short time (as this is being written), the game is just under $4.  There is absolutely NO reason to pass up this game at that price.  Hell, even at the full $15 it's worth the ride.
What you get is a beautifully-animated luchador-flavored Metroid romp in a massively sprawling world that was so good, they made it TWICE!  That's right.  Twice.  That means two times, you idiot.  You know how like in Symphony of the Night they flipped the castle upside down and you went through it all over again?  Well, it's kind of like that except the other version of the map is the DEATH MIRROR world that you can flip between in REAL TIME... after you unlock the ability, of course.  You are, after all, only a lowly masked luchador brawler to begin with, but as with all Metroid-style games, the more you play, the more powerful you become.
Not convinced?  How about you can play this game co-op with a friend?  No?  How about you can buy costumes for both characters that change the way you play the game?  Still no?  How about the game has amazingly realized mariachi-style music throughout the entire journey?  Not yet?  How about there is a MASSIVE screen-filling boss in the first third of the game that will scare the bejeezus out of you??  How about brain-teasing platform puzzles coupled with an insanely deep, yet simple-to-execute combo system???!  IS THERE ANY WAY TO PLEASE YOU?!?!  MUST THE GAME BE MADE IN UNREAL ENGINE FOR YOU TO BE SATISFIED?!?!
Listen, let's talk writing, then.  Are we going to talk writing or are you going to break my balls?  Good.  The writing is fantastically whimsical and funny.  Some of it is very cheesy, but it's always intentionally so.  The story is all about standard heroics - your lady friend has been kidnapped and you're out to save her.  But there's other things going on as well, in the background.  You'll meet the bosses long before you have to fight them and learn about them.  You'll find out that the main baddy, who is like Manny Calavera dressed as one of the Three Amigos, is only the main baddy because [MINOR SPOILER] he told the devil that he didn't have a job anymore.  What are you going to do about it, hombre?  Nothing?  Nothing?!?!  Aw, man, you're breakin' my balls here, you're breakin' my balls.
Look, do yourself a favor and get this game.  If the obvious references to Metroid aren't enough to convince you, maybe the endless meme-posters and indie-game tributes, hidden easter eggs, and odd obsession with chickens might be able to convince you.  And if you're still not convinced, then I suppose you can go back to your cookie-cutter AAA games that you've played a million times over.  Try something new, muchacho.

I have never been one for Metroidvania games. That genre has always been too punishing and bland for me. I see the appeal, but for me, it never lasts.
Guacamelee is firmly in that genre, and somehow I love it. Maybe it's the prevalence of save points. Maybe it's the fighting system that rewards variety and reflexes instead of perfect aim and conservation of ammo. Maybe it's just the amazing luchadores. I have never played a game in a world of luchadores, and I'm not sure one has ever been made before this.
There's a well-told story in a unique setting, an engaging combat system, a high level of difficulty, and a couple hundred in-jokes. There are also tons of secrets to find, dozens of challenges to beat, and a bevy of achievements with varying levels of impossibility. All told, this is a great game for fighter/platformers with a good deal of reward for those who like exploring.

Update: 600 hours in, I stand by this review. There's been quite a few improvements to RE:IS since I wrote this, I really recommend both this game and its DLC.
-------------------
When I first heard of Renowned Explorers : International Society (henceforce known as RE:IS) my initial reaction was along the lines of "what on earth is this?". I purchased it on a whim, and having now played it for nearly 100 hours and all treasures collected, it has definitely turned out to be one of my wisest purchases (and heck, i'm actually writing a proper review for once, my first one on steam.)
RE:IS is a roguelike in an Indiana Jones style - you and your crew will be having adventures all around the globe, from searching castles in the Scottish highlands to the tombs of  ancient pharoahs in Egypt in the hopes of finding treasures (and with over 100 treasures to find, there is plenty to see.) You'll run into a variety of characters such as bagpipe playing clansmen,  pirates suffering under a voodoo curse and a group of monkeys worshipping a giant fruit.
The game keeps a fairly lighthearted and humourous theme throughout, which is aided by its bright and colourful art style. Don't let this fool you however - there is a surprising amount of depth to be found in the games combat and exploration systems. Battles have three different approaches: you can befriend your enemy, offering them things such as compliments and peace treatires. Or you can take a straight up physical approach - hacking and slashing your way through hordes of your opponents. If you prefer a more devious approach, you can play mind games with your opponents, hurling insults towards them in such number that they run away from the battlefield sobbing.
Overall, RE:IS takes a refreshing approach to the turn-based rogue-like genre. The developers are very active within the community and listen to feedback and suggestions from players. The game is frequently updated with new content, and more has been promised down the line. I highly recommend purchasing this game.

So in this game you establish a team of 3 explorers, then go off on a series of adventures in order to defeat that dastardly Frenchman Rivaleux and his team of equally dastardly explorers. You have 3 options as to how you handle encounters: You can be Agressive, Friendly or Devious. These work in a rock paper scissors style system. As you complete these expeditions you find different types of currency, which can be spent on upgrading your crew in various ways. The in-game tutorials do an excellent job of explaining this to you, and prevent any confusion you may have at first.
The encounters themselves are fun and unique, even if you play through the same encounters again and again they always go a little differently, though they can be a a little cheap (and borderline unfair) at times (I'm looking at you, Vladimir). Unfortunately there are very little encounters currently in the game, so you WILL be playing the same ones again and again.
Overall I'd say it's an excellent game and well worth the price, with frequent updates adding more content. If you're at all interested in strategy or turn based combat I'd say this game is a must-have, as it's a nice blend of combat and RNG (generally to determine how many resources you manage to gather) with a lot of replayability and quirky, interesting and  generally adorable characters.
I highly reccomend it and would give it a 9/10.

Giant scorpions!  Pirates!  Sheep?  Welcome to the world of Renowned Explorers!  I'll start by saying I bought this game on a whim.  I was looking for something fun and challenging, but that wouldn't take a vast amount of time to complete. I would have settled for a "Meh" time killer, but I bought this and now I'm hopelessly addicted.  I can honestly say my first thought after an hour of playing was that I'd gladly pay for any future DLC to expand the game.  And that was after I'd lost five times.  It's a unique game that can be a bit difficult to describe, but rather than just shouting, "I love it!", I'll give it a try.   Basically you start by selecting a team of 3 characters from pools of 4 different types of explorers.  Each explorer is unique (some attacks abilities are repeated but the characters all have their own animations and it goes a long way to giving them the feeling of individual personalities) and has Skills, that effect how they play and their success rate on events that can occur while on an adventure.  After selecting your team, you start working your way through Adventures you want to undertake.  While on Adventures,  you explore locations on the Adventure Map searching for resources (used to upgrade your team) and events.  Events fall into three basic categories:  Adventure Wheel challenges (think The Price is Right), combat instances and story challenges (like choose your own adventure books). Lots of  events contain elements of all three.  Combat is tactical and features a unique system in which attacks are divided into Friendly (charm), Devious (psychological) and Aggressive (physical violence).  This ties into the flavor of your team.  Now at this point, we need to jump back to character selection.  Certain characters complement each other better when teamed together.  I've read some comments criticising the combat system as confusing and certain adventures as too hard.  The truth is, what team you put together determines which expeditions you're best suited to undertake and what tactics are best to use in combat.  *The game gives you all this information, you just need to read it.* When you select your crew, it tells you what types of team (Friendly, Devious or Aggressive) the character works best with.  It even gives examples in the character discription of the types of charcters they'd work well with.  It will even show you the type of team (Friendly, Devious, Aggressive) you're putting together at the top of the team selection screen.  The descriptions of Adventures tell you what type of team or what character skills are best suited for those adventures.  I imagine a lot of those people complaining did what I did at first, which is skim this information and go, "These three look cool together, I'll use them!"  Team Super Awesome may be the coolest looking group of explorers around, but it doesn't mean they'll work that well  together or that they have any hope of  making it out of Transylvannia alive.   This is a roguelike.  I recommend sticking fairly close to the recommended teams until you have the chance to get a feel for the Adventures and different characters.  For the combat system, it's one of my personal favorite things about the game.  You can overwhelm pirates with charm, beat the living daylights out of evil cultists, or even make an ancient goddess cry and run away.  The types of attacks you use (your Atttitude) versus the type of attacks your opponent is using (their Attitude) create a Mood (displayed in the top center of the tactical map) that grants various buffs/debuffs.  As a tip, next to the Mood display are little indicators showing how many of the other types of attacks you can use before your Attitude changes, which changes the Mood.  You can mix and match attacks, managing and manipulating the Mood to your advantage is part of the challenge.  Be aware, the AI can do the same.  Pros:  A wide cast of playable characters that feel like individuals (not just reskinned clones).  A fun art style that goes very well with the game's sense of humour.  The combat system is unique and challenging.  Tons of content and an enormous amount of replayability.  While there is some violence, most of it is slapstick or cartoonish, and  I'd say it's one of the safer games out here for younger players.  It's fun, which I know sounds rather simple, but I can honestly say at no point have I been bored or felt gameplay was tedious.  Stability (I haven't had a single bug or crash).  Cons:  A playthrough only consists of 5 Adventures.  You won't understand why that would qualify as a con until you play it and realize how much you wish you could squeeze in just one more  :)

I picked this up on a Humble Bundle for $1.01 because I absolutely love the first game. I love Real Time Strategy games, especially ones that focus on strategy of "muscle memory rush" tactics. Supreme Commander 1 broke away from many of the standard mechanics that have always broken the "realism" for me in my other RTS games, and in a wonderful way. I was always put off in other games that you were required to do research on the battlefield. I was often put off by winged aircraft that would simply float in place (not like a VTOL but like a blimp). I disliked how, in most RTSs, any non-land units (that would be sea and air) almost always seemed like an afterthought, being unwieldy, game ending, or extremely limited in options.
Supreme Commander 1 broke all these forms. Progression in SC1 is not determined by researching or by constructing buildings needed to construct other buildings. It was completely based on having engineers of the required tech tier. Your engineer drones needed to be more sophisticated to construct better buildings, but in no way was this ever researched. You were sent into battle feeling like you were in command of a front line, rather than feeling like your little outpost was the front-line, R&D, and everything else.
SC1 had a fully fleshed out air and naval structure with as much detail as the ground units, and as much fun to use as the ground. There was a strategic reason to pick naval, air, or ground power over another in specific settings. All aircraft would land when not in use to preserve fuel and, if they spent too much time flying, would need to refuel.
The immersion of SC1 was beautiful.
I even liked the resource system that is often complained about. In SC1 your units wouldn't wait until you had all the resources necessary to start a build project (and then somehow take all the resources at once away from the pool). You were required to manage resources by paying attention to your current stock and your input amount. This allowed you to either dominate in construction if you were able to plan constructions to begin BEFORE you had all the resources, but not use them all up before completion. It also allowed you to screw yourself by running your resources into the ground and having 15 projects all needing resources at once. This was an interesting mechanic to get used to, and provided me with a new challenge in economic management, as well as a new level of immersion.
Fast forward to SC2. Everything I've marked about SC1 as being unique was scrapped. Though the Supreme Commander "feel" is there at first, any fan of SC1 will quickly feel like this is a game of starcraft or age of empires with a Supreme Commander skin on it.
First lets talk about the good from SC2. It really did hold the graphical feel of SC1. It seems they were able to up the polygon count on their models for SC2 but this seems to come at the cost of a slight decrease in texture resolution, so you mostly don't notice it as everything kind of blurs when not zoomed in all the way. The game will be very easy for RTS fans not familiar with SC1 to jump into as it isn't as "different" as SC1 was to the standard mechanics of the genre. They've cleaned up the GUI and even added in a mini-map (in the first one it was dynamic zoom so in order to see the full map you zoomed out, you can still do this, but you also have a drop down mini map). With the "revamped" resource system you don't have need of the messy "resource production/consumption" icons that I frequently used in SC1 to see what was going on, so I guess that's a bonus too. They also added a nice feature that your buildings can have "add-ons" much like the main robot-suit in the first one could. These add-ons include things like shields, point defense tools, etc.
Next lets talk about the bad. I suppose if you haven't tried SC1 none of this will really matter to you. The game is a decent RTS as itself. But for fans of SC1 and the innovation they brought to the genre, be wary that SC2 may be a bit of a letdown. The advancement in the game is completely based on tech points that you generate over time and then open a tab to apply. These tech points do provide some interesting customization as they increase things like unit sight and health, but the small tech trees (where you unlock your units) decrease the amount of diversity of units you get. It also removes the immersion for me. That I was sent hundreds of lightyears to fight for terrain on a planet, and they couldn't send me with the schematics to perform my task feels like a game and not like a war.
They changed the resource system to be almost the same as in any other RTS. No you don't have units collecting resources, but you can't spend resources until you have enough to complete the build, and then they all deplete. While I originally thought this would be an interesting twist to SC, I found that it caused the game to feel like every other RTS. Though easier to manage, it felt like an artificial "dumming down" of a beautiful system.
Although there seem to be as many sea and air units as there are land, there are so few of any of them the entire system feels like its been simplified at the cost of strategic options. In the end almost all the units felt like an afterthought to me.
Lastly, though I guess I may be the only one with a complaint about this, but they made the air units permanently fly. To me there was some fun strategy in using faster aircraft to get past grounded enemy fighters before they could take off. I liked the realism of having to do forward notification to get my airships ready. I also liked the realism of all my VTOL aircraft having to land when not in use (yes, all the aircraft were, to some extent, VTOL, but none were blimps). In SC2 however, your ships just float there. There's always been something about an airplane floating in the sky that just broke immersion for me.
I would say that to anyone who enjoys RTSs, SC2 is a decent game. But if you really want an immersive RTS experience, I highly suggest you purchase Supreme Commander 1. SC1 will feel like a fresh take on an old gaming genre, with new ideas and mechanics. SC2 will feel like another good RTS just like every other you've played.

The sequel to one of my favorite FPS games. This game feels like it was made to make the series more accessible for people. The grenade particle effects are also gone from the first game :(
It's not all bad though! The long cooridor filled levels from the first game are gone. This game is changing it up every level. You even get to control an awesome mech to go down streets blowing up everything. This game is more difficult than the first one, mainly due to not being able to quicksave anymore. It has a checkpoint system this time around, which balances the game a lot better. The scares in this game feel even more terrifying this time around. The school easily has some of the scariest moments I have ever seen in a game. The new enemy types love to pop out constantly when you are least expecting it. The graphics have also got a nice upgrade. The deployable turrets were a fun new weapon, but I wish I got to use them more. The game is about 8 hours long, depending on how much you explore.

A shooter that simply ticks all generic shooter boxes.  Dimly lit corridors? check.  Warehouse/crates? check.  BOO! check,  bullet-time? check, Explodey tanks lying around waiting for you to make them go boom, crawlspaces? check! and let's not forget the bit where you're on a train and baddies keep coming at you from another track... etc
Environments: Corridors, do you like dimly lit corridors?  I hope you do.  You might be lucky and get some warehouse/crate action!!!  You get released from the tiny outdoor areas a few, all to brief times, then it's back to corridors and subway tunnels (yes, we're back to subway tunnels etc).  There are some better zones later on, big factory settings that at least have some sense of scale, but you wait a long time for them.
Shooty Bang Bang: The guns work, not much interest, the assault rifle is pretty much the entire game.  The hammerhead is nice, but no other weapon than assault rifle is necessary for 99% of the game.  Shotguns are cool for the things that charge you like abominations and assassins, but assault rifle is fine for them too.  Weapons that might provide some variety are castrated by lack of ammo.
Tank bits are fun, of course, tank bits are always fun.
The Story: Spooky bits are pretty much eye candy, there's no serious effect on the game, it's a straightforward shooty game with gratuituous spooky effects seemingly tagged on at the last minute to remind you that this is a FEAR game. Yes it does make you jump from time to time, effective in the same way as a screamer video on YouTube.   The levels are strewed with pointless info drops, saves having to script an interesting game I guess, having your plot all scrawled down on little data pads.  Ignore them.
Enemy AI: basic stuff.   You walk along, the game will auto-save to let you know there's a firefight coming, creep, crouch, bullet-time headshot them till they're all dead. rinse-repeat... in corridors.
The Ending:  Was that an ending? Ummm. ok...  I guess this was an Episode of something...
Overall: Meh, dull, unimaginative, fails to make any use of the IP.

The positive points of the game include smooth and beautiful object animations and well implemented physics. Due to the problems listed above, I couldn't progress much into the game to properly appreciate it. It was THAT annoying.
All in all, the game can be enjoyable if the user interface and responsiveness are improved. In its current state, the game quickly becomes irritating.

is a fairly short game that I think people might catergorize more as an interactive story than a game. However, the story itself unfolds in an interesting and compelling way and held me captivated all the way through.
is told through interviews of the wife of a murder victim, Simon Smith. Through these interviews, the player uncovers what really happened to Simon and why.
Even though the big reveal happened for me around the middle of my playthrough, there were still pieces to what happened left missing that made me want to explore more. Although I think a lot of people might be put off by the mechanics of the game as they can get a bit tedious (trying to come up with new things to search after a while was a struggle for me), I think it still did its job well enough for the length of the game.
If you're not a big reader and aren't the kind of person who feels compelled to find out every little thing in a mystery, I wouldn't get this game, but if you're looking for a simple mystery story to get immersed in for a few hours, maybe try this out.
I'm not 100% sure I would've gotten it at full price as it doesn't really have much replay value (I got it in a bundle) - so if you're on the fence, wait until it's on sale. The game looks great though, so I understand why the price is what it is. I thoroughly enjoyed the game, however, and would recommend to people who I know like getting lost in a mystery.

Difficult to review.  Certainly innovative. Also I'm trying to limit spoilers.
The game has strong resemblences to those wax paintings where you trace over them using a pencil or a jigsaw puzzle.  However the strongest resemblance is to the game "Hangman" played with words instead of letters.  If the word is in the video clip it gets added to your database.
The game plays through in only a few hours and even then is more interesting at the beginning.  At the beginning you pick up new clues easily and are soon busy assembling video evidence and getting to grips with the story of what occurred.  However once a key video clip is revealed you pretty much know what happened.  A lot depends on ambiguity over the question is one two or are two one.
Thereafter it was dredging to try to get 100% which I narrowly failed evem with cheat guides.  Some of the video clips are very short which makes getting the right word very difficult.  One tip - "Yes" and "No" bring up different and more useful results than Yes and No - which is bloody unfair.
The pay-off is a bit "Meh" and it would have helped to be told what had been the result at the end.
In the sale this will be coming in at a low price and at that it's worth getting for what is an innovative and clever idea.  I'd play until you've fully "cracked" ther case - or cracked it as much as the available evidence lets you know, get the ending, and get on with your life since beyond that point you`re chasing irrelevant fragments.
There's exceptionally low replay value.
It's innovative and clever but perhaps too clever for its own good.  A Dragnet style summing up of the participants' fates would have been more dramatic and satisfying.
A sequel would have to have multiple parts and multiple characters to sustain interest.  And despite the comments in the Wiki L.A. Noire is a far better detective game.
I'm damning here with faint praise.  It's very innovative for the few hours it will take you to break the case.  But its very high critical praise seems to value appearance over substance.

Highly recommended for fans of British or Scandinavian crime series, adventure games or narriative games. You (identity revealed later) is looking through an old corrupted database with short video clips of several police interviews with a woman about the disappearence of her husband. Type in keywords to search the database and find new clips, and slowly unravel the story of what happened and why.

HIGHLY RECOMMENDED...if caught on sale or in a Humble Bundle.
RECOMMENDED...at its current price-point on Steam ($6).
Her Story is both a full-blown story & narrative experience that gamers into those kind of games should most definitely experience for themselves. This is an excellent narrative experience that should not be missed, which is especially even more so true if the player catches this game on sale or in a bundle.
The question for most gamers is probably going to be this: is this game going to actually be worth the money? While the game is only currently $6 on Steam for its regular price - for gamers, that mileage may very likely vary. If there's anything that is a big question mark for this game, the length and replayability might be the biggest factors for many with this title.
Gamers might want to replay the game and see how quickly they can reach the important clips to get the player to hopefully be able to reach the conclusion of the game. Some gamers might get very quickly to the end of the experience, maybe not even realize an option they hit brings them to the end, might not have much of the database found, and might actually want to come back to continue where they left off or just flat-out even replay the story from scratch. Some players might find everything and be done with it for good. Again, the player's mileage may vary.
Without giving away too much, here's the story and set-up of this game. A woman is being interviewed a few different times - seven, to be exact - for the murder of her husband. Viva Seifert, as the woman being interviewed, completely steals the show here. The entire game is focused around videos of her from different interviews that are all chopped-up into separate files, which is surrounded by a completely immersive 1990's setting & aestetic.
The way Viva dresses, talks, acts; the writing and dialogue; and especially the computer the player uses to do the searches evokes a completey 90's setting + aestetic. Without the immersion factor; superbly written dialogue; and also the excellent acting from Viva Seifert - well, this game would most definitely fall apart.
Depending on how the player searches the huge database like one would use Google to search the Internet, throwing out keywords to get hits on the database to find clips to hopefully understand the narrative. Depending on how much the player digs into the database and how well, the player might experience and unfold the story in a different way.
While I have found most of the clips, I have not found all of them. So, some things that possibly might be ambigious for me, might not be for someone that has found everything. Some people might know more or less about the story + characters, depending on how much they might have seen & how they put together the story themselves. The player will have to put in the work here, since it doesn't always seem to spell everything out. The player must pay attention to the story, if they're going to actually assemble it.
Doing the searching for these clips can be addictive. Whether it's for seeing how many clips you find on your search; how much more info the clips holds in the story; and whether new characters, locations, and/ or whatever are introduced - and you might want to search on them further - this can cause the player to get completely engulfed and lost into the game's story + universe, which is completely what this game did for me.
With the excellent writing; very addictive nature of searching + digging for more information to bring out the detective in the player; and the wonderful acting + performance from Viva Seifert - this game completely shines. With twists, turns, and often very intriguing reveals - which can often make the gamer dig for more searches of videos - as a mostly narrative experience, this is a hard to put down game, for the time it actually lasts for.
Both expertly crafted and executed, this is an experience for gamers who love the 90's, murder mysteries, and narrative-driven experiences. For the current price of $6 and since this has appeared dirt-cheap in a Humble Bundle before, I do think gamers could do a lot worse and likely rent a horrible movie or spend more $ going to a movie theatre, in terms of the "bang-for-your-buck" factor. I spent 3.3 hours with this game, according to Steam - and I certainly don't regret one moment of my time spent with this game on my first (and so far only) playthrough.

is one of the finest examples of the
genre in recent years (the other being
). The combat system has a lot of depth and variety which is something that can be lacking in other games of the genre - allowing for dozens of combo combinations. The controls are very crisp and responsive - though, you will want to use a controller for the best experience.
What I love is how the developers designed the wrestling moves multi-purposefully. You use the same wrestling moves in combat as you do for platforming and traversing the environment. It's extremely satisfying and
. They also did a great job of steadily introducing new game mechanics (such as switching between the living and dead world, goat climb and goat fly). The great thing is - you learn these new mechanics via the level design as soon as you acquire them - never taking away control from the player and forcing a unnecessary cutscene. More developers need to design games this way.
There is minimal voice acting, but the story gave me a few chuckles with a few well placed memes and references (normally I don't like that in most games). The visuals of the game are quite unique and colorful - and it's wonderfully animated. The soundtrack is also stellar.
Guacamelee also provides quite a challenge. The bosses are well designed and there is roughly 20 hours of value if you are a completionist/achievement hunter. Some of the challenge areas remind me of games like
, requiring fast reflexes and good timing. You can bet you will be raging at some of them.
Overall, I highly recommend
as it's one of the most shining examples of it's genre. I'm looking forward to seeing what DrinkBox studios do next, as they clearly have some smart and capable game designers over there.

Guacamelee! is a fun, colorful game that combines brawling and platforming in a wonderful setting.
The gameplay is incredibly solid and always feels challenging without feeling unfair showing a great deal of thought by the developers. Combat moves have a place outside battle, not just for opening up barriers like in 'Metroid', but also for the platforming sections, leading to some very creative ways of using certain moves to manuver through levels. Speaking of special moves, the game is very smart about the way it teaches you, areas after getting a new ability will require that you use said ability in several different ways to progress teaching you all facets of each technique without spitting it out in a text box.
The story is admittedly a bit simplistic but it is populated by characters that are as colorful as the game itself which makes for a fun experience. Again, the world is incredibly vibrant and showcases cultures that so rarely get representation in games. Aside from the main story, there are plenty of sidequests and places to explore. You can help reassemble a Mariachi Band, reunite a girl with her missing doll stranded across worlds, and you can even go to Hell!
Hell is actually were the challenge rooms of this game are. The challenge rooms are, as the name would suggest, pretty challenging. Have fun with that!
Guacamelee! quickly became a favorite of my and earned a special place on my games list. I'd definitely say that you should get it. The soundtrack is also worth your money if you're thinking about that as well.

Blood Money is the 4th game in the Hitman franchise - released in 2006, 6 years before the next episode reached completion in development. It took IO Interactive quite a long time to develop the latest episode for the game industry's (probably) most famous assassin. As to what caused this postponement I do not know - perhaps the reception of Blood Money had been negative or somewhat mixed. My feelings about the game are only positive and I salute IO for making such an amazing, stealth-based action-adventure software that offers high replayability due to the various difficulty settings available.
Blood Money gives us a different setting in each mission. Hitman eliminates a gang on a riverboat in Mississippi, approaches a drug lord in Chile, takes down members of a rivaling organisation during a street festival, eliminates a sheikh in a casino in Vegas and more! Every level is very different from its predecessor - it requires different tactics and it is very important to pay attention to your surroundings, i.e. where the enemies are, what their patrolling route is, what disguises you need for them not to be able to recognise you etc. Attention to detail is top notch. The game looks good, runs well and has very decent voice acting. Music was composed by Jesper Kyd who later on presented us with the excellent score of Assassins Creed.
More than one solution exists to solve a mission. The game, therefore, is varied and offers replayability as some solutions require more finesse and while they offer you the easy way out (i.e. no violent encounters) the execution can hold you for hours. In fact, a higher difficulty setting allows you only to save fewer times so you really need to plan every move carefully. Higher difficulty levels yield you with extra money after the mission as the game offers no achievements. More money means better weapons and gadgets at your disposal. But if you prefer the stealth approach you will not purchase new weapons or upgrade your existing ones with the extra sum - you, instead, will use this to bribe key people to decrease your notoriety. Also, when you play the game for the first time, it is advisable to purchase information; information that helps you with the solution in each mission in the form of tips, personal messages.
In Hitman you need to obtain a disguise all the time to get past certain points in the level. While stealth-based games are many I do not recall any of these out there offering this option. In many cases you need to use more than one disguise and just to make the game more challenging you get extra money for reaching the extraction point in your tuxedo, how you originally started your mission. Even the story is interesting and has some surprises - just to mention the name of some locations towards the end of it would be a spoiler so you can find it out for yourselves.
Blood Money is an exceptionally good game. Absolution is the "next-gen" version of Hitman - but if you don't mind playing a challenging and exciting game that is 6 years old Blood Money is for you.

If you want the review summarized in a few words at the beginning of it, so that you can spare yourself the trouble of reading, there it is: this game is the next THE NEXT FTL (Faster than Light, come on, if you don't know what it is and don't have it, just buy it and play it already), but JUST A TAD OVERPRICED. Easy as that.
Renowned Explorers: International Society (REIS) is a game where you command a crew of 3 explorers on a quest to unravel as many treasures, gain as much renown and eventually rise to the top of the explorer society by beating you top rival... um... Rivaleux. Wowzers, very creative, I know :) So does the game deliver? Let's take a look at the good and the bad.
The Good:
1. Amazing replayability. No 2 groups are the same, they always yield different results in battle, and can be played in a plethora of ways.
2. Good AI. NOTE: I mean good, not great. On classic, it will exploit some of your misakes and forgive you others.
3. Unique locations with great art: the artwork of this game is great, the devs did am awesome job with it.
4. Unique Characters: your Captain and your crew members all have unique capabilities, and you are free to mix and match them to your heart's content, discovering the best combos and finding out what works best for you.
5. An innovative take on combat: combat can be won with friendship, deviousness, aggression and... guile. Why guile? Because you can mix and match all of those 3 combat approaches to achieve a combat status that best fits your next move at any given time, and thus win a battle more easily.
6. A game over that barely feels like a game over. Your crew doesn't really die... they just have "stuff" happen to them. Like spend the remainder of their lives repenting in an all-nun monastery. Well, if that was a 3 man crew... they have their work cut out for them.
7. Easy to roleplay: I am not a good roleplayer AT ALL. Yet I found myself putting lines in my toon's mouths. Say, my girl does an ew and shows some soiled undies to another female and I was like: "Geez girl, when was the last time you changed your knickers?!" - reaction: "Saddened". In another case she shows a snail and points at a guy and I was like "Sheesh, mate, even she knows that you are slow to get it up". And then I LOLED. And then I was happy.  And then I went to bed with a smile of my face. 'Bout that...
8. This game easily puts a smile on your face through dialogues, the encounters (charming wolves and sheep FTW), and the combat. Yeah, even when you're losing...
9. Tons of unlockables: the devs really went balls to the wall with this one. You have 20 unique characters, with every one of them available as a captain after you've played them a few times, over 100 achievements, treasures, and 4 difficulty levels with or without savescumming.
10. Ironman if you want: many rogue-likes (Lites?) have an imposed ironman setting. Here you don't. All that the non-ironman game does is to lock you out are the achievements, and that is a small gripe, especially when it comes to a game as hard as this one. 'Bout that #2...
11. The game is hard. It's brutal. It's so damn difficult to win. I love it. Even getting 2nd or 3rd place is an achievement. Hell, even surviving the whole ordeal is :D
12. 12 procedurally generated maps with tons of stuff to unlock on them.
13. Your experiences matter and the game teaches you as you go. I really like that about a game - it makes my subsequent playthroughs meaningful, and much more fun.
14. Tooltips give you an idea what to expect and even let you turn back and back out of a possible challenge, encounter or opportunity, which is a rare thing in rogue-like (lite?) games. You just need to read, you know...
15. The game gives you recommendations with your starting crew (every toon has 2 "best fits" so to speak), which saves you some trial and error time.
16. Once you get the hang of the entire system, just like in FTL, the game feels great to play.
And now, the bad:
1. Only a limited number of maps. 12 is ultimately too little if you want to play this game over and over.
2. The game is HARD. It will take you a good amount of hours to find a decent crew composition and make it work. And then you need to get used to the bosses... and then you need to get used to the levels... and then you need to learn which toons does what ability... and then you need to pick the proper maps to do it... and finally, you need to make it work. Yeah... that's a lot of info.
3. You can lose missions through no fault of your own. The map can screw you, the RNG can screw you, the enemies can screw you, etc. I had runs where I was consistently losing high % rolls... not a pretty sight.
4. Very high learning curve. Learning how every character, every enemy, every mood combo, every attack and so on and so forth works is a daunting challenge.
5. Overpriced. While the game is good, 20€ is too much. I personally bought it on HumbleBundle for the US equivalent of Euro and even had a % of it donated some to charity, so I feel good about myself. On steam, however, 20€ is a lot.
The conclusion:
This game gets an easy recommendation from me, especially to the gamers of the rogue-like (lite?) genre. The game allows you to do pretty much everything with it - explore safely, savescum, challenge yourself, find tresures, go achievement crazy and so on and so forth. It never makes you feel bad about losing too. Your guys don't perish - they just get to live a different life or flee. This makes it a great game for people who are generally sensitive or don't like to lose their in-game crew. All of this is a grat selling point to this game. Its setbacks comprise of a high learning curve, limited maps and TIME. Yes, you need time, and you really need to take the game in and let it teach you. Not everyone is ready to do that.
Any price reduction of 33% or more makes the game an easy purchase. It needs love in my opinion, because it does so much right, and it is a breath of fresh air to the genre, by letting you do whatever you feel like it with it. I have a ton of fun with it, and I will keep on doing so. 8.7 hours in, just a tad less than my play time in FTL, and this game still isn't getting old, and that is saying something.

The first problem I had with this game was the install. I got at least three errors concerning the Microsoft Redistributables, and that I had more recent versions than it was trying to install.
Next it auto-detected my graphics settings to be ~640x480, on a benchmark computer of barely two years ago. This made the mouse tracking on the menu about a quarter inch lower on the screen than it actually was, meaning I had to use my keyboard controls to efficiently rectify the issue.
Besides that, startup went pretty well. But then there's the tutorial stage. You have to play this to proceed to versus. In fact, from what I hear, you have to beat the entire single-player campaign (multiple times?) to be any good in versus. A-la-Borderlands with an online multiplayer arena.
Anyways, digressions aside, the tutorial stage: There is a five-minute-long animation that cannot be skipped, and plays every single time you start up this tutorial. This wouldn't be a problem if I was allowed the luxury of only playing the tutorial once.
However, about three minutes into the tutorial, my game crashed. This happened again, and I looked up how to delete the intro cutscene. Luckily I did, or I would have wasted a good 20 minutes of my life as the tutorial kept on crashing at this point or earlier. It was eventually determined that Battleborn's graphics engine is too unstable to handle the highest graphics settings they offer, and I had to lower them to allow it to run properly and without crashing on my computer.
After I finally worked my way through the uninspired tutorial stage, I attempted to lobby for versus. I waited for about ten minutes, and found one more player in a 6v6  match, before I decided to call it quits and give up.
This game is bad. It's buggy, it's boring, and it's dead. There is no point in wasting your money on this, when so many people already have and gave up on it since.

This game offers you something unique in an steakth game: Liberty. And by liberty i do not mean the false liberty you have in dishonored (i enjoyed both of them still). There's so much you can do, so many possibilities, so many ways to kill/subdue a guard, capture an outpost, bait animals i mean, this game's so huge. If i were to compare the raw material, the potential it had, i'd say it's on par with GTA 5, as there's so much the developpers could have done and there's so much I can do, on my part. And seeing them throwing that away really... saddened me.
Now the flaws in the game: first the travel system. It's very annoying to spawn in the middle of an outpost, having to sneak past guards (or kill'em) every single time i fast travel. There are also far too many loading screens, there's too much waiting time (it's my opinion, i know it's to give the game some rythme, but i didnt like it), the AI is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ BUT sometimes act like Aimbots. Late game is pointless. Evolving your base dosnt bring you anything, no satisfaction. And the endings leave you with a sour-taste in your mouth (for a first-timer on mgs).
On the other hand, the story is well written despite beeing a bit disjointed. The characters are stereotypes BUT it's well done enough to not be as bad as in Wolfenstein 2 for example, and so i actually grew attached to some of them.
.
Overall, i recommend it. For the non-fan, for the fans , it's simply too good to be missed. The sense of liberty you have, the story, the possibilities, the quality gameplay, it has almost everything a game could wish for.
I do not know why is the end game so lack-luster, but i'm fairly sure it's not Kojima's fault.
I recommend the game at full price (30€) if you can afford it. If it ends up on sale, dont even think twice about it and get it.

The game is good, but I'm not sure why this game is/was getting such unquestionable praise.
I'll organize this review in four parts, Gameplay, Graphics, Level design, sound and music, Story.
Gameplay:
The best thing about the game are the controls and the gameplay mechanics.  Snake controls like an oiled up greek olympian athlete, it's great.  Shooting mechanics are pretty good.  Theres a mechanic where time briefly slows down if someone spots you, which can create some pretty quick and tense moments.
The game provides you with a lot of tools to use in your objective, giving a bit of creativity in your play.
Despite that, the game was too easy for me... so eventually I got bored.  After a few hours your gameplay rythm will look something like this, choose mission, scan area for enemies, knock everyone out with tranquelizer pistel, use Fulton to steal people/stuff, leave after doing objective.  Objectives are usually very simple and lack diversity, so they got boring after a while.
Helicopters are pretty annoying too.  You have to use a helicopter everytime you want to enter the map and leave, which means you have to wait to be dropped off, wait to be picked up, and then wait to leave.  It doesn't sound so bad at first, but when you spend an accumulative amount of time in them you start finding reasons NOT to use them.
I like the idea of the IDroid, its like a cassette player that acts as a in game menu screen, you use it to manage the hub area (Mother base), resources, recruits, missions, and music.  Its pretty fun hunting down additional songs (All of which revolve around an 80s theme) by following the music.
Graphics:
Graphically the game is... servicable.  The character models are rediculiously detailed, like, so detailed that the muscles and clothing on Snake's body respond to his movements.  I'm always impressed with needless technical details like that.
The enviornments are an entirely different story, I wish the enviornments had the same level of love that was placed on the characters, but unfortunately they're boring.  Nothing to really write home about.  A positive is that the weather systems around the enviornment do actually impact gameplay, Sandstorms, night time, and rain do make you less visible, creating a window for some pretty interesting on the spot decision making.  Night time is pretty broken though, since you can choose what time to deploy (Even for main missions), it is irrefutably easier to go out during the night with thermal goggles.  Its actually pretty ridiculous.
I had to stop going out at night because I got bored with how easy the game is.
Perfomance is pretty good, it actually doesn't take much to run the game, which is fine because I prefer performance over graphical fidelity.
Level design:
This is an example of a game that has a pointless open world, I honestly think the game would have been better if it was more linear like MGS4.  There are two maps in the main game, Africa and Afghanistan, both are large but full of nothing.  There really isn't much to do in an open world outside of missions, this is even a problem in areas such as the main hub area, Mother base.  Mother base feels like a missed opportunity, the game tries to incentivise you to go back every now and again to raise unity "moral", but aside from a non consequential target shooting mini game, a few rough diamonds to find, and a few story moments this seemed like a waste of resourses.
Mission areas are disapointingly small too, it doesn't really take that long to finish one if you are pretty decent at it.
Sound track:
Good, very good, however there are some in game tracks that get WAY TOO REPETITIVE.  Like I said ealier, the game also has some licensed music that you can find.  I think you can also import your own music into the game as well.
Story:
Meh, the plot is really nothing to write home about as far as I know.  I'm not at the second half of the game, and as far as I know the story only gets worse from there.  The story tries coming of as a serious, but in reality its sometimes hilariously campy.  It's like watching a B movie with a constant.  They did a oddly good job immitating a "documentary" style when it comes to the camera work, but it also ends up making the more campy moments seem more surreal.  I often wonder if the game understands how campy it is and just rolls with it.
Overall:
This game made me feel like I was just going through the motions, running around, shooting and gathering resources.  And than one day it reminded me of No Man's Sky...  And I stopped playing ever sense.
It's NOT a bad game, I can see why people enjoy this game.  It just wasn't for me I guess.

And tons of fun video game and pop-culture references are sprinkled throughout the enitre game.
One particular thing I love is the optional depth to the game. If you're the type of player that only wants to stick to the main path and beat the game as soon as possible, you are able to do so. But for those who feel they've mastered the mechanics and want a bigger challenge, a little exploring reveals there is so much more lying beneath the surface.
I absolutely recommend this game to anyone who enjoys platformers, particularly those in the Metroidvania vein.

For simplicity, I'll be including my thoughts on Part 2 in this review as well, because they're pretty much the same and it makes more sense to me than writing two nearly identical reviews. I won't directly spoil anything plot related but things that can be considered spoilers for those who would want to go into a story as fresh as possible will be marked accordingly.
I'll just mark this in terms of pros and cons:
Pros:
+The humor in this is just amazing, it's something that's very subjective so your experience may not be the same, but this is probably one of the funniest things I've ever read overall. And for how long the story goes, the humor stayed surprisingly fresh throughout. Sure there were some kinds of jokes that were beaten into the ground, as well as some jokes that dragged on too long and weren't really that funny to begin with, but it feels like for every joke that failed, there were 10 that were really good. I was interested in taking screenshots of some of the funny stuff in this at one point, but gave up pretty much immediately after having that idea because there was just too much of it.
+The characters were surprisingly likeable (if sometimes painfully stereotypical), I don't usually wind up liking the "painfully stupid" type of character, and even in this story I didn't at first, but somehow over time, even they grew on me.

Highly recommended for fans of British or Scandinavian crime series, adventure games or narriative games. You (identity revealed later) is looking through an old corrupted database with short video clips of several police interviews with a woman about the disappearence of her husband. Type in keywords to search the database and find new clips, and slowly unravel the story of what happened and why.

HIGHLY RECOMMENDED...if caught on sale or in a Humble Bundle.
RECOMMENDED...at its current price-point on Steam ($6).
Her Story is both a full-blown story & narrative experience that gamers into those kind of games should most definitely experience for themselves. This is an excellent narrative experience that should not be missed, which is especially even more so true if the player catches this game on sale or in a bundle.
The question for most gamers is probably going to be this: is this game going to actually be worth the money? While the game is only currently $6 on Steam for its regular price - for gamers, that mileage may very likely vary. If there's anything that is a big question mark for this game, the length and replayability might be the biggest factors for many with this title.
Gamers might want to replay the game and see how quickly they can reach the important clips to get the player to hopefully be able to reach the conclusion of the game. Some gamers might get very quickly to the end of the experience, maybe not even realize an option they hit brings them to the end, might not have much of the database found, and might actually want to come back to continue where they left off or just flat-out even replay the story from scratch. Some players might find everything and be done with it for good. Again, the player's mileage may vary.
Without giving away too much, here's the story and set-up of this game. A woman is being interviewed a few different times - seven, to be exact - for the murder of her husband. Viva Seifert, as the woman being interviewed, completely steals the show here. The entire game is focused around videos of her from different interviews that are all chopped-up into separate files, which is surrounded by a completely immersive 1990's setting & aestetic.
The way Viva dresses, talks, acts; the writing and dialogue; and especially the computer the player uses to do the searches evokes a completey 90's setting + aestetic. Without the immersion factor; superbly written dialogue; and also the excellent acting from Viva Seifert - well, this game would most definitely fall apart.
Depending on how the player searches the huge database like one would use Google to search the Internet, throwing out keywords to get hits on the database to find clips to hopefully understand the narrative. Depending on how much the player digs into the database and how well, the player might experience and unfold the story in a different way.
While I have found most of the clips, I have not found all of them. So, some things that possibly might be ambigious for me, might not be for someone that has found everything. Some people might know more or less about the story + characters, depending on how much they might have seen & how they put together the story themselves. The player will have to put in the work here, since it doesn't always seem to spell everything out. The player must pay attention to the story, if they're going to actually assemble it.
Doing the searching for these clips can be addictive. Whether it's for seeing how many clips you find on your search; how much more info the clips holds in the story; and whether new characters, locations, and/ or whatever are introduced - and you might want to search on them further - this can cause the player to get completely engulfed and lost into the game's story + universe, which is completely what this game did for me.
With the excellent writing; very addictive nature of searching + digging for more information to bring out the detective in the player; and the wonderful acting + performance from Viva Seifert - this game completely shines. With twists, turns, and often very intriguing reveals - which can often make the gamer dig for more searches of videos - as a mostly narrative experience, this is a hard to put down game, for the time it actually lasts for.
Both expertly crafted and executed, this is an experience for gamers who love the 90's, murder mysteries, and narrative-driven experiences. For the current price of $6 and since this has appeared dirt-cheap in a Humble Bundle before, I do think gamers could do a lot worse and likely rent a horrible movie or spend more $ going to a movie theatre, in terms of the "bang-for-your-buck" factor. I spent 3.3 hours with this game, according to Steam - and I certainly don't regret one moment of my time spent with this game on my first (and so far only) playthrough.

No seriously, this game is charming, interesting and while on the surface, doesn't appear to have a lot of replayability due to the number of scenarios, actually hides an amazing amount of secrets in each location. So what does this game bring to the table? What makes it replayable?
It is designed to be played multiple times so each session will only last a few hours at most. You form a three person team from a roster of 20 characters divided into four specializations. The catch being that only four are unlocked at the start to be in the captain roll. Simply playing the game and running with different characters in the other two positions permanently unlocks them for the captain position in future playthroughs. On top of this you can choose how you approach your encounters, be it friendly, devious or aggressively so playing for or against type can throw your opponents for a loop.
Now the biggest drawback is the lack of locations to explore. Currently you have three possible starting locations and then choose from a handful of others. Your goal is to gain enough reknown to beat a rival explorer at a special party, but you only have time for a total of five explorations before the deadline hits and the most reknowned explorer is crowned. While I will freely admit to wanting more locations to explore there is a lot of replay value in what is currently available if you're determined to hunt down all the side quests or you want to nail a significant portion of the 100+ achievements currently available. Each currently available explorable location is stuffed full of interesting things to uncover. You can scour every spot on a playthrough only to discover a different event chain in that location in your next playthrough. The locations were definitely well thought out and had a lot of time and effort put into each one by the developers.
Would I recommend this game?
Yes. If nothing else, it's definitely worth a solid ten to fifteen hours of gameplay just to unlock all the captains and see a good chunk of the quest events. There are plenty more hours to be had if you want to find all the in game trophies and want to grab a good chunk of or even all the achievements. I just finished unlocking all 20 characters for captain use at nearly 13 hours and have only gotten about half of the in game treasure from various side quests and main quest chains and finding all of said side quests.

I have to say this is probably one of the most fun games I’ve downloaded since making a Steam account, definitely a pleasant surprise.  It’s a fun little premise based on running a team of three explorers through a handful of expeditions to exotic locations (pirate-infested isles, Count Dracula’s castle, the mysterious Shangri-Lai), exploring and gathering rare treasures.  Your time is split basically between three screens – the planning screen where you use the resources you’ve gathered to buy new equipment, unlock scientific advancements to improve your abilities, and gather an entourage of followers to increase the value of future resources.  It’s a nice little balance that allows you to take different approaches in how you improve your team.  Easy to use but requires some time and thought to really master and make the most of your choices.
The other two screens are the game itself.  The first is a map of the area where you pick what locale on the map to explore, trying to match your characters’ diverse skills to what the region is likely to yield.  IE, don’t send your party of fighters to spots where expertise in engineering or science is needed.  Finally the third, where you’ll spend a bulk of your time, is in the turn-based combat screen in which you resolve encounters according to your characters’ abilities in a kind of fun paper-rock-scissors dynamic that can see a friendly argument rapidly turn into fisticuffs.  The challenge of course being to balance it so that your own characters stay one step ahead of the fight by leveraging the skills their best at.
Altogether it’s a diverse little game that allows for a lot of play-throughs with different teams and styles.   It’s also the rare RPG where skills actually mean something more than just an alternative way to kill enemies.  The right mix of skills on your team can have your characters gathering tremendous amounts of renown (the way the game is scored) while a poorly selected and equipped team may end up just scraping by or eventually outmatched in the later stages.  It’s even possible to go through the game without technically ever getting into a physical fight – defeating enemies purely through the persuasive powers of your speech skill, a real rarity in any kind of adventure game.
I’d say it’s definitely worth a try if anything about the premise appeals to you.  The developers did a pretty excellent job of bringing the world to life and offering something a little different, and they’ve continued to tweak an already well-developed game in response to the community’s wants and suggestions.  And if it’s the art that’s maybe giving you pause, I’d advise you don’t let that dissuade you – it’s actually a pretty nice looking game when it’s running and while the cartoony style fits the sometimes humorous tone, this is a serious game that takes a level of skill and dedication to really master.

I'm not much of a stealth game player, but I found Hitman to be a very enjoyable experience. Blood Money in particular. I love the way that you can decide how to approach each mission. Either with brute force or cunning and tact. I found myself going back to earlier missions and trying to do better than before, trying to perfect my technique through trial and error (and a little dumb luck from time to time). Some missions can be difficult, but not so hard that you give up after a while. There are few feelings more satisfying than completing a difficult mission using only your wits and a few precise shots rather than blasting your way through security with assault weapons.

Hitman has always been a rather meh franchise. It has a great concept where you play as an assassin and are sent to kill people and then decide how best to do it. In practice... it's a puzzle game where the trick is to find the "correct" route that will lead you to your target and let you whack em. Not as fun as the original idea implies.
Well, that's what i'd say about the -other- Hitman games i've played. Blood Money on the other hand comes the closest to what it was trying to be all along. In this game you have a number of assassination missions, and there truly are plenty of ways of carrying it out. And it can get really really fun. Example... ah no. I'm not going to spoil that. You have to find out on your own! Guns, poisons, sedatives, fiber wire, and bombs are included among your toys, and that doesn't include any of the options that you can use once you on site. Some of which allow you to get other unwitting people to do your killing for you.
Anyway, it's a great fun game where you are sent to kill some people, and then choose how you shall go about it. If that sounds interesting... grab this during a sale. It's worth it. :D

I was always told that F.E.A.R. was the best of the series and after playing F.E.A.R. 2 I agree, I still have to play the third one though. As I expected, F.E.A.R. 2: Project Origin was a huge improvement both graphically and gameplay wise. I'd say it's still a great looking game and I could clearly notice how the gun handling was improved. I felt like on the first game the recoil was somewhat too much and needed more recoil compensation on the player end but on F.E.A.R. 2 I think they've "perfected" the shooting to better suit "casual players", while I think this is a good thing I understand if others think that the first game had more "realism", if you can call it that, to the weapons. One thing I still find to be rather "lazy" about F.E.A.R. 2  is that most of the guns are basicly just new skins of the older ones, you've got the assault rifle, the submachinegun, the "penetrator" but I gotta admit these new skins look pretty damn nice so I forgive them, one other thing, or maybe it was just me, I'm pretty sure they re-used the enemy voices and player and enemy animations from the previous game, I'm not complaining they did just the right job but I still find it lazy on the developers end. At the end of the day they did a pretty good job in keeping the shooting just as great as in the first game with improved visuals and gun handling, not to mention you can pilot Mechs on this one which I found out to present a nice variety of gameplay but, they did also put some turret segments in the game (I believe two), which I feel they didn't overdone it like some games. Still I think despite of having a great shooting experience, F.E.A.R. 2 wasn't that tense or scary as the first one, I think that's because of the improved graphics everything looks more "colourful" while in the first game everything looked kinda dark and sinister. In the end I think F.E.A.R. 2: Project Origin is a fine piece of work and definitely a great shooter with a nice continuation to the F.E.A.R. plot and the ending clearly gives you the clue that's more to come, I'm pretty sure you can't go wrong with F.E.A.R. 2: Project Origin, either if you're looking for a great first person shooter single player experience or a first person shooter with a paranormal twist to it, F.E.A.R. 2: Project Origin is clearly the game for you.

A sequel to the first FEAR which came out in '05, this game picks up almost immediatly after the first game. Gameplay is the typical FPS affair with various guns and enemies to shoot. The game changes things up with some turret shooting, mech fighting and a few neat set pieces. Slow mo is back and feels great as always. The story is told through in game cutscenes with good voice actors and cool effects. The plot is ok even though it can come across a ittle cheesy at some points. The haunting atmosphere is great, especially with the lights off. The only problem I can think of is the length of the game. I blew through it in a little under five hours but I was speeding through alot of the game. I didnt even read any of journals scattered throughout the levels that flesh out some backstory on whats going on. Ultimately, this is a great FPS with a effective horror theme. I could recommend this to horror fans and FPS fans alike.
