There are times that I'm pleasantly surprised by a game. Something good coming out of seemingly no where and catching me completely off guard. My time so far with Songbringer is one of those times. A very competent action-adventure game in the vein of the NES era Legend of Zelda games, with modern rogue-light procedural generation thrown into the mix for good measure.
Let's kick things off with the graphics because this is going to be make or break for more than a few people when it comes to this game. Yes, it uses pixel art and that is very rampant with indie games these days. That said, Songbringer is one of the better looking pixel art games I've seen of this particular style. The world feels like it has a lot of depth due to great use of lighting effects and shadows, giving it a more 3D feel than some other pixel art games. This is one of those games that screenshots don't really do it justice, it's best to watch the trailer and see how the game looks in motion.
On the flip side of things the game does sometimes over do it with the effects, or there's just simply a lot on screen at one time. This isn't helped by the fact that Roq (the player character) sometimes blends into the game world a bit too well. I had more than one fight where I lost track of Roq and it felt more like a confusing, hectic mess as I tried to figure out where my character went. Not exactly a deal breaker, but something to keep in mind.
Since I brought up combat, let's move onto that. After all, you are a shirtless guy with a sword you should expect there to be a lot of combat and there is. It works pretty much how you would expect for this style of game; you're free to equip weapons and tools as you like and use them in your own style and as the area demands. Overall I think it's done fairly well, but there's a few things that I think could be polished up a little.
It mostly comes down to feeling a bit on the slugish side of things, at least in the start of the game. Roq moves a bit slowly and there's no way to dodge or shield from damage, in the early game, so I felt like I was more reliant on the game's rather amble health drops than I would have otherwise liked. This does change after getting a couple of key tools, and getting more used to Roq's somewhat lunging attack pattern, but there is a definite learning period with combat. This isn't helped by a somewhat sticky world geometry. I found myself sometimes caught on a edge I wouldn't expect or my top hat drone, think Legend of Zelda boomerang, would hit something I wouldn't expect. It just makes things feel a little big rougher than it otherwise should.
My biggest beef with the combat was there was a couple times where I ran into unavoidable damage. The reason why this happens is that the game has a screen transition effect when Roq approaches the edge of the screen, much like Legend of Zelda, where the camera moves so that Roq is on the opposite edge, if he goes to the right edge to camera moves over the world until Roq is on the left side of the screen then play resumes. However, enemy positions aren't reset on these transitions so if Roq was fighting an enemy and triggers this transitions and then goes back to the previous screen, he may walk right into what he was fighting. This also happened to me a couple of times when leaving the store, the enemies outside of the store's entrance were standing in the doorway waiting on me to leave. I had not been fighting these enemies previously, I merely did not kill them before entering the store on that screen and they wandered in front of the entrance. This makes me think that the store may keep the previous tile active when inside, and the enemies were trying to get at me but I'm unsure on this one.
The other half of a Legend of Zelda-like experience would be exploration and Songbringer handles this through a seeded procedural generation system. At the start of each game the world is generated via a six character seed. This makes it so that each play through, if using different seeds, is unique. In the worlds I've generated the changes have been fairly vast, not just in landscape but also in that some items popped up much sooner than they did in other save files. This is because the game also allows for some non-liner gameplay. While it does hold true to the Zelda trope of needing some tools to progress past certain obstacles, large chunks of the world is also explorable from the start and depending on the seed this may include more than one dungeon from the get go. In my play testing of the game I accidentally beat what the game considered the second dungeon before even encountering the first without an issue. But, I've also had a world where I felt rather stuck, it may be I'm just missing that one thing that unlocks everything else, but it can be rather frustrating as well if you have a bad roll of the dice. Also, if you're looking for a more guided experience I wouldn't suggest Songbringer to you. It is very free form in its exploration and while it does give some markers on the map for goals it also expects you to go off and find things on your own as well and find secrets to the game's story without any prompts from the game.
Finally there's my last favorite portion of the game: the soundtrack. I'll be brief on it because I don't have much to say about it. I won't go as far to say that it's bad. I just really didn't care for some tracks, particularly the dungeon tracks. They tend to have long, droning notes that really grated on me. I understand the style they were going for, but I just honestly didn't like it.
So, wrapping up, is Songbringer for you? If you don't mind wandering around and learning about the world at about the same pace as the protagonist and the art style doesn't turn you off. I would say yes. It is a very good game and if you stick with it long enough to get a handle on how the game handles its combat then I think it is a worth while experience. Also, if you like the idea of starting fresh and having a brand new world to explore, it offers a lot of potential for replayability. If you can't stand procedural generation or pixel art I don't think the game will change your mind in the slightest.
Version played: 1.0.0

Songbringer is the result of one man working for three years on a procedural homage to the Legend of Zelda. Important to note is that this is most directly influenced by the original NES game, and not say, A Link to the Past or any of the 3D ones. You are given little in the way of instruction and essentially just nudged in some directions. There are dungeons that must be found, items to be plundered from them, paths that the items open up in the overworld, (slight mechanical spoilers if you want to figure everything out on your own):
Combat is fairly basic, mostly just sword swinging and hat throwing (it's a boomerang but more eccentric), but it feels good and hits have a good weight to them. Button mashing will get you killed fairly quickly, though dungeons are small enough and you keep any items or keys you've picked up within them so you can make a break through a hard room if you must.
The gimmick of the world shuffling itself based on your word seed is neat, though I don't know that you'll really want to play this over and over. Two or three runs should be satisfying. Still, they're solid runs. I'll be interested to see what speedrunners do to this game.
I raise slight issue with the claim that this game has hundreds of items; really, there are 5 elements that you can assign to most of your equipment, so in one run maybe you'll have a sword that shoots lightning and your bombs will spew acid, in the next you might decide to apply the traits to different items, but their utility isn't all that different. I ended up using most items as an overworld key more than a weapon. It's very light Metroidvania in that sense.
Music is neat and creates a nice atmosphere. Writing is charming enough.
TL;DR: If you like the feeling of exploring an overworld and going through each screen looking for secrets and whaling on enemies with a sword, bombs, and boomerang, this is worth your consideration.

One of my favorite new games of the year. I've always been interested in all the Indiana Jones, old mythos, and 19th century history, so this, naturally was an easy fit. But seriously, the game would be great without it. You get pretty attached to the characters you choose and in a lot of ways it feels like old world XCOM  - and yet completely refreshing.
There are two legit cons you hear more than anything else:
1) The game is too difficult
2) It should be longer
Personally I think the first one is a little dumb. Yes, there is RNG, but there is also, again, brutal RNG in XCOM, and it's no more crazy than that. I feel like the problem with the RNG is that too many people think that this game is like FTL, when it's really more like XCOM. The RNG isn't in the encounter, it's in the success. If your soldier misses a 85% shot on a mutalisk, he will probably, brutally die, I think the adventure wheel is in the same vein. Even more than the combat, which again, feels very XCOM. I read Abbey Games saying that they were implementing a difficulty feature, which will probably help.
The second complaint I wholeheartedly agree with. I would love this game with more goofy characters (or maybe an option to make and name your own character?), more areas to explore, longer quests, more treasure, more leveling up and all of that. I don't know how feasible it is, but maybe even open the game to modders in the future, because the template is all there, I would just love more.
But overall the answer is, yes! You should absolutely purchase this game. It's very fun, it's got a lot to offer, and from what I've read, it sounds like Abbey is planning on adding more to the game over time. If you're a little hesistant now, I understand - but at least put it on your wishlist.

Edit 3: They have made SO MANY improvements for this game that basically every minor complaint I had with it is now irrelevant.  There are more places to explore, tech is now no longer based on your team build, there are more events in locations and more interesting decisions to be made there along with tons of balancing patches.  You heard right BALANCE PATCHES IN A SINGLEPLAYER GAME to improve the play experience.  The Dev team is fan-freaking-tastic.  If you like rogue-likes, buy it, if you like turn based strategy, buy it, if you like adventure games buy it!  The only feature that might put people off is the learning curve.  You really do need to figure out the strategy elements in this game, which are a little weird at first, but after that the difficulty settings let you make this anything from hardcore score-attack to casual lunch-breaker game.  It's really flexible that way.
This game is great.  It has an awesome choose-your-own adventure style and a lot of replayability.  The mood and combat system is a bit confusing at first but it's not too hard to learn and it really makes things interesting.  There's a big FTL or Binding of Isaac kind of feel where it's a short experience that can turn out in different ways.  My only problem is that is simply doesn't have the unpredictability that those games do.  There are 10 different levels, 5 of which you explore in each playthrough, with their own strategies and secrets which are randomly placed on the map, but always present and always the same.  The characters abilities are slightly customizable over the course of the game but not a ton, this isn't much of a problem though as each 30 minute playthrough will use 3 out of the 20 characters.  However besides character selection there's little deviation between playthroughs.  In FTL or BoI finding the right weapon at the right time can swap your whole strategy, not so much here.  Your strategy is set by the characters and missions you chose, there's no evolution.  It may sound like I dislike the game here with this rant but really it's just that I love it so much and I see so clearly what it could be with more levels and more evolution.  If this gets steam workshop support or an expansion it could easily match the hundreds of hours Xcom, Isaac and FTL have gotten from me.  As it is now it's about 10-20 hours of great content, which was worth it to me but I can understand wanting more for your money.
Edit: Based on their latest patch I am now completely sold on this game.  Abbey has demonstrated that they are interested in making their game better on a consistent basis and ensuring it doesn't turn into a stagnant, formulaic experience despite being singleplayer.  This is more than I can say for Binding of Isaac and FTL, who recieved only spotty support from developers.  This pushes me from 7/10 to 9/10.  If they release a few more levels I'll send it straight to 11/10.
Edit 2: Well they released a new map.  I can think of no reason whatsoever not to recommend this game to anyone who likes turn based strategy.  My minor complaints and nitpicks have been blown into a fine red mist by the rocket launcher of amazing that Abbey is wielding.  They comboed their Impress with some follow up excite attacks and now I have become excited about their cause and stopped resisting.  I rate this game 11/10.  What are you waiting for?  Just buy it already!

This is the first game I'm going to try to refund on Steam.
I saw the comments about it being X-COM like and I thought I'd try it out. It turns out that there isn't much going for the combat other than a rock-paper-scissors sort of thing with three attack types. Of course, the game suggests building your team around one or two types, so you're going into a RPS contest without one of those choices. Each character has a small number of attacks to choose from, and they were mostly the same between the characters I tried. If there's some way to switch team members between expeditions, I didn't find it.
Between combats, the game has a dull board game feel, like playing Monopoly. Sometimes you roll on a wheel to see if something good or bad happens. There are different skills that influence this, but there's not much way to prepare for a particular type of area where different skills might apply, unless I missed that, too. I should note that the UI for this game is often confusing.
Also, there's some bug for unusual resolutions that makes the mouse cursor not line up with whatever position it's using for selecting buttons. I played this game on my TV, which obscures some of the edge of a standard resolution, so I clipped it a little in the video settings. I had to change resolution in the game to a standard choice and restart.
The point is, I don't want to play this game any more.
It's a fun game, which really causes you to want to keep playing. I've had a great time with it till now.

- Differentiated personalities, developed in a very creative way (each char has personal animation for each abilty, for example)
- Great Perk system with real impact in the game, giving even more flavor and variety
- A lot of replayability of every expedition without losing any of its characteristics, storytelling and general ambience
- Great graphics and animations, simple but very well done
- A lot of funny moments to encounter and laugh about
- Retry with different groups since gameply changes dramatically (for better or worse...)
- A ton of potential and expandability (free new expedition in the making!)
- Challenging
- Fun
Buy it, play it, enjoy it and pray for more games like this to be done.

While some may say Hitman shines in its gameplay, I enjoy the cutscenes more. Fapped to agent 47's voice.

To me this is the easiest game in the Hitman franchise, but it's also one of the best! The amount of varied missions here and the numerous ways to complete them result in endless replayability. I must have played 50,000+ hours on my retail copy, and I still find myself coming back to this game and finding new things I didn't notice before. Honestly there's not one mission I hate in this game, and each one is a nice sandbox-type map where you are thrown in and told to kill somebody; how you do that is up to you.
If you're new to the series I would suggest buying this game first and avoiding the mess that was "Absolution" altogether; or wait until it's extremely cheap. Blood Money was a near perfect game and should have been the standard that all future Hitman games followed. Instead of Blood Money 2.0 we got a ridiculous wall-hugging game--which might be alright in other games but for Hitman it's awful. Blood Money is not without it's flaws, though. The guards are way too gullible to manipulation; but man is it fun to trick them. They will follow blood trails, pick up dropped weapons, and respond to noises. At the time I had never seen AI this advanced before.
Bottomline: the amount of detail and things you can do in this game is amazing. If you've always wanted to play a game that provided hours of replayability as a hitman in a sandbox environment then get this game! The other games in the Hitman series are also fantastic, except for Absolution.

I can without hesitation reccomend this game. As of now I have 147 hours of playtime which is probably more than the average person would get out of it. It is not without it's flaws but in my opinion the flaws are not game breaking in the least.
Do not be put off by the first mission. The very first mission is a mandatory, linear, and all around just not very fun. It serves to teach you the mechanics without distracting you from the goal. There are other missions just like it which I feel are too linear, but nowhere near as bad as the first. I think this tutorial mission put off too many people who never got to the next one to find how "open" it could be and what the possibilites were like. It's not unbearable but it's so un-indicative of how most of the game goes and what makes it so good.
The menu system is pretty clunky. It seems to be really geared toward console gamepad controls. It's a small nitpick and you get used to it quite quickly but it can get annoying if you need to switch items a lot in rapid succession.
There is one fault with the rating system I will go into detail about next. There is a way to cause "accidents". You push someone off a cliff/down the stairs/whatever, or maybe you rig something to fall apart or explode suddenly to cause something large to crush them. Now while I love the concept and usually it is brilliant, there are problems. For example, I remember one instance where I wanted to get all accidents for the Silent Ghost rating (the highest paid rating possible). Well, pushing the guy down the stairs was the best way. So I push him and then he falls kind of slowly in what looks like a crawl down the steps. Then what happens? Apparently he didn't "crawl fall" enough and gets up and starts to shoot me along with everyone else. I had to reload and do this many, many times for it to finally work correctly. So I have a little problem with that but it happens relatively few times in the course of a playthrough.
So with the things that bother me out of the way, let me lose myself in the seemingly endless things that I love about his game. Starting with the Rating System. Now with this system you are awarded cash and a title depending on many factors including whether you did the optional objectives, how many innocents you knocked out/killed, how many times you alerted guards, how many bodies were found, how many "accidents" occured, what gun was used the most, how many shots hit their target, how accurate you were, noise level, violence level, and a whole bunch of other factors. Most of these come as a straight spreadsheet of info, but some are in the brilliant newspaper front page that you get afterwards. It gives a summary as an article of what you did, whether you silently exectuted the target/s quietly, or went and killed hundreds of people. Seeing the different ratings you can get for accomplishing certain levels of violence, silence, and ways to kill people, really increases replayability and makes certain "runs" pretty fun. Sometimes I just try to see how many people I can kill with a kitchen knife and still finish the mission. Or maybe i'll see how many accidents I can cause.
The custom loadout is really well done, but it has one flaw. You are limited in that you can only bring one weapon that you acquired from a mission. Like if you leave a mission with a Mosin Nagant sniper rifle then it becomes available with limited ammo for taking you with you on a mission. But what I don't like is that you can't have 2 rifles, 2 pistols, or 2 sub machine guns. You have 1 pistol, 1 rifle, and 1 submachinegun with no exceptions. I would rather have traded some of the other gadgets i didn't need for more flexibility but it simply wasn't an option. Still, the loadout system is fine despite that limitation. If you're really good then all you need are the syringes and the fiber wire most of the time anyway.
The writing is so hilarious. It is mostly self aware of how crappy it is at times and does it for comedic effect. Other times the writing is really witty and feels very real. Mostly everyone fits some sort of stereotype, almost insultingly so, but it has such a charm when a sailor with sideburns on the Mississippi says "Get lost Chum Lee." in a Cajun accent. This game has so much character in the characters if that makes sense. It feels very real, but at the same time it's so very surreal too.
The soundtrack is to die for. No really, it's like really well done mostly because of Jesper Kyd when he was, in my opinion, at his peak. It's a very teasy mix of classical and electronic rythums depedning on the mood and what is happening. Easily one of my favorite soundtracks.
Another thing I love about this game is the attention to detail. I'm always finding something new. I found out last time I played Curtains Down (a mission in which you are at a french opera house during a practice night). There is a guard constantly "patroling" with a group of people as a tour guide. This guard takes a break and goes into this small closet-like room. When he does you can quickly knock him out/kill him and take his clothes. So when you come back out the group starts following you as if you are the new guide. After a mintue or so of not talking to them they of course disperse sounding agitated in french. It's this kind of nuance and possiblity of discovery that helps me come back to play and see what else I can uncover. I hate to spoil a later mission but for example you walk into a high class party and the singer is absolutely, positively awful. First time I played I didn't even really notice I thought that maybe the game did it for a laugh, but then later you find out that she is the secret assassin there to kill you. That sort of blew my mind when I found out and yet another testament to the small things. You'll notice too that when you kill a contract they will appear in the main menu's chapel sitting in various spots as if attending. I could go on forever about all this little stuff but I think you get it.

It stumbles upon itself and seems confused as to whether it wants to be an action game, a cleverly crafted horror game, or a jumpscare simulator. The shooting mechanics are stale, the guns feel like toys, the characters aren't very likable and the plot makes little to no sense.
There are worst shooters out there, but there shouldn't be any reason to settle for this either.

A step backward for the franchise, shuffling the games studios didn't help, but the story maintains its excellence.  The biggest problem is the generic nature of the engine.  Without the F.E.A.R. name, this would just be another forgettable shooter trying to emulate the genre's best games.  If you're a fan of the series, it's worth playing but if not, then don't worry.

When my friend first gave me this game, I wasn't sure if I would really enjoy the game to the end. However, I was completely wrong and am truly in love with it! Guacamelee is a simple fighting adventure game that takes Juan in a journey to save the girl he likes. It uses a luchador theme that hasn't really been used much of anywhere making it refreshing and more fun. There is a nice combo system where you can chain attacks which is nice for those Street Fighter experts out there, but you can easily play through the game without doing combos or chaining your attacks.
There are 3 unique mechanisms which I cant really talk about without spoiling except for the attack skills. There are many skills to learn in the game that are used in order to unlock secret areas and progress in the game. The attack skills were very well made and are controlled easily. They are fun to use and experimenting with them in order to create your own combo to defeat the enemies and bosses is very fun. Bosses are also all unique to each other. They each try to force you to use certain skills to win, but are not necessary. Additionally, each boss is completely unique making the gameplay fun and non repetitive.
The soundtrack is good and worth a listen, but there was one problem that I had with the game. That is when you receive a skill, the game likes to strobe bright colorful lights at you, making your eyes hurt and sometimes giveing you a headache. But besides that, this game has a great fighting mechanic, good soundtrack, good art, and a cliche story with a refreshing theme.
Overall I highly recommend this game to everyone as it is short but has a good replayabliliy value. With a hard mode that actually changes the games text and NPC actions due to it being unlocked after beating the game once on normal. They also have challenges and other small mini games, secrets and side quests that help in exploring the world.

I didn’t think much of Guacamelee before I played it, but the roughly 5 hour experience was very satisfying. It begins like any typical videogame hero story, a weak hero goes about his day doing menial tasks that conveniently teach the player how to interact with the world when suddenly, the villain appears taking the love interest with him. While very cliche, it is still done well and throws in fairly interesting characters and amusing twists to fit the theme.
The traditional Mexican art style is an interesting new take that helps articulate the theme of the world, which is paired with a very catchy mix of Mexican instruments and techno. My only real complaint lies in the default female luchador design, whose extremely large chest is barely covered by a long white cloth wrapped around her chest. Then from her waist comes a long transparent skirt that might as well not be there. However there is an alternate costume that features her in more reasonable dress, though it must be bought ingame. There is also a reasonably large skin modding community for the pc.
At first glance, Guacamelee’s combat may seem button mashy, but that tactic will only get you past the first quarter of the game before It is harshly punished. Most enemies either actively dodge about, dig into the ground to avoid harm, or show no reaction to blows at all until death. The only way to reliably produce a combo with these enemy types is to keep them airborne for as long as possible which requires very careful timing. This is where most of the game’s challenge comes from as the puzzles are usually relatively simple and mostly only require figuring out with what timing to use which ability. The boss fights are much like these puzzle areas, usually actively punishing use of the same tactics that would be used on enemy groups. There are also plenty of powerups to find and purchase consisting of power grapples, health and stamina upgrades, and costumes. The power grapples are basically variants of the throws that either do focus damage, do damage around you, or simply do more damage to the enemies that are hit.
Guacamelee is a solid Metroid-vania with wonderful art and music that very much deserves your attention.

This game pushes all the right buttons for a satisfying Metroidvania style brawling platformer experience that doesn't overstay it's welcome.  The combat is challenging and rewarding.  It develops over time as you gain more and more traversal options which lend themselves to increased combo options.
If you pick this up, which I'd recommend most do so, I'd additionally suggest that you spend some time with the Combo Chicken to get a feel for what's possible with the combo system.  For most encounters you don't need to get too creative with your attacks aside from flair reasons, but late in the game there are a few fights that have the potential to be pretty rough unless you're pretty familiar with your attack options.  The game throws in additional movement and evasion requirements at you with the last two bosses of the game that demand that you're quick on your feet.
If you're into games like Shadow Complex, Dust: An Elysium Tale, or similar games, Guacamelee is definitely worth your time.

Cold War takes nearly every element from 2020 and improves it ten fold. The graphics are still somewhat primitive but improved greatly and it almost has a charm to it. Military wise its fun and easy to figure out and the new Merchant marine makes it ten times easier to move troops globally and invade island nations. The interface for managing everything is organised but can be confusing with some elements hidden behind too many other interfaces making it a maze to figure something simple out.
The Cold War campaign is well organised with the Atomic and Space races and the many conflicts and problems are there that were present in the 1950s,60s,70s and 80s.
The Sandbox mode is also still fun to play and a healthy mod scene makes it enjoyable to try different modes and scenarios.
Overall this game is definatly worth your time and money if you into this genre.

"Songbringer is an exciting new take on the classic Zelda formula. Its roguelike design makes for exciting worlds and dungeons that feel fresh and unique despite being randomly generated. Better yet, its frenetic combat and varied weaponry make these different world seeds all the more fun to explore.
While sharp difficulty spikes and frustrating boss encounters cheapen the fun, Songbringer’s main pull is enticing enough to warrant a playthrough (or several). And at just twenty bucks, it offers far more value than most games in its genre, right out the gate.

The Penumbra series was Frictional Games first series. Overture is the first game in the penumbra series, it features Phillip who is investigating a letter written from his dead father and ends up trapped in an abandoned mine. The game revolves around surviving and hiding, there are no real fighting mechanisms in the game. You can throw rocks or objects to knock out enemies (Dogs, Spiders, Infected) but after a while they will get back up again and attack you. This is a very puzzle heavy survival game, reading and taking notes are important but also some sounds can lead to become very important clues for some places. If you enjoyed Penumbra and haven't checked out Frictional games second series Amnesia, I would highly recommend it.

A creepy, modern dungeon-crawl.  Overture will keep you running and hiding from a multitude of enemies; frantically race your way through an old mining complex, listening to the babbling madman on the other end of your radio.  Clutch your tiny hammer in fear as an enemy slinks by, leaving you undetected... for the moment.
Interestingly, the only Penumbra game in which you can actually fight off enemies!  Let them have it while you can, the later titles don't allow such behavior...

The Hitman series has always been known for its mix of stealth and action gameplay, and this entry of the series is no different.
The game plot is revealed by a series of interview pieces with a retired police officer, in which he usually tells something about the death of a certain person that most people thought something (a different story to the public) and turns out it was something entirely different involving 47.
At first these don't make much sense, but as you play the game, you start to see where the plot is going, there aren't many remarkable points on it with the exception of the ending (which is amazingly delivered), so no spoilers.
The gameplay of this game follows the tradition of the old entries of the series, which is a good thing since it is what makes this series unique: you receive a briefing showing the place, who you have to eliminate, the background story of said person/people, then you choose your starting equipment and you are ready to go. What makes the game unique is that you can play in a stealth approach: observing enemy patrols, finding out how to infiltrate certain places, and planning a way to get close enough to take out your target or even how to take them down from afar.
One of the main features of the game that is still intact is that 47 is still a master of disguises and has the ability to change his clothing in seconds (it may sound a little weird, but it explains how someone can do the stuff he pulls off), which in most cases is the only way to access certain locations in the game. For instance, only workers can enter a part of the opera house that is still being build, I mean, you can enter without disguise, but that will attract attention AND the guards of the place.
An addition made in this game, is that now 47 can move faster while sneaking, in previous games, it was hard and painful to sneak around because it was too slow. He can now throw coins around to lure people to someplace where them and 47 can have a more "personal conversation" or simply use them to lure guards out of posts and such.
Although it is a stealth game, it is different from what the conventional stealth games are and play. In here, you don't use the darkness to hide, you use the people and your disguises, you can crouch behind something, but don't expect that to go unnoticed: people react to your actions, and someone sees you sneaking around or behind people, they will react properly.
It is weird that people only bother listening to YOUR footsteps. For instance, there's this guard walking with another close to him, he'll do his job normally, then later you take out one of the guards and take his place, the other guard WILL start looking back and perplexed stare at you. These things are a little annoying because it happens only with the player. Since you can't sneak all the time without calling unwanted attention, you have to adapt to survive, and having access to a plethora of ways to approach a place/person is what increases its replay value and makes it unique.
Also a new feature is the introduction of Accidents. 47 can now push people off rails, roofs, etc, or he can just knock them out and THEN throw them off such places. This adds even more different ways to complete the assignments. Since the money you earn is determined by your performance in the missions, things as killing innocent people or be seeing doing something suspect all count towards your final rating. If someone saw you, you CAN kill this people as a way to have no witnesses, but the game will not penalize you if you can make it look like an accident, this is a nice addition.
You can now also customize your weapons, like putting a silencer in your Baller pistols or SMG, or putting a more precise scope at your rifles. Upgrading equipment is also possible now, such as decreasing the time it takes to lockpick a door or increase the distance of where you must be to detonate your remote bombs.
A new possibility now in case things get hairy is the ability to take people as human shields. But besides the obvious purpose it also serves as a way to take someone faster to a certain place. For instance, instead of having to wait till the person is knocked down with the effect of some of your tranquilizer syringes and then drag them somewhere more discreet, you can grab then and "quickly" get them elsewhere and THEN knock then out without worrying with the possibility of someone seeing you.
In the graphics department, the game handles very well, its attention to detail is remarkable and every place in the game looks convincing, from a suburban house to a rehabilitation clinic or a Mardi Gras parade.
The soundtrack in this game is amazing, it server to set the mood for the missions but also to tell the player of the current situation, if something goes wrong and you're about to get shot by the guards, you'll know before hand because of the song that will start playing. The voice acting is really good, David Bateson delivers a believable cold Agent 47 as always, and Vivienne McKee does a great job bringing the faceless Diana to life in her "cold but sometimes caring" voice. The NPC's voices sometimes are goofy and funny but noticeable intended as a way to ease the tension in the game.
The big arsenal of weapons, equipments, and disguises give the player a lot of freedom to approach the missions. Being stealthy and infiltrating a place from the back or even the front, or simply go guns blazing, be certain that you can always surprise yourself when things DO work even when you try to be more creative.

Very very fine metroidvania with luchador theme. Do not miss this game if you like metroidvania style games at all. The soundtrack is also top-notch mariachi-electro fusion thing and I definitely recommend getting the soundtrack bundle.
In short, Guacamelee is exploration-oriented sidescrolling 2d action game with most gameplay mechanics lifted straight from Super Metroid and refitted with a magical Mexican luchador theme. Suits are wrestling suits and masks, weapons are wrestling moves etc. Even color-coded doors are here and they have to be opened with specific moves. Gamepad is almost mandatory, since you have to be able to control your character quickly and combo all sorts of moves in order to get through some later challenges. The game also features local co-op, where player 2 can just drop in and drop out whenever. I haven't tried it myself, but it should be at least a fun diversion and maybe provide some help in the trickier boss fights.
The game isn't flawless though. The difficulty curve is a bit uneven and especially two of the boss fights provide some nasty difficulty spikes. The fights are far from impossible, but they do require some very good reflexes and good control of all the moves in the player's disposal. Also the game world feels slightly small. Everything is designed quite tightly and there is not too much backtracking, but it feels like there should have been something more. Still, if you feel like 100% the game, the first playthrough should take somewhere in the vicinity of 10-12 hours, so it isn't too short at any rate.
Definitely get this game if you want a good metroidvania and/or love luchadors.

Supreme Commander 2 is the successor to the critically-acclaimed Supreme Commander 1 and Supreme Commander Forged Alliance titles made by Gas-Powered Games and published by Square Enix.  In the distant future, wars will be fought not by hordes of manned armies but rather swarms of drones remotely commanded by people in giant robots in the battlefield for some reason. This toned down sequel has drawn either much praise or a lot of vitriol from its community.  With such mixed responses, one may wonder if this game is even worth playing, let alone looking at it.  This review hopes to answer that question (summary below):
-Story:  Being a game published by Square Enix, one would expect story to be the primary focus of the game, but it seems that even the story in SupCom2's case was toned down in comparison to its predecessor (even though it was enough for me to want to see what the end looked like).  Throughout the 18 campaign missions divided equally between the United Earth Federation (UEF), Aeon Illuminate and the Cybran Nations, the three factions struggle to keep a fragile alliance together from internal plots to thrust one side into power over all others.  While this may sound dramatic, the tone never gets too grim while also avoiding an overly idealistic view.  The main characters sound like interesting concepts, but they're all executed in an uninteresting way with monotonous speech and limited facial expressions.  It also doesn't help that the FMVs feel lacking and empty.  Despite these facts, the campaigns still provide the benefit of practice for the multiplayer community, at least enough to familiarize the player with each faction.  It's still recommended to practice in skirmish mode and within the multiplayer community itself though.  Whether you care about the story or not, the campaign is at least something to pass the time and learn about the game.  Score:  3/5
-Graphics:  One of the main complaints voiced by fans of the previous Supreme Commander games is that the graphics in SupCom2 aren't nearly as spectacular as its predecessor.  While they aren't as bad as they could be, the presentation of the game is rather simple in a way that's almost lackluster in both unit and world design.  Even on the highest graphical capabilities, the game looks like something made out of legos almost.  The scaling is also a little strange, but it's understandable as to why the developers took this path:  They were betting on the idea that gamers in the start of the 2010's wouldn't be able to afford powerful computers with the best hardware on the market.   As a result, those whom had played the first game and eagerly awaited a new and improved sequel were disappointed while it didn't discourage newcomers from entering the franchise.  If you're the kind of person who doesn't care too much about graphics, this is the game for you.  If you wanted something even more realistic than the first, look elsewhere.  Score:  3.5/5
-Gameplay:  Another complaint by the fans of Supreme Commander 1 and Forged Alliance was that the gameplay was toned down in terms of complexity for SC2.  While Supreme Commander 2 is simpler than its predecessor in terms of strategic depth, this is not necessarily a bad thing.  The goal of the game is to assert your military supremacy with swarms of unmanned units while also avoiding total annihilation.  Units are constructed out of two resources:  Building Mass, and energy which is easier to harness since generators can be placed anywhere as opposed to mass extractors which are placed on strategic points and must be secured.  Instead of tiers, factions can invest research points that are accumulated over time to improve their units on the spot with increased gains in research the more research facilities are constructed.  Rather than requiring buildings dedicated to unlocking research though, one can just simply access their tech tree and spend points on what they can afford.  While this does sound better than the typical method of improving units, it can be tedious or outright absurd to feel the need to relearn upgrades every single game.  SupCom2 also benefits from allowing players to plan joint-operations with their land, naval and air units and the sheer size of one's armies, fleets and squadrons is still impressive with support up to as many as 500 units per team.  While some may complain about the downgrades given to each faction's late-game experimental units, they are still powerful enough to require planning to deal with effectively.  The view of the game is also impressive since not only is there a typical minimap with fog of war that's already drawn, players can zoom out and view the entire battlefield to coordinate multiple assaults in real time.  It may seem overwhelming at first, but it won't be take long to improve one's micro-management and multi-tasking skills.  To put it simply, if you're looking for a game with strategic-depth that's important for a long-term goal, play SupCom 1.  If you are more a fan for smaller-scale battles of tactics, SupCom 2 is the game for you.  Score:  4.5/5
-Sound:  Even though it seems that sound wasn't a high-priority for Supreme Commander 2, there's still a small OST that might have been complimented if it only had more songs and influences from the kind of music heard in games like Hawken or Battletech.  There is a recurring leitmotif here that may be detected on and off, but is rather downplayed in contrast to everything else.  Fittingly, there is dynamic music in Supreme Commander 2 that shifts to match the intensity of the battle with almost nothing but wind at the start and a building orchestra that climaxes once the battles rage.  The warnings for this game only tells you of critical information that requires immediate attention such as “Nuclear launch detected” or “Commander under attack”.  The voice acting for the game feels mostly restrained, with lines alternating between hit-and-miss sarcastic remarks and attempts to add character development that fall flat most of the time.   Not much to say here, but it probably could have used something more.  Score:  3/5
-Replayability:  Despite the divided fanbase in regards to Supreme Commander 2 and its predecessor, SC2 still has hundreds of players in the multiplayer community.  The community hub is still fairly active, and there is a modding community for the game as well, just like the first game.  Even if you're not into multiplayer, Supreme Commander 2 has a campaign that would probably last the average player about a week or a week and a half to complete just for the regular objectives alone.  For completionists, there are also hidden objectives to discover in each campaign mission to improve one's score.  There is also skirmish mode which can be played against AI with misleading difficulty values.  Fortunately the game's AI opponents are relentless enough even on Normal to improve one's strategy and drive them to feel accomplished as they eventually defeat their opponents.  The good news is that this game will last a good while for fans of short-term RTS games.  Average life expectancy would probably be around a month just for the singleplayer alone and several for multiplayer if it still lives on.  Considering that the story ending on a cliffhanger that probably won't be answered any time soon, if at all, SC2 is in no danger of being replaced by a sequel unless a spiritual successor is developed.  Score:  4/5
-Summary:  Supreme Commander 2 is the kind of game that's enjoyable in its own merits. If it weren't so conflicting with the lore, it's probably be more tolerable to SupCom 1 fans if SC2 could be thought of as a prequel in disguise as a sequel. If you aren't too judgmental about graphics or complexity and just wish to have a fun, futuristic short-term RTS, then Supreme Commander 2 is for you.  Overall Score:  18/25 or 72%.

Going back to play Payday The Heist after a haitus of of playing Payday 2 you see a solid game on par with the sequel, The Heist excels in everything it goes to accomplish except possibly Animations, But this was an early title for the company off the Xbox 360 so one would make a few exceptions for it looking a little stiff, What you come to see is an expertly crafted Horde Shooter with the horde being Common Cops to Swat that are hell bent to take you out on every heist you go on by throwing numbers over fire power at you in an attempt to take your gang and yourself out, On the flip side your set out with a standard pistol, and assault rifle to work towards unlocking other weapons and upgrade them by unlocking more for it to continue to progress yourself by taking money as a main replacement for XP, The game features 9 Heists with entirely different scenerios for each with each having their own enviorment to work in giving you room to breath and room for the cops to come at you, If your wondering if Payday: The Heist is worth checking out after playing Payday 2 and having enjoyed it then you will most likely enjoy this as well, It holds up to be on par in the same aspect as L4D1 is to L4D2 since both titles share the same systems and enemies.

Look, I don't know why this is getting such a bad wrap. It's a fun, engaging game with a surprising amount of depth. The mechanics are fairly unique; the skill trees last for a single mission only, allowing you to experiment with each character.
The co-op story mode missions can become a little repetitive, but are typically very fun. In true gearbox fashion, there is some outstanding dialogue and voice-acting - aside from Borderlands, I can't think of many other games that make me chuckle out loud. (Yes, there are some cringey one-liners, but it fits the schtick).
Imagine each story mission as a bite-sized, self contained Borderlands game, while the PVP is true arena goodness. Unique game modes, and some really cool maps round it all out.
The most significant issue I've got is that it's very hard to find a co-op game with what is now a fairly small player base. It sucks, because it's hamstringing what could be an awesome franchise.
TLDR:
Battleborn is really quite good. The small player base doesn't make it any less good, just more frustrating to get a game.

This game does have a few good things going for it.  the single player mode was pretty fun, and if there were enough people online to play it I imagine the co-op would be the same.  The game is plagued by 2 problems though.  the first is the tiny userbase for it.  Matchmaking takes a really long time and my first attempt I was matched with players at max level, despite being a low level myself.  There seems to either be no attempt to match players based on experience, or the player base is so low that there are no other options.
That alone would be a bad sign for a game which sets a great multiplayer experience as a goal.  The games other issue, however, is much worse.  The character balance in the game is so poor that it seems like only a few characters are actually viable.  I played as the one of the Tank characters, Montana.  His main weapon, a minigun, was so weak that sustained fire for about 30 seconds did not deal enough damage to kill a single other player.  It doesn't seem surprising at all that all of the high level players seem to use only 4 or 5 different characters.
I honestly expected a lot more from gearbox, especially considering both Borderlands 2 is probably the best experience I've had in a game since Half Life 2, but it is really hard to reccomend a game with such major flaws in it's multiplayer experience.

Renowed Explorers is a Roguelike-ish mix of Strategy RPG, Choose your own Adventure Book and planning sim from the Makers of Reus, a definitely wonderful god-Sim. But thats a different review for a different Day.
You pick a team of three archeologists from a roster of 24 people in 4 classes (Fighter, Scientist, Scout and Talker (Diplomat)) with yiur captian being limited to only a few people, but you unlock more as you play Expeditions with them.
The story is simple - Make it Big! Be the most renown Explorer in the Renown Explorers Guild, but you only have 5 months (say: expeditions) to do so!
the gameplay is pretty simple - When you start an expedition you are dropped on a fixed map of knots, like in for example FTL. Travelling between nodes takes provisions of which you start with a limit, which you cant surpass with restocks. As you traverse the map towards your goal you will see that some Nodes have Markers "There is Knowledge/Fame/Gold to be found here!","There might be an encounter here!", "There might be a XXX Challenge here. A YYY would be helpful". those nodes hold short events that will on success gain you some tokens or more information or on fail may cost you provisions, give your team debuffs or end up costing you Resolve (say: Lives). When you reach your destination, you will enter a bigger chain of events to ultimately resolve what you came for and finish the mission.
Upon finishing any tokens you gained through events and battles will be converted into your 4 base resources: Fame, Knowledge, Money, Renown and a mission specific shop will open.
On the world map you can spend your resources as you wish - Knowledge to write thesises (say: give your team various buffs), Money to buy more and better equipment and Fame to either get better Items in Stores or to hire an enourage, that will boost the amount of resources you gain from tokens.
Renown is your actal score, and you have to pass the renown of the Lists 1st to "win" the game.
As it was in Reus - the Graphics are beautiful, the characters and their animations are just gorgeous
Music and sound is nice to listen too and get you an an adventuring mood
Gameplaywise this game throws a few balls out there and manages to juggle them well. the combat system actually goes pretty deep with its Mood System - every character has Speech (say Magic) abilities that give certain buffs or debuffs (for example a flattered character will take more damage from Speech attacks while a confident character wil deal more physical damage) and based on the overall mood of your approach and the enemies approach (forceful, Devious or Friendly - yes, you can complement your enemies to "death") your team will get a global buff/debuff based on a rock-Paper-Scissors system. A Forceful approach against a peaceful enemy will leave you at an advantage while a devious enemy will have you gasping for air quickly
I have a little beef with this game, since it is mostly luck based. the Skill checks require your explorers to have certain perks to better their odds, but most of the time you will be staring into 30 to 40% chances top if your perks dont match up well.
There also seem to be a few bugs still around, like a memory leak on long sessions or that a certainBosses healthbar was imprinted on every space he stopped.
Also if you dont immeadiately invest a few points into the first skill tree (thesises) you will find yourself short on supplies quickly. And if they run out you will get arandom until-the-end-of-the-exploration debuff that will stack and might cost your head.
with that the shortage of Resources might end up leaving you dry during the end if you splurge too much in the beginning.
The replayability is very high due to the many different possible combinations of teams.
A Definite Must play for fans of Reus or the old Adventuring days in general

This game is fun!  The kind of fun where you sit down to play for ten minutes to see what the game is like and finally stop two hours later because of prior engagements even though you would rather stay and play.  The game is inspired by The Legend of Zelda but it is definitely its own game.  It is almost impossible to look anywhere and not see Zelda referenced when talking about this game.  I didn't realize it but this created some preconceived notions for me of what the game should be like.  I was immediately surprised by how fluid the game felt.  Play control is precise and responsive.  I never had the feeling that I had pressed a button but my action didn't take place as I wanted because of frame delays.  I have been using a controller and I feel that this the true way to play the game.  The design of the game is such that I would go so far as to say that a controller is required (a controller may actually be required, I haven't tried a keyboard and mouse yet).  It did take me a little while to get back some of my old school gaming skills and get to where I could attack enemies without taking damage.  Songbringer is challenging and that is probably what I enjoy the most.  You can't just stand there and beat on an enemy.  You have to move and attack and dodge and avoid the other enemies.
While I am only two hours in to Songbringer, I am enjoying the story and really like the manner in which it is presented.
I was worried about the graphical style but that was an unnecessary concern.  I sometimes have trouble with losing track of my charachter with pixel art style action games.  With Songbringer this has not been a problem, not even slightly.
I like the music of the game.  I won't try to classify it as I am not a music aficionado and wouldn't get it correct.  For me, the music always seems to fit and provide the proper sense of ambience.  The main theme and boss battles are exciting.  The level background music seems to fade away.  The music is still there but it works to create the environment not clash with it an make itself obvious.

Right now I am in the process of playing every F.E.A.R. game so it was at most a few days ago since I played through the first one. This means the memory about F.E.A.R. 1 is still fresh in my mind. First of all, the one main problem with the first game were the boring, grey, office building type levels. On the plus side the AI was fairly competent, the guns felt good enough and the story while scarcely told was enough to motivate at least somewhat to continue. All in all it was a mechanicaly excellent game.
Going instantly to the second game after playing the first one (with expansions) was a bit jarring. The game certainly looks nicer and while in its core it is with no doubt F.E.A.R. the differences in the mechanics can throw you off a bit. First thing I had to realize was that there is no leaning anymore. At all. This was an often used feature in the first game which saved my sorry♥♥♥♥♥♥more than a few times. Secondly the guns don't just feel as good as before. Thirdly the AI might be a lot more competent than it is in other games but it just does not compare to the first game where the enemies constantly flanked me, and I went down in a few shots even in normal mode. Generally you seem to take a lot more hits in this one making it a hell of a lot easier. And lastly, one of the most fun aspects of the first F.E.A.R. the "kung-fu-moves" are reduced. Normal punching and air-kicking is still there but my beloved "sliding" seems sadly gone.
The story is told much better and the "scares" while still not really scary at least to me, do a fine job at setting the mood especially with all the fancy new effects. I don't know how you could comprehend what is happening if you haven't played the first one though.
The levels were much more diverse but had still that certain problem of "I just know when the enemies must be coming because I am suddenly just standing in this big empty room". Also there is the unnecessary addition of notes to find everywhere which feels rather forced.
To sum it up comparing to F.E.A.R. 1: Levels more diverse, story better told, mechanics went downhill towards an average shooter level.
So all in all a slighty above average shooter.
Although not as brilliant as the original F.E.A.R, this is still a very fun, albeit simple, FPS with a corny but fun story and very solid shooting mechanics, oh yeah, and the mech sequence is bad♥♥♥♥

Firstly I would like to say that this game is not all that bad when compared to the other RTS games out there at the moment, however for the fans of Sup Com and Forged Alliance this game is a great dissapointment. There are a great many changes and the entire game feels rushed and less smooth than the previous two, here are a few reasons why.
The complex tech trees: Gone. You now start with one tier of unit and minimal choices. Some people prefer this over higher tier units smashing the lower tiers but its simply a lazy option taken instead of actually balancing the different tiers.
The choices between different commander upgrades: Gone. Research will give you all the upgrades there is no choice involved.
The fine balance between extracters and power and the need to control enough deposits: Gone. Pump out those generic one tier generators and you will recieve far more mass from them than deposits. There is nothing to be gained by pushing out to control a majority of the map simply turtle it out behind your shields (we'll get to those in a moment) and stock up on units/arty/nukes
The careful construction of defences and shields for maximum overlap protection: Gone. Spam those shields as close as possible and you can hold off the world. There are some small differences between the different races shields but they all can still all build as many as they want without even thinking about an efficent base design.
The unique racial differences and strengths and weaknesses: Gone. First designer "hey guys are we going to make the units and structures have different statistics like the first game and have counter intelligence options for complex game strategy?" Design lead "nah screw that it sounds complicated, make all the shields and other structures have identical stats and get rid of the other stuff". Very dissapointing since the units from the first game were so unique but now there is no difference in choosing one faction from another.
The detailed textures and environments that made it a great looking game: Gone. Its extremely unusual for a series to have a large gap between a game and its sequal and to not improve the graphical quality, this bucks the trend and goes backwards.
Well organised unit co-ordination, grouping and movement: Gone. Walking into each other, spinning on one spot trying to collect something right beneath themselves and refusing to move are now the norms.
There are more but to be honest I've got to go purge this game from my memory by playing Forged Alliance so this will have to do.

When I first bought this game, I thought it was trash.   Now, they've refined it into a very simple Legend of Zelda throwback with some ARPG elements.   It's a fun little time waster, I think the main draw is the replay factor, trying out different weapons, going for personal challenges, that sort of thing.  Either way, I pulled this up yesterday expecting to still hate the thing and I ended up wasting 2 hours without even realizing it.
The combat is extremely simple and this feels bad at first, if you don't like it, grab a bow.   This game feels like it's meant to be played as an archer.
Don't expect deep gameplay - The dungeons are all very similar and fairly straightforward.  The overworld is a direct throwback to The Legend of Zelda (original NES) complete with mazes, hidden passages, helpful AND pointless "friends" to flesh the world out ever so slightly.    The main thing to do here is collect loot and slay bosses.
I also really like how when you clear out an area on the map, the enemies are replaced right away, but in many areas, this is by "baby" versions.  Just a nice touch.  As well as the rats in the dungeons, this is great and makes it nice to go farm hp for the boss without being a slog in every room because the enemies just respawn.
All in all, coming back to bit dungeon II, I am extremly impressed.  It's not the next Elder Scrolls, but surely you knew that from the promotional materials.  You get a great little romp through a retro world complete with the feeling of perma death AND a continue that you can keep picking up. bit Dungeon II is a great way to introduce newcomers to the world of rogue-lite games, with its simple and fast combat, easy and low-challenging difficulty, as well as with its cute pixel graphical presentation. Simplicity is the keyword here, from combat and story, to the way the game looks and functions, and it can be its strength as well as its weakness.
From the very start, game is pushing you toward aggressive stance in combat: always rushing enemies and spamming them with attacks, while only occasionally blocking when you fight with some of the tougher boss encounters. It will take you 2-3 hours to complete the game after which you can do everything from the scratch while keeping your levels and gear. Speaking of story, there is none – you stumble upon the ghost girl who is asking you to find her tomb and bury her remains, and that’s all you’ll ever find out story-wise. Variety of the loot is also very nice, I suppose…
Thing is there is nothing else to review in this game as its pretty barebones stuff: you’ll experience everything so fast that you’ll just move on and forget about it, but while it lasts, you’ll enjoy the game constantly. Bit Dungeons II is a great game for beginner rogue delvers, but you’ll soon crave for something more substantial and challenging.

Project Origin is a direct follow up to the original game released in 2005. It took Monolith 4 years to cook up a sequel and they decided not to change much on the formula that has worked once. But 4 years is a long time and sometimes innovation is better than playing it safe. That's exactly why Project Origin falls short of its predecessor. The formula remained the same, but the audience has changed.
The game picks up right the time when the first games is about to end. To be precise, it starts a couple of minutes before the end of F.E.A.R. You are a part of Delta Squad and you're sent to place the head of Armacham Technology Corporation into protective custody. It's when sh*t starts to get serious and a nuclear blast bakes most of the city as a result of the original F.E.A.R. team's endgame. In the rest of the game you move in and out of underground facilities trying to achieve your ultimate goal. Even though the campaign lasts only around 7 hours the story is detailed and interesting. On the other side, you have to pay attention to every detail that happens around you or told to you on the comm because if not you'll find yourself lost in the web organisations and projects thrown at you in every couple of hours. At least if you do get lost eventually right before the end of the game everything will be cleared up in 5 short minutes.
The gameplay is very similar to the first game. Little has changed; slow-mo shooting is still great but the novelty has faded in the past four years. You will meet various enemies during your gameplay starting from soldiers, genetically modified monsters, mechs to ghosts even. The game will always try to throw something new at you which is nice, but eventually you'll immediately recognize the spacey room where a firefight is going to take place in 3...2...1.
AI was a strong part of the first game and it returns in the second one too. However, it doesn't always work like it meant to be. Sometimes the enemies will be clever enough to kick over tables and take covers, but in other cases they will try to rush you through the same door where you'll stand and shoot them one by one. The Delta Squad, your mates aren't the most brightest either. Most of the times you'll see them splitting up and getting killed (because of the story) and the writers could've written better lines for the voice actors too. Being a psychological game you'll never feel surprised of your team members being killed off. What is worse you'll never feel pity for them because they're unlikable, two-dimensional dolls.
Visually F.E.A.R. 2 is a real mystery. On one hand it presents a great world with some stunning lighting effects and great destructibility, on the other hand it's ugly. Everything looks sharp when you move, but stop for a moment a take closer look at minor objects, like consoles or books on desks. They look downresd, blurry and pixelated. The devil is in the details as they say. In the year when hardware pushing games like Modern Warfare 2, Resident Evil 5 or Killzone 2 were put on the shelves of retailers this kind of laziness is disappointing. One can look aside when it comes to these problems, but then there is the audio. The sounds of guns are just atrocious; every one of them sounds like they were taken out from an 80s Atari 7800 game. Every shot you have to take with the shotgun or machine gun irritates your ears. It's like firing with toy guns from the crappiest Chinese manufacturer.
F.E.A.R. is a decent shooter with its flaws and assets. The formula that made the first game great has aged greatly and the horror factor is M.I.A. in most of the game. Great number of "tricks" has already been used up in the previous title or other games. When the horror is present the game feels like a real successor of the prequel, but those moments sadly end quickly. It definitely has its moments when it comes to shooting (the mech scenes are great), but drawbacks won't allow to have an experience like with the original F.E.A.R. game.
Rating: 68/100; Replay Value: 2/5; To Beat: 7 hours; Played on: normal.

I never expected to feel as compelled and excited by playing a 2D platformer as I did with Guacamelee. Its hook is a perfectly crafted gameplay, a brilliant level design, and a unique humorous tone.
Everything is built around the abilities of Juan, the main character, and this seems to be the key of its success in all its fronts.
The game world is progressively unlocked as you acquire new powers, which allow you to access those small spots you saw at the beginning, that you were not able to access, but you knew you'll be able to reach at some point. It reminds me of those magic moments I had while playing "Metroid" (SNES), or the awesome dungeons of any old-Zelda game.
The combat system is brilliant, and this is thanks to the design of the foes inhabitating this crazy Mexican-fantasy-world. Each enemy type is built around one of your combat abilities, so as you progress in the game, and you get new skills, a new enemy enters the scene, asking you to masterize that new ability you just acquired. Without noticing, you end up fighting big groups of creatures, each one of a different type, asking you to combine ALL of your abilities in some sort of coordinated choreography. The best part is that you do not even notice of how you end up "playing piano" with your gamepad. And this feels really good. Everyone would like to learn to play a piano, right?
Totally recommended.

Blood Money rewards skillful play with the Silent Assasin rating which is also useful for keeping you hidden and earning money, keeping your bills low and making it so people don't recognize you as "THAT KILLER FROM THE NEWS!". Your actions are recounted in a newspaper with custom variables relating to you. The story is about people trying to catch you. It's surprisingly compelling. A welcomed change to all the other Metroivania wannabes. Guacamelee offers a fresh mix of style and gameplay one would expect from this sub-genre of 2D games. It avoids the weapon based shooting combat of other games by employing a hand-to-hand combo system that is quite fun to play with and can be pretty rewarding on harder difficulty because it requires the player to use a variety of moves to be successful. You'll find yourself excited to come across enemies just so you can pull off huge combos with wrestling moves in the style of Lucha libre. Defeating enemies will reward you with money that can be used to purchase more combat moves, outfits that offer stat boosts, or upgrading the health and stamina bar.
While not fighting a somewhat limited set of enemies, Guacamelee's main gamepaly is actually the level traversing and its focus on platforming. At its best, the game requires the player to use Juan's, our protagonist, short list of power-ups such as the standard double jump to the wall running ability in order to manuever through the environment.  Another power-up that allows Juan to switch between two worlds on the fly adds to the clever level design. At its worse, it is basic jumping from one platform to another, but that doesn't detract from gameplay at all. Players will be searching hidden areas to find chests and more powerups. If you want to know what they are, you'll have to play the game yourself.
Guacamelee is not only fun to play, but visually and aurally, it's a treat. The art is cartoony with a Mexican theme and littered around the environment are some nods to videogames such as Super Mario, Zelda, and of course Metroid. There are geeky internet memes injected into the settings as well.
The music is played in mariachi style that incorporates sythn sounds and beats with the traditional classical guitar and horns that's usually upbeat and fast pased. Some of soundtrack has two versions, which you can listen to by switching between the two worlds. They're all very enjoyable to listen to and nicely accompany each setting of the game.
Guacamelee is a somewhat short but ultimately satisfying game to play. Experienced players will finish it in around five hours while skipping certain hidden items. Doing everything and getting 100% will extend the game to an extra hour or two. Doing so will offer an extra ending. For everyone else, you'll be enjoying a good 8-10 hours of gamplay so do yourself a favor and pick up Guacamelee!

Songbringer is a 3/4th perspective pixelated, science fiction, action adventure game with light role playing mechanics. In the game, you play the role of of Roq Epimetheos, a dude in space who likes partying and making music. Cruising the galaxy with his buddy Jib, they explore space along with the rest of the crew of a ship called “Songbringer”. After crashing onto the world of Ekzera, it’s up to cool dude Roq and his robot friend to stop an ancient evil from doing ancient evil(y) things. Packed with pixelated sword swinging, dungeon adventuring, and not-subtle-in-the-least Legend of Zelda inspirations, Roq will travel through a handful of dungeons, collect power ups, upgrade his weapons, defeat bosses, and save the universe from *dramatic noise* the snake people!
Songbringer starts off with Roq crashed off his bike. After picking up the nanosword (or not), Roq will explore the worldscape with Jib. The player will go into dungeons, kill baddies, find some nice loot, and help save the world. As you explore the dungeons and follow the story, the game will hint of certain larger events playing in the background. It’s a fairly bog-standard story, but it works just fine. Roq and Jib have the occasional bits of back and forth banter. I was a bit worried the game was going to take itself too seriously or have the main character’s “dude” factor just become annoying. Luckily, the banter isn’t long between characters, and Roq’s dudeness is kept to a few lines.
Ultimately, “Songbringer” is Legend of Zelda in a pixel-art style with more memorable visual appeal. You have different dungeons with a few themes, some mostly-passable puzzles to solve, and then a boss at the end of each dungeon. Roq’s main weapon (if the player chooses to pick it up) is the nanosword. You’ll also have the opportunity to find a hat, and some different flavors of bombs, as well as some loot drops off of enemies and random items (if you attack them) found in the overworld.
Occasionally, Roq will also find currency to buy things from some cave stores. The things you can buy vary in usefulness, but it’s nice that there’s an option. What isn’t nice about the stores, is that there was an item for 420 diamonds, and I couldn’t buy it because the game wouldn’t physically let me pick up more than 255. I think it’s a glitch, but even if it’s not, the game doesn’t indicate in anyway that your maximum wallet size can be upgraded.
There’s also the crafting, which is limited (again) in usefulness, and you can only craft things (from what I’ve played) on the ship Songbringer, which story wise, you only can enter a quarter way through the game. I wish there was more things you could combine in the game.
The combat isn’t bad, and it felt quite rewarding (at times). However, that doesn’t mean it doesn’t have issues.
For one, the hitboxes. Because touching most enemies hurts you, it means you have to stay a good chunk back from the enemies, limiting the uses of the sword. This would be fine if Roq had any ranged weapons, but his ranged weapons just don’t do as much damage in comparison. What’s worse, is that the player has a “blink” ability that he’ll find which allows him to teleport a few feet ahead. This would be fine, but because Roq gets hurt by touching some enemies, it means causing you damage because you can’t directly control where you blink to in terms of visually seeing “where” you’ll end up once blinking. You can also sometimes lose Roq behind enemies or bosses, getting hit unnecessarily as a result.
These hitbox issues go double for the player. I died at the final boss a lot. Not because I didn’t do well, but because the player’s hitbox seems to change. Either that, or the attack hitboxes, meaning the actual attack’s hitbox, is changing. The final boss in particular uses a lightning attack that killed me despite clearly not being even close to the strike. Sure, the player has a shield Roq can find and then use if he stands still, but it takes a second to activate which again, means you can’t control when you’re being hit. This only happened with the final boss, but it was still frustrating. It doesn’t help that a lot of the bosses you fight, you fight in tight spaces, limiting the amount of room you have to dodge.
These issues could have been prevented if ranged combat was more prevalent and useful, or if the player had a shield they could pull up at whim, and not just when they’re standing still. The combat ultimately boils down to mashing the attack button, and since there’s no shield and no secondary attack with any of the weapons, it means just mashing the attack button while being forced (at least in the beginning) to take some hits that could have been avoided if the former two things were present.
However, regardless of the issues, I still had fun and played through the game even with my frustrations. The world’s are procedurally generated, and it works. I wouldn’t say it adds replayability, but it works fine. There’s also a co-op mode that I didn’t try, and a permadeath mode which was fun.
Visually, the game looks great. Even being procedurally generated, the world looks fantastic to wander through. Great weather diversity, dynamic lighting, reflections, and more. The choice of colors is appealing, and the game just overall looks good.
Audio wise, as said with other game reviews I’ve done, the music’s fine for the game it’s in. However, it’s not on the level that I’d buy the soundtrack. Take that for what you will. At the least, if nothing else, the bizarre tunes were nice to hear while exploring the dungeons. The sound effects are nice and punchy, and the music is technological and mysterious. Both fit the game just fine.
In terms of controls, I have a few issues. You can adjust settings between two different modes for graphical fidelity,there’s an option for an unlocked FPS, you can change the sound levels, and other basic things. You even have rebindable controls for both controller and keyboard, but there’s an issue, which is to say, you can’t actually see the controls. At one point, I wanted to look at the controls I set to make sure I couldn’t make them better. Only to find that you can’t do that. If you check to rebind the controls, you have to rebind all the controls, not just one button or function. It doesn’t even let you exit the menu until you rebind all the controls over again. It’s not (again) a huge issue, but it’s (again) noteworthy. Other than that, the developer gets plus one internet points for having a borderless window mode that’s actually a borderless window, and plus a thousand internet points for having that set to default.
Overall, I had fun with Songbringer. I’ve been told it’s similar to “Hyper Light Drifter” in more than a few ways, and both are $19.99. Regardless, the game was fun and refreshing. I don’t know if the price tag fits the bill, but considering my initial experience lasted eight hours, I’d say it at least is worth it in terms of a raw ratio of hours played to price. But, I’d still be more inclined to suggest the game on sale, arguing that it’s biggest letdown is the lack of combat and play style diversity, ultimately making each experience largely the same regardless.
