This is the only game this year where I couldn't put the controller down.  All I wanted to do was to play more when I was away from my computer. Guacamelee has superb game mechanics and extremely responsive controls.  Although you can fail a lot of times at a given mission, there is zero frustration.  Best way I can describe Guacamelee's gameplay is that it has a "flow" and once you are in the zone it's a joy to play.  There is no point where the game cheats, and every error is due to the player not mastering the controls.  Being Mexican, this game had me smiling at a lot of things, the humor, the surprisingly authentic portrayal of a lot of Mexican folklore, the subtle way that is was playing with telenovelas tropes. Drinkbox clearly did their homework. It is also by far the funniest game since Psychonauts.

Ever play Super Metroid or Symphony on the Night? Well ever wanted to play those games as a luchadore? Then Guacamelee! Is the game for you!
Guacamelee! Is a beautiful 2D Metroid-Vania game with a, awesome Mexican theme. You play as Juan Aguacate, A farmer who becomes a Luchadore to SAVE THE WORLD! When the El Presidente’s Daughter is kidnapped by an evil ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ skeleton called Carlos Calaca. Or if you’re me, you checked out the steam Workshop and saw a Johnny Bravo mod and played the entire game as him.
The gameplay is just so much fun! 2D exploration, Fun challenging platforming and a deep and satisfying melee combat system. The combat at first is simple until you find a gym hosted by a giant chicken who teaches you combos and how to master them. The satisfaction you get when you pull of a big combo multiplier during combat is one of the games strongest points
The platforming is interesting. It’s pretty basic at first. You jump platform to platform as usual and learn how to wall jump. But your skills are tested later in the game. Eventually you get the ability to change between the Living and Dead world. And platforms rearrange between them. This means wall jumping between worlds and timing it just right to land on the other wall or platform. It can be frustrating but the game’s controls are perfect. If you screw up, it is your fault.
Graphically this game is beautiful. The unique over the top Mexican luchadore style of the game is just so much fun to look at. And I mean look at. In the background there are several references to other games, Memes and websites which you think might just be annoying but it just fits in the world naturally. The game is hilarious. Throughout most of it I was laughing. (Probably because I was playing as Johnny Bravo and could not stop quoting him) The dialogue is so intentionally bad it is funny. The character expression and humour just leaps out at you and it is fantastic.
Guacamelee! Is near perfect. My only complaint is that it is over too soon. I beat the game in 3 hours and 47 minutes. I just wish it was a lot longer. But those 3 hours was one hell of a fun trip. 9/10

It's hard to talk about this game without talking about Metroid or Castlevania. It's an obvious homage to the older games of Metroid and Castlevania, what many would say is a genre in it's own right. (Metroidvania anyone?).
Guacamelee has enough cojones to stand shoulder to shoulder with these older titles
The game starts you off as a as a regular amigo "Juan Aguacate" who becomes the otherworldly super Luchadore to save El Presidente's Daughter the love interest of Juan. She has been kidnapped and whisked away to the nearest Casa de Muertos by the evil, Carlos Calaca and it's up to Juan to save her.
As you explore through the huge expanding and beautifully designed areas you earn powers and skills to help you fight of a number of different enemies and to reach areas previous inaccessible. It's the standard formula for Metroidvania games and it has been executed very well here, the game takes it a little further with the Dark and Light side switching that reminded me of Legacy of Kain, which does make for some great brain bending platforming puzzles.
The art design in this game is nothing short of stunning and there are pop culture references and meme's galore. It's packed with detail, especially when you start to see the game from both light and dark themes.
At first the fighting feels very shallow but it isn't until you gain all your powers and had enough training with the Combo Chicken that it becomes apparent there is a lot of room for creativity in the combat. Knock someone up into the air, jump after them and overhead smash them to to group, pursue them with a ground slam, catch them mid air from a bounce and pile driving them to oblivion. It's a very satisfying experience!
Too long? Didn't read? If you're looking for a Metroidvania game with kick♥♥♥♥♥combat, good laughs and beautiful artwork, you should play Guacamelee!

So when I started considering whether I should recommend this game or not, I realized just how split my opinion on this game is. While I enjoyed most of it, there was a huge spike in difficulty at around the 4-5 hour mark (well, 4-5 hour mark for myself) whereas the enemies weren't the issue - it was the platforming. There was a point when everything so far had been smooth sailing when it came to the platforming and suddenly the flow came to a stop because I had to perform the platforming only to fail - but mainly just to see what's ahead. And so I had to pause the game and think about how to proceed. It really halted my enjoyment because... I actually had to stop playing for a minute or so every once in a while. And it was boring. With that being said, the platforming then takes a huge dip in difficulty as well, when you gain a couple more powers that really improve the flow again. Just know that there's that one section which will probably make you stop... and think.
I must say though that I was pleasently surprised by how tight the controls felt - on a keyboard. Normally, platformer games tend to be rather clunky and nearly unplayable on keyboards but Guacamelee nailed it, in my opinion. And it's not just the controls for general movement. Even the controls for fighting felt incredibly responsive and I had no issues whatsoever pulling off some rather effective combos (though do keep in mind that I'm terrible at pulling off combos in every game, ever...) So yeah, the controls really felt good and if the fact that you haven't got a gamepad puts you off, then I'll tell you right now: 'Don't worry about it, brah, 'sall good.'
The story is very cute. The characters are very interesting. Though one of the villains did leave me a bit disappointed since you had very little interaction with him beyond the occasional warning and I feel like a bit more backstory would've solved that problem. I would also say that there's another character who gets you out of a rather tight spot who I would've liked to see more of - mainly because when I found out who he is, I chuckled and imagined some rather interesting future interactions.
With all that said, I feel like this game is worth a playthrough. I didn't really feel compelled to play through it again on hard mode nor to get the alternate ending (though that's mainly because I imagine that I'd have too hard of a time obtaining the final 2-3 orbs), but definitely worth that one playthrough. That's all for me, folks.
Sincerely,
Crayt

In a nutshell, this is one of those games that gets its hooks into you quickly. Definitely set aside a couple of hours to solve this within your first playthrough.
I bought this knowing exactly what to expect from the game and with no spoilers. You are presented with very little information at first, leaving your own assumptions to build the story for you. The first few videos may confuse you, or have you believing in something else completely unrelated to the core story. You will continue to poke around and start to separate the truth from the lies. When you finally get to the big reveal, you're in for a treat.
From a design perspective, information is presented to you in a way that is very clever. If you miss a key word, certain videos repeat key words to get you on the right track. If you hit a dead end, there is a history that saves your recent searches. You can also save videos in a timeline if they seem as if they hold a vital clue to getting a little further in the story. All of these elements will ensure your success despite the vague nature of the videos.
Highly recommended for those who are looking for something different or mystery fans.

As a fan of the original series I was not thrilled by Sumpreme Commander 2.
VERY NEGATIVE OPINIONS!!!
ISSUES:
1.  Lack size
Sup Com 1 in 2007 handled up to 1000 units per player on maps that were huge where it would take you a long time to travel from one end to another.  Sup Com 2 on the otherhand boosted the size of units, reduced the number, and shrank the maps where the scale of Epicness was lost.
2.  Economy
Sup Com 1 had a dynamic economy system where you could build howevery much you want whenever you want, but it's speed and efficency was determined by your production of 2 resources(Mass and energy).  Sup Com 2 attempted to simplify the economy where you had to have the amount of resources at the time in order to build the unit.  While making the game easier it also lost some of the difficulty from balancing you economy while fighting and became rush mode for whoever could grab the most resource points to win.
3. Campaign
Sup Com 1 had a large and unique campain for each of the factions each had about 6 missions, but each mission was well paced and as you progress the AI also progresses in the bacground which enourages the player to be as quick as possible, because otherwise the AI will have a large army waitting should they delay too long.  Sup Com 2 has a short campain which are shallow with scripted events and poor AI which have a single track mind to do one task where the play can take all the time they wish with little urgency. Poor ending vs Sup Com 1

.
4. Multiplayer
Sup Com 1 Forged Alliance expansion still has an active player base on Forged Alliance Forever.  Sup Com 2 does not.  Just be WARNED there is a lot of elitism in the community vs newer players.

I was lucky enough to be the first judge to play this game during the 2015 Indie Game Maker Contest. When I finished it, I thought to myself, “I may have just played the winner.”Several weeks and seven other judges later, that prediction was accurate.
This enchanting adventure game follows the title character as she gets roped into house-sitting for a friend of her mother. Corinne quickly gets more than she bargained for when it’s revealed the house is haunted by numerous ghosts. These aren’t scary ghosts, just confused people trying to make sense of their new reality. The player interacts with them on a daily basis while growing and selling flowers to earn money and purchase food so the spirits can have their breakfast.
The game is filled with stunning custom artwork, but don’t assume that it only won because it’s so pretty. This game has wonderful story and characterization and the adventure gameplay is simple but fun. It embodies a theme of “growth” in two ways – the literal growing of flowers and fully realized character growth for most of the cast.
Seeing it on Steam is a proud moment and I look forward to playing the updated version. At the current price, you can't go wrong! Check it out!

Absolutely love this game.  The campaign, while short, is quite excellent.  There's several ways to beat a level, with the biggest limiting factor being your creativity.  The only downsides I've experienced are difficult camera controls (quite frustrating at the beginning) and the lack of content.  Once you beat all the levels the sandbox is only so fun - I guess that says something about the limits of my creativity.  Regardless, this is a great game, and easy to go back to every now and then.
The actual building takes a lot of thinking.  More often than not, parts made specifically for a certain function aren't the best choice.  For example, the "wing" pieces actually aren't your best choice if you want to fly.  Sure they work, but they're not the most efficient.  Some people might see this as a con, but I think it allows players to really get creative with their ideas and provides a satisfying challenge if you're looking to make an optimal machine. Youtube is really great for giving ideas if you need them.
While the content is rolling out slower than I'd hoped, it's still rolling out, which is a big deal considering the early access label.  It's nice to see a developer stick with their product and still interact with the community years after release.  I'm really hopeful that one day this game will finish, but even with where it's at now, I'd still easily recommend it - especially if it's on sale.

Only started playing the other day, but I really like it. It's something between Dungeon Defenders, Orcs Must Die, Man VS Machine (TF2) and Borderlands.
You have a team of up to 5 players and can do co-op story missions (hunting for a boss like in Borderlands or defending against waves like in Man VS machine / OMD / DD) or versus missions of three kinds, where you play against the similar team of players, but both sides have AI minions that follow their own paths. It's such a pity this game gets so much negative feedback.
I really enjoy this game.
That said, it's not for everyone. I would suggest watching some actual gameplay before purchasing, to avoid passing up on an awesome title because it isn't what you were expecting when you launched it.
Also, note that there is a mandatory prologue/tutorial mission, before gaining access to both Multiplayer and Story modes. It doesn't take long to complete, and like all tutorial missions, gives you a basic feel for the game's combat and levelling systems. The mission itself takes anywhere between 20-35min depending on how quickly you run through it, plus animated cutscenes on either side of it, so allow roughly an hour of your time, before you really get into the game.
I would definitely recommend players play through the Story Mode (to be fair, I always opt campaign over MP in games. Just a personal preference)
Matchmaking can be a pain at times, but nothing that can't be remedied through Steam or Discord groups.
The only downside to this game is the lack of optimisation.
Any other flaw is nothing more than a minor irritation at best.
There's a terrible self fulfilling prophecy of this game being pushed to F2P, that has marred it since its early days. It's a fate that has become more common than not, among MP focused FPS/MOBA titles. The only way to stop it from coming to fruition is  to support the game, its developers, and community, instead of constantly wishing for it to fail, forcing it to the realm of F2P, to encourage a wider playerbase and deeper player pool.
It truly would be a shame to see this gem go.

Renowned Explorers is, in many ways, reminiscent of FtL: Faster than Light. You lead a crew through a series of locations, some of which are just text-based choices, some of which are fighting encounters, many of which give you the opportunity to gather resources that you can later spend on upgrades and items that improve your crew. The game puts you in the shoes of a Dr. Livingstone-like explorer, going through the ruins of ancient civilizations looking for plunder. It's very good in this way. The art style is incredibly cute and a great asset to the game. Not only are the twenty different characters you can take on an expedition instantly recognisable, the character portraits in-game change when you affect their emotions, which is a lot of fun (making sheep sad is especially rewarding). The music is good as well, never distracting from the game, always adding to it.
A game like this, however, lives and dies with its events. Such games throw a lot of text at you, and it needs to be enjoyable. This, the game succeeds at. There are quite a number of cute little unique responses that make you want to replay the game to see how different characters would interact (for example, a pair of Hungarian lumberjacks gave me some extra goods because they were impressed by my moustache). As such, the game is quite good. It falters a bit in the combat, though. You can use three types of attacks (friendly, devious, and aggressive) to solve encounters, and they affect what you get out of the encounter, but they do tend to play out the same way in an encounter. You can do some nice tricks with it, but it doesn't feel as deep as in FtL. Another negative in the comparison with FtL is that you never really feel pressured. You use up your supplies to move through the map, but there aren't a lot of events that mess with you, so you can usually plan your entire expedition and proceed unrushed. The events do seem to have a lot more variation than in FtL, and the perks that you can unlock for your characters throughout the game make for extra interactions and unique responses to events.
All in all, Renowned Explorers is a very good game. It's enjoyable and its humour makes it very replayable. The humour, graphics, and sheer variety of events makes up for some of its shortcomings and makes it a game that I would be more likely to pick up again than FtL, where I have kind of already seen everything it has to offer. It could do, however, with some more depth in its combat system.
Update: the More to Explore expansion has come out, and it has massively improved on many aspects of the game. A number of balance issues have been solved, the new expeditions showcase some of the best design the Abbey Games team has to offer, and by including new campfire stories, there is a new reason to keep coming back to this game and replaying it. I do wish the player would be able to customise his or her campfire stories at the start of an expedition, but the expansion improves this game on all aspects.

Board game lovers and traditional strategy game lovers will find enjoyment out of Renowned Explorers: International Society in more ways then one. Good balance and variety will allow for gameplay that has surprising depth despite it being very simple on the surface with its Rock, Paper, Scissors mechanics. The presentation works to a certain extent and the ability to customize your party and create different adventures is fun, especially if you get into your own immersion of giving the characters backstories on what has happened. Reasonable writing combined with gameplay you'll want to come back to makes a game that I really wish had a multiplayer element to it, but still works never the less.

This is somewhat conflicting for me. Yes, I would recommend this game if it was a standalone. It's a solid, albeit somewhat simple RTS that is easy for newcomers to dive into. With that said, it is a complete downgrade from SupCom 1/FA. To put it into perspective, just one of the five factions in SupCom FA has almost as many unit types as all four in Supreme Commander 2.
But back to this game alone. If you are new to the series and want an RTS with some degree of depth, then this is it. But if not, or if you're a more seasoned RTS player, than pick up Supreme Commander Forged Alliance.

Supreme Commander 2 is a mere fraction of the original Supreme Commander.  They took everything I liked about the original and either simplified it or cut it out completely.  I would not recommend this game to anyone and if I had to sum it up in a single word it would be "Consolized".

There is nothing, NOTHING redeemable about this game in comparison to the original, and I've only played it less than 5 hours. Get the first game if you want a good game, and then get the expansion to the first if you want a great game. Then mod it to become even better than that. Don't. Waste. Your. Money. On. Trash. This is trash. More below.
From the limited unit selection, to the insufferably stupid resource handling, and the unskippable cutscenes SupCom 2 disappoints across almost every possible angle to disappoint. In the original SupCom, you played as a nameless "Supreme Commander," a single human being trained and chosen to pilot an Automated Command Units, IE of a god-machine that, by itself, can level entire cities within a day, yet can rule if not destroy an entire PLANET within hours by creating an infinitely replenishing army of tanks, planes, and ships.
It was a game of epic scale, where it didn't matter that you had absolutely no characterization, because though you played a walking war god, in the universe that wasn't really all that special. The galaxy was full of war gods protecting or annihilating regular mortals. Again, I use the phrase "epic scale" to describe why it wasn't important that your guy had no character arc, because he/she didn't NEED any. You, the player, ultimately didn't matter in the so-called Infinite War... except you do; you become the most important person in a thousand year war fought with god machines that no one fighting it sees any end towards until-... Well, I won't spoilt it, get the first game.
This is the genius of the original SupCom and it was carried over to FA; what made you special and important and integral to the story wasn't that you had daddy issues or someone to fight for. No, none of that small-scale, whiny, too-human ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, it was all about your skill as a Supreme Commander. It was about how well you piloted your god-machine  and its countless legions of mechanized death. Sometimes. I say sometimes because sometimes, in both games, events overtake your skill and you still wind up losing, yet surviving to fight another day.
I get the feeling there's none of that in this piece of hot garbage. Don't buy it. I genuinely hate it. It's made by people who don't know how to tell an engaging war story, the promised improvements to unit movement never materialized (and being a technical and mechanics guy that was particularly biting), and the only reason that the game "runs better" than the first one is because, again, of a failure of scale compared to the first game. You can't make huge armies because of the clunky, counter-intuitive resource scheme, and forced SLOWNESS of making things.
And now the short of it: From a sub-par plot that fails at grasping the scale of the universe that obviously no who made this cared about, to neutered unit selection, a laughably stupid unit customization scheme, clunky resource management, and unskippable cutscene featuring god-awful angst and horrendous voice-acting SupCom 2 is a load of feotid shrimp wrapped in a diaper. Avoid, avoid, avoid. Go buy the first game.

However, these features that make it easy to learn also make the game stagnate before too long, so more experienced players may want to play the original Supreme Commander, or it's expansion, Forged Alliance.
TL;DR: Good for beginners, not for experienced players

Payday : The Heist is a 4-player COOP FPS. Frist of all, I love FPSs. But this game isn't some regular FPS you play when you're bored. It is more than that : the principle is, you load up before playing to one of the 9 playable heists (7 without Wolf-pack DLC). You unlock more weapons and upgrades as you gain more cash and reputation that gets you to level 3 skill trees ; "Assault", "Sharpshooter", and "Support" (Plus "Technician" when you have the Wolf-pack). There are little things that differ with the way you play during heists, but the scenarios are, in fact, the same. ;)
You may think, as the heists never really change, that the game may be annoying after 10 hours, but the thing is, when you grab friends and play, it gets really fun to play on the highest difficulties or even replay in normal mode the heists you liked (I assure you punching Taxman in "Undercover" is really fun). Even if it's not made like this (or maybe a little bit), Payday : The Heist has a really good replay value. Plus the DLC adds a lot to the basic game (3 weapons, A FCKIN TURRET, 2 heists, and more), and doesn't cost much (10 bucks, but you can get it on sale).
To finish this review, I'd like to say that this game is one of the most interesting, most fun to play and one of my favorite games ever. Thanks for reading! :ccskull:

You like Metroidvanias, don't you?
If you even slightly answered in the affirmative to this question, get Guacamelee.  It is a beautiful, well designed Metroidvania full of style, humor, and imagination.  The impeccable presentation certainly doesn't disappoint, nor does the consistently hilarious writing and thoroughly excellent platforming.
Speaking of which, Guacamelee has some unexpected influences, including Wall Jumping right out of Super Meat Boy.
There's very little to complain about, short of difficulty spikes that can be overcome with a little persistence.  Overall, it's an extremely well polished game well deserving of your time and attention.

FANTASTIC.
Guacamelee = A metroidvania with a mexican luchdor and a pretty damn good melee combat system.
Guacamelee is what's called a "metroidvania". An open world 2D platformer with certain paths restricted until you obtain new traversal abilities. You can also backtrack to previous areas with your newly aquired abilities and find power ups and other secrets. As far as this genre goes, Guacamelee is one of the best.
Graphics  - It's a great looking game. The art is colorful and fits the game perfectly. Whatever outfit your character is wearing, the animation is smooth and fluid. In addition, there are a lot of little nods and easter eggs to pop culture and gaming sprinkled in and it really helps to give the world character.
Story - No surprises here. Typical "rescue the princess" story we've had since the dawn of time. It serves the game well enough, but don't expect any curveballs.
Gameplay - Control is tight and spot on. Moving around the levels feels great and you're consistenly given new abilities so it never feels boring. There's also a healthy dose of combat that has enough depth to keep you interested. Those moves you use to open up new areas? They also function as attacks. By the end of the game, you have a great set of skill at your disposal to take out the bad guys.
This bring me to one of my few complaints about this Guacamelee. Enemies will gain one to 5 different types of shields in addition to being in one of two worlds you can switch between, the enemy only being attackable in one world. It can be a bit much to deal with later in the game when there is so much going on, especially when the enemies seem to get their shield back almost instantly. Small gripe, but not enough to ruin the game.
One more thing. There are some downright devious platforming sections. Nothing as bad as Super Meat Boy or IWBTG, but they can get a bit hairy. Especially when you have to double jump, wall bounce, uppercut, wall bounce, etc... all in one combination. If you're into that, you'll love this game and you do feel great when you finally nail it.
Replay Value - There is a "good" ending if you find all the hidden pieces of a certain item, secrets to find and areas to go back and get to 100%. There are also a few sidequests, and a "hard" mode. Once you've beaten the game and gotten the good ending though, you've seen just about everything.
If you're even remotely a fan of metroidvanias, or platformers in general. Pick up Guacamelee. It's one of the best in the genre and more than that, it's a simply a great game.
Simply incredible. From the gameplay to the art style to the dialogue. Get this game.

One of the best 'metroidvania' type games I've ever played.  Juan grows stronger and more fun to play the further you advance, and are then able to backtrack and collect items in areas previously traversed for even more buffs.  There's a decent amount of optional stuff to do even after you beat it, and there are two endings depending on how much you did.  While I didn't think I'd like the art style or the theme, but I gave it a chance and it grew on me to the point where I thought I'd die if I didn't have Taco Bell at least once during my playthru and the music is still stuck in my head!  Combat feels tight, and wrestling power moves feel useful and satisfying.  The game is full of interesting characters, colorful culture, and hilarious jokes and memes that throw many a nod to the 'net and the legacy of gaming.  This is one of the few games I feel respects the gamer, but its a two way street.  It does rely on some tight timings for some of the later environmental puzzles but it's nothing that can't be done without a bit of practice and determination.  Stick with it, you'll become stronger.  (I beat it without help from any guides or looking up videos.)  I feel this well-designed friction that makes players better at a game as they play it, is something missing from most games of this era and Guacamelee has that magic in spades.  The imperfections I've noticed: significant lag with fullscreen+vsync (I had to play in a window for no lag) and some of the gameplay techniques are not as well documented or demonstrated as well as they could have been.  Recommended for a must-play game of this decade!  Ole!

First of, I bought this game for the full price of 4€ and I found it worth the money. You can get much less for (e.g. a cappuccino in some cafés). However, this game could be so much more. I finished in it 1.7h according to steam play time, and that includes the first boss of the next playthrough.
But here's what I like and dislike.
PROS:
- I personally like the graphics.
- The background tiles remind of older games like Zelda Link to the Past (SNES), only less colorful and also a bit more simplistic.
- The enemy sprites are done in a bit more detail and there's a wide variety of them which I enjoyed slaying.
- Most important, even thought it was short, I enjoyed the time playing this game and did not regret spending 4€ for ~90 minutes of entertainment.
- Even without an intro/tutorial, I had no problem understanding what the stats did. Some of them I came to understand "later" during the game when I picked up items that boosted them, but I never felt like that was something I should have known earlier.
- I enjoyed collecting / comparing weapons and items. The system is kept very simple in that you equip the new found item or leave it behind. No additional storage that allows you to carry stuff around you're not using, which forced me to think whether I really want to e.g. switch to sword+shield from my bow for increased damage but with the downside of fighting closer to enemies.
NEUTRAL:
- The soundtrack isn't all that great but I didn't find it annoying and I find it creates a SNES like atmosphere, which I enjoyed
- The sound effects reminded me of zelda and at some points even mario games to the point where I wondered if they where copy/pasted. It didn't bother me though, as I thought they where fitting in quite nicely
- The game is quite repetitive, which didn't bother me that much due to it's shortness. For the price, I think it suits the game. A more complex game with longer runtime would fetch a higher price and be a different story altogether, so considering that, I didn't felt bored while playing it. Making the game a bit more difficult and maybe requiring
- In the beginning it felt strange that I could shoot diagonally with my bow, but after a minute or two I got used to it.
CONS:
- The animations could have been a bit better as they seem chunky at times, e.g. the walk animation is interrupted when running into a wall.
- AI needs an overhaul. The whole game is too simple because of enemies standing around doing nothing or getting interrupted with each of my (fast, consecutive) blows.
- Boss fights have to be way harder. I could beat every single boss in a matter of seconds by spamming the A button and I didn't even care about taking damage due to my interrupts. The boss was usually able to hit 2 or 3 times before dying and never made much damage.
- No tactics needed. It would be nice if the game would ask a bit more than just spamming the A button. One way would be to allow players to carry potions around but decrease the frequency of potions appearing in the game. This would require players to consider running out of potions, instead of just doing the only possible way - spamming and hoping for a potion or life leech hit.
- While fixing the cons above would make the game better, something that really bothered me was the non existing ending. I would have expected some sort of cinematic, text, note or event that informs me that I have done whatever the quest was in the first place. Unfortunately, there is no story telling as far as I had noticed and there isn't any sort of ending. Not even a "Yay you did it! wanna try again?" or a mushroom telling me that the princess is in another castle. Instead, I ran through the door behind the boss only to end up where I started, same level, same gear and all enemies in the starting area are now way tougher than before. While this is an ok way to continue the game (playing again on a harder mode), I was a bit disappointed and had a bit of a "wait, that's it???" moment.
All in all, I can recommend the game as I did have fun. If you think 4€ is too much to ask for 1.5h of entertainment, then leave it or get it on sale.
If you're the developer, please add some sort of narration. A character that will tell a short story of what happened (why the bosses have to be defeated) or some form of proper ending will suffice to make the game more enjoyable.

Though to be perfectly honest I don't even know what to say about this one. I played it for a bit once when I bought it, died once, then forgot about it for over a year (I think). Now I came back to it out of boredom and finished it under 3 hours.
You're some dude who wakes up in a forest, some ghost girl tells you to bring her spirit to her grave, you then proceed to go on a genocide crusade until you beat the final boss and the game starts all over again.
In all honesty there's less story here than there is in your average Zelda game, so I can't really think of anything else to say.
SNES style. Aesthetics are more or less Link to the Past inspired (the dungeons are blatantly Link to the Past). The pixel art is nice, runs at 60FPS. Had the game crash on me once for some reason, but restarting the game fixed that with 0 progress lost.
There's some chiptune music in the game, which I barely paid attention to simply because it was either too quiet or it wasn't playing at all (maybe that was a problem on my end, I don't know).
Is it good? Is it bad? I don't know, it's alright, I guess, but nothing you'll be humming to yourself after you finish the game.
It's Link to the Past with levels, stats, permadeath and Diablo styled random loot. There's melee weapons, bows and magic tomes, armor types and accessories. The Overworld map is fairly big, but it won't take you long to explore all of it. Once you beat every dungeon in the Overworld you'll unlock the Dark World which contains the final dungeon and boss. Beat him and the game starts all over again, but you keep your items and levels.
The store page says this game is difficult. After finishing it I can safely say the amount of challenge you'll find in this is about the same as what you'll find in your average Zelda game.
You auto attack enemies by bumping into them (someone's played Ys), but you can also attack manually by pressing the attack button (holding it lets you do a charge attack, which I found completely useless). All you need to do to cheese the game is get a decent melee weapon and just spam the attack button. I beat every single living thing in the game, including the bosses, by simply standing in front of them and hammering the attack button. I did not die once (except for the very first time I played this and was busy figuring out the controls).
I got this from a roguelike bundle which contained no roguelikes and I paid $1 for everything, which essentially means this game costed me a couple of cents. For those few cents I got a fairly alright Link to the Past clone (which is the only Zelda game I actually like). So for that I'm giving it a thumbs up. Is it worth its $4 asking price? Well if you're a rabid Zelda fanboy and you constantly want more Zelda to play I guess you can buy it for that much. If you aren't wait for a sale or grab it off another Humble Bundle, if it ever appears again.

If you are looking for a cheap and simple roguelike game with control  of attack button + WASD,  this is one of them.  I picked this game up and quickly learned everything I need to after dying for the first time (about 10 minutes).  The next 2 hours and 20 minutes (Total playtime 2.5 hours as of this review), I have beaten the game. This game goes on forever, after beating the game, you are back in square one but you still have your level and equipment.  You will continue until permadeath.
The objective of the game is to go and find 5 dungeons and kill a boss in each one of them.  After killing 5 bosses, you need to head back to the portal that take you to the "Dark World".  From there, you venture to find the final dungeon to kill a boss.  But this time, there is another boss and it is the final boss.  Killing him gets you that sweet chest to open. Unfortunately, as a DEX character, I got a STR weapon.  Which means, I have to go through the whole process again in the now Endless mode to get to the chest in hopes of getting a DEX item.
Now I mentioned STR and DEX,  there are stats in this game.  They are STR, DEX, INT, SPR, and CON.   So basically, you will be choosing to be STR, DEX, or INT characters.  It depends on your current weapon because when you level up, you will be getting +2 __ and +1 CON (where the blank depends on your current weapon).  There are also additional stats such as (chance to...)  Cleave, Lifesteal, Smite...and more.  So it is pretty refreshing for this simple game.
Pretty much have the idea of this game is about.
PRO:
*~2 hours to complete each playthrough
*Simple and fun - easy to get into
*Equipments are random which spice up the game
*can be challenging
CON:
*Not well balanced.  In my first complete playthrough, I had +10 Lifesteal chest item, that alone, I was just able to stand there and smack all but final boss to death
*Bow weapons might be little too good. Fire too fast and kill enemies before they get to you. Especially if it comes with +lifesteal, no need to run and shoot at all. Just stand there.
*Can be too simple for some people
*I have slight difficulty of hitting enemies with a bow because of simple up down left right and diagonal directions, just have to line up.
*With the right stat setup, can virtually never die.
If you find yourself playing past first complete playthrough and into Endless mode,  I think most people will quit after getting bored or losing their stacked character (somehow) via permadeath.
With all this in mind, I recommend this game.  With a bargain price and your willingness to give this game 2-4 hours, It is a good game to pick up and play.

Metal Gear Solid V is a great but very flawed game. I'll divide my review into two sections, gameplay and story.
Gameplay
While it does have the best gameplay in the series, it suffers from the usual problems of open world games. These problems are the open world being fairly empty, and gameplay repetition. MGSV has two big hub worlds, and inside both of them are outposts and more large scale bases, which you can infiltrate. These are all over the map, and in between them are vast expenses of nothing except scenery. This makes the open world kind of pointless, seeing as you only really want to get to the places you can infiltrate. Any time spent in the world besides infiltration is just a time consuming trek from one base to another, and all it really acts as is filler. Now getting to my other point, the repetition. MGSV has 50 main missons, and 37 of them are related to the games story. These missions are unique missions with different objectives, though they do usually share a similar theme of either retrieving a target, or eliminating a target, but this isnt always the case. The other 13 are challenge varations of the missions. I have yet to do them all, but they up the difficulty of past missions, and add a new twist to keep thing interesting. An example being a mission where you have to destroy a target located in an enemy base, but can now only use weapons and items you find while doing the mission. The ones I've played have been extremely fun, and a fresh challenge which still feels new, because of the added difficulty and new mission rules. These 50 main missions are the highlight of the game. Now lets talk about side-ops. Side-ops are very hit and miss. They have similar objectives to the main missions, but with no story. The problem with these side-ops is that they reuse many of the main mission areas, but just reuse them. No new rules or anything, just the same area with a different objective. Also, some side-ops sometimes have you go to random places in the wildermess on the map, only to usually do a quick 3 minute objective. So most of your time doing these ops is just spent traveling. And then the next side-op you want to do could be half-way across the map. So you either travel all the way over there, or call down a helicopter, which acts as the games fast travel and is used to leave the hub world. The problem is this still takes around 3 minutes. You need to travel to a helicopter pick up point, wait for the helicopter to arrive, and then your taken through another loading screen, and after that your finally allowed to pick another destination. Yet even after that you need to wait for the helicopter to make its way to the ground to drop you off. Travel time in this game is simply too long and tedious. So basically, main missions are good and side-ops are pretty boring and very repetitive. Now that I've talked about the basic aspects of the game design that effects the gameplay, I'll discuss solely how the game plays, and it plays beautifully. MGSV gives you so many options in how you can take on these missions, with multiple points of entry in a base and multiple ways to manipulate things inside and around the base. You also have a plethora of weapons which get better and better over time, giving you a great sense if progression. This progression also links with the motherbase building part of the game. This part being building your own mercenary group, Diamond Dogs, along with its base of opeartion. Throughout the game your able use GMP (the games currency) to expand your motherbase, allowing you to obtain more soilders. You obtain new soilders for your base by doing missions and recovering enemy soilders out in the field. You can scan any enemy soilder while in the hub world, check his stats, and knock him out and extract him back to mother base, he'll then be convinced into working for you, and become part of your team. The better people you have, the better your weapon and item arsenal. This is once again great progression, as it incentives not just running and gunning, but carefully considering your options when taking on a mission, as you'll want to maximize your rewards. There's also a multiplayer motherbase invasion mode, where people can invade your base, and you can invade theres, but I've had fairly little experience with this, as I've stuck mostly to the singleplayer, so I have no real opinion on it. So that covers the gameplay, MGSV does have some poor game design choices, along with some bad side-ops, but the gameplay and core 50 missions are more than worth the money, and has some of the best stealth gameplay to ever grace the industry.
Story (No Spoilers)
I've played every canonical Metal Gear game, and story wise, MGSV is the second worst, only beating out MGS: Peace Walker. MGSV's story is made up of two chapters, with chapter one consisting of 30 story missions, and chapter 2 consisting of 7 story missions, along with 13 missions that are past missions with different rules. Chapter 1 is pretty good, it has an interesting story and a solid antagonist. Though its not nearly as good as the other MGS games, its entertaining. The problems begin in chapter 2. Chapter 2 has pacing issues, where story missions just kind of appear after doing other various missions, and it all feels very loosely connected. Like, the ending mission of the game literally comes out if nowhere, and has absolutely no build up. Though I do like the ending itself and I think it sort of makes up for a lackluster chapter 2, it still feels out of left field. Also, one of chapter 2's arcs is unfinished. There was supposed to be a mission 51, which would explain a few stroy details in the game, but it was cut because of time constraints. Cutscenes and story details were released by konami though, so after finishing the game, be sure to look up these details for a better conclusion. Chapter 2 really isnt that good. But overall, I'd say the story isnt terrible, just really lacking, especially by MGS standards.
Conclusion
MGSV is an ingenious stealth game, muddled by some poor design choices and a lackluster story. So I'll sum up the game like this. If you solely play a game for gameplay and are a fan of the stealth genre, then this game is for you. If you play a game for story more than gameplay, and havent played prior MGS games, I wouldn't recommend it. Though I'd recommend MGS 1-4 as they are far more story rich. If you have played prior MGS games, I'd recommend this game either way, as it does give some story details MGS fans will want to hear, and I assume you like stealth games if you've played the other games, and the gameplay is great. So in conclusion, V delivers on gameplay but falls short on story, but I'd still recommend, as it truly is one of the best stealth games from a gameplay standpoint.

Navigating the Trilogy is simple: directional buttons, and "A" and "B". No, the old Konami code won't work in this game (I tried), but learning how to play was rewarding enough for progression. You play different roles which switch between scenes and RPGs to guide you through the story. It's simply straight up into a mash up of Bible Adventures and Pokemon. After some trial and error, I learned the importance of leveling up, equipping things, and using 'miracles" to my advantage. Especially for the pacifist who will see that refraining from a physical attack isn't going to help - at least use this holy "magic" to get around.
There aren't any real difficult puzzles to solve, but when you learn what you're doing, getting around isn't much of an obstacle. Although at the time I did wish someone seriously made a guide, I worked in the blind, but realized how easy it actually is if I just tried a little work. Playing and losing wasn't punishing, so it was worth a few hours of play. Perhaps the developer could have expanded this series with the Old Testament (after all, Adam and Eve already appears in the Rise RPG), and the stories continuing after the resurrection, including what could be the epic battle of Armageddon....but who knows?
Certain bible thumpers should be ignored (remember that bit about false prophets?). With its dry humor, flashy graphics, and simplistic format, I found it an entertaining introduction to the New Testament, blending key passages and the story to a new modern twist fitting our culture. What is the King James translation, when you have the Gamer's edition? This is no different than the existence of the LOLCat Bible. If you have time to kill, this should keep you occupied.

Shank 2 is the second game in the Shank franchise by Klei Entertainment, the wonderful people behind Mark of the Ninja. It's a moot point to discuss the merits of a 20 year game like Police Quest: SWAT but considering I bought this along with a majority of the Sierra catalogue on Steam, I thought it may be best to warn prospective buyers who think this game stands on it's own individually. In short: It doesn't.
Police Quest: SWAT is an FMV adventure game by Sierra intended to be played on PC. As previously stated, it is indeed a very old game, but despite that when I ran it on a modern PC with the bells and whistles, it works effortlessly, so it'll play as good if not better than if you played it when it first came out.
There's a lot of good with this game, albeit the majority of it lies in the gimmicks. In SWAT, you can allow yourself to be educated in the ways of Police SWAT training (Circa 90's in Los Angeles) and occasionally put some of the knowledge you get to the test in about 8 or so scenarios. The game seems to be overly detailed, which can be good if you're really REALLY into Police tactics and equipment.
Now for the bad, and hoo boy is there a lot of bad. After spending plenty of time on the range with small arms and Sniper training, learning about the various hand-signals and LASH radio system, as well as police tactics and lingo, you'd think this would allow some varied approaches to situations, right? No. Not at all. This is a walkthrough-mandatory game with certain missions. Your reaction time with weapons is irrelevent, if the game decides that a fragile old lady (literally the situation) with a gun taking a full 3 seconds to aim and fire on your team and you is what's going to happen, If you don't play according to the walkthrough, you will die and die a lot. What's worse is that the game mocks you for trying to do things without a walkthrough, by having suspects that warp reality to be in different places, depending entirely on what scene it is. That wouldn't be so bad, but this isn't a SCI-FI game.
Now, you might believe that you have the reaction time to shoot the old lady, and you're probably right and the game already trains you more in the use of your firearm than literally any and all other equipment. (There are no training missions in this game beyond the firing range) However, all suspects in this game up until the point where you get sick of the game and stop playing have cutscene immunity. By this, I mean that as soon as you deviate from the walkthrough, the game will take all control away from you, the suspect appears, and you die. So even if that old lady literally fumbles with her gun, you can't do anything.
What's worse is the equipment system. Because this is an adventure game, you select the different equipment/commands for the situation and use it appropriately. However, you are rarely going to have time enough to select the equipment and callout commands that you think would be necessary for the situation, since there's very little downtime in some scenarios. As far as I know, there's no hotkeys to remedy this.
I mentioned time there, and that's because the worst part of this game is the arbitrary time limits. One mission that deals with a bomb threat is what inspired me to make this review. It starts off normal, the SWAT team approaches the entryway of the building, and waits your command. If you don't act within literally 2 seconds, you die. This is the result of a Stealth approach, and there is ample time to respond to the shooter, but because the *game* decided you can't shoot, there is nothing you can do. Oh, sniper planted on the entry side to provide cover? No, you die. Click on the door and try to rush in? No, doors don't work that way silly. Oh, I got an item for thi- Too late, scrolling for the item you are interrupted and die. There's no reason for these time limits almost ever, they're just there to provide tension. The worst part is that because this game looks so dated, I started wondering how people with ruddy keyboards and trackball mice were supposed to react.
My litmus test for if an adventure game is worth it is if the gameplay is worthwhile. This title is not. It's inordinarily difficult to do a blind playthrough of and difficult even if you rely on one of the rare and elusive walkthroughs for this game. Watch a playthrough or letsplay of this instead and you'll save yourself the frustration.

Guacamelee is a rare gem and has been recognized as such by many review sites.
To quickly summarize, Guacamelee tells the story of Juan, a seemingly common agave farmer, living on the outskirts of a town where luchadores (a style of masked Mexican free-wrestlers) seem to be idolized by everyone including Juan himself, who appears to be an aspiring luchadore that just couldn't make the cut.
Everyone in town is preparing for Dia de Muertos (Day of the Dead), a Mexican holiday celebrating friends and family that have passed away, when a mysterious figure calling himself Calaca shows up with his minions and abducts El Presidente's daughter, a woman whom appears to have been a good childhood friend of Juan's. When Juan tries to stop Calaca, he is clearly outmatched and gets sent to the land of the dead, which parallels the land of the living. There, he finds a mystical luchadore mask which transforms him into a legit luchadore when he puts it on.  With his new-found luchadore powers, Juan will have to go back and forth across the land of the living and that of the dead, plough through hoards of enemies, navigate obstacles and solve engaging puzzles in order to catch up to Calaca and save El Presidente's daughter.
Stylistically, the game is remarkable and consistent in its theme. Personally, I'm a sucker for edgeless 2D visuals that depend on colour contrast alone, as opposed to lines, to mark the contours of objects. Other examples of this style can be seen in works such as Locoroco and Samurai Jack. Usually this style makes use of more saturated colours for the visuals to work and, as a result, everything feels much more vibrant and lively.
This edgeless visual style also lent itself very well to the game's very Mexican oriented aesthetic, which grew on me very quickly. Combined with 2D lighting effects and shader tricks, the game floods your eyes with graphical goodies that don't cease to amaze. Furthermore, most important characters have a very distinct style all to themselves from the way they look to the way they move and speak, which adds a lot of life and engagement to the experience.
The gameplay in Gacamelee is very solid. The controls always feel very solid and there's very good feedback for when you can and can't do certain things. You never feel cheated by the game and feel like you have complete control over Juan. This is fantastic for moments when you're trying to solve all the very well-tailored platforming puzzles sprinkled throughout the game.
In addition, a huge highlight of Guacamelee is the combat mechanics. I haven't felt this way about combo mechanics since I experienced the original installment of Devil May Cry for the first time. Sure, you can get by with doing basic combos or no combos at all, but you can get really creative with the combos you perform to the point where you feel like you have your very own fighting style. Even if you don't consider yourself great at performing combos, there's a friendly giant rooster and his skeleton there to help you get into it. Even if you get a little frustrated at first, stick to it and you will add a whole other dimension to your gameplay experience.
There are also many nuanced details in every interaction that I really appreciated. You can feel the impact of your hits, getting health and stamina increases is very rewarding and the same can be said for chaining particularly long combos. It's obvious that a lot of attention and care was put into designing a lot of these interactions.
Silent protaganists don't always work, but this is definitely not the case with Guacamelee. I really feel like I'm in Juan's lucha-boots when encountering story elements and the tight controls only reinforce the sense of immersion.
As I mentioned before, I fell in love with the whole Mexican theme and there are many references that made me want to know more about some elements of Mexican culture mentioned or displayed throughout the game. In addition to this there are many, many classic video game references to be spotted everywhere, from Castle Crashers to Majora's Mask to Super Mario Bros., Megaman, FEZ and more.
All in all, I think it's obvious at this point that I just love this game to the core. Definitely recommended, especially for the price at which it's being sold. Get this game.

The port is terrible.  It looks like absolute garbage on my 28" monitor.  The controls are very clunky: You have to be right on top of the bad guys to hit them with melee weapons and block is assigned to the same button as attack (you cannot remap buttons).  The ranged weapons (bows specifically) are wildly OP.  You can get some off-hand magic items but when they proc seems utterly random.  You end up mostly button mashing groups of badies.  The only factor that decides victory on a stage/dungeon/boss is gear.  You simply grind mobs to get gear.  You get 3 lives and then you're done and have to start over.  The result is you relentlessly grinding for gear before boss fights - going through the same maps over and over again.
This might have been cool on a cellphone but playing on a computer is a waste of time.  There are too many good games to spend time on something like this.  Great idea, poor execution.  2/10

I've heard people say that the FEAR sequels aren't worth the time to play, that they've decreased in quality over the years. However, since I loved the first FEAR and it's expansions and since FEAR 2 was relatively cheap I decided to give it a whirl, and I'm glad I did.
One of the things I loved most about the first game was the dynamic gore system, FEAR 2 amps the gore up, almost making the gore on par with Left 4 Dead 2 despite it's engine age. Enemy dismemberment is still brutal and satisfying, especially with the tight-as-a-toigar shooting mechanics. The combat is fast-paced and sends your heart rate soaring, with level design and first-person animations that are immersive and with an inventory that can easily be depleted if you're not cautious. Just like FEAR 1, the combat is the top-selling point making the entire gameplay experience delicious. The developers also improved on the combat, granting the player an extra two weapon slots, more powerful firearms including sniper rifles and flamethrowers and even the ability to further interact with the world in the form of creating improvised cover against enemy fire, you can slide out couches, push over cabinets, and yes, even flip tables
(╯°□°）╯︵ ┻━┻
While FEAR 2 improves on all of FEAR's strong points, all the weak points remain untouched. The story is yet again lacking, failing to grab my interest and any exposition to it results in my impatient finger-tapping, the characters all feel two-dimensional and seemingly only exist to die at a later point in the game. The worst part of FEAR 2 is quite easily the creepy little girl jump scares. Jump scares are cheap shots, with no build-up and having no need for atmosphere, they are a blemish upon this game. One thing I was dissapointed about was the removal of Q+E leaning, which left me more exposed to incoming fire that I felt was needed, as well as the removal of quick-saves, leaving me 100% dependant on the foul teet of autosaves.
Ignoring my quips, FEAR 2 is a really fun game, with it's combat, music, level design and explosive action, I'd definately recommend any players of the first FEAR to give this one a go.

Brief: Score: 72/100.  A good SHOOT ‘EM UP that’s definitely worth playing.
Phoenix Force is mostly about patience and avoiding damage.  The main gun is auto fire, so as long as you avoid damage you will eventually kill the enemy.  The more skillful players, who can memorize the bullet patterns, will be able to take down enemies by being more aggressive and jumping into the bullet hell more often.  Again, patience is the most power skill since one hit means death.  The enemies are basically all bosses. You meet a new boss in one level, then you face off against the new boss and a combination of the other bosses in later levels.  The game is a nice grind, since there are about 100 levels.  The graphics are passable.  Don’t expect to see amazing effects that you might run into in the top games in the genre.  Still, for the price, it’s a very good experience.  In fact, if you can pick it up during a sale, it probably is a must buy if you care about “bang for the buck” purchases.

The original Shank strongly harkened back to a Metal Slug type of game. The fighting system in Shank 2 is much more complex. You have multiple weapon loadouts and various combos. The style is very close to fighting games. You have fast attacks, strong attacks, juggles, grabs, pounces, counters, ranged, and grenades. You also can dodge with the right stick which adds a lot of depth to the game. It reminds me of a mix between the Arkham games and Super Smash Brothers. The game is much harder than the original Shank. Even on normal difficulty you need to really pay attention to enemies and learn the cues and how to counter them. This isn't really a beat'em up, but more of a metroidvania style game with a strong fighting system. I strongly recommend it, but only for people who like fighting games and a challenge

Hitman: Blood Money has been widely regarded as the best of the Hitman games. It offers a wide variety of nonlinear maps and numerous ways to execute your target. There are multiple incentives for exploring the levels; sometimes you can find disguises that would be near impossible to find otherwise. Other times you can find optional mission objectives like retrieving a briefcase full of diamonds.
The element that makes Blood Money stand out from the previous Hitman games is how you want to approach your target. For instance, say your mission is to assassinate a target in a mansion. You can kick down the door and gun down anyone between you and your target. You can pick the lock on the fence, climb up a drainpipe, sneak in through the window and garrote your target. You can drop down the chimney dressed like Father Christmas. And when it comes to killing the target, you can choose anything in between. Maybe you want to bring a sniper rifle and double tap the target through the window. Maybe you want to disguise as a butler and serve a poisoned martini. Maybe you want to break his neck with your own two hands. The choice is yours.
Where Blood Money stumbles is with its environmental kills. IO seems to adhere to the concept of "make the beginning first, ending second, and everything else afterward." The advantage of this strategy is that if anything gets rushed out, it will be the stuff in the middle that no one cares about. But when the beginning is an out-of-place linear level with mandatory gun combat, and (without wishing to spoil) the ending appears to not even be playable, then the best part is the juicy center. In this regard, Blood Money has a few blemishes on an otherwise flawless game.
Some levels have no ways of making the kill look like an accident (something that is almost required for the highest rankings), while others are downright ridiculous. One mission in particular sticks out: there are three targets and only one target can be killed in an "accident". The "accidental" kill is (hope you're ready because this will blow your mind) a suspended piano. Yes. A piano that the target willingly stands under and can be dropped by a landmine detonated remotely. Did I forget to mention that this mission takes place on Mardi Gras? Where there are people and witnesses everywhere? Another mission involves killing a target at a recreational center. The camera zoomed in on him bench pressing some weights, and the implication I got was to add some more weight when he wasn't looking and crush him. This didn't work, because the accidental kill was getting behind him and strangling him with the weights. I was fine with this until a guard saw me doing this and shot at me.
Overall, Blood Money is still good, even great. Nothing is more satisfying than watching a row of dominoes that you've spent the past hour or so setting up collapse one after another. If you play this game, expect barrels of fun as you set up elaborate death traps that the targets fall right into. But you should also expect some limitation to what can and can't work on a target.

This game.... is just boring!
The graphics are not bad and I do like the design of the phoenixes, but when it comes to a flying shoot'em up game, the most important aspect of the game is not just moving around, but also mashing the fire button until your thumb breaks appart from killing a bombard of enemies, and the collection of power-ups... this game has none of those.
Right off the bat, the only controls you have is the D-Pad (or WASD or arrows, if you please). The game fires by itself, you just have to move around and avoid projectiles and bosses from one-hit-killing you, which I'm ok with, that adds to the challenge, but when the challenge is based on just dodging... where is the fun?
And it's considered to be a "bullet hell" game, which isn't wrong, but... just fighting bosses really sets a limit, a no-enjoyable one. Sure! There're different bosses, but they tend to repeat them.
Do you wanna play this game with a friend? Well jokes on you! This game is single player... and it's not like there's a lack of characters to choose from, but you can only play solo. Just another forever-alone game.
Lack of power-ups and lack of enemies to kill (sure, some bosses send minions to kill you, but that's about it). It has a leveling-up system though and each character has their own particularity and special attack, I'll give you that.
Again, it is challenging, but it can be even more challenging when you:
- Go through a stage;
- Kill enemies and collect power-ups (again);
- ARE ABLE TO PRESS A FIRE BUTTON. This really pisses me off, it just doesn't give you any satisfaction. And I consider cheatting the power of having a turbo button, that's pretty much the same as auto-fire.
And yes, you can say I only played for like 15 minutes, that it's an indie game and that I got it for a really cheap price (I think it was 50 cents or so), but that doesn't make up for what I've experienced here, I played it for that time and uninstalled it, I wouldn't have paid 5 bucks for this.
I do see potential, but they need to come up with something better than that.
If shoot'em up games from now on are gonna be auto-fire... then I'm getting off this train.

My initial reaction was one of hostile confusion. While the format of interaction (searching through a database using keywords) was immediately comprehensible even without a tutorial, my bewilderment stemmed from completely not knowing the goal and not understanding how the game will check against its completion. Imagine a sandbox open-world title - maybe Minecraft; you are dropped into the world with no explanation, yet instinct or experience immediately imply the objective - "survive". But here... what are we doing here? And why?
So I dove in anyway, and it was only up from there. Yes, I suppose the "gameplay" is "groundbreaking" in that nevah-been-done-before manner. But that alone can not make it good; and in fact it's not that great. Limiting results to 5 from any given search feels asinine, yet is entirely understandable from a balancing perspective. What won me over in the end, was the quality of the narrative told within - its twists and nuances. I found the story supremely enjoyable overall, and had a lot of fun unraveling it. The game really managed to get me into a certain... "
" where I would stand up, briskly walk back and forth while ordering and sequencing in my mind the various statements, creating theories and evaluating them. It's not very hard though. I had a pretty good (and correct!) idea of what happened by the time I'd viewed maybe 30% of the video clips. Past that it was just about ironing out the kinks in my - eventually validated - assumptions... and getting the achievements. Which isn't hard either, considering the developers were kind enough to include all kinds of delightful methods of
improving your experience, should you wish to use them. Oh, and the acting of this one person we see on screen is definitely adequate, with some very minor areas for improvement. Like the whole product, I viewed it warily at first but then warmed up to it by leaps and bounds.
So yeah. If you insist on concrete, robust gameplay, Her Story might not be your cup of tea. Conversely, if you like experimental things or the "games are art" angle, you'll probably enjoy it. I'm recommending it with the caveat that a good command of English is required to fully appreciate the plot, even though subtitles are available.

Quite simply, Her Story does something different with the "video game" medium and does so successfully.  It's certainly more of a puzzle than a game, but reestablishing the boundaries of what is a "game" is something we should all be encouraging.  This is by no means a long an arduous experience, but at its current price; it's more than reasonable.  At the time of this writing, I've logged 5 hours of play and I'll likely never load the game again.  Beyond that fact, I would say the last 2.5 hours of my time logged was associated with achievement hunting.  Even so, I feel completely satisfied with the purchase and hope that others are encouraged to think outside the box and experience Her Story.

This game leans heavily on Analouge: A Hate Story. Not when it comes to the story, but when it comes to the uncovering mechanics. Sadly, it is actually worse than its inspiration. While Analouge paces the uncovering of the story "from the past" by allowing the player to access only a couple specific pieces of archived information at a time, Her Story just dumps the whole database on you at once and leaves the uncovering of the story "from the past" to your google foo.
Sadly for this game, I am really good at google foo. I am not bragging, but unfortunatly I stumbled upon the "twist" of the game ridicilously early. First three minutes, to be precise. While the story itself is still interesting, it had exactly nill mystery or atmosphere to it for me, which it obviously tried very hard to build with some of the clips hinting and suggesting wildly while not giving away too much. Too bad that someone savvy or lucky enough can just randomly scroll over right to the ending and spoil themselves within the mechanics to the game. Again, Analouge did this much more elegantly by limiting how much you can access. I am not going into details since I am trying to avoid spoilers to both games. Point is, Analouge had multiple moments of story discovery which felt like gutpunches because you uncovered resolutions to previous hinted or told stories, while in Her Story the pacing is left completely to the players hands. Without any guidance. There is exactly one single guideline, right at the beginning, and it feels like a tutorial guideline while also being one of the most important puzzle pieces.
The five video at a time search limit is a mechanic obviously meant to stop people from typing in some of the more obvious to occur words by obfuscating the database with 'filler' clips. Problem is this is quite a tad annoying as the filler clips are often under 10 seconds and not very interesting, and it also obfuscates any kind of overview one would have while doing an actual search. The other tools provided by the game are good enough, and the desktop enviroment is immersive and I'd even call it clever, if it hadn't been done before. No not by Analouge, but by an even earlier game by Love: Digital a Love Story. Now that I've written this out, "Her Story" seems to be a bit of a reference to these games, both ending on story? Or just coincidence? Anyway, even other games have been doing this before so while its nice, I can't give it originality points.
Loves games tend to include quite a bit of engagment with NPC's/characters inside the games world. Her Story also tried this, but this kind of interaction is surprisingly limited. The one time it did occur, it was effective and the game predicted precisely what I wanted to say at that moment. But otherwise you will feel isolated and as if you are watching an indie movie, not playing a game. As much as Analouge and other VN's get trashed for just being 'read and click' games, Her Story sadly has even less interaction for a game. What the game did make me, is pull out a pen and tiny note paper to write down all the search terms that came to my mind while watching the videos. Striking out terms as I search them was a small game in of itself, and felt very satisfying.
Her story is actually a interesting story, when we are talking about the story itself. It was surprisingly simple, when you break it down, but it is represented well, the acting is surprisingly good and I am sure if watched chronologically this would make for an alrighty thriller found footage movie or an ok episode of a crime TV show. There's been thought and details put into it despite the main premise being a bit... stretching believability.
Too bad about the pacing being dictated by pure luck. Still, this is quality work trying to experiment with the medium and format, and I certainly appreciate it. It doesn't have nearly the same catharsis or emotional engagement as Analouge or other Love games had for me, but it is interesting in its own right, hence my recommendation. I can see the criticism, and despite my general inide game elitism I can agree that this game can feel a bit of a chore and uninspired at moments, and that it has very little interaction to offer. The story itself is just a bit above average. And yet it is an interesting way of spending a couple hours, and if you are a person who appreaciates a bit more artsy videogames, the indie dev scene or alternative ways to tell a story, you should certainly enjoy this game.

I didn't think I would like this game, but I ended up really enjoying it.  I even liked it enough to play through it twice to get all the achievements.
First off, this is a rogue-like zelda-styled action rpg.  I haven't played a ton of rogue-likes, but this one is a little bit more forgiving since you have a decent health bar and one extra life.  If you die and use your life it is then possible to find another, so don't let the rogue-like element scare you too much if you don't play those very much.  That being said, don't expect to beat the game on your first try.  It takes some learning to master the combat and gain an understanding of the game before you can really progress far.  It is a challenging game, but once you get the hang of everything you can do pretty well.
I really liked the zelda-styled art direction.  It made the game feel familiar while still having its own personality.  The soundtrack is awesome, using retro sound bits and modern techno elements.  It is definitely worth getting the soundtrack.  I also really liked the combat system.  The controls seem simple, but mastering the positioning and timing takes practice.  The level up system also allows for a lot of depth, since you can choose how to specialize your character in each playthrough and you have to choose which weapons to use.  Since the enemies scale to your level the game is always challenging, but not unfair.
The downsides are that when you find a really powerful weapon and it doesn't match your build you may have to take it anyways just so you have a tough weapon.  With scaling enemy levels (including bosses) it doesn't really matter where you go first in the game, which makes progression hard to track.  It also eliminates any plot (beyond a very basic one at least).  That won't bother you if you are just looking for solid gameplay, good graphics, and a great soundtrack.
Anyways, I would definitely recommend this game.

Klei Entertainment did not disappoint with Shank 2. Inspired by Grindhouse flicks (from what I've read) Shank 2 places you in the shoes of Shank. I don't really know much about Shank since I didn't play the first game but I will give my 2 cents on the story and gameplay.
Story:
The story is kind of weak. Shank goes to his hometown to see his mother figure Helena. In between the 2 games a new military government has taken over and they are bad dudes/dudettes. Shank only starts fighting them because one of them makes him mad. After that he just mellows out on some booze before he goes to see Helena. The military sets the town on fire while he is drinking. When he attempts to get to Helena he sees her along with other villagers being hauled away by the military. So begins Shank's quest to save his mama.
You don't need to know much about Shank except that he is a cool dude. It would've been nice if he smiled or cracked a joke or did not sound like an old man in the restroom when he got hurt but that is just my opinion. You can also play as Corina, Shank's foster sister, in a level along with the multiplayer. She is a determined rebel member who is probably not a drunk. But you don't get to know her much either.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is excellent. You have a light attack, heavy attack, bombs, and guns. You can juggle people around using the light attacks. You can also pick up weapons on the road that are super powerful but only have a few uses like a bat, a pipe, an IV pole, and a sink. There is also a dodge mechanic which works really well. You can dodge at any point in your attacks. The dodge function will cancel out your attack so you won’t get hit because you are in the middle of one. There are also environmental traps you can activate to kill your enemies. There are a variety of enemies that will keep the game fresh. You have quick grenade throwers, regular dudes, fat dudes that laugh like Scooby Doo, and heavy dudes that go "hoo rah!" when they do a spin attack. Each game has a boss as well.
If you like beat em ups then this is a game you will not want to miss. A coop survival mode (I have not played) will add replay value and there are also leaderboards, a hard mode, and intel to collect. Getting achievements also unlocks skins.
Buy it!

Guacamelee oozes style and polish from every frame. It's a pitch-perfect Metroidvania (explorable map, powerups to open new paths, etc) with satisfying combo-driven brawler combat that stays both entertaining and challenging from start to finish. The game is also loaded with secrets that provide extra challenge for the truly hardcore, including a gauntlet-style challenge and (in the Infierno bonus content) a series of challenge rooms that test your timing, speed, and combat savvy.
The game also supports two-player (local only, I believe) coop, with the second player as the luchadora Tostada. A solo player can also swap to Tostada if they choose, though the game's script will still refer to the player as "Juan."
Playing with a controller is strongly recommended.
