I played the first FEAR game when it came out in 2005. It was actually one of the last games I preordered it and enjoyed it. Eight years later I finally got around to playing FEAR 2. So what did I think? Overall it wasn't a BAD experience. But there are some BAD things in the game I can mention. I remember the AI in the first FEAR game to be pretty good. Enemies would flank, take cover, etc. In this game they take cover but they'll also run right into the line of fire and do other assorted stupid things. The guns felt really, REALLY underpowered. One enemy took five shots from a shotgun before dying. Really? Oh, another piece of advice, ditch the pistol when you can. POS. Mission variety wasn't there. It was pretty much go to point A to point B and kill♥♥♥♥♥♥in between. You can walk around in a mech suit and get behind a large machinegun. That was as varied as it got.  There were some good things though. Level design was improved quite a bit. Instead of running around through office building after office building in the first FEAR game, you actually get some different environments. Special nod to the school map in this game, which I liked quite a bit.  The atmosphere was nice even with the obvious jump scares etc. There was a nice variety of weapons and the laser in particular was fun AND effective. The story was okay I guess. Thankfully you didn't have to memorize the first to enjoy this one. Oh, and the file size for the game is 12 GB which seems pretty damn huge for what's here but that's a minor gripe. Overall FEAR 2 gets a recommendation from me. You should be able to get it pretty cheap with the FEAR Trilogy pack during a summer/winter sale. Wait until then. 7/10 for FEAR 2 from me.

The characters look like they are talking and the captions show what they are saying, but you cannot hear them speaking.  It's not like having the voice acting is absolutely necessary to play the game, but I am annoyed that the game is not complete, particularly since there are only three scenes with voice acting in the entire game (the voiceover in the very beginning explaining the mission played without issue).
Long story short: these are great games, I wish the bundle had the bonus chapters that come with the collector's editions, and I had a minor issue with voiceovers in the first game.  Worth the price if you are really into hidden object games, especially mildly spooky ones.

A time and supply management game in the vein of Build-A-Lot, but with more resources.
You are an overlord in an afterlife community with many ruins lying about the map. These ruins must be rebuilt into their original structures. (No freedom of placement here, as with traditional city-builders.) At first, you have extremely limited space for food, resources, and money, as well as a limited amount of resources on the map (although the nodes do replenish over time). The game doesn't tell you this, but as you rebuild resource structures, you can place a worker there to start generating resources for your warehouse. As you upgrade your warehouse, you can hold more supplies and gold (up to 900).
It took a little bit for me to realise that you can grab your workers from the worker list in the bottom left and drop them where you want (go to that location first, then select a free worker). Once I figured that out, management was easier.
One issue: there is a quest near the end of the game that requires you to sell wood to the Capital. There is no resource known as 'wood'.
Pros:
+ trading cards!
+ cute graphics.
+ windowed mode.
+ simple gameplay.
+ always something to do.
Cons:
- short.
- the worker list is just a forward-and-back 'list', not a whole list.
- no achievements.
- no reply value.

You play as Shank. No, You do not play as a knife. (Shank - Prison slang for a homemade knife) Shank is the name of our fearless protagonist.
As Shank you can unlock and use various weapons that fall into two categories: Melee and ranged.
You can dual-wield pistols, blast multiple enemies with a shotgun or strike fear into the hearts of your enemies with a chainsaw.
There are also sections where you get your hands on a minigun and oh god is it fun to just let it rip and watch the massacre take place in front of your very eyes.
You can rack up combo-chains by launching your enemies into the air, shooting them and just being creative by using your surrounding enviroment such as holes for an example.
You can also pick up explosives such as grenades and molotov cocktails.
The only thing bad about the game and what also makes it worse than the previous title is that there is no co-op campaign anymore. Instead of that we get a new two-player survival mode tho. The survival mode can be played and beat playing solo as well. Survival mode offers various challenges and unlockable skins that you can use in both modes: campaign and survival.
To be fair then co-op would have made the campaign a bit too easy in this title so it's hardly a con but it's still less content for us since, well, co-op is still optional. I've played through the campaign 1.5 times but i would play through it again if it would have co-op in it.
Let's narrow it down, shall we?
+Fast, smooth and brutal gameplay
+Just the right amount of gore in both gameplay and cutscenes
+Awesome music that fits the game perfectly at all times
+Well done voice acting and animations
+Unlockables that keep you playing the game
+A whole new mode: Survival
-No co-op campaign

This is essentally the same game as Shank and comes with all of the same flaws, plus a few more.
Mainly, that the game just isn't very challenging and has been severely dumbed down for the casual market compared to old school beat 'em ups like Streets of Rage. Giving you infinite lives and checkpoints takes all of the fun out of this type of game. If nothing else at least offer an option to set limited lives and continues while retaining an "infinite lives" option for casual players who are just playing it through for the "story".
Speaking of story, it also took a turn for the worse. While the original Shank's revenge plot was at least interesting enough to care about, the plot in this game is just generic "B-movie" fare and makes no mention of the characters from the original at all. The settings are also a lot less diverse and interesting, boiling down to dark dismal jungle and industrial environments which are a lot less nice to look at. The added in-game voice acting is also unnecessary and for the most part downright cheesy.
Essentially the game retains the same flaws with little in the way of improvement, and a few additions that make the gameplay worse:
*Easy, short campaign, little to no replay value with the only unlockables being alternate costumes and character bios that add nothing to the gameplay
*Poorer controls than in the original (having to use seperate buttons to dodge left and right)
*A survival mode which had potentional but is multiplayer only (and with no one playing it online this mode is only accessable if you have a real-life buddy to play with)
I really can't recommend this except to casual gamers who typically play Facebook or Zynga games (and even then, the strong language and gore will probably be a turn-off to the type of people who play Farmville or Candy Crush Saga).

There are many games out there that even though don't appeal to me, I can understand the praise.
This one totally isn't like those.
To begin with, the full experience depends entirely on a single buton.
That's it. The same button to attack, to block and to use your special attack - infact pressing a button to attack isn't even necessary as your character does it automatically.
Somehow that design idea made into the final thing and never got changed even with lots of feedback about it on the forums.
You'll find yourself just mindlessly walking towards enemies, casually blocking and hoping for the best because a slight positioning failure means you can be hit through your block very often  (at least I like to tell myself that's the reason I got hit, because it makes no sense visually)
Then there are the items, which tremendously lack impact. You can barely feel any difference when equipping something new. What's the point of +3 str when huge enemies die in two hits? What does spirit even mean?
On the exploration point, it couldn't even be generic and bland. It had to be just bad.
You get to the desert and then there are endless rooms connected to each other at some part, for no reason.
Dungeons have you entering through the left just to appear at the botton of the next, and this happens furiously often.
Since there's nothing to find, rooms are the same, there's very little freedom to transverse through areas and they're just a corridor with a few enemies, luckly a key or a door, the level design is exclusively bad.
There's also no story, no purpose, nothing to put the setting into perspective. This is fine by itself if the gameplay could stand on its own legs but it clearly cannot.

This game is worth the price if you want to zone out for a bit and collect loot.
Once you figure out the few main mechanics, fighting your way through the world takes only a slight amount of focus. So the game might be reminiscent of an early Legend of Zelda title, but the dungeon bosses require virtually no strategy. I found myself defeating them boringly fast. The thrill of the dungeons is fighting the hoardes of enemies, but even that can get tedious if you're struggling to find the next locked door. It doesn't help that there isn't an apparent map screen (I couldn't find one), and the same music just repeats itself over and over. You may find yourself lost often, and I found that to be when the game was at its most grating. At times it felt like the whole game was just about grinding.

This is a tight, well-tuned metroidvania with spectacle fighter beat-em'-up combat. The combat scales from the trivial to the relentless:
- Some attacks can be dodged, others cannot.
- Enemies can be shielded with barriers that make them invulnerable until one of four specific attacks is used against them, or until they are pummeled with several attacks quickly.
- Enemies can be in either the land of the dead or the land of the living. They can attack you from either but you can only attack them if you're in the same world as them.
But you have several tools to outmaneuver them:
- Daze your enemies and then smash them around with wrestling throws to use them as projectiles or area-stun effects.
- Four distinct special attacks that launch you or your enemies in different directions.
- Turn in to a chicken and peck the bejebus out of your enemies to rack up higher combos.
- Freely phase between the living world and the land of the dead.
- Dodge through enemy attacks to rack your combos higher and negate damage.
- Lock enemies in aerial combos for a moment's respite from the earth.
- Unlock outfits with special powers.
If the game was only a beat-em'-up it would still be nearly worth the price of admission - but the various combat tools you attain are also the methods by which you unlock additional areas to traverse. The game strongly rewards exploration with both practical benefits (more life and more whuppin' fuel) and significant soft benefits (a better ending than the default for finding five main secrets).
All of this is backed by a crisp sense of humor, good writing, and a consistent mythology based in incan myth and mexican folklore. Critically, the controls are very tight - at least with an XBox 360 controller, which I had - which allows you to play with confidence that it won't glitch you out. If you have interest in metroidvania's or spectacle fighters, Guacamelee is well worth your time.

I get a strong Shantae vibe from Guacamelee; both games exist in a fantastic setting with an atypical occupation (Bellydancers in Shantae, and Luchadors in Guacamelee) and offer a constant stream of upgrades with corresponding puzzles. However, unlike Shantae, Guacamelee has a strong emphasis on combat, and the controls are completely tight.
Guacamelee doesn't seem to be a particularly long or challenging game, but it is incredibly fun and well made. There are dozens of references to other video games, both classic and obscure, and this is clearly a game made with a love of the craft. I definitely recommend this game, especially if you catch it on sale.
EDIT: I believe I spoke too soon as to the difficulty of this game. While the main quest may not pose much of a challenge, getting 100% complete requires split second combo reflexes the likes of fighting game professionals. If you are looking for a challenge, you will find one here.

In short:
Is this for hardcore bullet hell shmup fans?  No.
Is this a mediocre shmup that's worth $1, and you won't feel bad when you never return to it?  Yes.
This isn't an exceptional shmup, but it will give you a few decent hours for your purchase.  Each "stage" is just a single encounter, at first against a single boss-like enemy.  Soon you're taking on four strong enemies at once, and their patterns occasionally change.  Enemy health scales down when there are more enemies on screen, so it's the 1:1 battles that feel the most dramatic.  In the encounters with multiple enemies, you can sometimes kill one before they even get to their most difficult attacks.  The winning strategy is to focus on the one enemy with the attack that causes you the most grief.  That's the entirety of the game.
At the end of each encounter, you earn some kind of spendable currency and occasionally a relic that improves player stats.  You spend the currency on a purchasable 'level up' between stages; this is pretty silly because you can just forget to do it occasionally.  I'm not entirely sure it matters, as none of these upgrades really felt like they made any kind of significant change to the game.  It felt like the game just constantly scaled up enemy health to match my new abilities.
The game provides six playable characters.  I only bothered unlocking the first five, as the last requires you to clear 100 separate encounters that don't progress the game.  Only one of the characters is worth playing because it does the most damage.  The other characters are weaker and have slightly different firing patterns and different secondary abilities.  I never found a scenario where any of the other characters were more useful.
I know none of this sound particularly praiseworthy, so why am I recommending it?  Despite all these faults, it's an alright game and doesn't seem to have any major bugs.  I paid $1 for it, and I got four hours of decent play from it.  I think that's a fair trade.  Don't hesitate to throw in the towel once it stops being fun; I put at least 20 minutes into Stage 85, and after quitting, I'm certain I won't be back.  That's a shame, I'm genuinely curious what the last phoenix is like.
I guess there's a sequel.  I wonder if it's better?

Phoenix Force is a victim of the way that Bullet Hell games are designed and perceived, these days. Bullet Hell aficionados tend to be interested in difficulty and variety, and should therefore retreat to a safe distance and not bother with this game. There isn't much here to test the reflexes and mettle of those familiar with Touhou games and their ilk, and the aesthetic and mechanics of the game aren't anything special. Although the OHKO tightrope is firmly in place, plenty of BH players have supernatural balance and won't be in danger of falling to the wiles of this game,
Unfortunately, it's also slightly too difficult for any 'casual' bullet hell gamer (oxymoron?), or a newbie to the genre. I certainly am, and was flattened at several points during my playthrough - I'm not awful, but it was mostly bloody-mindedness that saw me through. This isn't a conventional 'beat the level, face the boss' style of game, either. You're solely confronting boss enemies, which vary in number and type as the levels tick by. Towards the end, I was relying on certain combinations not to appear; that feather-spewing pile of rubbish can go directly to hell without passing Go, as far as I'm concerned.
The gameplay is reasonably solid, with your weaponry and special ability being constantly fired or triggered at the appropriate time, meaning that all you need to focus on is the incoming barrage of projectiles...and where your bullets are going. The premise is a tad bizarre, but the different phoenixes offer some potential variety, although they're mostly differentiated by their special abilities. Otherwise, the game is just a straightforward slog through linear levels as the bosses get tougher and more numerous.
Honestly, it's all a bit dull. Marginally too tough to be an introductory entry to the bullet hell genre, but far too easy for seasoned pros - Phoenix Force lies firmly between a rock and a hard place, filling a niche that few people occupy. Some questionable design decisions and a dull, minimalist colour palette bog down an otherwise reasonable game. I can't see it rising from the ashes of my backlog ever again.

A game I had nothing but high hopes for, Planet Coaster offers a lot of creativity and flexibility in creating your very own theme park. But as for bringing a creative and interesting challenge to the table it appears to be severely lacking. With a screwy UI and complete reliance on youtube tutorials it feels as if there was no real intent behind making this a game as it was simply a creation kit, which would be okay if they weren't charging such a price for something that only lets you make a Theme Park. The base themes of the game are sparse and the dependence on the community to enhance that is very underwhelming, especially considering the size of the game.
Though some people likely enjoyed the experience of Planet Coaster thoroughly, I honesly found it frustrating and disappointing. I've always had a fondness for being creative and challenged, but the hoops this game puts you through to realise your dream park really put me off playing it. By all means, if you are looking to spend days, even weeks carefully crafting a beautifully sculpted paradise, then go nuts. If you're looking for a game to test your problem solving skills while allowing you to do so freely, this makes for a poor replacement for the old Rollercoaster Tycoons.
I'd personally rate Planet Coaster at a below average 36%

I don't remember the last time I enjoyed a game like I enjoy Planet Coaster. The game is super immersive, especially if you're someone like me who enjoys the atmosphere of theme parks and attractions. I bought this game while it's on sale, 75% off, but I feel bad, because I would pay full price for it -- but I won't argue.
The game brings a wild level of customization -- you can decide what kinds of condiments and toppings to put on your burgers and ice cream sold in the stalls. You can pay each staff member a different wage. You can create targeted ads. You can literally do anything to make the park your own. I've always been a big fan of the sandbox games, and Planet Coaster really brings me to my happy place with it. There really are no limits as to how detailed you can get with your constructions, whether it's a building or one of the rides, or they give you really cool placement-ready options if you're not so into creating your own. This is the fun part for me because I love looking at the scenery in real-life places like these, to look at all the details, and this game really captures that. Set the lighting, set the music, set the colors, set the special effects, you can do it all!
I've read a lot that people don't see the theme park management behind this game, but I'm not sure how they don't, as I've had no wishes that this game was more involved. You can set your funding however you'd like, put your money into research for new rides and shops, pay your employees more to make them happy, build more scenery, do some marketing, building a mountain, build a river, the list goes on. There are multiple game modes available and Challenge Mode is probably the closest to the traditional tycoon scene that I can think of, as your money is limited, refunds are small, and you have to get creative with your management.
Of course there's also your Sandbox Mode where money is no object and you can just play, or there's the Career Mode where you take the reigns on a failing park and bring it up to par. I've found Career Mode interesting because you can see the developer's creations and see exactly what is possible with the game and it blows my mind. It gives you inspiration and ideas and a solid base to make an amazing park, with some help.
Between the terraforming, the park management, the custom building possibilities and the DLC rolling in, I'll be a player for a long time to come. I'd recommend this game to anyone, 10/10.

The game has heart I give it that, but it lacks a proper budget to make the game work. Pretty much everything lacks polish. The game is extremely linear with almost zero side content other than the main quest, it's extremely short and every location looks the same, you can't distinguish a city from another, the dungeons all look the same. The music score is pretty good but it lacks variety, it's either soft ambient music or battle theme, there's nothing else.
The gameplay is the only saving grace, it's basically a simplified chrono trigger battle system with a weird "materia enhancing" mechanic that's pretty much based on luck, it works, it's not great but it gets the job done. Luckly some bosses are challenging and require some strategy but as you go forward you can figure out attack combos between some characters that pretty much break the game, you can one shot all the enemies in one attack all the time ... it made me question if the game was at least play-tested once.
In the end considering every pro and con i cannot as a jrpg lover suggest this game, it was at best prematurely released with a short and unoriginal story that doesn't have time to properly develop.

The Happy Hereafter is a casual strategy game. You manage the underworld and the poor souls who will become your slaves, err your workers. The aim of the game is to discover the entire map by unlocking all the areas, interact with some wacky NPCs quest givers, grab all the resources, build everything you can and upgrade it to the max. It’s a tiny persistent world, i.e. there aren’t several levels with different maps, you have one big map.
It’s a casual game so there’s no time pressure, you’re never stuck wondering what to do next as the game keeps throwing small tasks at you and can’t even choose where to build anything: everything have an already set place. The gameplay is how efficiently you’ll exploit all your resources and plan your crafting to do all the quests and finish the game. When you finish you can still keep on playing your little world if you want to.
It lasted around 6 hours and had a bit of complexity with the craft: you can produce several different food items, use them in a dozen cooking recipes; you also pick wood and stones and craft statues and other gift shop goodies. You can sell anything you pick or craft using a trading post and use your money to buy additional workers.
Expecting a trash game I was surprised by the overall quality. The graphics are nice, with a Tim Burton style. The music is calm and fitting, a bit eerie. The texts are fun to read and some quests made me chuckle. The game is pleasant and really well made and if you’re a fan of casual lighthearted fun, you shouldn’t miss it. Especially now since the game is on sale at a ridiculous price!

I'm about rep/lvl 155, so I'm going to say this: while this game has some better points than PAYDAY 2, the bad outweigh the good. This game is plain boring and is best gotten on a sale or something.
Remember, these are my opinions, but feel free to be a thorn in my side about my view on this game.
-Large maps
-Nice graphics, most of the time. For 2011, they're really nice.
-Genuine difficulty.
-Recognizable and simple weapons.
-CPU in this game actually kill enemies, unlike in PAYDAY 2, where they would rather stand infront of enemies and die.
-DLC adds some interesting content worth checking out if you like the game (3 weapons, 2 levels, a skill tree, and some other bonuses. Woohoo!)
-The RNG is very effective at locking whole areas of the map off, and the chance increases at harder difficulties. Not only does this stop roaming, but it also affects the difficulty for the worse. I've never had a closed door ♥♥♥♥ me over so many times.
-Outrageously high enemy spam as artificial difficulty, especially on Overkill and 145+
-Boring animations. A lot of reloads are lackluster, and there's no real fleshed out animations.
-Lack of community for PD:TH leads to frequent foreign visitors, low leveled players, cheat engine kiddies, or any of those in any combination.
-Some levels are intentionally made to be more in the cops favor than the player, most notably Heat Street and Undercover.
-Only about 10-12 maps, and a ridiculous level cap at 145 (that can be expanded by the DLC to 193!!) - hope you like to grind.
-The DLC only adds 2 maps and 3 new weapons, one of which is an ineffective full-auto pistol, a sidegrade to a starter weapon (albeit a very good starter weapon), and a single-shot, very large AOE grenade launcher.
-Ally AI never helps with objectives, just shoot their gun(s) and more often gets in trouble than it does help you get out of trouble. They also have a lot of trouble helping you up from incapacitation, especially from special enemies.
Overall, like I said, get it on a sale. PAYDAY 2 is a lot more fun overall.

It is a casual version of a city-building genre with predetermined buildings placements and almost none negative events to take care of. And the art design is great and coherent in the "cutesy-undead" style.
Downsides being, that it has only one map, which eliminates repetition of high-player-agency early game, where most city-planning happens, unlike later-game fine-tuning. And considering that all placements are uncustomizable it's better that way. You can chain games in this sub-genre one after another, pretending that you play different levels, while having new aesthetics every time. And the problem with the mid-game is that even with all upgrades, resource gathering is too slow and you just waiting with nothing else (like fighting fires, crime or epidemics) to do. Next is the story — you are just start doing stuff and don't know why, nor do you know who or what attacks your town. Speaking of which, defense is not only mechanically pointless, but even lacks any feedback, like your godhand throwing lightnings or something into enemies.
It kind of works with UWS UHD Surround, but GUI scaling hides important parts of the map from the player, so it's better to just play it windowed.
Overall it's a one nice and pleasant feelgood playing session of several hours with podcasts or youtube videos on second (fifth) screen.

There are tons of fun minigames, and some rather interesting HO scenes where you have to assemble stuff.
It's a very neat setting full of weird stuff. I like weird. And this is fun even without the shiny colours that usually draw me. It's certainly not bleak either!
I can also mostly easily understand what to do and why, unlike in most HO games where I'm left puzzling at the reasoning behind actions.
You can collect candy canes, and while they're not indicated on the map (I really would prefer more games to show where collectibles are still hidden), there's a reason to find them: You can buy cosmetic upgrades for your HUD with them!
Concerning the story...
The game crashed twice during a cut scene (different ones), but restarting, I could repeat the last action and watch the cutscene again without trouble both times.
There was one minigame that I skipped, because I couldn't see how it could be solved. (Made two screenshots of it, if anyone's curious.)
The first two Weird Park games are ok.
Nice setting and interesting story, though as is often the case, I didn't really know why I had to collect this or that to then to that or this with.
There's no fast travel map, or any map at all in part 1 and 2.
There are plenty HO games - though with an irritating misclick penalty (and no different difficulty settings) and when you go through a HO scene again, the previously removed objects are back where they were, including things you've gotten as reward and used/have in your inventory. Overall some nice minigames.
In the first part was 1 'remember the sequence', where you had to press different stick figure type drawings on piano keys, that was simply too long. First time ever that I skipped a minigame (that I know/remember/wasn't an accident).
2nd part had a minigame that I skipped too, as there wasn't really anything to go by to fill the image with bits from pressing buttons, except pressing randomly. (No clear way to tell what which button added.)
All in all, nice games, and the third's just great (I think I mentioned that before :) ).

The last true, classic Hitman game. Much better controls than the predecessors, very solid gameplay and very motivating.
Don't even bother with the dumbed down sequel "Hitman: Absolution" which was made by a different team.

When people talk Hitman there's usually one game they have in mind and that's Blood Money. Hitman is a series that boasted a novel concept which has somehow managed to remain pretty unique to this day (seriously - how many disguise-based stealth games are there?) and that gameplay evolved from game to game with Blood Money being the pinnacle (since Absolution went in a somewhat different direction closer to other stealth franchises like Splinter Cell).
Above all Blood Money is an action adventure game. Each mission provides quite a huge and open area with one ore more targets which need to be assassinated as well as the occasional non-assassination goal. Each map features many characters following basic routines and items or statics objects which can somehow be put to use. The beauty of Hitman lies in exploring the big and diverse environments, discovering usable objects, observing the targets and bystanders and then putting a brilliant plan together - and somewhat ironically the best and toughest plan is always the one where nobody dies, except for the targets of course. It gets even more complicated when you wish to make the deaths look like accidents and leave nothing behind (especially not that precious suit!). But even once you've developed that brilliant plan, there's still the matter of execution which requires perfect timing, with wits, patience and a good memory being the key to success - one mistake and everything goes to hell and there's not much left to do except mowing down everyone in your path.
As an action game Hitman is definitely sub-par but if you're up for it and are willing to spend ages on the same mission until you find and execute that perfect plan (or at least one perfect plan as often there's several ways to get that awesome Silent Assassin rating) there's nothing quite like it and a truly rewarding experience awaits you.
There's not much going on in terms of story, which is told through non-interactive cutscenes, but that doesn't keep the game from providing many very original locations and missions depicting the criminal underworld from a wide variety of angles, mostly ones you don't know from other games. To top it all off the action is accompanied by one of the greatest soundtracks to be ever heard in a video game, composed by legendary Jesper Kyd, providing a truly surreal atmosphere at times. What kind of graphics to expect everyone can clearly see on the screenshots.
Bottom line: if you are looking for an original stealth game or just want to know what all this Hitman talk is about - this is the game to go with.

Who would have thought a "game" where you just watch video clips (normally lasting, on average, between 9 seconds and a minute in length) would be so captivating? Her Story is indeed a captivating one, especially when viewed in a non-linear format as you try to piece together the mystery behind Hannah Smith and the disappearance of her husband Simon. Only some of the clips will allow you to discover the truth and whilst it is possible to just view the story in linear progression, it feels far more exciting to randomly search the video archives to discover a vague but important piece of information that draws you deeper into the story. This isn't so much a game but an arthouse movie, and the performance of Viva Seifert as Hannah is fantastic, relying heavily on body language to suggest all is not what it seems with what she says. It shouldn't work, but this is just simply fantastic.

F.E.A.R 2: Project Origin is the "official" sequel to the first game and is the direct canon to the original F.E.A.R (non-canon to the expansion packs: Extraction Point and Perseus Mandate) and I must say that F.E.A.R 2 is...lame. Unlike the legacy of the first F.E.A.R, the second game attempts to reestablish the horror elements and slowmotion gameplay as refreshing, but it leads to simple, generic, and typical FPS game. The game is very short as my first playthrough is 6 hours. The Alma sequences were not scary and relies very heavily on "jumpscares", which are very predictable. There is no psychological suspense or grave tension that the first game has. The "bullet time" in F.E.A.R 2 is not "well-spent", meaning that it's not necessary for you to use it. I find it as a negative aspect as the first game "recommends" you to use bullet time to ease off stiff, challenging, and difficult firefights; F.E.A.R. 2, not so much. And of course, there is no character development from any characters that you encountered as the high majority of them die off quickly and to be honest, F.E.A.R 2 is one of the very few games that I actually do not care about any characters or how they develop. It's too generic. Overall, it is hard for me to recommend this game to anyone, but I can only recommend to those who are interested in the F.E.A.R storyline. Lastly, the storyline of F.E.A.R. 2 does not follow the "Point Man" storyline. I strongly recommend for those who are interested to buy this game for $3.75; nothing more than that.

I like the overall atmosphere of the game and the concept behind it, which is to say it puts you in a haunted forest filled with ghostly enemies and resets your level and equipment if you die.  The abilities and items you gain throughout the game are sometimes interesting but you'll mostly have the choice of ranged and melee weapon types.  Magic type items are also available, but they're mostly just reskins of the bow item.  Ranged and magic items empty your mana pool but provide distance so the enemies don't hit you as often.  Melee is easier to hit enemies with but risks you getting too close to enemies and getting hit often.  There's a block mechanic, mind you.  The combat is deceptively simple and kind of fun, but the overly simplified controls may ruin some of that fun for you.
The game has multiple supported control schemes all enabled from the get-go.  The mouse controls are terrible, but you may find the WASD keys or the arrow keys plus the spacebar key are all you need to play this game.  You will, however, want to use the mouse to aim the bow and various spells.  That said, there is also controller support, and while I have not tried Xbox 360 controls for this game, it seems like it would be the optimal way to play this game.

A simple game for a casual game experience. That is what this game is, and that is what this game does well. Are you looking for a game you can sit down with for hours and comb through an engrossing storyline of epic scale, set in a sprawling open world of beauty and splendor? Well guess what folks, you won't find that here. Go in with the wrong expectations and you are going to be disappointed. See this game for what it is.
This game has a simple concept, simple gameplay, and a simple style. There is nothing groundbreaking or particularly innovative here. Go into the game with the expectation of a casual session of a few minutes to an hour where you can make progress and you will not be disappointed. When I say simple, it took me only a few hours to achieve 100% Steam Achievement completion, but that's what I expected. And you know what folks? I still go back and play this at times even after 100% completion because it is just simple fun. On the right sale, you can have a few hours of entertainment for less than the cost of a value menu taco... Sounds like more than a fair trade to me.

Pro

Con
I know it's a casual game, but it's far too simple, no challenge.
Very short (compared to the dev's other game "The Promised Land.")
Minions have to be micro-managed and dragged to certain jobs.
The game ends abruptly with "The End" on a black screen leaving you wondering what the goal was ....
Much of the map feels undeveloped with empty areas never used.
Overall, if you haven't played The Promised Land, this might be worth checking out, as it really feels as if this is the training wheels for that game. On the other hand, skip this game and play The Promised Land, for a much more polished, interesting, longer, and entertaining game.

Hidden Object games live from the stories they tell, some of them take a more "adventure" - Light stance in their task to tell a story. Weird Park Triology does a lot right, while only minor problems rise their ugly head during gameplay.
The three games have good graphics, only the third supports widescreen fully.
Original and fitting soundtrack to the game, some of the tunes catch the mixture of mystery, crime and actual horror or circus setting.
Not a lot of surprises here, some of the riddles are challenging enough not to let a gamer run through this game like a madman, and you should take your time to try out the riddles. If one particular riddle is too tough it can be skipped, or you can quit playing and continue later. The graphics of the hidden objects are quite well, especially the third part with the assembly HOS section is a real nice and relaxing part.
Now for the Genre-typical Scores:
I hope you don't suffer coulrophobia, since this story is about... Clowns, one Clown and a mischievously evil little entity that is. The story suffers some insignificant lapses during the three parts, those might be reasoned away with developing the villain and his victims (when you play the last part you'll finally notice why).
If all three parts would have had the technical standard of the last part here would be three plusses, my personal max score. Sadly the first two episodes are neither CE's nor are they fully compatible to widescreen (yeah, turning them into WS actually is changing them into uglyness). The game is on par with some of the other good HOG's.
There isn't too much to explain, only the last game has a lot of extras and a bonus chapter, which actually deepens the story behind the Series. Sadly, the first two aren't so well off with extras. Nonetheless, the Extras in the third part do some compensation.
Keep in mind, HOG's are casual games, they don't have much of a replayability, aside some sentimental value. But this triology includes three quite nice and well told stories, one which you actually wish to get deeper and deeper into. It has no fear factor - if you don't suffer coulrophobia - and is quite entertaining.
Last but not least:
19,90 € doesn't seem much for three games, but they don't have a really long playtime. And replayability tends to zero. Nonetheless, all three games are actually good HOG's with a lot of story to cover. So the price
acceptable. If you have a chance to buy it on some sale for cheap, do it. You won't rue the purchase.
I recommend the game on reasons of my given explanations, rarely was a recommendation so easy to speak out.

The Weird Park Trilogy is a great pick at a good price for three solid hidden object games that never drop below fairly decent quality. The atmosphere of the first and the game design if the third episode makes it especially noteworthy for any HOG fan.
Alawar made the right choice when they released Weird Park in the package format on Steam. While it certainly lacks extras like trading cards, the quality of the trilogy justifies the price. Let’s see in details:
Broken Tune is tries to sell itself with the visuals and atmosphere, not the story. The derelict amusement park, haunted by the ghost of a clown, works great as a setting, and it can make anyone forget that the game has almost no plot.
The game mechanics are barebones, but refined. There is a fair amount of backtracking and some challenging puzzles, but the main attractions are the hidden object scenes. They are well-constructed and a joy to play, even if some of them are reused several times.
The second part feels less intuitive. The playable area has expanded, but the game has little identity on its own. The number of the hidden object scenes increased, but their quality dropped.
The story brings back the ghost clown, who, along with his puppet, is now kidnapping children in order to place them in known fairy tale settings because… boredom, I guess. While the plot makes its presence known a lot more, it is paper thin and serves only as an excuse to change the scenery frequently.
The third part is, finally, plot-driven: a new protagonist ends up in the nightmare world seen in Scary Tales in order to free a kidnapped boy and the soul of the clown (who is suddenly a good guy now). There is even a bonus episode, where we finally learn the truth behind the jester puppet.
Gameplay is strange, as initially it focuses on sequential hidden object and fragmented object scenes before it settles on the traditional HOG mechanics. It also features cross-inventory item manipulation, a rare sight in this genre. This variety, combined with the abundance of story and stages, is the highlight of the trilogy.

What’s better than one game about creepy clowns? How about THREE games with creepy clowns! The minds behind these games clearly wanted to induce nightmares so play at your own risk!
The first game of the Weird Park Trilogy. You play a detective on a mission to uncover the mystery behind disappearances at an old carnival as well as find another detective who went missing there. The park is haunted by a dead clown’s ghost and the trickster Loki and both will eerily appear around the park to spook you, again, evil freaking clown.
The game play is basic hidden item fair. A fair share of hidden item scenes along with mini games and puzzles to solve. Nothing out of the ordinary. It has spooky music and voice acting, though it’s not the best. Everything you could want in a hidden item game is here, despite it being an older and more basic title.
The second installment unfortunately has little to do with the first. You play an entirely different character and, despite defeating him in the first game, you’re pitted against the evil clown Louise and Loki once again. The story is off the walls weird. It could be its own separate title and not even be linked to this trilogy and you wouldn’t notice. I found the story to be the weakest, and most annoying, of the three. Your a random guy who went off the road into Spooksville and you have to save kids you don’t even know.
The game play, graphics and music thankful make the game bearable. It’s fun to play and the puzzles are engaging. The voice acting isn’t stellar but it’s appreciated. Even if you feel the same way as I about the story you’ll be too busy finding hidden objects to really notice, too much anyway.
The final act in the war against Loki and Louise, you once again play someone different but you’re brought back to Fairy Gate Park as a journalist. Everything about this game is an improvement from the other two except, in my opinion, the story. The first game was incredibly spooky and unnerving, even causing me to be mad at it for the clowns in it. As the series progresses it becomes less and less scary and more mundane. The graphics have also improved from the first two but the voice acting really hasn’t. You also get a bonus chapter which shows how Loki became trapped in the record to begin with.
Overall this is a solid buy, even if one game isn’t strong on its own you’re getting three and that’s a great bargain.

Weird Park Trilogy are three games revolving around Louis Gauche, a clown that died during a representation. But there is also another recurring character, the real antagonist, which is Loki/Mr. Dudley.
Weird Park: Broken Tune was the first one to be released but I've played it in the Hidden Object Bundle 5 in 1. I enjoyed the dark settings and the soundtrack. But I had an hard time to find my way sometimes, relaying on the hint buttons. Besides, the ending was promising a real good sequel. In this opus, you're searching for a journalist that vanished and that was investigating an abandoned park that closed following accidents and the death of their clown.
But this is where Weird Park: Scary Tales happens. And it's not even a sequel to the story. You're on the road and you're suddenly distracted, sending your car somewhere you didn't know it exists: an old house and a little girl needing help... in another world. You have to save her and her friends, by re-acting some tales.
And to conclude Louis Gauche's story (which isn't really coherent at this point) with The Final Show, you're investigating the disappearance of another child and is sent to another world, where Louis Gauche, the clown, is finally understanding that he was manipulated and that he wants to save the boy that showed him that he could be a good man.
I hate when a trilogy is not making sense. I mean, Loki/Mr. Dudley is either a servant of Louis Gauche or his boss, we don't really have Louis Gauche's background coherent and I don't understand how he could have survived as you defeated him in the first opus. Also, the hero isn't the same each time, so, while you, the player, know more or less who to trust and the story, the character is completely unaware of everything.
If the graphics are very good and very representative of the ambiance of the story, the soundtrack is also good. As for the gameplay, it doesn't change: hidden object games and puzzles.
I would buy the bundle during a sale, mainly because I think that the price is not justified when you already own one of the game as part of the Hidden Object Bundle 5 in 1 - they did the same with another good game, Mountain Crime. Notice that I will buy the upcoming 4 in 1 though I already have the House of 1000 Doors. I don't want to miss the other games in it. But, yeah, for me, Weird Park Trilogy is worthy to be bought and played.

TL:DR- next to zero interaction, an interesting story that might or might not live up to the hype (depending on you), still a brilliant idea.
Her Story goes along with a certain "kind" of games born in the latest 4 or 5 years (i guess?). It basically is an FMV sort of investigative game that's splitted in about 270 short videos you have to get through in order to "guess-estimate" the truth. Mind you, there is no such thing as an end-game revelation, you will (would) just happen to carefully look for all of the keywords from the interviews and you will be able to get an idea of what happened.
It ends up being a bit too criptic and fragmented, that's perhaps what makes this "game" less enjoyable in a way, but i can see why the whole FMV is fragmented like this and thats how it actually works. BUT, but...this is a sort of halfway through, or perhaps more like, 75% through? :D of what it could have been.
I still recommend this game, because it is a good take and somewhat a brilliant one away from the stereotypes and classics of the genre. It also makes it suitable for mobile devices, and that is quite an achievement.
Pro's
- interesting story
- good acting
- brilliant concept
Con's
- very fragmentated experience (about 270 videos!)
- next to zero interaction
- brilliant in concept, but not in its shape.
- really aims a fair bit at nostalgic people, and with that being part of the "style" without it being actually purposeful to the game experience itself.

Pretty damn good game. Short but sweet. While not entirely bug-free, it's a lot more polished than its prequel. The game also seems to be a bit more clever with its scares, making the scary bits a lot more enjoyable.
The level design is on par with the original FEAR, though a little more varied. Paths to objectives are unrealistically complex, but fun nonetheless.
Combat is different. The AI seems to be less intelligent but can handle more damage and is more accurate when shooting. Some enemies towards the end can take a bit too much damage to my liking, but not to the point where it gets frustrating. There is no more peeking from cover, meaning you can't fight the same as you did in the original FEAR. On the other hand, it's much easier to flank enemies than it is in the original. While I prefer the original combat and enemies, I don't dislike the ones in FEAR 2. With the exception of fighting monsters, that is.
The game's biggest fault, is that they wanted to include more enemy variety and ended up with some complete BS monsters. There's the fast-but-weak creepy-crawly monsters that are just an annoyance because they do so little damage but are hard to hit and the puppeteer monster that takes a ♥♥♥♥♥on of damage, keeps running away and has the most annoying attack in the world. The latter monster is challenging, sure, but also a real chore.
The story is pretty fun, until you start to think about it and you discover some things that don't quite make sense (or aren't adequately explained, at least). The original game was the same, though.
Both FEAR and FEAR 2 are must-plays.

F.E.A.R. 2: Project Origin:
Intro:
Alma is back in the second game of F.E.A.R. named F.E.A.R. 2: Project Origin. If you enjoyed the first game this will be worth your money.
Do not expect this game to be a better version of the original game – there is no such a thing!
This game got some improvements compared to the first F.E.A.R. game, but a lot of downsides as well.
Graphic, controls, performance, & sound:
Graphic: The overall graphics got enchanted to look shinier and more modern - I especially like the blood which looks a lot more like liquid compared to the first one, plus an added effect, bodies also drop organs sometimes when they explode - however I miss the random body part (like a arm or a leg) that could fly off into the distance from the first F.E.A.R. game. Generally effects like: explosions, bullet impacts on surface or ground and shotgun bursts, looks absolutely terrible in my option, its way to white/yellow and without any detail, looks like something done in a hurry and is very a shame!
Controls: All controls can be customized and is a great way to use your own key liking. Also a new thing in F.E.A.R.2 is the sprint mechanic, however one thing I didn’t like is that you cannot toggle it on and off; if you toggle on your sprint it’ll last as long as the sprint meter is up, that can lead to awkward situations where you just need to stop up in a hurry even a half second faster count, if trying to avoid incoming attacks or taking cover.
Performance: I haven’t had any performance issues at all running the game maxed out, always on a steady/capped 60 fps even on a low-end CPU and a small amount of ram.
Sound: The sound effects work very well to create the dark and creepy atmosphere this game is going for. A common thing in the F.E.A.R. series is a high pitch noise whenever a scare is coming up, if I like it or not is the question, one could say it is hard to be taken off guard with such a mechanic.
Horror:
Scares in the world of F.E.A.R. is a great thing, and I like that Alma appeared this much in the second game, however, the same kind of scares appeared way too often which only made it annoying and predictable.
Asides from the point on scares (jump scares) this game has a surprisingly large focus on the small and creepy details of the horror genre, if one is to explore around like I did on my second walkthrough. I found a lot of things that I missed blindly first time, simply because I didn’t notice it, and that’s something I admire of a horror game. “You may not even realize they could be watching yah, aye?”
Artificial Intelligence:
The AI replica soldiers got a lot dumber compared to the first F.E.A.R. (or its expansions), their behavior is too monotonous, which makes killing them a little tedious and like a routine you go through.
Their awareness is also not working like it should: Moving from floor 1 and up in the right side by the stairs, the AI’s standing on the left side of floor 2 spotted me, because I had a flashlight on (they yelling: we got a flashlight over here) – even though a wall was blocking their sight on floor 2. Uh makes sense? I think not!
Overall:
Even though this review may sound rather critical and demeaning, I do not mean any of it in a negative manner, and the game does have its good moments. This review is simply based on my own perspective, from my experience and thoughts about the game and I’ll certainly recommend it if you enjoyed the original F.E.A.R. game or its expansions and couldn’t get enough.
The playtime value is about 12 hours.

Let's keep this simple: This is a resource management game on training wheels. For a younger audience, this could potentially be recommended, with caveats - but that doesn't make it a good game in the genre.
Developer Alawar and publisher Buka Entertainment are well known amongst casual gamers. Farm Frenzy and Treasures of Montezuma are two of the most well known series they've worked on, and the rest of their respective lists of mostly mediocre yet decent enough games are pretty long. They also collaborated on The Promised Land, another resource management game, but one I actually enjoyed; it was *heavily* reminiscent of Virtual Villagers, and even without ever managing to come close to the fun mechanics and attention to detail that made Last Day of Work's game a hit, it provided a few hours of entertainment.
The Happy Herefter feels like a game that attempts to capitalize on the moderate success of The Promised Land, and fails. There is nothing innovative about the resource collecting, building, crafting, quest fullfilling treadmill the game puts you on, and there is also no attempt at permitting the player any input or attempt at strategy. You follow the cues, you fullfill one (re)quest after an other, everything with an arrow pointing at things just in case you missed them. Except when you do miss them, because quests are worded awkwardly or mechanics are insufficiently explained. Certain mechanics also feel too much like busywork to be fun, like resources that deplete very fast but only for a few seconds - long enough for your toons to wander aimlessly around not knowing what to do and needing to be dragged back. There is a distinct lack of polish here, in the copywriting, in the UI, and in the mechanics, to the extent where it feels like no one really playtested this game.
So if you have younger kids, and if you are willing to sit around for a few hours helping them when they get stuck because something is worded wrong/awkwardly or a mechanic is badly explained, then this might be a fun game for them. It's utterly linear, impossible to go wrong, somewhat cute, with a silly story, and not too long. If on the other hand you're an adult casual gamer, might I suggest The Promised Land? Exactly in the same vein, just better executed and more polished.

Best thing about this game besides the lack of any time limits, is that it is more or less an open type world where the player controls who and what is being done.  Plus the town square can be built however the player choses by buying street lamps, paving stones, fountain, and benches.

Bit Dungeon II is a really short game that you should only get on sale. I feel like this game could've actually been pretty enjoyable if the creators worked for, let's say, one more year, because if there's one word that captures the feelings I have about this game, it is "incomplete". The artwork looked fine and I did kind of enjoy playing through it, which is why I'm recommending it, but, even though it is fine, i think it could've been really, really good.
The first impression was great, seeing a complicated stats system, many equipment slots, a seemingly big world to explore and the great artwork, I thought that this might actually be a great game. Much to my disappointment, the combat ended up being mashing your space bar quickly, the world was very small, the dungeons were really boring, the boss fights were short and the game was pretty easy and short.
I think that this game might have been amazing if they added in many moves and challenging, quick enemies, making the combat faster and more interesting. The world also needs to be way bigger and the boss fights need to be WAY longer, this game felt short and contentless. I did enjoy it for a few hours, and some of the stuff was actually really great, waking up and suddenly getting attacked by some mysterious person was the highest point of the game, but there wasn't much more to it than that. I think there's some great potential for a third game and, since I bought it on sale, I don't feel like my money was lost, so if it's on sale, don't let me stop you from getting it, but I personally think it was mediocre.

I bought this game for the equivalent of 1 USD. It wasn't worth it, and I'll be refunding it.
Consider: I played this for 83 minutes and beat it. I entered a new area identical to an old one with no explanation, so I closed the game to look if it was an NG+ loop... and it was.
Which is fine. Other games do this, but those games actually have substance. This game is a joke when it comes to design; its gameplay, insofar as it has any, is a puddle that won't even get your foot wet through your sock. Dark Souls, then, is a lake. Full of horrifying waterborne creatures with too many teeth, all too intent on tearing you limb from limb.
But yeah. This game is not that. The gameplay is as follows:
You get some inventory slots. From memory, you have a hat, a main hand, an offhand, a body armour, boots, a ring, a pendant... I'm not sure if you have more (I think there's 9?), but honestly it doesn't matter. You can't hold items, and all your stats (which level based on the weapon you're holding, as far as I can tell) apply to every weapon type anyway, so it's a game of pick up the stuff with the biggest numbers. If you're an archer but you find a nice axe, pick that♥♥♥♥♥♥up even if your strength is abysmal; all that dex you got from leveling up while holding the bow is just as well now, and the axe has bigger numbers.
You move with arrow keys or WASD. The only additional control is your choice of space, left click, or one more button that I never cared to use and thus forgot. The gameplay, unless you have a bow, boils down to walking into your enemy and hitting space really fast. If you have a bow, you stand a bit away from the ♥♥♥♥er and hit space really fast. Either way, the outcome is that they die and you gain exp. Don't worry about difficulty; the game's♥♥♥♥♥♥easy on NG, and you'll be bored once you're through with it since the game has no substance. Theoretically enemies could kill you, but it wouldn't be because of skill; it'd just be because the enemies had bigger numbers and became insurmountable unless you were willing to use the next bow you found off weak mobs to plink at bigger mobs for a while until they die.
Personally, I died once, to enemies in the final dungeon that appear to be copies of your character. I learned that I wasn't pressing space fast enough.
So that's the gameplay. As for the design... bitDungeon tries very hard to be the original Legend of Zelda. The mystery and wonderment of that game worked then, because it was 1986 and game design and technology hadn't come very far. Now that games like The Witcher are about, the appeal is kind of lost. bitDungeon plays exactly like The Legend of Zelda: You have room-sized square instances with a few respawning enemies in them, a map (but not in dungeons), and a character that moves in cardinal directions. Moreover, combat consists of walking up to an enemy and pressing a button.
Dungeons also play out like in the original Legend of Zelda; you walk around in a multi-storeyed dungeon until you get a hang of the layout, pick up some keys and kill some minibosses along the way while also vandalising the local equivalent of vases (seed pods, hearts, whathaveyou). Get big key, walk up to boss, hit space really fast. You get a nice item with bigger numbers as a reward. Kill four or five bosses, go to the Dark World (which is basically a ripoff of A Link to the Past, except the world isn't really mirrored), which is another overworld except even more maze-like because there's no map. Get a feel for the layout, find the final dungeon, rinse repeat. After the final boss (who is apparently the creator of all matter but still laughably easy to kill by hitting space really fast), there's a final final boss, whose health I couldn't even touched. You can just walk past him. Presumably the goal of the game is to run through it enough times to get big enough numbers to kill that guy.
Except wait, the game's bloody boring. Why bother? Just play a fun game instead. I feel dignified in refunding this game to get my single dollar back.

I played the original Shank some years ago on Xbox Live Arcade and didn't get around to playing the sequel until fairly recently. While I am disappointed that the co-op campaign of the first game was replaced with a mere wave survival mode in this one, the single player campaign delivers the same sort of experience as the first, a beer-soaked, white-knuckle, bullet-riddled rampage through a grindhouse version of South America, and that's nothing to complain about. I would best describe Shank 2 as a 2D "Stylish Action Game", a term that never really caught on, since people think God of War invented this style of gameplay when, really, Devil May Cry did it first- and better. To be fair, the Shanks are closer in style to God of War, and though there is a combo grading system in the game you can get by perfectly well by mashing the buttons until you have smeared your enemies into the pavement. Shank 2 delivers fast, brutal action, varied weapons and cinematic boss battles, and despite the short length of the game it is excellently paced and good fun to play throughout. I hope this is not the last we have seen of our headbanded hero and his messy adventures.

The Weird Park games tell the story of a spoopy ghost clown and his sinister little jester buddy, operating out of an abandoned amusement park. Each installment casts you as some kind of investigator looking into a part of the park's past, and having to assemble crests, collect socks, and shoot crossbows to solve the mystery. They're all hidden object games in that grand European style where the English and the logic are just a little bit off, but you can see the polish get layered thicker and thicker as the series progresses. Honestly, there's a lot of difference between the three games, so I'll talk a little about each one.
Broken Tune is the first in the series, and is about as straight-forward a hidden object game as you can get. You pick up inventory items, you use them on things, you find 12 doodads in hidden object scenes to get another inventory item. There are a few puzzles, but no gimmicks, no item combinations, and no map. However, the game itself is very well laid-out, with items arranged so that they will send you back to areas that have new points of interest. The uses of items are crystal clear, and the hidden object scenes are clean and detailed. One interesting feature of the game is that it is split evenly into two acts, with no backtracking or items shared between halves. The graphics are good, the voice acting is goofy, and it'll last you a good two hours.
Scary Tales is the middle installment and a huge step up from Broken Tune. This one adds more puzzles, cutscenes, and areas to explore. The game is also WAY longer, clocking in at nearly 4 hours. In terms of design, there's more variety to the different areas. The first third of the game is extremely open, allowing you to travel to many different rooms right from the start. This does make the opening act a bit harder, however, because you get a crapload of items at once and no real clear direction for using some of them. After that the game goes into some really creative places and plays with fairy tale concepts. It's a great game to follow the first with, especially since it's more difficult overall.
The Final Show is, unsurprisingly, the last in the series. Again it improves over the previous game, this time adding new variations of hidden object scenes, interactive items you can manipulate, an upgrade system (!), achievements (in-game, not Steam), and a map for ease of travel. Final Show is just as long as Scary Tales if not longer, and is split into convenient chapters with no backtracking between. It also goes full-on crazy with the setting, having only the tutorial set in the real world. Oh yeah, it has a tutorial, too, for some reason. The graphics are fantasic, and there are quite a few voiced NPCs in this one as well, as opposed to the mostly barren games before it. The upgrade system might just be cosmetic, but having something else to find in addition to the necessary items was a treat. There's even a bonus chapter you unlock after beating it that fills in some of the backstory, and is honestly one of the best-designed chapters in the series. My only gripe is that Final Show is harder still than Scary Tales, which pushes it into slightly unfun territory sometimes. In particular, some of the item logic is really questionable. Beyond that, though, it's easily the most polished and deep game of the three.
Taken as a whole, Weird Park Trilogy feels like a great way to get into hidden object games because each part of the series is so different. They form a spectrum from bare-bones to feature-rich, which lets you discover precisely what your taste is. There's even a complete story told across them, though it's perfectly goofy and predictable. It's also hard to beat the value, since you're getting 10+ hours of game in a genre where most will only get you 2. My one piece of advice if you do get into it, though, is to play on the lower difficulties. Whereas the "Expert Modes" in other hidden object games make the puzzles and searches more challenging, all it does in the Weird Park games is eliminate the highlights around hidden object scenes. It's an annoyance made worse by the amount of backtracking you have to do sometimes, because each scene has to be done multiple times at different points in the game. Remember that if you ever get stuck, too... go back and look for a scene that's reactivated. With the hints and the improvements of the later games, though, it shouldn't distract too much from the overall experience. No matter if you're new to hidden object games or an old hand at them, you won't be disappointed.

Man, I LOVE this game.
As with all "Metroidvania" style platformers you absolutely, positively must use an appropriate controller. You wouldn't use a gamepad to play Civilization, so you shouldn't try to use a keyboard to play Guacamelee... or Super Meat Boy... or Spelunky. You are setting yourself up for pain and suffering.
That said, I love Guacamelee like I love blessed few platformers. It's challenging, but not overly so (*cough* Meatboy *cough*) - and the writing, art style, and oh-so-subtle references to other games and pop culture are magificent in their execution. The game ramps up the complexity gradually, so you have a chance to improve as you play - and even avoid optional areas that may be too difficult for you (although there are plenty of bonus rewards for the adventurous).

Guacamelee is a game I can't say enough good things about.  It is a very well-crafted metroidvania game with a great combat system and a very unique setting.  I don't think I've heard of any other games where you play a luchadore.
From the graphical style to the music, the writing and the sense of humor, gameplay and combat design, every aspect of this game is top notch.  There are also a lot of references to indie and classic video games such as Super Mario Bros, Castle Crashers, Viva Pinata, and of course, Metroid.  A couple memes are thrown into the mix which may be an issue for some people, but only ones that would reasonably fit the game setting were chosen so I don't think it's a problem.
The combat system is fast, fluid, and a lot of fun.  You can pull off some great combos and it even takes some cues from fighting games, adding mechanics like dodge canceling of special moves.  The game also includes a set of alternate costumes you can unlock which affect your combat abilities and strength.
If you're a fan of beat-em-up games or metroidvanias, I think you would enjoy this game.  It has definitely become one of my favorites.

F.E.A.R 2: Project Origin is made by same development studio, Monolith Productions but had different publisher, which is WB Interactive Entertainment. The game has a different protagonist, Michael Becket, who gains fast reflexes after being captured and recovered at the hospital. From this point, you try to find out why Alma takes interest at you, what is your history with Armacham Technology Corporation and what to do next.
First F.E.A.R is known for slow-mo ability, smart A.I and great gunplay. Does F.E.A.R 2: Project Origin offer the same experience or is it better or worse?
Worse.
+ You can aim with iron sights now. This allows you to use sniper rifles, which is a great addition.
+ There are two mech-suit sections, which honestly are fun. Might be off-putting to some players, but I personally liked those sections. Offered something different for gameplay.
+ This game doesn't take your weapons away at any moment, so you can spare your equipment for difficult encounters.
+ Slow-mo: It still looks cool to kill enemies when time is slowed down. It's mandatory to use it in order to survive, which is fine in my opinion.
+ Scary factor: While some of these are predictable (No scares when human enemies are near), most of the time they might spook you.
+ You can now cook off granades.
* Graphics look better, but the style and lighting is much more bland, especially the lighting. Compare it to previous game and say which looks better.
* A bit more open areas than in first game, but they limit them with invisible walls and fences, which you could clearly overstep.
* Some in-game awards if you want be completionist, but they could've been steam achievements (Old game, so it's not in cons).
- A.I: I don't know why people say that A.I is better because in my experience, enemies are much more dumber than in first F.E.A.R. They manage to kill themselves with their own granades and seem to rush to player more often. There is also less interaction between enemy soldiers. What I liked about previous game is that enemies react to what you're doing. There wasn't much, but it was something and you could actually use their talk as your advantage. In F.E.A.R 2 only thing that I remember is them saying "He's too fast". A.I wasn't perfect in F.E.A.R but it was much more advanced than an average one, which could've been improved upon. Very dissapointing.
-Saves: Monolith Productions took off manual saves and quick saves and replaced them with auto-saves/checkpoints. I don't understand why they did this. Most checkpoints work fine, but some of them are plain horrible. For example, I finished off one turret section, decided to take some ammunition from dead replicas, noticed a rocket launcher. Then I checked its ammunation by replacing it with a weapon given by that one guy, and it disappeared. I wanted it back so I loaded a previous checkpoint, which WAS BEFORE THE TURRET SECTION!
- Story: This is a subjective thing and my opinion is that it isn't good. Most of the characters weren't interesting, except for
. Ending was pretty anti-climatic in my opinion.
- You cannot lean on to anything anymore. Why was leaning removed?
- Some gameplay elements: Melee strikes are still awful. In my playthrough, there were so many weird misses that led to my death. Now, playing on hard difficulty, the game is suppose to be challenging. It does that, but there are so many ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t moments. Sometimes it requires you to shoot enemies with shotgun like four times, but they can hit you from same distance only once and kill you.
- Hearing distance: Sometimes there is barely any audio cues when someone is approaching you. Usually that happens when they come from behind. If don't put your audio to maximum, you usually miss them and then enemy manages to kill you with easily. Sneaking type enemies almost always require slow-mo, which in of itself isn't bad but I wish there were more indications. That one tram sequence: I hated it. Audio glitched off, so I couldn't hear where enemies come from and that includes their weapons. This resulted in many unfair deaths.
F.E.A.R 2: Project Origin is plain average game. There are too many things removed and new additions aren't enough. For me, it's 4/10 or 5/10.
Like always, if there was something I missed, any possible mistakes or something that you thought was worth noting, please let me know in the comments. Otherwise, if you liked F.E.A.R, you probably like F.E.A.R 2 due to bullet-time and scares, but if you are a hardcore fan of the first game, you most likely dislike this one.

I liked borderlands, and I actually prefer co-op to PvP. In the weird Overwatch vs. Battleborn rivalry, I started out in Battleborn's camp.
Then, after actually playing it... Well, in the past 2 days I've managed to finish about 20% of the games I've played. In the past two hours, it has CRASHED my whole system twice--and I'm not running a junker--and "lost contact to Steam" twice. The fifth time was my internet dropping out, so I won't ding it for that, but it's getting incredibly frustrating.
Which brings me to the player base--they quit like children at the slightest provocation, like someone else playing "their" battleborn or just if their team mate screws up (admittedly, in my case it was falling off the map in the beginning which made me look like an idiot but not I'm not actually bad at the game). This would be fine, if the game adapted. But it doesn't--you can't join a game in progress, and it maintains the starting number of slots--i.e. 5-person lobby when everyone has left.
I can't even blame them, because the lobby design is the worst I've ever seen. Even when it's working perfectly, there are very long wait times for server rooms, and the game will actually quit looking for more players and just put you in a 2 person lobby if that's all it can find. You can't join a game in progress, which probably contributes as well.
The "battleborn," or rather, the big character selection, which should be a selling point, isn't, because the requirements are crazy. You get maybe 1 level a mission. If you complete it. And if you don't get disconnected. And if all your team mates don't quit at the character selection screed (seriously the game keeps going after that, wtf). You get maybe 1 character every 5 levels, ending at level 60, or if you complete their (usually PvP, but sometimes just excessive) requirements. Also two are available through missions, one of which I can't get because of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t defense section and crashes every time I've tried (four times in a row).
Also, there is a painfully small amount of missions, something like 6-8 30-minute levels, which they expect you to play over and over at higher and higher difficulties. Basically, 5-6 hours of actual content, that they are STREEEETCHING out with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. LAME.
On the plus side, it is funny. Sometimes it tries too hard, but I have enjoyed that part of it. ISIC has the best lines.
In short, DEFINITELY don't pay full price for it-- I got it through humble bundle and I was considering getting another one to give to my friend (I was hoping it could be thing for us) but it's so frustrating I don't think I can.

The ending was a little disappointing in the way it "wrapped things up" (I don't want to spoil anything, so I won't elaborate on specifics). Unfortunately, the way it concluded left me feeling unsatisfied - like I hadn't been rewarded for all of my hard work. Well, the minons' hard work...whatever. Also, the invasions (which I assume were included to keep the player on their toes) were easily overcome with a few clicks, and didn't really bring the element of stress to the table that this genre usually brings. In fact, there weren't any moments where I felt stressed or was punished for my mis-management. I'm not saying it needed to be super difficult, but maybe just slightly more challenging, or even offering a challnge scale option. However, I suspect it was the developer's intention to make the game relaxed without being boring. I think younger audiences will find this the right level of challenge though...unless they're some kind of child genuis.
All of that said, I'm still going to recommend this game - it looks great, it was engaging, it was cheap to purchase, and I had fun -  all qualities I value as a casual gamer. It would have been super amazing if there were some achievements included and some improvements to the above mentioned. But in the end, it's a casual, 'busy-work' kind of game that is worth checking out. If the hereafter is anything like this game, sign me up! As a master of course, not a minon. Cutting down trees and mining will never be my thing - in this life or the next.
