Have you ever wanted to don the mask of a luchador and heroically save your senorita, El Presidente's daughter, from the clutches of the evil Calaca?  Well then you should get off the computer and start getting into better shape!  But if you want to experience that epic adventure without all the sweaty exercise and horrible danger then Guacamelee is perfect for you!
Guacamelee is a metroidvania-style beat'em up from DrinkBox Studios.  You play the role of Juan or Tostada and set out on an adventure to save the world from the evil Calaca.  Throughout the game you'll unlock new moves from the Rooster Uppercut to the Goat Climb.  As you unlock more moves you'll be able to backtrack through the game and access areas that were previously inaccessible.
Guacamelee comes with Steam Workshop support and with it the ability to create and/or use custom skins created by the Steam community.  There are areas that act as arenas to fight in and test your luchadorian prowess.  There are only a few side quests in the game but they do add a tiny bit of background to the story of the game's world.
While replayability may be limited to just a tougher difficulty setting the game still has enough content in it to last you a decent amount of time.  Going for a 100% playthrough will take you upwards of 15-20 hours (or at least it did for myself...  I am kind of terrible at games though).
All in all, I do recommend this game to anyone looking for a good and funny take on an average day in the life of a luchador.

Guacamelee is a fantastic, witty and beautifully styled adventure through Mexican clichés and folklore alike. Being, as the name implies, a melee brawler you are eased into each new combo with clever environmental hints to break through to new areas. Platforming can be tricky but is thankfully forgiving with no health penalties for missing a jump. Upgrades come often and enemies vary quite nicely to keep the tempo going. Overall a fun adventure with drop in co-op to boot.
The only improvement would be well voiced characters, which in itself is difficult to do, but which does not detract from the overall game experience.
With incredibly smooth gameplay and comedic characters, this game is a joy!

You're thrown into an open world. You're given targets that you must kill, and in some instances, objectives to complete. That's it, the rest is up to you. You decide your weapon of choice to pull off the perfect hit; will it be the pistol? Shotgun? Assault Rifle? Submachine Gun? Sniper Rifle? You can spend the money that you earn from hits on different upgrades. Will you opt for a silencer on your pistol, or will you spend it on improved lockpicking skills? There are multiple different playstyles, and the choice is entirely up to you. Will you run in, guns blazing, killing anything that stands between you and your target? Or will you sneak in, using a disguise you stole from a guard that is now unconcious in the dumpster? How will you kill your targets? Will you poison their food? Strangle them? Snipe them? Rig a chandelier to fall on them? You choose how you play the game. You choose your definition of a perfect hit. First time players beware, however, you will find yourself spending lots of time doing trial-and-error to find the best ways to kill your target. If you enjoy games with linear gameplay where there's only one way to win, then you will probably not enjoy this game. However, if you want a sandbox stealth experience, where you get to decide how the game will play out, at $8.99, this game is perfect for you.

This game really kind of hurts to review. It's exactly what i was hoping, chrono trigger like combat, interesting rpg elements and a vast open world...
But it feels like it has no soul. I don't think i've ever seen a game that suffered so much for having a silent protagonist before. There's so many things going on it almost feels like a tales game or something else... and yet your character literally just sits there with a blank look on his face as bad stuff really starts going down... and apparently does not care at all. It feels like someone went through a checklist of chrono trigger or some other big rpg's, but missed the entire point of the game having a soul.
I am Setsuna is probably the most I've ever been disappointed by a game. I went into it REALLY wanting to like it... but as i played it just kind of wore me down. The combat is potentially interesting, but just feels stiff and lifeless. The animations have minimal creativity or visual interest besides fairly standard particle effects. I like how you can wait to attack with certain party members to add more depth to the fairly standard ATB gauge at this point, but the drop system is completely absurd, There's at least 30 different 'effects' you can trigger on any enemy, and apparently any one of those can trigger a special drop, which means bosses are a potential nightmare if you ever want some super special thing out of it, but of course the game doesn't tell you what you have to do to get any of these effects, so you'd have to go online and have your nose in a guide the whole time. The story as well, it feels so much like they're trying to make something deep and impactful, but they ended up making basically a really depressing take on Tales of Symphonia... except your main character apparently just doesn't care. A TON of stuff apparently happens offscreen or is never actually told to you that your character has said or does.
I feel the need to reiterate. I am not hating on this game because I don't like RPGs, i opened it up WANTING to like it... but this type of stuff happens constantly and between the non impactful (if potentially interesting) combat, the heinous potential requirements for getting loot from monsters, and the story which you're apparently being railroaded into without even being given any context really just ruins it for me.
Gonna give a few minor spoilers from the first 30 minutes now to present my point.
You walk into a snowy trail, run into some old guy, he says "huh, you must be this mercenary from this clan of super awesome mercenaries that's supposed to help me"
you: ...
old guy: well i guess you're not one for talking, lets complete our mission
(beat tutorial)
old guy: man, thanks for all your help, hope you don't get into trouble
you: ...
*suddenly a mysterious man walks out of the shadows after the old man leaves*
mysterious guy: (who definitly isn't evil) you're one of those super mercenaries, right? i've got a job for you to kill this one girl...
you:...
*time passes*
this is my first issue... you just.. apparently take the job? a silent protagonist is one thing, but they literally skip a huge set up for the story just stopping with 'i have a job for you' and don't even actually confirm that you accepted the job until you run into the person you're supposed to kill. Literally i was running around for 30 minutes trying to figure out if I actually had taken the job or told the *definitly not evil* man to shove it and hid out in the arctic.
*accidently run into the girl you're apparently supposed to kill*
girl: wait, are you here to kill me? wait please, cuz i'm planning on killing myself anyway, do you mind just waiting a while?
you:...
*you get knocked out*
and... yea, that's it. that's the entire interaction you have with this girl (who the townsfolk basically worship as their savior, again, ToS comparison) and then she takes you on as her bodyguard... apparently cuz you came to an agreement at some point that you'll help her go kill herself? I wouldn't even mind this so much if all of this wasn't just vaguely implied. The point of a silent protagonist is so you can project yourself onto them, but apparently this guy is making deals and taking jobs offscreen and I'm expected to know what has been agreed on?
This would be like if you loaded up final fantasy, some old guy just walked out and said "there's a prophesy for you to save the world" and the screen cut to black with you waking up on a different continent and no direction.

[Please note that this game, "The Happy Hereafter," is a slow pace game; it's not for everyone.]
There isn't much can be said about the game's visuals asides from that they're amazingly well done. Pretty much the same thing can be said about the game's audio. The visual and audio can be adjusted in the game's option menu.
The Happy Hereafter is an strategy simulation game. Where the individual can control the actions of their workers by assigning them certain task[s] to carry out like gathering resources from the environment around them. All the while maintaining their happiness that max level.
There are plenty of colorful and zangy characters to meet in the game. Some of them do have quests that needs to be fulfill.
There are plenty of artifacts to find and collect around the environment. Some of them can be easily found right away.
The building plans are locked because they're connected to the quests that given out by characters. They can be used to build new buildings in the environment. When building a structure it'll take some time. However, it can go much faster, only if add another worker to speed up the building process. [This same strategy can be applied to clearing away the garbage from roads and such.] The newly built buildings can be upgraded as long as the required item[s] are found.
There are two ways of scroll ("Click & Drag" and "Edge") in the game. There's little and/or no mouse control for "Edge" scrolling. There's plenty of mouse control for "Click & Drag" scrolling. I prefer "Click & Drag" scrolling it makes everything a bit easier.
There are total of five different trading cards. You only get the three of those cards from the game. There are several ways to get the rest of the trading card: Purchased from Steam’s Market; Trade with friends; Booster Packs and it’s Booster Pack Creator. Badge can be crafted and upgraded with these trading cards. This feature is only available for Steam’s version of this game.
Final thoughts, I definitely enjoying playing this game all the way through to the end. As for the replay value I would say it's low. I would recommend this game but not at the full price.

This game was a disappointment for me.  Not because the game is bad, it's not great, it is a fun casual strategy game, but it was a disappointment because it was a downgrade from a previous Alawar/Buka Entertainment game.
The Promised Land is a previous game from Alawar/Buka that was released in 2012, it was a game that I really enjoyed for what it was.  With this game I was hoping for more of the same but maybe a bit bigger of a scale or maybe with some more depth.  The Happy Hereafter however seems to be a downgrade on The Promised Land rather than improving on the formula that made me a fan .  For this review I'll touch on a few of the points that I felt really soured me on this game compared to the one that made me buy this game.
So the game is about starting off a colony, managing the workers that you have to finish tasks given to you so you can upgrade your buildings and continue progressing.  Right off the start the worker system showed a big downgrade from the previous game.  The workers are all generic and it doesn't matter what each one is doing, in The Promised Land, each character had a description, stats and preferred job(as well as disliked job).  Each worker in The Happy Hereafter is interchangeable, it doesn't matter what job each is doing and you can just throw them wherever and it doesn't make much difference.  In The Promised Land you had to plan out where each new worker went and what the best fit was to maximize their ability to collect resources and perform the best for your colony.  Each worker in The Promised Land could also gain experience making them better at certain tasks which again added depth in worker placement.  Workers could also be stationed in one area and they would continually work that area and if they ran out of resources they would patiently wait till resources spawned again.  In The Happy Hereafter if a worker tries to collect resources from a depleted area they will just wander back to town and if you didn't notice it (there is a pumpkin head character they hide behind) then you have an idle working doing nothing.  And lastly on the workers,  You can not assign more than one worker to collect resources from an area other than the very last resource you can collect, it really prevents you from progressing and puts you in a situation you don't need as many workers as you could have space for as most of them will stand around doing nothing.
There isn't really as much story as The Promised Land either, there wasn't much in The Promised Land either to be fair but again something lacking in this title.
Art is great in both games, again not much of difference or upgrade, but it's not terrible and is nice to look at.  It was pretty good in their previous game so why mess with it.
There is also random enemies that will try to pillage your storage area.  These are more annoying then fun to deal with.  They are also incredibly easy to deal with and pose no real threat, a couple of clicks and your back to the game.
The resources in the game for building and upgrading as well seem to be poorly balanced.  I had max workers on all areas to collect as much wood as possible and I was still constantly running out of wood, while having large stock piles of food, stone and gold (as well as other resources).  This could have been an easy fix by allowing more than one worker to collect resources from the mill, instead I had to constantly micromanage the workers to have one collecting while another was delivering.  As much as that might seem like it ads some difficulty or complexity, for me it just seemed tedious and takes away from the fun of these types of games.
To sum it all up, The Promised Land is 3$ more on steam, but you'll get a lot more out of that game compared to this one.  If you are looking for a short, casual, indie resource collection, strategy game, I would suggest The Promised Land over this game.  If you already have The Promised Land and you are looking for something very similar or better, skip this game entirely as I just didn't find it be near the quality or fun that The Promised Land was.

Solid Snake may have become the first video game character to official retire in MGS4, but the legacy of Big Boss had many gaps that needed to be filled and Hideo Kojima delivered in Ground Zeroes and of course Phantom Pain, possibly the pinnacle of the series with the best tactical stealth CQC sandbox environment to date. Konami really did Kojima dirty following the release, and with Kojima moving on to other things, I am perfectly happy with this final chapter of the saga done by his hand. In Phantom Pain we get the answers behind the creation of the "Outer Heaven" seen in MG1; why Big Boss seemed to come back to life in MG2 (the original 8-bit games before we even get to the MGS: Twin Snakes saga.) MG1 was my first NES game as a kid, and to grow up with these characters over 30 years has been an amazing and rewarding experience.

Ignore my play time, I play almost all games at work and dont have an internet connection so my play time is very wrong. At time of writing this I have probably just shy of 50 hours into the game.
I'll place the TLDR up front. This game rocks! Its a very good rebirth and improvement to the Rollercoaster Tycoon games. And make no mistake, this game was very obviously supposed to be a rebirth to those games.
Now, lets get into some detail. First off, people saying this game doesnt scratch the itch that Rollercoaster Tycoon left are simply on crack or its been so long since they played RCT they simply dont remember it. I do. I first played RCT3 just a couple years ago and fell in love with it, played it for hundreds of hours and still return to it occassionally. The game is very fresh in my mind. I got it on GoG not Steam for the fact checkers lol.
If I didnt know better I would be easily convinced this game is made from the same people as a masterfully done remake or sequel to RCT3. Except better. The game runs smooth as butter, everything is better; coaster building, management, graphics, terrain manipulation, the list goes on.
I mean you can make a mountain and create a realistic tunnel through it! No way in RCT3 to do that. Hell, you can make an entire coaster in an underground cavern/cave system.. way cool!  Customer feelings on coasters are much more realistic, you cant build something that just goes into a tight banked turn at 120mph and expect people to like it you have to take everything into consideration, yes RCT3 did have a similar system but not near as realistic. You could do crazy things that would literally kill people and they'd be happy about it. You could make a coaster very bumpy and very rough and it could still be a success. Not here.  The management goes way deeper you can customize and change almost everything.
Dont get me wrong, the game could use some improvement to make some things a little easier. Scenery/structure building isnt the greatest and can be a real pain when you want to do anything to extravagant. However scenery makes a big difference in how successful your rides and park are so it is kind of a mandatory deal if you want to make an insanely successful park. For instance having pieces snap to the track at the proper angle and placement(of course have an option to turn snap to off), like coaster doors would make it so much faster to build, instead you have to tediously and carefully tweak and retweak everything stop and wait for animations to see how it looks, etc. Duration on some animations would be very handy, coaster doors again, say you want doors on your tracks at each end of the station. The train goes slow coming and going, some coaster doors simply wont stay open long enough for the entire train to go through before it closes mid train and just looks silly.
I could get nit picky and go through and mention all the little things that I would like to see or that I was mildly dissappointed with, but overall I am very impressed with this game and am very happy to have it. My days with RCT3 are likely done as i have found a worthy and better replacement to it!
Yes, I recommend it.

That being said, the game does look great at 720p and on everything turned off, or on low.  The effects are really neat and I definitely enjoyed the anime-style cutscenes, it's very refreshing compared to CGI-everything.
The game looks great, and so far the characters are very well fleshed out and have their own universe about them, and the style is great.  However, with the performance issues (on AMD-hardware systems, and possibly some Nvidia/Intel systems) I would recommend writing to Gearbox about fixing some performance issues before balancing out character performance and meta-tweaks.
Gearbox has done some great stuff in the past, and definitely care for their writing and attention to detail, but we definitely need to not ignore this issue.

The biggest improvement has to be the multiple ways of approaching each level.  You could beat the level one way then talk to a buddy who did the same level a completely different way. The music was used well to heighten the mood when need be. As expected the graphics and game mechanics have been improved.
Cons: Although many paths exist for completing a level, Blood Money still suffers from the fact that once a sequence has been found for beating the level it is pretty easy.  However, this is still way better than the previous two games.  The game is only just good.  There are not many epic memorable moments and you never feel that involved with the level.
If you like the stealth action genre then this is a must play.

Neon Warp has a simple mechanic and is hard as nails. What kills all the fun is the poor implementation though.
There is no proper tutorial, so the first stages were just me fumbling around, trying to wrap my head around the rules. There is a grid of squares in 3 different colours. You are supposed to turn them into a single target colour. First you pick a starting square. Then you move to adjacent squares. If you move between 2 differently coloured squares, the target square turns the third colour.
I'll be honest, I didn't enjoy the base mechanic, but I don't fault the game for that. There is clearly a target audience, as evidenced by the ~3.5% of players who have unlocked all achievements. It just happens to not be me, even though I love most other logic and movement puzzle games.
What I will fault the game for is the very poor and unforgiving design. It forces you to complete a level within a certain number of moves. Even the lowest of 3 bars is very close to the minimum amount of moves, meaning you have to play near-optimally to even clear a level. Unfortunately the game only unlocks the next level once you beat the previous one. There is no skipping mechanic, no way to take a break from a level and advance elsewhere. If you ever get stuck, you're forced to beat your head against a wall. And you better plan out all your moves ahead, even on large grids, because there is no way to undo a move. Make one careless turn at the end and you'll probably have to restart the whole level due to having made too many moves. To give a sense of scope: Level 13 out of 150 had to be cleared in 26-34 moves, which is already starting to get pretty complex. I can't access later levels, but the 12 levels I beat were quite repetetive and I found myself bored of the unchanging rules and mechanics by the end. The store screenshots make it seem there are more mechanics in later stages, but I never got there and can't skip ahead to check them out.
Whenever I tabbed away or minimized the window I had to restart the game because the screen was full of graphical glitches rendering it unplayable. If you play on keyboard, never touch the mouse as even simply moving the cursor without clicking will move your square around!
Neon Warp is a one-trick pony that gets old fast. I was a bit frustrated with the game's difficulty for sure, but more than that I felt dissapointed at the game design and bored with the mechanic. I never really warmed up to the game. And it doesn't seem to be just me, looking at the global achievement stats: ~27% of players have completed 1 level perfectly. ~12% have cleared 5 levels (perfect or not). So within the first 5 levels, more than half the players gave up! Only ~6% did 10 levels perfectly (me included). And from there on we're pretty much down to the hard core of ~3.5% who unlocked everything.
If you think you're among those 3.5% this game is probably great for you! It has a ton of content with 150 pre-made levels and several time-attacks. All that for a pretty fair price (especially on sale). If you think you're not among this group - hands off! There are so many more accessible and enjoyable puzzle games than this!

Okay. So first things first. This is not Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance. If you go into this game expecting it to be like that, you will be disappointed. The gameplay, comparative to it's predecessor, is very different. Let's run through the biggest changes from the first game.
1. The Economy.
In Supcom FA you collected two types of resources; Energy and Mass. Mass was collected on specific points on the map through mass extractors, and you could build mass fabricators which turned energy into Mass as well. Energy was created through power generators which could be placed anywhere, and to a limited degree through hydrocarbon plants, which you could only build on specific points.
These resources would be stored to a specific limit, which could be increased by building Mass and Energy storage buildings, after that point your resources would be shared to your team, or if you don't have one, or they are also full, wasted completely.
Spending resources was done in a spend-over-time style. Instead of building a unit for 50 mass, you build a unit for 50 mass at a rate of 2 mass per second. This applied to all buildings and units.
This created a third, more silent resource called Engineering power. If you couldn't produce enough to outpace your resource collection, you would effectively waste resources, and so getting more engineers and factories was important.
Supreme Commander 2 takes a different spin on this concept. While the basics of Mass and Energy collection remain the same, storage is not a problem in this game. You have effectively unlimited storage, which, while it may require less work, less strategy on the part of the player, is not necessarily a bad thing. To some, the act of having to prevent your storages from being filled was tedious, and the storage buildings were, in vanilla gameplay, quite limited; locked to tier one only.
More notably, though, is the method of spending. Rather than keeping the spend-over-time model of the original games, Supreme Commander 2 vouched for a more standard RTS style of having set amounts, and paying all at once. To those used to games such as Age of Empires and it's ilk this change will not be too jarring, and is not a terrible system in concept, although I, and I think many fans of the original games prefer the old style, it is, when you boil down to it, preference.
2. Advancements/Research
In SupCom FA there were three "Tech Levels". You start at tech level one, and you have to upgrade your Commander and Factories to the next level in order to construct buildings and units of each level. Each level got exponentially stronger, e.g. tech level 2 is around 3 (?) times stronger than tech 1, and tech 3 is 3 (?) times stronger than tech 2, making it 9 times stronger than tech 1.
SupCom 2 completely abandoned this model, and made all units a singular tech level, but introduced a new mechanic and resource; research.
Research is a resource you gain slowly over time, and can be gained faster through the Research Center building, or a few faction specific ones such as the Cybran's Proto Brain complex.
Research points can then be spent on items in the research tree, which has five categories: Land, Air, Naval, Structure, and ACU. Research items can unlock new units, improve existing units, unlock new experimentals, give things new abilities, and make doing things cheaper/faster.
The abilities and upgrades you can gain from the research tree are nothing to scoff at, and are immensely important. They can do everything from giving your entire army shields, to making all of your mass extractors have anti air turrets on them.
The system, I feel, is very well handled, but may be a sore in those who enjoyed the tiers of the original game. It feels like an expanded version of the original games ACU upgrades, but more diverse and interesting.
My biggest complaint about this system is that, once you have unlocked everything in the research tree, there is no use for the admittedly quite expensive buildings, unless you are the UEF, and they have turrets on them, but even in that case they are subpar, at best, especially in that endgame scenario.
All in all, I think it's decently handled, but I think if they had kept the previous tiering system, and added research options to those tiers individually, it would be a more expansive, and even better system than what we have currently.
3. Experimentals.
This is where it hurt the most for me, in two ways.
On one hand, the experimentals of this game are rather dumbed down from the original game. Take the Fatboy, for instance. In the original game, this was a weapon of mass destruction; it was equipped with esentially battleship bombardment weapons, was amphibious, functioned as a mobile factory that could build most land units, and was an air staging platform, allowing planes to refuel on it. In SupCom 2, the fatboy is essentially just the first thing. A giant tank equipped with battleship weapons. While it's destructive power is still impressive, and definitely looks and feels cool, there is some diversity within each experimental that seems lost. They're more specialized in SupCom 2.
But, on the other hand there's more diversity in Experimentals in general, especially with SupCom 2's dlc. Instead of getting 4-5 experimentals, like in SupCom FA, you get 8-9 in SupCom 2. And some of these experimentals introduce new mechanics which are extremely fun. There's an air transport experimental, which can move other experimentals, a mechanic not found in the original game. There's a building that shoots out a long ranged beam that can convert enemy units to your side, even experimentals, if you can wait long enough. There's an artillery that can build units, and fire them across the map, even behind enemy lines.
There are a lot of things the experimentals in this game allow you to do that are simply not possible in the original game, but that being said, every experimental individually feels less incredible.
A great way to sum it up is:
In SupCom FA, you had the galactic colossus, which could shoot out a destructive laser and occasionally pull in and destroy a unit with a magnet.
In SupCom 2, you have the universal colossus, which can shoot out a destructive laser.
And you have a giant magnet on wheels which can pull in multiple units and destroy them.
Which you prefer is up to you, but they both have their benefits, I think.
The only major change other than that regarding experimentals is that, while in SupCom FA you build them with engineers like buildings, in SupCom 2 you build them out of their own factories. This, again, is a taste change. It requires less micromanaging, which some could see as better as it's less tedious, while others might see it as losing some of the strategy.
All in all, though. Supreme Commander 2 is an excellent game. It's just different. There are not many big, glaring issues that I found in my playthrough. There were just minor disappointments when not seeing things I liked from the original game, but, alternatively, when I went back to Supreme Commander FA, there were things I was disappointed not to have from this game (like the reclaim building. God I love the reclaim building. Stick one in your base when your enemy is gunship happy and just reap the mass.)
I'd recommend it to anyone looking for a fun RTS game that stands on it's own. I would not, however, recommend it as a Supreme Commander FA sequel. It simply isn't that.
For a proper score, I'd give it an 8/10.

The Happy Hereafter is a resource management game in which you are the mayor of a small town of Zombies and Ghouls. By letting your townspeople collect resources you are able to progress by constructing new buildings and upgrade existing ones, attract more inhabitants and discover the surroundings of your village.
There is a story, devided up in a lot of missions, which is mainly about developing your town and getting to know the characters you come across whilst playing.
Let me start off by telling what I like about the game. I enjoyed the graphics, the characters you come across and some of the missions. There are also scrolls and statues to be found that give you bonus material upon completing the game.
There were, however, a lot of things I did not like about The Happy Hereafter.
The story is basically a tutorial that lasts throughout the entirety of the game in the form of missions: gather this, build that, go there, andsoforth.
Secondly, gameplay consists of dragging and dropping villagers onto the resource to gather, buildings to build or research to complete. Nothing more, nothing less. You do not know how much resources there are left to gather per location and how fast they regenerate so as the map expands due to exploration, revealing new resource locations, this becomes increasingly tedious work.
The game is also not balanced. Villagers grow hungry during gameplay and eat your gathered food, but if you periodically perform a bit of magic in the circus their appetite is reset. Resources are plentifull in the midgame and apart from the bore to collect them, are quite easy to stockpile. There are some enemies that try to steal resources, but defeating them is easy enough.
Last but not least, I have encountered a few bugs. Some made the villagers non-responsive to me trying to drag-and-drop them, but I also had to start over once as the barrier I needed to clear in order to progress would not budge, no matter what I tried.
All in all, this is a game without enough varied gameplay, lacking a real story, poorly balanced and occasionally bugged. Though I like the concept, I cannot recommend this game.

The Happy Hereafter is not a terrible game. However, the reasons why I cannot really recommend it (even to fans of the genre) are basically these:
a) It seriously lacks replayability. Once you play through the "story", that's all there is to see. No other missions, no sandbox mode, nothing that usually make games of the city-building genre interesting.
b) It gets repetitive. Fast. It's like grinding through levels on a WoW character or playing a Facebook/mobile F2P game: build, upgrade, upgrade more, gather, build, rinse and repeat. There is no real depth whatsoever and the "challenge" is basically optimizing your material production so you'll be done with the game as soon as possible.
c) Short. You are done with the game in 4-6 hours or so, depending on how quickly you learn the ropes and how well you manage your workforce and assets.
Though it is very cute and the graphics and overall theme are very appealing (which is why I bought this in the first place), I'd only recommend this for younger players wanting to get introduced to the genre. For anyone else, there are better city-builders out there.

This is a hard recommendation for me.  On the positive it is a clever game with a few good ideas, such as the incorporation of RPG elements and focusing the game on boss fights.  However, the game is hampered by a few issues that put it a step behind other, better, shoot-'em-ups like Crimzon Clover.
The first is the fact that there is no slowdown button.  There is no control button to slow your phoenix down to navigate the more complex fields of bullets.  Instead, the analog stick is pressure sensitive.  So, when you're using the lighter touch on the analog stick you're sacrificing maneuverability for movement safety, hoping you can maintain control.
A second big problem is the way the game is structured.  Since you only have a single life per fight, if you get hit, you have to go through a continue screen that allows you to exit to the map or select another phoenix.  These menus are animated.  Overly-animated menus are actually a huge pet-peeve of mine because they add that 1 second that's just enough to be irritating between bouts.  On later fights where death is a regular risk, you will go through this a lot, especially due to the often imprecise controls.
Thirdly, there's the repetitive bosses.  You will fight the same bosses over and over, ad-nauseum, throughout the game.  As you move forward, many of these bosses with become harder.  Either their attack patterns will change, their bullets will move faster or start homing in on you, or you will see some combination thereof.  When the ideas for tough bosses run out, the game is padded out with fights against two bosses simultaneously, which is fine, but still repetitive.  After seeing the same skeleton boss over and over through the game it got pretty old.
Finally, and arguably the most important, is this is a very, very simple game.  Unlike a lot of the best shooters ever made, Phoenix Force does little in terms of gameplay.  You auto-fire during the fights, so your job basically becomes "dodge the things".  The bosses all move the same way, waving left to right across the top of the screen, and while their attacks are varied, simply moving in a U-pattern following them and focusing attacks on them between their pattern cycles will win you just about every fight.  What I'm saying is, there is no really unique concept here.  There are a ton of bullet hell shooters on Steam now and given the quality of so many of them, I cannot justify buying this game unless you have all of the other good ones in your library already.
Not to say Phoenix Force is a bad game, but in all of its simplicity and attempts to be a progressive experience rather than a flashy arcade game, it loses a lot of the fun factor so many other games in this genre have.  The reason people love games like Giga Wing, the Touhou shooters or the masterpiece that is Ikaruga is BECAUSE they are varied and challenging arcade-style experiences.  The lack of simple RPG elements does not make them lesser games, just as the presence of those elements in Phoenix Force does not make it great.

Hitman: Blood Money is a classic. Without a doubt, this is one of the best Hitman games in the series, which is unfortunate when compared to what Absolution could've been. As with the other Hitman games, you are an assassin with a very particular set of skills, hired to assassinate people unfortunate enough to have a contract placed on them.
Each level is appropriately huge and unique in their own ways, ranging from a deserted carnival to a colourful neighbourhood, to a sprawling casino. The way you kill your targets is all up to you; whether it be poisoning their wine, or dropping a chandelier on their heads. Every level is filled with their own quirks and tricks - again, it's all up to you to discover them.
The game may feel dated at times as the game was released way back in 2006, but IMO it has aged pretty well, assuming if you can get used to the controls.
If you're thinking of playing one Hitman game, definitely get this game.

Blood Money is by far the best Hitman game ever released. The amount of freedom you get in each level is great. You can go stealthily, and assasinate your targets silently, or just gun everyone down. The graphics aren't bad, and the way enemies react is awesome. The maps are beautiful and great. Gameplay is steady, stable and a fun. But achieving 'Silent Assasin' isn't easy, especially on the hardest difficulty. If you think Hitman: Absolution will be like this, you're wrong.

A simple, yet surprisingly mind-boggling puzzle game. Simplicity may be perceived as a negative connotation when it comes to games for many people, but Neon Warp's simplicity actually works in it's favor in the best way possible and becomes one of it's strength. The game has the kind of content that speaks for itself while still managing to be entertaining and being challenging enough to make you think, and it's simplicity allows players - experienced and new - to get into the game easily without much hassle.
Aesthetically, the game also impresses with it's beauty - it delivers neon tiles, as suggested by the title. Neon Lights also features a simplistic dark background that, combined with the aforementioned neon tiles, is very easy on the eyes; which could prove to be a major highlight for people like me, who prefer to play games at night rather than day.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

While Her Story has won numerous gaming awards for its innovative gameplay and presentation, ultimately I find it hard for myself to call it a game or a video game. Yes I enjoy Her Story immensely as while the mystery starts off slow, it begins to reel you in more and more as you try hard to discover more and more tidbits of video clips.
It has a great narrative, enhanced even more by the way you have to search for the relevant clues yourself. But this is always where the problem occurs when you have to think about Her Story as a "game". A game usually involves some kind of rules, and then a mechanic for which to interact with the game itself, and then either an end which you will win (or lose) the game or some way of ever increasing the difficulty of the game mechanic that makes you try harder. Yet when I play more and more, this does not have any of the elements in a game. The mechanic is basically a search tool for you to find all the video clips, yet the problem occurs when even if you reach the end (or if you cheat, just watch all the videos in the installation folder), you are not sure what the "end" is. The author has stated it is deliberate in which you as the player has to draw your own conclusion but while this is an amazing experience, i find it hard to call it a game. It maybe a new way of consuming interactive contents (a la the good old FMV based choose your own adventures) but when it has zero replayability, nor an ending, the gamer in me is left frustrated. I rather called this an FMV novel (a la the popular Japanese visual novels) than an actual game.
Nevertheless the time was well spent clicking through all the video clips and trying to create a mental image of "Her Story", it is no different than reading a mystery novel and trying to reason yourself what has happened. Just don't expect this to be an actual "game".

I was sold on the idea of this game being a spiritual successor to Chrono Trigger, it's the prime selling point of this game. However it is far from being anything like it.
While I do appreciate a Turn-based RPG that doesn't rely on random encounters, the placement for the common mobs are uninspired. Whatever happened to navigating through a certain location by dodging the enemy in order to not trigger an encounter? in this game, if you touch an invisible circle in the vicinity of an enemy, you will trigger a fight. It is nearly impossible to navigate through the lifeless walking animations of the enemies without triggering the encounter.
What really felt satisfying about Chrono Trigger's combat system is that it was quite simple, normal attacks/single tech/dual tech/triple tech/items. That was it, what was challenging was figuring out weaknesses, timing, or combinations to defeat enemies and bosses. In I Am Setsuna they ruined combat by making the system  more engaging instead of making enemies more engaging.
If you're looking for a turn-based RPG with a story hashed out of several Final Fantasy games, sure buy this game.
If you want to buy this game because anywhere you look the name Chrono Trigger pops up and you've got nothing but good memories about that game. Look elsewhere, because this game is nothing like it.

I am Setsuna in general I found to be a fun game if you just stick with the story content alone. The game itself is a hommage to a number of old jrpg giants during the snes era. Most notably Chrono Trigger. The Story itself can easily be a non cannon CT story set in the era of Zeal.
Pros:
Chrono Trigger Tech system done via FF7 materia style
Great Art work, atmospheric feel, music. Very appropriate. As a work of Art the game is great in it's own right.
Good Nostalgia feels from the days of the Jrpg legends and hero's of old. If your someone who really like's that kind of feel this game is for you.
Cons:
Outside of it's Art...the game has some real problems. First off Momentum is horribly explained.
Second...no New Game+... can't rightfully call itself a CT inspired game with no NG+
Third... no multiple endings, (personally I like the single ending it does have but come on guys... this is embarassing as a supposed CT inspired game)
Forth...no true replayability. Really sad point here for a CT inspired game.
Mixed:
The extra content after the game is very interesting but at the same time it also has it's problems. Min/Maxing Fluxes to totally pimp out your favorite characters is handled horribly. Certain things about the grind you can tell the dev team just didn't spend enough time thinking about. The content itself however can be pretty cool. For me personally I decided not to do it once I realized what I would have to do. The game is good but not good enough for me to want to put in that kind of time to finish the extra content after the main story, and yes it can be quite a grind but not the fun kind (IN MY OPINION)
In the end I am Setsuna is one of those Jrpgs that I will only really play once... and thats it lol. I feel like it falls short of the mark that it tries to hit. Overall though I had a positive experience.

Pleasant family-friendly building/resource management game, probably takes about 5 hours to complete first time through.
Resource management is crucial or you will be waiting around for building materials.  Personally I was always short of gold, but there is a limited production/trade chain which I could have used to better effect.  You also need to manage your own 'mana' to repel raiders and entertain your workers.  There is some spotting of objects scattered over the map but not much is made of this.
The map is small and building placement pre-determined.  There is a constant stream of directions from your 'assistant' which ensures no-one can ever get stuck with this game.  The instructions are not imo optimised - so you can ignore them and construct/upgrade available buildings as seems best to you - you will get the building reward eventually and the game doesn't quite run on rails.
And there is a very naughty leprechaun....

One of the most satisfying game ever made, in basically everyone's opinion. If you're searching for the best Assassination Simulator ever made look no further. If you're worried about story and plot and... stuff, don't worry all you need to know is explained to you in the very beginning. This game easily makes my top 10 of all time.

Oh! yeah... Mr. 47 is back in this new installment were the story follows the life of professional hitman Agent 47, as narrated in cut scenes by a former director of the FBI to a journalist who is interviewing him. The wheelchair-using ex-director recounts how his agency tracked 47 over a two-year period (but enough of the plot, don't want to spoil it for you).
Lots of improvements were done to the gameplay adding more simplified commands and ways to do stuff while using 47. The disguise works better than the previous games and using the split screens give you more insight of important events happening in each of the assassinations. As before there is more than 1 way to complete the missions, but this time every action you do has a consequence for the next mission, because if you go into a mission gunning everyone in your way, in the next mission the guards or the enemy will be able to recognize you quickly; that makes getting the "Silent Assassin" rating (keep in mind you will need patience and well-timed moves to get this rating) something critical, not just because you will get a lot of money for every mission (which will be handy to purchase weapons and upgrades). Plus you get to experience some random and funny events during the mission (won't spoil any of them, but let's just say you can see Mr. 47 dressed as a clown... XD).
Graphics are awesome and a superb improvement from their previous games in the series. Music is amazing and it really makes you feel like you are in a movie.
If you played the previous games in the series, probably you will like this one a lot and if you beat it once with random rating; want more? Get the "Silent Assassin" rating in all missions, I assure you will give you a good challenge and it will be rewarding!...

Really enjoyed this game. There isnt a lot of gameplay here but there is a great and original approach to telling a story. You play the game through an old style desktop and a video database search program. The only way to find video clips is to find them through the search engine. So for example if the woman mentions a name in one clip, searching for that name may bring up more new clips and so on. You have to find and watch these videos, some only a few seconds long up to a couple of minutes long, to try and piece together the story which revolves around the murder of a man.
Good points:

I'm kinda torn about whether or not to recommend it, as there aren't intensely strong reasons for either leaning, but I've ultimately settled on 'no'.
This is basically Virtual Villagers, but it doesn't run in the background, so you take a much more active role, which is pretty good, for the most part. Unfortunately, the way they've gone about this is to triple the level of micromanagement. For resource gathering there are basically three categories:
60% Short run: These resources have 5-10 units of the resource, so your people make 5-10 trips before they stop working. They will regenerate gradually, in this time they add to the one-shot category.
25% Stable: These resources are able to support up to one worker permanently .
15% One shot: There are a fair amount of resources, but they can only be harvested once before they need to regenerate.
Between the above, one-time resources and, one time production queues, there's a LOT of telling your villagers every. Single. Thing. To do.  At least they return to the town center so they are easy to find.
Periodically, you village is "attacked" by sprites that spawn from the same location every time and proceed to your warehouse to steal resources. The way to vanquish them is simply to click on the repeatedly. This is pretty silly, but I guess it's better than trying to incorporate some kind of extreme micromanagement tower defense...
The biggest problem I had with this game is that it was very hand-holdy, basically the entire game was a tutorial. There was a main game quest for, literally, every single building and upgrade. When it comes to these kind of village sim games, half of the point is that the map is very small, static, and unexplored. So, you're constantly thinking, 'dude, just leave me alone'. Obviously you're going to need to build a workshop type building at some point, and obviously you will need to upgrade it, it's not necessary to treat me like I'm four. You play games like this to explore and problem solve. That does not happen here. Even the things you know you will need to do at some point, like clear brush (without any special tools, just with hands), cannot be done until the main quest sprite places an arrow over it. That's pretty frustrating.
The interface and game, itself, is pretty bug free. Sometimes when one of the millions of quest windows pop up, it clicks through the world and pulls people off of whatever they were doing, but it's not a big deal. The greatest oversight is the wording in the quests. For example, there's one where you need to sell wood. Okay, wood is an actual resource that you get from trees or sawmills, but the quest actually wants you to sell planks, which is a production item made from wood. So I spent a good deal of time thinking that quest was broken. It only occurred to me it might have been referring to something else after a similar situation with a cooking assignment.
Ultimately, the game was not "unenjoyable". It was alright, although could have been a bit better. I have played 4.6 hours of it and that's exactly how much content there is. For the dollar-twenty I paid for it, that's pretty good, but I would have preferred it had more challenge, less tutorials, and more replay value in exchange for a higher price tag.

My mother had a Farmville addiction that was tearing the family apart.
Thankfully, she's moved on. Unfortunately, she's moved on to all the other facebook games.
I needed a cute little game to keep mother away from the facebooks, so I got this during the Halloween sale.
I wanted to test it out a bit before placing my laptop in front of my mother, so I decided to play for a few minutes.
Hours later, I ALMOST regret having started to play this game.
What at first had seemed like harmless fun has turned into a great part of my day that I cannot remember except for sparse moments of lucidity where I recall sitting in front of my computer yelling at little zombies to work faster.
This game is addicting, but not very fulfilling.
STORY:
There isn't much of a story, just enough to keep you from questioning why on earth you're sitting in front of a computer waiting for a little undead girl in an adorable dress to mine ore to build a house in a world that doesn't even exist.
ART:
The art is ADORABLE. Aside from the dopamine release when a project was completed, it was the art that kept me going until the end.
PACING:
The quests are appropriately paced to keep one interested throughout nearly the whole game, but they really start to lag towards the end.
This is an issue when you realize that the game will ONLY properly run in FULL SCREEN mode.
BUGS:
Speaking of properly running, the little worker zombie positively don't. In the beginning, while there are only a few zombies, the little fellows walk and work happily. However, after about a dozen or so, issues start to happen and you have a bunch of workers not working because they're stuck in between objects. This is easily remedied by clicking on them and placing them elsewhere, but it gets out-of-hand towards the end.
Buy this game if you like to make questionable choices with less than rewarding results!

This review was a tough one for me, because I am Setsuna is right on the line between a positive or negative recommendation.  If it were on a number scale, I'd give it 5/10.  The factor that tipped the scale for me was that this is first and foremost a nostalgia title, meaning that little of what we find here will be fresh and new.  Instead the intention is to remind us of some of the most classic (and not so classic) Square Enix titles such as Chrono Trigger and Final Fantasy.
The combat system is taken from Chrono Trigger:  It is a 3 person ATB battle with the ability for characters to perform combos if they have the proper techs equipped.  Techs themselves are equipped using the materia system from FF7, meaning that you will be placing magical stones into your weapons and armor (in this universe called "Spritnite").  You'd think this would be enough to make combat interesting, but unfortunately it is much too easy.  There are not multiple difficulty settings either, so if you don't like it... too bad.
The story draws heavy parallels to FF10, a choice that baffles me.  What this means is that the main story is very weak, and the game instead focuses on the inter-personal relationships between the characters.  Unfortunately the characters themselves are not that interesting.  I found myself ambivalent about continuing at most times, picking this game back up only when otherwise quite bored.
My overall recommendation is no, but again, this game was right on the line.  If you are crazy for good old ATB style combat, and don't care about easy difficulty, perhaps this game will be for you.

Hitman: Blood Money continues the trend set by Silent Assassin by making the game more accessible and less frustrating, while emphasizing cleanliness and stealth on the part of the player. This time around, 47 has some new gear that sticks around mission to mission, such as sedatives and poison that can be used on any food object, but the opportunities to use these new features feel very deliberate and pre-placed. In many ways, this sums up what Blood Money is all about: It's less a matter of coming up with your own, creative way to approach a situation, and more about finding all of the possibilities the developers have hidden away for you. As long as you approach the game like a puzzle - looking for weaknesses in the defenses of a given target - this is more interesting than limiting. The storyline and setting are fairly uninspired, however, especially compared to the previous games, and gives a definite air of 'different writers who didn't get it'. Still, for those looking to enjoy a competent and relatively easy social stealth game with some unique twists and awesome setpieces, this is the way to go.

This isn't what you'd normally call a game.
It really just is a videogame about a woman talking to the police. You get in the shoes of a person sitting in front of an old computer screen and review recovered footage from a case decades old. As you can already tell, it's not a game for everyone. You'll need patience and certain cleverness to get to the important parts of the story, as you need to use keywords or phrases to retrieve the videos.
The non-linear story writing is amazing, and depending on the order of your findings, you'll uncover the real sequence of events sooner or later.
Now the serious stuff, what really stands out in this game are the graphics, that's really what this is all about. You could almost believe it was an actual woman who was talking to the police. That and the fact I tried to clean my computer screen innumerable times (it has this weird dusty 90's computer screen tone to it).
Overall it was a 5/5

You have no goal, in the begining, don't know if you're supposed to search for some clues or whatever, only crappy search engine and hint that involves a murder. Engine that displays earliest 5 results which are searched on the words said in the video. Might be a social commentary on how governments waste a money on crap software and nothing works.. or it might be a cheap way to prolong the game.
Still it's easy to override using one same keyword once you figure it out. There's no reason to looking up videos based on mechanic since it makes you feel like some database input slave hired for cheap change.
The player is slow, takes a bit to load each of over 274 clips. You're supposed to watch, another crap mechanic that seems to be there only to prolong the time you spent inside the game (which is few hours).
Overall game part is total junk.
Still story part itself is quite interesting and revelead in interesting way. And that's why i'm still givint it positive recommendation.
If only it was served with a better mechanic...

However the phenomenal "experience" of the game makes up for it. The original game showed the promise of good storytelling, and this one realizes that potential. Much like the first I wouldn’t come for genuine scares but rather the eerie sense that pervades the entire experience, the terrible knowledge gleamed from what you’re allowed to know, and the growing tickle in the back of your head that things aren’t going to happen as they seem at first. It also succeeds in creating a doomsday apocalypse scenario that is somewhat unique, and at the same time actually manages to make you feel like the end of the world might be right around the corner.
A good "game", a revolutionary adventure.

I bet it's awesome with a controller sat 10 feet from a TV though.
EDIT: Addressing comments:
A: This isn't elitism, this is pointing out that the devs who ported this didn't give more than a cursory thought to PC gamers and that cursory thought was picturing us as a big dollar sign.
B: Before I paid I already had a working FOV fix researched and downloaded (for TPP) this is par for the course these days with ports - I was prepared for some "consolitis" but 0.4 hours of crawling slowly along the ground, interspersed with at least 20 cut scenes (thankfully skippable - although I had to work that out for myself) - unable to adjust camera speed or unable to bind more than 3 mouse buttons or unable to check controls were satisfactory due to W being practically the only control used for the first half hour (probably an hour from what I've read), navigating menus with arrow keys and enter because no mouse cursor, looking at 60 fps cap (on my 144hz) and a picture of a controller popping up everytime a cut scene became skippable ... was enough to tell me that I didn't need the full two hours for my decision to refund.
As I said, I bet it is really good on a big TV with a controller, either on console or steam. Unfortunately, I play at a desk on a PC monitor with a keyboard and mouse. So this cynical, ill thought, half baked, sloppy port doesn't float my boat ... but you fan boys are welcome to it .... in fact, that thought makes me happy.
You want a good review for your precious, go to the xbox metacritic ... and take your cleenex. Fap fap fap.

Hitman: Blood Money, as you probably already know, is a stealth game. What you may not know is that that only describes the game in part. Hitman: Blood Money is, in reality, one part stealth, one part sandbox, and one part puzzle. Stir well. Chill. Then dump it because it's POISONED. HE'S IN THE HOUSE. RUN! NO NOT THAT WAY! Perhaps your significant other can protect you. OH NO YOUR S/O WAS ACTUALLY A BALD MAN IN DISGUISE. You have died. Your final score is: 47.
In HBM, you play Agent 47, a clone who is the perfect murderer. This guy's a baller, let me tell you. Agent 47 couldn't give less of a damn even if you paid him a substantial sum to. He's already unlocked all of the no damns given achievements. This works to your advantage, because it means that you can take as many or as few lives as will ensure the completion of your mission objectives. Even if you translate that as "kill every last person in the neighborhood so that there are no witnesses," that can be arranged! I've done it, and it's a very satisfying strategy.
The biggest highlight of this game is that there are always multiple ways to complete your objectives. Some are flashy and more movie-like, like tricking someone into accidentally killing your target for you or rigging something to go gloriously awry at a fatal moment. Some are less rewarding but simpler to plan out, such as hiding in a closet and choking the target with fiber wire when they're all alone.
There's enough creeping around and hiding bodies to soothe the stealth goon in you, but there is also quite often a fair amount of problem-solving and planning. Figuring out how to go about each dilemma that stands between you and success is all part of the appeal, and it will often involve any number of outfit changes as you disguise yourself as one person to get closer to another person to "borrow" their uniform and inherit access to your quarry.
The levels have their hits and misses. Some levels have you waiting on (or missing) scripted events, and a couple are just downright confusing to memorize the layouts of. My least favorite mission takes place on a riverboat that I eventually had to consult a guide to find my way around. But then it's immediately followed up with a bayou wedding that's nothing but fun. There's a casino level that I'm no huge fan of, but it's worth completing to be able to play the level after, which is titled "A Dance with the Devil", and I shall leave it at that. My favorite level places Agent 47 in a typical suburban neighborhood with a target located inside of a house swarming with FBI agents. There are ups, and there are downs. But never give up, because there's always something better to look forward to.
In short, get Hitman: Blood Money. On a scale of 1 to 10 it's sooooo good.

Guacamelee is part beat-em-up, part challenging platformer and part Metroidvania explorer.  Does this sound like an appealing combination to you?  Yes?  Then just get it right now, because you will enjoy it.
Every part of this game is well done and polished.  The combat is smooth and gives a good feeling of advancement, doling out new abilities that both add to the fun of combat and give you an extra bit of exploring power.  The main game is challenging but definitely finishable, though I anticipate some people may have trouble with some of the bosses.  I'm not GREAT at beat-em-up type games but I found that I was able to push through some of the harder parts after no more than a few tries, with very few exceptions (and these exceptions were mainly bosses or challenge areas).  Where it really puts you up against the wall are the optional challenges.  Some are incredibly difficult platforming sections (one actually a little too difficult in my opinion, though I did manage it), others brutal combat sequences.  But these are all optional - Though there are some challenging bits in the main playthrough, for the most part it may only take a little practice to get through these.
The exploration is a real joy, though, especially once you get the ability to swap worlds at will.  Dual worlds is not a new concept (Zelda, Castlevania, and plenty of other games have used it), but it is not unwelcome and, even more, fits very well in with the story here.  And, by the way, the story is incredibly simple, and yet, tied with the sense of humor this game has, is well done and does not break the flow of the game.
Along with this, the visual style is incredibly bright, well animated and just full of visual treats and silly references.  It doesn't rely on these references to get anything across, they are merely little bonus details, but easily appreciated by fans of games in general.
The only criticism I have to offer is that I sometimes feel like combat is too hectic to tell what is going on and that the bosses may have a little bit of a difficulty spike, but other than that I heartily recommend this game.  All the pieces fit together into something fun, light-hearted and well polished.

I'd highly recommend Battleborn. Don't let the recent discounts deceive you into thinking lesser of the quality of the game. It was a smart move and it was needed to help stay competitive with other cheaper or free games of similar genre. Some may argue it isn't a triple A game, but its up to the standards of a AAA title, with some required improvements that have been addressed by the developers.
All upcoming maps and characters are free. One has been released, one announced, and one new game mode and three maps have been added since launch. Matchmaking is getting faster (although not as balanced), along with a weekly polish and character balances shows that Gearbox is aiming for the longevity of the game.
The art style is top notch, combining hand-drawn animations as well as CG. The writing is humorous and doesn't take itself too seriously, especially the banter between the large roster of playable personalities. Its similar to Borderlands humor but more refined and less meme-y. The campaign acts as a way to lay the foundation for its universe as well as provide a raid like instance for people to grind credit and obtain loot.
Aside from the campaign, the bulk of your playtime will most likely be designated in the multiplayer modes. There is Capture, Meltdown, and Incursion. It is important to note that this game does have complex mechanics and a steep learning curve, which is probably what strayed away some players initially. The game borrows mechanics from MOBA games, don't go in expecting it to play like a traditional FPS like Counterstrike or Team Fortress 2. People who come in with the mind set of a MOBA player and have access to quick twitch responses will be right at home. Character customization is vast offering a trait system similar to Heroes of the Storm. Stats can be augmented with gear that you obtain from loot packs or from the campaign.
Mostly my opinion, but don't let the discount fool you, it's a great game that needed the price drop to stay competitive. The game does have a learning curve, those who've played Smite or any other MOBAs should have an easier time transitioning, and those who jump right into competitive right after the prologue will not. Balanced matchmaking is almost nonexistent  due to its growing player base. If you were to start playing this game, I'd highly recommend doing a couple campaign modes first to get a some gear and a few rank ups, and then play a couple of bot matches, rather then jumping straight into competitive and expecting to have a good time. I enjoy it quite a bit and bet a lot of the ones who give it a shot will too.

UPDATE: So I recently got a new GPU (a GTX1070) and the game runs fine with it.Also they have kept updating the game and added a 5 v Bots mode that makes it a lot easier to learn classes.
I'll start by getting the big warning out of the way.
This game does not play nice with some AMD GPU's, I have a HD 7800 series card and the last two story missions have unplayably unstable Frame Rates. There are also two MP maps that have trouble, mostly with the frame rate yo-yoing up and down all the time. I have heard about some Nvidia cards having this trouble but it seems to be mainly AMD. So if you want to play this game I would check to see if there are any reports of problems with your card.
So on to the reason why you should play this game anyway!
This is a very fun first person MOBA, unlike Overwatch which is a TF2 MP Shooter with a MOBA flavour. Battleborn commits to being a MOBA. So you start every game at level 1 and level up as you kill mooks and enemy players. Of the three modes in the MP the one that is closest to something like DOTA or League is called Incursion. A single lane game mode where you have to try and take out the other teams giant spider robots whilst protecting your own one.
The best thing about this mode is that it cuts out most of the downtime that you find in a regular MOBA. Instead of games lasting an hour they last at most thirty minutes and you are fighting the other team pretty much from minute one. Instead of having a shop in a match you buy gear from your instead have a three piece gear loadout you carry into the game and activate by spending "Shards" which can also be used to build turrets.  The streamlining also affects your leveling. When you gain a level you open a menu and have a choice between three upgrades. The great thing about this is it lets you change how your character will play on the fly. An example is Miko, the pure Medic who can be geared towards clearing waves of mooks or even can become more of a battle medic that can stun enemy players for two seconds. (More than enough time for your teammates to kill them) or you can hear her to just be a even better healer.  The downside is that it takes a little while to get to know what upgrades come at which level but for me that just adds to the joy of mastering a character, being able to level up and just know exactly what skill to take in a second really helps in hectic fights.
The thing I love about the gameplay is that it is all about team fights. Whilst you can go on a one man killing spree sometimes, you will be unlikely to actually swing the match unless your team are backing you up. On the flip side a even slightly organised team can take down a player who is on a spree in a couple of seconds.  Each character has three skill they can activate along with the default attacks they have. Two can be used from the start of the match with the third unlocking at level 5, so like a Ultimate in a normal MOBA. Most of the non Ult skills can be used to help a teammate out. The melee fighter Rath can knock people up into the air and stop them from using skills for a second. Handy for him to catch up since he is melee only, but also can be used to keep a enemy in place for someone like Kelvin. A big slow tank, to get in close and pound them into the dirt.
Speaking of fighting the game does a great job at making the characters stand out. As of right now there are 26 characters in the game and only two of them could really be mistake for each other. With everything from a penguin in a mech to a weird mushroom throwing Kunai. You can always quickly know who you are up against, although mirror matches can get confusing. Overall the visuals in the game are very nice, there isn't really anything that blows my mind but they did a great job in making everything fit seamlessly together despite the varying sizes and races.
Stuff like that is what I think makes this game worth playing, the way all the characters skills interact with each other and play off each other. It feels great as a Miko to stop a frontline fighter in its tracks with a stun grenade to the face and then join your teammates in dog piling them. Or as the Sniper Thorn popping the head of a fleeing enemy as they try to get away from a fight.
Don't get me wrong, a lot of times you won't get that kind of game. I would say 1 in every 5 games is anything other than a stomp on one side or the other. But it is well worth it for when you get those nail biting matches that go right down to the wire. When you get your first robot knocked out in the first 5 minutes and then come from behind to steamroll the enemy to a clear victory in the last five minutes. When there are only few points in a capture  or meltdown match.
I am mostly talking about the MP because the single player/Co-Op campaign is just kind of OK. It mostly seems balanced for 5 people and the matchmaking system means you might have to replay the same levels over and over again. If you have a few friends I would recommend playing the story with them.
Another point that might swing you is the writing. Overall I think it is more hit than miss, the amount of barks and cross character chatter in the MP is amazing and really does flesh out the characters in the game. For me the only character I loathe is Orendi but other wise I found the cast growing on me as I played.
The writing in the single player is very Gearbox, which is to say they have a bad habit of just not letting a ♥♥♥♥ING JOKE DIE! Although it is free of most all of the meme talk people seem to complain about in Borderlands (Although tbh I never noticed that many memes in Borderlands 2)
So yeah, to summerase
PRO'S
-Deep complex Multiplayer
-Unique visual style
-Charecters are all unique and easy to pick out in a fight
-Team fight focused MP that rewards teamwork
-Single player/CO-OP campaign offers a good place to learn a character
-Cuts out most of the down time of a normal MOBA
-Generally fun and likable characters and a crap ton of voice work
CONS
-Matchmaking can sometimes hang for a long time for seemingly no reason (This happens regardless of player numbers)
-Matches can often be a one sided stomp
-Frame rate problems with older AMD cards and some Nvidia cards
-Jokes can overstay their welcome in the story

Shank 2 is a great sequel and in my opinion, better than the first game in basically every way.
The visuals are definitely an improvement over the first game, and one of the very first things I noticed was the larger variety in locations you visited. The first game suffered a bit from repetitive areas that didn't change very much, but in 2 you're always fighting in a different area from level to level which is a nice addition.
Another improvement is the weapon variety. You still have the signature weapons Shank uses in the first game, but there is a lot more to choose from this time around, and also you're able to pick up quite a few weapons that the enemies drop for a limited amount of uses until they break and they usually do fairly good damage. You can also change weapon loadouts in the middle of playing which is extremely useful, especially when you're on a boss fight and you don't have the optimal weapons equipped to do the most amount of damage.
Everything else in the game is quite similar with not much change. There are quite a few boss fights which are all fun and some are fairly challenging, especially when other enemies come out to join the fight. My only complaint of the game would probably be the length. It seems to be shorter than the first game, but it could be because I didn't die as often as I did in the first game. It's an action packed few hours, but it's a minor gripe. I didn't get to the play the multiplayer section of the game, but it would definitely add more replay value to make up for the shorter single player campaign.
Overall, definitely worth the money if you're into the genre.
