Shadows is an early access platformer bathed in the shadows. With the flood of early access games, is this worth picking up? Or is it just another early access game you can skip?
Finding yourself in a strange dark cave, you have no memory of how you got in there. Armed with only a jar, the fireflies you collect will light your way as you explore. But how can you get out? A huge hole in the ceiling of the cave seems to be the only way to get back to the surface but it's too high and wide for you to climb up. Be ready to construct a beacon to contact the surface with the pieces gathered from various spots in the cave. Be careful as many spikes threaten your life and every wasted second can mean death as fireflies escape. Will you find out how you arrived in the cave? Will you be able to escape the cave before the darkness swallows you?
Shadows main gameplay is the platforming, making the layout important to enjoy the game. The layout is very interesting, some parts you have to jump from the previous floor, and some you see before you reach the area. If there is an area that is well hidden, part of the particular passage will be shown. Many areas also have multiple ways to get past, letting you decide which way you can successfully do.  Regular, double, and wall jumps helping to easily reach each ledge and jump over gaps and spikes. For the most part it is very easy to get the hang of and easily jump over the areas that is certain doom. There is one part that is the harder than the rest, but it requires you to learn a trick with the jumping.
There is an interesting play with light and dark throughout the game. You somewhat have a time limit as fireflies escape over time, bringing the cave ever darker. The more you spend in one area, the more fireflies that escape. But it doesn't end there. Some exits are sealed if there is too much light, only opening up if you release enough fireflies. A prompt will show up telling you, but there will be a gray wall up to a point. Transportation to get to or out of an area are also not revealed if you are in the dark, causing you to collect more fireflies if needed. 50 fireflies are needed in the end, so this either has the player farm for fireflies or remember where they went to avoid losing fireflies to get to an area more than once.
When you lose all of your three lives, you can receive a screen based on what you have gathered. By default you will respawn at the start, with all the beacon parts and fireflies you had at the time. If you have one or more beacon parts, you can respawn where it was gathered with one price. The part will be lost if you have to respawn again. If 25 fireflies were in the jar at the time you died, you can release them and respawn in the room you died in. However, make sure you know how many you had as it will spawn you with 0 fireflies. Do you play it safe and travel back? Or do you risk it and respawn with fireflies or a beacon part?
A nice, calming soundtrack acts as a nice ambience for the cave along with a loud footsteps to give a sense of texture. This can easily be put in the back of your mind, trying to bring a calm vibe if you come to a difficult area or desperately looking for the last beacon part.
Shadows has a simplistic style, only using white, black, and shades of gray within a determined section of the screen. To give some variety, the background or forground can show some plants swaying, vines, and stalactites. Fireflies stray away from this, having a distinct yellow glow that points out their location on the floor. The memories are the opposite, looking like darkened fireflies swirling around in a circle.
Shadows ran very well throughout the whole experience. The simplistic style it has may allow any computer, new or old, to run it. The only thing that can be improved is the settings menu. There is an option to disable particles, fog, and lights but it is unchecked by default. As it doesn't have a title saying that it disables it, it may make more sense for it to be checked by default.
Right now, there are a few ways that Shadows has increased it's replayability. Multiple endings have been implemented this year, determined by what order you gather the memories and how many you collect. There is also an achievement to complete the game without dying, though don't go crazy trying to.
+ Use of light and dark
+ Good layout design
+ Simplistic and calming
+/- Somewhat confusing using the menu with the controller
+/- A bug has a chance to show up that disables the player's movement but it is fixed by exiting to the menu and going back in.
Shadows is a simplistic platformer that is playable from beginning to end. Having a calming atmosphere with a unique use of light and dark intertwined with the gameplay. Outside of a little adjustment to the settings menu, it would be useful if there was a way to distinguish a used save slot. The developer, Logan Apple, does wish the community to be involved with the development and has already implemented features that was asked and fixed bugs that was found. It will be interesting to see how Shadows will evolve over time as it is enjoyable and see what creations the level editor can make. If you are a fan of platformers or want a generally easy, chill game Shadows is for you.

If you came here looking for a review, you have come to the wrong place, but if you want some very ♥♥♥♥ing good brownies, you have come to the right place. You're welcome for an actual recipe, not a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ copy and paste pie recipe. Trust me nothing goes wrong with nutella.
INGREDIENTS:
1 c. unsalted butter
2 c. sugar
1/2 tsp. salt
1 c. flour
1 c. cocoa powder
4 eggs
1 (13-oz.) jar Nutella
5 Ferrero Rocher candies, unwrapped and crumbled
DIRECTIONS:
1. Preheat oven to 350 degrees F.
2. Melt butter in a medium-sized saucepan over medium heat. Add sugar, stirring until combined. 3. Remove from heat and add salt, flour, and cocoa powder, stirring to combine. Whisk in eggs, stirring just until the mixture is combined into a batter. Set aside.
4. Spray an 8"-x-8" pan with cooking spray. Pour half of the batter into the pan. Spoon or lightly drizzle most of the Nutella on top of the batter, forming an even layer over the brownie batter. 5. 5. Use a spoon or silicone spatula to cover the Nutella with the remaining brownie batter. (If you pour the batter straight on top of the Nutella, it will sink into the Nutella and combine into one marbled—yet delicious—mess.)
6. Bake until the top layer of brownies has browned and set, 28 to 30 minutes. It shouldn’t jiggle when you remove it from the oven. (The toothpick test doesn’t work here, since the toothpick will hit the Nutella layer, making the brownies seem uncooked.)
7. Let cool for 15 to 20 minutes, then top with a drizzle of Nutella and crumbled Ferrero Rocher chocolates. Cut into squares and serve.
Credits: ★ Billy

Hit and Miss:
- Some music, in my opinion, is terrific, other tracks just don't feel like they "fit"
- Some characters are very compelling, others are either poorly written or make some very stupid decisions
- Repetitive environments yes, but I feel like it plays well to the opressive atmosphere
Disliked:
- The visuals and gameplay lacks a lot of polish
- Combat is poorly balanced, and encounters are uninteresting, there are few "choices" to be made, I'm more just using the same strategy for 95% of encounters
- UI looks dated and frankly, ugly
- Many game systems are unituitive and poorly explained
- The story so far (4 hours in) doesn't make a lot of sense, many events and character choices make no sense or are riddled with tiny plot holes
- A number of bugs in terms of controller support, music playback, and UI elements

Vertical shooters are an interesting genre. They strip away any notion of exploration and (often) narrative to instead focus on delivering high speed action to the player.
Phoenix Force goes a step further and gets rid of everything except the boss battles.
There's only an implied story in this, as a Phoenix you travel the world (like, Earth) continent by continent, fighting your way through 100 boss fights. For your troubles each victory gives you some upgrade tokens (proportional to the number of bosses were in the fight), some stages also give you direct stat boosts for your team or, most importantly, add a playable phoenix to the titular force.
Every phoenix controls roughly the same, you move your mythological bird around using the mouse (move it too fast and it will lag behind the cursor a bit) and automatically fires up at the boss or bosses that swerve around at the top of the screen. Once you get hit by a shot from a boss you're dead and immediately thrown back to the phoenix selection screen to try again. Losing is painless, quick and expected along your journey. Each phoenix has a neat special power to differentiate it though, from a fire wave that triggers every dozen or so seconds to bullets homing in on your enemies to being able to teleport around the map (with a short cooldown).
These powers do a nice job mixing up the gameplay, and I felt myself switching phoenix every now and then to chance my approach to a level.
The earlier mentioned upgrade tokens are used to increase the level of your phoenixes. Fortunately, they all level at the same time, which means that if you've levelled up your standard fire phoenix to level 9 and then get the ice phoenix it will also be level 9. All of them are always the same level, meaning you are always free to try a different approach or strategy. This is a great thing.
Unfortunately, you don't really NEED to switch things up though. As with Japanese
(or 'Bullet Hell') games the primary concern lies in staying alive long enough to take down the boss. This means that mostly you'll just be swerving out of harm's way as the bosses shower you with projectiles of various types. The different phoenix powers mix things up, but not to a great extent.
Levelling up a phoenix in your team (and, with it, the entire team) will raise its attack power and lower the cooldown period between skill uses if it has any. It's a completely linear and straightforward system, but it does mean that you can redo levels to get a bit stronger before tackling a level you're stuck at. Unfortunately failing a level does not get you a reward, which means it can be frustrating to try and fail a level a dozen times, it would have been neat to have at least something for the player's troubles. A victory gives 5-20 upgrade tokens, so just getting 1 token every time you lose would have been a pleasant gesture.
About halfway through the game (just after winning your first battle against 4 bosses at the same time) you unlock Challenge Mode, which pits you against 4 random bosses you've beaten so far. This is the only extra mode the game has to offer, and I'm glad it's there, but it can be frustrating as well. You get upgrade tokens normally for each victory, but the main prize to aim for is the final phoenix, Lich, which is unlocked when you win 100 challenge fights. This is exactly as many levels as the campaign has. I made it through, but was thoroughly sick of them when I did.
The final phoenix definitely mixes things up though, and is arguably a lot harder to play as than the other 5. Its shots start off very weak, but gain strength every time you graze  (almost get hit by) a projectile. This was great fun, but it's unlocked so late that I was almost done with the campaign by then and I didn't end up using it much.
After 100 campaign boss fights the game ends. You get a short slideshow of the phoenixes congregating around a magical tree of some kind (which, if the map you've been traversing is any indication, is apparently in Portugal). Did the evil boss monsters come from there? I don't know, maybe. There's no story here either to make things clearer.
There is one thing I haven't touched upon yet in this review, and that's the actual bosses. 100 boss fights sound ridiculous on paper, no game has 100 bosses, and this game is no different. Each continent (of which there are 4 in the game, I guess Australia and Africa don't have giant monsters floating over them? Good for them!) has four or so different types of boss that it introduces. Each boss has distinctly different attack types, which range from easy to dodge (fire breathing dragons, giant floating eyeballs shooting straight-lined lasers) to downright nefarious (harpies showering the screen with falling feathers, flying demons that alternate spewing out acid pools and smoke screens) as you traverse the continents. Design and variety of the bosses is pretty good, with every manner of flying mythological beastie being thrown your way as the game progresses.
Each new boss type gets introduced in a one on one stage so you can get familiar with its attacks, but the rest are generally made up of different teams of bosses attempting to take you down. No level is quite the same, but some of them are pretty similar.
Phoenix Force sets out to do a simple thing, deliver excellent vertical shooter boss battles with minimal surrounding hassle.
It achieves this, but could have done with some more variety in its battles and maybe some of that hassle after all (e.g. a deeper upgrade system).
Definitely recommending this though, make up your own mind if it's a game for you.

Guacamelee! hits the right spot for anyone longing for a great action-adventure platformer with a unique setting and that little bit of Metroidvania magic. The game has plenty of off-beat humor - and tons of jokes referring to other games, as well as memes galore. Strangely, much of the fighting actually happens in rooms, though in many areas there are also enemies loitering around. The villains are decent - they have enough personality, although a bit more fleshing out would have been welcomed. The game does at times get frustrating - some of the platforming is pretty unforgiving, especially inside the blasted Tule Tree (or even worse, atop it). Likewise boss fights can be quite an infuriating experience, especially the one atop Sierra Morena. But the big final fight is satisfying, with a huge, intimidating last boss to go up against. Sadly, the ending is way too short, although I appreciate that it dares to not be all lovey-dovey in the end (unless you manage to get atop that awful Tule Tree). Overall a well-done game, and one highly recommended. 8/10.

Wow! This is one of the best Metroid-Vania games to come around in a long time. It is well paced. Well polished. Full of humor. And just plain awesome.
In this game you play Juan who is in love with the president's daughter. She is kidnapped by Calaca for some ritual (They need a virgin sacrifice; she tries to tell them she isn't eligible; they don't listen.) Of course, they kill our hero. That would be a very boring game if that were the end. But it isn't. Juan is given a second chance and becomes a luchador.
Through the game, you will be given new powers such as "Goat Run," "Goat Fly," and the ability to turn into a chicken. Yes, you can turn into a chicken. (If you get the chicken costume, you turn into an egg.) As with any Metroid-vania game, the new powers allow you access to areas you have discovered but couldn't quite reach.
One thing I liked was there weren't collectables on the levels per se. Yes, there are chests that hold pieces of heart (for life) and stamina (for special moves) or money. But you don't collect stars or tacos or something meaningless. T
There are some platforming and puzzle aspects to the game. Some of the areas where the orbs are hidden are challenging, but the regular areas are not too difficult.
The art is cubist and bright reminiscent of old Mexico. Combat basically consists of two buttons, hit and special. Putting these in combo will increase your combo meter faster and give you a money bonus at the end. Some monsters will put up a shield that you will need to break with the right special move.
This game is highly recommended.

I'd highly recommend Battleborn. Don't let the recent discounts deceive you into thinking lesser of the quality of the game. It was a smart move and it was needed to help stay competitive with other cheaper or free games of similar genre. Some may argue it isn't a triple A game, but its up to the standards of a AAA title, with some required improvements that have been addressed by the developers.
All upcoming maps and characters are free. One has been released, one announced, and one new game mode and three maps have been added since launch. Matchmaking is getting faster (although not as balanced), along with a weekly polish and character balances shows that Gearbox is aiming for the longevity of the game.
The art style is top notch, combining hand-drawn animations as well as CG. The writing is humorous and doesn't take itself too seriously, especially the banter between the large roster of playable personalities. Its similar to Borderlands humor but more refined and less meme-y. The campaign acts as a way to lay the foundation for its universe as well as provide a raid like instance for people to grind credit and obtain loot.
Aside from the campaign, the bulk of your playtime will most likely be designated in the multiplayer modes. There is Capture, Meltdown, and Incursion. It is important to note that this game does have complex mechanics and a steep learning curve, which is probably what strayed away some players initially. The game borrows mechanics from MOBA games, don't go in expecting it to play like a traditional FPS like Counterstrike or Team Fortress 2. People who come in with the mind set of a MOBA player and have access to quick twitch responses will be right at home. Character customization is vast offering a trait system similar to Heroes of the Storm. Stats can be augmented with gear that you obtain from loot packs or from the campaign.
Mostly my opinion, but don't let the discount fool you, it's a great game that needed the price drop to stay competitive. The game does have a learning curve, those who've played Smite or any other MOBAs should have an easier time transitioning, and those who jump right into competitive right after the prologue will not. Balanced matchmaking is almost nonexistent  due to its growing player base. If you were to start playing this game, I'd highly recommend doing a couple campaign modes first to get a some gear and a few rank ups, and then play a couple of bot matches, rather then jumping straight into competitive and expecting to have a good time. I enjoy it quite a bit and bet a lot of the ones who give it a shot will too.

UPDATE: So I recently got a new GPU (a GTX1070) and the game runs fine with it.Also they have kept updating the game and added a 5 v Bots mode that makes it a lot easier to learn classes.
I'll start by getting the big warning out of the way.
This game does not play nice with some AMD GPU's, I have a HD 7800 series card and the last two story missions have unplayably unstable Frame Rates. There are also two MP maps that have trouble, mostly with the frame rate yo-yoing up and down all the time. I have heard about some Nvidia cards having this trouble but it seems to be mainly AMD. So if you want to play this game I would check to see if there are any reports of problems with your card.
So on to the reason why you should play this game anyway!
This is a very fun first person MOBA, unlike Overwatch which is a TF2 MP Shooter with a MOBA flavour. Battleborn commits to being a MOBA. So you start every game at level 1 and level up as you kill mooks and enemy players. Of the three modes in the MP the one that is closest to something like DOTA or League is called Incursion. A single lane game mode where you have to try and take out the other teams giant spider robots whilst protecting your own one.
The best thing about this mode is that it cuts out most of the downtime that you find in a regular MOBA. Instead of games lasting an hour they last at most thirty minutes and you are fighting the other team pretty much from minute one. Instead of having a shop in a match you buy gear from your instead have a three piece gear loadout you carry into the game and activate by spending "Shards" which can also be used to build turrets.  The streamlining also affects your leveling. When you gain a level you open a menu and have a choice between three upgrades. The great thing about this is it lets you change how your character will play on the fly. An example is Miko, the pure Medic who can be geared towards clearing waves of mooks or even can become more of a battle medic that can stun enemy players for two seconds. (More than enough time for your teammates to kill them) or you can hear her to just be a even better healer.  The downside is that it takes a little while to get to know what upgrades come at which level but for me that just adds to the joy of mastering a character, being able to level up and just know exactly what skill to take in a second really helps in hectic fights.
The thing I love about the gameplay is that it is all about team fights. Whilst you can go on a one man killing spree sometimes, you will be unlikely to actually swing the match unless your team are backing you up. On the flip side a even slightly organised team can take down a player who is on a spree in a couple of seconds.  Each character has three skill they can activate along with the default attacks they have. Two can be used from the start of the match with the third unlocking at level 5, so like a Ultimate in a normal MOBA. Most of the non Ult skills can be used to help a teammate out. The melee fighter Rath can knock people up into the air and stop them from using skills for a second. Handy for him to catch up since he is melee only, but also can be used to keep a enemy in place for someone like Kelvin. A big slow tank, to get in close and pound them into the dirt.
Speaking of fighting the game does a great job at making the characters stand out. As of right now there are 26 characters in the game and only two of them could really be mistake for each other. With everything from a penguin in a mech to a weird mushroom throwing Kunai. You can always quickly know who you are up against, although mirror matches can get confusing. Overall the visuals in the game are very nice, there isn't really anything that blows my mind but they did a great job in making everything fit seamlessly together despite the varying sizes and races.
Stuff like that is what I think makes this game worth playing, the way all the characters skills interact with each other and play off each other. It feels great as a Miko to stop a frontline fighter in its tracks with a stun grenade to the face and then join your teammates in dog piling them. Or as the Sniper Thorn popping the head of a fleeing enemy as they try to get away from a fight.
Don't get me wrong, a lot of times you won't get that kind of game. I would say 1 in every 5 games is anything other than a stomp on one side or the other. But it is well worth it for when you get those nail biting matches that go right down to the wire. When you get your first robot knocked out in the first 5 minutes and then come from behind to steamroll the enemy to a clear victory in the last five minutes. When there are only few points in a capture  or meltdown match.
I am mostly talking about the MP because the single player/Co-Op campaign is just kind of OK. It mostly seems balanced for 5 people and the matchmaking system means you might have to replay the same levels over and over again. If you have a few friends I would recommend playing the story with them.
Another point that might swing you is the writing. Overall I think it is more hit than miss, the amount of barks and cross character chatter in the MP is amazing and really does flesh out the characters in the game. For me the only character I loathe is Orendi but other wise I found the cast growing on me as I played.
The writing in the single player is very Gearbox, which is to say they have a bad habit of just not letting a ♥♥♥♥ING JOKE DIE! Although it is free of most all of the meme talk people seem to complain about in Borderlands (Although tbh I never noticed that many memes in Borderlands 2)
So yeah, to summerase
PRO'S
-Deep complex Multiplayer
-Unique visual style
-Charecters are all unique and easy to pick out in a fight
-Team fight focused MP that rewards teamwork
-Single player/CO-OP campaign offers a good place to learn a character
-Cuts out most of the down time of a normal MOBA
-Generally fun and likable characters and a crap ton of voice work
CONS
-Matchmaking can sometimes hang for a long time for seemingly no reason (This happens regardless of player numbers)
-Matches can often be a one sided stomp
-Frame rate problems with older AMD cards and some Nvidia cards
-Jokes can overstay their welcome in the story
-ORENDI IS JUST TINY TINA AGAIN!

I am one of the 2K Bundle adopters. I'm giving this a thumbs up just because I'd like more people to play with.
1. To get the obvious out of the way - comparing this to Overwatch (which is a fun game lacking depth) is at best totally incorrect and at worst totally unfair. They are nothing like each other. Blizzard used the fact that both games offer characters with unique movesets and teamplay to utterly ruin Battleborn's launch (aside from the damage 2K did on their own). Blizzard is a marketing juggernaut, that's why people actually purchased a terrible game like Warcraft 3 and that's why World of Warcraft even exists in spite of being such an embarassing black eye on entertainment and culture - marketing. Diablo 3 is complete trash, and it's also one of Blizzard's best selling games. Starcraft 2 is nothing but broken online play and an anthology of fanfiction. Marketing is what makes this junk popular. Plain and simple. Battleborn never stood a chance against that. These are facts.
2. Personally I've never played a MOBA before and I'm having a lot of fun with it. The character designs are fun and unique, occasionally you get matched with cool people who actually are there to have a good time. I've already found a few favorite characters to play with (but the unlock system is neutering that fun, see below). Combat feels good.
3. I'd never pay for microtransactions in a retail-priced game. Isn't going to happen. Doing so makes you kind of stupid, and you're the reason the game industry is able to get more and more ridiculous with their pricing and awfulness by the year. I'm sorry if this describes you and you are insulted, but it's your fault we're all here. It'll only get worse.
4. Everything should be available at the beginning of the game, the progression unlocks make absolutely no sense whatsoever. At the very least, the "easy" characters should all be available at the start - why would you lock them until higher levels? In what way does that make sense? No wonder people who paid retail price are angry, there's very little to sink your teeth into right out of the box.
5. The 5 minute opener on EVERY SINGLE GAME is really annoying. I don't care about who is who. Can we just get to the gameplay please? I have practically destroyed my B button.
6. "Gear activation" costs? That's so dirty I won't even bother talking about it.
7. The story mode is fun, but you're most of the way through it within a few hours, and you can't really pick the level you want to play when you're public. I was forced to replay a level and I just backed out instead because that's not what I want to do. I want to finish everything and unlock all the heroes. Shouldn't have to, but oh well.
8. How about some more coop options for those of us who don't want to go PVP? There can be story mode, PVC, and PVP - what about those of us who don't feel like going up against jerkoff teenagers snorting Adderall that are taking a break between CS:GO MLG qualifying rounds?
I feel like this game has a ton of potential and I'm enjoying it a lot right now - but it'll wear off. There's just not enough here.

I love the original Shank. It's a fun brawler with a good story with over-the-top♥♥♥♥♥kicking.
Shank 2 improves the gameplay in some areas and downgrades it in others, but the main problem with this game is the story.
Pros:
-The dodge button was a welcome addition
-Adds more fun ways to dismember people, like throwing them in the air and shooting/slicing them
-Forward attacks involve more charging forward
Cons:
-A bit too tutorial-heavy
-There are way too many enemies to defeat. It makes the game not fun and more of a grindfest.
-The story is absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥ In the first game, the story was straightforward. Shank=good guy. Everyone else=bad guy. You kill bad guy. Also some backstory, but mostly that.
In Shank 2, you rescue your mentor/girlfriend and it's pretty dark and gritty. No. The story in Shank should just be him going around and killing things. I don't want to deal with moral choice in Shank. I just want to dismember people.
Also, Shank apparently has a daughter? This is wrong for a couple reasons. One, Shank is a terrible role model. He runs around getting drunk and killing people. Why should he care if he has a daughter? Two, Shank is such a badass that giving him a moral compass takes away a lot of that. It's like giving the Terminator a family.
Conclusion:
Shank 2 is more of a gritty grindfest than the over-the-top popcorn action game that the original Shank was. If you prefer a more complex story, then buy this game. I personally think that the story should complement the gameplay, and the original story did that a lot better. In Shank 2, the story and the gameplay don't match, and it detracts from the experience.

I love the F.E.A.R. series. That said, Project Origin is probably my least favorite. It took some  intresting directions, but it's oddly similar to Devil May Cry games in in that it has a tenous link to other entries in the series. The Point Man is nowhere to be seen, and  the combat mechanics are stuck in a bizarre transitional reality between the first and third games. You have very little health, but the controls are so stiff that you will find yourself taking unecessary damage constantly. The "cover" mechanic is laughable, and most guns feel very weak especially the pump shotgun- a game killer for me. On the upside, the mech sections are absolutely cathartic, the music is very strong and echoes the first game's score beautifully, and there is much more character interaction and good dialogue given the shift in cast from a lone operative to a Delta Force strike team. Bottom line, as a F.E.A.R. fanboy I enjoyed the game, but those just here for the shooting might want to skip it.

The Happy Hereafter is essentially Virtual Villagers - Lite set in Halloween Town.  Don't get me wrong, it's a good game on its own.  But there are a few lacking components and bugs that make it not as impressive as other similar titles in the genre.
For starters, it's incredibly short.  So short, that I finished it in two nights.  If you follow the quest order you can probably get another hour or so out of it, but that isn't a good thing.  There are a lot of stretches of time where you're doing nothing but waiting.  It certainly isn't as long or as tedious as Facebook games, but it lacks item collection or achievements like Virtual Villagers to help pass the time.  If I had known from the start to improve resource gathering facilities the second the tech was available, I probably could have shaved off almost another hour of play.
Second, the bugs.  And there are more than a few that can be annoying, if not progress slowing.  On occasion there are times where villagers stop gathering from resources at the bottom of the map.  While it makes sense for them to stop gathering when a resource has run dry and is in the process of regenerating, they don't always stop for this reason.  I found myself at the start of the game constantly having to reassign someone to harvest wood at trees because they just decided to stop working after collecting one load.  With a little luck I was able to get them to automatically harvest, as they are supposed to, but it did get annoying and tedious, especially at the start when you are entirely reliant on these nodes for resources.
Another bug that is annoying, but not game breaking in any way, re units sliding around or getting stuck on decorations.  Sometimes when you tell a unit to harvest something, it will show the gathering animation but they will slide all the way back to the town square.  This doesn't prevent them from completing their job, but it is annoying.  Also, idle units have a habit of getting stuck under things.  Benches, lights, buildings.  It is easily fixed by picking them up and telling them to do something, and doesn't harm your production since they were idle, but it is another minor annoyance that one would think could be easily fixed.
The characters are interesting and it's obvious that a great deal of effort was put into their creation, but they are sadly under-utilized.  Each character has one, maybe two quest chains, that are incredibly short, and then they are never used again.  The mermaid has I think 3 or 4 quests, spread across two "chains."  I say "chains" simply because the first chain has 2-3 quests for her and the second is a single quest given by the witch.  Once completed you will never see her again.  It's sad to see detailed characters and environments used so sparingly.
Ultimately, I have to say this game is a "Pass."  While it can be fun, for its length, bugs, and simple play-style, there are just better games of the same genre.  At sale price, it was a nice distraction; at full price it would still be ok, but for a few dollars more you can get similar games with more depth and over-all entertainment.
A good time waster, but sadly that is all it is: a cute waste of time.

Bought this at full price, a whopping $3.99 (US dollars) which is less than popcorn at the movies. I didn't really expect much and thought it'd be a very mediocre, forgettable, indie game.
I'm so glad I was wrong.
The Good:  It looks like a handpainted style game with a more cartoonish flair, and it's got a very cute whimsical soundtrack to go with it (the music that plays in the game, to clarify).  I love the fact that it has quests/missions in the first place, and they never make you feel too rushed but give you enough pressure so that you want to hurry up with whatever needs doing. The quests are worded in a very quirky style and made me chuckle a few times! I loved the fact that there were cutscenes within the game and they varied from traditional style cutescenes to an image artsy style cutscene, almost like a graphic novel. You start with 3 little "helpers" and it goes from there, depending on your resourcefulness and needs, and by the you can have many more, each working on permanent jobs or temporary ones. I like that you can always reassign who does what and when. And lastly, you NEVER have to save (omg what!). That's right, you can exit whenever you feel like it or whenever you draw parent aggro (girlfriend, boyfriend, wife, hubby aggro!), and when you log back into the game it starts exactly where you left off. Wish more games did that, instead of the runaround some games do to try and never let you exit their games. Yes, I'm looking at you Assassin's Creed. Also, there is a vendor system in place, where you can sell and buy. Comes in handy!
The Bad: bugs! Now, I only encoutered 2.5 bugs. One was when I first started the game, I was not able to use magic on an altar. I simply restared the game twice and never encountered this problem again. The second bug was when I was dragging a worker to a location, I got a popup tutorial (I had not ticked tutorial off at this point) and my worker disappeared from my screen! Turns out she ended up on a "dark" undiscovered part of the map. I got her back when I discovered the area, but it did take me a while to get there. And the 0.5 bug was more of a glitch "oversight" on the developers part. One of the components for building crystal houses is listed as "stones" but instead requires "gems". I was trying to upgrade my houses to a rank 2 but was unable to, I had plenty of stone, so I bought from gems from the trade post and sure enough I was able to upgrade to rank 3. Now the last bad thing, is the length of gameplay. It's short (about 6 hours) if you are playing to do the missions/quests, however, once you beat the game you have the option to keep playing.
Worth it? In my humble opinion, I would recommend anyone to buy this game. While it is short compared to most games out there it's got a lot of replayability, the game keeps you engaged and interested, and you can tell the devs put a lot of hard work into the game, so quality is on your side! Plus, at 4 bucks (3.99 US dollars) you can afford you buy it and hate it, but you will probably like this one. Hope you guys enjoyed it as well!

I was a big fan of the original Supcom. The level of strategy, the units, the huge maps. It was an overload of epic proportions for my young brain. I did not actually realize this game came out until I see it popping up on Steam on sale. Seeing as it was Supreme Commander I knew it would have to be good.
Well was it?
Yes and no.
What I like about SC2 is that they corrected some of the god-awful game mechanics present in the original, especially destruction of units. In Supcom 1, if a plane is spam hit by thousands of projectiles it explodes, and the model simply disappears in a cloud of white, instead of tumbling down to earth. Who the hell thought that was a good idea? If planes hit water they just explode in a cloud of white. Sinking ships sink straight through the map and vanish. They fixed these issues in SC2. When a dead plane hits the water it sinks and leaves wreckage. When a ship sinks it leaves wreckage. It adds for more immersion in my opinion. But that's about where it goes for me with this game.
The size of the maps have been drastically scaled back. Remember Seton's Clutch? That was a huge map in the original. plenty of room to set up forward staging bases, recon facilities and to hide experimentals from your enemy that you way nt to keep a secret. Well, now each base has a tiny amount of space apart from each other. The infamous corridor that was the home of so many ruined units is now a tiny walk.  Many of the maps have been smallified and that sheer size of strategy removed. That's something I don't particularly like.
Now lets go to the units. The race uses the original three factions, UEF, Aeon (Who are now simply known as the 'Illuminate') and the Cybrans. Design-wise, I think the UEF and cybrans stray too far away from their original feel and design. They seem too close together now. But moving on, many of the units present in the first SC are gone, replaced with single variants. Oh did I tell you the tech-level system was removed? Yeah, no more T1,T2, and T3 engineers to clog up your base. You buid experimentals in a seperate factory. SC2 has added many more experimentals to the fray, but at the cost of making them absolutely pathetic. Remember the Cybran's Soul Ripper? That thing could wipe out an entire base. Remember the Aeon's Collosus? That could take out Monkeylords in a heartbeat. They've all been replaced with inferior counterparts. The Soul Ripper II is pathetic. The new Collosus is also pathetic, but still looks pretty cool. The only way to truly win is to just spam a butt load of units at the enemy and target the commander. There aren't anymore of those close-call moments you get in SC where your experimental is assaulting the enemy ACU, and just as it's about to die the ACU blows up.
Also, the factions have become rather unbalanced. The UEF, as in SC1, are masters of artillery. They have the most powerful artillery buildings in the game. In SC1, this was the same deal, but it was balanced because the cybrans and the Aeon had their own artillery pieces. Here, they don't. The Cybrans do, but it's a pathetic cannon that doesn't have range on the UEF artillery. The Illuminate have no artillery, so build lots of shields!  Also, remember the Nukes? In SC1, one nuke could level a whole army. Now, the raw power of strategic missiles are gone. They're so pathetic. In SC1 you had to spam your entire army of engineers to get a strat. missile built. Here, they build rather quickly.
The graphics. It feels like the graphics have been improved in some places, and ruined in others. I just can't explain it.
So is SC2 a worthy sequel to SC1? Maybe, if you're willing to overlook the reduced strategic aspect, the pathetic experimentals and the graphics. Personally, i recommend Forged Alliance, a sort of re-done updated version of SC with the Seraphim as a new playable race. Still, SC2, not a bad game. 8/10

If you came here looking for a review, you have come to the wrong place, but if you want some very ♥♥♥♥ing good brownies, you have come to the right place. You're welcome for an actual recipe, not a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ copy and paste pie recipe. Trust me nothing goes wrong with nutella.
INGREDIENTS:
1 c. unsalted butter
2 c. sugar
1/2 tsp. salt
1 c. flour
1 c. cocoa powder
4 eggs
1 (13-oz.) jar Nutella
5 Ferrero Rocher candies, unwrapped and crumbled
DIRECTIONS:
1. Preheat oven to 350 degrees F.
2. Melt butter in a medium-sized saucepan over medium heat. Add sugar, stirring until combined. 3. Remove from heat and add salt, flour, and cocoa powder, stirring to combine. Whisk in eggs, stirring just until the mixture is combined into a batter. Set aside.
4. Spray an 8"-x-8" pan with cooking spray. Pour half of the batter into the pan. Spoon or lightly drizzle most of the Nutella on top of the batter, forming an even layer over the brownie batter. 5. 5. Use a spoon or silicone spatula to cover the Nutella with the remaining brownie batter. (If you pour the batter straight on top of the Nutella, it will sink into the Nutella and combine into one marbled—yet delicious—mess.)
6. Bake until the top layer of brownies has browned and set, 28 to 30 minutes. It shouldn’t jiggle when you remove it from the oven. (The toothpick test doesn’t work here, since the toothpick will hit the Nutella layer, making the brownies seem uncooked.)
7. Let cool for 15 to 20 minutes, then top with a drizzle of Nutella and crumbled Ferrero Rocher chocolates. Cut into squares and serve.
Credits: ★ Billy

Phoenix Force is the tenth game I have played through completely, and the fourth that I got all achievements in. It's a very, very challenging game, and I absolutely recommend it.
As for the story, a group of phoenixes is tasked with defeating hordes of enemies, before they can reach a dying tree to revive it. 100 Levels, and 100 Extra Challenges (to unlock the 6th and last phoenix) offer hours of challenging bullet dodging and thinking of which phoenix to pick.
Fury, the starter phoenix, is able to elimite bullets directly in front of him, Cryo will freeze all enemies for a couple of seconds, Tupa is able to teleport around on the field, Gaia simply has homing shots (which will always attack the nearest enemy), Gast is able to summon a shield, and Lich gains orbs shooting along with it the more health it drains from the enemies.
And with this force, you should be able to clear all the levels - but be prepared to get frustrated at some of the more tricky enemy types!

For three tiny games you can play for free, the Jesus Christ RPG Trilogy is not too shabby. It's easily the best Bible-based game I've seen (haven't played many, but I've seen some "shining" examples in the past.). If you have even an ounce of Biblical knowledge, you'll get a chuckle at the references. If not, you'll probably still laugh at the tongue-in-cheek writing and sometimes comical appearance of scenes due to the game's graphics.
Gameplay-wise, the battles, as long as you've paid attention to in-game hints and done everything you need to do, are pretty easy by RPG standards. There are very few enemies in the later two games, excluding bosses, that you won't basically one-shot. The bosses are at least fairly worthy opponents, but I don't see RPG experts having any trouble. It definitely put difficulty on the back-burner for the sake of telling the story. As someone who doesn't typically like having to repeat battles more than a few times, I welcomed this decision. Average players can probably finish all three games in the span of a few hours.
The music can get a wee bit repetitive, but some of the tunes, especially in the third game, are surprisingly catchy.
If you're looking for a simple, quick RPG with some interesting humor, give this one (three?) a shot.

Sequels are a funny thing. When a game is good-but-not-quite-great, we see the smallest solutions to itty bitty flaws, a few things that could have been spectacular given just a little more spit-shined development time. Yet those few tiny tweaks typically aren't enough to regenerate interest, never mind entertain for hours on end, when a sequel turns up. It' almost as if that game had its chance, and now we expect more, more, more.
Shank 2 doesn't reinvent itself in the slightest, which is why, more than most sequels, it's difficult not to compare it to the original. Developer Klei used past criticisms to patch its pants and glue its building blocks together. It shuffles its pieces around, finds better places for them to fit, and defies the idea that overhauling a flawed experience is absolutely necessary.
The result is, of course, a better 2D brawler, the kind most wished it would have been the first time around -- and it'll absolutely turn your Shank crank again.
Shank 2 addresses flaws Klei is acutely aware of, so it practically shouts about how much better it is now than it used to be. Main character Shank dodges with an effortless flick of the right stick, which is a massive step up from the clunky trigger/stick combo from the first game.
Attacking and healing aren't tied to the same button as they were previously. Where the animation system used to inhibit Shank, it now enables him: He moves faster, pounces farther and higher, and can switch between weapons mid-combo without a split-second delay signing his death certificate. In addition, exclamation marks above enemies' heads act as an instant-death counter-kill indicator, which is massively helpful for plucking particularly troublesome guys from a group. Also, disarming and executing dudes is quick enough not to break your rhythm, but slow enough to glorify the grossness of kicking a baseball bat down someone's throat. Uninterrupted murder is a beautiful blend of graceful fluidity and harsh ferocity, and few melee-centric action games achieve this kind of big-combo bliss.
The combat is improved for more than basic input reasons, too. Enemies attack in different ways from various places -- dudes chuck grenades from across the screen, careful shooters take precise pistol aim from above, and maniacal machine-gunners fire bursts in your general direction. Instant-kill pits make short work of bad guys (and you) too, and throwing switches to crush five guys beneath a shipping container is sickening fun. Each encounter is an unpredictable puzzle where evasion, aggression, and an impressive array of acrobatics earn you a personal accomplishment greater than any leaderboard high score.
Juggling and switching from your quick-attack shanks to a heavy sledgehammer to the shotgun aren't just cool-looking tactics -- they're completely necessary to surviving. By comparison, the first game is slow, unsatisfying, and cumbersome. (Really, you can never go back.) Shank 2 is demanding, and in a 2D action game so reliant on player precision, these simple tweaks make your life a hell of a lot easier.
Even the most difficult problems in Shank 2 have easy solutions. More importantly, its harshest conditions can't come close to the maddening challenge of its predecessor. This is perhaps the best step forward -- the first Shank had some ridiculously difficult spots. In Shank 2, you'll only bash your head against the occasional brick wall as long as you let it stand. When shotgun blasts or the scythe aren't doing enough damage to certain characters, swapping to the revolver or chainsaw is usually enough to take 'em down. Main character Shank no longer switches weapons on the fly during a level, though, and must instead trade gear between deaths. It's small inconvenience, but knowing weapon properties -- bonus damage against fat enemies or a knock-back effect, for instance -- and changing your strategy accordingly is the key to powering through tougher sections. Boss battles are a particularly great example of these and the rest of Shank's greatest design elements coming together. As bosses are meant to be, they're the final exam for everything you've learned along the way -- if you didn't pick up on and make use of something new and important, you're going to have a tough time with their interesting patterns and brutal attacks.
Co-op would have made the campaign a cakewalk, which is perhaps the reason it's single-player only this time around. Shank 2 trades the first title's local cooperative campaign for wave-based online multiplayer. It's both a trade-up and a trade-down. Clobbering coordinated bombers before they blow up supply caches for 30 waves involves all the single-player's best Shank-isms -- two players use the terrific combat, mount weapons, and set off traps to eviscerate and burn bad guys -- and requires serious skill. Dying doubles your ally's duties, plus they're responsible for reviving you, so bring a coordinated comrade or suffer the consequences.
Earning cash for kills to buy mini-guns, turrets, decoys, and, uh, a wild boar gives you a reason to seek out incoming enemies as well, rather than just let your buddy take care of the worst situations. There's an alluring draw to replaying the three maps with new characters, too -- each has his or her own statistics, like health bonuses, item discounts, or damage modifiers, and each match plays out differently based on how you experiment with various pairs. Survival Mode feels thrown in out of obligation rather than inspiration, yet it still brings enough new to the table that it'll melt away an hour in an instant.
Survival Mode is probably where most will spend the majority of their time -- Shank 2 is only a couple hours long, and there's little incentive to replay the campaign. Granted, the single-player is flashy, gorgeous, and where the coolest stuff happens, like escaping giant boulders and buzz-saws, fighting through a burning village, or exploring a massive boat with a bunch of diverging paths. Survival Mode is missing distinctive qualities to call its own, so it exists if you feel shortchanged but is inessential if you'd rather move onto the next great game in your library.
If there's one major change in Shank 2, it's the tone. Thematically, Shank was absurd. The game was dark and violent, which didn't quite fit in with the Luchadores, strippers, guys in gimp masks occupying each arena. Shank 2 is about martial law, facist oppression, and endangered family. It doesn't do anything to capitalize on this stuff, which is a shame -- the cinematics are still goofy, profane, and senseless, and some of the bosses are a bit out of left field, visually. The grim approach a nice touch to the gameplay, anyway, and fits into the grand scheme of making Shank 2 feel much more in line with itself.

Hard to ask such a high price when the majority of your game is built around replayability.  I didn't know this game existed until a beta came out a week before release or so, so it had very poor advertising.  As I understand it now has a cash shop for skins, which is the last thing it needed.  I don't even need to go into the numerous price drops.
Just makes me sad to see such great potential squandered. At this point, it's a good observation on how the things, events, and marketing surrounding a game's actual (really, really good) gameplay affects its success.

I predict (with everything crossed) that the reception will go up. It was a smart move for this game to go F2P. The Mixed status only comes from the game's decline as it continued to get overshadowed by other hero shooters.
The population seems low at first, but it appears to be climbing (Currently at yesterday's peak by 7AM Central Time). Wouldn't hurt to try it.
Hopefully it'll get more people interested now that there's no investment.
Now about the game:
It has a variety of PVP modes and gameplay is straightforward face value arcade shooting. Can be played casually or competitively (Draft mode to ban champions like League)
Some balancing issues but for the most part the learning curve is very standard and not too complex.
Loot boxes are exciting, seeing as they unlock actual gear you can use in-game compared to only cosmetics.
The 7 free hero cycle is also exciting, feels like an homage to League of Legends' cycle of free champions (What'd be the point of a F2P game if all of its heroes were available)
Leveling works in two ways (Commander and Hero rank). With every match you earn exp for both your own rank and the rank of the hero you played.
It's a fun game imo, wouldn't hurt to give it a go. Give it some time, it can be complex at times but well worth the "git gud" status.
The Full Game upgrade doesn't hurt either, seeing as this game is revolved more around multiplayer, the campaign does get a little upstaged. But it's still a great little list of WoW raidy type missions with Borderlands type humor.

I was in the mood for a mystery and I definitely got a great one with this game. Styled like the browsing of an archive of records in a similar vein to "Analogue: A Hate Story," it's worth a look for anyone who wants to sit down and puzzle out a story.
Not going to spoil much, as it defeats the point, but I will criticize by saying that there are too many "filler" videos. Videos where the interviewee just talks about her coffee or tea or repeats something she's just said. They would be a bit more seamless in a linear narrative but something like this which lets the player pick up the remnants in the aftermath of the actual events and try to piece together what happened, it does get a bit annoying to try to guess at the one word that is unique to a certain clip and then be rewarded only with redundant information. "Analogue" managed to avoid that kind of stuff for the most part so I feel this really has no excuse. Still, a fascinating game for anyone whose idea of video games isn't just trying to fill up bars.

[SPOILER FREE REVIEW]
Ok, for a game included in a US$1 humble bundle, I got my monies worth. You get about 2 hours (3 hours to 100% achievements) of gameplay which is basically typing in keywords into a 90's styled PC.
The 'gameplay' is to work out what to type in. Anything returning more than 5 results will only show 5 results and will only show the oldest files first, limiting what you can view and protecting the 'newest' files from being shown.
Once I eventually found the answers I needed (and I got my "ahh, clever devs...clever..." moment) I was satisfied, though if I spent anymore than US$1 on this I would have felt slightly cheated. It's a game that you could watch a youtube playthrough and possibly (depending on the youtuber) enjoy it more. I did enjoy the experience, though I'll be uninstalling it within seconds of posting this review as there is zero replay value (unless you want to grab the remaining achievements, which is basically ensuring that you watch every video).
tl;dr - For US$1 it's worth it if you like VHS quality 'who dunnit' and indie games.

Now 13 years old, the affectionately nicknamed Kotor is still worth playing. Sure the menus are clunky and textures show their seams from time to time, but the meat of the game, the plot and the character development, is still fresh. The story arc, like with the original Star Wars trilogy, is better if you've managed to avoid key spoilers. Even knowing what's going to happen doesn't stop the journey there from being wonderful because the main plot is secondary to the events happening on the planets involved in it anyway. In true Star Wars fashion, the mission at hand has our heroes hopping from one planet to the next and each layover is focused around getting entangled in the goings-on of that place and its people rather than moving the plot forward.  Captions are a necessity as some speak in their native tongues, further driving home the fact that the galaxy doesn't revolve around you as the player. The world and its people feel alive, though the lack of player accommodation can get a bit tiresome.
The world of Kotor may not be an 'open-world', but with a seedy card game-based gambling ring, a struggling racing circuit, and plenty of side quests, there are too many distractions to call it linear either. The same can be said for the physical act of playing the game as well. Straightforward violence with all its lightsaber dueling, blaster shooting, and Force pushing is always an option, and though it is a fantastic spectacle of parring and dodging, the fun of it wears out quickly. Thankfully, a number of encounters can be bypassed with a clever application of a character's skills. Computers can be hacked to shut down security systems, derelict droids can be repaired only to be sent against their former masters, and enemies can be persuaded to disband before a conflict even arises. For a game that was designed with the original Xbox in mind, there is a surprising amount of freedom in how the game is played.
That freedom is echoed in the game's approach to the player character's companions. Though only two can be chosen to leave the ship at any time, they all hang around and level up either way, meaning the dynamic can be altered to suit a situation as it arises. Simply talking to your companions can reveal a good portion of their character, but it's the personal quest each companion has that acts as their turning point. How players react during a personal quest will affect their compatriots for better or worse, providing some bit of control over their personalities, and giving the player the option of role-playing with the group dynamic in addition to their own created character.
At its core, Kotor is about a group of heroes struggling against the dark side of the Force while traveling through hyperspace and interacting with a wide variety of alien species, just like any good Star Wars episode. But Kotor offers more than just lightsabers and blasters, and it never loses sight of the legacy it's adding to.

As is now BioWare Tradition,Companions can be recruited and their characther can be built to play however you like.
The story of KOTOR is set in the middle the Extended Universe "Old Republic Age" roughly 4000 years before the events of The Phantom Menace.You play as a Jedi who has to stop the evil Darth Reven and his apprentice Darth Malak from discovering the powerful weapon called the Star Forge.
The game may not have the best graphics or the most engaging battle system,but it makes up for this with story and world design.The planets within the world look amazing and stand out.Dantooines lush landscapes with its intresting creatures is amazing!
Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic is a engaging,fun game and a must-play for any fan of BioWares Rpgs or of Star Wars and its expanded universe in general.

Her Story is an amazing FMV tale of mystery and intrigue where you must utilize your fine detective skills in order to piece together a story using archived video footage of 7 interviews. These 7 interviews detail the background of the candidate's missing husband. Viva Seifert, the interviewee, won numerous awards for her superb acting in this game, helping it become one of the most popular indie games in the summer of 2015. Even though I don't have many hours logged into this game on Steam, I have previously completed it with a friend.
With nothing much to start with, you first bootup the police video database and begin to watch a few seemingly non-interconnected clips, sporatically taken within the seven different interviews. Your job is to type in keywords discovered throughout your investigation in order to pull up other unseen clips. Some of these keywords are fairly obvious, such as:
, yet others are extremely obscure (the final keyword). A database tracker helps you visualize which/how many clips you have seen, and if you are getting close to the final tapes (in chronological order).
Throughout gameplay, there will be an active session of 5 or so clips, and if there are more than 5 clips for a search result, you must view some of them in order to have access to the rest. A very helpful feature is that notes can be added for each clip. This really helps if you leave and want to pick the game back up down the line. The depth in this game is magnificent, yet the UI can still use a lot of work. Other than that, this unique story is truly a masterpiece.

Guacamelee, without a doubt, is the best Metroidvania I've ever played, excluding any Metroid or Castlevania games. From the get go you're presented with a cool Luchadore theme, and tight controls. The game picks up heat pretty fast, and soon you transform from average farm worker to a luchadore, a hero of the people. This game follows the metroidvania tradition very well. You have areas to revisit, powerups unlockble through the game, and a 2D world to explore. The game is so much fun, you'll lose hours jumping and punching enemies. This game also has a great sense of humor, and has tons of references, like nods to Castle Crashers, Mario, Metroid, Mega Man, and even TF2. It also references a bunch of memes, which kinda get on my nerves, seeing things like Insanity Wolf or Me Gusta staring back at you.
However, every game has faults, and this game is chock full of them. First of all, the platforming will frustrate you to no end. Some of the platforming requires a lot of timing and fast reflexes. There were many times I almost went insane doing it. The game is short, but the time you get to have is great. I recommend using a controller for this, as a keyboard can really frustate you. I mapped all my keyboard controls to odd things, whicvh made the combat harder and the platforming as hard as well. Some things, like the sparring bot, just get ridiculous to use when you have your keyboard controls mapped to wild locations.
Despite its flaws, this game is very enjoyable, and easy to play. I'm looking forward to whatever this company puts out next. It may be hard to believe, but this is easily one of the most fun games I've played this year.

First thing to note is that this game was developed with mobile in mind.  Your character will auto-attack as you walk through things, but you can mash the space bar to attack faster.  While the game can be played with the mouse, I'd recommend using either the keyboard or a gamepad for the best experience.
bit Dungeon II is really addictive, but sadly not a very long game.  The entire game can be beaten in about three hours or less.  There also doesn't seem to be a true ending, as the game just automatically jumps into a New Game Plus when you finish it.
In this New Game Plus, you keep all your gear and currency, while the enemies and loot scale up to match.  You can play the game through many times while it continues to grow more difficult.  The game rewards you with some powerful loot when you beat it though, so it's clearly intended that you play it a few times.
The game could use more randomly generated content.  The overworld is static and while the dungeon layouts change, they're all picked from a small pool of predefined layouts.  A few more "Rouge-like" elements would take bit Dungeon II from a little replay value to a ton.
The loot is where it's at though.  bit Dungeon II more or less boils down to a short but addictive loot grind.  A lot of the replay value lies in trying out different character builds and the gear available to you.
If you can deal with a little repetitiveness, the game is worth the price, otherwise I'd grab it on sale.  I got my copy through Humble Bundle a while back, so I can't really say much more on the price.  It seems pretty fair, but people are likely to complain anyway.
With all that out of the way though, I'd have to say that bit Dungeon II is a commendable effort.  Even with these downsides, it has the right spirit.
I feel like if the developer had more time or resources to spend on this game, it could have easily gone from "good" to "great".
It is wicked addictive though.  If their next game is a "bit Dungeon III", I will definitely check it out.
(They've recently released a remake of the original bit Dungeon, formerly a flash game, to unfortunately mixed reviews, but I'll probably check that out too.)

One of those games that you really have to try for yourself, when you're bored and just browsing the free and cheap games part of steam. You can look in the sections for the awfully reviewed games, or the wonderfully reviewed games, and somewhere in between you'll find Jesus Christ RPG Trilogy.
Now, you might think to yourself, why exactly would I download this game? I'm not a religious person. I don't need to be indoctrinated.
The answers are very simple.
Do you want hardcore rpg gameplay, where the first thing that happens as soon as you step out of the first town is you are BRUTALLY MURDERED IN THE FOREST BY A PACK OF THUGS? That's not in the bible!
Do you want to recruit a band of disciples? Who doesn't like disciples?
Are you one of those people who likes to cure leprosy?
Do you want to control a character who *literally refuses to fight*?
Do you like chugging down wine in order to fight Lucifer and his demons to cleanse heaven of...
Well, you get the point.
The price tag is on point for the two nights of enjoyment I got out of this bizarrely compelling game. You expect some type of errors, or erratic gameplay, or something wrong with a free title, especially an RPG maker game, but there was never anything wrong.
You have to make decisions that require some thought, you get to baptize people. You even get to grind to beat up tough baddies. Do you really need anything else from an RPG?

If you like a game that feels like a cross between Freelancer and Starfleet Command, you could give Starpoint Gemini a try. I am certainly enjoying it!
Pros:
+Freedom to explore at your leisure. Do whatever you want inbetween story missions
+Lots of ships and equipment to choose from
+Tactical micromanagement a la Starfleet Command (targetting enemy subsystems)
+Excellent tutorial and low learning curve (but follow it to the letter, or it forces you to restart)
+Character customisation and RPG elements (levels, perks, abilities (called maneuvers) )
Cons:
-Poor voice acting. The writing is okay though, and you can mute the voices, so it really is a non-issue
-Occassional crash to desktop when jumping between systems seem common for many players (thankfully the game autosaves before a jump)
Comments:
Controls may feel clunky, but that's because there is a lot to manage. You can pause the game at any time by pressing F. During this pause you can do things like plot a course, check out the enemy ship's equipment and assign targets. Pausing mid-combat makes the game a lot more manageable.
Tip:
If you can't dock at T-gates or stations, it is probably because you are still in combat-mode. Turn it off by pressing the big red button at the bottom of the screen ;)

Hesitation.
It's on your face at the beginning, less so on hers. You're looking at a series of grainy videos from years past, recalling bad haircuts and embarrassing fashion choices. And her? She might be looking at being accused as an accessory to the murder of Simon Smith. Perhaps it's not so bad for you, in balance.
Sam Barlow's Her Story is a classic mystery game that subverts the 'choose your own story' genre for the Google generation (which my parents have caught up to now so perhaps I might even have them try this one out). Using a series of search words and phrases, you sift through a database of police interview videos captured many a year ago of one suspect: the titular 'her' in Her Story. Each video has been fully transcribed (in the background) so if a word is contained within it, it will show up in your search results. But it's not as easy as Googling, I mean typing in, 'murder' and 'suspect' and hoping to narrow down the field posthaste. Each video is loaded with a tantalising mixture of nebulous emotion, hard facts and delicious red herrings. The more you watch, the closer you get to the truth, or sometimes you find yourself going off on tangents on a hunch. There were a few times when I though I'd had it, only to discover a contradiction (which made me yell "Objection!" at the screen a few times) which required me to rethink my line of thought. This is amplified by the fact that the interviews take place over several days. The sense of time is palpable: the interviewee isn't in the same mindset every day so what you get out of her varies beautifully. It's worth mentioning that the acting by Viva Seifert is wonderful and makes the experience emotive and involving: there are times when she draws you into her confidence with throwaway lines and cheeky grins, and at times, she's in your face, telling you to go copulate with yourself. More colourfully, of course.
Put on your best gumshoes, grow out that stubble (ladies included) and don a trench, as to you prepare to lose yourself to Her Story.

Sequel to one of my personal favorite horror games and while it's not as spooky, it's definitely just as fun as the original F.E.A.R. and it gives way more backstory to Alma and Pointman than the original. This game is absolutely worth the purchase if you enjoyed the first FEAR and have yet to play this.
The story starts about a half hour before the ending of the first F.E.A.R. and you play a different soldier in the First Encounter Assault Recon taskforce. When the large scale explosion happens, your character is nearly dead and has lost a lot of blood. You wind up in a hospital, having been given Pointman's blood, and now you have his special skill of enhanced combat reflexes and can essentially slow down time to a crawl, to get the upper hand on your enemies. Pretty quickly, things get spooky, when you wake up in a hospital and no one is around. Things begin to go bump -- presumably in the night -- and it's time to arm yourself with all sorts of awesome firearms. The shooting is more intense than its predecessor and with way more fun weapons. The story is just as captivating, only this one has a way better ending that will leave your jaw on the floor and your eyes agape.

Do you like quick melee sidescrolling combat and adventure (and tacos). Then you'll love Guacamelee! This Mexican themed action platformer is set in in the colourful world of luchadores and the not-so-colourful world of the dead (which is still nice to look at anyway). The fighting is fast paced with plenty of moves and enemies to mix it up. There are also puzzle solving elements, where the player (that's you!) has to utilise the new techniques you have learned and quick reactions to solve them all. The music is also beautifully well suited, as are all the sound effects.
The game can be a bit challenging at times when you're facing multiple enemies in different dimensions, but by no means is it impossible. There is a hard mode available after completion of the game if you found the first run through too easy.
The game however, is quite short unfortunately. I finished it in 5:15, though that was with completing most all of the puzzles along the way (which probably made it easier for me anyway). That said, there are a number of side quests that I did not complete, and with multiple costumes also available, combined with the hard mode, there is some replayability in this game.
Another feature, though I have not tried it out, is co-op mode. Could be fun, but not necessary anyway.
The story isn't too bad - typical save the princess stuff with a Mexican and underworld theme mixed into it. The dialogue can be funny at times, but I think the only decent material was when references to other games were made. I feel like the developers tried too hard with this, and perhaps should have been more subtle most of the time - to me it seems they relied upon it too much.
Guacamelee is fun, beautiful to look at, and engrossing, which is why I recommend it, but considering it's length, I would wait for a sale so as to get more bang for your buck.

Guacamelee is a platform brawler with a solid, simple combat system that provides depth while also allowing for plenty of combos. The world also follows a Metroidvania style structure which gives you lots of places to explore as well as plenty platforming puzzles that make good use of the control scheme. I highly recomend a controller.
The game also contains plenty of humour with a ton of references to games like Metroid, VVVVV and Castle Crashers to internet memes.
2 player local co-op is also available.

It was a really excellent casual playthrough.  Loved the "paintings in motion" style visuals. As for the bad, even after beating the game I'm not quite sure how the talisman / spritnite system works.  The magic system is more complex than I'd like, although the difficulty is forgiving enough that it was still possible to push through the final dungeons by having good weapons and spamming aura and flare.  I'd guess that some of the optuse descriptions are translation issues, so you might want to check a wiki for help in making sense of it all.
Overall great game, if you enjoy SNES RPGs or are looking for a short linear JRPG, it's definitely worth a playthough.

The trailer does a good job advertising this game like it's a darker version of Link to the Past. It had me so hyped I decided to put five dollars into my Steam Wallet to buy it. Big mistake. Once I got the game, I quickly realized that the gameplay doesn't live up to the polish of the trailer, and only resembles a Zelda game on the surface. While the world of bit Dungeon II looks visually interesting, there is little to no story or exposition to explain what's going on. I'm supposed to transport a dead woman's soul apparently...but why should I care about her? Who desecrated her grave? Where the heck am I supposed to be going? It's a shame there's not more background about the world of Bit Dungeon II, because I really would have liked to know more about the world.
Mechanically speaking, there are an abundance of collision issues with the game, especially with walls and destructible objects. Colliding with these objects makes the character sputter back and forth, to the point that you'll be pushed into the room you were previously in. The depth of the battle mechanics is woefully shallow. Point. Click. Kill. That's all there is to it. The puzzles are disappointing too...they consist of moving rocks over switches, and that's about it. I was hoping to acquire different tools to solve different types of puzzle challenges, but the game emphasizes action over puzzle solving.
TL:DR Bit Dungeon II looks awesome in the trailers, but doesn't live up to the hype.

So, Planet Coaster. It's pretty well-known, and has accumulated a fairly large following over the past year it's been running. I personally enjoy this game, especially if you can get at the very least 15 fps on medium graphics. Now, I myself do have a low end computer, but it has about 8G of ram, so I think it can handle the game smoothly enough for me to REALLY enjoy it. The coaster editer has a couple issues concerning smoothness, continuous roll, yada-yada ya, but the spline system is good for casual players to jump in and do whatever you want. I, myself, have prior experience with the spline system, and about 15 minutes worth of Nolimits2 coaster creating experience, which for me is enough to say that the coasters in this game can get fairly smooth. Another thing is the terrain option, and building system. Both of these are probably the best I've seen before in a theme park simulator, and I LOVE it. Especially the terrain system, which is so easy to use but so hard to master, and that makes it awesome. I usually only play in the sandbox mode, and I have only played this game for about 4-5 weeks on and off, but that's enough to say that this is a truly phenominal game. And considering I haven't touched the tycoon simulation part, that's a pretty high rating. I didn't really come here for the challenge, but I've heard a lot of mixed reviews on the difficulty. Some say it's not hard at all, some say it's farly difficult, but I think that that depends on how much experience the player has with tycoon games, and how good they are in general at time management and buisness. The community here is actually pretty peaceful in comparison to a lot of others that have become kinda relevant, and irrelevant ones (Geometry Dash, the new FNaF games (5, 6, I dunno but maybe 7, I have lost count ever since sister location), Cuphead, maybe Roblox, etc. (not gonna include Undertale because that fan base is irrelevant at this point and has dismantled after it lost its popularity). Since Planet Coaster has accumulated a fairly large following, there are bound to be youtubers playing this. Some new, some NoLimits 2 fans, some migrating from RCT3 and RCTW, some fans of City Skylines, and many more. One of these youtubers have created a Planet Coaster community inside of the Planet Coaster community, named Channel5Gaming. I've been there before, and I've had some fun there. I think most Planco players know that youtuber, and from what I've seen a majority enjoy his content. I think that Channel5Gaming has brought a lot of good to the community, and a bit of bad (but hey, any fan base or community can't be perfect), but planco's fan base is pretty close. I think that I might have rambled for too long about the community, mostly because I'm kinda inexperienced with the game and I don't have much to say other than so far I've enjoyed the game, and all updates and DLC (despite not owning any planco DLC, but I will soon). This has been my review, and I personally recommend this game to almost anyone who is interested.
