You've been given access to a police database containing videos of a woman being interviewed over the disappearance and possible murder of her husband: you'll slowly uncover what happened and why by searching the database and listening to what she has to say.
Her Story is a detective game that challenges you to make sense of what you're looking at and come up with effective search words to unlock more, hopefully important, video sequences: it won't be everyone's cup of tea but it's an interesting experience for sure.
-simple yet effective art style
-decent, if minimal, soundtrack
-Viva Seifert gives a great performance, her acting and body language add a lot to her lines
-a very interesting story featuring a few twists and appropriately mature content
-requires you to listen and reason to come up with valid search terms, the detective work is enjoyable and taking notes is almost a must
-not everyone'll appreciate the simple gameplay or the fact you're simply looking up and watching videos, for some it won't even be considered a game
-going through inconsequential videos can get a bit dull
-depending on your skill you might easily find out what happened or be left stranded
-while the interface is simple a small tutorial'd have helped players realize how it works (e.g. how to fast forward or rewind videos)
-not very long (I'd say 2/2,5hrs to find out what happened plus another hour if you want to watch all videos you've missed) and no replay value
I sadly can't plainly express many of the things I liked about the game as doing so'd require me to detail certain events or dialogues: doing so'd lessen the experience of anyone who hasn't played yet so, as usual, I'll be very vague. The story and narrative are, imho, pretty great and manage to stay enthralling even as you necessarily uncover them out of chronological order. There's lots to watch and you'll be faced with mature themes, sordid stories, false leads or simply useless bits of info.The fact you only hear answers without the starting questions means you'll have to think about what you're watching to make full sense of it: more reasoning'll obviously be needed for you to find out leads and decide if and how they fit in the investigation. It's difficult to remember every possible keyword so taking notes'll help you remember what to search for and, for some, it might be a great external tool to organize leads and try to understand what happened.
I have to admit that, at times, watching useless videos can get dull: of course they're there to make sure things don't become too easy but watching her answering how she wants her coffee each day isn't exactly fun. Depending on how good you are at guesswork and/ or your luck you might also find yourself stuck without knowing what keywords to use: other times you might have an hunch on what happened but find it hard to come up with the right word to find the video you're looking for. As a whole the system works though and I had no problem in finding enough leads to be given the option to exit the database and finish the game.
Her Story'll sit well with fans of the detective genre as the basic gameplay found here is all about looking for clues and making sense of what you find, there's also a good story here for those that value narrative over gameplay: if you are in the target audience the game will be a rewarding and original experience, one I thoroughly enjoyed.

I've been playing UG:CW for a while now. And I actually came to the store page to see if it was still in early access as there was some bugs that were beginning to make it difficult to progress in the campaign mode.
I loved this game from the beginning but became more frustrated as I noticed there wasn't much improvement over the months and I began to feel like this was just a rushed game since I couldn't get past the bugs and glitches.
First, the A.I. would seem to glitch and keep running but not move anywhere. I would attack the said unit with calvary and the calvary would join in the glitch and not attack. Then I will have to retreat but can't seem to get my calvary away from the glitched A.I. and then some skirmishers will come and mow down my calvary.
Second, my own units will act sporadic, and I don't mean routing or falling back, I am talking about going in for a charge they will just stop moving. I don't understand why I tell them to charge by either pressing the charge button or double clicking the enemy, but they will sometimes just stop and will begin to continue firing after a couple seconds.
Third, when I am zoomed out as far as I can from the battlefield I will try and have my units move, but when I click them to a location they will begin attacking an enemy. As in, when I click to go to a forest line where there is no enemy they will will move towards the closest enemy to them which can be in the opposition direction. It makes flanking very difficult as I will have to zoom out, get to my units, then zoom back in to initiate an attack. I've found out that zooming back in will mitigate the problem, but it becomes annoying.
This game has so many awesome features and I really enjoyed it thoroughly when it was in early access, but I don't know what the heck happened because I just can't seem to use many tactics now as they seem to be bugged or the units are glitched and get stuck on parts of the battlefield that I don't want them in.
Please fix this so I can come back and enjoy the game! Please!
But at the current time of this review, I can not recommend playing unless you want to feel frustration.
Edit:
I thought I'd add to this so it doesn't sound like the game is rubbish. The game itself aside from the glitches and bugs I feel is very enjoyable. Its unique in itself with making decisions based upon your own choices and how battles are played out by your own strategies. The game is well balanced as I've never felt that the enemy has been too strong or given any handicaps, but what does make it difficult is when your own units glitch out and you just get massacred since they are unable to move. Which is really my only complaint, but once that is fixed then I'll feel that the game is even and totally playable.

I Am Setsuna doesn't actively do anything wrong, it just doesn't bring anything new to the table. There is not a shred of originality to be found here. It has heart but it has no substance. It ticks every JRPG cliche box and despite being wrapped in a neatly presented package it manages to be utterly forgettable as an experience. Tropes and conventional gameplay aren't inherently a bad thing, and although i enjoyed some of my time with Setsuna i couldn't tell you if it was merely due to my own blind nostalgia for the silver age of JRPGs of the early 00's. The story of a maiden sacrificing herself for the sake of the world? Yep it's Tales Of Symphonia and Final Fantasy X.
The characters are alright though nothing special. The everpresent  piano music is pleasant and fits the snowy setting, my favorite tunes were the world map and Kir's theme.
The battle system is essentially 90's Final Fantasy ATB. You attack, wait for your attack gauge to refill in real time and attack again. I was admittedly never a fan of ATB to begin with. I much prefer properly turn based battle systems like Nocturne's Press Turn Icon system or QTE based attacks like Paper Mario 2. Or even something as outlandish and awesome as Shadow Hearts 2's Judgement Ring. The most in strategy you get in Setsuna is to accumulate enough special points per round to add a bit of extra damage with your next attack by pressing a button wth the correct timing. There are also some combos available when combining specific skills but fudge me if i can figure out what makes what combo. Once i had the Blowbeat combo with Endir & Nidr i just kept spamming that on every random encounter. It stuns enemies and deals a ton of damage, devastating anything that stood before me and making any remaining battles a joke. Not that many of the battles left much room for strategy anyway, usually it sufficed to spam your strongest attacks and heal whenever necessary.
What i was sorely missing throughout the entire game was world-building. Mainly due to a complete lack of flavor text. Take Golden Sun for example, you could click on every stove in every house and get a little line about whatever dish was boiling in that pot. And the text would differ for every single house. The most you can interact with Setsuna's world is by finding sparkling ingredients scattered across the land. Even NPCs rarely have anything interesting to say. There is some background story written in your journal, but why the hell wouldn't you put your world building into the actual world instead of hiding it away in walls of text. It's FFXIII all over again....
Further grievances listed for your convenience:
- The world is map is extremely rudimentary, no encounters or treasure chests just more sparkly ingredients to be found. And you can't run on the world map making going from A to B a slog.
-There are too many different vendors, you could have easily combined them all into one shop for items & equipment. Splitting it into 5 different stores is simply inconvenient.
- There aren't any inns and save spots will not restore your health. You gotta rely on skills and items to heal.
- There is apparantly a cooking mechanic but good gravy it's obtuse. You need to have the specific ingredients and talk to a specific NPC in order to acquire a recipe. I went through the enitre game without finding a single recipe.
- Locked chests you're not allowed to open until the very end of the game, have fun backtracking everywhere.
- A severe lack of sidequests make the world feel even more empty. I have read that there are some character specific sidequests very close to end game but just like the recipes i never encountered one.
- Objective negatives are no auto-save, no maps and unskippable cutscenes. All of which is inexcuseable in this day and age. Also during one boss fight the game froze on me...Had to to do the entire battle again. Annoying.
If you're looking for alternatives to I Am Setsuna here on Steam, i'd say for memorable characters and a vast story i recommend Trails in the Sky. If you're looking for something original and unique, go with Undertale. And if you're looking for something traditional i would still recommend Tales of Symphonia over I Am Setsuna.

In Shank (1) you could only shank one guy, thus why it was just called "Shank", singular. It was a good fight and I enjoyed shanking that guy, but I always felt as if more could be done with the concept. It seems that I was not alone.
In Shank 2 you can can shank two different people for a total of two shanks. That's *twice* the number of shanks that you got to perform in the first game, which is a significant improvement if you're the number crunching type (and I am). I know that they say that quantity should be subservient to quality (i.e. was Aliens better than Alien just because it added an "s" to the title? I'll leave that for you to decide, but the answer is yes), but for my money I'd rather get to enjoy shanking two different guys over just shanking one*, and I think both the developers and you will agree.
Shank 2 delivers.
*It's possible to replay the game on two higher difficulties, giving you a total of *six* possible shanks. I don't know why you're still reading this and not clicking the buy button so you can start shanking the first guy already.

Despite the inaccuracies, the possibly offensive content, and the skimming through of the Stations, overall it is a well-made RPG with great, inoffensive humor in the face of a very heavy story.

I really can't recommend Starpoint Gemini. This was LGM Games' first project, and I'm afraid it shows. I can see what they were going for, but it just doesn't come together in a satisfying way. Presentation-wise, the game manages to look dated (ship models) and beautiful (nebulas and planet vistas) at the same time. I can live with that. I could't live with the voice acting though, which I'm sure must be done by the dev team, or someone they kidnapped off the street. Fortunately for the sake of your sanity you can turn this off. More worrying though is the UI, which is confused, overly complicated, and a royal pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Even basics such as turning your ship aren't handled well: you can either left click to turn the ship towards the point you clicked, which is useless for anything to the side or behind you, or you can hit the A and D keys which turn the ship in what seem like 30 degree increments per press, with multiple presses resulting in prolonged spinning until the key presses wear off. It's manageable once you get used to it, but it's painful and makes combat a drag. That's a pity because the combat engine is fun at first, it's nicely tactical and lasers sizzle and whump appropriately, but I found it soon became frustrating due mainly to the very high early difficulty; your ship only has a narrow firing arc, everything else it seems can out-turn you, so lining up to take a shot means your front shields are quickly toasted with you being barbequed shortly afterwards.
The other problem is that the living universe is merciless, and high level rogue (pirate) ships crash your nice low-level party with frustrating regularity. I had to replay the first mission about four times because I kept getting jumped by high level pirates that laid waste to everyone including my puny level 1 ship. It's a pity the quicksave button doesn't work, because you have to save a lot... except it doesn't actually let you save during the prolonged and tedious dialogs and during mission events. Eventually you start to get a handle on things, and there were moments such as the first time I flew inside a nebula that the game almost starts to sing, but then it's gone. Side-missions from stations largely involve flying to a point and clicking a couple of icons, or flying to a rogue ship and getting blasted within seconds. After a few hours I realised that I just wasn't having any fun because I'd played this game before in much better forms. However, the silver lining is Starpoint Gemini 2, which is apparently so massively better as to be a completely different game. I'd start there if I were you.

Don't be turned off so quickly by all of the other bad reviews – I would say that some of these people are stuck on "beauty is skin deep."  I can agree with the other reviewers in some aspects; if you have big standards for shiny polish on games, you might want to avoid this one.  The graphics are dated, the controls take some getting used to (I keep having to look at the configuration to figure out what I pressed by accident, even after 15 hours).  There are bugs and CTD's.  You can’t dock with T-gates sometimes or steer.  The camera gets stuck at odd angles on occasion and you have to change sectors to fix it.  The music selection leaves a bit to be desired.  The radio chatter is repeatable.
One guy complained the tutorial was too long!  I found it was just right for the complexity of the game and it got the basics down quite quickly.  You just have to wait patiently for them to read all the text on the screen out (there is no “click to skip”).  As for graphics, the sector backdrops are a bit washed out for my liking, I love the colorful and crisp sector graphics in X3.  The music, though quite good, has a very limited number of tracks and is quite repeatable.
HOWEVER, this game has engaged me happily for over 20 hours now, and I’m only halfway through the campaign with very little extra exploration.  The campaign can be challenging at some times, but I found it was a bit too easy to make money and afford a dreadnaught.  It seems you need to do this in order to make good progress in the campaign.  At one stage in the campaign you lose your ship, however you keep all of your equipment and cash.  No problem, at that time I had enough to buy three new dreadnaughts.  So yes, the campaign is a bit out of balance sometimes.
In the campaign, there is a lot of "fly to this sector, blow up this ship, then fly to that sector."  But it's all wrapped up in a package that keeps it enjoyable, as you search for derelict ships to loot, Rogue containers to crack open and steal goodies from, and fight off pirates that randomly attack you.  You can speed up monotonous travel by getting a T-Drive, but then you miss out a lot of the sightseeing opportunities along the way, and also chances to dock at stations to find better equipment than what you already have.
If you are excited by the prospect of boarding and capturing ships, this game does it nicely!  If you love to customize ship equipment (weapon slots, shield slots, engine slots), you'll enjoy this game.  If you want to play with over 50 different ships, each having different special abilities, you'll enjoy this game.  If you like RPG-style characters, where you can focus on specific weapon types (beam vs. plasma) and improve your skills as you level up, you'll enjoy this game.  You can even hire different officers, each which will add to your perks or boost one or more of your ship stats.  The game gives you the possibility to line up your stats and perks to make an ultra-powerful beam-equipped ship destroys everything easily, until you hit an enemy who has shields and equipment specifically set up to resist beam weapons.  Then you’re screwed.  What fun!!!
The game has many aspects familiar to Freelancer - faction names and how they're handled, station names, station designs, radio chatter, jump gates.  It also shares common control mechanisms with Eve Online, including 2D controls, ship configurations and character skill leveling.  I wouldn't call it a "rip off" of any other game; rather it combines many of the great elements from other games, while setting up a solid new story and universe to enjoy them in.  It's all tied together quite well in an engaging way, and I am continuously reminded of fond times I had playing Freelancer and Eve in years past.

I have had two different experiences with Her Story.
When I first played the game, I began fiddling with the search engine trying to uncover what happened to poor Simon.
I did not get very far, and began to lose interest and decided to play something else.
A few monthes later, I decided to boot up Her Story again. It was nagging at me that I could not understand this game at first, and I wanted to know exactly what you are supposed to do in this damn game. I begin looking through the search engine and watching clips again wondering what was going on, and by chance I had discovered a huge revelation about the game that completely turned Her Story on it's head.
It was surprising to see my innate assumptions about this murder case get blown out of the water, and even then it just continued to slap around my unfounded conclusions as to what was actually going on. The games plot has serpentine twists that remind of me of the early works of M. Night Shyamalan film. I found my self going back to my personal video archive to cross reference new footage, and then finding even more revealing tidbits helping me piece together the entire narrative of the story.
The closest analogy I can compare as to what kind of gameplay experience Her Story contains would be that of taking a 1000 piece puzzle, opening the box, and dumping the pieces on your table. Digging through each piece until you find the ones that connect, and the connecting the chunks of information you have, all the while looking at each piece for every minute detail. You can not rely on merely observing the same patterns over and over. You have to pay attention to whats being said, certain details and clues, the appearance of the subject, the times and dates of the videos, everything. I definately think keeping a pad and paper is a requirement for this game, because once you start digging deep into this game you will need it.
Whenever you engage in something, you have a preconceived notion of how something will work; there is always a structure and a expectation of how to interact with that structure. Her Story tears this expectation down not only in how you experience the content, but how you engage with the structure of Her Story as a video game. The game does not hold your hand and lead you on a linear path to understand how the story gets from point A to point B. Other than a couple of readme.txts placed inside of the game. it does not really tell you what you are doing, or why you are doing it in  the first place. The game does not time you, the game does not grade, the game does not give you a score or tell you what you have accomplished. The game does not give an elicit definition of the challenges and roadblocks that will set before you. Only when you have researched and observed enough significant videos to give you a understanding of what exactly happened during the murder of the man named Simon will the game nudge you into giving you an answer, and once that happens you will know exactly what Her Story is.
One of the criticisms I have seen is "Her Story is not a game! It's just a bunch of FMV clips!". I have noticed people who say this have put only an hour or less into Her Story. As much as I don't like being dismissive of people's personal opinions I have to say it...their opinion does not matter. They have not put in enough time to understand what this game is. It is definately a game. It will challenge you, it will make you think, and most of all, you will have fun. Considering it accomplished all of these parameters for myself, along with a sense of personal satisifaction for getting to my own personal conclusion and closure of the game, I have to say this is a very good game.
Positives-
-Enthralling Story
-Immersive Experience
-Ambiguous Nature of game leads to satisfying investigating
-Wonderful perfomance by Viva Seifert
-Tense and atmospheric
-Engaging and entertaining plot twists
-Incredibly detailed in its clues and hints
Negatives-
-Does not immediately grab attention
-must be focused and pay attention at all times
-Ending may not be satisfactory for some people
-Not for everyone, will have a niche audience
-It's ambiguous nature and lack of solid instruction
may confuse and turn people off
-requires a solid investment in the story which some people
may not have

The longer I play the less I like this game.  Buried beneath some truly punitive design choices lie some of the best battlfield mechanics that have ever been devised, unfortunately this is less of a game and more a guided tour.  While looking at Game-Labs' labor of love is encouraged actually interacting with is not.
Within the first few hours of play it became apparent that my enemy was not the Confederate States of America, or even the supposedly advanced AI, but rather the Clock.  I lost count of the number of times I carefully maneuvered my men into advantageous positions, utilizing the admittedly wonderful route planning features, to set complex assaults in motion; only to meet with failure despite the Rebels fleeing in disarray because the timer ran out.  By the third time you reload to win a battle you had dominated with manuever, tactics and strategy in order to win by weight of numbers alone the game will start to lose it's luster.
Complicating this are some truly glaring mistakes which defy all versimilitude.  Artillery, the King of Battle, for instance becomes useless without time for bombardment to provoke natural evolutions in positioning which can be taken advantage of.  In defensive actions it's maddening to watch as your cannons belch cannister shot directly into the melee without the defenders suffering any collateral damage.  Ditto for the ability to enfilade friendly forces to great effect.
Far from putting positional advantage within reach Cavalry units collapse the moment they enter the range of even the most numerically inferior blocking forces' guns.  Skirmishers, while incredibly useful in early battles suffer from a dearth of supply as the game progresses, ultimately becoming useless since the superior weaponry that they naturally rely on (such as scoped and repeating rifles) never become available in numbers which scale to match the increasing unit sizes.
Perhaps the worst aspect of this experience is that there is no reward for undertaking it.  Completing the Campaign does not unlock anything to incentivize you to play again.
Who This Game Will Appeal To:  Hardcore Civil War Buffs.

+ The gameplay is a ton of fun. It feels very much like borderlands
+ 25 characters to unlock and choose from all with different playstyles, and unique abilities to learn.
+ A unique upgrade tree to enhance your characters weapons / abilities which resets after each mission. Each mission is designed to be played at anytime as they start off easy, and let you gain experience to level before fighting the bosses.
+ An interesting "loadout" system, where you basically equip items that you get from loot (mainly from bosses), which can then be used to give various interesting buffs throughout a mission.
+ The overall artistic direction and graphics of the game are absolutely fantastic!
+ The levels all feel very grand in scale and highly detailed
+ You can build various turrets, drones, and so fourth which can help aid you during difficult sections.
+ Lives.... Unlike borderlands when you go down while playing solo you can actually revive yourself by finding and using lives. This is a huge sigh of relief for solo players out there.
+ Each mission, and all the bosses feel unique and actually fun to play through. Each boss has unique mechanics which you must figure out in order to defeat them, and are often very challenging.
+ The animated 2D cartoon-style cutscenes are an absolute joy to watch
+ There are 9 missions, with each mission being about 40mins long with about 2 major bosses in each. I felt like this was plenty of content
for this game especially considering the added replayability with the amount of characters. About 6 hours to finish the game solo.
+ Comical dialogue with some very good voice actors
- The game seems to be focused towards playing co-op with 2-4 players, so if you choose to play solo it will be very challenging at times and can be frustrating.
- The cutscene during the prologue mission is a bit too long, and the rap music did not match up well with what was going on in the scene. It was pretty cringe-worthy to sit through.
- The story... I'm not sure if it was just me, but I had a very hard time understanding what was going on story-wise. Characters tend to talk in the background and are hard to hear as you are mowing through enemies.

This pretty much recaptures the magic of games like Chrono Trigger, Granda, Breath of Fire III, Suikoden and so many more, just on a smaller scale.
I wish the studio had been given more money to make this game "complete" in a sense.
There is little variety in monsters, environment, NPCs, overworld or anything else for that matter. The item system and battle system feel underdeveloped and unfinished - I mean there are only 2 pieces of gear per character and fights last for about 10 seconds of the most part.
Everything repeats over and over again, yet the story and genuine writing, as well as the terrific atmosphere, keep everything worthwhile. Especially with the astoundingly well written soundtrack - which again fitting to the lack of budget - is only one Piano, all the time. Still it evokes more emotion than all that bloated orchestral score we all grew accustomed to over the years.
Sometimes the story felt like it needed more time to evolve and many this seemed underdeveloped. It's intesteresting how this game, even with so little of it, still manages to blow other major titles out of the water. This game would need an instant remake with a budget 10 times as large by the same staff, so they can give us more of it, every little detail that it deserves and we nostalgia fans crave.
If you like 90s RPGs and are tired of all those soul-less major JPRGs this is a must play.

A charming JRPG with a great soundtrack and an interesting battle system,
is definitely worth your time.
It is a little short compared to many other JRPGs -- coming in at
20 hours -- but for good reason; it is not unnecessarily padded with fetch quests, grinding in preparation for overpowered bosses or slogging through random encounters.  I don't completely hate these things, but
is a refreshing change of pace that demonstrates how unnecessary they can be.
The battle mechanics feel very much like a combination of two of Square Enix's most popular (
and
).  Techniques and Support Abilities slot into your equipment (much like materia), and characters can work together to perform devastating Combo attacks (assuming that they have the right techniques equipped).  Throw in a new "Momentum" mechanic that gives each Technique a bonus effect when timed correctly (e.g. heal the user, apply a status ailment) and you have a plethora of different tactics to choose from.
My only problem with the game is that the Save points can be quite far apart, especially inside some of the later dungeons.  This isn't a difficulty issue, but a scheduling one --
isn't a game that you can drop into for less than an hour.

This is a great game.
Pros:
- Looks Great
- You don't have to win every battle in the campaign (which contributes to realism)
- Your armies are completely customizable-- you get to pick exactly how many men are in each unit, how many divisions you'll have, what kind of units you'll have, and even what they're named. You want an infantry unit with 1719 guys running around with farmer's rifles named Dave's♥♥♥♥♥ You can have that.
- VERY user friendly. If you're new to rts games, this will help you catch on fairly quickly. If you're experienced, you'll enjoy the various nuances of the game.
Cons:
- Calvary are underpowered in general, but especially ranged calvary. They'll take one shot at the enemy, then immediately turn around and retreat.
- Charges were a big part of the civil war, and were known for being very effective. In this game, however, the charging unit will almost always rout before whomever they charged at, even under the best conditions.
Overall, I really liked this game. It's realistic enough to make it challenging without forcing you to micromanage every little thing. It's also really good at surprising you-- just when you think you've outmanuvered your opponent, something will change on the battlefield to make you sweat.

Starpoint Gemini is an RPG tactical simulator focused on the control and strengths of individual vessels. In SPG ship captains and their skills make the greatest difference in large-scale battles. The games is set in a science-fiction universe where various thriving technological directions exist side by side.
After spending almost twenty years trapped in the so-called Stasis rift anomaly, unaware of the passage of time, player reemerges into normal space to find Gemini and indeed everything he knew, had changed beyond recognition.
The Gateway stood as the entry point to the Gemini system, but events that took place two decades ago closed the wormhole and practically sealed the system off of the rest of the universe. The isolation and the appearance of countless anomalies enabled unforeseen technological advancements. Political intrigues, greed and lust for power have shaped the fate of Gemini and it is almost time for reckoning .
Players will freely traverse the rich and filled vastness of the Gemini star system, fight skirmishes with rogue ships, trade commodities, research anomalies, buy new vessels, upgrade their ships with state-of-the-art technology, increase their experience and rank to learn more powerful maneuvers and ultimately use all that in large scale engagements against other fleets of hostile ships. Gemini is a dangerous place with riches waiting to be claimed by the more daring and capable captain.

I think this game would probably cause some really mixed reactions from the gaming community.  Some would probably praise it for the unique way in which the story is told, while others would likely criticize it for its ambiguity.  Personally, while I see both sides, I definitely think that Her Story is something special.  The plotline can get frustrating because not all the details are revealed and you have to fill in the blanks as best you can with your own theories, but that's what I love about it.  I love that I felt like I needed a pen and paper to write out a timeline of events in the order in which I believe they took place, and then talk to someone else and realize that they came to a radically different conclusion.  It's only a few hours long, and finding the last few bits of story in the database can get really frustrating, but overall, I highly recommend it.

bit Dungeon II is a simplified rogue-like game with a few souls-like elements.
It looks good, has a pleasent pixel style. Your progress only shown on a minimap, so a mental map is pretty much needed for navigating through the maze-like world. Creature variation is good enough. They mostly behave the same way, but there a few special units needing different approach.
The gameplay/combat however is so simple, that there is no real way of being good at this game. There are a few actions aside from walking into enemies and auto-attack them, but in a rogue-like where you can die and lose almost everything there is not enough control. Boss fights are poorly developed. You just have to have proper gear and basically run into them until the special attack kicks in and the boss dies.
Enemies level up with you (at least that is what i think anyway) so there is no reason to grind for xp. Items can be collected, these are the things which can make a difference, but drops are extremely random (after i died the first time on level 43 i found a legendary lvl17 staff in the open after a few minutes at level 6, the best weapon since I played the game). There are rooms scathered in the world where you can pick a stat bonus for yourself, when you level up you gain stats automatically. Black coins can be gathered from chests and fallen foes, which can be carried over through "incarnations". I recently found a room with epic chests which can be opened via coins. There are also lesser starter items available in these "shops" available on the cheap.
Overall, bit Dungeon II is an enjoyable title for a few hours, worth a try if you already have it, but it cannot be taken seriously in the end due to its random nature. This is one of those (nowadays pretty frequent) occasions where features were so simplified that in the end it hurts the game itself. I would say the game is too casual, does not build upon skill, still it punishes you for being "bad" at it.
Graphics: 7/10

Replay Value: 6/10

bit Dungeon II is a Link to the Past meets the Souls series(as in Demon's Souls and Dark Souls, not as in Soul Blazer) with the original Grandia leveling system.
If those are games that you love then definitely check out bit Dungeon II.
There is definitely some buginess to the game(bosses and invaders tend to lag when starting their dialog. Sometimes the controls will lock up when the randomized loot is generating), but overall the bugs do not ruin the experience.
Gear is also nearly 100% random, with the only exceptions being certain basic gear vendors, so planning to level up your character a certain way from the beginning may ultimately cause more harm than good depending on the RNG.
For your first few attempts, try to be fluid in your character build, trying out all of the different weapon types and deciding on your preferred playstyle, then attempt a true build once you understand how the character building works.
::FROM THIS POINT ON I WILL BE WRITING A SHORT PRIMER ON CHARCTER BUILDING. FEEL FREE TO STOP READING IF YOU PREFER TO FIGURE THESE THINGS OUT ON YOUR OWN::
The character building is surprisingly deep, despite the simplicity of this game.
Like in the original Grandia, each weapon type is linked to two or more stats(daggers are dexterity weapons, great axes are strength weapons, staves are intelligence weapons, etc), so if you level up while using a weapon with a particular stat focus, then your character will gain additional points to that stat(all weapon types increase constitution as well).
The Souls games influence much of bit Dungeon 2, but in terms of character building, the Souls series influence is apparent in the weapon damage scaling.
Weapon damage is improved based on the stats that are attributed to it(these appear on the bottom of each weapon's stat description, annotated with an asterisk*), so a weak dexterity weapon like a dagger will generally be far more effective on a character with high dexterity than a much stronger weapon that does not use dexterity to scale its damage.
Of course, you can find an off build weapon that is powerful enough to outclass build centric weapons, but these should be avoided during early leveling if you have already increased a particular stat upwards of 50 points, since focussing on a new stat after that much investment may impede your character's growth, and keep them from getting strong enough to stay competitive as enemies get stronger.
Final note: Every enemy in the game scales with your character's level, and you can level your character well beyond level 100.

Disclaimer: We write long reviews. Due to steam's word limit, we can't upload our full review here. Don't complain to us, complain to Steam. As such, a link to the full review has been linked at the end. This is a majority of our review, with all the unnecessary bits cut
[Purchased Copy]
The game tries to play similarly to Zelda in many aspects, but there’s quite a few things that makes it differ, namely the times it doesn’t try to be Zelda, and instead tries to be Dark Souls. For one difference, you kill enemies automatically. While you can press the space bar or the A button on your controller to swing your sword or shoot arrows, the game will automatically attack the closest enemy with whatever weapon you have. You can also defend by holding down the attack button. The combat is simple, and in almost every aspect, too simple. We really wish there was something more to the combat, but there’s not. For example, sure you can use a bow, but why would you when it’s almost never as strong as the weapon you’re holding? And, unlike the melee weapons, the bow uses energy. Once you run out of energy, you have to wait until it replenishes. This both unnecessarily slows down gameplay, and slows down combat in general. Then the problem with the melee weapons, is that you almost never have to do anything strategic. The only boss we actually had to think about for any time at all was the end boss because his hits took out half of the player’s health. Other than that, by 45 minutes in, there wasn’t a thing in the game that could kill us, and that’s not a good thing. Especially not when the game is barely three hours long. The enemy variety is vast, and many of the designs are actually pretty interesting to look at.
Eventually, enemies will randomly drop one of two things; coins, or items. These ‘coins’ can be spent at certain caves randomly around the map in exchange for chests with nice armor or weapons, while finding items could be armor, jewelry, or weapons. There are a few special effects these items can have, but the vampire powers that allow you to steal health we found the only really nice bonus effect. Eventually when you level up, stats are automatically added to you. This is good in some aspects, but it largely defeats the purpose of leveling up if it’s done automatically, and it would have been better to just restrict usage of certain weapons and armor until you’re a high enough level. Eventually you’ll uncover areas on the map where you have to go into what could adequately be described as fortresses, kill some enemies, and then kill a boss. These areas are good to break up the monotony, but they themselves don’t really differ from one another. To put more bluntly, one fortress has no real difference from another except for a few minor details, and the enemies within. They can be changed up, but the theme of them never really changes, and thus aren’t differing enough to be memorable. The landscapes you traverse in while having different biomes, are both easy to get confused, and are easy to get lost in. It doesn’t help that the map in the corner is really too far zoomed in to really be of any help either. Once the player kills enough bosses, you’ll enter another world, kill a bunch of ghosts, kill the final two bosses, and that’s pretty much it. The story is lackluster, and is trying really hard to do something that’s simply over its head: making the player care. The biggest problem is progression. In the game because the leveling up process is automatic and borderline pointless, there’s few points of progression. The only two main ones are when you spawn, and when you enter the other world.
There’s also the problem of leveling and more standard ‘RPG elements’ that the game includes. When we mention that the leveling up process is borderline pointless, we should add that the majority of things you can improve are pointless. Basic things like damage, stamina, health, armor, etc are fine. However, what’s ‘Berserk’ ‘Spirit’ or ‘Constitution’? The only way you as the player can change things is through finding randomized armor and weapons that arbitrarily upgrade your skills and thus, you have no use in half of the skills. We still don’t know what the skill ‘Intelligence’ does, and the game isn’t keen to explaining any of these things. As a matter of fact, the entire menu has barely any options at all, and no explanation for what these things do in-game.
We certainly didn’t see any difference in playing between having ’14 spirit’ and ’22 spirit’. We thought that we were just doing something wrong, but we couldn’t find a single difference in having half of the skills differently. Even with armor at zero, the vampire armor and weapons that stole health from enemies negated all the effects. Maybe they have to do with using the ranged weapon, but we couldn’t figure it out.
To start off, the visuals are great. We’re a sucker for pixel art and nice visuals, and this certainly at least fits the pixel art category. However, that’s not to say the visuals are amazing. They’re okay and get the job done, but it’s not really the levels or visuals themselves that are nice, but it all together as a package. The enemies and character designs specifically are really great and fun to just look at, and would fit right in a game like Dark Souls. The armor and weapon designs are great as well.
The audio is well done too. It’s not amazing by any means and it certainly doesn’t break any land records for in-game soundtracks, but it gets the job done. As we’ve said with most of the games we’ve reviewed recently, more tracks would be useful, but the ones present do at least present the player with a well-manufactured ambiance.
The controls were…okay. Both controller and keyboard we had no specific problem with, but really a problem with the control layout in general, like the fact that you have to hold the same button you attack with on controller to block. It’s both frustrating and unnecessary. For example on the controller besides the analog sticks, the player will only use a grand total of three buttons. It’s nothing players can’t get used to, but it’s not nearly as fun or as difficult as it could be. The settings you can/can’t change are also random at best. You have no rebindable keys which for a PC release isn’t excusable, you can turn music on or off, you have shadows, and you can delete your save. That’s pretty much it. Oh, and there’s no way to actually exit the game, at all.
Despite all these gripes, we still enjoyed the game. While the game has many shortcomings, few would be those that we’d consider to be really things to completely turn a gamer away, but certainly things for a gamer to consider. The game is still both fun and enjoyable for what it’s worth, and we enjoyed our time with the game. Sure, it did cost us $3.99, but that $3.99 earned us three hours of game. Was it worth replaying? Not particularly, but it was fun for what it’s worth, and the price tag helped. It’s by no means a great game, simply a game with many minor flaws that could be fixed. That being said, we’d still suggest the game to a fair degree. It does have flaws, and make no mistake that those flaws all together could easily turn players the other way around, but individually, those flaws could be seen as minor gripes in a simple, decent little Zelda meets Dark Souls lookalike with some oddly placed roguelike elements.
PROS
- Nice visuals and character design
- Short, but just long enough to get some fun out of
- Audio is simple, but fitting and provides good ambiance
CONS
- Level progression is pointless
- you're pretty much a god less than half-way through the game
- settings are pathetically lackluster
- Are you serious? There's no quit button?

I Am Setsuna is a decent JRPG, but the developers' boner for Chrono Trigger shines through a little too much at times. The combat and skill system is nice and fun and carries the game more than the lightweight story. The plot is very simple: You go to a town, solve their problem and move on, while gradually unveiling the mystery driving the quest.
The problem is that the story utilises too many RPG tropes without understanding what makes them effective. At several (several,
...) points in the story I had to pause and take a deep breath because of the characters' stupidity. You'll see what I mean right from the start, when the main character joins the party. The plot should have been drawn out a little more to make it cohesive; as it stands, the character development happens at the pace of a six-year-old changing their mind about what kind of ice cream they want, and with as much logic behind it. To compare it to CT (because the game itself does so in the description), Lavos is a tremendously effective villain despite having no personality, because throughout the game you see his effects on the history of the world. Here, the main villain had zero effect on me because of poor storytelling.
Aside from the plot, it has many good things about it, though everything comes with a caveat: the art style is cute but not particularly memorable, the soundtrack is great but gets a bit repetitive at times, and the combat is fun but quite easy. Still, I did enjoy it and would give it a lukewarm recommendation, although absolutely not at full price.

Wait that's not right...
I am Endir.
Yes, despite the title of the game, you aren't in fact Setsuna, but rather her bodyguard and former assassin, Endir. "I am Setsuna" is another one of those nostalgia gimmicks designed to bring oldschool JRPG fans back in time for a classic experience. The problem with this is a little something I like to call modern standards. It just doesn't work, and is probably one of the most boring and cringeworthy games (if you can even call it a game) that I've played in quite a while. Bare bones writing and lazy anime tropes combine to form one of the most frustratingly bland concoctions in my history of gaming.
It's exactly what you'd expect from a JRPG - real time, turn based combat. Great, I love me some turn based strategy! But gods, not like this. The standard enemies are incredibly easy. Each round of combat lasts for no longer than thirty seconds, bust out your strongest move, kick a couple asses, and you're done. There's no challenge, it isn't fun. The standard foes drop items that serve no other purpose than as a source of income for your party that you then spend on a new set of weapons to match the level of the next area, maybe even a few potions and ethers too, which are immediately consumed during boss fights. Maybe the basic baddies were one hitter quitters, but here's where the game starts to struggle with balance. The bosses are impossible. I found myself spamming potions and phoenix downs quicker than I could damage, resulting in an endless loop of hurt until my resources were exhausted and the boss emerged victorious.
Ugh, don't even get me started on the story. Shadow of Mordor did this and was one of the many reasons it turned out to be a hot mess. Darkness falls across the land and it's up to a lone hero to sacrifice themselves for the greater good of humanity. This nonsense is the definition of cliche and is clearly the result of lazy writing, awful time crunching, and a minimal budget. It's the typical JRPG get-out-of-jail-free card. This method also proved to be detrimental to character development. There's such a wide cast of beautifully designed characters whom were bogged down by unimaginative, stereotypical personalities. The hot-headed brute, the silent assassin, the compassionate healer, the insecure mage, the valiant knight, the list goes on. Their conversations are like those a pair of grade schoolers would have; slow exchanges consisting of obvious statement-making and dumb question-asking. Even the side characters in every copy-pasted village were copy-pasted models with copy-pasted personalities. If anything, this game is just a P.T. clone.
If there's two things I really like about Setsuna, it's the art and music. Despite the horrible writing and gameplay, it's fairly generous in terms of visuals and sound. Setsuna's soundtrack consists exclusively of minimalistic piano solos. Additionally, the game itself looks like a painting. It's one of those snowy log cabin scenes you'd see hanging on your grandmother's living room wall. As much as I could complain about the music and setting being obnoxiously consistent throughout the entirety of the game, I just can't, because it never got tiring. Though this could be an issue for some folks. There's something about a steady snowfall paired with a gentle piano rhythm that managed to keep me calm on this torturous adventure.

EDIT: So it was brought to my attention by several people that you actually can save at any point on the world map, not just at save points. My other objections to the game still stand, however, as does the ultimate "not recommended."
"I am Setsuna" otherwise known as "Where the ♥♥♥♥ is the next save point, you dirty sons of ♥♥♥♥♥es, I wanted to stop playing an hour ago."
Don't get me wrong, the game looks charming and like a visually modernized classic JRPG. Mind bogglingly it's only the visuals that have gotten modernized. The design and mechanics are straight out of the sewage pit of bad game design of 25 years ago, tolerated today because of the patina of manchildren's nostalgia laying over them like a crust of dried excrement. Blunders such as the inexplicable lack of regular save points being particularly outrageous.
A note on whether this game is turn-based. It is absolutely NOT. There isn't even an option to toggle between its hectic buttonmash arcade garbage combat system designed by aliens and proper turn based RPG combat. No, you'll regularly have your characters die because you took a split second too long targeting a heal on them, or wasting your expensive rez potions because the boss will decide to do his big aoe a second after you use one on one of your characters.
The other unfortunate blunder that this real time arcade buttonmash combat system sets itself up for is not allowing you to bring your full party of 5. It's already hectic enough just managing cooldowns on 3 characters and frantically buttonmashing their abilities so they don't get killed a split second before they can fire them off. No, you can only ever bring 3 characters even though there are 5 of perfectly balanced roles in your goddamned party. I guess they do all pop out for group dialogue scenes, which I guess is something.
Another irritating thing is the total thematic disconnect between the game mechanics and what's being presented on the screen. At one point I had a horde of savage beasts attacking a village. And they were led by... a giant clockwork golem using time magic. What the *♥♥♥♥*? No, this was never remarked upon by any of the characters, it was just there because it was "a monster." Have you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s never heard of the concept of monster ecology? Evidently not. There's also fat, cute, floppy seals as monsters. And their abilities are... poison based? What the ♥♥♥♥ once again. And when dying they self destruct and do area damage around them for no reason. Just like real seals. There's also an enemy called a "roly poly." If you're at all familiar with the English language, you might assume that's a a giant beetle. Haha, no. It's a tiny squirrel ROLLing a giant snowball. :rfacepalm:
So yes, charming visuals, decent story, decent if sometimes irritating music, but that's about all that's positive about Setsuna. On the other side you have the deeply frustrating WTF alien combat system, full-retard pacing/placement of save points through the world, and generally the suffocating funk of a slavish attachment to terrible, outdated game design, and I found at best a very mixed experience leaning rather more heavily to the negative than the positive.
What they could've done differently? Not stop at the visuals when modernizing the game. Proper turn based combat allowing you to use your WHOLE PARTY, not this real time twitch buttonmash arcade nonsense that people on the forums insist is actually turn based. Another thing that just *might* have helped is actually playing through the goddamned game before they shipped it. Jesus Christ, at one point I had to keep going for about an hour past where I wanted to take a break because it was TWO HOURS between save points. Two anxiety filled hours of me crossing my fingers that the game wouldn't CTD or I wouldn't wipe to some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and have all my time wasted.
Another fun example of the lack of save points is the very beginning of the game. The VERY BEGINNING of the game. You have one save point before one of the advanced combat tutorials where you fight  a polar bear monster. Okay. And then you fight TWO MORE BOSSES without a single goddamned save point. If you wipe to either of them, it's back to the tutorial with you. And sitting through the opening credits. Are you ♥♥♥♥ing kidding me? And yes, that did happen to me. If the game hadn't been a gift, I would've refunded without a single moment of hesitation at being forced to replay half an hour of dialogue and trash fighting because the drunken monkeys they had designing the game couldn't be bothered to put a goddamned save point in the town the first boss fight takes place in.
Near total disaster of a game. If, like me, you're a player of western RPGs and wanted to use Setsuna as an introduction to JRPGs, yeah, you're not gonna have a good time.

Guacamelee! is a humorous 2D platformer with a Mexican Día de los Muertos esthetic. Consisting of side-scrolling combat, jumping puzzles and boss fights, the gameplay strikes a balance, being challenging yet fair.
Progressing through the game unlocks new abilities and areas. There are also new enemies and puzzles that provide opportunities to use these newly acquired skills, so the game becomes more complex and harder. Compensating for the difficulty, the game allows you to respawn from numerous checkpoints or whatever ledge you fell from. This prevents frequent deaths from breaking the game’s flow, and allows the player to learn from failure and quickly adapt to overcome a hard part.
I hate excessive dialogue in games, but fortunately Guacamelee! has just the right amount. It has enough to move the story along and even work in some comedy, but it doesn’t overstay it’s welcome. This is necessary in a game where parts must be repeated until gotten right. Having to scroll through the same dialogue over and over again just to get to the point you failed at before is an annoyance from an obsolete era of gaming.
Guacamelee! is not without its flaws. It can be a bit repetitive at times and get slightly boring, but it’s not enough to hinder the gameplay significantly, and the soundtrack and colorful animation inspired by traditional Mexican folklore give it a unique style that almost had me buying this game on looks alone.

Consider this rating rather neutral than negative. I was disappointed, but I wouldn't say the game is a complete failure. There're just too many better games around and I didn't feel it lived up to my expectations.
I love hardcore roguelike games and dungeon crawlers. Sadly, this game is neither one of those things, or at least fails at being them. It's the easiest, simplest, one button mashing, casual grindfest I've played in some time. Even games like Clicker Heroes have more challenging and rewarding gameplay. I finished the game within the first 60 minutes and didn't have to use anything but WASD and hold BLOCK (the game actually auto-attacks enemies, so if you position yourself face-to-face with an enemy and hold block, you're invincible - even against bosses!) and without losing even half my health. The only time I died was when I wanted to unlock the last remaining achievement, which was for dying for the first time. To my surprise, when I tried to kill myself, I actually got revived a few rooms back with all my stuff and progression! Not very rougelike, is it?
I simply can't figure out how to fail or even have a slightly hard time at this game, which is making it very unenjoyable and pointless to me. The only challenging part of the game was navigating through the map, which is very chaotic, unintuitive and sometimes seems random (meaning it's NOT randomly generated, like you'd expect, but sometimes you leave a room through the top door and enter the next room through another top door, instead of the bottom one, as would logic dictate). You can't even leave breadcrumbs on your way, because every time you clear a room and leave, all the enemies and objects in it immediately respawn.
I might have given up on it too soon, but what other choice did I have after finishing the game twice and getting all achievements in 3 hours? Or maybe I'm just too spoiled by games that are actually thought-through and challenging. Either way, this game seemed very cheap, buggy, extremely easy and with very little replay value.
But since I got it for about half a dollar, I can't really complain that much. At least I got some trading cards and 100% achievements out of it!

Whilst it is short for a JRPG - 16hrs to complete including a couple where I just sat and grinded levels - I am Setsuna is a beautifully crafted, winter-themed adventure that is enjoyable but sadly lacking an indepth character development and combat system compared to other JRPGs.
- 3/5 - short, linear, good but didn't make me feel engaged throughout.
- 3/5 - Much of the same throughout. It was suitable for the game but didn't really blow me away.
- 3/5 - With the exception of a handful of skills that can be used by all heroes your characters are locked in the abilities they can gain. This character development was further let down by a lacklustre weapon/accessories system. It then got to the point where I was only using 3 of the possibly 7 characters as their combo was the best at mob clearing. Rinse and repeat until I got to a boss. The combat system was the biggest let down for me as I would have liked heroes that could learn a variety of skills (consider Red Mages from early FF games) but what I was given were characters that were limited in what abilities they could have which resulted in this selection of a few heroes to use for most of the game.
3/5 - I thought I would add this here because the game does a decent job of introducing and developing characters individual stories (with the exception of the 'player' character who has some shady background that is never fully explained). Models were nice although I can't get past the legs having no knees or feet. Your characters walk on what can only be compared to stilts. Enemy models are pretty limited and at times are just different coloured variations of one another depending on the area you are in. There are some unique enemies thrown in here and there but not a lot. You'll fight penguins at the beginning, and you'll fight them near the end. Some are black whilst some are brown and their abilities vary as much as their colour scheme.
I am Setsuna is a fun JRPG that whilst lacking in areas does enough to be enjoyable overall. Whilst I recommend I am Setsuna for fans of JRPGs you may possibly consider waiting for a decent sale if you are not entirely sold or sure about what you are getting yourself in to.

The facts:
If you're expecting fun right out of the box, you're going to be disappointed. Your first couple of hours of this gaming experience are spent not playing the game, but watching videos. You'll waste a lot of time pausing, rewinding and trying to figure things out because tutorial doesn't match the game you bought. You're better off looking for YouTube let's play videos than anything the game will direct you to. This game is going to require a hefty commitment of time from the user to learn the basics. I'm sure this is one of those games where you get what you put into this game. If you have the time and you're up to the commitment required to dig for the answers then this is probably going to eventually be a lot of fun.
In Conclusion:
Massive learning curve. No hand holding. If your idea of fun is spending hours rumaging through nested menus then this is your game. You'll start off with a "tutorial" and by tutorial I mean a bunch of YouTube videos. The first video will scurry off immediately placing a ride, adding the exit / entrance paths. Which sounds great! Unfortunately, these videos don't match the actually game.
New users will start off on a map without the premade paths shown in this first YouTube tutorial; which means, you have to figure it out on your own. Pause the video, the bottom right conrner has the menu item you require to add the paths that the developer's YouTube tutorial will start with. Paths have a habit of defaulting into an elevating ramp. You'll have to fight with the UI to get it to match. As a fan of the film Memento and the game Gone Home, I have a certain bias towards exploration of perception, memory, and non-linear discovery. If you disliked those titles, then chances are you won't appreciate Her Story and you can feel free to disregard the rest of this review.
The "gameplay" consists mainly of using an artificially constrained search system to find video clips from a series of police interviews with a woman (played by British athlete and musician Viva Seifert). The implicit goal is to uncover the story / most of the clips, or at least the important ones.
My initial impression upon realizing that there is no apparent gameplay other than searching for clips by keyword was... "doh, is that it?" However, the story and the excellent acting by Viva Seifert quickly drew me in and compelled me to find out the rest.
Clips are indexed by transcript words, so you can search either by words or names you hear in clips already seen, or by whatever relevant words (or phrases) you can think of. As such, the video clip archive is a sort of graph connected by the keywords and you can follow the graph edges or blindly attempt to jump to other parts of the graph.
Thus what we have here is an interactive, non-linear experience of uncovering a complex, intriguing story (sufficiently qualifying a "game" by my definition). The non-linear aspect refers to the order in which every player might view the clips - this can of course impact the nature and quality of the experience. However, in my opinion, even if the clips were viewed simply in chronological order, the story is still intriguing enough to stand on its own.
The writing is brilliant, and far more intricate than it might appear at first. Even now, after considerable reflection, and even after having posted this review (yes, this paragraph I edited it in shortly afterward), I am still poring over analyses.
The story alone is a worthwhile watch. But the FMV archive presentation is a brilliant interactive storytelling experiment and the combination elevates Her Story to, in my opinion, possibly one of the most noteworthy games in history, doing something that has not been done before quite like this, or, in my opinion, quite so effectively. Her Story deserves the long list of accolades it's received.
Some clips are very hard to discover via keyword search, and this acts as a sort of challenge element to the game. If you're actually going for this, (or, in general) chances are you'll need to take quite a few notes. However, there are ways to make this easier or bypass it completely, for those less inclined to take on the challenge:
To make it easier:


Although, I would only recommend doing this first making an effort to play the game as intended, there is a way to view all clips in chronological order:
Or you can just look up a chronological compilation on youtube if you don't care about the completionist achievements. (but, again, I recommend actually playing the game first)
Why is Her Story's presentation formula so effective?
Consider a typical, linear story presentation. A good story will captivate you and have you guessing at least sometimes (especially mystery type stories). But presenting the material the way Her Story does, out of order and interactively further accentuates that feeling of engagement, stimulating you at every point to analyze the material, judge, make connections, extrapolate, make guesses.
As mundane as an FMV clip show may sound, this kind of presentation can be remarkably effective at engaging the mind of the audience. It is intrisically a more active and mentally demanding experience. But aside from that formula itself, the material, the script, the story, the acting is cleverly tailored in its complexity and ambiguity to maximize audience engagement, yielding what is likely to be an unforgettable experience.

True confession: I am, and have been my entire life, fascinated by history and particularly by the American Civil War. So, therefore this game stands almost zero chance of getting anything but a great review from me. Now, all that said, when I actually began playing this game, I found it to be as exceptional as I had hoped it would be. This is a kind of grand strategy game (ish) with your management of your Army and skill points outside the battlefield. Decisions have to be made, resources (which can be sort of sparse (particularly Army/unit leadership resources) have to be managed well, etc. And then within that grand strategy is the actual RTS battles themselves. This is where the game really shines (although truth be told, I'm a dork for the management side of my Army -- research to name every brigade after a historical unit, etc). The game, inside the battle itself is unforgiving. Make a mistake and the AI WILL take advantage of it. The higher the difficulty level you play at, the more formidable and punishing your mistakes will be magnified. This game will teach you real fast, the value of maintaining cover at all possible costs, covering your flanks effectively, establishing a good solid battle line, proper deployment of your experienced troops vs your green troops, along with many other things.
All in all, if you are a American Civil War buff -- get this! If you just like a good challenging game -- get this and set it to the highest difficulty. You will not be disappointed. This is a solid A++ game in my book.

This game has been one of the most enjoyable strategy games that I have played in a long while. While I still remember spending countless hours playing Sierra's Caesar 3 way back in the day, as well as the orginal Rome:Total War, I was encouraged to find that there are still some great quality strategy war games being made.
While I had never played the first version of Ultimate General, I had stumbled upon this game many months ago during the Beta release. Coordinating your armies can be a daunting task unless you have a good idea of how you want to engage your troops. This game allows you to detach skirmishers from your regiments and re-attach them at your convenience. Soldiers may become fatigued, lose morale, or run out of ammo during battle, but if you are well organized you may position re-inforcements to take their place. One way you can replace tired troops is by selecting the "Fallback" feature which many strategy games lack. Your troops can disengage properly without receiving a devastating volley from the enemy and they cover their retreat in an organized fashion.
I feel that there are many positives to this game, too many to list.
The only negative, at this time, I can think of would be this; Prior to any battle, the game shows you where your troops and the enemy will be deployed, where re-inforcements will come from, and what locations must be captured or defended. It is very important to remember this information, however, when you are in a large battle and you sometimes don't finish the battle in one sitting, It would be beneficial to be able to have the option to review that information the next time you load your campaign. (Sort of how Age of Empires 3 did)
I highly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of AOE, Total War, and the early Sierra games like Pharoah, Zeus, or Caesar. It has nothing to do with city building, but plenty to do with warfare and maintenence.

Now that I'm really thinking about it, I think this might actually be the first dedicated American Civil War game I've ever played. I've certainly played alot of mods, custom scenarios, and other stuff along those lines, but not a game specifically focused on it...
UG:CW is, obviously, focused on that conflict. You get to either fight individual battles or partake in a quite lengthy campaign as you build/maintain your army and fight numerous battles over the course of the war. To me, this game kinda feels like a Total War game, but lacking the high end graphics, animations, and other technical aspects. Other differences being that there is no terrible diplomacy system, the battles you fight are already set and have specific conditions/goals, and your only real concern is winning battles. I actually like this approach because while the "sandbox history" of games like the Total War series or Paradox Games' (Europa Universalis, Crusader Kings, etc) can be very fun, sometimes... a game that trades that freedom for attention to detail is pretty cool too.
In that regard, my history nerd-side got quite a bit out of this game and gave me some insider knowledge that certainly helped while playing the game. I have this massive "atlas book" focused on the ACW and the maps in there match what I saw in this game, as did the generals involved and the overall course of battles. It is heavily scripted, but there is room for differences should you manage to succeed where history failed. That can be very rewarding, with it often meaning you can win battles before enemies are heavily reinforced. Other knowledge, such as how the minie ball (aka, rifle bullets) was the major killer of the war (after disease) or how artillery was very strong at close ranges but hadn't quite become super-lethal at longer ranges just yet, ended up being invaluable. Lastly, that the battles of the war gradually changed from resembling the Napoleonic era towards resembling WW1, and how that changes how you have to approach the game. In other words, this game is a treat for history nerds like me.
..Which may very well have made the difference between winning and losing, actually. This game can be pretty tough, and I was playing as the USA (the CSA would be harder, and by all accounts is). You often find yourself fighting battles with small forces awaiting reinforcement, forcing you to make do with what you have. These moments generally were the toughest parts of the game, since it often means you are outnumbered or racing against time to take an objective. The steamroller approach can work in bigger battles when you have all your forces, but much of the rest of the time you need skill to win. People complain about this, but I'm ok with it. After all, battles don't always happen when you want them to.
Less good is the "prestige" system in the campaign. Basically, you earn prestige from winning battles, can spend it in order to get more money, weapons, etc, lose some from draws, and lose alot from losing battles. It is this last point that is the real issue, because those prestige losses can be huge, and if you lose more than you have it is game over. So you can't really afford to lose battles. I didn't have this problem since I was playing as the Union and my approach to strategy games is to stack the deck in my favor before ever reaching the battlefield. But I am worried about it when I try to play as the CSA instead, since the real ACW (and the game) was very much a case of the USA tapping into their huge resources while the CSA had to fight with what it could scrape together.
One more point to raise about the campaign is that battles and the overall campaign is influenced by your performance. Specifically, enemy armies continually increase in strength as the war continues, but you can mess this up if you keep inflicting huge costly defeats upon them. I though that this was a pretty cool way to let the player "alter" history to a degree, but it ended up being a little disappointing too. Because if you repeatedly crush the enemy, or inflict massive losses in the early stages of a battle they will have much less later on.
This was highlighted for me strongest in the Battle of Gettysburg. The first day was an intense defensive battle that had me have to fight hard to not get overrun by the CSA. But because I inflicted such heavy casualties first during Day 1 and then during the Day 2 assault on Little Round Top, the CSA attack on Culp's hill didn't really happen and the infamous Pickett's Charge on Day 3 was so feeble I ended up charging them instead. The game continued to be challenging and interesting throughout, but repeated early success probably ended up ensuring that later battles like Gettysburg and Cold Harbor ended up being much easier than they ought to have been because the enemy had little to fight with. With that said, the later battles like Cold Harbor when it became a proto-WW1 ended up being the most costly battles I fought.
Anyway, that's enough for this review I think. As usual, I'm only stopping now because if I don't I could keep going on and on. I don't want to write that much and chances are you don't want to read it. XD
Is this game fun? Reasonably. Does it immerse you into the ACW while balancing historical accuracy with freedom to change results? Absolutely. Would I recommend it to others? So if you are a history nerd who has even a passing interest in the American Civil War, consider checking this out. Most regrettable purchase I've ever made. I've never seen so many bad decisions in a video game before.
Here's my experience with it:
I played two betas of it before and played the same PVE mission twice. The shooting mechanics are fun enough, but as for the rest of it...
I launch the game for the first time after buying it with 30 minutes before work, first thing you have to do in the game is play through the prologue. There's no character selection, you're forced to play as the worst designed character I've ever seen and I literally never had a problem with character design of anything, I never care about that, but this time I'm just thrown into the game with a character that I can't stand, in a game that boasts having 25 cool different characters that give you all kinds of gameplay variety.
The game starts off with an intro animation, weird crappy art/3D mix instead of just animating the models at a good framerate and making it look smooth and nice. Fine whatever, but it's an unskippable intro video that lasts almost 10 minutes, a video that shows absolutely nothing interesting, showcasing 5 random characters without almost any backstory, most of it is action that is crappily animated at low framerate trying to make characters look as badass as possible even though I'm sitting there bored out of my mind and feeling like my time is wasted. So with those 10 minutes wasted I start the mission, play for like 10 minutes and I feel that I don't have time to continue since I have to leave, so I exit the game.
I come back home with 2 hours to spare before having to go to bed, I have to pick between this game and another new game I got, so I decide to go with this game, since it's light and somewhat casual enough to play and what am I greeted with? Same freaking prologue that I can't skip, same intro video that still can't be skipped, it was faster to google how to get rid of the intro, exit the game, delete it and restart the game than to watch it again. Fine, I play through the mission, sure enough at the end I'm greeted with another unskippable animation, shorter this time, but still annoying and pointless with some stupid attempt at character building in a game with 25 characters. At this point I decide to do the next mission alone since I feel more comfortable playing that way.
Upon starting the single player mission I'm greeted with a queue informing me that I'm waiting for a server, this is frustrating since I'm just playing alone and I don't need any server, but it's okay, I get it, Borderlands was a cheater paradise and this game wants to avoid that, it's a necessary evil to some extent. So the game starts and it's the same mission that I played twice in the beta. Now that's fine and all, I expected that and I just felt like I'll just have to go through it to unlock new content, about one hour in I reach almost the end of the map as I'm greeted with a disconnection icon in my single player game. I realize that my internet connection decided to crap out and restart, but the game didn't care, I got kicked out of my single player server, no progress saved, I will now have to beat that mission all over again if I want to advance. At this point I no longer have time to play again, I don't have time to do anything, I have to go to bed soon, but the game wasted all of my free time that I could've spent playing the other game I had.
To make it worse, there are a ton of terrible decisions in this game, it's PVP oriented for whatever reason with a dead playerbase already, you have to grind and keep playing over and over to rank up and unlock stuff, you have microtransactions in a 60$ game, you have gear that has the worst utility I've seen in any game yet and I can't even refund this because I bought it outside of Steam. Thanks Gearbox, Borderlands was fun, but this game is just a mix of terrible decisions, terrible designs that try to be original for the sake of being original and end up being unappealing, game mechanics that try to be original and end up being uninteresting, unskippable cutscenes all over the place(especially those pointless character and boss introductions) and the freaking online only restrictions that don't have any safeguard against disconnections or any kinds of issues.
