If you learn one thing from this review: DON'T PUSH THE "DELETE SESSION DATA" BUTTON"!!
It will not just clear out the session videos, IT WILL RESET THE ENTIRE GAME, and you'll have to start all over.
Now that that's out of the way.
"Her Story" is a very original game where you must enter keywords to search through a database of video clips to investigate the story behind a murder.  The clips are of a woman named Hannah who was called in seven times for questioning.
As you already know, the UI of the game is clunky, and that's part of the challenge.  You play the game with a simple search engine on a simulated Windows 95 PC.  The object of the game is to find and view the ~270 video clips in the database.  To do so you use the search engine to find video clips by entering keywords that match Hannah's answers.  You can only see the first five hits, but when you find a clip that you haven't seen before, it's marked with an icon.  There's also a search history and a utilities menu with the above mentioned dreaded button.
New hits are easy to find at first, but later in the game you must dig through your notes and try clever word pairings to get new ones.  After that, you'll be guessing words, so towards the end of the game it becomes a bit of a grind.
You can't hear the detective's questions, which is frustrating.  It'd make more sense if I could attempt to predict the questions, rather than try to predict what Hannah will say to an unknown question.  So your best strategy is simply to make note of important words Hannah says in each video and use them to search for more.
The interviews are well performed and the story takes some surprising turns.  I found myself yelling at the screen in surprise and hastily pounding in search queries.  I formed my own theories about why Hannah did what she did, but unfortunately there's no way to confirm them.  When you've watched all the videos, you're done.  They could have made some videos findable only if you enter search terms that show you know what's going on, but the writers did not do this.
While "Her Story" is original and entertaining, it's a foreshadow of the kind of detective game that we'll hopefully have some day once we've developed the AI to parse and respond to natural language queries.  Then, we can play the detective for real.

Star Wars Knights of The Old Republic... Ohhhh boyyy is there alot to say about this game.
One of RPG juggernaut BioWare's first titles, this game is a classic Star Wars experience.  I'll separate the attributes of the game so this review is waaaayy easier to read but first a little general info.  KOTOR (Knights of The Old Republic) is an action RPG set in the Star Wars universe about 2000 years before the events of A New Hope.  Despite being 2000 years ago, the game still has blasters, lightsabers, starships etc. the date is very hard to notice.  You start off creating your own character and choosing between (I think) 3 classes, Soldier, Scout and Scoundrel.  You can be male or female, white or black or what have you, then you get to choose Skills and Feats.  Skills are pretty self explanatory but Feats are kinda like a mix of perks and abilities from other games.  For example, an ability Feat would be Sniper Shot, which is an accurate attack for blasters while its melee counterpart is Critical Strike, the Feat's effect is that it deals more damage and has a chance of stunning enemies.  A perklike Feat would be Gearhead, which passively increases your Repair and Security Skills.  After all the Character select stuff is done the game starts proper, now I'll go onto the Categorized stuff below...
1.  The Story:  The Game's story and characters are excellent and it is the game's strongest aspect in my humblest of opinions.  Most of the characters are likeable but it would really depend on what kind of player you are, some you will like more than others.  All the characters will react to the decisions you make, also the things you say to them and will like/dislike you accordingly.  Every character has defining traits and their own story arc which can be completed depending on how invested in these characters you become.  After characters, the story itself is pretty inuitive and flows nicely, the pacing and atmosphere are especially good, I never felt that I was being rushed.  If you're someone who likes a much more fast paced Star Wars game I reccomend The Force Unleashed but more on that later.  There is an alignment system where you can make good or evil decisions, and that in turn raises your Light/Darkside meter.  Characters in the game will actually comment on your demeanor or appearence based on your alignment.
2.  The Combat:  The game's combat is.. uhhhh.... unique.  Its semi-turn based with real time fighting, but you choose your moves when combat opens and then let the sitution play out, choosing new moves as time goes on.  I liked the combat for being more intuitive than it seemed at first.  And it gets very intuitive, with you needing to pay attention at times in order to make the ultimate build.  This is only the case for Normal mode and above however, for Easy mode you can go however you want really, just use common sense when you choose what you feel would be the best character.  The blaster fighting I found a bit boring at times but the MELEE fighting looks awesome.  When you close into melee with an enemy you will engage in a duel where you are parrying, striking and just looking awesome.  There are also items you can use that you may find in your travels like shields, grenades, and stims which provide buffs or damage enemies.  There is an inventory and you can customize how your character looks with different armor, weapons, etc.  You can customize your companions inventories as well.
3.  The Soundtrack:  This game has an amazing score.  The OST is very fitting for nearly every situation with there being a very small few oddballs at times.  You can tell that they spent alot of time on the soundtrack.
Conclusion:  An excellent RPG and an excellent Star Wars game, a must play for anyone who likes good charcters and a strong story, as well as a must play for Star Wars fans.

This game is in a lot of ways better than Shank 1. There are a lot less "cheap" deaths, although a lot of the enemies themselves pull some pretty cheap/unblockable moves. The result is that most deaths in this game feel a lot more justified than in Shank 1.
The original game's controls were dumb enough - it required 12 buttons to perform all actions, completely ridiculous for a fighting game with such a shallow combat system. This one is even worse, with 14 buttons required. They added a dedicated "pick up/use" button, and added 2 (!) dodge buttons. These add absolutely nothing to the gameplay, but make it so that you have to map a couple controls to the right analog stick... really really stupid. Do you want your dodges to require you to move your thumb from attack/jump controls? Probably not.
They mostly got rid of the QTE type boss fights from Shank 1. Boss fights in this one involve shooting your guns A LOT, maybe 300-500 hits kills a boss. They feel more like Mega Man bossfights than fighting game boss fights. When EVERY boss gets to half health, you can grapple to trigger a short cinematic.
Presentation wise, this game is quite a few notches below Shank 1. What little story there was there is pretty much eliminated here. Cutscenes are quite poor quality, and some of them look like they were hand drawn, scanned to 720p and then stretched poorly to 1920x1200. The game takes place in south or central america, but all voice actors sound like they're white game developers from Seattle. The drop in quality makes me think the budget for this must have been a step down from Shank 1.
Due to less cheap deaths, I'd say this game is better than Shank 1 by a hair, but still pretty poor. The controls are stupid and overly complicated for such a simple game, the combat system is still pretty much button mash with the occasional jump out of the way, and the presentation is almost non-existent.
I WILL recommend Mark of the Ninja, don't be scared off of it because of this, but by the same token, don't by Shank thinking it'll be the same quality as MotN.

A number of reviewers made the same points, so I will be brief.
The good:
-Looks nice.
-Feels like a great game, especially during the first 5 hours.
-Army customization, upgrades and different weaponry are nice touches.
The bad:
-The AI is broken in various ways. For instance, it often charges irrationally, and seemingly to make up for this the developers gave it some super powers.
-Cavalry is useless, even against lone skirmishers or undefended artillery units. You are always better off investing the money and manpower in an infantry unit.
-Battles are heavily scripted, to the point of having a broken logic. You are supposed to defend a position. You do it and thanks to the AI's suicidal charges, the enemy gets almost completely wiped out or routed. Then the game hits a point in the script and you are prompted "Our position is being overwhelmed! We must fall back to that place!" Then the script magically teleports your whole army to the hill behind the position where you were doing just fine. Then you watch the comedy of the enemy trying to charge your new position with 10% of its starting force because you had killed or routed the rest before your position was "overwhelmed."
The ugly:
-No matter how badly you beat the AI, it keeps making up its losses and more. This renders your actions completely inconsequential. After 50 or so hours, (or sooner if you are smarter than I am) you realize that you are not playing a strategy simulator. You are instead playing one of those clicker flash games in which the numbers keep increasing as you upgrade your skills but nothing else changes because as your income increases so do the cost of future upgrades.
If that sounds too abstract, here is the same point made in concrete gameplay terms: I first played two campaigns with CSA. The first time when enemy kept making up their losses regardless, I thought "Well, I am a noob. So, I didn't beat them hard enough in the beginning. That's why they recovered." But then I played the same campaign again. Even in the easiest difficulty and right after I consistently mowed down 70% of the Union army battle after battle, the next battle they always had 10k more soldiers than they did before. Then, I said "Well, they are the Union after all. They had a larger population than the rebels" and I tried out the Union campaign. Who knew the South could replace 200k+ losses and keep pressing towards the DC? I didn't. They kept coming, their numbers kept swelling no matter how many I killed.
The Verdict:
I wanted to like this game. And to be honest, I enjoyed it for many hours. But the enjoyment was in part due to the illusion created by the game, the illusion that my actions and decisions mattered. Once the illusion was shattered by the realization that no matter how well I play, the AI will be able to match and raise my hand, the enjoyment was replaced with disappointment and frustration. Overall, I would have to say, the experience ended up being negative.
PS: I aslo want to respond to a common objection to negative reviews with many hours: "You played it for 70 hours, how bad can it be? Grow up and get a life!"
It is possible to enjoy something in the short term although the enjoyment is replaced by discomfort after a while. If you think that this is impossible, try telling that to a heroin addict who wishes that he had never done that first shot.

Although the developers advertise that they fixed/improved it, I have screenshots for each battle and experimented with numbers, and it turns out that you still have to think a lot in camp whether to improve your numbers, unit size or equipment, because every improvement might be mirrored by the AI twicefold. For example I noticed that before achieving a crushing victory at Port Republic, the AI armory was 21-26%, after it was 39-44%, that is after I killed more than half their force. So basically the reward for crushing the AI was that I play a harder battle at Gaines' Mill, I am better if I skip the battle. I don't want to spend time calculating the scaling instead of actually enjoying the game, but this degree of brokenness makes me to (or makes me stop playing). And I will mention here that actually this is a pretty good game, except for this (horrendous) downside.
I am a developer myself and I know that at some point you have to draw a line on a product, say that it is what it is and move forward. But adding (back!) a no scaling checkbox, that would apply to normal difficulty too is not that hard, since they had the feature before. Unless they fix scaling or introduce a no scaling option, this remains a negative review. I will update it according to future updates.

Having played this game, both as Union and Conferederate, for many months, I find the mechanics of the game to be very addictive. I have found myself playing for hours without even realizing it.
However, I feel the game was rushed into production with the premise.... this is good enough.....
More specifically, the game lacks polish and flexability.
For instance, the campaign game follows the course of the actual battles during the war, but the army management, where you actually build your army, seems to be designed for PvP play rather then any historical immersion.
The major personalities of the war are present, but they lack, personality...good or bad, commanders are just presented for their historical context, their abilities or limitations in real life not withstanding.
You have the ability to outfit your army and customize their arms, but it seems most of the available muskets,  rifles and cannons are just meant for eye candy, as they never appear in the numbers required to outfit a unit.
Winning or loosing a battle does not seem to affect the course of the game, you are stuck in the same battles as the historical counterparts, no matter how you performed in previous battles. There is also no strategic benefit or consequence for winning a battle, apart from a possible buff for the next battle.

And all of the battles devolve into "capture the flag" , where everything revolves around capturing a key terrain feature, rather then focusing on the enemy army. In fact, once the terrain requirements are met, its best to husband your units and ignore the enemy until time runs out.
The custom games are very limited, as you are forced to use one of the premade battle maps and then pay for a limited supply of arms and men.
The pre-made historical battles are very playable and enjoyable, but from these you can also see how the army management system does not do the game justice.
Overall, Ultimate General seems to have potential, but given its built in limitations becomes rather repetative and dull once you've gone through it a couple of times.

A blown-up sequel to the original Ultimate General: Gettysburg game, which was itself an updated and  more complex version of Sid Meyer's Gettysburg from days past.  In a nutshell - a wargame where you move around units composed of individuals, not square cardboard pieces with numbers on them, and watch them duke it out.  The game is executed well -- it's beautiful to look at, it's relatively easy to understand the controls, and it provides a lot of replay value.
It's not perfect, mind you.  There are some tactical quirks to the AI, and occasionally some gunk gets in the works and you see tiny, almost-panicked units rout a complete and full-strength enemy unit (or something like that).  The terrain can sometimes be hard to read (there is an option to increase the depth of the terrain on the map; I find that essential, but still occasionally have issues), which is a factor in a game that attempts to realistically model the benefits/costs of fighting uphill vs. downhill.  The campaign model in this one (which is greatly expanded and modified from the relatively basic sequential battle system in Gettysburg) can be a bit complex and challenging.  And the game does not hold your hand at all -- you really do need to know at least some basic military tactics and concepts to function well in the game.
On the whole, though, it's an excellent wargame, albeit not something with copious depth (like, say, anything by Gary Grigsby).  Great for people of intermediate wargame skill (like me), but I'd think that hardcore grognards may find it too easy or simplistic (or both).  Given that it's a very small development team (who have proven to be quite good at responding to user feedback on both their games), it's an impressive achievement.  I wish I had more time to dive into it....

It seems most of the negative reviews come from people who paid $80 and are angry that the game has gone on sale a few times in the last 2 months since release. Kind of a dumb reason to give a negative review of a game considering that has nothing to do with the actual gameplay, so:
Game is a lot of fun, great borderlands style humour throughout the game. Has fun MOBA style first person PVP, as well as 8 "missions" you can play co op or solo with varying difficulties, each mission is an hour or so to complete, so that makes the single player roughly 8-9 hours total. Not too bad for the single player experience in a mainly multiplayer focused game.
Folks seem to also be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥about microtransactions. Just to let prospective buyers know, these transactions take form of taunts and skins, nothing that actually effects gameplay. There is no "pay to win" here of any kind. Anything that effects gameplay, including heroes, can ONLY be earned through play, there are not even any short cuts to buy. With this in mind, I do not understand why people are upset over it. Even with the skins, you can earn them through normal play if you really want to.
There is also a random RNG loot system present, a cross between Overwatch's random loot boxes but the loot feels more like Borderlands, with it being items that give various small buffs (Nothing huge, just 5-7% of this or that stat.) you get a good few rares and epics just from doing one single player mission. Def enough to put together an OK loadout within your first bit of gameplay.
I have encountered no bugs with the game in my time playing it, all has run very smooth, the game does not seem hugely graphically demanding as it seems to run on a heavily modified version of Unreal Engine 3 with DX11.  Program is 64 bit.
Balance I cannot as of writing comment on too much. I have no unlocked every hero, there are quite a few (All unlocked for free just by playing the campaign or doing random stuff in game.). Now the fact that you have to "unlock" heroes through play is something I can def say is a negative, I feel that in this type of game that all heroes should be unlocked from the outset, the artificial gameplay walls seem odd to me, though you start with a lot of heroes at the beginning, and they seem to unlock fairly easily so far. Still, having to unlock the heroes through gameplay at all is definitely still a negative.
Overall the game does get my recommendation though, it's fun, it oozes style and the co op and PVP are a good time. As of writing, the game was in the latest humble bundle, so the playerbase has sky-rocketted. If I understand correctly, before the sale there was around 1000 average players on an average day according to steamcharts, that is now MUCH HIGHER. It may not be millions or something, but definately is not a dead game by any stretch.
If you can get it on sale, it's worth your money. At full 79.99 (As of writing.) though, I would probably pass on it.

So, since a lot of my childhood memories on a frying Pentium 4 are to be credited to this game, I felt like I needed to make a review.
It was at the time when it wasn't that hard to get started in it, or I was too stupid to notice. I just had fun. Than you could actually get into a server and play normally without repeating that you want a clean game.  But yeah, back to present.
There are two major things crippling Nexon: Zombies to the ground.
Number one - latency - You may be thinking "They do two latency updates a month, it's fine." But it is not. On a good day you're going to freeze randomly, teleport, or stop while other players are moving, approximately 2 times each/game. On a GOOD day. It quickly gets annoying, and at turn, frustrating. Not even your fancy overclocked processor can't save you here.
Number two - balance- Oh where do I start with balance? Perhaps on a store having items selling for 20000 currency (quite a bit) that you can easily obtain as daily rewads? It makes less than little sense. And oh yeah, if you want a character skin, you're going to have to give it 10 dollars, because why not?
But, the major imbalance occurs in actual multiplayer matches. If one, for example, somehow earns an M4A1-Dark Knight (rare modified M4A1 with stackable buffs), there is no way anyone can kill him. You can use your shiny CS:GO skills, but it just isn't enough. He will rain victorious, while others will be cursing the day they got the game. Since it runs on an old "create your own server" system, matchmaking doesn't exist. Ranks don't exist. Balance doesn't exist. You can get experienced, yet fair players, or raging kids with shiny guns and no skill.
Zombies are relatively fun, just make sure you get a reliable processor. It utilizes an ancient-era-AI system, where it generates each zombie as a unique AI, causing big PC-s to cough a hairball. There isn't much unique about the gamemode, though it's nice, I guess.
Nowadays, I only boot the game for daily rewards and to check new updates. There is just very little charm to vouch for the game, though a bot TDM can sometimes be fun. I honestly doubt I'd get Nexon: Zombies again, if  it wasn't for my childhood. It earned my upvote years ago, but not now.
EDIT: Today the devs brought back the long-anticipated Mileage Auction, which is a regular auction where currency is mileage, obtained from various decoders; the main one being the mileage decoder. Sadly, the mentioned decoder was discontinued today. Though, the auction works well, no crashes or bugs. This is a big step in the right direction, as weapons can be bought from other players with their prices. There are a few compromises, mainly being the 30% comission for selling guns, meaning if you ask for 1000 mileage, you will get 700. I personally think that is fair, considering the fact that we got the whole system.
Also, I am getting a strong feeling devs changed something with bots, and for the better. Even the "easy" bots now duck for cove when detected, they are now getting to spots they couldnt get to previously. As an example, bots now smetimes climb the ladder on the map Santorini. They also seem to camp less often and actually go in groups, which is a nice change. It may just be my imagination, but I think it is not.
Another side note; Today, devs are starting to host a play time event, where you get different rewards for playing for certain times, meaning you will get 500 mileage if you play for an hour and a half. Seems fair to me.
I have never had this much fun in this game, since I stopped taking it seriously, and it instantly feels much nicer. Even a few games with bots proved to be quite fun, where before they would just stare you down for a century before actually pulling the trigger.
EDIT 2: I have started playing with friends, and to be honest, the more "naked" players run around the map with starter mp5-s, the more fun it gets. People are assaulting the toxic community, and Im not gonna lie, its there. People are right on that front. Just get a bunch of friends while theres an event running and you are all-set.
Also, I noticed people call this game p2w. Now, I dont cmpletely agree there. Sure, the decoder system is pretty bad (with trieal guns and all), but I wouldnt completely give up on it just yet. As I mentioned in the previous edit, the mileage auction is back, so you just need a fistful of luck to get a permanent weapon and assuming you know how to work money, you should be able to trade guns around. Plus, they do an event for every update, so for as long as you participate in most of them, you will have your guns.
Now, I believe the deciding factor here is time itself. As Im writing this edit, my counter is crossing the 350 hour milestone, and I believe I have enough to be content (40 perm guns, including the wretched AK-47 Paladin) So, if you are okay for spending this much time in the game, you will have more then enough to have fun with.If, on the other hand, you are not, then just walk away. Either way is fine. I feel like I have to repeat that you should not take this game seriously. It is a little Korean FPS that does have a bit of charm to it. If you compare it to CS:GO or COD, you need to take you hand out of your crack and into your wallet.

At first I wanted to play this game just to see how bad it was. I wanted to laugh at the mediocrity of this game. When I closed the game and went to sleep, I had a dream. I don't remember what the dream was, but when I woke up all I knew was that I had to come back to this game. I played it some more, and my eyes were finally opened. I had found the missing pieces I was looking for, the evidence to finally convince me that God is real.
Seeing Jesus fight demons with his friends made me believe! I was shocked and angry. How could they not tell these epic stories in the Bible? How could they not tell me about Jesus using his super powerful Exorcise spell to send demons to hell? The more I saw the true story of Jesus, the more furious I became. Seeing the challenges Jesus faced as he ran out of potions and MP made me feel like I finally had discovered something truly amazing. This game was portrayed the events of the past more accurately than the Bible itself. The gameplay, the story, the music and sounds, the dialogue of NPCs, everything about this game was just absolutely perfect.
But then I stopped playing. After playing two of the three games in the trilogy I just quit. I don't know why, but I did. Perhaps I had something I needed to do, or somewhere I needed to go. After I stopped, I completely forgot about this game. So much had happened in my life after that, and I felt lost. Thats when I remembered about the trilogy, and how I never finished the third game. I immediately stopped whatever I was doing and came back to this game. Playing this finally gave me the direction I needed in life. I felt invincible. Invincible with the protection of God himself. I had found a new purpose in life playing this game.
And that purpose was to serve my God.

Said abilities are useful in both movement and combat. Like a punch that propels the player quickly forward, used to thump butts OR reach difficult areas.
Many a pop culture reference can be found, along with chuckle-worthy dialog throughout the three to five-hour campaign. Hidden or optional areas not necessary to "beat" the game provide the greatest challenge in terms of combat and/or platforming.

I got this game in a bundle and i have to admit i wouldn't have gotten it otherwise because i haven't heard of it before.
And now i ended up playing it more than any other game i got in that bundle!
This game is awesome!
The game has a simple concept. Forest area, desert area, ice area, night area etc., all connected and each one has a blue fire that serves as a save spot and fills your energy, and each has a dungeon you have to go through and defeat a boss in order to open a portal to progress further. The game never tells you any of this, but it's really not that hard to figure out just by exploring a little. You spawn randomly in one of those areas and explore. Where you spawn, there will be a cave you can enter to pick up your starting weapon, and everything else is up to you.
It's very simple to play, yet has a lot of variety in how you build your character through gear. A lot of different weapons to choose from, each with their own playstyle. I ended up doing a DEX build with katanas and daggers which allow you to go invisible for a short period and sneak attack enemies, but have occasionally gotten other weapons if they were better.
Worked out pretty well because i finished the game once, and got to the last boss the second time around on NG+. NG+ works the same way it does in Dark souls pretty much. You get to keep your levels, your gear, and the whole game resets with stronger enemies.
Speaking of Dark souls, this game is heavily inspired by it's death mechanic. You pick up a ghost lady you need to escort to her grave and she acts as an "extra" life and you better damn well take good care of that life. If you die, you only have one chance to go retrieve the life where you died, and if you die the second time before you recover your life (ghost lady) that's it, game over, you start from LVL 1 again and you loose everything. So it's Dark souls mechanics mixed with roguelike elements. And it works great!
And speaking of biting the dust, i died, as mentioned, at the last boss on the second playthrough because my controller turned off for some reason. And what would have been a rage moment in any normal circumstances, or any other game, here it was just "Well ok, that was stupid, but now i get to play again and try out other weapons, see how far i can come!". The game has a lot of replay value!
And while i got it in a bundle, it's well worth the full price if you're into those kinds of games, and if that's not your thing, still check it out on sale, it's worth it!
It's also worth if you're an achievement hunter. Achievements are pretty easy, you just play the game and you'll get them all eventually.

Star Wars Knights of The Old Republic... Ohhhh boyyy is there alot to say about this game.
One of RPG juggernaut BioWare's first titles, this game is a classic Star Wars experience.  I'll separate the attributes of the game so this review is waaaayy easier to read but first a little general info.  KOTOR (Knights of The Old Republic) is an action RPG set in the Star Wars universe about 2000 years before the events of A New Hope.  Despite being 2000 years ago, the game still has blasters, lightsabers, starships etc. the date is very hard to notice.  You start off creating your own character and choosing between (I think) 3 classes, Soldier, Scout and Scoundrel.  You can be male or female, white or black or what have you, then you get to choose Skills and Feats.  Skills are pretty self explanatory but Feats are kinda like a mix of perks and abilities from other games.  For example, an ability Feat would be Sniper Shot, which is an accurate attack for blasters while its melee counterpart is Critical Strike, the Feat's effect is that it deals more damage and has a chance of stunning enemies.  A perklike Feat would be Gearhead, which passively increases your Repair and Security Skills.  After all the Character select stuff is done the game starts proper, now I'll go onto the Categorized stuff below...
1.  The Story:  The Game's story and characters are excellent and it is the game's strongest aspect in my humblest of opinions.  Most of the characters are likeable but it would really depend on what kind of player you are, some you will like more than others.  All the characters will react to the decisions you make, also the things you say to them and will like/dislike you accordingly.  Every character has defining traits and their own story arc which can be completed depending on how invested in these characters you become.  After characters, the story itself is pretty inuitive and flows nicely, the pacing and atmosphere are especially good, I never felt that I was being rushed.  If you're someone who likes a much more fast paced Star Wars game I reccomend The Force Unleashed but more on that later.  There is an alignment system where you can make good or evil decisions, and that in turn raises your Light/Darkside meter.  Characters in the game will actually comment on your demeanor or appearence based on your alignment.
2.  The Combat:  The game's combat is.. uhhhh.... unique.  Its semi-turn based with real time fighting, but you choose your moves when combat opens and then let the sitution play out, choosing new moves as time goes on.  I liked the combat for being more intuitive than it seemed at first.  And it gets very intuitive, with you needing to pay attention at times in order to make the ultimate build.  This is only the case for Normal mode and above however, for Easy mode you can go however you want really, just use common sense when you choose what you feel would be the best character.  The blaster fighting I found a bit boring at times but the MELEE fighting looks awesome.  When you close into melee with an enemy you will engage in a duel where you are parrying, striking and just looking awesome.  There are also items you can use that you may find in your travels like shields, grenades, and stims which provide buffs or damage enemies.  There is an inventory and you can customize how your character looks with different armor, weapons, etc.  You can customize your companions inventories as well.
3.  The Soundtrack:  This game has an amazing score.  The OST is very fitting for nearly every situation with there being a very small few oddballs at times.  You can tell that they spent alot of time on the soundtrack.
Conclusion:  An excellent RPG and an excellent Star Wars game, a must play for anyone who likes good charcters and a strong story, as well as a must play for Star Wars fans.

This is the most accurate ACW game I've played and probably one of the most fun tactical one's. I'll address the elephant in room first. The graphics look like that from a game from 10 years ago. If you're looking for a game that shows the sweat on the brow of the soldier you this isn't your game. That being said it has to be one of the most comprehensive tactical strategy games I've ever played, taking into acount the reload time of your soldiers, their morale, their condition, the weapons stats, the cover that they are in, etc. The coolest part is there are several differant modifiers available to help you improve these stats through unit veterancy, allocating weapons, assigning commanders, etc. which helps this game stand out from Empire Total War. Customizing your army is one of the best parts of this game. It's a constant balancing act of acuring the best weapons for the cheapest cost for the most soldiers. This balancing is depedent purely on ones gameplay within the campaign. Though even losing battles there are so many ways to play around lack of equipment, lack of man power, or lack of money by tailoring your army to work around it. So though you may lose here and there, the game may punish but it's never unfair with what you can or can't do. The tools to beat the odds are always there. So 36 hrs in, I can say I love this game in every aspect; the accuracy, the gameplay, and the balancing of the game.
TL;DR It's essentially Empire: Total War with worst graphics, better more balanced RTS gameplay, Better more customizable army compositing, a better and more realistic logistical system, and no grand strategy map to worry of. The gameplay alone makes up for the lack of those two aspects from ETW. Would buy again.

I recommend this game only to people of a very niche market who like playing oldschool RPG games - this is not a good entry game to the genre as it lacks much of the charm of it's predecessors that it attempts to emulate.
I have mixed feeling about the game since I'm a fan of the genre and this is a very solid nostalgia trip that doesn't have any glaring bugs that made it unplayable or hang progression.
It's a fairly straightforward 20~30 hour oldschool-esque jRPG game with clear homages to Chrono Trigger and a few other SNES jRPGs.  Let's start with the good, it has a fairly interesting combination skill system of item hunting, selling materials to unlock abilities to then equip into "materia" slots that are given per level but also attached to some more powerful talismans (bangles).  You then go about upgrading these skills through use in battle for slight bonuses or star levels and combine them with other allies' techs for Double or Triple techs.  It was fun experimenting and finding a slew of different abilities to prepare for boss battles and deal with specific mechanics.
The combat unfortunately is poorly balanced, hinging almost entirely onto either extreme ease of instantly clearing the entire screen with powerful AoEs to receive the best materials for even more skills - to the extremely quick party wipe from a boss monster that acts unexpectedly.  It's encouraged not to "grind" in this game as it's entirely possible to clear it without over leveling but making sure to collect material for appropriate abilities to trivialize even the hardest of boss encounters (Which sadly is a small handful at that).  If you insist on grinding experience - you can easily find a few high enemy count areas or a few of the "Special recolored" beasts to farm for a quick boost if you want some padding.
The dialogue is cliche and the overall overworld, scenes and dungeons all give a samey reused assets vibe (Lots of snow, lots of blocky dungeons, same houses and NPC models).  The story just seems pieced together and the illusion of choice in dialogue in apparent extremely quickly when all choices don't lead to any sort of branching path.  Sadly by some weird design choice - they made the sidequests entirely unavailable until the very end of the game or after you've cleared the final boss at least once.  So the "linear hallway" complaint can be seen here even further as many players will miss the sidequests completely even if they return to exploring because a lack of any hints (I randomly wandered back to every town and wasted a few hours searching for quests before figuring out I had to have the appropriate party leader to talk to a particular NPC each time to start a sidequest).
The piano music while beautiful at first, quickly becomes a not so memorable grouping of sad piano pieces which only feels tedious rather than creating a somber tone.  The only upbeat piano piece was actually distinct for this reason and wins some points in this category.

This is a classic JRPG at its finest. The piano music is simple and effective, the battle system is classic 90s, as is the story; straightforward, simple, compelling, and engaging. I am Setsuna is an incredibly strange game. Inevitably you will hear how "classic" it is, in both positive and negative reviews. But in reality it's not very "classic" at all. It is actually VERY experimental in terms of JRPG games. It's very much like Chrono Trigger, if Chrono was much deeper in it's mechanics, and didn't try to make you like it one bit. I am Setsuna is a moody, charisma-less game that took me a few hours to get into, but once i started to understand it, I really, really started to like it. It's like sitting down to talk with a stranger and spending the first 30 minutes thinking how weird the person is only to come to find that they are actually fascinating once you get past the weirdness. Weirdness in the case of IAS being it's quirky acoustic-piano soundtrack, omnipresent snow, tedious menu-system and off-kilter mechanics. What you come to find, though, is a compelling story about duty and purpose, a uniquely melancholy tone and atmosphere, and DEEP RPG mechanics that are fun and rewarding to master. HIGHLY recommended for any real JRPG fan, but understand that this is fruit you have to work to get a taste of.

I am setsuna is a game changer in this AAA world. The music, nostalgic battle system, and setting is amazing. 'I am Setsuna' is a old-school inspired JRPG that mixes gameplay from the likes of 'Chrono Trigger' against the themes present in games such as 'Final Fantasy IX'.
I loved the 'Chrono Trigger' battle system from the moment I first played that game almost two decades ago. It's a simple turn-based battle system that allows you to combine your character attacks to boost damage. The system in 'I am Setsuna' has a few additional quirks - some which work and others that are a little too complicated or random - but that is the basics.
'I am Setsuna' is a budget title from a new developer (working within Square-Enix) and that sometimes shows. The entire game takes place in snowy environments and while I didn't mind that - it game the game a more intimate feel in my opinion - that won't work for everyone.
The game is also quite short by the standards of JRPGs. I completed the game in 14 hours - though I haven't done any of the end-game content - and some may be disappointed by that. But as someone in their 30s with less time on my hands I'd prefer a shorter RPG rather than a 50+ hour monstrosity that I never end up finishing.
The characters in the game are charming and the dialogue is mostly pretty good. The story is simple but effective and the themes are relatable. This isn't a game that descends into incomprehensible mumbo-jumbo towards the end.
I'd recommend the game wholeheartedly to those that love JRPGs and especially those who grew up on the 16bit / 32bit JRPGs from Square. For a first time effort from a new developer this was really promising and I hope they get another opportunity and a bigger budget so we can really see what they are capable of.

I am Setsuna is a pretty enjoyable game for the most parts. However, there are also problems.
TL;DR:  I liked the game, only the ending let me down.
You start off as a masked mercenary...i have no idea anymore, what his name was, as the game let's you rename every playable character and just me being me, i renamed him to Vari... after a first tutorial mission you get a contract to slay "the sacrifice", a girl from the village of Nive, that got chosen to be sacrificed in the Last Lands, so the world shall be save from monsters for a little longer. This girl is Setsuna. Things however go a little different and you end up being in her party to escort her to the Last Lands, to see her sacrifice through.
The game then plays out as your average JRPG. After a few more minutes you got your first party of three characters together, three more you will get throughout the near future and a sevenths one in the very end, from which you will have three in your active fighting party. Combat is pretty turnbased. You have a bar, that is filling up and showing when you are ready to attack again. You can boost your ATB via items and both passive and active abilities.
On a world map you travel between locations, which can be quite annoying, if you -for whatever reason-want to get back to a place long ago, because you can't skip things llike caves or mountain passes, so you have to choose to enter this location and fight through it once again.  At least i haven't figured out a way to skip this.
The game throws a lot of text at you, so if you don't like reading, iiiiii would not advice you to get this game, if you plan on enjoying the story. Occassionally you get asked about your opinion during the chats.
Personally i liked the story throughout most of the game. Sometimes i had this feel "Yea, pretty darn predictable, because have you ever had this kind of scenario play out differentlly in a story? I think not."  But there also have been some twists i haven't forseen, which was nice. In the end the game closes a circle, you will notice it, once you reached it. As you can see I didn't even play an hour of this game and it really turned me off at that point.  In general, the core mechanics just feel really bad.  Not to mention trying to give feedback on the forums only got me attacked, so the overly defensive community can go play this game amongst themselves as it dies.
- Forced to play the prologue with multiple unskippable cutscenes
- Even the single player Prologue is all server based
- Jumping is way too floaty.
- Movement is too slow.
- There is a small delay between moving the mouse and the on screen cursor moving.
- There is a server-side delay when using jump pads.
- There are server-side delays when destroying objects in the environment.
- There is a server-side delay when shooting projectiles.
- There are delays when using my abilities that make them no fun to use.
- Having to stop mid-match while I'm alive to do upgrades is completely counter to a fast-paced shooter
- Zero feedback when holding Z to respawn so you have no idea if it took or not (you already have a circle around the number, just make a UI swipe element around it).
- Performance is really bad.  It's even sub par on a single player Prologue map with no enemies and most effects turned down...completely unacceptable for a fast paced shooter
It all just points to the fact that they haven't really fixed the core experience that people originally complained about in the 3 months since launch, so it's not worth my time to put any more effort into it.  I'm sure some people will enjoy it, but I'm mad that I wasted my money on it and my time downloading that 15 GB.

I wanted to like this game, but the mechanics are very clumsy.  If your key word search has more than 5 hits, you can only see the first 5.  You can line up some clips, obstensible to play in a sequence, but you can't re-arrange the clips, nor can you remove them.  You have to drag other clips on top of the ones you want to replace.  Worse, you can't even play the clips as an extended sequence.  Each one has to be played individually.  There's a big difference between making something challenging and making it tedious.  As it stands, the game play falls very much in the tedious category.  It's a shame because the story itself seems interesting.

The concept of the game, in piecing together a story through video clips, is interesting. All told I think I quite enjoyed the different sort of game experience, I just I wished there was a bit more to it. It was a bit thrilling at first learning more about the story but after awhile if you are trying to hunt up all of the clips it can get tedious. You can get through the game pretty fast if not trying to view every tiny clip. I did hunt up all the clips (some pointless) with not but the time wasted to show for it, there was nothing in-game to reward me like I was hoping. I wish there was more to the ending as well.
I recommend if you enjoy a different kind of game experience and/or if you enjoy crime stories. Just don't feel the need to be a completist.

I ♥♥♥♥ing loved Shank. I’m putting that out there up front. I loved every minute of playing it. It was really really hard. It’s been a while since I’ve played a game like that. Now, when I say “really really hard,” I don’t mean impossible. Super Meat Boy is impossible. I mean really god-damned challenging. Shank is by no means a perfect game, but it’s so much fun. Even if you aren’t a fan of beat-‘em-ups, I still recommend giving Shank 2 a shot.
We’re going to pretend like I know what happened in the original Shank. Right? Right. What’s research?
Shank 2 is, as previously stated, a beat-‘em-up game in which you play as (appropriately) Shank. Shank is a member of a rebel group who is defying the warlord, General Magnus. Magnus and his militia have taken over the government, essentially throwing the entire system out of whack. The militia is tearing the cities the government controls apart, taking in slave labor, burning entire villages, the whole shebang. For a game whose story is completely unimportant, Shank has a considerable amount of thought put into it. I mean, don’t get me wrong, the story is a tired tale that’s been done a million times over, but it sets up an excellent backstory for Shank.
Shank’s mentor, Elena, has been captured by the militia. Not only does she mean to world to Shank, but she also is the leader of the alliance group. It’s up to Shank and his partner Corina to save Elena and take down Magnus once and for all.
The first thing you can note about Shank is that he is BADASS. He uses a flipping chainsaw and shotgun to take out hordes of enemies, cranes, superhumans, and airplanes. His weapons actually range from machetes to molotovs. Yeah, how flipping cool is that? Unfortunately, Shank isn’t a relatable character in the slightest. I know that the game wasn’t going for an emotional tale, but what’s the point in having a backstory at all when you can’t feel any emotions toward the characters? Shank, and even Corina, to an extent, were too Gears of War-like for me to actually care about why I was killing all of these deranged lunatics.
Putting the stupid characterization aside for a moment, I’d like to discuss the flashback I was continuously having during my playthrough. There was a game made for the SNES called Blackthorne. Maybe you have heard of it. In, a badass character runs around shooting a shotgun to save prisoners, etc. I haven’t personally played the game, so I can’t attest to how good it is, but I’ve seen in played and learned about it. There are so many callbacks to Blackthorne that it isn’t even funny.
Let me give you some examples. Blackthorne’s signature move was shooting with a shotgun… one handed and backwards. Guess what Shank can do? Of course, there is the obvious saving prisoners from the bad guys… I could go on, but I think you get the picture. Before you go calling Shank and Blackthorne the same game, though, recognize that Blackthorne was actually a cinematic platformer. This is a genre that isn’t really touched on as much nowadays, with the exception of the recent re-release of Flashback. My point is, whether they meant to or not, the developers of Shank made Blackthorne cool again.
Before we dive into the gameplay, let’s talk about the art of the game. The animations are all very comic-book-like, which I’ve always been a fan of. The animations are simple and cartoony for such a violent game, but this is hardly detrimental. What isn’t the best part of the game is the music which is… bland. Sure, it sounds epic… at first… and then it gets repetitive and fades into the background. There isn’t anything wrong with it, per say, but it isn’t as good as I would like it to be.
Shank is hard. I know I’ve said that a lot, but I’m trying to ingrain this into your mind. There are two modes of the story: Normal and Hard modes. Normal mode is doable, but Hard is… ♥♥♥♥ing hard. In Normal mode, you get plenty of health powerups, checkpoints, infinite lives, etc. In hard mode, you get very few powerups, next to no checkpoints, and infinite lives. To give you a quick perspective, I beat Normal in about four hours, give or take. I have yet to get past the third level in Hard.
Some of the better things about Shank are his weapons. You see, there are a variety of weapons, like I said earlier. Each weapon has a different amount of damage, speed, and some variation of stun. You will be able to find which weapons work best for you as you play the game. You don’t unlock all of the weapons until the last few levels, and by this point you’ve probably already figured out what you wanted. For instance, my lineup was the Chainsaw, the Shotgun, and the Grenades.
I like that the game balances out the weapons. You have a real chance to figure out which weapons are best for your playstyle. If you’re like me, you like to deal with one problem at a time. This is where the Chainsaw and the Shotgun came in handy. If you like to take on lots of enemies at once, you may find that the Pistols and Machetes work better for you. Even when it seems like a weapon is unbalanced, you’ll find that it has a certain ability, like leaving enemies burning in your wake. The weapons are arguably the best part about the game.
The gameplay is pretty straightforward. It’s almost, but not quite, button mashing. The enemies range quite a bit in size and power, so some weapons will work better on them than others. For example, when I was in close quarters with several enemies, I’d end up flailing about and murdering all of them with my Shotgun. If I needed to clear the field and make space, I’d use the Chainsaw. You’ll find that just using one will not work. You’ll need to chain combos together to help you take down the multitudes of enemies.
Speaking of multitudes of enemies, there are quite a bit of them. These basic enemies range from swordsmen, to female ninjas, to guys with pistols, to guys with machine guns, to guys with axes, to midget bomber, to gigantic ♥♥♥♥ing cretins… There are so many. Each level may or may not present you with different enemies. Occasionally, this could just mean the same enemy reskinned, but some levels do include zone-specific enemies.
The best enemies are the bosses. And there are not as many as I would like. The levels in Shank only end up being about 20-30 minutes long apiece, and there are only eight levels. This does mean there is variety in bosses, but there aren’t enough. For such a BA guy, you’d think he’d constantly be taking on guys three or four times his size.
That being said, the bosses are awesome and also not. Each one of the focuses on a different aspect. For example, there is a psychic boss, and there’s fire boss, and there’s a strength boss. Each of these bosses seem perfectly fit for their levels. Alternatively, there are minibosses in some stages. For example, the crane I mentioned earlier. It has been a long time since I’ve had this much rage towards a boss in a game… You can’t hit the crane unless you’re using your gun. The crane repeatedly tries to smash you with a boat that takes up a third of the screen while guys with pistols try to take you out from a mile away. It’s tough. But I beat it. I can’t get past in on the Hard mode, but I got in Normal.
The bosses are not awesome in some parts… Mostly because they all use the same tactics. To a degree. They have a predetermined moveset that consists of maybe five moves at the most. Once you take out about a third of their health, they all call backup. It’s the same thing every battle. On top of that, once you figure out the movesets of each boss, they aren’t that hard to beat. Hell, even the final battle against Magnum I beat on my second try. For a game that can be as challenging as Shank, the bosses aren’t hard enough.

Overall, despite it's drawbacks, I'd have to say I recommend this game.  It's the last game in the era of "classic" tactical shooters, like SWAT 3, Rogue Spear, Ghost Recon, etc, where you had to play it extremely slow, you actually completed objectives, and the game revolved more around the atmosphere of the levels and the actual gameplay, rather than the cinematic events and story-telling that would be featured later.  Some games such as GRAW 1 and 2 for PC and Operation Flashpoint Dragon Rising tried to recapture this sort of style, and did so admirably but were never as influential as the previous titles as they weren't able to gain the traction and acclaim that their predecessors had done so seemingly with ease.
Unfortunately, as the last game of the "classic" tactical shooter era, it's not all that great.  The AI can become glitchy and shoot walls, some lights sear right through the textures and you can see them from anywhere on the map (this is a rare glitch, thankfully), and planning your own routes and picking each individuals gear is completely absent.  Instead, you're given a preset path which you can choose to follow (you often probably should, since it feels as if the missions are designed around following these paths, and if you stray off the path, you'll often find nothing of interest.  Instead of choosing each soldiers load out, you pick "kits" for the whole team, which are pretty diverse, but picking your own gear is much preferred.  As for the AI, you'll often see your team mates shooting walls, trying to get at enemies, and they won't budge until the enemy is dead, or they die.
So how, how can I recommend this game despite all this?  Well, for one, the HUD is very neat and tidy.  There are a few squad commands at your disposal which work quite well and is very easy to adjust.  The missions have a nice flow to them and are quite addicting.  While not as large in scope as Ghost Recon's, they offer interesting settings with very nicely detailed environments which the mappers clearly at least TRIED to make feel "realistic".  Some of the very first levels you play are actually quite memorable.  In terms of replayability, the game is largely more linear than in the previous titles I've mentioned here, but again, it tries to make things more interesting with the nicely detailed levels and memorable settings.  The graphics are quite nice, but are tarnished by the "sweat" effects which replace the brutal blood and gore you'd see in Ghost Recon after firing on enemies (though thankfully there's mods which replace the sweat with blood).
Overall, the sum of its parts adds up to a game with a more linear structure to the levels which makes the overall gameplay feel faster paced, with a lot of the more complex features of the previous titles either being skimped over, or altered/simplified for ease of play.  If you're looking for a game with memorable settings, decent gameplay, and is easy to get into, I would recommend this to you.  If you're new to the tactical shooter genre, I would also recommend this to you.  And thats where its strengths are, it services both groups while still managing to be fun.  It's not better, but it doesn't necessarily need to be.

I've only put a little over and hour into it, but I'll summarize what I've experienced thus far:
It's a cross of Rainbow Six: Rogue Spear and Ghost Recon 1. It's developed on Ghost Recons engine, so the main menu to the actual in-game graphics and interface are near identical. You can't customize your loadout, although there are a lot of varied presets to choose from.
You manage one team which consists of three operators including yourself (other teams non-playable). Commands are basic and to the point, hitting a sweet spot, although you'll more often then not, rarely use it, unless of course you have a weapon not ideal for CQB, which is directly tied to the team loadout presets you can choose from.
The part that makes it similar to Rogue Spear and Raven Shield is the way missions are structured and play out. Every mission is pre-planned, and you have to follow the waypoint system that's in place. There's a mini-map that shows your surroundings and building layout. Enemies will pop up as red dots once you make visual contact with one.
There's also an auto-aim system directly in line with Rainbow Six 1/Rogue Spear where your crosshair will snap and lock onto enemy targets torso or head respectively. This can be toggled off if you prefer to aim manually within the gameplay options.
The story is somewhat interesting being it's based on the movie/novel. Instead of all the story elements being exclusively in the pre-mission briefings (similar to Ghost Recon 1), there's additional intel which comes in the form of press clippings or general news covering the ongoing situations from a civilian perspective, which can be amusing since you know what
went down.
All in all, for the price it's available at now ($4.99), I'd say it's worth it. If you liked Ghost Recon 1 and Rainbow Six: Rogue Spear, you'll most likely enjoy this as well, although it is more simplified and restricted compared to both games, it's still a good experience.

tl;dr: For $60, this game is pretty terrible. SMITE is, in my opinion, a better (and free) alternative.
If for some reason this game drops in price, as in... a sale, I'd recommend not touching it unless it was at least 50% off.
If this game becomes free... (highly likely, given its wealth of poor reviews and lacking playerbase) then... what've you to lose? Only disk space and time. You might even like it... Though I can't say you'd have anyone to play it with.
$60: 4/10 (The devs need to have a sit and think long and hard about where their game is going, and need to change quite a lot if they want it to succeed. Not likely, considering the game has been released.)
$30: 6/10 (The graphics are okay, but the characters require more balancing and maps need to be redesigned.)
$15 or less: 8/10 (For a multiplayer MOBA, it really should be free... but it has a storyline and some minor replay value... Good with friends.)
There's been an influx of games into the MOBA genre such as SMITE, HotS, and Paragon (and this game of course) in a relatively short amount of time. They all try so hard to bring something new to the table without taking too much from other games of their ilk...
Regarding this, I believe they all try a little too hard. Games these days are being transformed to cater to a more simple type of folk than the game would normally host.
Casual gamers.
It's not a bad thing, by far. Pandering to the casual gamercore by way of simple game mechanics is a good way to generate more revenue without upsetting too much of the hardcore fanbase... Unless you push it a little too far.
Battleborn is by no means too simple, which is why it perplexes me that I stopped liking it soon after playing. I wanted to like it, but I couldn't find it within me to give this game a decent rating.

The original Knights of the Old Republic was a classic, and an icon for the karma based RPG genera, which I would have highly recommend for anyone looking for a good RPG where your choices actually mattered. However, with that said, it has aged terribly, in fact, it has aged worse than most games made in the late 1980’s and that is a serious statement. Just trying to get it to play on Windows 7, which will soon (from the time of writing this) no longer even be supported, took a bit of work. Trying to get it to play in Windows 10 is about as fun as unskipable cut scenes (which thankful, this game doesn’t have many of- hint it’s the space bar). However, getting it to run on a modern OS isn’t the game’s main issue, it’s getting it to run on modern monitors. This damn game, even though it came out after wide screen monitors were already a common thing, does not support wide screen resolutions, forget about HD resolutions. So unless you plan on playing this on an old square low res CRT monitor (and yes, by the time this game came out both widescreen and highres CRT monitors were also very common) to get it to run in widescreen you will need to pull out your hair before you get it to play properly. If you want to play it in HD Widescreen on a modern OS, have fun, I’ve spent more time trying to get the damn game to work than I did replaying it. If you’re a masochist you should use this patch:
. At the end of the day there are millions of PC games, thousands of which are really good games worth playing, half of which are probably better than this game, and I own hundreds of them, and I still haven’t played them all. So this is a final goodbye to a game I used to love. I will never play SWKOTOR again, and that is a little sad because like Morrowind (which has aged wonderfully and I highly recommend) it was a game I constantly want to replay, but unlike Morrowind, I can’t do it without spending more time trying to get it to launch than I would spend actually playing in any given session. This came has caused me so much anger and frustration I am giving up. My recommendation, if you have a life and value your time, don’t bother. Go find another game which you will be able to enjoy without wanting to shout from the top of your lungs for hours on end- before you even spend a single minute actually playing.

This game does a great job of providing tactical level command, set in an operational storyline that takes you through the Civil War. The graphics are well done. The AI is fairly good, and challenging.  The options you have in each battle are wide open with the exception of holding victory locations and the dreaded battle timer - however, you can customize your Corps units, weapons, generals, and recruitment. You can also determine where you spend your "capital" points.
Commanding units and giving orders is relatively easy, the interface is quite user-friendly, and overall - I loved playing this game through and seeing how my different Corps excelled, grew, shrank with losses, and how the weapons developed over the course of the war. The challenges on each side are quite different, I played through both from the time this was a limited release.
The Union - you have the disadvantage of mostly being on the offensive and digging out well-entrenched Rebel forces. You also have to procure your weapons, because the ones you might pick up from the battlefield from the Rebels are horribly outdated and not useful. You will be hard pressed to build a big enough Corps, and equip them, to overcome your casualties and beat the Rebels. Your advantages are plenty of recruits, access to advanced weaponry (if you can afford it), and being on the offensive always gives you the initiative to strike the enemy at their weakest points and control the momentum of the battle.
The Confederacy - you have the disadvantage of numbers, you are always outnumbered. Your weapons are heinously outdated, and you don't have access to the Union's advancement in weaponry so you are forced to find ways to capture Union supplies and weapons. Also, you are often times forced to defend positions based on victory locations and it's not always ideal. However, if you can find ways to make sure you have mobile reserves, cover your flanks as necessary, invest in short-range artillery to decimate Union ranks, and run down retreating Union Forces to capture their supplies, your defenses can become impenetrable.
Overall - 8/10.  I've been in the military for over 20 years, have re-enacted Civil War battles, and have been playing war games both electronic and board for nearly 30 years. This game is fun and addictive, and easy to put away and come back to later as you have time.

This isn't the most accessible game out there (would have really liked to have seen a tutorial), so be warned up front that you'll probably need to read some guides before you really get a handle on this game. I've had many hours of fun with this title, finding it to be a unique and innovative approach to the RTS genre.
The game's campaign takes you chronologically through the major battles of the civil war with a persistent army for you to command during and manage between battles. Having an army that you need to manage and carry from one battle to the next adds a great degree of importance to your tactical choices. Each battle has win/loss/draw victory conditions and rewards and this is one of the few games where it may be beneficial to skip (if a minor battle) or fight for a draw or loss if you think pushing for the victory will cost you too many men. I would recommend saving frequently and maintaining several save files so that you don't have to start completely over if you take horrific losses in a battle and find that you just can't recover two or three major battles down the road.
The gameplay itself is quite fun, with a unique way to control your unit's movements and with a focus on locating and occupying advantageous terrain, flanking, and unit morale. As an added bonus, knowing your history oftentimes can be beneficial (I may have forgotten what Stonewall Jackson was up to during Chancellorsville during my first campaign and received a nasty surprise on day 2).

Gameplay
Casual sandbox physics simulator. Endless possibilities and creative freedom. Besiege offers a growing number of parts/weapons/tools at your disposal to complete a variety of challenges. Physics work believably, constructing and testing different machines is challenging. Each zone consists of one objective and the ability to construct a new machine or edit the previously successful vehicle. Simple in nature but the difficulty slowly rises as you must become more creative in your designs. One zone you might grab and carry boulders to a marker, and the next you could be constructing flying machines to take down gunships.
Controls are widely customizable in terms of part functions. Camera controls are a bit awkward once you start driving/flying your machine, making it frustrating to operate. Currently includes a nice sandbox mode for testing builds. Besiege seems to be regularly updated which is a nice thing to see in an Early Access.
Sound
Fairly absent of any noticeable music, not entirely a downside but it would help break up the silence and occasional animal/soldier sound effects.
Graphics
Simplistic and charming. Environments are created on an endless plane and while these structures are constricted to a small area, they appear more like artistic renders than simply blocks waiting to fall over. Enemies and objects are minimal but beautifully crafted. Destruction works in an enjoyably fluid way, meaning each piece and part reacts accordingly once effected by another object/weapon. Visual effects like fire/smoke/sparks are mesmerizing and even more so once you slow down time using the in-game slider.
Replay Value
A great deal of replay value is possible in Besiege and the increasing number of updates add new parts to tinker with. However this is largely dependent on the players creativity. Starting out it may seem a little rocky but once you familiarize yourself with the function of each part you'll begin to create more intricate machines. Each zone offers the same objective but the creative control aspect makes for an infinite number of ways to complete it.
Wrapping Up
Charming, challenging, and enjoyable. Easy to learn but hard to master. With a very reasonable price tag, Besiege is a solid Early Access title that is shaping up to be an incredibly worthwhile game.

OVERVIEW: Rainbow Recon - Lite
+ CQC sized maps
+ Ghost Recon ('01) engine
+ One shot kills (unless your hitting appendages, vests)
+ Mission Editor (located in the game's folder)
+ Mod friendly
+- No Planning
+- Limited gear selection
- Partially derped TeamAI
- Occasional model glitches (ex: hand through weapon)
- Less popular = less available mods
VERDICT: A great way to introduce others to the world of tactical shooters from yesteryear before throwing them into the more hardcore establishments. Also great for getting your fix when short on time.

REVIEW:
This game is what could be considered a streamlined, slightly more user-friendly approach to the classic tactical shooters. It's not as in-depth as the Rainbow Six or Ghost Recon games of the past but has just enough to make it enjoyable.
Because of this, when you don't have the time to go all-in with the other games you can still get your fix when you're waiting to leave for that VA appointment, or some such. And THAT is exactly why people should get this game. It's not Rainbow Six, nor is it Ghost Recon. But it takes a bit from both and it's still a hell of a lot better than most games being made today that toss around the words tactical shooter like a grain of salt. Besides, you could take the assets from this game and port them over to Ghost Recon for more variety.
Based on the events of the movie with the same name, in singleplayer you play as an operator within the FBI under units like HRT and Spec Ops throughout the eleven mission campaign. Mission types consists of a number of objectives like clearing multiple floors, rescuing hostages, disabling alarms and the like. Although I prefer the hardest difficulty level, there are two others that players can choose from. I don't use them so I can't go into too much detail but they most likely involve less opposition and what not.
Even though there is a single plan, by default, that's based on speed and objective completion, don't expect to be drawing up your own. There's no pre-mission planning involved. Of course, you can always stray from the path anyways. Still, if you were to use the provided mission editor in the game's folder, you could modify it all you want along with everything else by creating your own mod. However, given the date of when this game was released, creating total conversions could pose a challenge.
Your gear selection is based on pre-selected weapon loadouts (HRT Stealth, Spec Ops Recon, Open Assault, etc) that contain variations of kits based on how you want to approach the mission. However, some don't appear until later missions due to their not being entirely necessary until then. Personally, there wasn't a single time that I needed a weapon that wasn't already included in the game to accomplish the missions.
Team members' actions can slightly be controlled by basic commands like choosing whether they should hold fire, stay put, or telling them to open a door. Very basic but for the most part they serve more as a mobile spawn point should you go down. Support units have their own plan and clear out other areas of the map.
Multiplayer and Coop is there although I haven't attempted these yet. I'll update this review then. But the possibility of running the campaign with friends is present. As for replayability, you can try different difficulty modes, mods, create your own missions, play FireFight which has you clearing levels of enemies, or you can LoneWolf various missions.
Ultimately, this could be viewed as an expansion of sorts but released as it's own game. Nevertheless, one shouldn't over look it because they're comparing it to the classics. Instead, compare it to Call of Duty and then you'll see what I mean.

If you liked the original Ghost Recon and the original Rainbow Six games you'll probably like SoAF. This game isn't quite on the same level as the aforementioned games, but it's definitely up there. In SoAF you can plan your strategy for each level, and execute it in whatever fashion you like. The game feels a little linear at times, but it's also 12 years old now. SoAF is a pretty solid Rainbow Six/Ghost Recon clone, so if you're jonesing for a tactical shooter, then consider getting this game.

I would like to preface this review by saying that I LOVE the original Ghost Recon. I have beaten that game at least eight or nine times. So imagine my surprise when I first load up The Sum Of All Fears and find out that it looks exactly like Ghost Recon! It was developed in 2002, one year after Ghost Recon, by Red Storm Entertainment, so it really shouldn't be a surprise that the engine and essentially everything else is pretty much the exact same. This would most likely be a negative point on most reviews, but considering my love for Ghost Recon, this was very welcome!
However, there are a few changes, and they make this feel more like an expansion pack, rather than a standalone release. The Sum Of All Fears is quite literally a dumbed-down, streamlined version of Ghost Recon. Plain and simple. You don't get to assemble your own squad, the waypoints are pre-plotted for you, the skill-point system is gone, completing special objectives nets you no reward other than personal accomplishment, I could go on. This time, the game is focused on the story, which is actually based on a book, so I don't see why all these features had to be cut out. It's not like they had to spend their time coming up with a plot to this game. Maybe they didn't follow the book, I don't know.
The story follows you, a randomly generated HRT member, as you tear through West Virginia, killing tons of rednecks in news stations and underground complexes. Then, after the second mission, some♥♥♥♥♥♥decided to detonate a nuclear device in a football stadium in the middle of a game. That stadium is in Baltimore, Maryland, and a quick Google search shows that the Baltimore Ravens were completely wiped out by this bomb, along with whatever team they were playing (hopefully the Bengals), as well as hundreds of thousands of fans. If you ever want to get America's attention, you screw with its professional sports. 9/11 has NOTHING on this attack. Those towers were home to about as many national sports teams as Nebraska. Maybe this will take the focus off of 9/11 and this will be the attack everyone refuses to stop milking for the next three decades. That's enough to get the entire country♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥enough to form a special task force in order to hunt down these monsters.
Football is great and all, but what makes me mad about all of this is that the nuke was detonated late December, 2001. The Wire, a prolific television show set in Baltimore, first premiered June 2, 2002. These terrorists effectively destroyed any chance of that show ever being made. Mother. ♥♥♥♥ers. Okay, you don't have to tell me twice, let's go kill everyone even remotely related to the plot.
What did stay in this game is the stiff, tactical shooter gameplay that made Ghost Recon so much fun. One well-placed bullet can take a bad guy down, but that goes both ways. The AI can be a little dumb at times but Jesus Christ, once they get you in their line of sight, it's a mad trigger dash that usually ends in you eating a bullet. I know the game is tactical, and it's trying to be as realistic as it can, but when you get shot and don't die, your character takes about three minutes to forget about everything around him and fliiiinnnch.
I appreciate that the developers actually made your character acknowledge when he's hit in a way other than annoyingly jerking your camera around, but it's really just a death sentence. You have no control when your character decides to do this, so by the time you are playable again, the enemy has probably shot you ten more times, and you are now dead. Good job. Thank god you can switch teammates.
The game doesn't really look too exciting, but something about the slow, trial-and-error gameplay just twists my ♥♥♥♥♥♥s. Filling a bad guy full of lead and then watching dust fly out of him like he's been sitting on a shelf for 3 years prior to this mission is really satisfying to me, and the game has a few extra options that add a little replay value onto it. If you gave me a choice, I would definitely choose Ghost Recon over this, but I'm happy that The Sum Of All Fears exists. There's 12 missions for you to complete, as opposed to Ghost Recon's 15, and in the end, spoiler alert, you do get the guy. But, the damage is already done; that universe still won't have The Wire. Shiiieeeeeeeeeet.
