Take the Cake is a cute and casual platformer.
The player characer is a smoky blob who is on a quest to retrieve stolen cake from robots of mysterious origin. As you would expect from the genre, the player encounters a stream of new environments and mechanics to overcom. The primary mechanics being that you can grow or shrink in size and your feet are conditionally sticky. Jumping into the ceiling from below (or the floor from above, depending on the direction of gravity) will stick you to that particular surface.
These mechanics are how you'll navigate environments and solve the puzzles, which are generally very light. There are optional collectibles availible which inject a little challenge for those looking for it.
Take the cake is cute, competent, and casual, but you may be disappointed if you're looking for a more engaging experience.
Really fun game, has enough content and replayability to warrant the $60 price tag.

Half Borderlands styled dungeon crawl with raid bosses and half Super Monday Night Combat type MOBA shooter.
This game is nothing like Overwatch, but seemingly that doesn't stop people from comparing the two. The only key similarity between the two is the fact that they're both cartoon styled shooters with multiple playable characters. Surprisingly, even though everyone has been slamming this game since release, i gotta say, this game really isn't half bad!
The best part of Battleborn is easily the story mode campaign, in which you set out to clear dungeons of monsters and robots and, well, whatever really. You can play this mode with a maximum of 5 other people and it really is plenty of fun, if you've ever played Borderlands you're right at home here. You unlock new gear after every mission which you can then equip for your characters and make them even more powerful.
Multiplayer in this game is closer to a MOBA than it is to Team Fortress 2, you level up, you kill minions, build turrets and try to kill other players using a plethora of different characters. Fairly basic stuff with a couple of twists, if you've ever played a MOBA this will also be fairly familiar to you.
All in all, the game really is good fun. It's a very strange mix of different genres put into a single package but the value proposition isn't really that bad to be honest. You've got a very replayable single player/coop campaign and the MOBA style multiplayer mode on top of it. There are also bots in case you're wondering if playing with other people might prove an issue because of the small playercount.

DISCLAIMER: I bought this at the discounted price of €23,99.
TL;DR > While I Am Setsuna is cute and its ambiance perfectly crafted, the simplicity of the equipment system and of the combats generally leave you feeling like you played a very, very long demo.
I am NOT recommending this game: I don't think it is worth its price, and it has the same failings as "Child of Light".
So the longer version is that I was honestly pretty disappointed.
When you sell me a game that is supposed to be the spiritual child of Chrono Trigger and Final Fantasy VI, and you put forward a combat system, I expect really nice combat sequences, hard bosses, difficult encounters.
That will never happen in "I am Setsuna".
Much like World of Warcraft, the game generally feels like a power grind. You will almost never die, unless you really try to, and while the combat system is full-feldged, the over-simplicity of the combats themselves means that you never have to really understand it.
On the graphics side, 10/10. Beautifully done, very nice animations, the snow gimmick is nice to look at. The world is willfullly baren, which ends up being a tad boring after a couple of hours of gameplay.
One caveat is that the monsters generally look like cute fluffy creatures you would rather have as pets than kill, but maybe that's just me.
On the general side there are a couple of bugs: doing a print screen while walking will skip a frame, allowing you to pass through walls ; some skills are written in another language than what you have selected (some are entirely written in French when you ahve english selected, for example), but nothing preventing you from enjoying the grame.
One thing that is absolutely horible is the controls.
ESC exits the game, always.
Menus are by default navigated through the J, K keys
More or less everything on the controls side gets some getting used to.
As for the story I won't comment on it seeing as I have yet to finish it. It's touching but pretty stereotyped - nothing to write home about.
Generally speaking I give this game 5/10, with the possibility of being noted 8/10 if it was priced at €20 without discounts.

Could be finished in as little as 20 hours without too much trouble, or take a bit longer if you take your time to see everything there is to see in the game.
Like earlier JRPGs it does run afoul of a few awkwardly written dialogue scenes and does rely heavily on the classic tropes of the genre.  This could be either a positive or a negative depending on the gamer
Overall, if you're a fan of this genre it's definitely worth a look

Would i recommend the game to a casual player who wants an even playing field for everyone... mostly no, that is if you are staying f2p or if you're willing to invest some hefty time into this "amazing" game.
You would think that since this is cs 1.6 with mods that it would run easy on older machines, but you would be wrong there either because there are 2 hack detection softwares running alongside which doesnt even do any good and 1 of which is just a trainwreck in a way that it takes as much cpu as the game itself every 5-8 seconds for a brief moment causing fps drops and making the game one hell of an experience, with lower end machines atleast.
The game also has 5 servers which are: Europe, NA, Russia, SA and Turkey. Now the Europe, russia and turkey servers are pretty good and unless nexon fks up with an update(which has happened in the past, but got fixed pretty fast) the ping should be good, but that is not the case for NA or SA. From what i gather it seems that the SA server only gives good ping to Brazilian players, that is lower than 100, which is well, pretty ♥♥♥♥ty for other SA countries but well, what can you do. Now i dont use NA server that much, but from what i gather the NA server is just horrible, most of the players there have around 200 ping except some rare specimens who get around 20 ping for unknown reasons, i have only heard a rumor that the NA server is located somewhere around other side of russia to which i dont know how true that is.
Now for the updates. All the content(guns, maps, features, etc) updates CSNZ gets comes from cso korea i believe and the time stamp between new update there and here is somewhere around 12-4 months, but mostly its around 6. Updates mostly center around 2 game modes, that is zombie hero and scenario mode, which is understandable since its the 2 main things the game focuses on at the moment, because all other human vs human modes have already been fked with OP guns.
Now, the p2w aspect of this game is what i have heard the most noise about, and i can perfectly agree with that to some extent, to have BEST newest weapons you need special decoders (which are basicaly cases from csgo) which you can only BUY with REAL money, but there are also other decoders which you can get from events for free and which feature older or new and not so strong weapons, but there is also a special event every 6 months that lasts for 1 month called the auction event, which lets you use in game currency to buy most weapons in the game and its the best chance for f2p's to get a brand new arsenal of guns, not including weapons that are newer than 6 months.
Now there are also all kinds of classes(character skins) in the game, which for the most part only give you a slight(5-15%)exp and point boost and all kinds of stats in scenario mode, but there are currently 2 special classes, which are again, p2w exclusive,  which give you certain bonuses in certain game modes, like for example damage display in zombie hero mode and better stats in scenario mode and which feature different hand/glove models.
Now for the game modes, the most important thing about the game. There are dozens of game modes. 11 game modes feature zombie elements, which range from pvp with humans vs zombies, to pve with teaming up with 3 other players and building turrets, watchtowers and some other crazy stuff to defend your base again waves of zombies to after a while, either get rescued by a chopper after certain waves or beat 1 final boss, to pve with 9 other players using your best guns to advance special nexon created maps with swarming zombies a obstacles to finally reach 1 final boss on all kinds of difficulties, to other amazing game modes with cool concept. Now there are 5 human v human game modes, which are original, tdm, dm, gun deathmatch and basic, which most of which are mods from cs 1.6 brought into csnz with basic mode beeing the only exception, but what human v human modes suffer from are insanely OP weapons unless you have classic weapon restrictions which basicaly only lets you use cs 1.6 weapons, which is the only way you are gonna get a normal match. Now there are also mini-game modes such as soccer, which is selfexplanatory, hide and seek which has a cool concept, gotta see it for yourself to understand realy, sudden death which is a number of players in a small map with a knife and a deagle at the center of the map, kinda like mini hunger games if you would, fight yard which is human v human with classic weapons lying on the ground, a mod from cs 1.6 basically, and a hell more minimodes which are pretty fun if you can find a good room where to play.
Now for some random facts which doesnt realy need a section, but still worth mentioning. There are a lot of turks in europe servers, in fact turkey servers are most of the time emty as far as i know. In NA servers the most spoken language is spanish for unkown reasons. This is one of the best purchases I've made on steam this year.  At its heart, it's a Metroidvania-style game, but the surprisingly good gameplay mechanics, atypical but highly amusing lucha libre setting, endearing art style (nice change from all of the retro/pixel games lately), and witty dialogue make this a clear winner among similar games.
Combos are easy to string together, but still offer a lot of versatility. The platforming aspects, while at times challenging and requiring creativity, are not completely unforgiving and don't require split-second precision (i.e., Super Meatboy).  There are enough side quests to add some flavor, without turning the game into a massive collection of fetch quests.  And there's no need for constant backtracking and revisiting old areas (although you do get skills that unlock certain secret/optional rooms, those entrances are clearly marked on your map so you don't have to waste hours checking every wall in every previous area for a secret).
Bottom line, it's just plain fun.

The game is much maliged by long term fans, though I don't really understand it. The game has all the essentials that the first one did. It  may not seem to push the envelope technologically as its predecessor did, but  FEAR 2 isn't a slouch in that regard either. In all, I enjoyed the act of PLAYING much more with this sequel. FEAR was a great game, and it wowed us all with its chip melting tech, but it also felt flimsy at times, almost like being in a diarama, however beautiful. FEAR 2 is solid, like a rock. It has weight, and more importantly, it has colour. What was excised from the formula has, I think, done more to strengthen the gameplay than weaken it. And it's ironic that critics bemoan the perceived loss of certain atmospheric and narrative elements in favour of increased action. Let's face it, FEAR was never 'scary'. It was tense, sure, but Condemned - THAT'S a scary Monolith game. The FEAR series has always been primarily for the action, and this second game delivers.

Gameplay
Casual sandbox physics simulator. Endless possibilities and creative freedom. Besiege offers a growing number of parts/weapons/tools at your disposal to complete a variety of challenges. Physics work believably, constructing and testing different machines is challenging. Each zone consists of one objective and the ability to construct a new machine or edit the previously successful vehicle. Simple in nature but the difficulty slowly rises as you must become more creative in your designs. One zone you might grab and carry boulders to a marker, and the next you could be constructing flying machines to take down gunships.
Controls are widely customizable in terms of part functions. Camera controls are a bit awkward once you start driving/flying your machine, making it frustrating to operate. Currently includes a nice sandbox mode for testing builds. Besiege seems to be regularly updated which is a nice thing to see in an Early Access.
Sound
Fairly absent of any noticeable music, not entirely a downside but it would help break up the silence and occasional animal/soldier sound effects.
Graphics
Simplistic and charming. Environments are created on an endless plane and while these structures are constricted to a small area, they appear more like artistic renders than simply blocks waiting to fall over. Enemies and objects are minimal but beautifully crafted. Destruction works in an enjoyably fluid way, meaning each piece and part reacts accordingly once effected by another object/weapon. Visual effects like fire/smoke/sparks are mesmerizing and even more so once you slow down time using the in-game slider.
Replay Value
A great deal of replay value is possible in Besiege and the increasing number of updates add new parts to tinker with. However this is largely dependent on the players creativity. Starting out it may seem a little rocky but once you familiarize yourself with the function of each part you'll begin to create more intricate machines. Each zone offers the same objective but the creative control aspect makes for an infinite number of ways to complete it.
Wrapping Up
Charming, challenging, and enjoyable. Easy to learn but hard to master. With a very reasonable price tag, Besiege is a solid Early Access title that is shaping up to be an incredibly worthwhile game.

An excellent RTS, have had a blast playing this.
With 3 unique factions to choose from, there is great variety in play style available with the higher level units in each faction offering greatly different approaches to a battle (highly recommend the Infinite War Battle Pack DLC as well!).
The single player campaign offers a story covering 3 friends from different factions as the galaxy is threatened with the possible restart of the epic war that ended at the end of the previous game.  The story itself serves the purpose but is not something you'll get overly concerned about, however the campaign missions themselves do offer a good variety of scenarios to handles that will offer challenges that you won't get in the multi-player side.
I love the play style of this game, more so than other RTS games I've played, which is largely down not having arbitrary rules to restrict the way you play, with 2 key ones being:
The ability to smoothly zoom right out and view the entire map (also multi-monitor support, so you can also keep an interactive map on a second screen)
The ability to build what you want, where you want, so long as you can get a construction unit there safely (not to say that it won't be destroyed by the enemy, but that's a different matter...), no restriction on having to build beside other buildings or within a certain 'zone'
Despite frequent comparisons to it's predecessor, the scale of the battles is still fairly epic (more so than other RTS games I've played) and there are other areas that it is better than the game it follows:
- Unit movement is smoother, moving an army of hundreds of units results in few instances of units getting stuck as the army tries to move through a narrow area or through buildings.
- graphics are clearer and more impressive looking, and seems to handle large armies better in terms of game performance
- more variety in types units available
- streamlined economy management making it easier to keep control of your unit building
Regarding the economy, in this instance you have to have the resources available in order to build a unit, so if you don't have the resources to can't build more but the units already being built will finish building normally.  In SC1 there was income per second and usage per second, the more you build the more your usage per second would be, however when your usage was too high and you ran out of stockpiled resources, everything would grind to a halt - resulting in a few frustrating minutes of trying to find the biggest drains and stopping them so that some units could actually finish building (or worse yet, you would have to switch your shields off since they use your energy as well).   SC1 had a good idea, but IMO was rough in implementation, SC2 however smooths this out so you can concentrate on what matters in an RTS, strategy.
Not to say that SC1 did not have some things better, as most players of both games will point out, SC1 had much larger scale battles and much larger maps.   This is indeed true, but is not an issue that cannot be resolved via the games Modding system - just install one of the available Scale Mods that are available, which will return the game to the scale of SC1 and increase the unit cap  (you can also return to economy model of SC1 if you desire as well)

I sort of feel like this game doesn't get enough credit.  Not to say that there aren't issues.  It seems to have very specific themes it's trying to evoke, rather than touch on a large spectrum of emotions/music/landscapes/etc. like other more grandiose RPGs, which you might call a con.  As in, there's always snow.  It's always serious.  You always hear piano.  Etc.  But I did feel immersed in this world.  The plot seems half-baked sometimes - there are obvious throwbacks to CT/CC, as a little wink to aging JRPG fans like myself - but I don't know that I need much more from a game like this.
The combat system really is fun, though.  At first I didn't understand what the hell Momentum Mode is (many aspects of the game are often not very well explained - for instance, I don't think I got a single recipe until I had already beaten the seven endgame character sidequests), but once I figured it out, it allows for quite a lot of variability.  There are 60+ Triple Techs, and it's fun just fooling around with your spritnite to see what kind of combos you can pull out.  The music is actually quite good, even though all you ever really hear is a piano.  The graphics are splendid, too.
I admit that it's difficult to recommend at full price, but it's 40% off right now, so if you like JRPGs I'd say give it a go.

bit Dungeon II is a tongue-in-cheek mash-up of the The Guardian Legend and Dark Souls, with a Rouge-like(-like-like-like) perma-death consequence system + Diablo-style  "loot treadmill" that propels you (at hilarious speed) through its semi-procedurally generated dungeons.
If it wasn't clear from the game's title (or the way-over-the-top festival of jargon and videogame argot that was my first sentence), this game, like most Rogue-likes, is very self-aware ("self-conscious" might be a better word, with its connotations of over-wrought affect) and the overall game design is extremely sparse/generic (in the literal sense of that word).
All of which is to say that if you're looking for an immersive adventure experience where the mechanics exist as footnotes to the story (and not the other way around), this is probably not the game for you.
Here are three things that I really liked about bit Dungeon II:
- It takes about five minutes to figure out how to play. If you're familiar at all with min/maxing for DPS and high-drain, the learning curve will be practically non-existent.
- You can do a complete run-through in about an hour, if you're about your business and the RNG gods smile upon you (i.e. you get the drops you need when you need them).
- The simple scenario design and the settings are excellent: just really, really good art design and direction throughout. I enjoyed every environment in this game, which...I mean, that's saying a lot.
Here are three things that I didn't like:
- The sound design is garbage: from the idiotic, try-hard EBM chip-tunes to the arbitrary compression and processing on the blips and bloops (seriously: if you worked sound design on this game, you are definitely doing it wrong: play a Jun Fukuda game and try to learn something), I'd say the whole thing is pretty much a tear-down. There are no redeeming aspects to this game's sound design. I hope someone reads that and it hurts their feelings.
- A little more variety in the main character's gear would have gone a long way: the hats are cool, but all other armor looks the same (all boots, for example, are just color-swaps with all other boots).
- I played the game on my Xbone gamepad. Generally, the experience was flawless, except for the bits where I had to navigate menus, e.g. the start and pause menus. I kept doing stuff I didn't want to do because of bad layout or unclear button functions and that could probably use a little clean-up.
tl;dr Definitely play this game: you will have an awesome time.

Pls allow me to say that I truly appreciate the time and effort that the devs obviously put into this game... I love the concept and framework that the Ultimate General Series has built and Civil War is an impressive sequel to Gettysburg... that being said, I hope the next installment ( which I will purchase regardless ) offers much more polish in the end product.
Pros
- Ability to create and custom equip army
- Unique art style
- Great sound
- Multi-stage battles
Cons
- Terrain glitches causing units to get "stuck" ( i.e. water crossings )
- Enemy units practically "flying" across great distances
- Enemy cav sometimes glitches through your lines with no collision at all
- Enemy units route through your lines and reform on your flanks
- Units in melee can be fired upon by nearby units with almost 0 fratricides
- Poor continuity in some of the multi-stage battles ( i.e. Unit dispositions )
- Enemy units seem to have 0 condition/morale modifiers ( allowing them to sprint/reform continuously )
- Routed enemies tend to build up on edges of map rather than fleeing the field
- AI makes outright silly decisions ... ( Too Many )
But I digress... the game needs some polish but this is obviously a labor of love and a definite upgrade in the series

This is by far the best Civil War video game I have ever seen. It is very well made. The campaign is great, and allows you to allocate your army's resources as you see fit - you can choose to have a lot of cavalry, artillery, can choose their weapons - and the differences are meaningful without there being a single obvious best way to go. The battles are pretty well done, and it is not an easy game to master. It takes some time to learn the tricks.
The only downside I'd mention to it is opposed to the last game they made, Ultimate General: Gettysburg. In UG: Gettysburg, each battle would operate in phases and players would have choices about how to deploy during the next phase. For example, on the 1st day of Gettysburg, Union players could choose to pull back to Cemetary Ridge or to try to hold the Confederates at Oak Hill. Confederates could choose whether to do a frontal assault or attack from two sides. In UG: Civil War battles operate in phases, but the phases are pre-selected and don't have to do with your performance. Sometimes this can cause a bit of a headache.

This game is my second one ever on Steam to have > 100 hours invested.  It is excellent in many ways.  I jumped onboard the train right at the beginning because I had played and enjoyed Ultimate General: Gettysburg.  To be honest, I wish I had waited until the official release, as I wound up restarting the campaign several times just to make sure the changes were incorporated along the way.
The battles, strategic, and tactical gameplay in this are top-notch.  Even preparing your armies for battle in camp is an enjoyable experience.  Yes, the game could have a bit more polish and detail, but that said it isn't a premium $60 game.  You get incredible value for $30, and a heck of a fun time to boot!

- 2 level progressions, first one being your commander rank which is your personal rank outside of play and then there's the second one being the in-game level system which resets every time you complete a match, which is a upgrade system for that one match, what it does is it gives you helix points to upgrade your character (This can be the means of changing a special attack to make it function differently for example)
- Devs are communicating alot with the community! as well as putting in changes from feedback of the community
- Campaign with up to 9 missions each can last up to 30 or so minutes
- Spec ops, which is the dlc content of this game, they're special missions which lasts around 15-25 minutes and is packed with a bunch of lore! they use a system with "ops points" which makes the game harder the more you earn them along with unlocking skins, taunts, and titles for you to use- There is still one more yet to come!
- Each character has a set of challenges they can do, example: kill (this thing) (this many times) which will unlock xp for the character as well as credit, some specific ones unlock taunts.
-Loot boxes and gears which is dropped by minibosses and bosses, can also be bought with credits you earn from a game which gives you small bosts such as more shield strength or damage.
with gear there comes loadouts, you can put up to 3 gears in a single loadout to put into a match which you need to pick up shards to active (shards is the in-game currency to buy turrets, traps and giant robots to help you in your defense or attack)
- Good balancing, some things might be alittle strong but nothing too gamebreaking, it's mostly about knowing your enemy and working together as a team
- There are 4 gamemodes in this game currently along with 3 maps for each mode

there is 3 control points you need to hold to win (the more control points you own the more points you get) There's structures you can build to speed your allies up, verelsi scouts spawn too which when killed drops shards and shared xp to you and your teammates
Defend your (2) sentries from being destroyed by the enemies, aswell as trying to destroy their own, there are multiple structures you can build to defend your sentry with- along with the merc camps, on which you need to kill thrall mercs to get these mercs to fight for you.
2 lane gamemode, Prevent the enemy from sacrificing their minions to the altar while trying to get your own into theirs, when the score hits 300 or if there is 10 minutes left of the match the gamemode will go into the "Finale" on which teams gets super minions, if a team gets one of their super minion in their last altar, they win instantly.
A gamemode which shares the same maps as capture does, but the objective is to kill verelsi (AI) which is scattered around in stations on the map, and collect their masks, at the middle of the map there is the delivery point of the masks which scores your team points, only two times in the entire match you're going to fight a boss verelsi which drops alot of maks for you to pick up.

Every person who approaches this game can have a unique introduction to the story depending on what words they search for and how they piece things together.

bit Dungeon II is the sequel to the popular free to play game, bit Dungeon (duh!).  After the success of their first title, they decided to create another one with some improvements here and there.
There's no intricate story, and this game doesn't need one.  It's simply drops you into the world and you begin your run.  The actual story is that your loved one has passed away and you want to meet with her again, so you clear the dungeons, etc.
I fully recommend this game, not just for the initial play through, but because you can come back to it later and play through it again if you'd like.
I'm going to break this review down into a few sections so it's easy to digest.
Upon clicking "Start Game" you'll be dropped into the game world with no armor or weapons.  If you press the "ESC" button, it will pause and bring up a menu that explains the very simple controls.  I chose to play with a keyboard because I didn't feel like getting my game controller back out (laziness).
After beginning, you're left to gather up weapons and armor, fight enemies to earn EXP and gain levels, and wander around the overworld clearing the 6 dungeons.  Because the game's difficulty and levels scale with your own level, you can tackle the dungeons in any order you'd like.  This leaves it up to the player to choose their strategy.  I really like that aspect about of the game.
At the end of each dungeon, you will fight a boss and upon winning - receive a chest with a powerful weapon (random).
You have 1 extra life, so if you die, you lose that life - but you can pick it back up in the same position that you died.  A tactic I highly suggest doing.  If you die twice, it's game over and you start back at level 1 and the game resets.
Upon clearing the overworld, you enter the Dark World, and from there you clear another dungeon, fight some bosses and clear the game.  You can actually start back at the beginning and clear the game AGAIN with the items and levels you already gained.  Meaning you can grind and grind until you get totally sick of the game.
This is where bit Dungeon II shines a lot.  The overworld stays the same between play throughs, but the inside of each dungeon will be different.  There is, I believe, 7 different layouts, and 6 dungeons total (correct me if I'm wrong!).  So that means that you're going to have some variation each time you play.  Of course, you'll memorize these if you play through a few times, or die a few times, but it still keeps things fresh.
The actual dungeons are identical to the old Legend of Zelda games.  I mean, they have the same look and feel, and that makes this game super easy to pick up and progress through.
As I mentioned before, you earn EXP and gain levels from fighting enemies and bosses.  The enemies and bosses own levels scale with yours, so that allows you to progress through the game in any order you'd like.
The weapons, armor, and accessories you pick up also scale with your levels, so you can keep getting stronger and stronger.
Each item you pick up carries some stat boosts, so you can pick and choose which items have the best stat boosts for your current play through or "skill" set.
As for the weapons, there's one handed weapons, two handed weapons, ranged weapons, and magic weapons.  It's up to you which one you use.  All of them have their pros and cons.
Since I played on the keyboard, it was just WASD and then mashing the spacebar A LOT.  Some people might not care for this, I didn't mind it.
I can honestly say the graphics are enjoyable for what it is - it's supposed to be a retro inspired game.  I love the graphics, but that's just me.
The music was enjoyable, different music for different areas.  The sound effects are the basic 8 bit sounds.  I love that about the game as well.
There's 15 achievements, and I would say the average full play through from start to finish, should unlock all of the achievements.  You get one for each boss fight, and then you get one for picking up certain items, and so on.
I think I covered most of the aspects of the game.  I paid under a dollar for this while it was on sale and I'm happy with my purchase.
It took me a little over 3 hours to fully complete the game and all of the achievements, granted I died a few times before I got the hang of it.  But after seeing that I'm transported back to the start of the game with my newly acquired armor and weapons, along with my levels - I can see me coming back to this game.  Perhaps even speedrunning it at some point (yes people run this game).
In closing, do I recommend bit Dungeon II?  Absolutely!  You should grab it and play the crap out of it.  Just watch the video for the game and you'll see what it's all about.  If you're into these types of game, you're going to really enjoy this title.

Let me preface by saying that I've not played any other Metal Gear Solid title; I have no real basis of comparison.
This is a decent stealth/cover 3rd person action/shooter.
Pros:
The gunplay feels fairly satisfying, and while the game would certainly prefer for you to take your enemies alive and Fulton them away to safety/employment, you're not really obligated to do so.
The weapon customization is welcome.  Many of the choices are largely cosmetic, but the ability to choose a short barrel vs a long barrel, or swap your medium-power combat rifle ammo for a smaller supply of high power sniper rifle ammo, is helpful.  The most important aspects of customization, for me, are suppressor, optics, and underbarrel attachments.
Mission rewards feel tangible.  You do something, you get paid for it.
Lots of side missions that let you experiment with different play styles.  Open world lets you wander around and kill/extract whoever you want at your own pace.  Not a great way to make money, but a good way to get personnel and resources.
Cons:
The cover and stealth mechanics don't feel as tight as those in, say, Splinter Cell: Blacklist.  They're functional enough for the game, but I frequently find myself trying to stick to a wall and getting spotted by an enemy 150 ft away, despite the fact that every other time I've immediately covered next to that wall.
The tech tree unlocks are clearly resource/time sinks, and unlocking the various trees frequently doesn't give any new customization parts, just a new base model.  As the game has no resource or time cap, it makes everything feel a little... unimportant.
I have no idea what the ♥♥♥♥ is going on in the story.  None at all.  I'll admit I haven't prioritized it heavily, but I went from apparently nuclear powered robots the size of skyscrapers with unpronouncible names in Afghanistan, to rescuing war orphans and avoiding gratuitously nude zombie snipers in Africa, and there was something about a disease whose infection vector is the language you speak?  Like, this is all over the place.  What the hell?
The online connectivity is a little unstable.  Not usually a huge problem, but when a large portion of your cash and resources are stored online (why, exactly?), it's frustrating to suddenly lose access to them due to server instability.  Oh, also, if you are doing a FOB mission (Adversarial PvE with decent rewards) and you get disconnected?  Instant fail with maximum penalty.
Overall verdict: It's not a compelling narrative, but it's good casual fun.  I'd personally recommend picking up on sale, and playing with a gamepad.

The Good: Excellently crafted story, likeable characters, dialog choices are fun, engaging combat, deep customization and leveling, captures the Star Wars feel perfectly
The Bad: Weird combat problems, ugly and dated visuals, stiff animations and some iffy voice acting, some dialog trees are just broken or off, every planet is laid out to similarly
BioWare is a company that revolutionized the action RPG genre for the western era. In a time where Japanese RPGs dominated the market, BioWare was sitting in a little studio churning out one of the best RPGs of all time. I remember when I was younger how much of a big hoopla this game was. For someone who didn't own an Xbox or a PC that could run the game it still slipped under my radar. I eventually got a chance to rent the game years later on 360 and quickly got bored due to its age. I finally picked it up again on the PC and I am glad I did. The game may feel very dated and old (an entire decade), but there's no denying the excellent story and well crafted atmosphere that truly feels genuine in the Star Wars universe.
You play a custom character that has to defeat the evil Sith Lord Darth Malak. He has found some sort of Star Forge to use against the Republic, so you are shadowing his footsteps to find the Star Maps to this Star Forge. This takes you across several planets such as Tatooine, Dantooine, Kashyyyk, Korriban, Yevin, and even Taris. You acquire companions along the way of all types and endure some pretty tough battles and story choices. You have to constantly choose between the light and dark side during choices, and there's plenty of ways to go about the story.
Firstly, you can choose any world in any order. Each one is roughly laid out the same with a large hub area then an area beyond where your main quest and some side quests lie. I got rather annoyed with the constant similar layouts and wished for variety. Each world has the Star Map area blocked off until you fix some global catastrophe on the planet. Some are so serious that your decision will determine if you are allowed back on later. Besides running around and talking to people to get quests and buy stuff, the combat and customization is fathoms deep; fans will be pleased.
You can customize your character with a plethora of items such as implants, shields, different weapons from lightsabers, blasters, vibroblades, belts, armor, robes, headgear, and I haven't even started on leveling up. You should pick your character based on how you're going to fight. I chose to use melee weapons because you eventually go through Jedi training and get your first lightsaber. I have to say that this brought a smile on my face when I inserted my crystals and watched my character whip around those sabers with the classic lightsaber sounds. Nothing can top that.
The game allows you to customize all your items by inserting upgrades that you find or buy. This is mandatory because there really isn't a "most powerful weapon in the game". You just get a powerful weapon and you have to upgrade it or it won't do you much good. Other than this there is the deep leveling system. You can choose an attribute, feat, power, and skill. Feats effect what you use physically in combat and what combat attacks you can use. Powers are force powers and there are plenty of them. All light and dark powers you can possibly think of are here. I had a lot of fun using them in combat and getting an edge over certain enemies. The level cap is at 20, but most people probably won't even hit that by the end. I finished at level 18 and didn't have too hard of a time finishing it. You can even choose how your companions level up because you can control them too! This is great for people who like a variety and can't have every skill available for your character.
Combat is turned based with die rolling behind the scenes. I really would have like real-time combat, but what's here is exciting and fun on its own. There are tons of different enemies to fight on each planet, and some are harder than others. I found the game really hard at first, but after a while you will level up and find the game very balanced. There are some issues in combat that just really annoyed me. There seems to be a targeting problem in small areas. When you click your action you want the characters will get stuck in an endlessly looping animation if there is someone in their way. This can cause you a battle because you have to disengage and restart the attack or move around the obtrusion. This happened quite a lot, but you will learn to just live with it.
While the story is interesting and choosing how dialog will change it is fun, there are some issues here. Instead of your choice being final, some dialog trees will allow you to go back and change your answer or no matter how you persuade or force persuade neither will work and you can't continue the dialog. This is usually in side missions, but I have never seen the persuade option fail so much in a BioWare game. No matter how much I leveled up my persuasion attribute I failed an awful lot. Other than this though, my other issue is that some dialog just drags on way too long. I found myself skipping a lot of it or just reading ahead of the voices. These, again, are just minor issues that can be overlooked.
The graphics in the game look old and terrible these days, but back in the day they looked amazing. I can see why it looked so good then, but you can still feel the Star Wars atmosphere and that's what counts the most. The character models and animations are stiff, blocky, and repeat a lot, but overall it works. Even some of the voice acting is spotty at best, but overall it is pretty good.
KotOR is an amazing Star Wars experience, but the age may turn a lot of people off. My biggest issue of all is that the game doesn't give any clues on where to go ever. You get no hints and are left on your own to just figure out what to do. I had to use a walkthrough through most of the game because I had no idea where to go, or some quests were very cryptic. This is a huge no-no for me and really hurt the score the most. Overall, this is an amazing Star Wars game and any Star Wars fan will love this game.
~Score: 8/10

Star Wars Knights Of The Old Republic Review
Intro. Star Wars Knights Of The Old Republic or KOTOR for short is a classic video game. It is one of Bioware's first RPG it is a very popular game from 2003. This game is the precursor to Bioware's Mass Effect and Dragon Age games.
Pros
1 Star Wars KOTOR is a great roleplaying game with a great story that is comparable to the quality of the starwars movies. It has a very interesting plot with a very imersive world, well written characters, is true to Star Wars lore and is a joy to play through multiple times for the story alone.
2 The gameplay in the game is very fun your decisions in the game have benefits and negative if you decide to follow the dark side or the light side of the force. There are often many different outcomes to a quest, adding more to the replay value. The games combat is similar to dungeons and dragons with attack damage calculated like a dice role, so how much damage you do can depend on luck making the game more challenging. There are also many mini games throughout the story adding variety such as swoop racing, space fights, card games, arena battles and riddles just to name a few. The game does not feel repetitive with all the extra mini games.
3 The mods for this game are wonderfully done there are well over 1000 mods for KOTOR including, KOTOR 1 restoration mod, yavin IV planet mod, Solomon revenge the brotherhood of shadow, and many many more mods. There are many mods that fix parts of the game you may not like mods adding content mods fixing bugs, and mods restoring lost content. Some of the fan mods even have voice acting, 3D textures, dialogue and extra stories that are higher quality than the content in the game. Most KOTOR mods come with a TSL patcher that makes installing and uninstalling them very simple just run the installer to install the mod.
Cons
1 A rule is said about KOTOR and that is that it's impossible to run KOTOR without the game crashing on you at least once. The game even crashes in speed runs. The game is really buggy and unfortunately many of the wonderful mods don't help how the game can crash during cutscenes, movies, loading screens and such. The game can be fixed to run well even on modern systems. I have played through the game on windows 10 both the steam and disk version and it had some issues but I was able to beat the game with only a few crashes. The community support to fix any issues you might have is very good but there are many problems in KOTOR due to the game running in a awful engine. Despite you likely having to change game settings a few times and it crashing on you a few times I still recommend the game. If you want a game just like this that is more stable and crashes less try KOTOR the sith lords 2, but I am one of those people who think KOTOR 1 is  better.
2 The game is very old and does not look very good. The game looks like a ps2 era game and is quite dated by today's standards. There are many mods that improve the graphics of the game, there are mods the redo most of the textures in the game even texture mods that fix the textures of mod content so if you don't mind installing a few texture mods you can improve the look of the game Its effects animations sounds and much more. The game even with all of the setting cranked all the way up and with all the texture mods the game looks much better but still looks dated but it doest look like its 10 years old if you mod it.
3 KOTOR had some issues with the game being rushed and it having cut content. KOTOR the sith lords had this issue too but that game at least had a new steam update that officially added that mod content into the game, adding controller support, and improving the games performance. Sadly KOTOR 1 does not have these improvements but some day it may get such improvements. The game feels well made in a few areas but empty in other parts of the game. You will want to mod the game to get more content because the old KOTOR series 1&2 had development issues.
Thoughts
Kotor 1 is a classic and a excellent game despite these issues. if you want a more stable game I would recommend you try KOTOR 2 but I personally found KOTOR 1 much more fun as i have beaten the game multiple times while I liked KOTOR 2 but I could never enjoy it enough to play it through. I think KOTOR 1 had better sound was more imersive as a story, was more fun, and it has more mods than KOTOR 2. The best way to describe this is if mass effect or dragon age was a Star Wars game but older. The game was the first bioware game to have the first "romance scene" ;)
To Conclude
Do I recommend you buy this game? Yes I do recommend this to anyone who wants a fun game with a great story, TONS of awesome mod content, a game that immersises you in the star wars universe like no other game I have ever played and is really fun and has great replay value. If you consider mod content to the game it has enough replay value to play the game over 12 times playing each class each difficulty, each mod that is incompatible with other mods and playing different decisions. The game is unstable and will crash on you at least once but I found the steam version to crash less than my disk version of the game. I recommend that you buy the game and see all the wonderful mod content, the great story and get immersed  into the world of starwars in a story as good or better than the starwars movies.

tldr: The best new game in this genre in a decade.  Civil war improves most aspects of the general simulator genre.
The battles: fun, easy to get into, difficult to master.  Best interface/userinteractions in a game like this by a wide margin, ever.  The AI isn't great (I'm a big proponent of human opponents), but it's still really fun because...
The armies: Rather than moving units around a campaign map you choose from battles from different years of the campaign.  The army management system has more in common with xcom than it does total war.  At times it can feel a little tedious (I felt the same way about managing 20+ xcom soldiers) but it also adds a lot of depth to the game.   Want to win at Gettysburg as the Confederates.  Be prepared to spend many many lives and still not make your objectives.  30,000 men died fighting me to a draw on normal mode and those lives were simply not replaceable.   You're left locked in the same proposition that the North and South found themselves in during the war - the South needing decisive, efficient victories and the north needing a bloodbath.
Campaign evolution: Over the course of the campaign new guns come into use, earthworks and trenches proliferate, and the size of your army grows vastly.   The new guns drastically increase the killing power of each brigade, especially defenders, and pose interesting problems and opportunities for each side.  In the first battles you're handling maybe 4-6 brigades and in the final years of the campaign you could have something like 150.  You may need to set aside an afternoon for some of the battles: your left-side flanking maneuver might be made up of 25 units (maybe as many as 40 if you've sent out all your skirmishers).
This is a great game and it will influence many games to come in this genre.

I'm not exactly sure what my purpose in the game is other than killing enemies and defeating dungeons in different areas that are designed around a certain color palette and elemental theme (forest, jungle, nether, ice, desert, etc.). Thankfully there are no puzzles in this game when it comes to progressing forward in the dungeons, you just have to hit every button you find, pick up the keys, unlock the doors, and keep moving.
My first run through I got to level 3 before dying. Second time was similar, as was the third and fourth time. The fifth time, however, I got through the game once and then died at Lvl 83. As you can see, it's very easy to master and the only thing stopping you from progressing is failing to pick up stronger gear that are color-coded for your convenience in regards to overall rarity and strength. White -> Blue -> Green -> Purple -> Orange -> Red. Funnily enough, White, Blue and Purple were the most commonly found in my fifth playthrough, while Green was just as rare to find as Red. Funny, eh.
Bonfires are spread throughout the lands and offer both a full restoration of health and a quick look at your stats. They have unlimited uses, which is awesome. Another thing to mention is that you will not lose all your accumulated moolah when you die as long as you don't delete your save. You do start from the beginning at Lvl. 1 with no armor or weapons, but you are seamlessly reintroduced to the beginning with some weapons being located right next to your respawn point, which allows you to get back into the action.
The bosses were fairly easy for me: Just get up close and keep wailing on them. As soon as I found a strong enough 2-Handed Axe, Hammer, or Sword I abandoned the shield in favor of pure power. I also avoided magic staffs and bows because they take up much more stamina/magic than simply swinging a sword, even if you have to get up close and personal with enemies. It's much like Hotline Miami where foes don't bother you if you just get in there quick and hit them before they hit you. They're also scaled to your level so you won't encounter the problem where you're getting barely anything for experience when you kill an enemy that you first met at the beginning of the game; everything is still a threat but much less so if you paid mind to upgrade your gear.
It's very fun and the achievements are very easy to get; in theory you could get them all in one persistent playthrough.

So I believe I am ready to write a review for this game. It's been about two months and I feel that the game has progressively albit slowly gotten better. It is still an intense game visually speaking and there is no way (that I know of) to turn down or turn off effects from various abilities. Star Wars Knights Of The Old Republic Review
Intro. Star Wars Knights Of The Old Republic or KOTOR for short is a classic video game. It is one of Bioware's first RPG it is a very popular game from 2003. This game is the precursor to Bioware's Mass Effect and Dragon Age games.
Pros
1 Star Wars KOTOR is a great roleplaying game with a great story that is comparable to the quality of the starwars movies. It has a very interesting plot with a very imersive world, well written characters, is true to Star Wars lore and is a joy to play through multiple times for the story alone.
2 The gameplay in the game is very fun your decisions in the game have benefits and negative if you decide to follow the dark side or the light side of the force. There are often many different outcomes to a quest, adding more to the replay value. The games combat is similar to dungeons and dragons with attack damage calculated like a dice role, so how much damage you do can depend on luck making the game more challenging. There are also many mini games throughout the story adding variety such as swoop racing, space fights, card games, arena battles and riddles just to name a few. The game does not feel repetitive with all the extra mini games.
3 The mods for this game are wonderfully done there are well over 1000 mods for KOTOR including, KOTOR 1 restoration mod, yavin IV planet mod, Solomon revenge the brotherhood of shadow, and many many more mods. There are many mods that fix parts of the game you may not like mods adding content mods fixing bugs, and mods restoring lost content. Some of the fan mods even have voice acting, 3D textures, dialogue and extra stories that are higher quality than the content in the game. Most KOTOR mods come with a TSL patcher that makes installing and uninstalling them very simple just run the installer to install the mod.
Cons
1 A rule is said about KOTOR and that is that it's impossible to run KOTOR without the game crashing on you at least once. The game even crashes in speed runs. The game is really buggy and unfortunately many of the wonderful mods don't help how the game can crash during cutscenes, movies, loading screens and such. The game can be fixed to run well even on modern systems. I have played through the game on windows 10 both the steam and disk version and it had some issues but I was able to beat the game with only a few crashes. The community support to fix any issues you might have is very good but there are many problems in KOTOR due to the game running in a awful engine. Despite you likely having to change game settings a few times and it crashing on you a few times I still recommend the game. If you want a game just like this that is more stable and crashes less try KOTOR the sith lords 2, but I am one of those people who think KOTOR 1 is  better.
2 The game is very old and does not look very good. The game looks like a ps2 era game and is quite dated by today's standards. There are many mods that improve the graphics of the game, there are mods the redo most of the textures in the game even texture mods that fix the textures of mod content so if you don't mind installing a few texture mods you can improve the look of the game Its effects animations sounds and much more. The game even with all of the setting cranked all the way up and with all the texture mods the game looks much better but still looks dated but it doest look like its 10 years old if you mod it.
3 KOTOR had some issues with the game being rushed and it having cut content. KOTOR the sith lords had this issue too but that game at least had a new steam update that officially added that mod content into the game, adding controller support, and improving the games performance. Sadly KOTOR 1 does not have these improvements but some day it may get such improvements. The game feels well made in a few areas but empty in other parts of the game. You will want to mod the game to get more content because the old KOTOR series 1&2 had development issues.
Thoughts
Kotor 1 is a classic and a excellent game despite these issues. if you want a more stable game I would recommend you try KOTOR 2 but I personally found KOTOR 1 much more fun as i have beaten the game multiple times while I liked KOTOR 2 but I could never enjoy it enough to play it through. I think KOTOR 1 had better sound was more imersive as a story, was more fun, and it has more mods than KOTOR 2. The best way to describe this is if mass effect or dragon age was a Star Wars game but older. The game was the first bioware game to have the first "romance scene" ;)
To Conclude
Do I recommend you buy this game? Yes I do recommend this to anyone who wants a fun game with a great story, TONS of awesome mod content, a game that immersises you in the star wars universe like no other game I have ever played and is really fun and has great replay value. If you consider mod content to the game it has enough replay value to play the game over 12 times playing each class each difficulty, each mod that is incompatible with other mods and playing different decisions. The game is unstable and will crash on you at least once but I found the steam version to crash less than my disk version of the game. I recommend that you buy the game and see all the wonderful mod content, the great story and get immersed  into the world of starwars in a story as good or better than the starwars movies.

TL;DR: Knights of The Old Republic is a classic RPG and an essential purchase for Star Wars or RPG fans. If you are a casual gamer, or do not want to any reading, I would pass on this game. The textures may be outdated, but the gameplay and atmosphere stand strong. The depth of this game is incredible, and titles like these come MAYBE once a decade.
So, I get why you make not like KOTOR.
It's slow to start.
You have to learn D&D terminology and do a little internet research to make a good build.
It's turn-based and feels awkward at times.
The narrative drags along at first, and since you don't begin as a sith-slaying god like Obi-Wan or Skywalker, you may want to quit out of boredom.
But honestly, please give this game a few hours to see if you like it. Knights of The Old Republic is one of the best and most in-depth things about the Star Wars franchise, and definitely their best game next to Battlefront II and Republic Commando.
You begin as a lowly republic soldier whose fate lines up with some heavy hitters in the galaxy. While KOTOR sort-of starts off like Morrowind, where you assist a character in saving the world, it is soon up to you to bring down the Sith armies and rival gangs, and to restore order to the galaxy.
On your journey, you will have to make many black-and-white moral decisions that have little to no ambiguity, and pretty barebones consequences. I don't really mind this honestly: it's Star Wars, not exactly a franchise known for grey areas.
You will also meet many well-rounded and relatable characters along the way:
Carth Onasi is a hardened Republic soldier who's seen more than his fair share of combat, and holds deep inner turmoil for what happened in his past. He tries to keep on the mission at hand, and is a strong leader despite his occasional cynicism.
Mission Vao and Zaalbar are two rebellious, street-smart characters who are on the run, and have to look out for each other to survive. Their bond reminds me of something out of a movie.
And the list goes on. KOTOR's allies that you discover on your journey to the light or dark side are ultimately what make this game so much fun. You may often see your allies talk amongst themselves, and occasionally even fight over small issues. This creates a sort of humanity and real vibe to the world you are playing in.
KOTOR also divulges topics like religion, politics, racism, and more, often directly in the dialogue, or in situations with NPCs in the world. I've had to save racially oppressed aliens more than a few times from the punk♥♥♥♥♥humans.
The Empire, while not an official superpower yet, holds control over the planets they conquer in a fascist, do-as-we-say kind of government. This was very interesting to see, as similar imagery directly alludes to Nazi Germany in The Force Awakens.
The items and environments in KOTOR are fantastic and do the franchise great justice. Nothing I saw in-game took me out of the experience in any way, and the pace felt fine as I played.
There are also many things to do apart from the "main story": you can help merchants, save or kill civilians, break into apartment rooms, go after bounty hunters or do bounties yourself, participate in duels, gamble, race swoop bikes, and the list goes on and on.
While KOTOR sticks to the basic premise of jedi=good, sith=evil, there is enough creativity in the story for you to be the character you want to be. The story is not a one-note, drab playthrough; there are many different ways to play. The characters feel human enough that there is often moral conflict when in different situations.
Honestly, I haven't even finished the game and I could write forever. KOTOR belongs up there with the likes of Baldur's Gate, Planescape: Torment, Deus Ex, and System Shock 2 for the best RPGs of all time.
Get this if you like Star Wars or RPGs.

Her Story is quite a novel way to present an interactive story game - on one hand it's daring and innovative, on the other it has its flaws. One aspect that can be considered a flaw is that it's not very realistic despite using FMV - what the player does in the game doesn't make any sense in real life. You have to find video fragments to reassemble an old crime story - you can search for words (apparently the fragments are text indexed), and you can find more clue words in the videos. IRL you'd just pull out all the fragments and reassemble them (yeah, the game comes up with a reason why, but it's kinda lame to be honest).
But, as we know, it's a video game, and it doesn't have to be realistic to be good. The story and the acting are very well done, so if you manage to suspend your disbeliefs, hunting for the main story elements, then the small details to fill the gaps can be quite engaging. As it's done in a sandboxy manner, it is inevitable that it becomes a little flat towards the end with lots of fruitless searching, but until you figure out the main plot outline, it's really first class fun.
You'll get through the best part in 60-90 minutes, so adjust your expectations accordingly. From my side, it's definitely recommended.

While it keeps most of the mechanics of Shank, Shank 2 is ruined by the need to carefully block opponents instead of building awesome combos like in its predecessor. This not only messes with the fluidity of the game, but spoils most of the fun as well. It's a shame too, because it could be a very promising title. Would not recommend unless you are very much into defence driven action. If not, the first Shank will keep you more than satisfied.

The original Shank and Shank 2 are fundamentally the same game. You will be doing the same combos with the same weapons on the same enemies.
They did add some fun tidbits such as weapons enemies drop that you can then pick up and beat other enemies with. Some of those weapons are insanely powerfull which only adds to the fun. However, I did not find myself using most of weaker pickups because the game’s balance was more focused on Shank’s default weapons so you cannot combo as well or as quick.
Bosses are considerably more enjoyable than the original Shank. While they are fundamentally repetitive, they feel challenging. Add that to the bosses are no longer tanking you with their health pool and you have a very enjoyable experience that will leave you screaming at your screen with excitement.
Another definite positive is enemy animations. Though it might be unimportant to game play, it defiantly adds to atmosphere. After a brutally insane and satisfying combo, it is fun to watch your beaten enemies roll around on fire or with limbs missing.
However the biggest negative is the story. If the story was bad in the first Shank, it is even worse in Shank 2. The story seems to have no point what so ever and you will find yourself wishing it was not there. The ability to skip cut scenes is the greatest thing I could hope for while playing Shank 2.

After playing 100+ hours in this game I am disappointed that it suffers from the same issues it predecessor Ultimate General: Gettysburg did. Although some fun improvements have been made, they ultimately don’t make that game worth the time.
The Good
The new army camp screen where the player can build their army is an excellent addition.  Recruiting and leveling new brigades and officers, outfitting them with better weapons, and spending reputation points for more money or better weapons gives the player a real sense of achievement as they progress through the campaign.  Sadly this is the only positive for this game.
The Bad
1:  The balance in this game in non-existent.  2000 men infantry brigades routing to 150 men skirmisher brigades and melee cavalry brigades with 3x the men being unable to rout or even push back lone artillery brigades to name a few examples.  Yes I know I about being flanked, that is not the issue.  The balance is also incredibly inconsistent for player vs the AI.  When the player is on defense with superior cover that AI brigades seem to have a much easier time dislodging and routing them player does in the opposite situation.
2:  Since the battles are recreations of actual events it makes them very scripted which is to be expected, but that takes away a lot of the potential strategy a player could employee to achieve a better victory with less loss of men.  Combine this with a battle that has the player attacking a defending AI and the player is guaranteed to take more losses in men and equipment then with be rewarded for winning the battle.  On several occasions I tried to flank the enemy lines only to have the enemy receive reinforcements from behind me making the flanking maneuver pointless.
3:  Any battle that is more attacking of a defending AI will always result in a net loss for the player-ALWAYS.  Try to be smart and flank the enemy, nope doesn’t work.  Try to do something other than continuously throw brigades against a defending entrenched AI, not gonna work/would take too long for the time provided.  Even if you manage to win a Victory in the battle it will cost you more money to rebuild your army than what is gifted to you for the Victory.
I want to like this game but there are many issues and inconsistencies that make it more aggravating than its worth.  If you can buy it on sale for less than 5 bucks I’d say go for it, but otherwise don’t waste your money.

Ultimate General: Civil War is a fun game when you first play it. I've even written a few guides for the game.
It bills itself as an authentic historical game with good AI. At first glance, the game does all of this wonderfully.
Deeper analysis of the game reveals fundamental design problems that only become visible with time.
Many of these problems are known to the developers. However due to the mechanism the devs use to solicit feedback these issues remain unaddressed since early access. Other problems are more fundamental, such as a lack of true player agency (a la Mass Effect 3)
Once you get past being beaten by the AI in the beginning and get used to the quirks of the game then the advertised 'strong' AI vanishes. Each map basically devolves into one of two strategies depending on if you are on offense or defense.
The challenge the AI provides against you is not in the AI being smart. Rather the challenge is in the sheer numbers the AI has versus you.
The problem gets worse if you play on half speed. With careful micromanagement, it's possible to defeat armies with 5x the number of men you have as well as drive back the relentless AI charges (if you aren't playing offensively that is). You can even cancel AI charges if you do things right. The AI pretty much always reacts the same way to you and it is easy to learn how the AI reacts and do the same thing every game. This is a regression from UG:GB where the AI had different personalities and acted differently.
Some of these problems with AI involve various bugs. These include AI breaking charges if you reposition units, AI favoring charges even if the unit is exhausted (which you can halt the advance by micromanaging artillery). Others are more fundamental. For example, early on in early access the AI had problems defending their artillery. So the game devs, instead of making the AI better at defending their artillery, made artillery invincible to melee.
Similar examples of game mechanic problems exist elsewhere. Melee mechanics were broken since early access. 2 brigades of 200 men in melee will perform 4x casualties as 1 brigade with 400 men in melee. Thus, some players (in a single player game mind you) liked to stack lots of tiny cavalry brigades and abuse the melee mechanic bug to beat battles. This bug was reported and these players complained the game was 'too easy'. Instead of fixing the broken melee system (or *gasp* asking the players to not use such strategies in a single player game), it was decided that 'cavalry was too powerful' (since this was the most commonly abused unit). Thus, cavalry got nerfed to the ground so much that the only way to use them is to abuse the melee bug. A 400 men cavalry brigade can't even chase down 90 skirmishers without getting routed.
These issues of game design, where bugs are not fixed but instead hidden, permeates to the entire game. It results in unrealistic situations that hurts realism of the game. Such as 750 cavalrymen who manage to surprise 200 artillerymen from the rear failing to beat the 200 artilleryman and instead being routed and losing half your men. BUT if those very same 750 cavalrymen were dismounted before engaging the artillery, then the results won't be as disastrous (AI will still not lose men though thanks to invincible AI artillery). It results in the best way of dealing with artillery being shooting them (and eating canisters to the face) rather than charging the cannons. It results in on harder difficulties having to play the game a certain way rather than having true agency.
On the topic of player agency, UG:Civil War does a poor job of this. On easier difficulties player agency is somewhat there as the AI is not gifted tons of men to produce artificial difficulty. Thus as the game goes on if you manage to defeat the AI (where the AI loses 3-5x your men) the AI won't be able to reinforce. This creates other problems such as the 2nd half of the campaign being too easy.
Due to this complaint (and also due to complaints from players exploiting game bugs and AI weakness on higher difficulties) combined with the lack of difficulty levels, hard and legendary difficulties are not only incredibly broken but also unfun, a tedious chore, and lack player agency. The AI patently ignores the 'army intelligence' screen where you see how many men it should have and deploys much more men than the number shown. This means you can't play with a small, elite army that's lowered the AI army strength, no, you have to bring as much men as possible.
Since the game ignores the army strength on higher difficulties there's no point to capturing or killing AI at all. Instead it's a matter of force preservation (since you only get limited recruits). As the AI is gifted a new army each time you destroy an army, the facade of player agency collapses completely. It simply does not matter what you do or how many men the AI loses.
Fundamentally these problems are a result of a lack of dynamic campaign. This is compounded by game bugs exploited by players on hard/legendary that were never fixed which makes the game 'too easy' for them. Or the lack of a true dynamic campaign where you can choose to end the war early if you manage to defeat the enemy army.
No, the solution chosen by the devs was to brush the bugs under the rug and just give the AI more men (or men invulnerable to their weakness such as invincible artillery). This doesn't result in a fun game. Rather it results in a game where battles become a CHORE to micromanage and abuse AI weaknesses (not to mention all the small bugs which still have not been fixed). It's not any more challenging or hard in a tactical level.
One aggravating factor which lead to these decisions has to do with feedback. Due to the many different ways one can play a game, issues which may crop up for some players may not crop up for other players. Similarly, due to the vast difference between normal and hard in difficulty (different AI bouses), playstyles/bugs which may work on normal may not work on hard.
Instead of soliciting feedback from the playerbase as a whole, the general impression I have from watching the game progress since early access is that a small privileged group of testers (who tend to be experts and or play using certain strategies) have their suggestions favored more by the devs. This isn't necessarily the fault of the devs, as these players are simply more active in providing feedback.
This generally wouldn't be a matter if it wasn't for the fact that some of these more active players have a habit of discounting other player's problems (since it doesn't occur for them with how they play). This leads to issues where unless a problem is faced by a majority of players, problems which only affect some players are routinely ignored or outright dismissed. It also leads to poor balance changes and honestly a terrible experience for new players who are thrown into the game (eg the patches making the first intro/tutorial level harder and harder and harder to the point where new players have to go on the forum and ask for how to beat the FIRST LEVEL).
Many of these fundamental issues would be solvable if there were modding support by the devs. One would think the modder DarthMod would have supported modding in his/her commercial games, having come from the modding community.
Instead, impediments to modding were added on purpose to reduce the basic modding possible in UG:CW.
I would honestly prefer to play the first early game access version of the game rather than the current version of the game as it is now. I lack faith the devs will be able to fix fundamental problems based on experiences since early access.

Battleborn is probably my favourite game that is currently in my library.  I truly cannot understand why people are giving this game anything but positive reviews, but I will try and break my own down as fairly as possible.
TL;DR This game is a romping good time with a vast array of heroes and the classic Gearbox touch that I loved from Borderlands.  The biggest negative is the depressingly low player population.
For those who want an in-depth review, here we go:
Graphics/Artwork:  It is clear from the beginning that Battleborn shares the same artistic genre as Borderlands, though with a different spin.  Shadercells abundant, the game is very much a moving comic book.  The game is visually attractive, there is no arguing that, though the myriad of colours that will erupt somewhere on the battlefield during even a single match may turn some players off.  Personally, I find it adds to the fast-paced, almost chaotic nature of the combat.
Gameplay:  The game has both a story and a versus mode, both heavily reliant on the multiplayer/co-op aspect of the game (more on that later).  The story is not very long, and you can probably crank it out in a few hours if you went non-stop.  The writing and the dry, sarcastic humour of the story is fantastic.  I frequently found myself literally laughing out loud at some lines that are so casually thrown in by the heroes.  The multiplayer is split into three game modes, though more are promised in the future.  You have Capture, a domination-style match, Incursion, an escort the drones so you can kill your enemies' sentries, and Meltdown, the most MOBA-y of the three styles.  Each is fun in their own right, though each plays fundamentally differently.  It will take some time to figure out which one you prefer.  I see many people posting "Sick, a MOBA shooter I am totally in" which disuades those who just want the unique take on an FPS, or bums out the MOBA fans who don't like Capture or Incursion.  But trust me, everyone will find a game type they like.
Heroes:  The best part of the game.  Battleborn currently boasts a roster of 26 heroes, and every single one is unique.  You have can play as a tank, healer, sniper, witch, knight, support, a rogue, fencer, a robot, a penguin riding in a mech suit, an ice golem, a mercenary, a bird-man, a smuggler, an elf-like archer, and the list goes on.  Every single hero has a unique personality and play style, and you will quickly find which ones are best for you.
Leveling/Meta:  There are essentially two different forms of leveling up in this game.  During each mission or match, your hero will level up their specific mutation path, letting you choose from two (or sometimes three) perks.  You can reach level ten in each match, allowing for a unique play experience each time, though after you find your role you will often only tweak one or two each match.  Your heroes also level up outside of the match, up to level 12.  This allows you to unlock skins, taunts, loot packs, and mutations - which add a third option to certain levels when you level up in game.  This means that there is an actual sense of achievement for gaining experience at the end of a match, and you become stronger as a result.
Microtransactions:  Purely cosmetic, as they should be.  You can pay for a nicer looking skin or a fun taunt, but everything you need can be purchased by playing and accumulating in-game currency.  I have not spent a single real dollar buying loot crates, and still have a heap of credits left.  However, when they released Alani, the first bonus hero, she was technically free, but cost ~40k credits.  Doable, but not really worth it.  Buying the season's pass gets you all future DLC and heroes, but at a real cost.  Still, the season's pass is cheaper than that of most other games, and we are already getting content for it.
Community: We all know Gearbox rocks.  Borderlands and its sequels were amazing, and the studio behind them and Battleborn are one of the few that still respect and value their player base.  They release weekly updates showcasing fan art, members of the Battleborn community, and in-depth news and updates.  I have missed that feeling in most AAA games lately.
The Bad:  Like I said earlier, the population of this game is painfully low, usually between 600-1000 players at any given time.  As a result, wait times for matches can be ridiculously long.  I got in a win streak with a random group, and noticed that in six or seven games I had played some of the same people twice.  Furthermore, players may find initial frustration when trying to find their role.  Not all heroes are meant to run in and deal massive damage quickly. My prefered role is a hero that can apply a massive overshield to herself and allies, while targetting enemies for extra damage.  But her own damage output is weak compared to many heroes.  The game is balanced if your team recognizes the need for both damage and support, but it can be frustrating when they don't do that.
This game is fantastic, and it really does make me sad to see it misjudged and pushed aside.  It is a quality game with much more value than what is on the surface.  Do I recommend Battleborn?  Yes.  A thousand times yes.  If you like a unique take on an FPS with witty, fun characters that span a massive roster, a good story and some awesome multiplayer from a developer that has a proven track record, give Battleborn a try.  I will see you on the battlefield.
