I love Setsuna's OST and art direction. The story, although a easily summed up as a *very* poor man's Final Fantasy X, is functional even in its worst moments. I don't mind the lack of sidequests, since it makes perfect sense within the narrative. I'm even okay with most enemies being minor model variations of earlier foes, because they at least behave a little differently and the codex cleverly explains the similarities as evolutionary adaptations of the same family.
If that as all I had to say about the game, I'd give it a thumbs up - $40 would still be crazy steep, but I think you could have a decent time with this hypothetical game for the sale price. Alas, the combat exists.
tl;dr: Inexplicable design decisions render combat tedious and mindless. You're still forced into it constantly.
I am Setsuna desperately wants to be Chrono Trigger in battle. You can only have three characters in battle, there's an ATB system, enemies wander around the map in groups and jump in to combat, and you even have pair and trio special moves.
So where's it go wrong? Those three characters are the only ones gaining EXP at the full rate, so everyone else ends up underleveled, which kills any motivation to use them unless you want to grind. You don't, because the ludicrous cost of items and equipment relative to enemy drops means the only economical way of restoring MP when there's no save point is levelling up. As a result, you either just mash attack until victory or have to grind even more so you can afford the items you need to grind and use special abilities with any consistency. Which might not sound so bad, but remember that you're grinding to pay for items and main party equipment, then second party equipment, then to catch your second party up with your first party. If you're like me, you very quickly say "**** this" and just use the first three characters for the entire game.
But hey, I've played plenty of great games using the same party in nearly every battle, including most of the JRPGs IaS wants to be. It still could've joined them if its battle system wasn't garbage even when you've got the items, equipment, and levels to fight properly. For starters, you can only equip a tiny fraction of your special abilities, and the screens to equip said abilities and see which ones are part of combos are separated by several menus, both of which are themselves separate from the menu for buying abilities. So you'll either look it up online, spend a totally inordinate amount of time doing it the way the game intended, or just stick with whatever you accidentally find. Which won't be many, because there are remarkably few combos relative to the number of skills.
Next, the battle system is heavily dependent on positioning but, and I cannot emphasize this enough,
Boss knocked you out of position for group healing? Tough. The 'X' formed by your combo is completely off center? Deal with it. Even better, the game has the bombs from Final Fantasy, except they're
to explode on death no matter what you do, and if they stand right next to your party (which they almost always do!) your choices are to either eat their self destruct damage or just stand there and hope that they're nice enough to move away eventually.
Even that could have been partially excused if you could set deployment positions in battle or if the game remembered where you attacked from relative to your enemies, but you can't and it doesn't. No matter how you approach a group of enemies, both parties jump to the same positions. You'll have some bonuses if you attacked from behind, but that doesn't help much if all the bombs are right in front of you.
Lastly, there are normal enemies that are black, and then there are special enemies that are black. Sometimes the special enemies look like entirely plausible normal enemies, but then you attack and discover that their defense is so high that most of your party is literally incapable of dealing damage, and they may even have heals to cancel out whats left. You then have no choice but to run, but you can only run if you have a consumable item, and you're going to use a ton of those running from battles where all the bombs spawn on top of you.
I have a lot of patience for bad JRPG combat when everything else is done well, but I am Setsuna does combat exceptionally poorly and almost everything else is merely acceptable. Not recommended unless you have saintly tolerance for the combat.

Wow... Where do I begin?  The games background, that is to say the setting, is rather boring.  Snow and ice everywhere, with very little color variation to break up the monotany.  But (and this is a big BUT), I have never been moved to tears so quickly by a campy JRPG story.  Even FFVII took an entirnity to get you connected to it's cinnamon roll character.  Setsuna quickly managed to make me curious as well as to make me rethink my understanding of human psychology.  As the story goes on you become not only more attached to her character, but more afraid of losing her.  As before the end of the first chapter you know it will happen.  It is filled with moments of impressive character developement and is perhaps the first game since Danganronpa 2, to truely make me feel the loss of a character.  And now the white waste of setting makes some semblence of sense, there is no real happy ending for anybody in this story, no bright colors, no spring in sight.  It's sad that the only really colorful character (literally not their actual personality) is Setsuna herself, fitting, but sad.  The ending may change this review, but I don't think I'm wrong in saying, that after the final boss, you will have beat the game, but it's going to feel hollow.

This game is a bunch of fun, and thus should be played. The level design is solid and generally works well to suggest the tactics you should use to overcome its challenges. The open-world-ness functions well, with basically very few changes from the old metroid dynamics. Which is definitely not a bad thing, because it works well.
The combat is just great. It's never too easy, and never too hard. It's rare to find a game that has that good a balance, but this is one of those games. It's also fun, and pretty smooth to control and chain up combos.
The art design is fantastic. Every area is brimming with tons of details which fit in perfectly. Excellent work on the levels and also the characters. Hell, especially the characters.
The addition of tons of things to do off the beaten track (see previous notes on metroid open-worldyness) is very welcome, and while some games would be comfortable to not put a lot of effort into these bits this does not do that. They are all still meticulously crafted. And often very tough. Which I heavily approve of.
The story's pretty boring, but it doesn't tend to crop up very often so it's not really a problem. That's pretty much the only negative I can think of about this game. The characters aren't really ever explored that much either, but yeah. Perhaps that's just a leftover from the metroid style - because they were all about isolation (and the story developing through your actions alone), so adding a bunch of other characters and extra story into that just doesn't fit too well. But yeah. A very minor negative.
Summary:
A very fun, challenging, open-world 2D puncher-platformer, with excellent art, good level design and great combat mechanics. It's a joy to play, and you should totally get this in your hands and face right now.

Fantastic game from both the standpoint of a Civil War buff and a fan of tactical battlefield games.
Every battle feels engaging and some of the best AI I've ever seen in a war game.
It made me want to learn more deeply about the tactics of each battle being fought rather than just the grand strategic narratives every ACW buff knows.
That said... I hope there are more updates to the game.
There is a heavy bias to the selection of battles to the Eastern Theater, the one everyone cares about. Outside of that theater you have a grand total of three battles: Shiloh, Stones River, and Chickamauga. I get that one problem is how heavily involved engineering and naval support was in the Western theater, particularly any battle on the Mississippi River, whereas this is a pretty typical napoleonic infantry-cavalry-artillery game, but that's kind of the point, isn't it?
Even aside from that, there are many important battles in the Western Theater which could probably be accomodated in this game: Vicksburg (post-Grant's landing), Chattanooga, Perryville, Franklin, Nashville, and/or the Battle of Atlanta.
This is also kind of part of a mild pro-Confederate (or at least pro-Virginia) bias in terms of the battles chosen. All of the battles I named above were Union victories, since outside of perhaps Chickamauga the Union consistently won major battles and offensives in the West.
I get it, I'm from Virginia, I love all the Eastern theater battles, but even then most of the battles chosen are from the first two years of the war, and there's only a few that take place after Gettysburg.
The only battles between Lee and Grant are Cold Harbor and Richmond? The Wilderness, Spotsylvania Court House, North Anna, the siege of Petersburg? Nope.
I get that you don't want to have too many Union victories (although as I said you're slightly short now), but from a tactical or even strategic perpective most of the battles of the Overland Campaign were either Confederate victories or inconclusive - not until Petersburg did Lee ultimately break.
So bottom line, the game is absolutely fantastic, but seeing as the devs are so amazing at providing updates, I'd love for the broader story of the war to be covered, rather than just the popular history version which ignores everything west of the Appalachians and anything after Gettysburg.

As an old player of Sid Meier's Gettysburg, I have really enjoyed this game.  It adds the critical element of continuity between battles (you keep your army), which for me, makes a campaign-style game much more engaging.  I usually don't care too much for real time games, but this one is manageable.  The balance between infantry/skirmishers, cavalry, and artillery seems about right and the battles are fun.  On top of all of this, it has caused me to study up on Civil War battles and learn some history.
From a gaming standpoint, the one thing I would like to see is an ahistorical option that reflects pathways in the War that may have occurred particularly when the outcome of a major battle is substantially different that what happened historically.  I also don't fully understand the scaling mechanic of the game.  It might be nice to have a bit more transparancy on this or even better an option to adjust the magnitude of the scaling.
Even after 259 hours (at this time), I'm still improving my technique, and in fact, will be starting a new Confederate Campaign (on normal) because I just lost the last one at the final battle (Washington) basically because I didn't have enough troops in one of my Corps.
All-in-all, I applaud the designers and hope there is more of this style of game down the road.....perhaps a fantasy setting that allows for more flexibility in battle sequence and overall goals.

Her Story is quite a novel way to present an interactive story game - on one hand it's daring and innovative, on the other it has its flaws. One aspect that can be considered a flaw is that it's not very realistic despite using FMV - what the player does in the game doesn't make any sense in real life. You have to find video fragments to reassemble an old crime story - you can search for words (apparently the fragments are text indexed), and you can find more clue words in the videos. IRL you'd just pull out all the fragments and reassemble them (yeah, the game comes up with a reason why, but it's kinda lame to be honest).
But, as we know, it's a video game, and it doesn't have to be realistic to be good. The story and the acting are very well done, so if you manage to suspend your disbeliefs, hunting for the main story elements, then the small details to fill the gaps can be quite engaging. As it's done in a sandboxy manner, it is inevitable that it becomes a little flat towards the end with lots of fruitless searching, but until you figure out the main plot outline, it's really first class fun.
You'll get through the best part in 60-90 minutes, so adjust your expectations accordingly. From my side, it's definitely recommended.

The people who say that Her Story isn't a game are the same people who buy Call of Duty and Assassin's Creed every year.
So the game starts up and I'm sitting there infront of a CRT monitor, reflecting lights from within the room and showing an old desktop screen. I hear fans and hard drives whirring in the background, giving a fantastic feeling of ambience. Then this soft music starts to play as I delve into one of the most gripping game encounters of my life.
As Her Story unfolded before me I was unable to look away, with certain parts of the story sending tingles of excitement up my spine. The story is deep, meaningful and dark. I actually filled three pages with scribbles to keep notes on the story instead of using the system provided by the game. I feel that's how the game should be played. Scoring down key points, linking parts of the puzzle together like a real detective.
Viva Seifert's (Her) performance is amazing, portraying a range of emotions and mental states through each of her seven interviews, making the character feel completely real. The writing is also worthy of mention. With each of the interviews you can sense the growing tension between "Her" and the police detectives filming the ordeal. As she progresses from pitiful widow to potential murderer, the transformation of the situation is enthralling.
The only criticism I can provide for this game as this will be a one-time trip as it offers almost no replayability. But that's okay, the first time will be unforgettable anyway.
All in all, Her Story is very rewarding when the player submits to the experience and gets really engaged. A must play.

First off, I love bit dungeon. I play it all the time. So when I saw BD2 i had to buy it of course.
First impressions were good. It's not the same as the first game, but still enjoyable and much more varied.
My first problem is that other then in fortresses, i didn't find a way to regain your health, only by killing the purple demons who appear in rooms you already killed everyone in. If you are just running around outside as you most likely are, there is no way to replenish your health.
Another problem is that often you manage to click and change your weapon to one that's just laying around without noticing it.
The bigest issue though is that it's buggy.
Often when you walk around the screen keeps jutting and shaking as you go, and I'm not sure if it's only on my PC or everyone finds this, but often when you pick up a weapon, the associated special attack doesn't work well. (sometimes it works on one screen and stops working on the next)
This wouldn't be that big a deal, but I accidentally switched my ice hammer off for an ice cube.
The ice cube didn't reside in the weapon slot, but still i couldn't carry it at the same time as I carried my weapon.
So i accidentally picked up the ice cube that was right next to the door and then left the room... Returning instantly I found my 25+ atk weapon has disappeared, and I was left with an icecube that had NO powers. I couldn'T even get out of the sewers/catacombs under the fortress as I had no means of attacking. This is a huge issue because of course i was forced to let the monsters kill me and go back from lv 19 or 20 to lv 1 and start the game over.
--------
So can I recommend it?
It is a really nice looking game if you like the art style. It is in the same style as Bit Dungeon, just way more varied, more in depth and less repetative. It has a nice variety of style through the overall map, and it's procedurally generated meaning you'll have different worlds every time you start a new game.
It is also kinda buggy, The controls are a bit weird, not very responsive, sometimes I click an enemy to hit it but my guy just walks there, or I am in the middle of a bunch of monsters, my special attack doesn't fire and even if I'm clicking I'm just changing my weapon to the one right next to me and just get mobbed and killed in seconds. Also I found no way to replenish your life outside of fortresses.
Honestly, If I wasn't such a huge fan of Bit Dungeon I probably wouldn't like it that much.
So I'll recommend it but only half heartedly. Only buy this if you really really like the style!
It's been out on steam for over a year now, I hope these bugs will get fixed soon so I could give it a higher score.

I sit here in shock after playing this game for about 5-ish hours. At level 123 I was about to face the final boss. I had grinded for hours for the best gear I could find, the best stats that would help me kill bosses better. I had prepared myself, I was ready, this had to work right?
I approached the boss, stealthing in, critting him for well over 3k hp and hitting him relentlessly only to discover that he had taken my health down to a third and was gearing up for another attack. I barely scratched him and I had no extra life, so I charged in once more for my final attack......
Bit Dungeon II's story is more or less non-existent, save for the fact that you are supposed to free this ghost girl from her grave. You have no name, no history, no clue about who you are and why you have to help her, but not all heroes
get proper information at the start of their journey.
Bit Dungeon II has some of the most fun, and addicting gameplay for a 2d, dungeon crawling, RPG. I had gotten tired of the one button press, boring rpgs that had the same attack animation each time, and the enemies would die in the same way for the most part. This game changes that by automatically attacking, and allowing the player to use special, weapon-specific abilities at his command, which are tied to the resource called stamina (purple bar section). It may sound very easy, but when you face off against a horde of enemies guarding a chest or a boss who can easily 3 shot you, you'll see just how difficult combat can really be.
The controls are pretty much straightforward, once you actually figure them out that is. One button is configured to Guard/Special Abilities (a weird combo but it works). There are also buttons for the Main Menu, Stats and Inventory. This makes it a simple-enough game, with some hidden mechanics worth trying.
There are many weapons in this game, which was pretty nice overall, but I really enjoyed the ability to use any weapon I found, if I wanted to. Even though there wasn't an official class system, the game would grant you stats catered to what you were building when you levelled up. Greatswords would generally give you strength (more physical damage) and constitution (more health and stamina), while staffs would give you more magic oriented stats such as intelligence. I liked the ability to dual wield weapons, so I grabbed two daggers myself, and found the most addicting style of gameplay.
Each weapon had its own special abilities. For daggers and blades, you could walk around in stealth, and you'd get an insane damage bonus for
damage. If you were seen, or in combat prior to this, you'd have to walk around for about 2 - 3 seconds before you'd go back to an undetected state, allowing you to deal surprise damage again. One thing that was very clear to me was that each weapon had very distinct strengths and weaknesses. This made it very crucial to identify my ideal playstyle, and test each weapon enough before sticking to them, and once decided upon, stick to it. Stealth gameplay was great for assassination on a small number of targets, but if you ever got surrounded you would most likely die. On my first playthrough, this was my fate as I realized simply building dexterity wasn't enough to survive.
There were 4 main areas in the game and around 8 or so dungeons. They were not randomized, so it was possible to memorize layouts or plan strategies for approaching them. In my experience, dungeons were my favourite places to be, as the rat-like creatures which feasted upon previously killed enemies dropped health potions fairly often and prevented me from dying. Bosses were pretty varied, and had unique mechanics tied to each of them, though some weapons were a little better on some than others.
If you died, you were allowed one respawn if you had the extra life from the ghost girl at the start. If you managed to return to the place that you died, you could pick up that extra life and repeat the process again. I loved this mechanic, as it didn't make death such a scary prospect.
I didn't quite like the equip/inventory system as it took me a while to figure out that I could only have one of each type of item at a time. This made the inventory almost useless, as it was only to look at my existing items and figure out what I would aim for next.
As stated before, there was no tutorial or guide to the game so the initial learning curve was rough, and it was only after my second time seeing "Game Over" that I finally understood how the game worked at each section.
And finally,
.
Bit Dungeon II is one of the most fun 2d RPGs I've played in a long time. Some people may say the first was better, I wouldn't know since I never played it. But don't let that turn you away from this game, it's definitely a fun one. If you can get it on sale, and you don't mind spending a little extra time to learn the mechanics, this game is definitely worth buying.

This is a great modern take on the classic JRPG. The comparisons to Chrono Trigger are apt, if not unfair. I am Setsuna is very reminiscent of Chrono Trigger through it's battle system, world design, story telling, character depth and overall story arc, but does not have the benefit of nostalgia or a littany of "Best games of all time" lists from the past 20 years. Go into this game with level expectations, do not start this up expecting one of the greatest games of all time. I am Setsuna is an incredibly engaging JRPG for those who miss simpler times and want an adventure.
Pros:
- Beautiful world and character design
- Fantastic soundtrack
- Deep battle system (very similar to CT)
- Distinct charcters (follow typical JRPG tropes, but executed very well.)
- Solid storyline
- Strong sidequests that add to character depth
- Hidden worlds and bosses that help develop the world around you
- Clocks in at about 20+ hours, doesn't overstay its welcome
Cons:
- Can be very grindy (mostly due to tracking down items for Spritnite)
- Flux system can be confusing at times
- Can be somewhat predictable
- $40 seems like a lot for a classic style JRPG (though I do not regret my purchase)

The term FMV - full motion video - is usually a red flag when looking for a quality game. Few FMV-based games have managed to hold up and the ones that do tend to use FMV more as a supplement to the core gameplay (often as a storytelling enhancement).
All that has changed with Her Story - it is the first game I have played that successfully uses watching FMV as the focal point of gameplay.
The game's central trick involves the interview videos players watch to discover the story. For each video, players have to figure out what questions were being asked, at what point in the investigation each response occurs, and which parts of the response warrant further investigation. This lack of context is a brilliant step forward. For years, developers of FMV-based games have tried to make players react to videos that follow a predetermined structure - like filmmakers do.  By removing the context of these clips and not trying to tell a story in the same way a film does, Her Story allows players to participate in the crafting of the narrative. It's a fascinating process for the player, one that leads to the unique discovery of a story with a few clever wrinkles that relies heavily on acting of the actress playing the interviewee (which is thankfully on point).
It's not a perfect game. The act of searching usually involves specific words mentioned in clips or thinking of alternative ways to search for the same thing, but it sometimes turns into the boring, repetitive task of searching common words for new leads. Even worse is that some of the clips (specifically a few clips that consist of the interviewee only saying limited phrases like "Yes") cannot be found without some help provided after "completing" the game (and beyond achievement-hunting, these clips don't have much value).
These criticisms don't take away from the fact that Her Story is a revelation. Beyond the intriguing story, the clever idea of search engine as gameplay mechanic, and the comment it makes about the way technology and media can cloud our ability to understand reality, Her Story is a game that has finally figured out how to turn the passive experience of watching video into an active process of playing a game. It should be remembered as one of the important video game milestones of 2015.

Shank 2 seems to think that for a good sequel, you need to add a bunch of gimmicky crap.
All a sequel needs is a fresh coat of paint. Exhibit A: Portal 2.
I think the best way to put it is this:
It's rather liked getting bopped on the head once ($9.99), given five cookies (Shank,) then bopped on the head again ($9.99), and promptly kicked in the shins (Shank 2.)
Don't get kicked in the shins.
Keep your ten dollars.
Go buy Subway sandwiches for yourself and a friend.
It's valid sustenance, you'll develop social skills, and you won't repeatedly pound your head against a terrible for a bad decision. Assuming you don't add mayonnaise.
Shank 2's Final Score: 5.75/10
Letter Grade: F
Verdict: Worse than mayonnaise.
Mayonnaise's Final score: 6.0/10
Letter Grade: D-
Verdict: At least some people like mayonnaise.

Absoutely amazing game.  The story is comical but also not just a joke.  The music and art are phenomenal.  If I had to describe it using other games as a basis of comparisson, the map and sidescrolling non-linear gameplay reminds me a LOT of castlevania symphony of the night and the metroid franchise which is a GREAT thing.  The combat itself has a simple combo, grapple, and special attack system that works very well and is highly responsive.
I have seen the negative reviews complain about difficulty, but an important thing to remember is the games of the era this game is created in the essence of were all very difficult and chalenging.  This game is very non-punitive though.  For example, when you die from a platforming section, you simply spawn back to the start of the room.  Yes, you must complete whatever series of jumps or wall flips it has for you, but it doesn't rewind you to your last save point to do so.  In short, it has the skill elements from games of the past, without the frustration that can go along with it.

The platforming elements are a bit different in the way that you combine fighting moves to traverse the more challenging segments. You can use an uppercut to get to a higher place, or a side kick to get to that distant ledge.
Overall, this is a very genre blending game. It's a 2D-action-platformer-beat 'em up-metroidvania. And it somehow manages to be very good in all those elements. Would recommend it to anybody who likes these elements!

Graphics: Typical indie pixel show. Nothing worth pointing out here. Not particulary offensive to the eye.
Gameplay: Nothing too complex overall, can complete the game with pretty much the space bar and movement keys.
Music: Not bad, but due to the size of the game the soundtrack variation is short. Becomes quite repetitive after a while. For some reason there's no music in the Dark World. I don't know what this was trying to achieve really. It didn't come across as dark or forboding, just a boring area with no music.
Sound effects: Nothing worth pointing out. Beeps and boops. Stuff that would have been standard about 30 years ago.
Replayability: After one (almost completed) run I didn't feel like going back to it again. If I had completed the game I have serious doubts there being any point in going back to it.
Positive points: Pacing of the game felt alright, until the Dark World.
Negative points: (These will need their own sections)
-Zone borders: Too often I would move in to another zone accidentally while trying to dodge an enemy. Zone crossing is just far too sensitive for this kind of gameplay.
-Item disappearence: After crossing a zone every item from the previous zone, excluding chests and keys, is erased from that zone. This can include equipment you accidentally picked up and left your old, better, gear behind. I can understand that if they didn't have this system the zones would all clutter up and cause the game to become a complete mess. However, there are work arounds for this. For example, including an inventory so players can pick up items and store for later or discard (not just placing back on the ground again but completely discarding them). There could have been a storage chest at the bonfires where this extra gear could be stored and withdrawn later on.
-Enemy placement: I lost count of the number of times I crossed a zone or room in a dungeon and suddenly get mauled by 3+ enemies crowding the door. This just shouldn't happen, it's lazy design. Why should a player be punished for simply entering a room or zone as they should do. To prove this is lazy design, the enemy spawns are all random. You may or may not end up getting your face ripped off upon entering a zone. There's nothing done to prevent this from happening. Just sheer laziness. Something like this is unforgivable in a game where there can be permadeath.
-Enemy AI: There's more or less no AI to speak about. Unless they're right at a zone entrance as explained before, no enemy poses much of a threat, especially if you have a bow weapon. Not even bosses pose much of a threat (although I never got to experience the last boss of the game due to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t explained with enemy placement).
-Dark World: This whole area is just stupid. Really really stupid. You get placed in an area with no music, 1 type of enemy which is just spammed throughout the whole place which has 1 attack and poses no threat at all unless you're unlucky and get a bunch of them in your face upon entering a zone. There is no map, as for some reason it treats the Dark World as a dungeon, even giving you UI elements for keys despite there being no keys or locked doors in this particular area. As a result of there being no map in this area, I had absolutely no idea where I was going or whether I was going in circles. It didn't help that so many of the zones in the Dark World look exactly the same (Boring black/grey zones with black ghost enemies everywhere). I did eventually find the dungeon of the area, but I did come close to just closing the game before I even got there.
Final throughts: I only played one run of this game. I got to the last dungeon and died due to getting killed at the entrance of a zone I crossed in to. I wasn't about to go all the way back through the Dark World again due to there being no way for me to retrace my steps back to the dungeon. Even if I had completed the run, I doubt I would have felt like going back for more. The game even seems designed for one playthrough only due to the limited amount of achievements it has. I ended up unlocking all of them in the 2 short hours I played this game and obviously this was intentional.
If the devs could do just two simple things to make this game something I could come back and complete, it would be to fix enemies crowding the doors and zone lines, and give the Dark World a map. Maybe also give the player something they could use to indicate where they've been to previously. Currently I would not recommend spending time on this game until these things have been done.

While this is with out a doubt the best 'looking' tinkering/machine building game I have run across it certainly is NOT the most intuitive.
After playing for a while and blowing past all the lvls (Was here for the building anyway.) I really started to look into what could and could not be done with the base vanilla game.
As is turn out that is not allot. Most of the amazing builds you see on youtube and on the workshop are either made via an old glitch that has been fixed or using a building tool mod.
-The base game dose not let you angle blocks other than 90` meaning everything pretty much has to be square.
-You can set a 'mirror' mode but it only works on placing and not deleting.
-After you place blocks you can't move them individually, meaning if your machine is 2 pieces and needs to be realigned you need to completely delete one of those pieces and rebuild it in the desired location.
Keep in mind though that after installing a 3rd party mod, all of this stuff is immediately and perfectly remedied. So that makes this a perfectly price worthy buy if you like to build stuff and don't mind messing around with mods (Non workshop~Workshop only has creations as far as I can tell, not mods.)
On a side not, if modders have a dozen different building tool mods I I don't see why the devs don't take a hint and expand. Its been proven that its very do-able and also it seems like a good % of players are allready using them anyway.

Her Story is a game where a series of interviews regarding a case has been transcribed, split up into short segments, and put on a database. The interviews are all one-sided; you can only view the responses. You can only search for words used in the transcription (or your own tags for the video) and the goal is to put everything together and figure out what's happening. As you learn about different characters and situations you can tailor your searches to see if there are more videos that mention that subject and eventually see more and more of the archive.
There are some clips that are very difficult to find normally so you may want to try one of the strategies in steam guides (or go to the install directory) to watch them all after you finish your playthrough.
There are two main ways people look at what's presented depending on whether or not you believe the final interview. I don't think there is enough evidence strong enough to completely discount either theory and there's no way to get more from other sources or really corroborate evidence to form anything solid. Pick whatever feels right for you and enjoy the story you want.

You can't really even mention this title anywhere without being bombarded by arguments that it's "not a real game", as if that actually matters. It's systematically downvoted and 0-bombed and trolled pretty much anywhere it's discussed and reviewed. I'm certain this review will end up getting a handful of automatic thumbs down from people who hate that this kind of thing even exists and want to fight against... whatever it is that it represents. As if this game being made and being successful means that every developer in the world is going to drop everything to try to imitate it. I don't get that line of thinking.
Really, who cares? Whether it's a proper game or not, it's a unique experience that's highly experimental and plays with interactivity in a new way. It's not entirely successful in what it sets out to achieve, but it's interesting and it's cheap. I might agree with the notion that it's a bit overhyped. This wasn't really game of the year material for me so much as it was a fun diversion that was fun to unravel, with a cool idea on how to interact with a story. But I don't regret spending time with it, and I'm glad that we live in an era of gaming where developers can try new things that are worth talking about and debating.
Don't take this one as the bold new face of indie gaming, because it's not. It's a story, most of all. One that you might get wrapped up in, or you might not. I love working out a mystery, so I did. The central mechanic works very well if you don't try to break it. That is, if you mostly follow the story as you discover pieces of it, searching keywords related to things you just discovered, or trying to fill in the gaps as things come into view. I've heard of plenty of people "breaking" the game by accidentally stumbling onto big revelations by guessing key words rather than following the trail of clues, but that doesn't mean you ruined iit. The big twists hidden away still leave a lot of holes in the story when you find them, and if all goes well, you'll feel a definite sense of the whole picture coming into focus as you explore the database.
The really cool thing it does, one that I thought worked well, is let the player define their own victory. It's easy to discover the biggest twist early on without meaning to, but even once you know it there are a lot of other details to fill in. While playing, I went from a fuzzy sense of what happened to a more defined picture, and without viewing 100% of the clips, I eventually found I could explain every little detail. Things clicked into place and I felt like I "won", even though the game didn't tell me that. Evoking a sense of personal victory without actually telling the player that they beat the game is just really clever, and is what makes this worth playing yourself rather than just watching someone else on youtube or whatever.
It's a good conversation piece, as well. The "ending", such as it is, can be interpreted in two different ways, so even once you've put together the overall story, it's worth searching for evidence towards one side or the other. I can see it as a good game to play with someone else, or to share experiences with afterwards. I liked what it did, and got a satisfying amount of entertainment out of it, and you might too if you're not hung up on the whole "not a game" thing.

At first, the game was really pleasing to the eye. The graphics, the music, the gameplay, and the voices. Holy hell the voices - it's one of the coolest features of the game. However, as I progress through, it went kind of dull and lead to many question marks in my head.
What I like:
1. Voices and Music
Japanese voices. Really awesome and suits their character. Voices are only in battles, though. The music is great, too. As a piano lover, I could listen to the soundtrack all day.
2. Battle System
I really like how there is an extra twist to the battle system in where, when you press a button, it triggers an event that will increase your attack or tech damage, buff your stats, or heal your comrades. I also liked how you can combine your skills with other comrades through Combos. It adds flavor to the turn-based genre and I quite enjoyed that.
3. Skills / Techs are equipped, not learned through levels
In Most JRPGs, you had to reach a certain level to learn a skill. In this game, you get them from creating Techs called "Spiritnites". You equip them to your character so that they can use it in battle. This way, you would need to strategize on what Techs you need to use in battles to come.
What I dislike (Major Emphasis):
1. A single and linear path
It's like following a one-way road. You know EXACTLY where you are going to next. It rarely gives a sense of exploration as you're traversing through the lands. I find it quite irritating.
2. Some of the story's plots doesn't make sense
Let's give one example: You go to this town, it's deserted. A boy tells you they are kidnapped by monsters in a cave. You rescue 3 people. When all is done, you go back, around 10+ people are in town. I've been trying to do the math, but it just doesn't add up. Seriously.
3. Decision making
Your main protagonist (Endir) cannot talk, and instead you are given speech bubbles for him to choose. But it doesn't really matter what you choose, really - they end up doing the same thing when picking any of the speech bubbles. Let's say you tell your friends, "Kill her!" Then everyone will say no and continue doing the other speech bubble you were "supposed" to choose.
There is just one exception though - a decision that, if answered incorrectly, will take you back to the beginning of the level. But apart from that, that's it.
--
All in all, it left me really unsatisfied. The story was what got me down. I didn't buy it on sale because it had good reviews, and as a spritual successor to Chrono Trigger I thought I was going to be delighted. I was quite disappointed on how it all turned out.

I was hoping for this to be a lot better - especially at the price point it's selling at.  They threw around some very famous titles in an effort to sucker people ( like myself) into buying this game.
The game itself is short and greatly lacks in any sort of content.  You battle the same ten enemies over and over again with different color skins but nothing new.  After you've played the game for an hour you've experienced nearly the entire game.  The items, food, and spiritnite aquisition system is awful.  Forget about even trying to find recipes for food unless you have a guide that tells you which NPCs to talk to and what they're looking for, because you'll have no idea until you actually gather the items.  The consumable items are bland and very standard.
The battle system in this game has a faint resemblance to the "good ol' days" but that's about where the positives end.  The momentum and flux systems in the game are very very poorly explained and are not very fun to use.  I liked the idea of the combo system like they had in Chrono Trigger, but the system was very poorly executed and you end up spending a great deal of time even coming up with a decent spiritnite combo build that you end up just throwing your hands in the air and saying "screw it".
Another shortcoming of this game that I really wanted to enjoy was the artwork and soundtrack.  I should have paid heed to the reviews before.  This game lacks in both artwork and soundtrack.  While the soundtrack isn't awful and I do love piano, I don't want to listen to it through an entire game.  I also get really bored looking at snow and ice caves for an entire game.  The lack of effort and imagination put into these two areas are really what killed this game for me.  The lack of imagination really came through in the rest of the game too which is incredibly unfortunate.
The characters in the game are incredibly flat as well.  There's very weak character buildup and a poor mish-mash of intermingled stoies that bring the group together on the journey.  None of them have very outstanding personalities and none of them are very memorable.
The reviews and description of this game that say it takes you back to the "JRPG masterpieces of yesteryear" obviously have never played said masterpieces.  Even comparing this game to those that this is supposed to pay homage to is quite sad and it makes me weep for the future of JRPGs.
The game did have a lot of potential.  The snowy landscapes are beautiful but some diversity would have made this game amazing.  The sound track is also nice, but also needs a lot more diversity.  The characters could have easily been fun and memorable with a little more work as well.  Overall, the story I think is what had the most potential, but due to the shortcomings in almost all other aspects of the game, the story gets kind of ruined.
Overall, I can't recommend this game at this price.  If the game dropped down to about $9.99 then I'd say it'd be worth a run through... but for $39.99... I feel cheated.

If you like gritty, serious games that shine a light on the flawed reality we call real life, you should consider this free-to-play title. It is, albeit unintentionally, a perfect metaphor for existence.
Gameplay centers around matching three or more of the same number, a mundane, repetitive task, just like real life. You are given objectives to complete, just like real life, and a limited amount of turns in which to complete them, just like real life. These turns symbolize the rapidly passing minutes in each hour, hours in each day, days in each year, years in each life. These similarities may seem trite to you, but I haven't gotten to my point yet.
Gameplay that may seem satisfying at first becomes less and less enjoyable as time goes on. Just like life, it gets harder, and as it gets harder, you realize how arbitrary and unfair it can be. The sheer amount of luck involved becomes more apparent as you progress, and are given less room to fail. Often you will be put in circumstances where the only moves open to you do nothing to help in your objectives, and only serve to waste the limited opportunity you've been given, but the alternative is to do nothing. Earlier in the game, you had excess available moves, and could afford to waste them. Now you cannot.
I am not one to believe that the universe is completely random. Making smart decisions increases your chances of success, and making stupid decisions increases your chances of failure. Just like real life, though, in this game you can often make all the smartest decisions available to you, and still fail, because of the conspiring of circumstances. Whether these circumstances are procedurally generated (evolution), or the work of the unseen devs (a Creator Deity), they can render your efforts useless, and make it seem as if hard work is not worthwhile. This is nonsense, and I will tell you why.
While you are not always given opportunities to succeed, sometimes you are, and if you are not ready for those opportunities, you will not be able to take advantage of them. Sometimes life conspires against you, and though you do the best anyone could do, you fail. Rarely, you are given copious opportunities, allowing you to make big mistakes but still succeed in the end. This is less common as you progress through the game, just like real life. But the most common opportunities for success are narrow openings. You are given the chance to succeed, but in order to do so, you must do everything right. Any failures on your part are fatal to your efforts. This is different then the circumstances in which your efforts are meaningless, in which success is impossible; in these instances, success is possible, but. very. difficult. Just like real life!
As in real life, if you have capital available to you, you are able to buy your way into having more of a chance at success. Also like real life, you can spend your capital and still fail, if circumstances are strongly against you, or if you make poor decisions regarding the opportunities you've been given. In a delightfully self-aware statement, the developer has made it so that real-life money is the capital used to give oneself an advantage in their simulated reality. Truly an artistic irony.
What is the moral of this game, and this review? Nothing in life is completely random; by making good decisions, you'll get farther than by making asinine ones. But there are always elements outside your control, that will turn the best laid plans into paper mache. You simply must, if you hope to progress, always act as if making good decisions matter, because eventually it will, and when it does you must be prepared to make such decisions. I'm about to make a good decision now. I'm uninstalling this game.

Pros;

A large amount of historical battles to choose from allowing you to really feel like you are part of the campaign.
Decent AI that moves to counter you and often takes you by suprise.
Glorious graphics.
A competant learning curve throughout the game.
Historical figures that you can recruit to lead your men.
Lovely music and sound quality during combat (if a little repetative at times).
Honest to goodness had me at the edge of my seat focusing hard at the higher game levels to win battles.
SO MUCH MORE! SOOOOO MUCH!
Cons;
AI scaling is a bit wonky, you often end up being heavily outnumbered leaving some battles impossible to win if you try and increase the size of your army.
Routing AI often flee through your troops when you really can't afford to chase them and they end up coming back in perfect flanking positions.
Veteran costs are a bit extreme considering battle rewards (even with maxed out politics, economy and training perks).
Leaves you wanting more skirmish battles and minor engagements.
Flanking seems a little random at times, i.e flanking an enemy often does very little compared to what it does to you.
Cavalry vs routing inf brigades needs a buff.
Cavalry AI is often a little unresponsive.
Improvements needed in the future;
Ability to have a multiplayer feature for historical + custom battles would be AMAZING!

The gunplay is tight and twitchy, rewarding focused headshots, pre-emptives, and well cooked grenades.  Perhaps the worst thing about this game is the fact that you can get the same experience pretty much verbatim by playing the original.  There are a handful of superficially 'new' grenades, one gun that feels somewhat different, and some pretty sweet power armor...otherwise this is shinier FEAR 1.  Start there if you're new to the series and come here when you want some more slow motion FPS intensity.  If you like the FEAR series be sure to check out Vanquish on a console near you; it takes some inspirations, but elevates them to a whole new level

You can't really even mention this title anywhere without being bombarded by arguments that it's "not a real game", as if that actually matters. It's systematically downvoted and 0-bombed and trolled pretty much anywhere it's discussed and reviewed. I'm certain this review will end up getting a handful of automatic thumbs down from people who hate that this kind of thing even exists and want to fight against... whatever it is that it represents. As if this game being made and being successful means that every developer in the world is going to drop everything to try to imitate it. I don't get that line of thinking.
Really, who cares? Whether it's a proper game or not, it's a unique experience that's highly experimental and plays with interactivity in a new way. It's not entirely successful in what it sets out to achieve, but it's interesting and it's cheap. I might agree with the notion that it's a bit overhyped. This wasn't really game of the year material for me so much as it was a fun diversion that was fun to unravel, with a cool idea on how to interact with a story. But I don't regret spending time with it, and I'm glad that we live in an era of gaming where developers can try new things that are worth talking about and debating.
Don't take this one as the bold new face of indie gaming, because it's not. It's a story, most of all. One that you might get wrapped up in, or you might not. I love working out a mystery, so I did. The central mechanic works very well if you don't try to break it. That is, if you mostly follow the story as you discover pieces of it, searching keywords related to things you just discovered, or trying to fill in the gaps as things come into view. I've heard of plenty of people "breaking" the game by accidentally stumbling onto big revelations by guessing key words rather than following the trail of clues, but that doesn't mean you ruined iit. The big twists hidden away still leave a lot of holes in the story when you find them, and if all goes well, you'll feel a definite sense of the whole picture coming into focus as you explore the database.
The really cool thing it does, one that I thought worked well, is let the player define their own victory. It's easy to discover the biggest twist early on without meaning to, but even once you know it there are a lot of other details to fill in. While playing, I went from a fuzzy sense of what happened to a more defined picture, and without viewing 100% of the clips, I eventually found I could explain every little detail. Things clicked into place and I felt like I "won", even though the game didn't tell me that. Evoking a sense of personal victory without actually telling the player that they beat the game is just really clever, and is what makes this worth playing yourself rather than just watching someone else on youtube or whatever.
It's a good conversation piece, as well. The "ending", such as it is, can be interpreted in two different ways, so even once you've put together the overall story, it's worth searching for evidence towards one side or the other. I can see it as a good game to play with someone else, or to share experiences with afterwards. I liked what it did, and got a satisfying amount of entertainment out of it, and you might too if you're not hung up on the whole "not a game" thing.

I bought Blood Money back in 2007 when I seen it on a shelf at EB games when they still existed for 10 dollars. I knew basically nothing except from what I had seen on a G4 episode of X-Play. I came home, popped it in my white xbox 360, and spent the next few weeks playing this game.
Tons of weapons from pistols and rifles to knives and fiber wire, Multiple ways to complete each mission, Great stealth system, All around amazing game.
There are 4 difficulty levels that all scale very well. Each difficulty level brings in less help from the agency you work for and more ways to get caught and screw you over in the long run. It's punishing but it does it in a great way.
Since you get to play out each mission like you want to, It can lead to great satisfaction when you find new ways to eliminate your target and walk out like nothing happened. From setting it up as a "Incident" to blatently shooting them in the face you can feel like a true assassin to a petty criminal.
I don't want to say anything about the story since spoiling anything is never fun.
There are minor bugs and glitches with AI and the game enviroment but I have never come across anything game breaking.
All in all It's a great game. I recomend picking this game up whenever you have the money to enjoy this cult hit.

I would love to like this game, I really do. But it has one fatal flaw that ruins the entire experience.
No free save option. Checkpoints only. And they are rare.
I played through an entire chapter without finding a checkpoint, only to die on the boss.
Bottom line: When I had to replay the entire chapter, was when I said: I'm out!

I am just going to get right to it.
The world design is incredibly repetitive, especially for the many dungeons that only come in 4 flavors, Snow Forest, Ice Cave, Blizzardy Mountain pass, and weird grey magictech ruins, all of which use repeatedly recycled traversal puzzles.
The world as well is very linearly designed with dungeon areas having to constantly be transverses to move forward, which makes any situation where you find you need to back track a absolute chore until very late in the game.
And Backtrack you probably will, as without a guide it is very easy to accidentally miss some important item drops needed for crucial abilities later on because you didn't kill a certain monster in a certain way to get a certain item to get
an ability that turns out is practically mandatory to beat a boss.
The Spiritnite equipment system in itself is deeply flawed as it limits the amount of abilities you can have at any give time, yet has little tactical value due to the wildly unbalanced abilities letting you easily find a dual tech or 2 that will let you coast through 80% of the game while ignoring nearly any other tactical option.
The story and characters while serviceable and far better then most of it's contemporaries is uneven, feeling both dragged out and rushed at the same time, with weird little nagging plot holes from what I can only assume came from content being cut.
If you like piano heavy music this game is your soundtrack and is genuinely the highlight of the game, but for others it might just come off as too artsy and pretentious in combination with the rest of the package.
I know I sound really down on I AM Setsuna but there is an enjoyable game to be had here and even shines in a few spots. Just do not go into it expecting the second coming of Chrono Trigger as the Devs being a bunch of industry rookies simply did not have the chops or the time to even come close to perfection.
Knowing the history behind this game's incredibly short development time and small kickstarter scale budget, I may be more forgiving of the games shortcomings then some might, but the game is still a far sight better then most other modern low budget JRPGs like the constant stream of DLC laden crap Compile Heart ♥♥♥♥♥ out every couple months riding entirely on fan survice and endless vapid voiced over dialog where nothing meaninful is ever said.
I am Setsuna has some real problems, and the buyer should be aware before they blindly jump in, but you can do far worse as far as JRPGs on Steam go.

I recommend this game and all of it's assets and flaws to anyone looking for a story-driven sandbox title with a uniquely ridiculous and campy world that could have only come from the mind of Hideo Kojima.

Hearts are the energy system in this game, failling a puzzle takes a heart, you have to have a heart to replay a puzzle. Hearts regenerate with a increasing length timer  You can Buy Gems with real money to buy hearts and many boosters to get you past hard puzzles.

It's a solid game and contrary to popular belief, plays nothing like Overwatch. The only similarity it may possibly share are the character lineups, but that's something to be expected from any 'arena shooter revolving around classes/heroes. I was actually in the midst of writing a wall of text but it was slowly turning into a fullblown essay which mainly derived from my frustration with this game; which is not something I want this 'review' to focus on. So I'm going to keep it very brief and concise for a change.
Cons (applies mostly to PvP):
- Questionable to Horrible matchmaking.
- Spamfest of skills often obscuring screen like magic gnomes joypuking on your face.
- Friendly and hostile units blocking your sight and colliding with your skills.
- Somewhat difficult to track your target(s) because of the above two points.
- Disconnects/Leavers that leave an entire team crippled in versus.
- Absolutely nothing to compensate for the above point.
- People who play this game thinking it's Overwatch.
- Questionable character balance.
- Campaign somehwat easy (even on advanced) only getting difficult in 4-5 player parties.
- Lack of players for campaign matchmaking making full/filled parties really rare.
- Campaign is forgettable and short; doesn't really capture any attention to the story.
- Probably more..
Pros:
+ Despite the cons, the Campaign is enjoyable action-wise.
+ The characters, their different or similar personalities and voice lines.
+ Interesting and clean artstyle.
+ Great soundtrack.
+ The humor which relates to the character voice lines really.
+ Oscar Mike & Whiskey Foxtrot.
+ Orendi & Shayne/Aurox.
+ Okay now I'm just naming irrelevant things to extend this 'pros' list..
So yeah.. when it comes to quantity or severity, the cons outweigh the pros from my (current) perspective. That doesn't mean it's a bad game... right? So would I recommend this game.. For it's full price, definitely not. Not to mention there's still the season pass that will add new story missions and characters. Or even the microtransactions for 'special' skins and taunts.. ..not sure what they were thinking adding those to this full retail game especially in it's current state.
Even though it's nothing like Overwatch.. this game in it's 'fullest' is priced at a higher value than even their Origins edition (which are mainly skins). That would indicate either the campaign or the difference in games is enough to justify a higher price tag, which obviously isn't the case in my honest opinion; by far.
Putting it bluntly.. Get the digital deluxe edition when it's on a decent sale and I'd say it's fair enough of a deal to get your money's worth especially if you're into Borderlands' gameplay. And solely on that condition will I leave this recommendation on a 'Yes' note.

Let me preface this review by saying it's going to be very heavily weighted towards negative points. That said, I would still recommend the game for its price, especially on sale. I got it for $1 and I'm more than confident I got my money's worth out of this game. It is FAR better than many other free or $1 games I've played.
bit Dungeon II is what I'd describe as an action-roguelite. It's halfway between a twinstick shooter and an RPG with roguelike elements tacked on (most prominently, permadeath.)
The game immediately throws you in the deep end. First you see the title screen, then from the moment you hit "play game" you're more or less on your own aside from some short instructions if you figure out how to pause the game (ESC key.) NOTHING is explained clearly. You have to figure it out on your own. In a way I feel like this was sorta a good thing, since many roguelikes do the same, giving you nothing but a list of key binds and maybe a general overview of your objective.
PROS:
+The game is well polished for its price, and well worth it on sale.
+It features "8-bit" (note the quotes) graphics which look pretty nice for what they are. I've seen a lot worse in more highly priced games *cough*Teleglitch*cough*
+There's a wide variety of equipment to be had, and there's a lot of different designs for each piece. They are all represented correctly on your character sprite too, which I think is super neat. There's a lot of games out there like this that don't bother, or will only show weapons/shields on the character.
+I like the way the game starts with dropping you in the deep end of a story that is never really fully explained. You'll have to make guesses as to what's going on, which I personally find pretty interesting. I cannot say the same for the way the game drops you in the deep end of its mechanics though.
+There's a few different classes of weapons which all have their own combat styles, more or less. Each relies on a certain stat (or two) which means you'll have to decide what stats you want to focus on and can make it painful when you have to give up a rare weapon due to not having enough points in its particular stat.
+You can play this game one-handed, either one hand on the keyboard or one hand on the mouse. It's pretty simple.
+Combat is fairly straightforward and easy to learn.
+It's "open-world" so there's some exploration to be had. Not sure if the map is somewhat randomized each time because I did literally everything there was to do in the game on my first run.
+The game scales as you progress story-wise, meaning that you can grind for the next dungeon if you want and it won't scale until you've beaten the current dungeon. This, IMO, is a good thing unlike certain other games which continually scale to attempt to keep the game challenging and therefore defeating the purpose of levelling up to begin with.
+The game is infinitely playable, it loops and continues scaling until you die for real. Technically this is a good thing, I personally find that kind of replayability extremely dull but eh.
+Enemies are randomized every time you enter a room, and corpses are permanent in dungeons. This becomes pretty neat when certain corpse-eating enemies start appearing and getting stronger the more corpses you leave behind in a dungeon.
CONS:
-The game is too easy. I literally beat the whole game and got all the achievements in one run, my first run. It would be MUCH tougher if you did not have the "second chance" life token, but unfortunately you NEED to keep that on hand to beat the game properly.
-The game is pretty imbalanced.
--Some weapon types are clearly better than others, apparently due to how the damage is calculated which is never made clear. Weapons that use more than one stat to determine their damage always seem to be better. This also happens to coincide with the fact that you can use a shield or spellbook with the two weapon types that let you do that, which makes spears and knives much better overall, especially since they also hit faster than the two-handed weapons. Probably. I didn't try staves.
--Some enemies are complete pushovers, whereas others will remain tanky no matter how far you get into the game. There's not really much in between the two extremes. The tanky ones, as a result, also tend to be the ones that do the most damage.
--I found the majority of the bosses to be FAR easier than hacking through the dungeon to get to them. In most cases, the small bands of enemies and attrition from working your way through will wear you down much faster than the boss.
-The game drops you in the deep end and nothing is explained. You could well end your first run by not investigating the nearby cave at the spawn point and picking out a weapon, since you cannot fight without one.
-The combat is very simple, which makes it a little uninteresting. All you do is walk into enemies to auto-attack them, and you can press spacebar/left mouse to spend MP to attack at will. What this turns into for the melee weapons is "mash spacebar to win" except for a few enemies who will tank that.
--Holding the attack button is meant to charge up for a special attack, but it was pretty inconsistent and did not always work. That's also the same command for blocking, which also did not seem to always work.
--Bows make a complete embarassment of most of the bosses, not least of all the final boss who lazily followed me around the room while I popped off shots until it died - it fired a grand total of 4 projectiles so clearly it was meant to be able to retaliate at range, but it didn't try.
-There's a few puzzles but they're ALL really easy to solve.
--The mazes may initially be confusing but there's a VERY obvious clue as to how to solve them in every single maze. On top of this there are NPCs who will outright tell you the solution.
--There's a few "push the blocks onto the buttons" puzzles but none of them are actually challenging at all.
-The game makes a point of saying that you lose EVERYTHING when you die, equipment, levels, everything. However you get to keep your money, which can be used to buy some pretty strong equipment if you know where it is.
-No save function, so you have to beat the game in one sitting. The game is actually kinda lengthy so you'd have to leave it on when you're busy.
-Enemies respawning every time you leave a screen and return can get annoying, especially when a lot of them can turn invisible and block your path/surprise attack you.

text:
"I am Setsuna" is a gorgeous game with an indie-developer feel and real solid, finished and enjoyable gameplay that you may find from a typical modern Square Enix game. This game was inspired by Chrono Trigger and Chrono Cross with obvious hints to the Final Fantasy franchise. However, all of these references shadow this game. With the summary of the game alluding to the Chrono-franchise, I feel they inevitably force this game into their shadows.
The Chrono-franchise was folds upon folders deeper and more unique than this game. The only hints you may feel from "I am Setsuna" in relation to these games is the sound track and subtle environment details from time to time. The combat system is Final Fantasy 13 without any player movement (the enemies move). The combat system lacks severely in complexity and description. In Chrono Cross, the player could talk to a village elder and chose whether or not to have an indepth tutorial on battle - not to mention, the battles got more complex as you played the game when introduced with new magic and items.
This game is very shallow, they provide no character depth in the first few hours and the story is only sad feeling due to the music, not the content. The level design is very linear. The battle items show their worth but the standard items are useless outside of gaining profit. The game makes it a point for you to explore (if you go in to the menu and dig around a bit), but the exploration is poor and minimal at best.
The game punishes you for not grinding, but that only happens later... There are no signs of it wanting you to do that in the first place. It feels simple, it feels easy, until you get one particular boss fight, then good luck.
This does not go without saying that this game is very unique and rather enjoyable! It's the first JRPG (turn/time based) within the past 10 years that I've played that was enjoyable to look at and interact with. Its simpleness is somewhat refreshing and the art style makes you yearn for more. I want to see more concept art, more character art, more environments. I want to read and see more about the tribes and characters, where they come from. It is a really pretty game and it's perfect for those entering the JRPG scene; those needing a warm up from our high-quality-graphics-obsessed-era to the good ol' JRPGs with hard-to-look-at-graphics from back in the day...
I recommend this game because it feels independent, it feels cute and rough around the edges, but looks like a kids game with some mature ideas. It's a game that will make you want to play more RPGs.
The music man. The music.

I am Setsuna is a game designed to mimic RPGs from the "Golden Age" of the 90s. Chrono Trigger is the name I see thrown around most often in comparisons, but I feel that comparison is part of why this game let me down. Don't get me wrong, I am Setsuna is not a terrible game, but it's not a game worth paying $15+ for. It's pretty short, has a minimalistic story and flat characters, and a poorly explained combat system.
The setting is unique, and it did a good job of grabbing my attention intially. The soundtrack is pleasant, it's nearly all piano and it does wonders for establishing that unique setting. The game is meant to feel lonely, and it does. But at times that loneliness lends itself to tedium and boredom as all of the environments blend together.
The combat system tries to encourage mixing and matching characters to find the best team for certain fights through combo attacks. This is I am Setsuna's attempt to reproduce one of the best aspects of Chrono Trigger's combat system, but it ultimately fails for two reasons:
1. The characters can only equip a small amount of their usable abilities, and every character involved in a combo attack needs the correct ones equipped to use it. Switching abilities out takes time and there is no system in place to have saved sets of abilities, which means it is very time consuming to switch in and use other characters. Characters outside of the party recieve reduced experience as well, so constantly switching is necessary to keep them all at an appropriate level.
2. The game explains which abilities are used in combo attacks in a menu hidden away in the codex, I found it only after I Googled the combinations and it was pointed out to me. So in order to figure out which abilities characters need the player must navigate their way to a completely different section of the menus to reference the necessary information. It is extremely cumbersome.
I am Setsuna is a game that was created with a noble idea in mind. I want to see more traditional JRPGs come out onto Steam, but I think that Tokyo RPG Factory needs to rework a few things in their next entry. The inventory system needs to be streamlined and the combat needs to be better explained. While I do look forward to what they produce next, I do not recommend buying this game unless it is $15 or less, even if you are a dedicated RPG fan.

One of the most artistic and genre-loyal games made in recent years, I am Setsuna is sure to delight anyone who ever fell in love playing traditional Final Fantasy/Phantasy Star type games in the 90's and earl 00's. The combat system is fun and engaging, the music is amazing, and the art and story are top notch. Strongly reccommended.

I really wanted to like this game.  Unfortunately, I don't and that's too bad.
The battle system is inelegant and fairly opaque... but has a lot of promise.  Some of the mechanics aren't explained well in the game text (for example: the explanation of what upgrade material does.  Figuring out how it actually works is very expensive).  I'm blaming the translation which feels about half-way done.  Game balance is wonky and I'd say that monster damage is too high past a certain point in the game.
Dungeon designs are awful.  It's all squares with monsters connected to other squares with monsters.
The player has negative agency throughout the story.  Other characters will literally ignore anything you say or do to push along the main plot.  Nothing you choose to do matters in the slightest (except for one dungeon but it doesn't make sense why).  This is probably the biggest hit against the game and they'd have been better off not even allowing the player to pick dialogue options.  You can tell that there is an intended voice for the main character (generic shonen hero) and shame on you for not playing into it.
The story writing is... just boring.  It just never hooked me.
Otherwise, the game's aesthetic is pretty solid.  Character designs are good.  Music is decent... maybe a bit repetitive in some areas or forgettable in others.
The UI is passable, though it could use few quality of life improvements (mainly cleaning up the interaction between talismans and spritnites, how things are sorted in various screens).
Overall... the longer I played the game, the more its flaws seemed to stand out and the less I enjoyed it.

CONS:
I couldn't quite finish this game.  I got to the final dungeon, went a ways without finding a save point, got killed by 3 of the dinosaur thingies, and rage quit.  The game is really easy for most of the game, but hit massive difficulty spikes that were out of place and not fun.  The game systems were poorly explained, and was missing a lot of features that I consider standard for modern RPGs (auto-save, sell all buttons, clearly designed tutorials, etc.)  For instance, it was REALLY difficult to figure out which spritnite to equip in order to enable combos.  Why...?  The story was also not very well written or fleshed out.  It felt like a super dumbed down version, and poorly written version at that, of the Final Fantasy X story.  That wouldn't be a bad thing as I really like that game, but the fact that it had no soul made the story an afterthought.
PROS:
The music and visuals were very solid, although they had a 3DS RPG vibe to them, which for being on PC didn't look all that good as far as character models are concerned.  There was a good variety of skills available, although at the end of the game I just spammed fire 2 and cyclone (which you get at the very beginning of the game, btw) and killed all of the end game trash enemies (except the afforementioned dinosaurs).
VERDICT:
Overall, I am on the fence on whether this game is something someone should play or not, and I am going on the negative side.  If you want to play a game like this, go with the original and play Chrono Trigger, or pick up Final Fantasy VI or something on Steam, but I would say this one could be skipped.

Admittedly, I was apprehensive about getting this game, at first. With how it advertises itself as a love-letter to JRPG's, I was concerned it would be too derevitive to hold my interest. However, I'm glad to say I was proved wrong. Though it certianly calls back to older games I've played before, it holds a certain charm that's all it's own. Individually, each aspect of the game can be said to be a bit generic. The combat system is like some later titles of Final Fantasy, the writing isn't superb, and the music is essentially on par with similar titles. However, together, these things create something that's rather charming, which the art style only helps to add to. I have yet to finish the game to know for certain how invested I am in it, but I really like where it's going. Here's hoping things continue along this positive trend!

I really...really...really want to recommend this game. It's got a great musical score, great artistic style, humor, interesting and seldom-seen-in-a-video-game Mexican-theme. And I've always loved Metroid style games.
** BUT **
The platforming sections of the game are ridiculously difficult. Needlessly difficult, I'd add. I'm still stuck on the section in the Tuli Tree, where you must do a series of wall jumps combined with flipping in and out of the land of death. I cannot do it. And I'm no stranger to platformers!
I wouldn't have a problem with this kind of difficulty if it were only used sparingly in areas of the map with hidden power ups or bonus content. But to make just getting to the next dungeon/temple/castle/level this ludicrously challenging is too much to ask! I play games to be entertained; if the gameplay turns into a repetitive series of failures that's no fun at all!
Part of the problem is that the controller layout isn't ideal. A few glaring control issues: One, Right-Trigger to switch between light and dark worlds!? Bad button mapping! Also, when playing two players, we often accidentally enter the bubble mode, which is disaterous if we both do it at once! And the button placement for "chicken mode" isn't so good either. Rather than doding (left trigger) I sometimes bump the left button for Chicken mode. And on top of all that, there's no way to re-map the buttons.
So, DEV...  before I could recommend this game to anyone, PLEASE fix the level designs and button mapping!
EDIT: I changed my mind on this one. I gave it rest for a while then came back to it. As I had previously said, it IS insanely hard! But I did finally manage to make more progress. I'm now all the way to boss fight with Calaca! It's definitely a good game, although, I still wish they had made a easy mode!
