An intense, and somewhat unique experience, as well as being a sequel to one of the scariest and most action-packed games, FEAR 2 delivers an incredible experience with a fun slow-mo mechanic, big weapons, mech combat, and thrills that will keep you at the edge of your seat.

Because Alma is Alma. Whoever never played FEAR can't understand why.
Anyway, FEAR 2 is putting you in the shoes of Michael Becket, a sergeant in a special unit, used to answer to any kind of special missions involving paranormal (F.E.A.R.). Unfortunately, he's sent to retrieve Aristide, the mighty CEO of Armacham Technologies, that has something to do with the current problem in Auburn district. After a powerful detonation (the ending of the original F.E.A.R. game), he wakes up in an hospital, with people trying to kill you and with Alma Wade, the powerful spirit, taking an interest in him.
The plot serves to erase Perseus Mandate (a weak link) and Extraction Point (one of the best add-ons I've ever played) and to make a continuity in F.E.A.R's universe by the original developers. While I find it interesting as it's focusing also on Alma Wade's personality and her conflicted feelings. It's true that in itself, Armacham is a company with many secret projects (Origin is one of them, hence the title of the game) but I'm more attracted to Alma's struggling and story than Becket's.
Anyway, FEAR 2 is a FPS, like the previous game. While in FEAR, your HUD was pretty simple, in FEAR 2, it's more elaborated, like you have connected glasses or helmet on the head. However, Becket, during the story, will acquire a power that the Pointman in FEAR has: bullet time. True, Becket isn't Alma's son contrary to the previous hero and the previous antagonist. But trust Armacham to play with your character.
Anyway, that bullet time is very useful when you have to battle strange creatures or Replikas, clones and soldiers that are controlled by telepathy. You're not alone to fight: the rest of your team is helping, though they're nearly all affected by Alma apart for your lieutenant. Anyway, you fight, you shoot and you take advantage of your environement. You choose which weapons to use, you improve your power thanks to syringues and you collect information in the form of folders. That's how the story is also revealing itself.
FEAR 2 has some hard passages, mainly in the high difficulty (hospital, research center, the last fight). While it's well-balanced, you have to be resourceful. Even when piloting an EVE (big robots), you need to take into account everything.
However, FEAR 2 is perhaps more tragic than FEAR in the sense that Armacham never hesitated to cross lines for experimentation. It was already creepy to learn Alma's story in FEAR, here, you're learning that she wasn't the only one to be exploited like a piece of meat. While it makes sense to explore an hidden hospital as you were operated, to try to find a way out of Auburn destroyed or to put an end in another hidden compound, it's shocking to find the truth in a school and mainly what's under it.
While the previous game was mainly set during the night, this one, when outside, is a daylight game. However, as you're in a battlefield, the graphics are showing this world in chaos, whether you are. And they're pretty good for this game. You're not let down during your hallucinating periods (Alma's doing) or when you're in the real world. Alma herself is less creepy in her adult form but only because she wants to appear normal in Becket's mind - else, she's still the creepy young adult that seeks revenge on the world for what happened to her and her sons.
The soundtrack is also very good, fitting to the fights or to the important moments. The voice actings are also good. If anything, I've two favorite tracks that I've listened a lot when I used YouTube as my playlist.
Anyway, I loved this game. I'm just sad that there is no Steam Cloud - the technology back then wasn't spread or existing for other games - though it's been a long time since playing but I remember when I changed desktops, that's how I discovered that I've to unlock everything again, as the game has ingame achievements.
Like any FEAR, even FEAR 3 that I still need to play, the best is still the plot and Alma. FEAR 2 is an excellent sequel, though I wish Extraction Point to be still cannon - forget about Perseus Mandate. That game is a must-have.

If you like match-3 games that get you to look at the board differently, Legend of Numbers is worth trying out. Its boards have two types of tiles: the usual kind that can be matched in the usual rows/columns of 3, 4, etc., and those that can only be combined with an exactly matching tile. These two types of tiles can block each other, which adds an extra level of tactical thinking to the game: is this the tile I want to create with this match? Is this a good or a bad spot for it? Is there a way for me to maneuver a particular tile where it'll make the best match?
I don't know whether I'll enjoy this long term, but the first hour or so has been a fun experience, as I start learning the new rules, and figuring out the best ways to solve the board.

Battleborn is the most enjoyable multiplayer experience I have had.   It requires miles of patience, and rewards patience tenfold, handily.
Battleborn is a first person MOBA, where you can also go on WoW style dungeons with the heroes.
Battleborn has 28 classes that you must learn, and you want to get them all from rank 1 to rank 15.  As you level the classes, you are constantly rewarded with skins, taunts, loot packs, and most of all, skill as a gamer.
Every hero in Battleborn has a laser specific role, and it's up to you to figure out what that role is, and how you play that role early game, mid game, and endgame.  In game, you level the heroes from 1 to 10, and every level you select a helix choice that augments your skills in one way or the other, so the amount of build differences there are per class are dauntingly high.
There is a long period when learning the classes, where you just can't seem to do anything right.  You're not killing anything, you're getting killed all the time, and the skills just don't ♥♥♥♥ing work.  After you endure this humiliating initiation for a few ranks, you start unlearning how *you* think the hero should be played, and you start adapting to the way the hero *does* play.
Also, please remeber that someone playing ambra at rank 1 will have an entirely different playstyle than someone who has max rank and has unlocked all the helix mutations.
When you perfectly learn, and the hero clicks, it's one of the best experiences I've had in gaming.  It makes you feel so god damned good, and you wonder why *everyone* doesn't play this hero.  You'd be happy playing this *one* hero from here on out, and you go through this experience with every hero.
Early game heroes feel weak, and are quick to die.  So, clearly, you don't want to die.   If you die to enemy plaers, they will get a boost of experience, so repeatedly dying results in a very strong opponent.
The goal of the multiplayer is *don't die* and *focus on the objectives*.  In meltdown, you kill the minion creep wave, not the enemy players.   In capture, you work as a team to dominate the map points.   In incursion, you lead your creep wave to the enemy sentries, and destroy the sentries.
Please, if you have MOBA experience, play Battleborn like a MOBA.  Play safe, don't die, communicate with your team, and don't die.
T is push to talk, Y is party chat, B teleports you back to base, refilling your health and shields.  If you don't see a healer next to you, and you have low health, run back and teleport, every time.
Good luck, have fun!

Let me start off by saying I love this game.
TL;DR     It’s great fun, but some serious changes have to be implemented to revive the community.
It’s nothing like Overwatch. Overwatch is like TF2. The closest thing to Battleborn is probably SMITE.
Battleborn is a fun mesh of FPS gameplay and MOBA-esque PVP. I feel like that’s the problem with it, though. FPS games persist because they have strong communities of people who enjoy playing the game. Don't get me wrong, it's more fun to win than it is to lose. MOBAs are renowned for having toxic communities that harass and plague its own player base. Battleborn’s player base has dwindled from the time of its launch. There’s no denying that.
Can you still find a game? Yes
Will you spend a long time in que? Yes (Based on my experience, anyway.)
But most of the games I find have at least one toxic player that drives away their own team. Since the game does not have a content release schedule or rewards system that caters to the FPS crowd, the hounding of experienced players drives away anyone who wants a casual PVP experience.
I’ll be completely honest: I can’t speak for the MOBA crowd, because I don’t like MOBAs. I don’t like how they control, I don’t understand them, and I hate the communities. I’ve tried playing DotA, DotA2, League of Legends, Heroes of the Storm, Smite, and Paragon. In every one of them the learning curve is such that I have no patience to learn how to play the game “right” and I can’t play the game the way I want.
That being said, Battleborn doesn’t seem to cater to the MOBA crowd either. Battleborn doesn’t punish people for going off on their own like MOBAs do, there isn’t a jungle to level or hide in to surprise your enemies, and the ‘towers’ (Sentries in Incursion mode) don’t function like the towers in MOBAs.
Battleborn, in short, takes some MOBA elements and lets you play them in an FPS setting. The game is great fun, but some serious changes have to be implemented to revive the community. I love this game; it’s the closest thing to a MOBA I even remotely enjoyed playing. I have poured over 200 hours into it in the first couple of weeks it was out.
Sadly, I haven’t wanted to play it recently because I have better things to do with my time than sit in queue for 5-15 minutes looking for a game, just to be ♥♥♥♥♥ed at by someone that doesn’t think one character belongs on the team, and then to have our game ruined in the first five minutes because someone rage-quits leaving us at a disadvantage.
I still would recommend Battleborn to anyone who likes Gearbox, FPS, or just wants something different. It’s fun as hell, funny, and has a lot of depth.

Let me start by saying that I really do like this game. The elements of design are excellent, especially in terms of sound and graphics. Building divisions and brigades, arming them with quintesential weapons of the era, and assigning leadership is engaging and interesting. Getting into a nasty exchange of musketry and cannon fire is a gleeful pleasure to watch and winning said fights is rewarding. But where things begin to fall apart for me is when the game starts to get bigger.
When I say bigger, I mean that in terms of the size of your army. Very rapidly, you will find yourself on titanically big maps, attempting to control dozens of units in an army that must be well over 70,000 men strong. You will also be forced to control that army in 1500-3000 man clumps, and organize them in a manner which will allow you to carry the day in battle. This is not easy.
This game is, quite frankly, not meant for people like me who simply do not have the headspace to manage such a colossal endeavor.
The game really shines when you are on the defensive. The nature of commanding such a vast array of troops lends itself to defensive fighting in almost every way. Reaction times are not as readily punished on the defensive, and understanding where the enemy will likely move towards and planning ahead for that assault is incredibly rewarding. Going on offensives, however, is a different animal entirely.
I truly believe that this game would beneift hugely from the inclusion of a cooperative game mode, wherein a friend could be given command of parts of your army. Being able to split the effort of commanding massive armies over multiple people (just like command structures in real life) would, in my very humble opinion, make this game one of the top 3 in my library today if not the very best.
Today, I can hardly stomach the idea of playing any of the battles past the second or third year of this epic American conflict. I'm not ashamed, merely dissapointed that I cannot enjoy what is perhaps the greatest American Civil War tactical and strategic game that has every come out. I say this as a reenactor, a gamer, and a Civil War buff: I cannot recommend this game.

Guacamelee is a Metroidvania-style game with a strong emphasis on platforming and brawling. As with other games in this genre, you have some freedom to explore the world, with access to new areas controlled by gaining new abilities. Exploring this beautiful Mexican art inspired world is made easy with the game's great map system and fast travel points. Blocked areas that require specific abilities to enter are color coded and are marked on the map making them easy to go back to once you have the ability to break them.
The platforming sections are mostly challenging. You'll be combining precision jumping, special moves, roll/dodge, and switching worlds to reach distant platforms. The combat provides a good challenge as well, and as a luchador you will punch and grapple your way through different enemy types that you'll be facing in bunches. As you go deeper in the game, these enemies will have different types of shields requiring a certain type of move to break. Some will also exist in one world or the other and you must be in the correct world to attack them.
It took me around 8 hours to finish this in my first playthrough, but there's some replay value to it as you can play as other characters with different attributes. There are also some side quests, collectibles, and you can continue exploring the world after you've beaten the final boss. Highly recommended.

I had high expectations for this game ever since I saw a trailer for it. Boy, did it meet and excel past the standards I had. The combat is extremely fluid, the platforming puzzles are very tricky, and hot damn the graphics are stylish. Guacamelee is a Metroidvania game, fyi. I have yet to test co-op, but with how combo-friendly the game is, but I don't doubt for a moment it would be fun. I haven't beaten the game yet, as it's fairly challenging; I regret not buying it sooner, and so should you.
P.S: The game has epliepsy warnings for good reason; I highly recommend a controller, although the game certainly is playable on keyboard as I have noticed.

I've been meaning to make a review for this game, but I've just been too busy playing the damn thing than to make time to give it it's well deserved praise! I'd like to give this a proper review so hopefully I don't get too drawn out with it.
TL;DR: Planet Coaster is the Disneyland of Theme Park Simulator games and playing this game gives me the same feeling as watching a fireworks show at the park or even hearing the music being played just as you enter the gates! that feeling of childlike abandon coupled with goosebumps and feelings of nostalgia!
Like many fans of this genre I was introduced to it by Roller Coaster Tycoon, this game had a huge effect on my life that I became obsessed with Theme park design, coupled with the fact that I live nearby various major theme parks fueled my obsession. I've always created parks I wanted to visit or rides of my favorite TV shows/ video games that I hope I could one day ride myself. I've had all past games of Roller Coaster Tycoon and each of them fed my hobby of Theme park building. Then came a game I was so eagerly awaiting to be released(I won't be mentioning any names) it promised limitless possibilities (and grid-less building!) and couldn't wait for it; Then I saw the first trailer, lets just say I was distraught with the result and thought the genre was dead but then came Planet coaster
This game gave me the same feeling as watching the fireworks at Disneyland. from the first trailer onward each news of this game added more potential for that perfect theme park builder/simulator I've always wanted! There's just so much care and detail that has been put into this game, not only that but you can tell that the team that made this game are fans of Theme parks themselves! This was made by the same company that was hired by Disney to make a 1:1 recreation of Disneyland for a video game so of course this game has good Theme Park design under it's belt!
The emphasis on theming you parks is what really drew me in. Sure you can plop down a few Rides and call it a park, but they added a game mechanic that boosts your rides if you take the time to actually theme and decorate your rides for your guests enjoyment. Speaking of the guests, the animation and design of the people really brings the park to life, you can zoom right in with the guests and walk along side them as if your actually there in the park! I remember playing RCT3 and zooming down to the guests view, but I don't feel as if I'm actually there. With Planet coaster those rides really tower over you, and going down one of the hills on a roller coaster feels more real than riding POV in RCT3.
If your a fan of Theme parks this should definetly be in your library.

I cannot find a reason to play this game instead of doing either of those two alternatives. I am Setsuna is a charming game that hearkens back to the old single-player RPGs that I used to play in my youth, where graphics didn't matter nearly as much to me as the story. In the case of the story of this particular RPG, the similarity between some of the core narrative concepts of a (begrudgingly admitted) favorite of mine, Final Fantasy X, was what drove me to finish it.
I am Setsuna performs in most ways that you would expect an RPG to perform - there is a host of memorable characters that you eventually befriend on a long journey, the world is filled with interesting little tidbits of knowledge and lore, there are dozens of treasures to be collected and the combat system is engaging and challenging when need be. The musical score stands out as being one of the more memorable aspects of the game to me, as nearly every single instrumental is composed of artfully constructed piano pieces that both establish the deceptive intensity of the main character's story and draw you deep within the story with recognizable melodies. The world is wonderfully put together, simple enough to not detract from the stylized nature of the game but detailed enough to make you appreciate what you're looking at.
The few legitimate criticisms that I have are small gripes that mostly stem from the relative simplicity of the plot and a few systematic frustrations that made me put my controller down and go "okay, well, that happened". This is one of many stories much like the role-playing games of the 1990s so a bit of tropey goodness is expected, but something about how the dialogue is written and the characters interact with one another takes away from the sorrow that could be inherent in Setsuna's journey. It seems impersonal, almost overdramatically written, and you find yourself witnessing tragedy and crisis being solved in a matter of moments, so it's hard to invest in a story where everyone seems to have the same lukewarm answer. If you watched as much anime as I did in high school (you can laugh if you want, WHATEVER MAN) you'll quickly notice that most of the main cast follow stereotypical archetypes, which can get a little bit boring if you enjoy more to your characters than the most basic of personalities.
One thing I will mention that irked me in particular was that there are a very sparse number of save points and no ability to turn on any sort of auto-save feature. If you get stuck on a boss fight, you very well may have to repeat the last fifteen or so that you needed to get through to get to that point. Come on, man. Save points EVERYWHERE is like RPG 101.
I am Setsuna is a cute game and I reccommend it to anyone looking to play something familiar, sweet and a little bit sad and loaded with nostalgia that will make you want to pick up all your old favorites again.

This game is a great modern-day JRPG. I won't compare this game to any one other JRPG out there because there are plenty of other reviews that already do that. I'll be touching upon how this game's battle system, story, music and world map are when related to some JRPG's that you might have played before.
Battle System
The battle system of this game reminds me a lot of Final Fantasy VII. I actually enjoy the ATB system and it works for me since it provides some sort of real time engagement during battle rather than the Breath of Fire IV style of selecting your moves against the enemy every 'turn'. It allows for better immersion and a more rewarding victory.
You engage in battle like how you did in Guardian's Crusade - walk upto a monster and engage it. The difference is that the battle mode doesn't switch you to a different system and keeps you on the same screen so the end of battle rewards and exp screens are super quick to get out of.
What I really like about this game is that non-active party members also earn EXP while not in battle so you can switch in a character you want to play at any time without it being at a disadvantage.
The Talisman 'fluxation' system is quite complex and useless in my opinion and I didn't even have to use any of it to beat the game. The Spritnite and fluxation seem to me like a desparate attempt to re-create the Materia from FF7.
Story
I would say that the story seems quite linear in the sense that you are guided every step of the way. There is no room for exploration until almost the end of the game. There aren't very many hidden things to explore - I've found them all and it took me just 15 minutes to find them all.
The story does offer some surprises that completely blew me off my feet. There isn't any voice acting - something you'd expect in a modern-day JRPG.
Music
The music is heavily influced from the Final Fantasy series. Although the Final Fantasy music albums are pure bliss, Setsuna does not do a good job with their music as many people seem to think. Their themes seem out-of-place in particular parts of the story. I would rate the music in this game to about 5 on a scale of 10.
World Map
The world map is beautiful in the sense that the artstyle is amazing. The map is almost entirely covered with snow and the artists did a great job of drawing it out. The individual areas are just reskins of areas visited previously in the game. The team has repurposed a lot of textures instead of creating new ones that makes me feel like the game lacks visual appeal. You tend to stare at the same blue frozen ground all the time for about 60% of the game.
All in all, it is a good JRPG experience but not worth the exorbidant amount of money that they charge you for it. I completed the game in about 16 hours (including all hidden areas) and was surprised at how short the storyline is. I would recommend getting this game during a sale.

Before I get to the review, I am aware that the game wasn't finished properly, and that Konami made some big mistakes. However, nonetheless, this game is still an experience to behold.
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is definitely one of my favourite games I have played this year. At the time of writing, I have been playing this since Halloween, all through November. I had a bit of a horror binge throughout October, and I should have totally been playing this instead.
MGSV has shown me some of my most enjoyed storylines, settings and characters this year. Having played other entries in the Metal Gear Solid series (never touched the first two Metal Gear games), I will admit that when I first heard Kiefer's voice I found it a little jarring. However, despite my love of David Hayter's quips and voice (which has more gravel than my garden path), I have come to enjoy Kiefer's performance. Once you play for a while, you warm up to it.
Furthermore, the endless attention to detail in this series, from character and story events taking places in an entirely plausible timeline across the whole series, as well as music and thematic choices, and the whole, gigantic, artistic vision that Hideo Kojima has created., come together to form a true marvel.
Additionally, some of the characters and themes explored within MGSV have made me feel so much more empathy, horror, dread, joy and countless other emotions. Seriously, this has put to shame some of the horror games I have recently been playing in terms of atmospheric tension and instilling a feeling of anxiety.
Gameplay is great, I love the various weapon mechanics, and pro and cons between lethal and non-lethal weaponry. My favourite little detail so far is firing a bolt-action sniper from a prone position, rolling away to evade a spotlight, and then performing the bolt reload before I can fire again. These little things all help to build up the game even further.
All in all, an amazing gaming experience, definitely worth full price, let alone a sale price. I would honestly recommend this to anyone who enjoys a fully comprehensive single player experience, with a great story and characters to flesh this out into an all time favourite of mine.

Let me start off by saying I love this game.
TL;DR     It’s great fun, but some serious changes have to be implemented to revive the community.
It’s nothing like Overwatch. Overwatch is like TF2. The closest thing to Battleborn is probably SMITE.
Battleborn is a fun mesh of FPS gameplay and MOBA-esque PVP. I feel like that’s the problem with it, though. FPS games persist because they have strong communities of people who enjoy playing the game. Don't get me wrong, it's more fun to win than it is to lose. MOBAs are renowned for having toxic communities that harass and plague its own player base. Battleborn’s player base has dwindled from the time of its launch. There’s no denying that.
Can you still find a game? Yes
Will you spend a long time in que? Yes (Based on my experience, anyway.)
But most of the games I find have at least one toxic player that drives away their own team. Since the game does not have a content release schedule or rewards system that caters to the FPS crowd, the hounding of experienced players drives away anyone who wants a casual PVP experience.
I’ll be completely honest: I can’t speak for the MOBA crowd, because I don’t like MOBAs. I don’t like how they control, I don’t understand them, and I hate the communities. I’ve tried playing DotA, DotA2, League of Legends, Heroes of the Storm, Smite, and Paragon. In every one of them the learning curve is such that I have no patience to learn how to play the game “right” and I can’t play the game the way I want.
That being said, Battleborn doesn’t seem to cater to the MOBA crowd either. Battleborn doesn’t punish people for going off on their own like MOBAs do, there isn’t a jungle to level or hide in to surprise your enemies, and the ‘towers’ (Sentries in Incursion mode) don’t function like the towers in MOBAs.
Battleborn, in short, takes some MOBA elements and lets you play them in an FPS setting. The game is great fun, but some serious changes have to be implemented to revive the community. I love this game; it’s the closest thing to a MOBA I even remotely enjoyed playing. I have poured over 200 hours into it in the first couple of weeks it was out.
Sadly, I haven’t wanted to play it recently because I have better things to do with my time than sit in queue for 5-15 minutes looking for a game, just to be ♥♥♥♥♥ed at by someone that doesn’t think one character belongs on the team, and then to have our game ruined in the first five minutes because someone rage-quits leaving us at a disadvantage.
I still would recommend Battleborn to anyone who likes Gearbox, FPS, or just wants something different. It’s fun as hell, funny, and has a lot of depth.

PLEASE READ FOR AN ACTUAL REVIEW!!!
Firstly, I have played this since launch and in seeing the reviews for this game I find that I don't think people understand what reviews are for. In this review I will give the pros, cons, and why people are wrong on their opinions. And yes opinions can be wrong.
What is Battleborn. Battleborn is a FPS with a MOBAesque aspect depending on the multiplayer game mode. There is also a fun story component to the game allowing players a different type of challenge, especially on the harder difficulties. For PvP, players pick a unique character from a rather large roster (once all characters are unlocked) and battle. You battle your opponents, collect shards (currency), buy gear, and build defensive structures all while competing to out do your opponents.
Pros
This game has hilarious commentary, especially in the PVE games
Diverse range of unique characters
Currently 10 story mission that will take about 30 min each to finish on the easy difficulty
Constant developer update with free content on a regular basis
4 game modes: 3 PvP modes and PvE in the form of the Story
Has a MOBAesque aspect for two of the PvP games modes for those that like that style
All characters can be unlocked thought game play.
NO PAY TO WIN
Gear optimization to play a character how you want to play them. There is no perfect combination of gear (for most characters)
Achievements and unlocks to work toward for increased gameplay
Leveling mechanic that allows for specialized customization each game based on what you are trying to do
Cons
Story is a little confusing and there isn't a lot of cohesion between the missions IMO
Currently there isn't a punishment for leaving a multiplayer game
Matchmaking isn't perfect
Allied Player collision is annoying
Low PC player base (I blame people not actually trying the game for any length of time)
Bad marketing
No PvP tutorial (but honestly it isn't that hard to grasp the concept)
Can't switch your character after its chosen
Why people are wrong (these are things I have either read or heard people say)
Its the same as Overwatch. - NO, just no. On the surface they are similar ie. Team based objective oriented maps with unique characters. If you actually play both it should be apparent to everybody that there is a BIG difference between the two, both of which target different players with some overlap of course.
Some characters are too similar. - I don't understand this complaint. Yes, there are characters that have a similar role, appearance, or play style, but you can find that in any game if you look at them objectively.
The community is toxic. - Really, have you even played LoL or Dota? Those are horrible people. The people I've found are pretty cool for the most part. There are toxic people don't get me wrong but again, any game that has you interact with others has the same problem.
It cost to much for what it is. - This one really pisses me off. People pay full price for Overwatch which literally lets you only play capture and/or payload maps with no other real option. RB6 Siege only has a multiplayer mode that ends the same way 9 times out of 10 and a vs bot (terrorists) mode, again no real story. Battlefied and Call of Duty haven't really changed in the past 10 years but people still pay full price for them every 6 months. Then you have Battleborn which offers a fun series of story campaigns you can play with or without friends, three multiplayer modes each one played differently than the other. It also has unlockable characters with with their own set of achievements which can take about 10 or more hours before you finish all of them allowing for a tremendous amount gameplay. You then have customizable gear allowing you to play a character differently based on the gear. BUT ALL OF THIS ISN'T ENOUGH TO BE PAY FOR!?!!?!?!??!? ARE YOU KIDDING ME!!!!!
I really wish people would give this game a chance.

You can, however, fight the lack of variation by becoming a varied fighter yourself. Some achievements are in place to encourage you to make more stylish kills, it's just not enough to make the game really stand from the crowd. Regardless, it's fun - just not that great.

I'm going to feel like such a nitpicky jerk talking about this game's flaws, because everything else is just really good. But we'll get to them.
Guacamelee! is a muscular Metroidvania, a world where the mask is a very literal symbol of strength and the powerups are sealed behind openings that only ancient body-press techniques will open. Its world is a bit more linear then some Metroidvania-inspired titles, but there's still a pretty solid amount of nooks and crannies to break open and revisit with new tricks.
Just about all of your movement or "unlocking" abilities are combat-oriented-the blue doors are unlocking by dash-punching, for instance, giving you regular new tricks in fights. Things that don't move you tend to move enemies, so you're almost always able to keep a combo going, either by reaching someone or hurling someone into a distant group. The fights are fast and fluid, and a little bit of dimension-changing thrown in offers a manageable issue that'll still keep you on your toes.
The platforming's fine, too-just as some enemies only exist in one of the dimensions, so do some blocks and walls, making you keep switching to get past things, have safe landing points, etc. When it flows, it's a real joy to bounce around the game.
Problem #1 is that it doesn't always flow, though. Hazards (spikes, nasty water, thorns, etc.) tend to have a pretty big hitbox, and even nearly-but-not-quite grazing something can send you spiraling to the ground below-this is a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥on vertical segments, especially since there's no safe-fall. Thankfully, these are few and far between. Still, though, landing in water or falling off into a pit teleports you to solid ground, immediately-it's actually worse to land on a platform below where you were. A strange choice.
Problem #2 is that our hero, Juan, presumably a técnico, has a pile driver move. He really shouldn't-that's for rudos.
Those are nitpicks, though. Overall, the game's just fantastic. If you need a sidescroller, this thing deserves a place in your library.

Guacamelee is an indie Metroidvania, it has a fantastic soundtrack, unique art style and great gameplay.
Gameplay wise, Guacamelee isn't particularly innovative, throughout the game you'll explore levels that are full of various platforming and combat challenges, these elements are polished to a shine. The platforming controls well, and has a lot more variety than one might except from a Metroidvania style game. Similarly, the combat system takes a more traditonal beat-em-up style and infuses it into the game, while it might not be comparable to some hardcore action games, it is a satisfying system overall, and I had lots of fun racking up high combos.
In traditional Metroidvania fashion, you'll find yourself gathering new abilities throughout the game and then using said abilities to progress through new areas. The game has a fair amount of optional secrets, which will motivate players to backtrack through previous areas to find powerups. Personally, I liked how the games combat system and abilities worked together. A majority of the abilities you get are multi-purposed, one use being how it helps you explore the enviroment and the other use being how it helps you in combat. For example, the uppercut ability allows you to break various red blocks throughout the enviroment, but it also adds a uppercut to your character's repertoire in combat. This means as you get more abilities, the variety in both combat and platforming increases. The system works near perfectly.
My main problem with Guacamelee is a minor one and it has to deal with the games sense of humor. To be frank, I found the games attempt to be awful. The games references to the Metroid series didn't come off as funny, but lazy. The game also has some weird obsession with some bottom of the barrel Reddit memes, they aren't funny or orginial. It's not a major complaint, but it's annoying to me that the humor has to resort to "lol me too references" and "xd reddit memes" considering the work that was clearly put into the games world design.

This was a short but very creative and compelling little game. I think it's particularly fun for those of us who enjoy digging through files in a computer searching for that "one" file you know is out there; as well as for those who enjoy unraveling a murder mystery little by little, connecting in your head seemingly random dots into a coherent narrative.
It's not like most games in that it has a clear and explicit goal or a win state, nor does it informs you about the rules and mechanics of the game, which you have to deduce by yourself as you go on. It relies instead on your own curiosity and motivation to understand the story underneath it all. In that sense, this game is more akin to one of those viral marketing campaigns for movies. And if you enjoyed one of those, then I think this game is right up your alley.
I would sum it up by saying that this game lies in the Venn Diagram intersection between a crime documentary; nostalgia for the aesthetic of Windows 95 and the early internet age; and the thrill of spying into someone else's computer and frantically searching for their porn stashes before they return (not that I would know...)

Along with KOTOR II, the best games period.  The production values unsurpassed.  Lucas did for gaming what he did for "science fiction" films in the original Star Wars series.  While "graphics" are a bit dated, the audio--voice, background music, special effect sounds--remain top-drawer, worthy of a high budget blockbuster film.  For me, this is what makes the game infinitely replayable.  These are real actors doing the dialogue, and they are perfectly cast.  Most, if not all, of the Brits in the games are from the Royal Shakespeare Company.  The ambient music for Kashyyk fit perfectly, such an otherworldly sound.  I spend a lot of time fooling around on that world just to get caught up in it.
The dialogue branching, another factor in making it replayable, is also incredibly complicated.  I honestly can't figure out how they did it.  All the actors had to record all the lines in-character, and they never fail at it.  How they were able to branch to all the possible outcomes, all the while keeping the plot consistent, is a monument of what can happen when technology and theatre unite.
Of course they aren't perfect, but they come as close as any have come to it that I've experienced.  I'm not sure we'll ever see again the near-perfection of plot*, character and scene, as it must have cost them a bundle.  After Bioware handed off the franchise to Obsidian, it developed the Mass Effect trilogy, which was similar to KOTOR I & II, so I really see it as a Pentalogy.  Still, despite their fervent attempts, ME never gives that total immersive effect the overarching storyline gave KOTOR.  It comes close enough, however.  I replay all five games in sequence twice each year at Christmas and on my birthday.
*Okay, KOTOR II's original plot was only great to a certain point, then apparently they ran out of money.  However, the Restoration project and Aspyr has done much to improve it.

Fabulous party game, for anyone. Second best of all the Jackbox games.
Here's my rankings for the game, best to worst;
Quiplash 2 - fun with funny people
Tee K.O. - fun with creative people
Fakin’ It - fun with people you know well
Guesspionage - fun for statistics nerds
Trivia Murder Party - fun for trivia players who like RNG
While I do recommend a console version of these games due to practicality, these games are great for any group larger that 4. Always a blast to break out at parties.

Since there are 5 party games in one game I'm going to be reviewing them all and thankfully for me, I have tried out all the games whether that be sacrificing my friends' time to play some of these games or playing it with my family members.
Let's first start off with Quiplash 2: Whether it be family members, college mates or steam users this game is crowned as the best thing in existence.  This just like the first predecessor is really fun and enjoyable, there are lot of new things that haven't been introduced in the first game, such as the fact that you can create your own prompts, I have so far 2 episodes I made with a lot of crazy prompts such as "help!  A gargoyle stole my cheese pizza".  There's also new weird characters that you randomly play as such as a weird turqoise cat or a gray vampire coffin or a yellow (demonic voiced?) star.  They also changed The Last Lash level, instead of getting a prompt you're given either an acro prompt, a comic prompt or a word prompt and not only that players award the answers in medals so that is something new.
Up next is Trivia Murder Party: This game is one of those trivia fact game host show things that would see on your television.  Only Trivia Murder Party takes place in a saw themed place where players play as plushies to try and escape, everyone gets a multiple choice trivia to answer, if one or more plushies doesn't the answer correct they would have to survive "The Killing Floor (not the game Killing Floor) where in The Killing Floor, players/player have to play mini games of death whether it would be answering as much easy math problems as you can or spinning the loser wheel or remembering patterns.
Next up is Tee KO: Tee KO is similiar to Quiplash but only instead of filling out prompts you are drawing t-shirts and filling out slogans for these shirts.  Once you've done that, other people are going to use your as well as some other players artworks and slogans to make their T-Shirt.  Once they've done that then it's voting time to see what T-Shirt is better than the other one.  This game is pretty complicated in my opinion, a lot of people I showed this one were pretty confused by it.
Next it is Guesspionage: Guesspionage is a game that is all about percentages, how high or low it is.  One player is given a question and has to estimate what percentage he or she thinks is appropriate for that question.  Once they've done that, other players in the game are given two options of whether the percentage should be higher or lower.  When they finish doing that the real percentage is given out to players to see if the player given the estimation was higher, lower or spot on.  It has some pretty interesting gameplay, I must say.
Last but not least is Fakin' it: Fakin' it has a very 60's cartoon look, in this game players have to work together on finding the faker.  Players are given tasks on their phones, tablets or laptops while one player (which that player is the faker) gets a different one, it is up to the faker's job to try and blend with the crowd.  Some of these tasks are: pointing to one or another, making weird faces, holding up a number of fingers or raising your hand.  Once players are told to stop doing these tasks, they have to vote on who the faker really is.  This game is definitely NOT recommended to anyone who wants to play this game over online because of these tasks given on your phone.
And now the final conclusion on these games:
Quiplash 2 is great especially that they added the option of creating prompts, Trivia Murder Party is fun, Tee KO is pretty confusing at first but eventually you'll get used to it, Guesspionage is pretty good, Fakin it is alright but not terrible.
Overall: buy Jackbox Party Pack 3, buy some beer, buy some friends and have a wicked party.
Cheers

Guacamelee! Gold Edition is a Metroidvania Mexican styled action platformer.
The very first impression of the game is that it looks awesome. A wonderful and colourful atmosphere that reminds me the good old times of Monkey Island. In addition to that, the writing is sharp with a lot of funny dialogues...or to be more precise, the dialogues are mostly monologues since our mexican hero Juan will not say any word during the game.
Regarding the combats, I would say that are interesting but they can also end up to be quiet boring. Juan has some standard attacks (punch, kick) but he gains many power ups as he goes deeper and deeper into to the game.
My humble opinion is that a medium experienced gamer would need about 10hours to finish the game. But if you want to push your self to the limits you will have to try to unlock as many steam achievents as you can. This is a real challenge, especially if you try to win all gold medals in the El Infierno area (I think I spent two days for this...nightmare).
As a conclusion, I would say thay Guacamelee is a great game with humour, fantastic world design and interesting battles. Even if someone is not a lover of 2D platform games I believe that Guacamelee has something for him as well. Finally, if you do not have a CONTROLLER, just do not play the game. The first few hours I tryied it with the keyboard and I can assure you that you will not be able to keep up with steam achievents.

I rarely write game reviews, mostly because they don't usually hold my attention for long & after playing for a while I end up feeling "well that was good but it could have been so much better".  This game, however, I wholeheartedly endorse.
I own its predecessor (Ultimate General Gettysburg) which, while an enjoyable game, had various shortcomings and a lack of replayability, all of which have been more than addressed in Civil War. There's dozens of different ways to approach the Campaign promising years of enjoyment. Supply lines, skirmishers, cavalry that can dismount - these have been added without increasing the need for micromanaging & turning battles into a chore. Line of sight is easier to understand than the previous game, making artillery much more effective - and it clearly shows when units are blocked, flanked, or simply need a rest from battle.
And then there's the whole economy side of things, with money and reputation earned from success in battle and allowing you to grow & equip the army under your command. In many games this kind of thing can be a confusing chore, but in Civil War its a delight.
If you're a fan of any kind of tabletop war gaming, I think you'll love this game. I know its going to soak up a lot of my limited spare time over the months & years ahead.

Along with KOTOR II, the best games period.  The production values unsurpassed.  Lucas did for gaming what he did for "science fiction" films in the original Star Wars series.  While "graphics" are a bit dated, the audio--voice, background music, special effect sounds--remain top-drawer, worthy of a high budget blockbuster film.  For me, this is what makes the game infinitely replayable.  These are real actors doing the dialogue, and they are perfectly cast.  Most, if not all, of the Brits in the games are from the Royal Shakespeare Company.  The ambient music for Kashyyk fit perfectly, such an otherworldly sound.  I spend a lot of time fooling around on that world just to get caught up in it.
The dialogue branching, another factor in making it replayable, is also incredibly complicated.  I honestly can't figure out how they did it.  All the actors had to record all the lines in-character, and they never fail at it.  How they were able to branch to all the possible outcomes, all the while keeping the plot consistent, is a monument of what can happen when technology and theatre unite.
Of course they aren't perfect, but they come as close as any have come to it that I've experienced.  I'm not sure we'll ever see again the near-perfection of plot*, character and scene, as it must have cost them a bundle.  After Bioware handed off the franchise to Obsidian, it developed the Mass Effect trilogy, which was similar to KOTOR I & II, so I really see it as a Pentalogy.  Still, despite their fervent attempts, ME never gives that total immersive effect the overarching storyline gave KOTOR.  It comes close enough, however.  I replay all five games in sequence twice each year at Christmas and on my birthday.
*Okay, KOTOR II's original plot was only great to a certain point, then apparently they ran out of money.  However, the Restoration project and Aspyr has done much to improve it.

I bought the first game on a Steam Sale, but loved it so much that I bought the second one at full price and bought this third one almost as soon as it released. Definitely worth it. If I had a nickel for every time I've packed my laptop to a house party JUST FOR THIS GAME, I'd have enough money to buy the trilogy. You just need your laptop and an internet connection to start it up. Listen, the game uses your phone as the controller, which means literally every single person you ask to play with you immediately have a frame of reference for how it works. That's priceless. No teaching controls, no explaining mechanics, just "look at the TV, go to that site, enter the code." I don't care if you have an Android, iPhone, or cheap knockoff iPad; if you have an internet browser, you can play this game. The games offer the prompt, then your phone's browser lets you submit your response. Super easy. I've seen socially reserved people suddenly become the funniest f***er at the party, not because they're social butterflies, but because they were witty with their lies on Fibbage.
PLUS, the games are presented in such a way that it can behave like either Apples to Apples or Cards Against Humanity. It's good to play with kids, college students, or adults and still have a good time. The prompts are never inappropriate, but you're responses can definitely be. Players can adapt the game to suit your own friend bubble's sense of humor and it's brilliantly handled. There's also a secondary prize in most games (the best ones at least) based on who had the most liked responses, which people can pick after the answer has been revealed.
This one comes with 5 games and all of the best ones have an 8 player cap. Each game takes about 10-15 minutes to play, but they have TONS of questions and prompts, so you'll almost never hit one you've seen before and it's pretty easy to corral people to try it out because of the play time. Each game has an announcer that briefly explains the game and the rules, while also presenting the prompts. They're sorta funny; they get some laughs for being super cheesy. You won't want to turn it off for being annoying, at least. They're a little self aware, honestly. Quiplash 2 and Trivia Murder Party are THE games you need, though.
Quiplash X is the first game you're buying this for. At the start of the game, everyone gets two prompts that they have to make up a response for. Prompts could be like "A sitcom where two pairs of twins marry each other" or "Titanic 2: _______". The catch is that one other player has your same prompt, and everyone is going to vote on the best response of the two. You get points based on the number of votes you get. Sounds simple, but that's why it's so good. It's probably the most approachable Jackbox game.
Trivia Murder Party is basically a trivia game, only you're trapped in a basement and the bad guy from SAW is going to take you out one on one based on who gets the answers wrong. It's pretty fun, has a lot of diversions, and promotes just the right level of competition. You really have to play it to get how it works, but I like it and I don't even usually like trivia games.
Guesspionage is pretty funny. You basically guess at statistics and get points for how close you were. Prompts can be anything from "Percentage of people who make their beds in a hotel room" or "Percentage of people who enjoy pickles." It's pretty funny and a good conversation starter.
Tee K.O. is like Pictionary, except you're prompts are for T-Shirt designs, every prompt is given to two random people, and everyone else votes on the best one. You make the drawing using your touchscreen and get points based on the number of votes you got. It's basically like a blend of Drawful and Quiplash. Pretty fun and rounds off the pack nicely.
Fakin' It is basically a "Who is the spy" game. It's alright.You get a prompt and have to raise your hand if it's true. People can call you out if they think you're lying, so there's a good balance between telling the truth and lying just to avoid being called out.
Seriously, though. Get this. It's a great game to break out at a party or just with a small group of friends and super easy to set up.

So, I just finished playing this game a few hours ago. I really liked it.
Very cute, very charming, lovely scenery, interesting world, solid game mechanics, enjoyable characters, and of course, excellent music. It's pretty much got everything, but it's all on small scale, and intentionally so. It's not some grand, epic adventure like most RPGs try to be. It's a very humble game, consistently so throughout pretty much all of its characteristics. All the aesthetics are kept simple, but because of that, everything can pretty much look exactly as its designers want them to look like and doesn't need to press against any modern graphical limits. The basis of the plot is a fairly well-established scenario, nothing huge or groundbreaking, but because the central idea is so well established these days, it draws more attention to the more subtle details of how it goes about playing it out. The music is kept very simple, only a piano throughout the whole game. Normally, I'd express doubts about limiting an entire games score to a single instrument, but the piano music that plays throughout the entire game so perfectly expresses both the immediate and overall tone of the game's events, as well as represents the games scope and the quality with which it meets that scope. It's because this game, in so many of its aspects, modestly doesn't try to puff itself up as a big deal, that its so easy for us players to accept the game for what it is and see it's more subtle, charming characteristics shine through.

bit Dungeon II is a very simple Rogue-Lite Dungeon based RPG which was likely developed with Mobile Touch/Mouse as the main control method.
Don't think that a Mobile port is always a bad thing, in fact, this game actually pulls off the mobile port somewhat right because it doesn't charge a ridiculous price like many other mobile ports.
The game is likened to the original Zelda title because of how the game is set up. There is no tutorial to tell you what to do and many people would be irritated with that fact, I actually liked journeying throughout the world trying to figure out what to do. I've gotten to what I assume is the final boss a couple times. The difficulty really depends on what drops you get because the game at its heart is a Rogue-Lite Dungeon RPG. You progress from dungeon to dungeon and fight each boss until you can get to the Final Dungeon. Sometimes you will have good runs and sometimes you will have bad runs.
The game is a little buggy but it seems that a lot of the bugs I use to experience have been patched in the past few months and that pleases me a lot to see a developer patch and support their game post release on Steam, because all too often I see games that could be very good just left as abandonware on Steam.
bit Dungeon II will remain a game that I will play periodically because of how enjoyable it is. If you enjoy Action RPGs with permadeath you will enjoy this game.

Its with a heavy heart that I don't recommend this game.
It just does too much wrong for me to say otherwise and that is a huge shame!
Lets get the negative out first, starting with; The game explains nothing.
When you
play the game you can't attack. This will probably cause your first death. You might stumble across the nearby store or you might be like me and think that is a dungeon and not a store.
Even if you avoid that mistake, it costs 8 black coins to buy a weapon. What is a black coin and how is it different from regular coin?
!
Black coins are just the regular currency in the game and that is fine, honestly. Money gets called all sorts in games and its not a big deal then either, but for the longest time I thought maybe money came in other colors too but it doesn't as far as I can tell. Designer just wanted to be original I guess so moving on, or rather
moving on because I almost quit when i couldn't attack anything! Let me explain.
You need money to kill things but you only get money from killing things which you
without a weapon. You do not start with one and the fact the local store sells some is meaningless to you because you have no money to buy them and you can't steal them either. So the obvious thing is to run around and try to find a weapon and/or money. This becomes a
problem because the enemy can body block you. You have no invinc frames after a hit and you can
get stuck and get a game over before the game has even begun! Walking to a new screen also confers no invinc frames or delay on enemy spawning so you can die in a room before the room has visually spawned on screen due to enemies hugging the doorway! Bad game design choice there.
It gets worse though because to swing your weapon you tap A. You hold A to raise your shield, if you have one and you also hold A to use your melee special attack. Do you see any overlap? So the game decides for you if you are raising your shield or taking a smack to the face.
The developer also added to the steam description "inspired by Dark Souls" and I am glad it was only inspired by it because it just can't pull of dark souls at all. Which is actually kind of a shame but  I bring it up now because I feel the games lack of explaining
is because 'dark souls did it' failing to remember that dark souls actually points out a lot of stuff and tells you what
Which brings me to problem number four if you were counting, which is what do stats
I experimented and found out that Dexterity increases crit rate as well as the damage of weapons that are marked xDex with similar stats boosting damage in similar ways but any auxillary effects outside of boosting damage for the other stats is just completely unknown. What is +10 berserk and is that good or bad? Should I replace my +5 Phase with it?  What even is Phase?
Which segways nicely to proble-- you know what why even count? The game has lots of problems  so here is a helpful tip for you, when you level up your stats go up.
This is
important information because if you used a sword for the first 20lvs of your career and then decide "I'm going to be a mage" you are not going to have the stats for a mage. You either need to die and start again from scratch to rebuild as a mage, or you are stuck with sword and board for the rest of the game. Not explaining this to the player is unforgivable to me because players are inquisitive by nature and are going to switch weapons around only to get very rudely shafted without even knowing.
Speaking of weapons...I mentioned before how you press A to swing your weapon? Or you can just nudge enemies by walking into them to auto attack. Is this Hyglide? Is that what we have become? I mean I partly don't mind it because when I enter a new room I can kill the enemies that hog doorways (and there are many!) but at the same time it takes me right out of the game when I can kill things without actually doing anything. I feel the game should choose a method of attack and stick with it, not have both. I would be fine with pressing A for my special attack and nudging for regular attack if they ever revisit the system.
Overall I am sounding very negative about the game but here is the thing. The game is good after you get over the hump of getting a weapon and figuring it all out. Its no masterpiece but I can actually stand to play it rather than getting bored and moving onto another game. It also wears the original Zelda game on its sleeve like a huge blister that it wants to show to everyone so I hope you like burning the bush or getting lost in infinity mazes.
I want to touch on the good aspects of the game but even the things I like, have a negative aspect to them. For example if you bring up your inventory then the music stops. I like the music and the game already has a pause button, so it feels odd and is very noticable. You also have no inventory bag so you have to decide there and then what to take with you because when you leave the screen all items are gone, I like this because my choices have impact and weight but if i kill a badguy the loot doesn't drop straight away.
Often I leave rooms just as the loot is spawning because there is a delay before it even spawns the animation that shows loot dropping and if I go back to get, whatever it was that might have dropped, then its gone already.
The best way to sum up the game is that it feels like a game in early access/late beta. I could forgive the flaws-- I'm lying, I couldn't, but I could be hopeful that the flaws will be fixed one day. As it stands at present however, I feel like people need to read my review before playing the game, so that they know how to play the game. I even looked for a Bit Dungeon 2 wikia and I found one...Every page was empty! A sign that people are just not getting over that inital hump.
Developer, if you read this, put the price of the game up. Get that coin and reinvest it into this game (or a sequel) and address these issues. The game world is beautiful and despite the ambitious nature of the game (dark souls + zelda 1) the game is its own beast, but as it stands right now, it needs TLC.

A number of the issues people have been complaining about have been sort of adressed. There's a pseudo-tutorial when pressing escape (not that anything tells you about it) so you aren't left totally without any information. There's a minimap showing your surrounding, so the maze-like world isn't impossible to navigate.
So that's good. However, it is far from enough. The game is still incredibly obfuscated (not even the dedicated wiki know what the stats do!) and difficult to navigate, lacking a sense of direction, and basic features (like key-binding, which is a pain with non-standard keyboards).
There isn't much to the game either. There's been some effort to make the enemies different (with some being invisibile, while other parry or use beams) but in the end you handle all of them nearly the same: run into them until you kill them, parrying when you see them wind up for a hit (or just fill them with arrows). Bosses are probably supposed to be different, but I wouldn't know, they all died easily to the same tactic of circling them while spamming attack.
On the plus side, the graphics are OK if you're into pixel-art, the soundtrack is tolerable, and what little of the story we get is cute.
So if you really want a Zelda remake with random loot a-la Diablo, you should give this a try. Otherwise, I'd stay away from it.

If someone knows how to do it properly, please comment and let me know. The game is kind of short, but you can spend as much time as you want grinding for XP, coins, and stat orbs. It would be nice if the game told you more about how to do stuff (like closing it) or what different things do, because it took me a while to figure out that the camp fires were checkpoints. There may still be more stuff I simply hadn't figured out yet too.
In the course of building your character up to be able to beat the final boss, you will easily get all of the achievements, as long as you can actually beat the final boss, who really is the toughest enemy in the entire game. It's easy to get the basics of the game once you start playing, the only real advice I have to offer is to check for hidden areas, which I kept forgetting to do after finding one.
While the game doesn't have anything to especially amaze a player, it's definitely enjoyable. I approve.

The metroidvania subgenre's popularity has erupted with the popularity of downloadable titles and the burgeoning indie scene. Their emphasis on exploration and character building make them instant favorite for those looking for those looking for retro gaming experiences with contemporary flavor. In addition to that contemporary flavor, Guacamelee is also spiced with chili powder and served with a shot of tequila. It's a south of the border styled adventure packed with plenty of platforming and pugilism as well as a sexy senorita in distress. It also might be, surprisingly, one of the best games you will play all year.

You play as a simple agave farmer named Juan who finds himself having the worst Día de los Muertos celebration ever when and evil Charro named Calaca abducts El Presidente's daughter and sends Juan to the underworld. In a small stroke of luck Juan is resurrected and transformed into a luchadore so that he may rescue El Presidente's daughter and stop Calaca from wreaking havoc among the living. The plot is Guacamelee is what pico de gallo is to a taco, it provides color and flavor but certainly isn't the main attraction. The healthy dose of humor and Mexican culture and folklore do distinguish Guacamelee from its contemporaries however and give it a unique ambiance.
Unlike most metroidvania styled games, Guacamelee places a huge emphasis on platforming and some optional areas have an almost Super Meat Boy like difficulty requiring quick and precise actions to traverse the obstacles laid out. Most of Juan's offensive repertoire doubles as a means to navigate the environment. A Street Fighter style flaming uppercut acts as a super jump, a charging maneuver that can be devastating to your foes is also effective when it comes to smashing blocks. By the end of the game these abilities can be combined into lengthy, deadly combos and used to reach far off platforms. Juan also eventually gains the ability to swap between the world of the living and the world of the dead and much like The Gianna Sisters, things change between worlds, opening up new passageways and allowing Juan to reach previously inaccessible areas.
The fundamentals of combat are simple enough on the surface with one button throwing punches, another dedicated to special attacks and one used to grapple enemies once enough damage has been doled out. Grapples are very effective for crowd control since once an enemy is in Juan's grasp the game slows down and an arrow indicates where your foe will be tossed and throwing your enemies into each other is always a good idea. Special grapple maneuvers can also be purchased at the games save points for additional offensive options. Costumes, health and stamina upgrades are also available for purchase. Combat starts out simple enough but over the course of the game's six or so hours enemy types are mixed up and combined with the platforming ca pose a satisfactory challenge. Some enemies have shields that require a particular special to bring down. Bosses also challenge your mastery of Juan's skills and many offer multiple phases.
As with any metroidvania game backtracking is a necessity if you want to grab every secret that Guacamelee has to offer and this is made painless as a result of a fantastic map and plentiful fast travel points. Blocks that require specific abilities to break are color coded and their location is marked on your map making them easy to find on repeat visits once Juan has the proper skills to smash them. Chests are also marked on the map. Rounding out the distractions are a handful of side missions who can be found by talking to the citizens of the two towns you are able to visit. These missions involve everything from simple mini games to talking to every citizen in an effort to gather the ingredients necessary to make the world greatest enchilada. The only problem with these side missions is that they are very centralized and don't really require any exploration. It's easy to complete most of them within a matter of minutes.

Guacamelee is one of the best platforming games i've played the last year.
The game is going with a mexican style and everything that relates to it ( Chili peppers, Dias de los Muerto's, Luchador's, Mexican Music, Pinata's) can be found.  Guacamelee is presented in a colourful way and with a very cheery and memorable soundtrack. The fighting system is enjoyable and gets expanded over time with a ton of unlockable moves.  On top of that, it's also possible to earn outfits and upgrades.  To add to the charm, Guacamelee is littered with game referenches to games like Grim Fandango, Super Mario Bros, Castle Crashers and Viva Pinata.
Next point of discussion: the puzzles. There are a ton of little side puzzles that are harder than the main-path, but offer small rewards like extra coins for upgrades. These puzzles range from fairly easy to mindbending hard. Sometimes puzzles require you to remember a set of moves to use to get to the end-goal, while other times figuring out which moves you actually need to get the reward is an excersize on itself. To make the puzzles even harder, switching between the living world and the dead world is often necessary to reveal / hide platforms and obstacles. Often you will find yourself thinking about how you will have to tackle a puzzle and learning the muscle memory of the moves before you're actually able to pull it off.
The story is fairly straightforward, but because of the small cast of interesting characters and the funny written dialog it feels fun to follow the story. Besides the mainstory, there are always a few little sidemissions to keep things interesting. The aforementioned puzzles are a side-mission on itself.
Finally, the bossfights require you to use all the skills you previously learned in the game and are often pretty hard, but you never feel like you will need to google for a solution.

The best sequel yet of this unique series of stealth games, Hitman Blood Money ups the ante by making assassination a more interactive and rewarding experience. A lot of the old quirks like instantly changing clothes (which allows you to breach area quicker than humanly possible) are still there, since the gameplay hasn't been overhauled but rather improved tenfold. While yes, you could either go into a mission guns blazing and slaughter every witness in sight, or sneak in with a rifle to silently assassinate your target, the game now offers you a new method of killing: accidents. Missions have scenarios that allow you to take out your target in a manner that makes it look like their death was a matter of circumstance, and the game actively encourages you to finish your missions in this manner, creating a new mix of creative thinking and hair-trigger timing for players to complete.
Buy this game. It is good. That is all.

Fans of classic Defender-like arcade shoot'emup action will be entralled with Paladin and its city protecting space action. With multitudes of upgrades and ships, a rad as heck soundtrack, and massive bosses it's a Defender for modern times.
In the spirit of Puppygames' classic brand of modernized classic formulas, infused with a bright and flashy visual and audio style Paladin takes the classic arcade shooting formula of the 80's and gives it an addictive flair with frenetic and fast combat through waves of increasingly chaotic variations of alien baddies. From Qix-style line creating spiral enemies to homing-missile launching dive bombers, the range and diversity of clever enemies to dodge and destroy is impressive.
It's intense, flashy, bright, and attractive. It's addictive and it sounds damn good to the ears. Paladin is a bliss-out for retro arcade fans.

I got this game on a bit of a whim remembering it's win at the Game Awards this year, and it was definitely worth it. I'd say that very often, I dislike story heavy games, even if the story is well written and interesting, it just seems like a movie that's crammed into the middle of a game rather than an experience that grows out of it.
But Her Story manages to create a narrative that works tremendously well as interactive media. The story itself is nothing special, but the way the player is allowed to discover it is. Almost no piece of the story is revealed unless the player seeks it out, making it feel as though he or she is the one in control of the story. It seems like such a non-linear story which can be discovered in any order would be a haphazard mess, yet somehow it all ties together very well, preserving enough mystery to keep things interesting without ever being too confusing to care about. The events that take place are also open enough to interpretation that any player is bound to continue to engage with the story even outside of the game.
I'd normally like to say what other games are similar to this, but I don't know that there are any. Maybe the Ace Attorney series? Though comparing these to things is a bit of a disservice to both, so I don't know.
I think Her Story is at the very least a well put together experiment in game narrative that is refreshing in a sea of games that deliver story through cutscenes, morality meters, and dialogue trees. It's not for everyone though. I don't know if I'd even consider this a game so much as interactive media. It's not exciting, it's not technically impressive, but it is something that I don't think we've ever seen before.
Not exactly a "game," but a great interactive story.

The closest thing to Sid Meier's Gettysburg! you can currently find. Very solid top down civil war game.
Many people complain that the historical battles are too scripted and vote the game down. This is silly to me, as the same battles in campaign do NOT script your forces to giving up ground, and you fight with an army that you have personally chosen and set up as you like. Historic Battle mode is doing as advertised, you have to overcome the historic.
Campaign is the strongest portion of the game. You begin with a few premade units on level one, after that you create new units, divisions, and corps out of infantry, skirmishers, cavalry, and artillery. You can arm and train these units any way you see fit. Personally I have a 450 unit of cavalry equipped with the longest range skirmisher rifle available. Sniper Cavalry. Yeah.
Before patch 1.4 (I think) I would not have recommended this game. After this patch, units properly face the enemy when moving or flanking around the enemy. Previously the unit would turn 90° and drag the flank through the battle. Now they continue to face the enemy, and march into position while maintaining formation. Two units can coninutally fire and move to pincer the unit from both sides, previously you would distract while one ran behind.
I will say that even on easy, this game is NOT for the faint hearted. You have to lose or save scum for a while to figure out the mechanics. Even when you do, you will make mistakes, and they will hurt. Thankfully the game tracks how decisively you win, and factor that into how much weaker the enemy army would be after that, so it is an even handed system.
As I write this review, the game is 30% off at $21. This is a steal if you enjoy non-basebuilding RTS, or ever enjoyed Sid Meier's Gettysburg!

While crafting a badge,I recieved a coupon for this,I could tell what it was,but thought I'd give it a try anyway.
Firstly to address the elephant in the room,yes...it's an Achievement bomb game,you get a ton of achieves just for starting the game,and then a bunch more for every level you complete.
The game's a standard 2D scrolling rage-platformer,frustrating but not too hard. I won all 30 levels and got all achieves in about an hour. [And I suck at platformers,so it probably takes less time than that]
Gameplay:The game is all about jumping over obstacles,though the problems come in the physics.
The jumps are floaty,your character feels like it has no weight,you'll get used to it after a bit,but it's frustrating at first.
There are some horizontally moving platforms that you stand on,but don't move with,meaning if you stand still it'll just slide out from under you,so you have to walk with it...the vertical ones however,work normally.
There's also some boxes that can be moved,but the game never utilises this feature at all,they're just there.
I will say that once I learned these quirks,none of my MANY deaths seemed unfair,as other hazards work as expected.
Artstyle: The game sports what should be a neat artstyle of all black with white shading,it looks good in the screenshots but in the actual game you can see how messy the lines are,it just looks cheap, And the player character is weirdly lopsided, watching it run is rather uncomfortable.
Music: I approve of a rock soundtrack,but it seems too high energy for a standard platformer,it would go better with a racing game or a shooter,it's fine at first,but there's some issues here as well...
There's only a few tracks,to make up for this they reuse the tracks only slightly sped-up or slowed-down,instead of just having more,and everytime you start a level over it resets to a random song/tempo,considering how much I died, the music got old REAL FAST.
Once you get used to the above issues though,the game plays fine,I've played worse,And I encountered no bugs to speak of...so the game is...playable I guess? The problem is there's no reason to play it,unless you just want a larger number on your profile's achievement showcase. The art style ends up being kinda tacky, and the gameplay is the same as any other rage-platformer you've ever played [give or take].
I only paid 25 cents for this,so I don't want to be too hard on it. It's fine for what it is,though I can't honestly say I'd recommend anyone buy it.

This was one of the most basic looking games I've ever played. It has almost no visual style that doesn't just look poor. An example would be spike floors that appear around the middle of the game are barely approachable without instant death.
The game relies very heavily on trial and error in a few stages, but is otherwise pretty fairly designed. You will need to watch the timing and movements of hazards more than the hazards themselves. On some stages the hazards were hidden by visual design flaws. A light color would almost totally obscure small floor spikes, making them very hard to see. I was able to get past it eventually, but not without eye strain.
I've been playing this game on mute; sound is not what I'd call great. There seem to be no sound effects at all. Music track are grating and annoying, and they reset every time you die, so it's a bit like hitting the skip button through an album after about 30 second into a song.
One very odd design mistake is that the instructions on stage one were incorrectly showing that I needed to press the up key to jump. This was wrong. The SPACE BAR is jump.
I didn't feel like this was time well spent. I've played worse games, but I've played many better ones for sure.
As of the date of this review, I found that you can super jump in certain spots to bypass obstacles. Just tapping the space bar repeatedly will launch the player quite a bit higher than normal, and since there is no falling damage the player only needs to watch out where they land. An easy way to see what I mean is right at the beginning of the first level. Just tap jump repeatedly to launch the player up. Wish I'd have known about this earlier.
