A really fun, and really charming Metroidvania beat 'em up in a Mexican world.  The gameplay gives plenty of that Metroidvania style (with objective markers which'll help people who have no idea what they're doing when they play these).  The combat is surprisingly fun once you unlock a handful of special moves, allowing you to make up all kinds of cool combos on the fly.  You could argue the game pulls the "Stick you in a room with enemies" too often, but the combat was fun enough that I didn't mind.
The game's moderately difficult, but most of its difficulty comes in optional areas, so it shouldn't be that hard to complete for most.  I do hear the keyboard controls are poor, however.
The much praised humor was a bit hit or miss for me.  The game as a whole was charming and funny, but at times it descended a bit too much into referential humor that just made me groan a little.  Do we really need a move called the Dashing Derpderp?

Guacamelee is likely my favorite title of any video game ever, which makes it a good thing the game that actually bares it is so awesome! Drinkbox Studios, developers of one of my other favorites from recent years, Mutant Blobs Attack, has completely outdone themselves with not only their best creation yet, but one of the most fun and charming games of the year.
In a world that all but worships Luchadores, Juan is just a normal guy who hope he may one day have a shot with the governor's daughter. But when a band of demon's attack he is sent on a one way trip to the land of the dead, he must don the mask and become a Luchadore to save his beloved (and as it turns out, the entire world).
It's a setup seen a million times, but here it's tweeted and turned into a hilarious and unexpectedly engaging tale. Full of terrific and hilarious writing, as well as fantastic characters that while encompassing cliched roles, are all fully developed and likable (even the villains, crazy as it may sound). If this was a movie I'd have been impressed, but when paired with the great gameplay it's truly an amazing experience.
For fans of metroidvanias, this is the equivalent of being serenaded by a mariachi band outside your window. The world strikes the perfect balance between size and navigability,making it almost impossible to get lost but hiding tons of secrets to find. In classic fashion certain areas are blocked off until you collect the requisite move, but what Guacamelee does that not many games of this sort do is make almost every move you gain equally usable in combat and exploration, keeping both parts fresh throughout.
The combat system is easy to understand and yet full of depth in how you use it. Only a few buttons are used but combining them can produce a wealth of different moves, and it's up to you to make the most of them to rack up huge combos, or just stick to the basics and punch everyone in the face. Boss fights require a bit more planning in how you approach them, and this does present a slight problem as they put up a much better fight than most of their minions. Thankfully it's usually just a matter of memorizing their patterns in order to finally beat them.
Platforming is the other half of the package, and the level designs are outstanding. Utilizing familiar moves like double jumps and wall jumping, they place you in new and creative scenarios that proved a joy to navigate. It's not until you begin to use one the most prominent mechanics though, switching between the world of the dead and that of the living, that the levels really take off. Because some platforms (and in combat, enemies) can only be seen in one realm or the other you have to quickly switch between them as you jump from point to point in an amazing display of platforming genius. Even the early sections top anything Mutant Blobs had to offer, and the quality only goes up from their.
A couple of minor playability problems do pop up, with the somewhat clunky controls being chief among them. Because you are required to use the stick and buttons in conjunction with one another to pull off most special moves, it can lead to problems where you are pressing the stink in the opposite direction you need to be heading  often sending you off a cliff or into the path of an enemy. They aren't bad, but they could have been better and make some of the more difficult sections terribly frustrating. I also wish that side-missions were highlighted on your map, as there isn't any indication of them in the game and without the achievements informing me of their existence I'd likely have missed them.
Despite these minor issues Guacamelee is an all around excellent experience that makes it easy to gloss over the few rough spots. The art style is brilliant and creative, the gameplay very enjoyable, and the soundtrack a freaking incredible blending of contemporary hip-hop and rock, and traditional Mexican Ranchera music. It's a great deal of fun and incredibly charming though and through, and most of all a game everyone should take the time to play.
Viva la Drinkbox!

First of all, let me state the obvious: This game is nothing like Overwatch. If anything, I'd say it was more like Super MNC, in the fact that it's a First Person MOBA. If people would just look past the whole "Overwatch clone" thing and give it a try, they might actually enjoy it.
The PvE mode is fun, and you can play it with a group or solo if you wish, though I would recoomend playing it with a group.
The queue time for PvP can take a while. Some people have complained that they've waited for upto 30 minutes for a game. Me? I've really only waited about 3-5 minutes on avereage, so it's best to play during peak times or on the weekends.
Also, the notion that the game is "dead" is pretty misleading, given that I have little trouble finding games. I'm not sure if these people are playing at really odd times or are just REALLY impaitent.
Yes, there is a microtransaction store in this, but it's only for cosmetic items, such as skins and taunts, and the store itself is burried away in the gear tab, so it isn't front and centre when you start the game up. Say what you will about microtransactions in paid games, but no one is forcing you to buy that stuff, so you can't complain.
My only complaints are some optimisation issues, not to mention a pretty bad game crash when I first started the game up, but that was fixed after a system restart and hasn't happened again since (I think it was a Windows 10 problem more than anything).
If you enjoy MOBAs or enjoyed the Borderlands series, you should deffinately give this game a look.

Almost didn't get this game because of the negative reviews. Love for Borderlands sent me to Youtube for more research. What I saw convinced me to buy and I've been having a blast so far. I haven't had to experience matchmaking since I've been playing with friends (and my wife loves it too). The campaign is fun in and of itself. Tried some private matches with bots as well. Enjoying those a great deal.
If you mainly want to pown people in multiplayer pvp matches and teabag them afterwards, this probably isn't the game for you (from what I've read in the negative reviews). If, however, you just like the liquid-smooth shooter mechanics and frantic run and gun that Gearbox provides, this gives you lots of ways to enjoy that- a campaign that you can experience alone or with friends, and with a bazillion (real number) of combinations of gear and characters for variety; or three different MOBA-style modes of versus gameplay, with two maps each, and bots who fight well (but sometimes do make some interesting/stupid strategic choices during gameplay).
The versus and campaign maps are well-designed, the characters have interesting abilities and playstyles, and the boss fights (campaign) can be quite interesting with multiple phases. Collecting loot and managing your loadouts is a mini game in and of itself as you seek to min/max aspects which synergize with various characters.
I'm not sure I would have paid full price for it. $30 seemed like a sweet spot for me, so I picked it up on sale. It's too bad that this game apparently let down the ultra-competitive twitch gaming crowd, but if you're a more casual gamer who likes MOBA, tower defense, and first person shooters, this throws all three together into a medly of mayhem I recommend.

Don't get this game expecting it to be one in the traditional sense. You type keywords into a search engine that queries on subtitles contained within video files. When the keywords you type match words in a video file, the search returns videos based on those criteria, up to a maximum of 5 videos at once (there are more than 200). What I just explained is the entire game.
It is an interesting concept, and the novelty will keep you interested for about the first 50% to 75% of the videos. After that, searching for the correct term to find new videos can be frustrating. I didn't see any reviews that really summed it up accurately so here goes:
Overall, this felt like I got the same amount of content as the Tina Tina expansion, for 3x the cost.
1) It's mostly arena and 'defend the tower' episodes.
2) The game may as well have been released episodically.  Each episode is 30min-1 hour playing solo, or 15-30 min in a group.
3) There's only 8 episodes.
Basically, it was built to have a story as an option but was hoping people would be sold on the PvP aspects.  Even if it's not open world, from the folks who did Borderlands, you'd expect more play time for the solo mission.  In BL, you could always coop and go from arena to arena, including in the expansions.    Other than the fact that there's 18 people you can eventually choose from, it's just... You can get a lot more game for a lot less money.    Unless the season pass starts kicking out 12-episode storylines and they promise 5 of them, I'd take your money elsewhere.
The one exception would be if you have friends who all agree to play together.  If you're all really into it and don't mind playing the same 8 maps over and over, it might not be terrible....but only if you get it on summer sale.

Battleborn started as a fairly decent game that went downhill in it's months, with actual reasons behind it. I first played the open beta because it seemed cool, it was made by the same people who made Borderlands, so that got me hooked onto it. A lot of it's humor seems to be coming from Borderlands 2 other than the slightly worse Pre-Sequel, and much of the gameplay style seems fun and original, co-op slightly resembling Borderlands however, but all of Borderlands mechanics seemed to have been adapted and changed into Competitive Play.
Then Battleborn got ultimately thrashed by Overwatch, people made unecassary comparisons due to it's art style and class based mechanics. From playing both, they're both entirely different games, however, quality-wise, Overwatch seems to be a more well-developed 2016 game than Battleborn.
Competitive Play is a nightmare, with queues that take up half an hour, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ match-ups (Teamed with people who just started playing against people who know the game like theb ack of their hand), and the most common complaint, the player base that stooped beneath 1k, which i'll talk about later. There seems to be balance issues between characters as well.
Co-Op seems, sadly, the highlight of this game. Co-Op actually manages to be fun, but with a few game-breaking bugs in the way, more infamously, players and enemies getting stuck outside the map, and on another note, there are only a few co-op maps.
In it's recent months however, Gearbox seems to be doing such a♥♥♥♥♥♥job at promoting it and upkeeping it, the game fell apart. Gearbox is desperately trying to keep this game alive, despite it already being practically dead at below 1k people. A surprising two million people played the open beta, then bugs, microtransactions, and it's competitor, Overwatch killed it.
The game's dead and mangled guys, don't put $60 into this, or summer sale wise, $30.

Ultimate General: Civil War is a solid indie Civil War game and is well worth checking out for strategy fans and for people interested in the American Civil War. It's not quite the deep, complex, free-form Civil War game that I've been hoping to see from Creative Assembly's Total War series, but I can't really expect it to be. Overall, I recommend the game! It doesn't have the polish of a bigger-budget title, but what it does do well, it does really well, and it provides some deep and compelling strategy gaming.
Those of you who do try it out will find a game that does have some genuine innovations. Strategy game developers like Creative Assembly should definitely look closely at Ultimate General's unit movement commands. Drawing movement paths and including a "fall back" command are things that should probably become standard in real-time strategy games -- especially those with historical or realistic settings.

While combat is a staple of metroidvanias, Guacamelee has a beat  'em up feel to its system. Combat is done by chaining punches together with the main attack button. As you progress you will learn four combat special moves executed with another button or key and a direction. These can be chained together for long combos. Also there is a grab move that can be executed on enemies have taken enough damage. The basic system is simple and common to many fighting games and brawlers, but I have not encountered it in a 2D metroidvania before.
Guacamelee also has a heavy focus on precise platforming sections. These sections can range in difficulty, from simple to hand-cramping tough.The aerial acrobatics that your character is put through defy easy description, or even recallable button input. But after that last time he had to do a wall run, air dash, dimensional phase, double jump, flaming uppercut, and punch for that little extra distance.... I really wished I could have just reach in and given him a good length of rope.
Overall a really great game though.

I am Setsuna is a good throwback to classic JRPGs of previous generations, combining many elements of classic genre examples to varying degrees of success.  The plot may seem familiar to fans of Final Fantasy X, and the battle system will absolutely feel familiar to fans of Chrono Trigger (its most obvious inspiration, even copying some Tech and weapon names).
The soundtrack is beautiful, although only having a piano for the entirety may actually be a turn off for some, as it can begin to feel "samey" after so many tracks.
The battle system is quite fun, borrowing the Tech and Combo Tech systems from Chrono Trigger quite successfully.  Battle animations are quick, which is very refreshing compared to many modern JRPGs that suffer from horribly-paced battles.  Experimenting with the various combinations of Techs for the characters offers some very nice customization options and gives the player something to try and optimize.  Even after beating the game, I don't quite understand the Flux system, and the method for getting better loot from enemies (defeating them with combos,  links, or other conditions) is similarly under-explained.  There are some interesting systems at work here, but they ended up being a bit too obscure.
The plot moves along at a solid pace.  The story isn't amazing, but I thought it was more than good enough to motivate me in moving forward.  There were enough mysteries about the world, the characters, and the presence of monsters to keep me guessing.
The environment is an entirely snow-bound world, and most areas feel very similar.  I was okay with this, but my personal tastes don't tend to mind "recycled" environments that much (Dragon Age 2 is one of my favorite games, for example).  Some may find the constant snow areas dull, so it's something to look out for when purchasing this game.  The snow-bound world is, I believe, central to some of the main story themes and captures the feeling of the downtrodden world quite well.
The game is obviously a low budget offering, but I think Tokyo RPG Factory did a very admirable job capturing the essence of what made JRPGs so enjoyable on the SNES.  Definitely recommend!
The biggest pros are the battle system, the excellent pacing of the battles themselves and also the plot.  Things I consider pros but others may not quite agree are the soundtrack (beautiful piano pieces, but only piano), and the story's ability to engage the player.
The biggets cons are the obscure systems in place, seemingly cobbled together.  The low budget is clear in certain aspects of the game as well (animations, effects, in-game character models).  Environments being very one-note (snow) will be a detractor for some.

I am Setsuna is everything I would have expected from a JRPG inspred by Chrono Trigger.
The music is delightful and the characters are people you really grow to care about.  The artwork is beautifully executed in a classic style remniscent of everything I loved about games growing up.
If you love RPGs or are thinking about trying one out, this is definitely worth a purchase.

If you've never played the original Shank, then I suppose Shank 2 is as good a place to start as any. Events in the past game are barely referenced to, if at all. So how well does Shank 2 fare against its predecessor?
To begin, the first Shank wasn't a remarkable game. Even with its short single player campaign, the plot was weak and the gameplay repetitive. Shank 2, with its superb art, suffers a similar fate but with an even weaker story and more uninspired foes.
Gameplay-wise, Shank 2 tries hard to be diverse. There is a large variety of actions and attacks at your disposal and in moments of high intensity, it's all too easy to get buttons mixed up, resulting in eventual death.
To encourage replayability, Shank 2 boasts a leaderboard that tracks player scores built up by combos and items collected. Additionally, there are a dozen or so alternative skins unlocked by completing achievements. If you're not interested in those, then one playthrough may be enough.

In June of 1994, Hannah Smith walked into a Portsmouth police station to report that her husband went missing.  A few days later, she was charged with murder and referred to the Homicide and Serious Crimes Division.  Most of the evidence surrounding her case was destroyed during a major flood in 1997, but some of it was recovered.  After filing a Freedom of Information request, you have now been given access to the remaining video evidence.  What really happened back in June?  Was Hannah guilty?
Created Sam Barlow (the writer behind Silent Hill:  Shattered Memories and Silent Hill:  Origins, formerly of Climax Studios), Her Story is a police procedural that puts you into the role of investigator.   While you start out with just four videos, you can search the fictional Portsmouth LOGIC database for additional entries using terms gleaned from the videos.  For example, in one video, Hannah might mention "stories".  Searching for "stories" in the LOGIC database will bring up eight more videos, some of which will clarify those stories a bit more.  As you continue your searching, you begin to unravel more of Hannah's life, the people in it, and how she became a murder suspect.
A compelling narrative, haunting soundtrack, independent film-style presentation, and a fantastic performance by Viva Seifert make Her Story worth looking into.

This is a fascinating... experience. There's a little bit of a game to it, piecing together the videos to make a cohesive story, but most of it is just exploring the content in whatever way you can to make the story.  Some of the 200+ clips are hardly worth watching, but most are fascinating, and putting the pieces together to figure out what happened (or may have happened) is a challenge I've never seen in a game before.  Very unique, and very much worth experiencing.  It's about 3-4 hours of time investment (and there are ways to make it much easier to see everything), and well worth it.

It's a detective game in the purest sense. There are no concrete answers and it's up to you to figure almost everything out for yourself. If you're adverse to getting out a pen and paper to keep track of things, this is definitely not for you.
However, if you want the immensely satisfying feeling of watching the pieces falling into place as you progress, I'd definitely recommend it. Her Story nails the atmosphere and mystery to a T and the lack of "gameplay" actually helps add to the immersion factor.

I think I am Setsuna is a great RPG game. I love playing it and it is very beautiful. As a standalone game it would make my top 20 games. A big problem everyone seems to have is that its not Chrono Trigger. While it might not be fair to compare a spiritual succesor to its progenitor, if you market it as an asset then people are going to compare them. This game is not nearly on the same level as Chrono Trigger, but it is good in the same way that DarkSouls2 is not half as good as DarkSouls but as a standalone game is still pretty fun.
I really enjoy piano music so the soundtrack being somewhat limited in instrumentation didnt bother me at all, but if youre used to typicall rpg soundtracks with electronic and guitar stuff then it might get on your nerves. The combat is very standard for JRPG's nothing to unique minus the momentum feature. I really enjoy JRPG's so the tedious battles that happen over and over again dont really get to me.
The price is very steep. If you have the money, theres really no reason not to get it. If you have to spend a lot of time deciding which steam games to spend your money on (like me) then maybe look at other choices before this one.
The fact that your choices dont really change very much is nothing new. Thats a standard troupe in RPG's simply due to the massive amount of time it would take to make branching storylines for every dialouge option. Giving the player the ability to chose is simply a mechanic to make the game feel more immersive.
TL;DR: The biggest issue with the game is the pricetag, if you like JRPG's then get it. If not, then go over your other options.

I'm not sure what to say about this game.
The first thing most people look for is the gameplay. Fairly standard stuff, almost exactly like Chrono Trigger with the addition of "Momentum" effects that can almost entirely change the use of an ability.
The graphics are good, the snow trails are fun, but I wouldn't say it's anything game changing.
The style seems almost... sporadic. I mean, the environment is consistently snow but the characters seem almost conflicting in style. And maybe one of them actually seems prepared for that much snow.
Crafting kind of exists, but not in a sense that you have to manage what you have in your inventory or what you're picking up. Especially because it's very difficult to get what you want to drop if you need to craft something because they couldn't go with simply RNG, they made it so you have to kill an enemy a certain way to get a certain item. Which is as awkward as you think it is.
The price is a little high, but I think they claimed that from having decent voice acting for each of the main characters. I can't say it's particularly good voice acting, especially because it's only during combat and when you get hit they say the same thing over and over (Endir, the guy you start playing as, actually says "Sweet" in Japanese, I looked it up)
But there are two things that kind of ruin it for me, at least.
1) There are no secrets, and there have been no reasons to explore anywhere off of the path for the entire time that I have played, not that that stopped me.
2) The game gives you choices and does nothing with them. There's probably like 1 or 2 actually meaningful choices somewhere in there, but it gives you so many other times to choose that don't have any effect on the story.
I have not completed this game, but after the first few hours of "Oh that's pretty" and "This story is really interesting," it became "I wish there wasn't this much snow between me and the next story event that I'm trying to get to." I lost interest in doing anything but watching, because only watching was rewarding. Combat is just abusing your attack button. Exploration has nothing to offer. I doubt you'll ever feel hard-pressed to get enough cash to buy items. And managing random stat boosts - managing items in general - feels tedious because the bonuses they give are too small to be noticed. Maybe pick it up for 10$, but then again you could buy Undertale for that much.

Guacamelee caught my interest as soon as it launched on Steam, I still remember that day because on that day Spelunky and Papers, Please were also released on Steam. Having previously played Dust, I think that these two games are very similar yet very different. Guacamelee takes place in a mexican town and tells the story of how you save the world of the living from merging with the world of the dead. I found the graphic style to be really nice and it certainly looks pretty well considering the world in which the game takes place along with the soundtrack which actually made me remember of Total Overdose because it has that very specific latin/mexican feel to it. Now, for me the best part of Guacamelee was the combat, executing combo after combo using different skills and rolling in order to avoid each enemy attack felt really satisfying and that's where I think the game really shines and was probably one of the main reasons why I kept playing it in the first place. Overall I think that if you played games like these, so called "metroidvanias", which have alot of backtracking such as Dust An Elysian Tail which I also loved you will certainly have a great time with Guacamelee, I highly recommend it specially if you enjoy some brawler action yourself, either solo or co-op.

I don't think I've played a funnier, cooler, more beautiful, better sounding game in, I dunno, ten years? Twenty? Forty? No wait, I'm not yet forty myself...
The POINT being, this is really frigging GOOD!
Guacamelee is a "metroidvania" style platforming, exploring, brawling adventure game. But instead of aliens and vampires you have goats, esqueletos and gratuitous Spanglish. And luchadores! Viva!
(This is also really frigging MEXICAN, in a goofy stereotypical pop culture sort of way. It's brilliant.)
The presentation is bueno excellente! It's vibrant, colorful, full of life and personality and delicious flavor like a giant piñata bursting with goodies - and I'm NOT just talking about the graphics, impressive as they are, which for blessed once is purely because of incredible visual design and not just technical wizardry. Oh no: the soundtrack, too, is extremely rich and atmospheric, changing with your surroundings from the happy mariachi tunes of the sunny Mexican town to the kind of muted, surreal fusion type thingy of the World of the Dead without skipping a beat or even dropping the tune.
And then there's the writing! The awesome, hilarious, beautifully cliché and even touching dialogue. All the little nods and winks and shoutouts to a million other games. The hot double-entendre-loving witch. The drunk pistolero with his head on fire (the Devil did it). The chicken thief. GOATS!
Seriously, video games CAN be art.
If you could re-bind the controller buttons (personally, I'd prefer to dodge with the left bumper and turn into a chicken with the trigger), this game would be downright perfecto; as is, it's "merely" MAGNIFICO.

With the latest explosion of independent game developers, the gaming industry has also seen a rise in retro-style graphics. Not only have "retro" games become a rather popular choice among gamers and developers alike, but the rogue-like genre has also seen a surge in popularity. That said, it's these factors that make "Bit Dungeon II" by Kinto Games an absolute no-brainer for entertainment when it comes to blending the retro feel with the "hardcore" feature of rogue-like games.
First and foremost, if you are familiar with the NES days of old, the overall feel of the game, right from the get-go, is "Legend of Zelda." It follows the same formula with the player moving across the landscape with shifting blocks that resemble the different areas of the world map. In each of these areas, just like LoZ, there are enemies that constantly respawn upon re-entering them. Much like its predecessor, Bit Dungeon II also follows the "lacking storyline" approach as it gives no real indication as to what the player's purpose is, but that's what really makes this game so great. It draws upon this nostalgic feel, this idea that the player's imagination needs to kick in and fill in the holes, which in turn makes the experience simple but immersive.
Now on to the real meat and potatoes of BD2. As the name implies "Bit Dungeon II" is a dungeon crawler. The setup, much like most of the other features, is in the likeness of "Legend of Zelda." The player needs to explore the various dungeons that dot the large world map, and in turn, seal them There are plenty of tricks and turns that will completely throw our nameless protagonist off course. Ultimately though, the player will have to solve puzzles and navigate through a maze of rooms in order to find the black "boss" key. Once found, it's time to take on the boss of that particular dungeon and conquer it, moving the player one step closer to sweet victory of beating the game.
Now, this all sounds fun and somewhat like a rip-off of LoZ in the fullest, but its about to get so much better. Not only does the player have to seal each and every dungeon to beat the game, but they only get one shot to do so. Well... two, perhaps. Essentially the player gets two lives, one given at the start of the game, and one extra life to try and retrieve the bonus life given to them. If at any point the player loses both lives (dies twice), our hero is forced to restart completely over, losing all gear that was found along the way as well as any bonus stats that might have been accrued.
On that note, the true depth of BD2 comes from the RPG elements that are incorporated. Ultimately, the player is on the biggest grind of grinds just to find bigger, better, badder gear. There is a plethora of options to choose from and this gives the player the ultimate freedom to create any type of champion that their imagination can muster. From the typical critical-striking assassin to the fire-spell slinging, shield-packing, axe-wielding nightmare of a heavily armed pyro-knight... the possibilities are limitless. Each item that is "dropped" gives stats to the player and each stat governs a particular trait. Again... there is no tutorial on this, so let the imagination run wild!
This is the part where the cons come out, but honestly... aside from the slight and rare bug, here and there, BD2 absolutely delivers. Its replay value is through the roof, and although it can get somewhat frustrating at times, the very "risk/reward" model that BD2 offers is exceptionally gratifying. When it comes to dungeon crawlers/RPG/Rogue-like games, Bit Dungeon II definitely takes the cake and is guaranteed to leave you satisfied.

Many years ago, a company called Uber Entertainment released a game called Monday Night Combat.  MNC was a third person MOBA, where the player played the role of a gladiatorial athlete/clone in a stylized future sport.  I loved this game and it's sequel, Super Monday Night Combat, but neither game really had much staying power.  The games still exist, but the lobbies are mostly empty, and I've been left with a terrible itch.
Thank you, Gearbox.  You have scratched and satisfied that itch with Battleborn.
I love this game.  I love smashing bots.  I love pushing up the lanes.  I love experimenting with loadouts and the helix skills to find that perfect Orendi or Alani or Oscar Mike build.  I love the back and forth of a good 30 minute verses match.  In comparison to another hero-based shooter that came out a month after Battleborn, the matches are much more satisfying, like a holiday meal in comparison to a couple candy bars.
It's also nice to see a company get microtransactions right in this sort of game.  No power boosts or access to microtransaction exclusive gear.  Nothing that changes the dynamic of gameplay, resulting in cries of "pay to win."  Just taunts and skins.
If there are only two problems with the game right now, it's that it came out just before another, equally fun, better advertised hero shooter that's soaked up a lot of attention and playtime, and that the match waiting times are a touch long.  Never more than five minutes, but still a touch long.  I'm hoping my review may convince you to give Battleborn a chance and help swell the ranks of players to help with that last bit.

Battleborn is an excellent example of a well made fusion between a MOBA and a shooter. Add Borderlands' fun artstyle and you have an extremely addictive experience in both PVP and the PVE campaign.
Battleborn's campaign is relatively short, but it provides a very diverse range of beautiful environments with great replay value, offering bosses that can be farmed for better gear to give you an edge in future games.
Criticisms that could be made of the game in its current state are a somewhat cluttered HUD that could be problematic if you are playing at a low resolution, and somewhat long matchmaking times. However, it really depends on what you are interested in playing, as modes such as Incursion tend to take 3-5 minutes to find, but meltdown can be a little longer.
Gearbox works tirelessly to update the game with new content and balance patches, and they frequently interact with the community via the subreddit.
In conclusion, I would say that if you enjoyed the Borderlands franchise you will love the humour and characterisation of this game, and it is also a great option to SMITE and Dota 2 players who are looking for a more long term attraction through the loot system.

Her Story is a generic first person shooter set in the second world war complete with recharging health and cover mechanics. You and you generic team of tough stoic hardmen battle countless nameless grunts while wisecracking and alpha-fiving each other before heading back to the base for some no homo shared beers and communal butt massages.
Not really. What it involves is acting (detective like) by sifting through all manner of video's trying to look for clues in the matter of an unsolved murder "Her" (Hannah, played expertly by Viva Seifert) husband has been murdered and it's up to you to discern what/ if any role Hannah played in her dissapearance.
You do this by searching a police database for keywords you can think up yourself by watching random episdoes of CSI ("Murder" albibi" etc) and also listening for specific names (or trying to ascertain patterns) and thus searching for words not traditionally associated with dead bodies, missing persons and so on.
The game is well acted and written and features an intriguing story that keeps you interested in finding out more. It's cool as a feminist to see a game feature a female protagonist (kindof.....) although she might be a little more Basic Instinct than Manic Pixie Dream Girl if you catch my drift.
What's intriuging is even after you have found all the videos (or so I'm told, I haven't managed it yet) the game's plot is still Nolan-esqueily (its a word if you want it badly enough to be damnit) ambigious and people still debate whether or not Hannah was a Martian space alien or a Transgender Somalian lesbian (it's possible they debate two more plausible scenarios but that would be too spoileresque).
So the game is interesting and features a pretty chilling performance from bunner boiler Seivert (she is her character damnit). In particularly one song gives me more goosebumps than an aspiring SEAL listening to Adele during Hell Week. Overall the game is interesting and worth a purchase if you live above the benefit line.

I am now 26 years old, twice as much as I was when I first played this game. I was already impressed with Bioware's Neverwinter Nights at the time, but the hundreds of hours I spent on KotOR really set the bar for all future RPGs for me. Features you love games like Jade Empire, Mass Effect, KotOR 2 and Dragon Age or even Arcanum, The Elder Scrolls and newer Fallouts for were pretty much all introduced to me by KotOR. A great soundtrack, deep companion stories, good/evil choices that make a difference in the storyline, plentiful side-quests, plot-twists, they're all there. This game was certain to become a classic the moment it hit the shelves in the second half of 2003.
Definitely among The Essentials.

While the combat might be a little uninteresting and the graphics are dated, the personality and detail of the world around you more than makes up for it. Every companion has a story, a personality and enderaing reasons why you should dedicate time and energy to become friends and, in some cases, lovers. The Soundtrack is also amazing! For example: Manaan has a haunting, mysterious vibe that suits the water planet. Dantooine's Jedi Academy has a very relaxing and rustic theme that suits the zen like surroundings. The world seems very real and believable and feels like a world actual people could live in
Every planet has a style, for example Taris. Taris is sophisticated and futuristic until you go deeper into their city to find the undercity, a dark and dingy home of criminals and beggars. Plauged with monserous creatures and a deadly plauge that you can cure, if you feel like being generous. You can also look out for yourself, become a dark jedi and choose some fun, but evil, choices like Selling a vital cure, telling a wookie to kill his lifelong friend and just being a♥♥♥♥♥♥in general. In KOTOR, your alignment (Light or Dark) actually influences your ending. There is so much to do in this universe and it is an experience you can't miss! So go and buy this game, you and your wallet won't regret it.

Sparkle 2 is a game very similar to Zuma, but enjoyable in its own right.
It's quite a casual action based casual game, where you need to shoot balls at others in order to create matches of 3 or more. The queue you are shooting at is constantly moving, and if too many balls go past the line at the end of the path, you lose. It's a simple objective, but very fun as the game progresses and comes up with more intricate map paths, and powerups.
The powerups offer a decent amount of customization and strategy before you go into a level, but I found myself not changing through many because it felt like they didn't do enough to bother with it.
The powerups in-game are very fun and satisfying. Some do things like move the queue of balls back, where as others will give you awesome weapons that allow you to blast through rows of balls to buy yourself some time.
Overall, it's a very easy game to pickup and learn, but I had so much fun playing it through that I have to recommend it.

I am Setsuna essentially sets out to be a modernised tribute to the 'golden-age' of JRPG's from the mid-ninties. Every review you will read for the game will mention how the combat system is essentially lifted straight out of Chrono Trigger, and that is in no way a bad thing. Likewise, the inventory and skill systems seem very reminiscent of games of this era.
The plot of the game is deliberately very sombre, and coupled with the almost exclusively piano-based soundtrack (which, by the way, is very good), it gives the game a definite unique and recognisable appearance.
If you like snow (who dosn't?), then you'll find the world that I am Setsuna takes place in to your liking. Almost every single environment in the game is absolutely covered in the stuff, and it can make the game seem a bit 'samey' at times. The dungeon environments are repeated occaisionally, and re-skinned enemies are fairly commonplace, but given the fact that the game is suitably short compared to those that influenced it, it dosn't pose too much of an issue.
The majority of the games characters are incredibly well designed, with clear hints towards character classes seen in similar RPG's, but there are some who are a bit on the dull side, and these are the ones which will probably be left out of most players rosters because of it.
Overall, the game runs very well (despite some early issues with XBO controllers which are now fixed), and given its deliberate simplicity (due to the 90's influence), it looks very pretty in a modern engine and will even render at 4K resolution while maintaining a steady 60FPS. The framerate is particularly pleasing as a lot of the games which influenced Setsuna are locked to 30FPS or in some cases 15FPS! The main storyline is more than interesting enough to keep you playing, and are plenty of side-missions and optional super bosses to satisfy completionists.
Recommended for any fan of 'golden era' JRPG's, and those looking for a casual and modern introduction to the genre.

When I saw this game was in production, I immediately started looking at PS4 bundles and started shopping around.  I realized it wasn't going to release for a while, but I kept my eye on it with it on my Amazon wishlist.  Just before release, Steam popped up announcing that it was going to be released on Steam, and I immediately bought it.  Here's my completely biased review of this game (since I bought it!)
My Rating: 7/10
Story
The story starts off similar to how Final Fantasy X revealed itself late game.  You are recruited to assassinate a girl, whom you find out is already destined to die.  Due to her destiny, you decide to protect her until she dies by her own means.  The game does not get too complex with its story.  It is very linear, and the surprises feel more aimed towards young children.  That was a bad guy?  No way!  (Sarcasm)
Setting
The world is covered with snow, and is being increasingly ravaged by stronger and smarter monsters.  This makes sense, as you progress through the game - it gets harder (obvious in an RPG).  I always had the feeling that after the "next" boss, a time portal would open up and take me to another time.  But...oh right, this isn't Chrono Trigger.
Similarities
Yes, this is NOT Chrono Trigger.  I swear it's not the same game.  I mean, abilities are the same...you even get to learn X Strike and Frog Squash...but this is NOT Chrono Trigger.  You even have a bad guy with a big scythe trying to kill you.  You get weapons with descriptions nodding to CT heroes such as a spear with magic twins imbuing their power to it.  Well, you get a Buster Sword too, so yeah there's that.  Gotta love Square Enix for their cameos.
Gameplay
Although the battle system is a Chrono Trigger clone, the game has some incredibly unique accomplishments.  Learning skills for instance - you trade in body parts of the monsters you massacre, and combine them to buy the skills - and this is how you make currency as well.  The modification of each skill is something I have not played around yet myself, but you can modify an AoE spell to not only critically hit more often, but also to heal you each time you use it (Momentary Recovery).
I haven't beaten the game yet - as it has scaled in difficulty a little faster than I cared to spend grinding experience and ability modifications, so I can't say whether or not there are more tricks and surprises for me to see.

If you never heard of Zombie Estate the first two were on Xbox 360 originally years ago. They were amazing games. This is the updated version with some new things plus.... ONLINE play for up to four players! Something many people wanted on 360. Its old school sounds, graphics...etc in a pixilated flat but 3D looking world where you face wave after wave of zombies. There are three "difficulties" to play from. Casual which is short and has some continues. A harder mode with less continues and harder enemies. And a unlimited mode where the enemies are random every wave and get stronger as you go on. Probably the funnest mode with 3 other players joining you!
You have a few levels to choose from, 100 weapons and tons of characters and hats. As you kill enemies drop money and ammo. Money gets used after each wave at a store on the level. You can use money to buy weapons and use in game coins (given after each wave) to upgrade them. And after a game, even if you lose, you earn Zombie coins to unlocks new characters (with different stats and unique weapons). Or you can unlock hats, which have higher costs but give you boosted/unboosted stats.
There is PLENTY to keep you busy for a long time in terms of unlocking stuff. Some of the weapons and characters are hilarious but fun to use. Like a man whos starting weapon is a bacon slicer that shoots slabs of cooked bacon at enemies to kill them. To guns that have elemental damage. To guns that call in orbital strikes. The levels always leave room for you to learn who to use and with what weapon in hat depending on where you are in the level. There are lots of enemies with varying abilities and weaknesses.
You can use a controller or mouse and keyboard. And from what I seen people on systems as far back as Win Xp seem to be able to get it to work. I have had no issues, well aside from getting to bed four hours late because I was in unlimited wave mode. lol. If you do have any issues I'd say please be patient with the creator, hes always getting feedback to patch any issues. We already had a patch, thats how dedicated he is!
And the maker has said he may release free updates in the future if the game does well. Personally I am biased towards this game having played it for so many years (well the 360 version which had less content). But its probably one of my favorite small time made indie games. Defiantly give it a try, its only $5 which is amazing because I'd easily pay $15 or even $20! This is also a one man production by a man who has spent his free time putting this on PC. I honestly hope he does great!

Battleborn is an excellent example of a well made fusion between a MOBA and a shooter. Add Borderlands' fun artstyle and you have an extremely addictive experience in both PVP and the PVE campaign.
Battleborn's campaign is relatively short, but it provides a very diverse range of beautiful environments with great replay value, offering bosses that can be farmed for better gear to give you an edge in future games.
Criticisms that could be made of the game in its current state are a somewhat cluttered HUD that could be problematic if you are playing at a low resolution, and somewhat long matchmaking times. However, it really depends on what you are interested in playing, as modes such as Incursion tend to take 3-5 minutes to find, but meltdown can be a little longer.
Gearbox works tirelessly to update the game with new content and balance patches, and they frequently interact with the community via the subreddit.
In conclusion, I would say that if you enjoyed the Borderlands franchise you will love the humour and characterisation of this game, and it is also a great option to SMITE and Dota 2 players who are looking for a more long term attraction through the loot system.

Battleborn is a true Gearbox game. The story, the graphics, the incredible diversity of locations and character personalities. It reminds me greatly of when I first played Borderlands 2. I had no idea what was happening, but dang, was it fun.
Learning how to be better at Battleborn is very different from learning to be better at Borderlands. The one thing that comes to mind is the loadout system. In Battleborn, you can equip 3 items at a time to give your character specific stat boosts, like shield penetration or bonus critical hit damage or extra health. Similarly, in Borderlands, items had their own unique stat bonuses as well, but arguably impacted gameplay less than items do in Battleborn. However, in Battleborn, each item comes with a small price. Rather than have the stat bonuses immediately, to use them, you have to collect these yellow shards in matches. Items costs a higher shard price the more rare it is. Commons cost the lowest (they can even cost 0) and legendaries cost the highest (1800 shards). Depending on who you are, that could be a positive or a negative for you. On one hand, it does provide an extra level of depth to the game, but on the other hand, it can be confusing, knowing when its best to use one item over another.
Speaking of items, you can get items just by playing the game, and you can save the in-game currency you get for completing missions to buy loot packs to get more items. You can either get the currency by playing the story mode or by playing online.
Next. Oh, boy. Characters.
In typical Gearbox fashion, this game has a freakin' huge range of characters both for you to play and to face off against. With such a large selection to choose from, with everyone from calm, fancy, bowler hat wearing robot snipers to crazy, demonic, 4 armed psycho girls with pillars of shadow and fire, to sarcastic, pistol-weilding elf chicks who just want to get on with their lives, I garuntee you'll find a character to love, be it for gameplay or for personality. The game's humor is, if anything, slightly toned down compared to what it was in the Borderlands series, but it still maintains its classic charm.
In all honesty, the only major problem I see with this game is the PvP online multiplayer. It takes a bit (5-10 minutes) to find a match, and you'll see the same people over and over again. I personally don't mind seeing the same people over and over again, as it helps to adapt to different styles of playing while also allowing you to experience online. However, if you feel that the PvP experience is just some infinite torture device manufactured by Gearbox to slowly pry out the soul of whoever is playing it after reading the other reviews for this game, then try the story mode. Get together with some friends and run around, have fun, try stupid combos and loadouts.
While this game is on sale, I would recommend giving it a try. Play it and make your own opinions, ignore the reviews comparing this game to Overwatch and saying how bad Battleborn is because it doesn't provide the exact same experience.
Hope to see you there,

A simple and easy action-adventure RPG/dungeon crawler. Good enough pixel graphics and animations, barely any story, not much variety in puzzles/levels. Plays like a simpler Zelda with dungeons filled only with enemies, buttons, and door keys. Press every button and kill every enemy in a locked room and eventually you'll reach the end. One of the only puzzles was the 'endless maze' type of puzzle where there are multiple exits and you just go to the exit that doesn't have the bush next to it.
It's pretty good for power trips because once you power up above the difficulty curve you can just walk into most enemies and you will automatically kill them. Level ups come pretty often. There's one button to attack, charge attack, & defend. I didn't like using mouse (because you need to move the mouse cursor to face the enemy) so I just used keyboard for both positioning (and attacking always goes in the direction you face). Instead of WASD+mouse I used arrow keys + space but it may be possible to use a controller instead. It's a simple enough game to play in windowed mode while watching something else on the side.
Death is pretty forgiving as long as you stay in areas you're strong enough to get through. When you die you leave behind an extra life token. If you die before you retrieve it then it's game over. Otherwise you can die as many times as you want as long as you can retrieve the token each time. However, I've read that the final boss removes your extra life (so only one try) so be prepared for that.
I liked lifesteal + constitution/defensive stats just so it would be easier to not pay too much attention.
I ended the game at level 74 and went from a Lvl 19 Vampiric Sword of a God to a Lvl 32 Vampiric Spear of Death and skipped all other weapon drops. Once you beat the game you start again from the beginning with all your items and coins but I stopped playing so I don't know if there's anything different.
Other random thoughts:

I would have liked:
Worth a look if you like simple zelda-like RPGs and like to power trip. It may be a little more difficult if you aren't a seasoned gamer but I'd say you can always grind to beat the power curve and then power-trip to the end.

I think a better healing system needs to be in place though to balance the fact its all too easy to get hit unfairly as lose health or even die when moving between areas- at the very least health potions need to be more common.
There are a lot of positive aspects that could be built upon for a sequel since I feel this game is going in the right direction, alot of good aspects are in place such as random items and events.   Another issue with most RL games and BD2 suffers from the same problem is that items are law, you find some of the best items/weapons in the game and you are almost guareented to finish the game, RNG goddess is unkind then you'll die alot.
Rogue-likes are really tough to judge and review honestly since they vary greatly in difficulty and what is consider fairplay mechanics.  I've played quite a few terrible rogue-likes that are more or less for masohist players, whilst this one is better than most, it still occasionally punishes the player severely, especially on bosses with some being overly powerful - like 2/3 hits your dead.  Rogue-likes and Rogue-Lites always walk the tightrope when it comes to balance vs fun, some have become big hits and others have failed miserably - this game is not a hit, but this game isn't  bad either however I wouldn't even recommend this game at the moment, however a few patches and upgrades could make a huge difference.
I think this game would benefit from a reward system so as you play, you can unlock more rewards which will help you each time you die, such as starting with boosted stats, ability to keep item(s) or starting at a higher level without making the game 'too' easy.

One of the most memorable video games ever created. Not because it is particularly innovative, but because the mixture of shooting, climbing, creeping, thinking, laughing and simple astonishment works perfectly. The rhythm of the game is fast-paced and action-packed, and includes some fun, well-thought-out dialogue. I am Setsuna has no rival. There's no other game, despite Killzone 2 on the visuals, with the same level of quality as this. The game is almost perfect in every stage, and it has online coop and deathmatch; there's no doubt that it's one of the top three games for the PC, and one of the five best games of this year.

: Toyko RPG Factory
: Square-Enix
==========
I am a huge fan of Chrono Trigger. This is a well-known FACT about me, everyone knows it. When I Am Setsuna hit the Steam Store, and boasted Chrono Trigger as a direct inspiration, I knew from the get-go it would be an RPG I just had to have. I was not disappointed. The story is a bit cliche, having played other games with a very similar storyline, but I Am Setsuna found ways to set itself apart from other games. Not going to dive too much into the game's story, as it's something you want to experience for yourself. Just know that Setsuna is the center of it all.
While this is definitely a good game and a good RPG, it is somewhat overpriced for what it offers. I would not recommend buying it at full price...wait for a sale, for sure.
==========
Many aspects of I Am Setsuna were directly drawn from Chrono Trigger, the most prominent of which is the base of the combat system. Each character has their own action gauge that, once full, allows them to take an action. This action can be a simple attack, using an item, or using a technique. What I Am Setsuna brought new to the table is the spritnite system. Spritnite, put simply, is a stone kind of like Materia (remember Final Fantasy VII?). You can assign spritnite to any character who is compatible with it (only certain characters can use some spritnite) and these stones grant the character special skills and abilities. These abilities can then be combined with other character's abilities to perform devastating attacks. Remember the Double and Triple Techs from Chrono Trigger? Yeah, I thought so!
Progress is made by moving your party through each area and interacting with NPCs, fighting battles, and looting chests. It's your standard RPG fare. If you've played any RPGs in the last decade or so, you know how this works. Fight battles to gain EXP, level up, get stronger, and equip the best weapons and armor you can find.
Each character has their own equipment, spritnite, and accessories (Talismans) to manage, and as with most RPGs perhaps the biggest job is managing your inventory. After battles you receive EXP, items, and gold, and you can use this gold to outfit your characters and buy supplies like Potions and Ethers to restore your HP and MP. It always pays to be prepared for whatever you may run into.
==========
Setsuna boasts a cute sprite-ish artstyle that will heavily remind you of the olden SNES RPG days, though they are three-dimensional now. The influences are plain to see. The character models look great, and when you equip new weapons they are shown on the character. Small detals like this help with immersion, and impress me when they have it.
The biggest complaint I have about this game is the lack of varied environments. Set on a giant snowy continent, I Am Setsuna is literally covered with snow. Everything is ice and snow. I'm not even kidding. While it's not a huge deal, it does get a bit old and kind of ruins the excitement of exploring new areas when they all look so similar. Half the fun of RPGs, after all, is exploration. When everything looks and feels the same, your drive to actually run around and see your surroundings is nonexistant.
==========
The soundtrack to this game is absolutely beautiful, if a bit simple. You can definitely hear some influences from older RPGs and trends. There are no English voices whatsoever (that I could find), but the Japanese voices sound just fine. The characters only have voiced lines in battle anyway., and I'm sure they aren't very important or have any bearing to the story.
==========
I Am Setsuna ran great on my mid-tier custom rig, with full 60 FPS at all times. Full controller support with my Logitech F310. No slowdown, lag, or random crashes were experienced, and the game just ran very well overall. I can't imagine too many people having issues running this game, unless they are sporting a toaster from 1993.
==========
A touching story and engaging Chrono Trigger-esque gameplay really makes I Am Setsuna worth a try. It's like a love letter to the older RPGs of yesteryear, especially if you grew up in the SNES era of gaming. Like I mentioned before, try to snag it when it goes on a sale. it's good, but not $40 good.
==========

==========

I'm not sure I would call this a game so much as a non-linear immersive detective story.  Get out your pencil and notebook, brew some strong coffee, and dive down into the rabbit hole.  The less you know about this the better.

So, it all begun with simple "I'd like to try something different." And I'll be completely honest with you - this game sucks. More on that matter a little later, but be advised, there's a good reason for me saying that.
Now, when we know what made me buy 'Her Story', let's just focus on something a little more different - my experiences with this game.
Feeling like solving a puzzle, burried deep down is some PD archives? Check.
Wanting to move your brain cells a little, don't really want all elements on the table from the start? Check.
Want to grab a pencil and an old-school notebook you were hiding for occasions like that? Check.
This game has it all - surprise, not-too-linear story, element of fiding a secret and solving it completely. This is why it took my heart in an instant, and left me craving for more.
Now, you've been lured by me saying that this game sucks, and promised to shed some light on it:
Remeber the amazement you felt the first time you've watched 'Sixth Sense'?
BUT THERE IS ABSOLUTELY NO GOING BACK FROM KNOWING THAT BRUCE WILLIS IS ACTUALLY DEAD.
The same problem is with 'Her Story' - I want more, much, much more; I want to bury myself in that story again, feel it once again and have that ':O' face while watching the clips and typing new words into the search box with my cheeks red. Knowing how it ends (although a big plus is the 'opened ending', leaving you free for interpretation: basically, there're two theories and both have their point) makes you wanna run and cry into a pillow, because you already know all the secrets. That's the only problem with it, honestly.
3 amazing hours to get to know the story, one more to make it 100% to get the 'bigger picture'.
Worth your time, worth your money.
Now, make yourself a favor, make a cup of coffee or your fauvorite tea, (grab a cig if you smoke and you're 18 or older), take a small notebook and a pencil. Sit in front of your computer. Give up the cinema, spend 3 comfy hours at home, while being a detective, the audience, the judge and a director at once.
Thank me later.

This indie captured my attention because of the various positive reviews, the many awards AND the price... XD
The game presents itself in a very minimalist form: you directly see the desktop of a "windows 95-like" computer and a search engine window you should use to search and play clips from the police database. These clips are all related to a Murder and show small sequences of a girl under interrogation and you have to understand what really happened.
- The story. It's so intriguing the fact that you have to reconstruct the events from these short clips. It may sound simple and boring but I can assure you that the totally random way you may find clips make the experience very complicated, contradictory, difficult and deep at the same time. I came up with few theories often contradicting each other so I had to keep searching to understand the truth. And towards the end When you think you understand the story, everything loses importance with a couple of lines, kind of revealing a very small detail giving the whole story and situation a new unexpected perspective and with an important context.
- The Gameplay. It's really simple: you have a search engine where you can write words thinking of tags or even part of speech. This makes the game a virtually unique experience for every individual, because when you see a clip you might think of a word or a clue or a name or a sentence to search for, while someone else could think of something else, hence the search engine will show different clips to different people. This makes the game addictive because you don't want to know more: you NEED to know more as the clips' order is not chronological, and you can hear everything and its opposite. Very innovative and intriguing.
- Soundtrack. It's not really outstanding, but it is a really nice background during the "search engine" sessions ( it stops when you play a clip)
- The "environment". It's funny how simple things give the game a little depth. You have some files on the desktop... And there's even the Recycle Bin too... With a couple of files deleted...
- Reflection. You'll notice sometimes your own reflection on the screen in different ways: light neon flickering, Police lights with syrens. I admit I almost jumped off the chair the first time I saw it... I was somehow scared of a kind of horror turning, or something else... XD
- You're pretty much on your own. I must say it took me less than a minute to understand how it works but I admit it made me feel kind of... alone. You're simply thrown to the desktop and search engine and you're there. There's no dialogue with nobody else, nothing to do but search and play clips.
- You don't have a system to put aside various clips to build back, piece by piece, the interviews as whole like a puzzle, maybe to see them from the beginning to the end. And this is somehow odd because that would really help a lot.
- Gameplay. Yes, because there's a simpe (and lame ) trick to find and view all the clips in chronological order. And besides that you migh run out of interest if you believe you get what happened. You might be wrong and there will be no explanation or epilogue, just those "couple of lines" I've mentioned before revealing another imortant information but that's all. You might even have totally misunderstood the truth and you're gone. That's supposed to motivate you to keep on searching, maybe even all the clips, maybe in chronological order, but that doesn't seem a good way to set a game, where the story is the true essence. If the heart of the game lies in the story you MUST make sure the player ends the game with the awareness of AT LEAST the key events. But that's not assured as the conclusion script seems generated by the number of clips visualized, not by the Visualization of Important clips. I've solved this by viewing 100% of the clips, and by viewing the entire last day interview in chronological order.

Payday The Heist is a four player cooperative FPS and a fun one as well; Playing as one of four professional heisters you will engage in various criminal activities such as stealing a panic room filled with cash and intercepting a truck transporting gold ingots all the while defending yourself from waves of police who assault and attempt to capture you over the course of the game.
Although the levels themselves are static there will always be certain elements, such as the location of the cameras in First World Bank or the petrol canisters in Heat Street, which won't always appear in the same place each playthrough. If you are a relative newcomer however you can choose to play these missions offline in order to get a feel for them before playing online cooperatively with either friends or random players.
If you successfully complete these missions you will then receive cash the level of which determines what rank your character is as well as what weapons, gear and perks they can choose before you start the game. Even if you fail however you may still get rewarded with cash, albeit a lot less, for taking part in activities such as shooting the security cameras.
You can appreciate how they managed to include stealth segments that you were able to participate in for a limited amount of time such as no mercy, the diamond heist, and counterfeit (provided that you own the Wolf Pack DLC) and how this informed the design decisions they made in its sequel.

Sparkle 2 is an enjoyable addition to the Luxor/Zuma type of match 3 game.
A line of different colored balls slowly creeps forward and you have to shoot balls to match 3 or more to make them disappear.  If they reach the end of the line before you get rid of them all, it's game over (though I'm assuming you can keep trying after failing).  It's in the Puzzle category, but it's acutally an action puzzle rather than turn-based or one that just sits there while you decide what move to make.  In this game you have to think fast and have good reflexes sometimes.
Occasionally you get power-ups that will help you.  Fireballs that destroy balls.  Color Match that makes several balls all the same color.   There are ones that slow the train or make it go backwards for a short time.
There are also equipable power-ups that you can choose once you've unlocked them.  Such as unlimited swap of whatever colored ball is currently next in line to shoot.  Or every 10th ball you get is a fireball.   You can try out the equipables and customize the way you want to play the game.
There is a main story with a path that you follow, but there are also other game modes that you unlock along the way.
Graphics are nice.  I especially like the details on the balls (no jokes please).  They aren't just a solid color, there is a pattern to them that is nice.
Music is very nice.  To me it has a sort of fairytale classical style.  Kind of hard for me to describe.    It sets the mood perfectly for a jaunt through the creepy forest.
I haven't finished the main story yet.  I might be halfway through, going on the equipable power-ups that I have yet to unlock, but I'm not sure, and I've played almost 3 hours according to Steam.  And I haven't played the other modes yet, either.

So I’m going to base this review on my personal and my friends’ opinions when we got to play the game together, this is going to be a partial review because we didn’t play Fakin it as I’ve read from reviews that the game isn’t fun at all.
Overall, the game is really enjoyable to play with your friends for a couple of hours, this game brought us some laugh out loud moments and really gives you that feeling of togetherness when you have your friends over. What’s great about The Jackbox Party Pack is that you don’t need to prepare anything like extra controllers or anything like that to play with multiple friends on the couch; all you need is a laptop, an internet connection, and smartphones which I’m sure everyone has. What I also like about this game is that it caters to everyone; be it your family or friends, and is relatively easy to get into, as friends who watched for just a couple of minutes would already understand how each game goes (some of my friends aren't really good at english). Now, on to each individual game the pack offers;
This game is the ultimate source of laugh out loud moments that you can have with your friends since it gives you the option to make your own prompts where you can add some inside jokes that are sure to give your group a good laugh.
This game has the longest lasting appeal as me and friends have played this game over and over for hours without getting bored. However, as many of the consumers have stated, the trivias are mostly ‘American’ trivias that most people who lived outside the US won’t get. For example, the game asks which presidents where democrats and which of these people were once hosts of a show like Family Feud. It’s a damn shame because I really wanted my friends to not get confused 80% of the time by these questions and actually have a clue of what they should choose as the answer.
As you can probably tell from the name of the game, this is a game about guessing, as in guessing percentages. The guessing happens the whole game, it gets boring fast and it doesn’t really give you any sense of competition or achievement when you actually win the game since it basically crowns the best guesser.
My review for this game will be taken by a quote from my friend; “If we drew the shirts and make all the words, why is our shirt just mixed pictures and words taken from someone else’s efforts?”. This game isn’t fun because all your hard work will be used by someone else to win the game and even if you win, you won’t win by using your own drawings; this game is unsatisfactory and the scoring system is really confusing.
, Get this game for Quiplash and Trivia Murder Party, and get it if you have friends who aren’t really into games but is looking to meet up and have fun, or if you have any friends at all for that matter.
IMO the best of the series.  A must get if you enjoy playing games with your friends and family.

Battleborn is a diamond in the rough, but a bit more diamond than rough, I think. It has a few flaws, like some of the map optimization, and the queues for multiplayer could be better, but I honestly enjoy the hell outta Battleborn. The saturday morning cartoon scifi setting/aesthetic is fun, the maps and art style are great to look at, the humor is top notch Gearbox-style goofiness and black comedy that has me almost constantly giggling, and the characters are excellent.
Seriously, the characters are the best part of the whole game. They're all fun and varied and extremely endearing, in the same way that the casts of the Borderlands games are, and it's taken very little time for me to fall in love with most all of them. The lore unlocks you get and dialogue snippets you hear mid-game re: the cast are all delightful.
I don't think it's fair to compare Battleborn to other games; it's honestly its own thing and it's very much worth playing as such. I've found it pleasantly addictive, and when you get in with the right people both the PvP maps and the story missions are great fun to dig into. And hell, if you can't or don't want to get into multi, there's always singleplayer and bot modes. It could use a little more polish around the edges, but BB is honestly fun and enjoyable and it's well worth getting and playing.

It's an FMV game, and as such it's already a niche title. The only thing you're doing in it is typing in keywords in a search box and watching videos. It's not exactly innovative or original, similar FMV games existed before, but the game is well aware of this and tries its best to deliver a non-linear murder mystery. There are two major twists to be found, and there's a lot of psychological drama. The actress performs quite well, and the story works even if it's a bit too far reaching at times. However, if you suspend your disbelief just enough (no, there's nothing paranormal about it, not like that) it does deal with some interesting themes.
There's not a lot of gameplay to speak of, as you can see. There's a minigame easter egg, but that's it. If you ever liked FMV games and don't mind a neat idea, then give it a shot. If you're looking for something more substantial with deeper mechanics, look away.

Playing this was an interesting experience. You are given access to an old police computer terminal and video clips of a woman being interviewed. It has a really unconventional style, which will probably catch you off guard if you're expecting more traditional gameplay.  It isn't clear what your goals are, who you are playing as, or what information you're trying to uncover. And I don't think that's a bad thing. The game intrigued me and had me asking questions all the way through. I wanted to keep digging deeper into the clips so I could learn more about this woman. The more you uncover, the more questions you begin asking yourself. I don't want to say much more about it. I think it's best to go in blind.

An interesting take on explorative narration. Be aware that this game has set aside very few explicit rules and mechanics, opting instead to focus entirely on the player's drive to find out the truth to the story.
The story itself is unique and interesting, but doesn't really offer anything groundbreaking in terms of worldviews, or really anything that relates to most people.
At the end of the day it's basically an audiovisual/verbal version of those hidden object search games, but it's still interesting enough to be worth a try. I found it refreshing to see something new being tried in this manner, but the experience never striked me as anything revolutionary.
Would recommend if you're able to get it on sale, as I don't think it's quite worth the price point for all the content being accessible in under 3 hours.

IMPORTANT NOTE:
. IT IS CRITICAL THAT YOU UNDERSTAND THIS FACT.
First off: I generally do not like puzzle games. Especially most type of point-and-click "adventures", which more often than not rely on you clicking everywhere, hiding things in places that make no sense (I'm looking at you,
with your rotten lemon...).
reminds me of those point-and-click games, only that you actually have to pay attention to get the clues you need to keep going further: you listen to a video snippet and with what has been said, in most videos, there will be one or two (or more) keywords that you have to use to keep going.
So, I guess you could call this a "watch-and-type" puzzle game.
The basic premise of the game is trying to understand a murder from snippets and searches. As you progress in the story, you start piecing things together. The story starts to unravel itself and you slowly see more and more of what happened and who the protagonist (antagonist?) is.
This means that you'd want to play as much in one sitting as possible, and keep a piece of paper with a pen/pencil handy to take notes. This will be a tremendous help to you. If you're a fan of any narrative-based investigative crime show, chances are you'll love
.
The interface is minimalistic and simple. You have a search bar, a history, a clock and a few other things that benefit to be read from an immersion perspective, but nothing that's actually required beyond that (well, some might be for achievements, but that's a different ball game...).
It's so simple that if you're used to using Google or any other search engine, you'll be right at home.
Did it work for me? Yes. A resounding yes.
Why? Because I'm weird. I love fetching things online that somehow my friends always seem to miss or be unable to find. I always see it as a fun puzzle to solve, and this game is right up my alley in that fashion.
Of course, your own mileage may vary.
